So, here i am again, about 40 hours later, reviewing the game. I have fought Risryn 3 times, all of her 3 levels. Love it, wonderful game. BUT IS IT NOT NOOB FRIENDLY. "oh but they can be countered". Yes, they can, but spammers use them mid way through their assualt when you least expect it. All i want in this game, is for their to be proper match making, so im with people my level. And also, developers, if you're reading this, please listen to your audience... nobody asked for a chaotic, awfully made 3v3 where it's essentially who can push who off of the bridges or ledges first. If this game was free I would reccomend it, but If i had played it before, then i wouldnt pay £20 or however much it is, for a game that is plagued with a cancer, a cancer that is growing like the population of Brazil.......spammers (and the guys that add you on steam just to shout at you for winning hahahahaha)

Well, first off, this game looks amazing. It has a number of very well designed areas, with a really good color palette. Now, since it's a combat game, the control system is very important. Which they got pretty spot on, if you ask me. Although this game isn't unlike other fighting games, where button bashing works almost always. Proper timing and patience will be needed, if you wanna be good at this game. While, the combat is fairly good, some other elements of the game get pretty annoying at times. Especially the camera, as it gets locked during a fight, and if you get cornered, you're practically blind. Then again, since this game will be getting constant updates, the developers might find a fix or a workaround for this problem. Another problem you most definitely will face is, getting outnumbered in a fight, a lot. Many times, it's more than two opponents you have to face, and frankly it's incredibly unfair, even if it's just the AI opponents. If you, by any chance get caught between two or more opponents, you might wanna get ready for a barrage of attacks from more than one direction. Although it can  be countered by moving to the sides, and singling out opponents, it still sucks to get kicked in the skull from behind when you're guarding the front against another opponent.
Even with all this, once you really get into a fight, and start dodging hits and countering in an epic fashion, the excitement you get is like none other in this game. With some practice, you can easily get used to the fighting.
Online interaction with other players is through seamless encounters in the various areas. Communication with other players is limited to emotes, but you can request others for co-operation or a friendly fight.
The main problem though, in this game, comes in the online part of the game. I don't know how this game's servers work, or how many there are actually, but the game lags often. Maybe it's only when the server is crowded. We can't really tell, because there is no indication of what server we are in, or where the server is from. They probably made it that way for the immersion, but it would definitely help if we knew what server we were in. The develpoers are certainly aware of this problem, and have said that they are working on fixing it. Possibly more servers, or better optimized servers. Any way, the lag ruins the gameplay hugely. If you get into a fight, with lag, you'll see yourself teleporting here and there, and getting hit even though you dodged on your screen. Just imagine yourself playing in 600+ ping. Yeah, that bad. Until they fix the lag problem, I won't be playing a lot of this game. Although you can just play in the offline mode, and avoid the lag altogether.
In the end, it's a very good game, with a unique concept and engrossing gameplay. It looks beautiful, plays well. What's not to like about that?(Apart from the obvious problems I stated) If you're a fan of souls-like games, then you might enjoy this. If you like those arcade fighting games like Tekken, etc. you might still enjoy this.(Seriously, you can pull off really cool moves in this) I do recommend this game,despite it's current flaws, because I believe the developers will fix them as soon as possible, and the basic framework of the game is solid. Well, that's it for this review. Cheers.

This game is beautiful. Chilling, Moody, exploratory, fun. But hell... what did they do to this New Lands???
This version is dull, boring and stupid, honestly. Let's list it:
- First and foremost, the camps to recruit new units are damn too far away. So far away. I have to spend days just going out recruiting and not only that, I have to "manually" attract the peasants with coins (like they are carrots) because if I just give them coins, they walk so slow they won't make to base before night and will lose their coins to the monsters. I have to spend days recruiting just a handful of people. Super boring.
- Expanding borders is stupid. Having multiple walls is basically a waste of money, because archers will only gather in the farthest border. But archers in archer towers will stay there even when they are needed at the farthest border. Another waste of units.
- Monsters waves are simply unbalanced. They take many more days to come in largers groups. But if they did, we would be unprepared because of all the hassles above.
- You have to run miles and miles and the horse is always tired. ALWAYS.
- Because I have to expand my borders to try and diminish the hassle of recruiting (making a shorter path to new recruits to walk... very slowly), I simply cannot manage fights on both sides. This was super fun on the original game. I didn't have to have such distant borders and could watch both sides during a Red Moon.
It is shameful to say all of this. Kingdom is a smart and beautiful game. Apparently they tried to expand the length of the game without really thinking about it or balancing it. I played and enjoyed several hours of the original one, but couldn't stand much in this new version. Can't recommend this. Buy the original one, much better.

In this game, you spend about 90% of the time waiting : either by riding from A to B, or looking the battles of your little army (and facepalming at their pathetic aim) or just plain damn waiting for the night or the day to end. So when you "play" this game, basically you do nothing during 90% of the time.
It's also very casual and doesn't offer more depth than an average free strategy flash game.
It's a pity because there's a lot of nice bases in there, and with more evolutions and a better & faster control over everything, with a waiting time divided by 2 or 3, it'd be an hell of a game. But here, it just feels a total waste of the little time I'm allowed on this planet.
- Good gameplay bases, and the little which is here is decently tuned and balanced (once you have understood how everything fits together)
- Visuals and world have a lot of charm
- Most of the control is indirect, which leads to annoying situations : you can't decide where your soldiers stand ; eg: if you're attacked from the left, you can't tell your soldiers on the right to rush to the left
- You have to guess the game mechanisms and some are very not obvious : eg: the regent appears once you have upgraded enough your town hall ; you can
plus some more, over several times in the following days
- Archers can't stand on wall, while the walls block their aim, so it leads to ridiculous situations where you need 10 arrows and luck to kill 1 defenseless enemy
- Randomization of the island geography has low influence on the gameplay (ie: you still end doing more or less the same things in the same order), but has a great influence on the outcome --> luck matters more than skills
- Gameplay is 1D : only left/right, no up/down
- Horse gets tired all the time ; to lower that, you have to let him eat some grass for 5 seconds to get a 45-second buff, but there's no grass in the forest

Playing this game is kinda like eating a big wonderful pizza and finding out, after you already ate it all, that it was made of badly rotten♥♥♥♥♥♥ But enough talk, let's make it short:
PRO
- Incredibly addicting gameplay. Very well thought structure, challenging and fun
- Beautiful graphics. Lovely pixelart, with the exclusion of the horse's head: it clearly suffers of some horrible deformity
- Good, immersive soundtracks
And now the reason why no one should ♥♥♥♥ing buy this game even at 0.01$ as long as no one fixes it.
CONS
- 100% ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI. For istance:
You will see a compilation of suicidal workers, archers that can't hit a perfectly immobile rabbit (a rabbit big as a dog) in 7 shots from distance of 5-6 meters, archers that will try to shoot arrows at enemies while overlapping walls or directly aiming the wall, workers that will go out of the protected area during night one after the other trying to chop down a tree and die, archers that will shoot 12 arrows in arcs trying to kill a single monster behind the wall and always hitting the wall, farmers not going to farm for no reason or farming a different lot every day making the others rot.
- Bugs mixed with the AIs and ragequits
But let me make it clearer for you with few actually real, personal experience examples that should make you understand why this game is absolutely rotten and unplayable (to be fair: you can win, but it will depend greatly on luck and absence of bugs, not on skill. In fact the same person could easily win or lose a run with the same valid technique).
1) You have played for a couple of hours. You don't actually have money because it doesn't matter how long you've played, there will ALWAYS be periods of time where you don't own a f*******g penny. You have put yourself a lot in the game and you have the keyboard destroyed because you have wondered between the borders of your hardly built kingdom. You are in front of the most external wall, it's almost night, and your workers, that you already know are almost ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, are out of the walls. You wait for them to come in. The monsters approach the wall. The workers start to run inside the protected area (not before they have seen the monsters approaching since a couple of days before. As I said, they're not exactly bright). And they run SLOWER than they walk. What? Did I miss anything? The monsters♥♥♥♥♥♥some of them, but luckily (considering the workers' hammers costs a lot and that you don't have a penny) one can miracolously reach the protected area, and you let out a sigh of relief. Just after that, the survived worker starts to overlap the wall being attacked by the monsters. Why? After some back and forth, he succeed to be hit by the monsters and he becomes a useless beggar. Your walls are badly damaged and you have no more workers, or moneys to make other ones. The run is lost.
2) You have played for a hour and a half. You're doing a great job, you've kept the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ workers in the safe area, and you've survived the abyssal incompetence of archers (you can actually buff them making them good, but the truth is, the standard is excessively bad. Also because you have to pay costantly to keep the buff, and I already explained you how the game works, also considering it won't let you keep more than a modest quantity of money). You're completely stuck because your archers can't hunt♥♥♥♥♥♥and you've taken down all the trees you could cut without risking losing your retard-workers that will gladly cut the trees 5 miles afar from the safe zone and then stay there scratching their fat asses. You have managed to have a basic farm and ONE farmer that will allow you to buy other scythes to make other farmers to have a good, stabile income (at least for the rest of the summer) and to go on with the run. The first day he prepares a lot to plant. The day after he changes idea and he prepares another. You're already sweating blood knowing how buggy the game is, and that if the farmer bugs, you've lost the run. But hey, the day after, he's still cultivating the same lot, and you see the corn growing more and more. Then the corn becomes taller that the farmer, and you know the day after it will be harvested and you'll be able to play instead  of just going back and forth looking for deers that just aren't anyway. The day after, the farmer starts to prepare another lot and the corn rots. The farmer is bugged and the run is lost. Alt+F4.
3) You have played for several (and I mean SEVERAL) hours, you've already defeated a portal, blood moon event occoured, and the left part of your reign have been destroyed for the 80%. But you have played well: before night, you have made new archers, and also fixed the walls. The archers are also 100% buffed. All the archers go on the right side of the reign and stay there. After a couple of in-game nights, you have been completely destroyed. The run is lost. Alt+F4 again.
4) You have played for three hours circa. The level is quite easy, so you could go on pretty well with just a couple of farmers. But now you have hundreds of miles of lots ready, and you just made something like 6 farmers. But hey, guess what? They stay right there and do nothing. The money start to run lower and lower and you need them more and more, and you just thrown a small fortune in the WC. Yep, the run is lost.
5) You have made the left external wall too near to a monster-portal. That mean archers, everyday, wander too near and starts shooting at the portal, triggering it and making monsters go out. Everyday, they get hit by the monsters, lose their bows near the portal, and start goind back and forth because they want to pick up the bow, but they're afraid of the portal. The result? They keep staying out of the safe area, completely unarmed, and you can't do♥♥♥♥♥♥about it. Everyday you lost people and money. The run is lost once again.
Look at my play time. Pretty high, huh? I tried my best to like the game, and for a lot of things, I honestly liked it! But when it comes to "Oh come on... that's not that AIs are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... it's my bad!" or "That looks like a bug... but hey, it just happened 3 runs on 4, I can deal with it" or "Ok everything went in the sewer, but it's not because the AIs are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I had to fight with bugs, it was totally my bad!", you can tell yourself ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for some time. Not forever.
CONCLUSION
The game is simple and 2D. The challenge in the game is pretty high, but in these conditions, it becomes a war of luck and tears when something bugs or the AIs start to kill themselves... or both. So hey, I have an idea... what about fixing this fuc*ing game? It's not big deal, and I know quite something about games. Just show a little care for your product, for god's sake. ABSOLUTELY to avoid as long as it's not fixed and improved.
And just to point out, I also own Kingdom: Classic and it has the same problems, with little worst AIs. Good luck with that one either.
P.S.: I'm 100% ready to change this review in a super positive one immediately after the game is fixed.

This game is one of my favorite all time games. The last horror game that I absolutely loved was Amnesia the Dark Descent and after that I thought no horror game would ever be as good, until they came up with this and many people refered it as Amnesia from the point of view of a baby.
Now if you think you were absolutely defendless in Amnesia, you can guess that it gets even worse because, how what can possibly a baby do against the things that lurk in the shadows except from hiding in places he can only access? You won't be completely alone on the baby's adventure though, they were kind enough to give you a teddy bear companion that could talk to you and lights up when you hug him. Which is a very recomforting item in the middle of a very messed up baby's world.
What I liked the most is that, since the protagonist is still a baby well the way they see the world is so much different of what it is. And also since some parts of the game is going through the memories, well it's no secret that human process memory very different before the age of 3, so the vision of those memories is a pretty disorted world from what it actually is, making the experience even scarier for the player.
Since the begining I had a pretty good idea of what was going on, nevertheless that made me constantly worry even more about the baby and feel powerless at the idea. Even though my suspicious were true it still managed to give me a shock in the ending, because the game is truly immersive. I'd try to play in one sitting for better experience, and also because unfortunately I've heard people complainig that game files got somehow deleted after a while of not playing (I don't know if this has been fixed in a patch though, since it's been a while since I heard those complaints).
So to wrap this up, if you want a unique and genuine horror experience, it's worth checking this title out, it can get spooky without the need of cheap jumpscares, it has stealth elements, a loyal companion and an eerie environment.
Update as Nov 2016:
Saving system may still mess up somehow, so take my advice to beat it in one sitting or ASAP.

Granted, it takes a lot for that to happen nowadays, but I never felt like it truly hit the horror mark.  That said, I would still recommend this game because it's fun, interesting, and has a lot of cool atmosphere, but don't expect to crap your pants with any jumpscares or whatever.

Very underrated and one of the finest games of the genre.
+ Amazing story with great characters.
+ Looks great and can run well on most systems.
+ The gunplay is nice and each gun feels different.
+ Cars have a lot of weight to them which makes driving very fun and satisfying.
+ Police can remember your license plate and appearance, which makes escaping the cops more challenging than in your average open world crime game.
+ Lots of collectibles.
+ Small things like buying food, bribing the police, etc. make this game stand out.
+ The game does a great job at capturing the 40's/50's atmosphere.
- Limited hub world. While you can travel around the city, there aren't any activities or side missions to do and you can only travel around it mid-mission.
- The DLC's are very lackluster.
The empty hub world is what really holds this game back, but fortunately the good outweighs the bad. A must-have when on sale.

The build up is extremely badass, as Vito and Joe try to make their way up the ranks in the Falcone mafia by carrying out awesome hitman jobs and car chases, but towards the end the game feels rushed as it gives you an ending which is left unanswered and most likely will never be answered due to Mafia 3 taking place in a different time era and being created by a different set of developers.
I'd give this game a 9/10 because this is honestly THE GAME for anyone into late 40's/early 50's America and if you want a solid third person action shooter game, give this one a try.

Old review ommitted.
****Update
Well, I gave this game a good amount of more time spent with pvp and exploring the whole game itself.  And I can say that it "had" promise, but it is brutal in a lot of aspects of the game.
Let me hit the pvp area first.
1)  Pvp is extremely brutal.  There is no assistance to make the warbands closer to even in rank.  The more experienced warbands should cleave their way relatively easily through the lower ranked warbands.  Stat upgrades alone make a big impact and skill upgrades make it even bigger.  Not forgetting the weapons that the more experienced warbands have as well.  Starts making a big difference almost right out of the gate.  These problems alone make it difficult to get a group to continuously play in a "seasonal" type setting.
2)  If the game freezes, lags out, computer crashes, or pretty much anything that cuts the match short while its your turn, your whole warband goes out of action.  So that way, when you get back online and reloading the game, you can find half your warband all screwed up with injuries with no rewards (stuff from scavenging as that is the only way to get money) to help recuperate the severity of the penalty.  You only have the option to voluntarily bottle out to avoid this from happening.  Too severe and can really destroy your motivation to bother playing as you may find yourself being outstrengthed quickly when crap like this happens.
3)  There is absolutely no control from the number 2 thing mentioned above.  There is nothing that asks both players if the match played was on good standings.  There is no in-game league set-up.  And no "boss" that can override and simply make the players replay their match.  So there is no avoiding the #2 from happening.
4)  Really disappointed with the pvp mechanics of the game.  They could implement stuff to help those who would like to play in groups stay relatively competative instead of forcing them to remake and rebuild their warbands through either more brutal pvp or through repative pve.
5)  There isn't a good way of finding out what the opposing warrior's stats and abilities are.  As of right now, the only way I know of is to pull up the map and hover over their emblem, or by getting within charge range or shooting range to find out what they are.  The formost mentioned takes time even if you are an experienced player.  The other two are risky as you must get into a risky situation to get there.
6)  The Impressive's (or big guy (or special tough player)) are op'd.  In one turn, they can take out one of your hero's or leaders even at the rookie stage of the game.  The only thing you can do is pit your impressive against theirs and hopefully win by either outrolling them and/or with assisting them with ranged characters.  And if you don't have an impressive, well...good luck winning the match as it takes a minimum of three hero's to take one down and losing at least two of your hero's in the exchange.
If you have played Blood Bowl in a league, then you would understand what I mean by all of this (#1-#4) through and through.  If not, then lets just say that in pvp, you may get really mad if #2 happens or if you have a bad match.  There is simply no coming back from something like that in a "seasonal" type thing unless you are willing to put in some time to rebuild.
A little sidenote.  Players can adjust their warband by playing with fewer warriors, using basic weapons, and the such like to match their opponent.  But this takes a great deal of effort.  Even more so if you were to play in a group as you may constantly be doing this.
So, pvp was a bust for me.  I tried it.  And I don't much like it due to the brutallity of it.  One warband gets ahead and the others fall further behind with no hope of competativeness.  And I am not one to put in a full days work to rebuild my damn warband either to try and be competative in a group that has played 5-6 games each.  So this has been really disappointing as the ability to RolePlay your warband in a group setting gets dimished after a loss or two....
Now for the pve.
Because its playing against the computer, it can get boring and quickly.  So, you have to be really liking the games appearance and storyline to really be into it.  Anyway, here is a quick double take of the pve.
1)  Once you get a certain knowledge of the game, it gets relatively easy to get wyrdstone (basically gold to be turned into cash later on).  New players may find it somewhat of a challenge, but that should be shortlived to about a week give or take a few days...
2)  Visually, this game is not quite where it should be imo.  It lacks fluf or uniqueness.  If you see one rat, basically you seen them all kind of concept.  This also applies to terrain.  The maps feel identical.  Buildings, traps, walkways, etc...  pretty much all the same with slight variances.  More or less, it feels like you are in the "ghetto" part of towns.  And that is about it for that.
3)  Storyline is unique to each race.  However, it is straight foward.  Once you play a warband to its completness of the storyline, you have no need to play it again outside of wanting to.  Nothing will change.
4)  The computer matches your warband for difficulty reasons.  This is a good concept that I haven't really seen much of in other games.  I liked it and hope to see it more in other games.  The good thing about this is if you had a bad run in a previous match or matches.  The computer will match you with difficulty so that you don't feel overwelmed or helping you avoid that hopeless feeling.  And it does help you continue your warband...overall anyway.
Overall
There are alot of abilities and progression that you can choose from while building your warband.  It does take time to get the experience for your warrior's though, so be ready to be disappointed when/if they die or get that injury that greatly affects their progression or usefulness.
Looting shouldn't be the only means of gaining compensation for your warband.  Losing fights in pvp or pve (ie: bottling out) should not mean that you get nothing along with injuries and upkeep to pay for warriors.  This whole setup in regards to compensation sucks.  And can lead to frustration to the extreme of deleting your warband (repeatedly in my case).
Pvp sucks due to what I mentioned previously.  There can be a lot of twerks and implementation that can lead to better gameplay experiences and less getting frustrated to the point of quitting the game altogether.  There is a difference of "taking a break" vs "I would rather play something else."
And with that, if you are looking for the short term game that you play on occasion, then this game wouldn't be a bad purchase.  I would get it on a deal or sale.  10$ would be the most I would consider to be a proper priced game (and that would include the DLC too).  If you are looking for something that you want to play daily, don't bother.  If you are looking at the pvp, then be prepared to deal with the frustration or don't bother with this game.  It's too brutal to play casual pvp and progress your warband.  In otherwords, don't buy it for the pvp aspect.

It's Horror Movie, The Game!
Resident Evil 7 manages to take the best tropes and cliches of the horror industry without making it feel forced, cringy, or overdone in a way that actually fits well with their already existing story. Taking inspiration from games like Outlast and Alien: Isolation, you'll find yourself running and hiding a lot from some of the overpowered baddies.
However, not all the villains are overpowered, because your standard "zombie types" still exist here, and the game retains it's action elements despite all the reviewers saying it doesn't. Only once did I not have enough ammo to deal with the zombies that faced me, and I only just ran past them without a care in the world. Having at least a little sense of conserving ammo and health should be enough to get you through this game without worry. This didn't bother me, but it may bother some who truly don't like this part about the Resident Evil series.
Also, the overpowered invincible enemies that chases you also has problems too. They don't run very fast and have very short term memory. Which means if you got a firm grasp of the level design, you can often outrun them. But they can sneak up on you if you're not careful. My biggest criticism is that there are clearly rooms that Jack and some baddies won't chase you to. It breaks the immersion and the terror.
Nitpicking aside, this is truly the best Resident Evil since RE4, and I hope Capcom doesn't ♥♥♥♥ it up in future titles.

Well, first off, this game looks amazing. It has a number of very well designed areas, with a really good color palette. Now, since it's a combat game, the control system is very important. Which they got pretty spot on, if you ask me. Although this game isn't unlike other fighting games, where button bashing works almost always. Proper timing and patience will be needed, if you wanna be good at this game. While, the combat is fairly good, some other elements of the game get pretty annoying at times. Especially the camera, as it gets locked during a fight, and if you get cornered, you're practically blind. Then again, since this game will be getting constant updates, the developers might find a fix or a workaround for this problem. Another problem you most definitely will face is, getting outnumbered in a fight, a lot. Many times, it's more than two opponents you have to face, and frankly it's incredibly unfair, even if it's just the AI opponents. If you, by any chance get caught between two or more opponents, you might wanna get ready for a barrage of attacks from more than one direction. Although it can  be countered by moving to the sides, and singling out opponents, it still sucks to get kicked in the skull from behind when you're guarding the front against another opponent.
Even with all this, once you really get into a fight, and start dodging hits and countering in an epic fashion, the excitement you get is like none other in this game. With some practice, you can easily get used to the fighting.
Online interaction with other players is through seamless encounters in the various areas. Communication with other players is limited to emotes, but you can request others for co-operation or a friendly fight.
The main problem though, in this game, comes in the online part of the game. I don't know how this game's servers work, or how many there are actually, but the game lags often. Maybe it's only when the server is crowded. We can't really tell, because there is no indication of what server we are in, or where the server is from. They probably made it that way for the immersion, but it would definitely help if we knew what server we were in. The develpoers are certainly aware of this problem, and have said that they are working on fixing it. Possibly more servers, or better optimized servers. Any way, the lag ruins the gameplay hugely. If you get into a fight, with lag, you'll see yourself teleporting here and there, and getting hit even though you dodged on your screen. Just imagine yourself playing in 600+ ping. Yeah, that bad. 8/10
An unique horror experience that puts you in the small shoes of a 3-years old child, trying to survive the horrors of the dark.
The principle is the same as many survival horror games - survive and don't get caught, while you find items and complete puzzles to progress. But right as you start the game and try out the controls, you see how different it feels, since you're in the role of someone incredibly young rather than a fully grown adult. The character moves faster when crawling, but you need to stand up to reach certain things or climb up a ledge. All items used throughout the game are related to toys a young child would have - toy keys, shapes to fit inside a shape mold (squares, triangles, etc), among others.
I won't spoil the story, but I'll say it's certainly interesting and the Prologue (free DLC) expands on it, explaining the events before the main game.
Highly recommended.

I thorougly enjoy this game. It offers the tactical gameplay I have been craving. I entered during the early-access period and while for awhile it was dissapointing, the developers have certainly delivered on their promises. Mordheim offers a rogue like flavor with the ability of your warband members to become severly injured, both physically and mentally, and even die during the campaign. The ability for you to play against other people and have the same consequences of playing the campaigns is a big draw. Don't fret however if your warband becomes crippled. Your profile maintains passive advancements for being a warband leader, such as lower cost hiring of new warriors, or training old ones. So if you need to dismiss either a few people or your entire warband you still maintain some key forward momentum.
The few complaints I have include the extensive load times, and a bit of lack of explanation in some abilities. The self cast abilities and some spells don't quite have enough explanation for what they actually do. So unless you can remember rather well you either have to test it once during the mission or write it down. This is balanced by the fact that the advancement is paced well enough, that you use the abilities with such a high occurence to become familiar with them until you purchase and train in your new ones.

Well, gave Mordheim a go, and here is my impression of the game.
First and foremost, the campaign itself seems a bit weak. The game is propping the AI up so the thumb is always in it's favor when it comes to warband balance so get ready to fight tooth and nail through every mission as your enemy seems to be just showered in equipment as you try to peice together scraps for your own warband. I worked on a skaven warband for a bit, after a bad total party wipe though, my urge to go back to the game and start just is not there as I could just read a book or watch grass grow for the same effect.

Mostly the design of the game is solid. Fundamentals like the Stragey and Offence Point systems combined with the various actions are clever and I assume lifted straight from the tabletop. I especially enjoy the ambush mechanic and they are generally well balanced against each other.
The maps look nice and are interesting but they need to open some buildings up a bit, it is too easy to turtle up inside a fortress of a ruined tudor building.
Customization sucks though I would expect it to be a lesser priority.
Collision meshes are too big and frustrating on characters making them silly road blocks for your following characters and making it difficult to navigate.
However the biggest problem is that inspite of the level of tactical play offered your ploys will too often become undone by the rng. Your strategy may be sound, you may get the drop on the enemy and be able to focus your strengths, but then you will get ♥♥♥♥ed over by the rng.
That is this game in a nutshell, the rng ♥♥♥♥ing you over, again and again. You will do little or even nothing wrong but a set of ridiculously bad rolls (or lucky for the enemy) will see you fail and punished hard. This game and world is meant to be harsh but somewhere someone forgot the game part of that equation, and it's implications. This is less a game and more an exercise in random-fueled frustration.
For example I just had my entire warband of 7 take on the enemy commander of a weaker warband, and 2 whole rounds of my team missing, he pummeled my leader and gave him a skull fracture causing him to be stupid for the rest of the campaign. I could not have weighted it more in my favour but all that invested expense, time and effort is now wasted on a useless leader.
Maybe if they introduce say three warband fate points I will give this game another shot, until then, ♥♥♥♥ this game.

Empire Total War (ETW) is by far one of the greatest turn-based strategy games I've ever played. In my opinion, ETW takes place in one of the most fascinating centuries in history. I love learning about certain eras of history, and the 18th century is one of them. Anyone that is new to the Total War series, ETW is a definite must have game.
This is no game for the faint of heart or some chump looking to pacify his or her ADD for a measly thirty minutes. Empire is all about micromanaging every aspect of your country. For those who don't have the balls to handle everything that's thrown at you, there is hope. You can opt to have the computer manage the economy and construction for you. However,  in doing so you will only cheat yourself by reducing the game to a cheap simulated version of Risk. At the very least, I'd recommend a sold hour of gaming time, so plan accordingly.
I'm a pretty hard-core gamer, which means I love playing games on the hardest settings. For better or for worst, my satisfaction can only be quenched  by conquering a game while the odds are stacked against me.  If you have a top-shelf gaming machine with all the bells and whistles, I recommend maxing out all the graphic options. In doing so, you'll truly appreciate all the fine visual details this game has to offer.
Lets get down to what really matters. Here's the good, the bad, and the ugly:
The Good:
* ​​One of the most immersive strategy games available in the gaming market. In-fact, any stand alone game in the Total War series is worth its weight in gold.
* ​The replay value of this game is off the charts. Each playable country offers slightly different types of challenges. Although the overall objectives are still the same: Manage resources. Build-up your military. Go kick the sh*t out of people.  You'll quickly realize the road to success is not identical for each country.
*​ This game is cheap as hell! Seriously, $9.99 + tax! That's nothing less than highway robbery!
*​ Spending your Friday night playing this game with a full rack of your favorite beer and snacks is going to = one hell of a good time. You'll be bewildered at the countless hours that just fly bye.
​The Bad:
* ​The load times can seem very tedious.
* ​You not owning this game is bad. It's more than bad, it's an f'ing tragedy! What are you waiting for?! Go buy this game!
​The Ugly:
* ​There is no ugly, there's only you still reading this instead of playing this epic game!

People who have seen me tear games like Borderlands and Republic Commando to shreds (games with larger fanbases), might be expecting me to do the same to a much smaller game that no one really remembers, but as far as personality, good game design, and storytelling go- Pajama Sam is one of the better examples out there.
I know what you're thinking. "Dude? For real? You're favorite games are The Last of Us and Spec Ops: The Line! Those games are INTENSE! And you're suggesting a kid's educational game from the 90's belongs up at the top of the list with some of the greatest games ever?"
In my opinion? Yeah.
See, Pajama Sam was a game DESIGNED for kids, but the developers had enough mind to add enough humor that only adults would get. I'm not saying there are any sex jokes, and there aren't, but there are plenty of jokes that I know would go over most kids' heads. The game is also much more maturely designed. Of all of the Humongous Games, you mainly are told specifically what to do (Spy Fox, Freddi Fish), or you meet completely foolish characters that tell you what they need but are more than capable of getting the job done themselves (Putt Putt). But Pajama Sam did something different... it plays with empathy. Think about it. You run into situations, and mainly Sam reacts to the situation or you- the player- does. Otto can't go out on the river, just as he can't move along the land since he's a boat. The King can't move because he's rusted to the track. For the few seconds you speak with each character, you feel sorry for their problems (mainly Otto's stupidity) and solve them yourself.
The game also does incredibly well with it's design. The artwork is beautiful to look at, and the way each frame is shot to emphasize different perspectives and imply you can move in different directions makes the game very clear and concise. It's not like some point-and-click games where you stumbled across a door fifteen times and didn't notice it till you looked up the FAQ on the game. And, yes, the game is simple. It is easy. But, like I once told my ex, it doesn't have to be hard to be good. The voice acting is decent. as are all the sound effects, and the music is very ambient and creates a lively atmosphere.
The game revolves around a large puzzle for one of your three lost items, and each item has two randomly-selected puzzles that can be mixed and matched any which was, creating a lot of different "games" for you to play through. Of course, I got each different puzzle for the missing items after playing three times. But with this, and the 20 missing socks you can find, Pajama Sam could take up roughly 2-3 hours for you to play in its entirety, where you can take 40 minutes of your day to sit down and relax to the Land of Darkness.
Pajama Sam may not look like much, but of all the old point-and-click games I've played as a child, this one certainly has a lot more substance to it. There were the second and third official ones (we don't talk about the fourth), but the first one really got a strong identity for the character of Pajama Sam and his world of imagination. It's no masterpiece, and I'll never try to sell it like it is, but it is really, really, really good. It's a lot better than a lot of games I've played out there. Granted, it may not be for everyone, but it still is worth checking out for anyone looking for a very unique video game.

It's basically a copy of the Kingdoms: Classic game, except with some very nice retextures and more maps and things to do. First of all, the point of the game isn't to kill off the enemy, but instead to hop on a boat and get out of there. This is nice. Although this seems like a small problem, I was really annoyed by how my archers were shooting 89 degrees in the air in attempt to hit a rabbit.
The game also brings itself more problems. You no longer get a daily income after about 3 days. This means that if you ever run out of scratch, you're dead. This wouldn't be a problem, however, if you could have more control over the game. The guards always covered the right while the enemies came from the left. My farmers worked on the left while the enemies came from the left. Eventually, this led to a downward spiral of "Stop. Don't. Come back." followed by poverty and loss.
I really hate to dislike this game, but it falls too short between "challenging" and "playable" that it reaches neither. It becomes a game of how long the enemy takes to kill you and "I wonder if I'll get any money tonight".

Easy to Master:
Although there is a lot of grinding, it is the most enjoyable grinding I have played in a long time. However, late in the game, once you discover the optimal strategies, it becomes a little too easy.

The fighting system is awesome, everything else reeks of technical issues and poor design choices. I've had fun with this game and I'm going to keep playing but it has too many issues for me to recommend it at this stage. Wait for the devs to fix things before you buy it. I'll try to keep this review updated.
THE GOOD:
- Fighting system is 9/10. This is clearly where most of the effort went. Dodging and parrying attacks feels incredibly badass once you get used to it. Customizing your moveset is a lot of fun, there are a ton of moves to learn from 4 different fighting styles, and there are endless ways to chain them together. One on one fights are super intense. The only real issue with the fights is that the camera goes to a weird place if you get backed up against a wall, which doesn't help when you're already cornered.
- The art style is nice.
THE BAD:
- Bugs and crashes galore. When I first started the game I instantly clipped through the ground and died.
- The single player campaign is very short, and once you beat it there's nothing else to do in single player exept grind NPCs for new moves.
- It isn't possible to fast travel between areas, even after you beat the game, so if you want to go somewhere you've already been you just gotta slog there on foot.
- Fighting random players with online matchmaking is fun but the servers have been down for hours every day since launch.
- Online fights have no timer meaning that your opponent can just run away from you forever if they're about to lose.
- Sick of random 1v1 matchups and want to try a new mode? Well too bad matey, because that's the only mode there is.
- The PvP reward system needs work. When your rank goes up you just get a random item that might be a duplicate, with no guarantee that you'll ever get anything cool. You are not alone in this world though as your faithful friend, Teddy, an actual talking teddy bear, goes with you, helping you out and keeping you company.

It's a nice spooky game with interesting imagery and gameplay, so this definitely comes with a thumbs up from me!

Among the Sleep is a horror game from the perspective of a baby. I really wish I could say I liked it more. I mean, your walking animation is just adorable, with your little star pajamas and clenched fists waving around full of infant determination. Sprinting is walking on all fours, which is also clever.
Other than that, there's not much to the game. How could there be? The game can be finished in about two hours, including the prequel free DLC and even then it doesn’t have much to show for those two hours. The boogeyman can barely catch you, except when he's scripted to show up on your tail. There are no mechanics except some very light climbing and block pushing. It's baby's first puzzle game, which is odd, since it seemed to be a game
a child, not a game
a child. By the end, the game does have some interesting elements with adult themes that a baby couldn't understand, but it's not much to go on. Seeing normal things from a very low perspective also make some mundane things very menacing, but there's not much more to that either. The game is set in a well-realised, but a bit trite nightmare otherworld that almost every other horror game has been putting out since Silent Hill.
Among the Sleep is okay, but I would not recommend it to anyone but a diehard horror fan that wants to try everything.

Many of the negative reviews that I see are either because the game is challenging and the person lost, or the reviewer was expecting the game to be a CCG, which it is not.
Yes, the game can be difficult, but that is a positive in my book.  Not knowing if the next card drawn will be fantastic loot or possible defeat makes the game exciting and keeps me looking forward to the next scenario.  And yes, there is randomness in this game.  It has cards and dice, what else would you expect.  The randomness does not, however, mean that there is no strategy or tactics.  Crafting a team with decks that can handle a wide range of challenges is fundamental to the game.  I have also seen comlaints that about the Stash only holding ten cards.  This adds to the strategy and, yes, you will be forced to make difficult choices about which cards to keep and which to get rid of.  Having access to every card in the game, through your Stash, would greatly diminish the challenge.
The game is less of a CCG and more of a Living Card Game.  There is a difference and if you are expecting a CCG, you might be disppointed.
To sum it up, I really like this game and recommend it if you are looking for a game this is a little diffierent from most other digital card games.

I had to come write this review because there are many misconceptions and bad information about this game that nearly made me avoid buying it - Which would have been a terrible mistake, because the game is stellar.
So before I give my mini review (I'm still under 10 hours into the game) let me address the elephant in the room- 'Losing cards' you have paid for or earned- Its just not true. Your collection never loses anything, ever. Your character may lose access to that card if he banishes it (or through other means) but the card itself remains in your deck and collection. This really was confusing at first while reading the reviews and discussion and the way its explained by most led me to believe that you 'lost cards'.
The way this game works is that you have to think of this as being composed of many 'decks'- Your character decks are all separate, as are your 'stash' and 'collection' decks- When a card is lost from your character deck it merely is moved to your 'collection' deck and then is randomly shuffled back into the game during scenarios- The fact is, you never actually 'lose' any cards.
-The 'p2w' aspect...Non existent. Now, perhaps on android that might be true (I dont know) but if you buy this game and the DLC, you have everything- Forever. Things you 'buy' from the shop or get in chests will already be in your collection at that point (assuming you have the DLC) and right now I picked up everything for around $10.
Now onto the 'game'- This isnt a typical CCG where you build decks and play single matches- This is so unique and different that it needs to be approached as probably a separate genre- This is more character building/scenario grinder comprised of using a limited amount of cards to build a deck out of whats available (again, what is in your 'collection' doesnt actually give you access to those cards all the time- They are shuffled into the game world and have to be brought into your character deck through gameplay...Confused? I bet- So was I and it took a good 3-4 hours to really see how the system works and the beauty of it- To get out of the mindset of how most CCG's work and look at this as something more.
Had I paid full price for this game and all the DLC I would have been really happy- In fact, I will be going to try and get the actual tabletop version of this game because its a blast and I would love to play this with others.
The artwork is top notch, game mechanics are simple enough to grasp but complex enough to really have to put time into this and build synergy and strategy.
On the negative side- Stash size needs to be increased (10 cards seems way too small) and multiplayer added- But thats it and those are minor things in the scope of this wonderful and unique game.
This should be overwhelmingly positive on reviews but there is so much misunderstanding and misinformation that people are thinking they are losing cards or approaching this as a standard deckbuilder CCG and not something else entirely.
-Anyhow loving the game and I hope they continue to release DLC adventures and hopefully multiplayer and more game modes- VERY happy with this purchase and I almost didnt buy it.

I did not expect RE7 to not only return to old school survival horror (with combat, puzzles, not the hide and seek stuff like Outlast), but to do it in such an incredible fashion, as to be IMO the best survival horror RE ever made.
Yes, even better than REmake.
The story isn't as cheesy as a B action movie or as cliched. Hell, there are even some emotional bits here and there and they work as intended i.e. they are not unintentionally funny or cringy. The game is not gore orientated, it is very atmospheric and quite regularly genuinely creepy. It's not very scary, but it does have jumpscares which are earned and not cheap.
F-uck me, Resident Evil has earned jumpscares. Is this real life?
The combat does its job, it's ok. The boss battles are great. However, the game is much easier than the old school horror games and does become rather action heavy towards the end. There is little enemy variety. Fortunately, the good greatly outweighs the bad.
Capcom delivered a classic RE game in 2017. Maybe there is hope for humanity after all?

Boy, I was in for a wild journey. Although I loved the fixed camera angles in the old games, the first person element was well integrated in the atmosphere of the game and it didn't feel alien. On the contrary, it made it more immersive. Furthermore, the game exhibits a captivating narrative which is enhanced by the development of the antagonists, i.e. the Bakers, etc.. Superb sound design and voice acting increase the terror already induced by the spine-chilling settings. The scarce ammo and the fight or flight dillemas revived resident evil memories of old and thus were more than welcome. In general I felt that this game was a distilled mix of the things that made resident evil a game of suspence and sheer horror.

This game right here is the first one I ever owned, and I couldn't resist picking it up again. Just like I remember it, the game is an excellent point-and-click adventure, one that you can play over and over thanks to the main 3 items randomly changing locations. I always loved this feature, because every time you start anew, you have to solve different puzzles to beat the game, rewarding each replay with variety. Sure, I hold this game on the nostalgic pedestal a bit, but not without good reason.
Now about the Steam version: I'm a bit disappointed. I've ran my original copy in the Scumm engine before and reached the same performance differences here: voice dialogue loads faster then normal, so characters talking in cutscenes sound like they don't take a break to breathe and just go into the next sentence. Here and there I see animations changed or cut out altogether, particularly during the intro dialogue with King where he says "Loop-de-Loops" and his face doesn't move. The game is still fully playable, but these emulation problems still got to me. It would be unreasonable to recommend getting an original copy and seeing for yourself, as this game was designed for Windows '95 and the like; the game would most certainly not work without a virtual machine. Even still, if you remember this game, played it or not, this purchase it still worth it.

Kingdom Newlands is a great sequel to the original Kingdom game with a lot of great additions. The game is a really simple with simple AI and simple controls but the game gives off a horror survival vibe that you can’t shake off every night with the enemy creature called “greed” try to destroy your Kingdom (the enemies are called “greed” because they want your gold and stuff and they also want your crown). The change of breaking the portals so you can build a boat to escape is a welcomed addition to the game unlike the previous game where you just had to hold out for as long as possible which made the game feel sort of futile since destruction was inevitable unlike this game that has an ending that where you win and your kingdom is saved (now before you correct me, yes the old game you can destroy the portals and your kingdom will be save but you have to do so in less than 25 days thing is kind of dumb since there are achievements for lasting 100 days which at that point you are screwed either way since its winter you have no income and the “greed” will just break your walls and take your crown anyway).
The AI is a downside of the game but if you have played the previous Kingdom this AI is certainly better, for starters they actually run to their destination (not all the time but they can unlike in the old game where they never run at all even when it night time). The upgrades for this game are okay they almost always have a use even if you don’t use them but there are some that just become a necessity like the “Baker Hermit” or “Ballista Hermit” which you really need in the late game. Besides those minor gripes, I have with the game it is very solid, I don’t think I have even encountered a bug at all during my time playing. So, if you like the 8-bit aesthetic and survival resource management gameplay experience then try this game out.

Penguins Arena: Sedna's World is a penguin themed first-person shooter intended for children, developed by
in December 2008. It's a multiplayer game where players try to knock each other off of an iceberg and into the water. There are four different game modes and each map contains five different temporary weapons or powerups that give the player an advantage. The maps are all very small, thus the rounds are really quick and furious.
The online multiplayer of this game is practically dead and the artificial intelligence is not very good, often the opponent just falls off the cliff by himself or he just won't let go and the round goes on forever. If you want to buy this game, I would recommend you to get some friends to play it with you, if you play alone you probably won't have much fun. Also the game is pretty repetitive due to the similarity of the maps and the game modes, so it might get boring after a few rounds.
Still it's overall a fun game with cute graphics. It's nothing special, but it has a basic and easily understandable gameplay and the powerups enhance the fun. There's even a map editor, which I really like. You can download it
or download custom maps created by other users
. Even though the game was released five years ago, the developers recently announced an upcoming update, so let's see what the future holds.
Penguins Arena: Sedna's World is great if you want a short-term fun game to play with friends and nothing too serious. Also it's a nice alternative for children to the many violent first-person shooters. The game is only available in a bundle, which is in my opinion not worth the price if you'll only buy it for this game, but if you can get it on sale it's worth a shot.

FlatOut 2 was a great followup to the original FlatOut. It didn't take itself seriously and had nice graphics and style to boot. In 2007 BugBear decided to tweak it, repackage it and call it Ultimate Carnage. It's basically the same game but with some added modes and upgraded visuals. There's better textures, water, debris effects and reflections on the cars themselves. On the audio side the soundtrack has been replaced with lesser known tracks but they're mostly good although it gets repetitive after a while.
This is kind of a tough game to judge. It's fun, entertaining and has a lot to like but if you've played FlatOut 2 before then you'll feel more than a little sense of Déjà vu. It has the same cars, same tracks, same game engine and even the same physic glitches. It's pretty much FlatOut 2 with some new paint and chrome which is more than a little disappointing. Fans of the series would eventually get a FlatOut 3 from a different studio but the less said about that the better.

SPOILERFREE REVIEW:
I personally don't like the GTA Series all too much (maybe GTA 4 a bit), because the story is too loose and the freedom too big. I always end up strolling around doing nothing and never feeling I experience the game as a whole and as a story. So GTA always feels too much like a sandbox - and I get bored fast in sandboxes since after a while everything feels the same.
In addition GTA usually has bad car physics. That is why I only liked GTA4, which had some physics and therefore a little challenge while driving fast or around corners.
Mafia 2 got me hooked up from the very beginning. I never played part 1 because I didn't have a powerful computer by that time but I only heard great things about it so I jumped on M2 in a sale to try it out. Mafia 2 takes you by the hand and leads you from well scripted story mission to the next. It tells a moving story where the main character isn't dragged into the mafia by accident, he chooses to be a mafiosi because of easier money, girls and other stuff.
When you follow Vito, you get to experience the city which is modeled with a lot of loving details. You have a lot of freedom but you never feel "lost". Basically what you will end up doing is follow the story. This will take you around 12 hrs (without DLCs). It will start off slow and will be getting better with each mission. The game is obviously based on some mafia movies and themes like money, betrayal and family wars are the main drive behind it - this and of course your main Character Vito Scoletta, who is much less black and white then all the other game characters in recent games.
Especially if you are used to arcade/mainstream games or racing games keep in mind that in the beginning you have very old, slow cars and that there is an easy to learn, yet sometimes challenging car physics which makes the game much more interesting then just the brainless car physics in most GTA titles.
Graphics are still fine, although in 2010 by the games release, I really hoped for better facial animations.
BOTTOM LINE
Despite all the freedom you will be ending up playing the game failry linear, which is, if you are looking for 12 hours of fun gameplay and a well told story, something you should totally look forward to doing so. If you like that you have the feeling of being in a big world with your own choices, but taken by the hand (instead of having too many things to do at once) - you will propably like this interpretation of an "open world".
If you like story - go for it.
If you like mafia movies - go for it
if you like the 40s and moreover the 50s to some extend - go for it
if you like to plan ahead how long you need for a playthrough - go for it

It's a very linear 3rd person shooter, think max payne, but you really need to use cover effectively like in gears of war.
The story is great, but calling it an open world is an insult to open world games.  You have only one path, you can wander around but other than smashing stolen cars for money, robbing stores or getting in shoot outs with cops, there isn't much to the 'open world'.  I didn't find a single side quest, I bought the deluxe version with all the dlc, but I probably won't bother.  Think 'Max Payne' with a godfather/good fellas backdrop.
Also, there is no fast travel, and no inter mission saving.  More than half your time playing this will be driving somewhere very slowly.

A cheap death can set you back to the beginning of the level.  And believe me, there will be cheap deaths.  Keyboard smashing cheap deaths.  Guys spawning behind you within 3 feet with automatic weapon cheap deaths.  Falling cheap deaths.  Getting hit by cars cheap deaths (sometimes police on regular patrol).
The game is rough around the edges.
There is stuff to collect, but it doesn't seem to do anything.  There are no upgrades.  There are some much better guns.
But outside of the magnum and the tommy gun, I didn't really use much else except for the shottie.  The shottie that is ridiculously accurate at 100 meters.
You do get a better tutorial on fighting at some point in the game, from then on as long as you're patient you'll win any fist fight.
It's a fun shooter, but don't confuse it with saints row or assassin's creed or far cry or grand theft auto.  Call of duty in third person would be more accurate, something akin to gears of war only not as good.  Fun, but VERY linear.
Don't get me wrong though, I REALLY enjoyed shooting up places and taking on armies of guys, just me and my shotgun.  Sometimes you fight with NPCs who are invincible, and get this, they actually HELP, instead of just getting in the way like in most games.  It's fun, but not very sophisticated.  The level design has a lot of variety as well.  Stealth sort of works.
I'd definitely recommend the game, but don't go in expecting what I expected.  It's a fun, linear shooter with a good story which rips off tons of plot elements from a variety of famous gangster films.  You can wander, but just to find collectables which do nothing.  So, I'd recommend not doing that (unless this is the only game in your library).
Don't pay too much for it, I think I paid 10 dollars for it with all the dlc, it's too old and lacks too much depth to be worth much more.  The ending gave me little interest in the DLC.  You'll see what I mean if you play it all the way through.

As a long time Resident Evil fan, I was distrusting of this sequel because of the mix of horror genres that are not particular to the series: voodoo, supernatural, and creepy kid to name a few. The game draws from the first Resident Evil and seems to have taken cues from Silent Hill while making nods to classic horror films. When Resident Evil 4 first came out, it was also in the vein of a new twist on the genre, Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Invasion of the Body Snatchers being central inspirations. Only, RE7 is without series creator and veteran Shinji Mikami and that may be why RE7 feels a little off-the-rails.
Still, I recommend it as a solid horror experience. First-person view fits right at home in Resident Evil and I hope to see future sequels have this look. Where it truly falls short is how it has traded gameplay for the inclusion of setpieces (four to be exact) that  go from best to worst and don't seem to meld well together. They feel disparate from one another as if developed by different teams and stitched together post-production. The first two hours will draw you in through its spooky mansion exploration, but as the story and characters are revealed there is less of a survival-horror experience and more what appears to be a playable version of Saw, and a drawn-out segment that takes place on a ship.
Once its over, you can't help but wonder if its worth playing again because the second half is filled with cutscenes, wresting control from the player. As a horror experience it's a great title, just don't expect this to be the royal return of Capcom's best-selling series as promised. RE7 might have fared better as a spin-off title and leaves much to be desired for the long-time Resident Evil fan. For that, DLC might be the antidote you're needing to justify the purchase of the potentially lackluster base game.

TL;DR: The fighting and world are well crafted with some minor bugs. The PvE is experimental, with the world and experience being your story more than the actual narrative. 8/10. I would definately buy this game if you like martial arts and if you like old martial arts movies/stories.
I understand this game can be very polarising, but the game has surprised me to such a degree that I felt like giving my two cents on the PvE and PvP parts of the game.
The PvE is itself two parts. There is the story, which as you have read by now is quite minimalist, and there is the actual world you play in. This world is acts as a place to meet other players as well as enemies to face even when the story is finished. Some people complain about the shortness of the story. While this is understandable it does really nail the feeling of a genuine martial arts narrative.
The story itself to me is completely ingrained in the world and the player experience, as you are able to continue learning moves and start your own school after the main narrative.
Effectively this means that if you see the whole world and experience as the story you'll have a much more rewarding experience, as the world seems to be set up to really fill in the gaps with personal experience. I realise this is very much an experiment, and for some people this might be a failure. I personally think the developers got it spot on.
The PvP part of the game is excellent. There is sporadic PvP happening throughout the main world, depending on what players choose. I have yet to see any real ganking or trolling, people tent to ress each other after combat (which everyone can do for anyone). There is no chat, but there is a streamlined emote-wheel which does the trick when it comes to player interaction. My interactions with other players have been pleasent, and less pleasant players don't break the game. Dying has no penalty. It does not cause loss of progress and there are plenty of checkpoints to respawn at. The fighting mechanic is the deepest I have seen in any game so far, and I am barely scratching the surface.
There is however a steep learning curve, so you have to be willing to put in effort to get most out of the game. Some reviewers have complained about people blocking all the time or exploiting a single move, but there are ways around every fighting style. It seems to me like people complaining about this haven't really gone deep enough into their own style yet. I don't want to say 'get good', but I am warning other people that these reviews do not represent my experiences with the game. The 1v1 combat is instanced, but takes place in areas you will be familiar with if you've played through the story.
The design and atmosphere are as well crafted as the fighting styles, but this is of course partly a matter of taste. If you are familiar with martial arts you will recognise a lot of moves. A lot of love has gone in to this. There are server performance bugs, the gameplay itself is well optimised. There is one bug that is not server related right now (4/9/2017) that causes the loading screen to get stuck in a black screen while respawning on occasion. The devs have responded to it all and are working on it. They seem to be invested in the community. I would say the bugs are minor and probably will be adressed.
8/10 with bugs. 9/10 if they adress them properly.

It took me about ten hours to become Absolver, which marks the end of the singleplayer content. If you want to play offline there isn't much here.
The core of the game is duelling an evenly matched player and that's a beautiful thrill. I've played for 30 hours now and so far two out of three matches were exciting, with me and my opponent both thinking "I will win this one" until way past the midpoint of the match.
I read some reviews that state a level 30 player will never beat a level 60 (current cap) player. They're wrong. Winning a duel is about the flow of your moveset, your ability to recognize and remember your opponent's moveset as well as endurance of focus (yours, not your player character's).
One level up gives you one point to invest, which raises a stat by one half to two percent. A few percent bonus on your damage, vitality or stamina won't help you if you can't land a hit, and whether you can land a hit is not determined by these stats but by your skill and moveset.
The quality and versatility of the moveset will be most important to the outcome of high-skill play. That's where Absolver is a deckbuilding game; the more moves you unlock the more options you have for your moveset. Fittingly, some NPCs refer to 'fighting' or 'drawing a weapon' as 'folding' or 'unfolding'.
When you start a new character your level resets but you keep your moves, so you can build a complex moveset right away and don't have to endure hours of getting back to where you were.
In the open world (more like labyrinth than expanse) the game doesn't restrict, reward or punish you for however you interact with your fellow Prospect. The serene art-style and soundscape however inspire nearly everyone to be cool to one another. I also love that there is no chat, only a handful of gestures to convey basic thoughts and feelings.
For me, in Berlin, the servers are very reliable. Especially for a game that apparently launched to better sales than anticipated. I'v had two infinite connecting-loops and one hard disconnect in 30 hours, that's better than acceptable. I do hope the ping will improve, right now executing a move is satisfying but doesn't feel quite immediate.
There are some rough edges in the production, like the artificial intelligence. Outside of combat NPCs are running back to their posts like mental moles.
But the core experience is extremely polished. Hitboxes, animation, responsiveness, input design, visual effects and acoustic feedback are spot on.
I'm pretty sure I'll be playing this for months at least. I recommend that you do likewise.

They released this game too early. The core gameplay is unique and thought provoking, but is placed in a game where there isn't much to do.
The visual audio experience as a whole is 10/10. The simple yet beautiful art style with lots of attention to detail in its dark-souls-like level design means I don't get bored of running through the same zones looking for new moves and items. Nylon string guitar with orchestral backing shines through in a mysterious soundtrack that flows with the action. The 'thud' of punches and combo audio queues are all very satisfying and add to the intuitive combat experience.
The meat of this game is the 1v1 PVP combat. This is a PVP game. If you want to beat up on npc dummies all day and feel powerful, you can do that here but you will get bored. This game is all about improving yourself as a player as well as growing the abilities of your avatar. Fight deck customization and player reactions and reads is what this game is all about. It makes every fight unique, and there's always something to improve upon.
The game launched with server issues, but they've gotten much better. They're adding 3vs3 PVP, ranked matches, and spectator mode. I enjoyed this game at launch, but it should be more mature in 4-8 weeks. They're also adding more combat styles and moves.
Right now there are 4 very unique combat styles and over 90 bare-fist martial arts moves to build your style with. There are also sword moves, but they are more difficult to aquire.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Dark Souls PVP but wants it faster and with greater depth.

Double Dragon: Neon is an absolutely fantastic video game.
Double Dragon: Neon is everything it wants to be. Not only is the gameplay satisfying, but it also delivers spectacularly with the soundtrack, forged by the man Jake Kaufman himself. This game is wonderfully tongue-in-cheek while also paying homage to the earlier games of the series. Now, while I want to call this game perfect in every respect, it sadly isn't. However, I still feel very passionate about just how great Double Dragon: Neon is.
Now as you all probably know, this game is a sidescrolling beat 'em up with co-op capability, and it's great. The gameplay has a decent sense of depth for a 2-D beat 'em up since you are given the ability to dodge and perform combos with a bro. The sound effects are all robust and clear and really give you the sense that you are beating the living daylights out of someone. The voice acting and kind of humor this game has are both delightfully silly. And to top it all off, the hype soundtrack is not only fitting for this game, but it's also available for a free download. This game is just bodacious-- and for only $10!
The bro-op really is just boss, by the way. Juggling your opponents together to utterly annihilate them, the high-five mechanic that allows you to split health or give each other double damage, and sharing (or fighting over) money and healing items. It's friggin' bro-op.
Now I could go on and continue singing this game's praises, but it does have a couple issues. The netplay leaves much to be desired, and the game is capable of stuttering and crashing. I personally have not consistently experienced the latter, but they are definitely issues that have needed to be ironed out. Fighting Roxy, that jetpack girl, is also pretty bogus. That last part doesn't really matter, though.
Now this part of the gameplay here you may love or hate, as it is quite different from the other Double Dragon games. As you progress through the game, you'll grab these nifty little upgrades called Mixtapes. These are, in essence, how you level up your Billy (or Jimmy) to make him stronger. You can equip two different Mixtapes at any time: One of your Mixtapes will be stance which boosts your stats passively, some of the stances having unique effect on gameplay. The other will be your Sosetsuken, otherwise known as your special attack. Grabbing more of the same Mixtape will enhance it, making it more powerful. In addition, you can actually upgrade the maximum strength of your Mixtapes at the Tapesmith. This all adds a sort of RPG feel to the game, which I personally have no issue with. If you feel like the Mixtape system cheapens the game, don't worry! The harder difficulties will still prove challenging even with a maxed out Mixtape.
Even with this game's issues, I would absolutely reccommend this game. It really is a solid game that's even better with a bro. Or you could buy Nekopara, I guess. If you're a dweeb.

TL;DR Imperi is an hour's worth of casual click-strategy and definitely worth the ninety-nine cent price tag.
You play as a Romanesque governor, sent to some minor province to help make it flourish. These actions include recruiting soldiers, fighting for more land (and thus the potential for a higher population), taxing your population, planting crops, and purchasing grain.
Short and simple, the text-based interface is intuitive and it makes for some fun. Overall, I get the feeling that this is a first attempt in a long learning process, and that Nuts and Volts could definitely be on the path to releasing more complex games in the future.

Hiiro is a calm platformer game focused on exploration.  It's Seiklus meets Fez . . . literally.  Things are straight lifted from Fez.  A tribute is one thing, but the resemblance is uncanny: in Hiiro, you walk around exploring the world with platforming mechanics and collecting yellow cubes, just like in Fez (except there's no 3D mechanic here).
It's not just the concept, though, there are other things too.  Just compare the animation at 0:35 (notice Gomez's body language [he's the guy in the middle, without the eyepatch]:

To this animation in Hiiro, which occurs when a large cube is collected at 0:21 (again, look at the character's pose):
Even things like the design of the collection menu and giving large cubes a Tetris-like texture on the surface (in Hiiro's menu) seems straight from Fez.  I can't ignore this, and it's the main reason I cannot recommend this game.  I haven't played Seiklus for a long time, so I can't say if anything was lifted from that too, but the Fez similarities are way too close for me to ignore.
Adding to this, the game is somewhat broken.  Ladders are near impossible to climb unless you get really lucky with your double jump (I could never get the ladder with a single jump or the up arrow; I always had to double jump to try and get it).  This is the only real problem I've found so far, but it's a pretty big one, since ladders are the main way you progress get to higher areas.  Thus, exploration becomes frustrating every time you come across a ladder and try to climb it, which may take a few minutes *each* to finally grab onto.  I have no idea why, but it's pretty frustrating.
It's a real shame, because from the description on the store page, this game seems like a real passion project, a love letter to games the developer enjoyed and was influenced by.  The art has a nice style, and I enjoyed exploring this world (though I haven't explored much yet, mainly because of the ladder thing).  But the game goes beyond a tribute with the things copied from Fez, from a love letter to a clunky copy.  I’d just play Fez ($10 USD) or Seiklus (free) if I were you.
