As a remaster of FlatOut 2, and being a FlatOut player for over 10 years, this game feels refreshing arcadey and VERY nostalgic.

The game itself is fantastic - best racing game I ever played. The focus on destruction is hilarious and fun. Some of the music is great too, especially if you like hard rock / metal.
However, when you first start the game, it won't work work. No error message, it just won't start. It deserves a thumbs down for that alone. To fix it, you have to install Windows Live Marketplace (WLM) a.k.a. Games For Windows Live (GFWL) first. If you sign up for an account you'll be disappointed, because GFWL insists it needs to download an "update", but then says "Can't download the update. Make sure that you are connected to the internet", offers a broken "support" link, and forces you to sign out of GFWL. This problem is caused by Microsoft, but the game developers have refused to fix it for YEARS even though they keep trying to sell it!
Since you're signed out, you can't play multiplayer and more importantly, YOUR SINGLE PLAYER PROGRESS IS NOT SAVED on exit; you'll be left with nothing unlocked so you can only play the initial maps. I've experienced the same thing on two PCs, one running Win7 and the other running Win10, and before that I was completely unable to make this game run on another Win7 PC.
Edit: Edit: other reviews say Ultimate Carnage is the same as Flatout 2, but sadly it's not. The gameplay and maps ARE almost the same, with only minor improvements, but the graphics of FOUC are hugely improved over FO2, the user interface of FOUC is much more polished, and the soundtrack is new. I hate that I had to switch to FO2, though FO2 is certainly still fun.
A couple more things: (1) even broken I still would buy it when it is heavily discounted, as the initial maps are fun and there is a party mode (turn-based multiplayer stunts) which doesn't have any upgrades to lose on exit (but might be too challenging for actual parties). (2) The mouse cursor is broken in GFWL; use the keyboard to navigate it (Tab, Enter, Esc and arrow keys) (3) Microsoft somehow offers two versions of the GFWL installer (gfwlivesetup.exe) in different places and I tried both of them on Windows 10. One of them is 70 MB and is self-contained; the game is incompatible with this copy and WILL NOT START. The other is 628 KB and downloads the rest of itself. This copy worked for me on both Win7 and Win10 (Sorry for not offering a link, as I lost track of where I got it from). After installing it, don't worry about logging into the marketplace, it is not necessary.

Save Jesus is a fun point-and-click puzzle game. The stages are played with true physics where you manipulate a rolling ball to wipe out enemies and leave Jesus unharmed. The format is similar to Angry Birds with levels that can be completed and then attempted again to receive the maximum 3 stars. The game is the perfect length for a casual gamer but may be too repetitive for players looking for 10+ hours of gameplay. The presentation is clean with sharp cartoon visuals alongside very funny voice over jokes thrown in occasionally. I found the main villain to be extremely funny in his laid back evilness !  I was quoting all of his sayings after finishing the game. I would love to see that character return in a sequel or another game. Perhaps where you play as him in the time machine and have to kill historical figures from different periods.

Save Jesus is a physics game where the goal of the game is to get a ball of something (called a weapon) to collect stars, hit the romans, and don't touch Jesus.
The game has a very nice difficulty curve, with the earlier levels being signifcantly easier to lead and teach you how the game works. Some of the later levels are actually quite hard to get 3 stars in, but I was able to 3 star all 50 levels. Overall, the game is still on the easier side of these kinds of games, as I was able to beat all 50 levels in under 1.5 hours. I tried to grind out the rest of the achievements, but I got bored and annoyed by the complete 50 levels using the different types of weapons (essentially making you do each level like 7 times).
The game is very lighthearted, and overall presents itself as a relatively enjoyable game.
Rating: 7.3/10
Recommend Price: $0.79 or under (it is a bit short)

Context: I grew up playing RE.  I remember when RE opened and Chris Redfield was smoking a cigarette.  The 90s were awesome.  RE remake, RE0 and RE4 were my favourites, played them over and over and over again, on the hardest difficulties.
Details: the protagonist, who I presume to be a mild mannered guy who doesn't like to offend anyone and has a tendency for misplacing things, is looking for his wife, who 3 years ago decided to work for some family in the middle of nowhere, and who he abandoned after not hearing from her for a time, despite knowing the location of her workplace. Why did the wife go work in the middle of nowhere for some random family?  Was she a babysitter, a chef, a housemaid, the gardiner?  We don't know.  Why didn't the husband give her a call, go to her workplace or phone the police when he stopped hearing from her?  Not sure, but right out of the gate the plot is hollow and you know you are playing as a guy who is a loser.  Many of the responses I have received is that this is all explained in the game and the guy is actually the coolest RE protagonist ever.  I doubt it, but even if we accept that...
Having received an email one day containing two new videos from his wife (one of which should have prompted him to phone the police and FBI), he decides to visit her workplace alone and unarmed (despite the contents of the video which, I repeat, should have prompted him to phone the police and FBI).  On the car ride there he's on the phone with a friend and tells the friend he doesn't know if it's actually her.  It's a very odd phone call to be making, makes no sense, and cannot be attributed to being "lost in translation" from Japanese to English.  But whatever, let's just play this game.
Within minutes of the protagonist's arrival at the workplace: there she is, in some random guy's dungeon.  The couple have the most unrealistic exchange you would expect between a husband and wife in such circumstances, and the immersion in the game is immediately lost.  Then the crazy begins.
It's clear the protagonist's wife has suffered some mental ilness/RE infection during her stay in captivity and is suffering from Stockholm syndrome; not to be unexpected. Crazy wife decides she's going to help the protagonist escape the dungeon she's been living in for 3 years... by throwing him through walls and doors with the strength of the incredible hulk and attacking him with a knife. Also not unexpected.  I get how zombies(RE1+)/infected townsfolk(RE4)/Africans (RE5)/abandoned wives (RE7) behave.
What was unexpected however, given that in previous RE games the protagonist dies when attacked, if he/she cannot fight off the attacker is that: he survives a knife attack from his wife, in which he is repeatedly stabbed all over his body with deep wounds, has his palm pierced by the knife, which is healed by pouring alcohol over it.  As if this hand hasn't seen enough, it's stabbed through the palm again by a screwdriver, such that it is stuck to a wall.  The protagnost tries hard to pull the screwdriver out of the wall only to have has hand cut off by a chainsaw.  I figured the "You Are Dead" screen would appear, or he would pass out and find himself attached to medical equipment.
Remember when RE4 scared the hell out of you because you were going to be chased by a chainsaw?  Well, RE7 brings back the chainsaw, except this time being cut by a chainsaw will be about as fatal as being hit by a lightsaber in the new Disney Star Wars movies, i.e. it'll just leave a scratch. Unless it's part of a scripted part of the combat (press A, press A, press A), in which case you lose your hand.
His left hand chainsawed off and bleeding all over the place for several minutes, the protagonist conveniently finds a handgun and 3 clips of 9 mm bullets (which he loads into the gun despite missing his left hand).  These bullets are insufficient to drop his wife, despite hitting her directly in the head and knee caps, so he resorts to a trusty handaxe that spawned out of thin air after his wife threw him through a door previously barricaded by layers of wood and nails.
Having survived this ordeal by pouring alcohol on himself, the protagonist finds himself chased around a similarly enclosed space by the dungeonmaster and his cliched deep south incestous family, has his foot cut off by a shovel, then manages to put it back on.  So the protagonist has lost his hand and his foot, but both of them are put back on, and I am supposed to keep enjoying this.  I tried.
He watches a black police officer have his head cut off by a shovel - not at the neck, but mid-face, it just doesn't make any sense.  (Where are BLM and the SJWs on that one?)  Meanwhile your protagonist is unloading more 9 mm into deep south dungeon keeper to no avail.
You can't drop him.  I mean, you're swinging a knife into his neck, head, hamstrings, back, chest, eyes, but he's undroppable.  You shoot him all over the place and he doesn't drop.  I know RE bosses are semi invincible, but it just doesn't make sense this early in the game.  He cuts off your foot again, because apparently that's what this guy does. He stabs you in the gut with his shovel, lifts you into the air.
How does his shovel do these things?  How is it you can fight back with guns and axes, but not your fists?  In the earlier combat with the wife you had the "mash A, mash A, mash A" prompt to fight her off, but not with deep south dungeon master.
Why can't you run away when you hold shift?  Don't ask me. What I do know: apparently you can still live, even though you've lost your limbs, are in immese pain, and have lost enough blood to feed a vampire colony for weeks.  Finally, if you do drop him, do you really care to keep playing?  I don't.
Sorry for upsetting so many players.  I wanted to be one of you.

I've been a pretty big Resident Evil fan ever since I played the Wii edition of RE4 almost a decade ago (I know, I'm a real heathen). I've played through a lot of the classics (though I've yet to play 2 or 3) and the only game in the series I'm pretty indifferent towards is 5. I even liked 6 in a weird, sick way. All that to say, there are some common elements throughout the series I love, horror being one of them.
Resident Evil 7 is far and away the biggest departure for the series, and I'm happy to say it's a good time. However, some of its changes are fairly serious misteps, in my humble opinion. While many would assume the camera change to first person was the most signifcant change, I would disagree. The series switched from isometric fixed camera angles to over the shoulder camera angles before. Far and away the most significant (and worst change) is the tone. No longer is there the charming and vibrant cast that pushes you forward, or the cheesy one-liners that makes you crack a grin. It's a much more serious affair, with the only offbeat moments being some ridiculously over-the-top (read: great) boss encounters. Ethan is a dry character, plain and simple, and so are all the other non-antagonist personalities that show up. Give me Leon, Claire, or hell, even Steve over Ethan, his wife, Alma, or not-Chris any day of the week. I'm a fan of the core RE characters. I love 'em. Thankfully we got the stellar CG movies like Vendetta to give me my fix, but I hope we get a return of some great personalities to the main series.
...Now with that out of the way, the core of the game. The overall structure is certainly a throwback to RE1, with the exploration of a spooky manor and backtracking to previous areas. Visually it's pretty stunning, though I did get a fair bit of screen tearing in my play through (that's honestly probably on me for not knowing how to properly optimize my recently bought gaming rig). I really appreciated the amount of environmental detail in it, they really nailed the vibe of a trash house. The overall game story was fine, though nothing to write home about. The villains certainly provided plenty of memorable moments, but the core "man searches for his wife" horror story didn't do much for me. Again, this kinda fell on some limp characters.
Onto the meat of the game; the mechanics, exploration and horror. It definitely feels different from prior REs for me. The weapon upgrade and treasure system from RE4 doesn't make a return, which is a shame as I thought those systems were incredibly rewarding and engaging. Instead, improvements are few and far between, and they are either gotten through searching the environment, buying them with antique coins hidden about, or solving a puzzle to get them. I appreciate this approach as well, and I think it served the game well. Capcom stuffed coins in places you wouldn't expect, such as underneath dressers or in small corners of the room, basically invisible even when looking straight at them. This may sound like a negative, but I love games that give purpose to taking in your surroundings, and this certainly was one of those games. Exploration never felt confusing like in some of the previous games, but it also never felt to linear like 6, so I think they really nailed it here. As an aside, I loved the optional VHS mechanic as well, particularly the Birthday Party segment. The horror was a little more mixed for me. There were plenty of tense and skin-crawling moments throughout the game, but I wasn't a fan of the heavier emphasis on visceral gross-out scares. Granted, there's still plenty of spooky moments for people who like the more Fatal-Frame style ambience. As far as tense moments go, I still think the Verdugo scene from RE4 reigns supreme, but there are some pretty solid onese here for sure.
Anyways, a bit of a long review, I apologize. Definitely one of the best horror games in years, and one that I could actually class as a game. Whole heartedly recommend if you like horror or exploring detailed and spooky environments! Recommend less so if you only really cared for the amazing cast, lovable cheese factor, and warm heart of the earlier games.

You will learn how to avoid, or deal with, loss.  You will make choices, knowing that there is no "best choice."
Loss: Yes, random rolls can pile up, forcing you to lose a treasured unit.  You are fighting with other mercenaries over the "City of the Damned", people will die.  You might actually care for them.  It will hurt.  You may quit.  Or you may find the young replacement and swear at how wortheless they are compared to the veteran that they replaced.  It feels like a warzone, and that's what I wanted.  Learn to dodge.
Choices: The optional objectives are woth more than the primary.  The primary is, usually, easy.  Beat the not so smart AI.  When just starting, I did lose a few primary objectives.  You learn to stick together, and if you don't start together, get together ASAP!  Then you start winning primary objectives.
You start looking at those optional objectives.  And realizing that if you want to accomplish them, you might have to break out of your comfortable, stick together, everybody comes home safely routine.  Maybe you start taking risks.  And you like the rewards.  Then somebody gets caught alone against a swarm, or maybe just a single impressive unit.  And it hurts.  And you wonder if those rewards were worth it.
Stick through it, learn.  And you can find yourself making most of the optional objectives and making it home in one piece.  And sometimes you look at the map/setup and realize it's the day to just hunker down.
Those two things are why I love Mordheim.
It does have some negatives. Managing inventory during a mission could use the ability to drop items. I get annoyed when the enemy routs immediately after I take down the one guy I needed to take down, only to not get the chance to grab his token before the rout ends the mission.  Deployment could be made more user friendly (selecting deployment from the map instead of cycling). The game has gotten a LOT better since it first came to Early Access, and I hope they continue working on some of those.  But the good things more than make it worth dealing with the few annoyances in the game, in my opinion.
I hope they continue, either through DLC or just updating the game itself, to develop more warbands, more equipment, more customization of models and more mission types (story or procedural).  But I love the game as it is today.  I would just love to have more too :).

It's not often someone walks away from a game in seething frustration to revisit it months later and fall in love with it for some of the same reasons they walked away from it in the first place. I think this game gave me Stockholm Syndrome.
Mordheim is a simple but punishing tactical strategy game in which you control a small band of rats, a small band of lunatics, a small band of sexist male humans, or a small band of sexist female humans (The 4 base factions) and pit them against other small bands of random types in a winner-take-all quest to gather as many glowing green rocks as you can, or else your sponsoring organization (Doritos?) defaults on your Sally Mae college loan and then it's game over for you.
But before you can enter the city with all those high hopes ready to be dashed to bits, you get to design your own band! The character models all look great, and there are small amounts of custom textures you can apply to give all your goons a personal touch. You also have the option to give them backstories, probably so it's all the more sorrowful when they see their ultimate end. The leader of my mercenary band, Herbert Halfscrotum, is still alive and kicking.
Mordheim promises permanent deaths and injuries for your band, and has a million ways to ruin your expedition. Spells can fail, prayers can backfire, attacks can go horribly wrong, traps are everywhere, random neutral demons can hound your entire band into an early grave... even the rocks you are there to gather can drown you in negative effects. This is a great game for pessimists, because everything will go wrong and it pays to have contingencies.
Gameplay is rough and slightly unbalanced in your enemy's favor. I don't think the RNG is rigged, but the AI warbands DO get a health and damage boost over yours, even on the lowest difficulties. I think this is to compensate for their blatant stupidity. Regardless, they aren't pushovers, and I've found the best tactic around is to let them split up like fools, let them charge you one at a time, and gangbust them Clockwork Orange-style. It may sound dirty, but more often than not, missions can feel like an uphill battle with the AI having an overt handicap as well as almost always having a higher power rating than you. I'd give that last comment a definite, but I actually ran into a band with 1 less point than me... but it was in a not-for-keeps exhibition. Go figure.
There is a good game behind all this polarization, even if some people can't find the fun in something they can't consistently steamroll. If you were like me and fled in frustration over a lack of noob-friendliness, constantly cursing the RNG for why your heavily-armored tin can couldn't make that climb check and sustained permanent brain damage, consider swallowing your pride and giving it another go. You already bought it, after all. Just grab a few beers (or kale smoothies, or whatever), make a band you really believe in (All hail Herbert Halfscrotum!), and wade back into it. If you haven't purchased it yet, consider giving it a shot... even if you wait for a sale.

Double Dragon: Neon is an odd case. This isn't really like the arcade games, it's more of an action-rpg with beatemup elements. Yeah I know, it's confusing isn't it? Just hear(read) me out.  Technos Japan, the original developer of Double Dragon, also created the Kunio-Kun franchise. Remember NES classics like Super Dodgeball and River City Ransom? That's Kunio-Kun. Neon is a combination of RCR and DD. You collect or purchase and upgrade mix-tapes to improve your stats as well as use special abilities. This game is made up of 10 missions, all of them linear, with a structure that mostly adheres to the arcade games.
Now if you just want a straight-up Double Dragon beatemup without all of that RPG nonsense, I'd suggest Double Dragon Advance (GBA). It is in my opinion the best entry in the classic series. In any case, we're strictly talking about Neon for the rest of this review.
Some days it just doesn't pay to hang out in front of your boyfriend's garage, as Marian gets kidnapped AGAIN. This time around the villain is a lovely chap by the name of Skullmageddon. A silly name deserves a silly character, and he's all that and more. This is the goofiest and most 80s entry in the series. Along with a ton of familiar names (with not so familiar faces), there are a handful of new enemies and bosses to contend with. Aesthetically this game is very well-done, with a truly excellent soundtrack that elevates it to another level.
Since these days it apparently isn't enough to make a game about beating hundreds of people up, Neon features RPG elements. Trying to ignore them in search of a "legitimate" challenge will just frustrate and anger you. There are 20 mix-tapes, 10 are special moves, 10 function as stat-boosting equipment. You can switch mix-tapes at any moment in the game. It's strategic in a sense. You can switch to a magic-boosting tape and fling a few fireballs, then switch to your absorb tape to replenish some health. You can even micro-manage like you're playing a JRPG with an ATB (active-time-beatemup) system.
The actual fighting is comparable to the previous games, although slightly stiffer. Some moves have been changed around or removed, but classics such as the flying knee and spin-kick are always handy. The most important move is the duck. When you duck an enemy's attack at the right moment, you get the glow and do 4x damage for a few seconds. Also while ducking you can do an evasive roll. This is an extremely useful move to master. Overall the fighting is standard, but it's enjoyable. It could be more satisfying I suppose, but juggling an enemy never gets old.
As you'd expect from a Double Dragon game, Billy and Jimmy can team up some brotastic bro-op fun. Just don't expect much if you attempt to play online. I've tried hosting a few times and the results were pitiful. Players would jump on, play for a minute or two, and then just leave. I'm not sure what the deal is here. I've read that the online doesn't function properly, or it has issues with certain machines, or it only works when it's raining in Georgia. Whatever the case, it's a darn shame that more people can't enjoy this game online, it's way more fun with a friend. There's always local-play at least.
There are other issues with the PC port, such as memory leakage, crashes, and so on. I didn't really experience anything firsthand, so I guess I lucked out. While there was a patch early last year, it apparently didn't go far enough in fixing the game. Abstraction Games, the team responsible for the Neon port, had ONE TESTER working on it.
What the Butt?
ONE TESTER!
I couldn't believe it. Let's figure this out.
While the PC can be considered an easy platform to develop for, you have to account for a multitude of variables. How do you expect to make a game that's compatible with every PC, when it was only tested with one?
Another problem with having ONE TESTER is that Double Dragon is an online co-operative game. You can't possibly expect ONE person to test a TWO player game...can you?
At the very least a beta-test should have been done. It's not like volunteers are that hard to come by. Hell, it seems like these days we're all beta-testers (especially whenever a new Assassin's Creed is released). It'd be nice to beta-test a game for free instead of paying for it. Wow...ONE TESTER...I just can't get over that.
All in all Double Dragon Neon is a good game. Its quasi-beatemup/RPG elements give it it a rather unique spin, and I can't recommend the soundtrack enough. Just do some research, hold your breath, and hope for the best if you plan on getting this port. It just might crash and burn on you.

From developer Ebullience Games and publisher Top Hat Studios Inc. comes a slice of life, romantic visual novel.
Valerie is a normal college student with the ability to see people’s red strings – that connect them to their soul mate. Playing as Valerie, you take her through two different stories of romance, with four different endings. Take her on an adventure to find her soulmate, or to create her own fate in this visual novel.
I wasn’t expecting too much of this, as red strings seem to be a very big genre. They’re not normally done really well, so I didn’t think that anything like this could be any decent, and I only downloaded it to grab the four achievements and up my Steam achievement number and my TSA score.
What I didn’t expect, was to actually really, really enjoy this story line. I thought it was really quite sweet and almost innocent in a way. Aaron and Valerie’s line was the first I focused on, and it was sweet, but I confess, I liked Luke and Valerie’s lines much better. The story line was a really well done one, and I think that it was made brilliantly. The visuals are wonderful to look at, and it’s wonderful to play.
I would definitely recommend this one to people who like visual novels! Also to achievement hunters. This only took me under an hour to complete all the achievements. Penguins Arena Sedna's World is an extremely barebones king of the hill shooter. You play as a penguin throwing snowballs and other, slightly different colored penguins trying to push them off an iceberg and into the shark infested waters below. The maps are fairly varied with some being big arenas with lots of trees covering the edges making them long and sometimes frustrating to end and others being so tiny that a single explosion will throw half the players into the murky depths. Some of the maps even have collapsing glaciers that makes the play area smaller the longer the game drags on.
There is no health for the Penguins your only weapons are the slow firing snowball and your rather weak punch. Your 3rd weapon, which is both the best and the most risky, is yourself. By running and jumping you can pick up speed and by hitting other penguins transferring that speed into them sending them flying with incredible force. Of course, if you miss or get hit when moving that fast you'll often end up killing yourself. You can also pick up various power-ups on the map ranging for a brief invulnerability to snowballs to a small supply of rapid fire fish or an exploding fish that functions much as a grenade.
Graphically and musically the game is nothing impressive and there is no storyline, no voice-acting or really anything other than your basic deathmatch. The few different modes available only really allow you to change the number of teams in the match and whether or not your additional lives should run around as bots, fighting until you die and take them over, or simply be additional respawns that can't get themselves killed.
Although Penguins Arena is a fun little multi-player game it suffers from a number of rather major faults. The lack of any additional modes means that it gets repetitive within a couple of games and the lack of anyone else playing it online means it's only really fun when you can manage to gather a bunch of friends to play with, the bots available in single-player are simply not up to par.
All in all, not a game I'd recommend you get unless you plan to get it with a couple of friends so you have someone to play with and even then I doubt you will get through many matches before the repetitive nature of the game forces you to stop and go find a better alternative.

It's been a while since my first review of this game, so I felt it would be time to give out a more proper one. It's a good game, but not without several problems.
Empire: Total War, set in the 18th century, is a game I reccomend to the player who likes the idea of massive, 18th century-style land and naval battles. The game also has a very large campaign map, including India, Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, and the Americas. There's also a lot of colonialism involved as well, so if you like all of these things I mentioned, you'll probably like this game.
However, don't expect multiplayer to be a fun experience. It's still active, but there aren't many people playing. There's a good number of players here that will mistakenly or purposefully break the rules set by players hosting their games. Even hosts will break their own rules.
You also need to consider the fact that there are many players on here that have adopted the use of specific units that are simply OP, which therefore ruins the historical atmosphere of this game. Historically, most 18th century infantry were armed with highly innacurate guns, so they gathered in very large formations and fired at each other. They were called line infantry. This type of warfare was in no way meant to prolong the life of an individual soldier at all. The entire point of this type of fighting between infantry units was to use overwhelming force and numbers of troops and firepower to overcome the other side, which meant that line infantry would have to have some serious discipline and toughness. You'd rarely ever take cover, and if you were in the front lines, your slim chances of surviving the battle depended on how fast you could reload your gun and if you could make your shot count before the other side did the same thing you were meant to do.
Now, you'd think line infantry would be the staple unit on this game, and therefore they'd be pretty effective. However, their historical use as the essential staple unit for 18th century armies can easily be rendered useless on this game with just three types of units: Riflemen, skirmishers, and light dragoons.
The sad fact is that on multiplayer, the only three types of effective ground units that have any form of effectiveness on this game are the three units I stated above, aside from artillery. True, line infantry still have their uses, but not by much You see, the problem here is that skirmishers and riflemen have guns that can shoot farther than the muskets used by your line infantry, and they are unfairly accurate, meaning that your line infantry will be dropping like flies just trying to close the distance to take on the skirmishers and riflemen. They also reload their weapons incredibly fast. This is in no way historically accurate, because the guns used by lighter infantry forces at the time, no matter how far they shot, were still incredibly accurate and would have taken a long time to reload. Not only that, but we're talking about guns that weren't easy to aim with.
I could understand how lightly armed riflemen and skirmishers could give line infantry some serious trouble in, say, a bunch of forests, but they are so overpowered on this game that they can easily take out line infantry on an open battlefield.
Then there are light dragoons...
Light dragoons are soldiers riding on horseback, equipped with modified muskets that have shorter barrels. Therefore, they'd be less accurate, right? In real life, yes, but in this game? Wrong. Would it be easy reloading these guns on horseback? No, because muskets need to have the projectiles loaded with ram rods, primed, blah blah blah, shoot, repeat. It's difficult enough to do all of this while standing on your own two feet, but on horseback? That's bound to take longer.
Light dragoons can be incredibly dangerous to line infantry due to their superior speed, and because this game has overpowered them, every single soldier in a unit of light dragoons fires his gun, even the ones in the back. None of the troops in the front ranks of the dragoons die, and for some strange reason, a good number of the shots fired hit their mark. Sometimes, This means that you'll be having large numbers of line infantry dying all at once, which can cause a morale shock.
So unless you make rules against the use of light dragoons and skirmishers on the games you host in multiplayer, you'll be seeing these units being used on a constant basis, throwing all of the great historical accuracies of 18th century warfare out the window.
Now that's been explained, I should tell you about a few problems with other aspects of this game:
1) Despite the fact that Empire has a very large campaign map, you will be disappointed to find that almost every single battle map looks the same. Same texture, same everything. Yes, some buildings will look different depending on what part of the world you're in on the campaign, but you will quickly realise how bland the atmosphere of the maps are when you fight battles. Building detail in towns is also severly lacking.
2) The AI is incredibly dumb at times, so dumb that the developers decided to buff up the stats of the AI's units to compensate for their stupidity in the higher difficulty levels.
3) Individual troops in your army lack spatial awareness when they enter buildings or defend/attack fort walls in a siege battle. It's a horrid sight to see at times. Troops just move through each other in a frantic motion. Path finding on walls is also terrible.
4) Some sound effects for this game are awful, especially for muskets. For example, when a unit of line infantry fire a volley at the enemy, you only hear a 'poof' sound. These are primitive gunpowder weapons. They should be noisy and make a loud 'bang' when fired. Instead, the muskets used by your line infantry sound like fake guns used for movies in Hollywood.
5) You won't hear any general's speech before battle like you used to in Rome I and Medieval II.
6) There isn't much voice acting. You won't get to hear any voice acting at all when you initiate diplomacy, and the few bits of voice acting that you do here on this game tends to be subpar.
7) Melee combat between infantry units looks decent, but not amazing. The combat animations are too drawn out and look more rehearsed than realistic. Some of the combat animations are so terrible drawn out that everything looks unrealistic.
8) Because of the way the death animations work on this game, cavalry takes forever to take out a routing unit. Many times, an unnecessarily long combat animation has to be so terribly drawn out that it takes longer than needed for the cavalry to take out the routers. It'd be more convenient if the cavalry just swing their swords at boom, the routing units die faster.
9) Artillery units can be glitchy, even in multiplayer. Sometimes, they won't fire their guns no matter how many times you order them to.
10) On the campaign map, the AI controlling Britain, the United Provinces, and France tend to ignore India for some reason, so almost every single time you play this campaign, the Marathas end up becoming an OP faction.
11) There are no marching tunes with fifes and drums on the battlefield for any of the factions. This feature should have been implemented by the developers. I can understand that some players might find them distracting, but an option could be made to just turn off those marching tunes in the game.
12) Naval battles can sometimes be a little glitchy. Ships will sometimes move unnecessarily slow even when you order them to move faster.
This game can still be enjoyed despite all of these problems I mentioned. However, it will never be as great as it could have been. There are, however, a few mods for this game that you can use to make this game more enjoyable. Keep in mind that the mods are, unfortunately, not supported for Steam as there is no workshop.

I feel like this game should have some sort of trigger warning; but at the same time, the trigger warning would spoil the story. That said; it was a very interesting game. The developers did a good job creating a game that did feel like you were controlling a toddler (There are moments when you're running and the baby can trip and tropple to the floor). The themes and how the game sets things up is also very interesting.
Graphically; the game is par-core. Generally very good texturing; you do have to spend a lot of time up close and personal with them after all. Very creepy at times. ((Especially the long trails of dark-ooze in some levels). Sound design is also -very- good. The little disturbing noises really add to the atmosphere and had me freezing in spots, listening and looking about for a monster.
All in all, I definately would suggest this game: It's not very long and the story is interesting. Perhaps not quite as scary as some games out there; but definately nerve wrecking. 8.4/10.

A lot of anti-fun in this game.
First, there is a limited number of turns to complete each scenario. This is your main enemy, not the monsters or the traps. And the only way to defeat it is to get lucky. Because if you're not, nothing is going to save you, and your 20-minute session is wasted (not entirely, but see below).
Second, after both defeat and victory, you must decide which cards to keep, and which to discard. This is both boring (requiring quit a lot of inventory management across all participating characters) and painful, especially after a victory. "Here, " says the game "take some cards as a reward! And now decide which one you will keep, because you have no more free space in your stash. Oh, and cards picked up during the scenario also compete for that precious free space. Nice evening to you!"
I can't recommend this game. I found myself wanting to avoid playing it, if only to evade endless card management and painful, yet almost meaningless decisions about which cards to keep, and which to drop. If you want a single-player CCG, get System Crash instead, or Card Hunter. This one sucks.

I had been following the development of this since witnessing it's announcement right before GenCon 2016. As a huge fan of the tabletop game (I own all the base sets and all the ADs for them except Mummy's Mask) I couldn't wait to get this.
I have to admit I still like playing the tabletop version more, but the frustrating thing about the tabletop version is when you just want to play solo there's a huge investment in set-up time. Especially if you're currently in the middle of a campaign with other people. You have to keep track of everything so you can put the box/decks back in the correct configuration as the state of the box is part of the game.
Enter this. I bought every version of this game on all my devices as soon as it was available. I was happy enough playing it on an Android emulator on PC, but I was already yearning for a native PC version. It's here and it's great!
If you've played the Pathfinder ACG games before, not sure why you're reading. There's definitely differences here and there, it's not a 100% true to rules conversion, but it's so close it doesn't matter. If you don't like the little additions like extra cards, runes, etc.. you can largely ignore them and play close to the tabletop rules. Not having to set-up, tear down, look up rules, forget to do things, etc.. is worth any small difference.
If you have not played the tabletop version at all, think of this game as an RPG in card form. Your hand basically represents your weapons, armor, items, etc.. as well as your hit points. There is a blessings deck that represents a "timer". What you do (mostly, there are twists and turns), is take a party of adventures (decks) of different classes and powers and rurn through scenarios trying to defeat a Villian and their henchmen by cornering them and defeating them. You do this by closing location decks. Each location has 10 cards you have to "explore". They could either be "boons" (items, weapons, blessings, spells, allies, etc..) or "banes" (monsters, traps, henchmen+villians, etc,,). As you go through scenarios defeating villains and solving scenarios your characters grows by gaining new powers, upgrading existing powers, increasing their deck (health) or hand size, etc.. Kind of just like leveling up a char in an RPG. While exploring you're turning a blessing from the blessing's deck every character's turn. There's 30.. so you need to defeat the villian in typically 30 turns or you fail and have to retry the scenario.
There's so many small nuances in each character, in the items, locations etc, that there's always something new to discover. Some scenarios even change things up where maybe you're trying to recruit allies before they all get eaten, or maybe there's two villians instead of one. I don't want to spoil anything so I'll stop there. But mostly it's about cornering a Villian and defeating it.
Each character has their own strengths and weaknesses in their attributes (STR,DEX, etc..) and powers (maybe the char gets an extra die when they are fighting alone at a location, or maybe they can add dice for combat. You'll most likely need a diverse party because there will be certain checks (maybe to close a location) that some characters will have an extremely hard time achieving. This game is all about using the correct characters/items/combo to increase your odds of succeeding at a check whether it be combat or not. And just like an RPG, there's a huge amount of luck involved due to the dice rolling aspect. I've seen a lot of people complain about RNG blah, i always fail blah. No, you just didn't strategize to maximize your chances or use the correct char. Sure.. you can get into a rut of bad bad rolls, also good rolls. But even 50-50 odds have a chance of not going your way for a long streak. It happens.
The game is extremely nuanced and it's a ton of fun. If it sounds like your cup of tea get it. Maybe watch a youtube playthrough or two to see an experienced player play it.

After seeing this post on the Absolver subreddit, it came to me that Absolver is indeed, in a number of ways, the offspring of For Honor and Dark Souls.
Yes, I hate comparing it to Dark Souls like far too many game journalists do nowadays, but Absolver genuinely does contain familiar elements from the series. Cairns are the equivalent of bonfires, protecting you from any enemies harming you as well as respawning you, but while you can level up at them you can in fact do that at any point of the game..... just don't do it in combat, I forgot and learned the hard way.
Don't worry, the whole review is not all about Dark Souls references, but when it reminds me so much of the series, I had to note these down and the rest of this section will tick off the rest of the necessary Dark Souls mentions. The layout of the world is somewhat akin to it, as well as how you have to kill certain bosses to progress to another area, and how areas are interconnected, allowing you to swiftly move from one to another. The story is also laid out in a similar way, with the occasional cutscene to provide some context, as well as how equipment works, heavy armour slowing you down but providing superior defence and vice versa.
Okay thats enough Dark Souls references, I don't wish to be seen as one of those "The Dark Souls of..." journalists. In fact, combat wise, its a blend of the aforementioned series and the recent For Honor, which had potential and a great combat system but was poorly handled. Absolver takes elements of its combat and makes it work, but alas there is no gore here, so don't go expecting decapitations.
Your sole goal in Absolver is to defeat the Marked Ones so that you can become an Absolver. I went in expecting a good number of bosses to fight and to spend a decent amount of time in this. Four hours is all it took for me, 10 bosses and that was it, and for the most part that time was spent grinding or luring enemies out one at a time so I could actually have a fair fight.
The bosses have minions, a pet peeve of mine that I have mentioned time and again, if a boss is weaker than the player character, I can understand minions, but if they're just as strong or stronger then cut it out with the minions, it takes what should be a fun and challenging duel and just turns it into a slog of killing several enemies one at a time. The second to last boss fight was an exception though, it was two enemies I had to fight but it still felt fair, as I had plenty of room to maneuver around and set up punishing combos. But oh man, the final boss fight is easily my favourite, two humans of equal power going toe to toe, fighting to the point of exhaustion, your reward being that you become a fellow Absolver.
To learn new moves, you have to track down an enemy with the moves you want and then just block while they hit you until you learn it, and then you have to kill them. Its a slow process and I got along just fine with the starting moves of my chosen school. Apparently the class I chose could duck and leap around during combat but I had no idea how to do it so stuck to dodging. Most of the attacks looked the same to me anyway, although to be honest I never really payed attention to enemy fighting styles, except for Jinn Mesca. Jinn's fighting style stood out to me because it was a drunken fighting style, like Bo Rai Cho's from the Mortal Kombat series and Jackie Chan in his Drunken Master films. Its definitely a style that I will go back and learn at some point.
Speaking of Mortal Kombat, the idea of running around beating people up and progressing the story was vaguely reminiscent of Mortal Kombat Deception.
Back to the game's combat, you can utilise swords and a few other melee weapons too. Swords can be found spread throughout the world and give an edge (pun possibly intended) in combat, but sadly they break rather fast, although you can acquire a permanent sword from the last boss. You can even set up a sword deck, unfortunately it is agonisingly slow and frustrating building a proper one. This is because you have to grab a sword, throw it at the feet of an enemy and hope that they decide to pick it up and use the move you want enough for you to learn it before the damn thing breaks.
You also have shards that regenerate as you deal or block damage, these can be used to activate abilities like regenerating health for a short time or a shockwave to knock enemies back for some breathing room.
Thankfully, the deck building system is incredibly simple to use and can be completely customised to suit your playstyle, assuming you have the moves unlocked.
Multiplayer is interesting, you don't summon other players for help or PvP, you see them running around the same world as you, ready to fight or help you at any notice. You can always go offline if needed though, this is best if you are aiming to learn new moves and don't want someone coming along and killing your enemy, in an honorable but misguided attempt to help you.
Most of the players I met during my time were incredibly helpful, showing me items I missed or assisting with difficult fights. One group attacked me while I was afk but revived me instantly, I still have no idea why they did it but not long after I met them again and they saluted, I assume as a means of apology. There's no text to talk with others in Absolver, the only way to communicate is via emotes.
I have to point out a few issues that really irritated me over the course of the game. The camera is just awful at times. I am not a fan of how it auto locks on to an enemy when you engage combat and I detest how clumsy and slothful it is when trying to switch between enemies when fighting multiple opponents. A good portion of my deaths occurred as a result of this and the camera getting stuck on a wall, obscuring my vision.
A few more things to point out: the Marked Ones fully regenerate if you leave their zone, but you don't which is infuriating, and bosses seem to respawn every so often so that if you get there just as one is beat then you need to wait till they respawn.
I can definitely see myself sinking more time into this game and building a truly fearsome deck to crush other players with. But Absolver definitely needs some tweaks to it to be even better than it already is, thankfully the community is off to a strong and helpful start.

Double Dragons Neon is an interesting adaptation of the classic beat'em up.  I call the game an adaptation and not a remake as it plays differently from not only the classic Double Dragons but other beat'em ups also. In this game, you have to collect tapes that can either improve your stats or give you special moves, the more tapes you collect the more powerful you can become.  Several times however, I have had to grind some levels over and over just to get new tapes in order to defeat the final boss. I guess this is the developers way to lenghten the game but for me, it took me out the experience.  Another issue I had is the awkward roll/dodge/run commands.  Despite these issues, the game does provide a good retro/nostalgia experience if you are someone like me who grew up in the arcades around the 80s/90s with a fun soundtrack and interesting visuals.

Is a great turn based game that provides plenty of challenge for those who are used to strategy games. The injury system is good and challenges one to have to make tough choices if one is left with a asset thats injured beyond usefullness. Haven't tried much of the multiplayer out yet but if its anything like the single player campaign its bound to be tough and fun. One thing I wish they added was an option for a local match against friends like one is playing the table top game at home they may still add the option later which would be fun and make the overall replay value worthwhile. I do recommend this game if your looking for a good turn based tactical game that gives one plenty of options to customize ones warband and take it online against others. I think there is room for more warbands to be added in the future. Played this game a lot while it was in development was impressed with its improvements showing the development team knows and cares about what they are doing. Building up a warband expect to have losses even if you win which makes the game fair in my view. The AI also looks to pick off your most vulnerable you just have to adapt and go after them the same way. Give this game a chance and you most likely will like it for one reason or another think advanced battle chess where it gets progressively tougher every match.

This game is just like the Kingdom: Classic with the grow and survive basis. The difference? There is quite a rush to end. Instead of growing larger and surviving on one island, you have to travel to another island to start over again, which in turn make the difficulty harder. You might leave the first island in 10 turns then leave the second in 20 turns. The reason why to leave? From what I have experienced, you don't get stone buildings or walls so it forces you to go to the next island before defences start falling and you get overrun. This is the type of game that is great for those who like to start over and make everything progresively harder as you restart to make it a challenge.
Personally, I don't like that kind of gameplay. I loved the classic because it makes you build larger and larger while defending while staying in one place and because I didn't feel as rushed, I felt more like I was being pressured to make better decisions with my resources. Why did I give it a positive review then? Because I still enjoyed the game. Yes I got a refund, but just because it isn't my cup of tea doesn't mean I didn't have fun while playing it. I'm pretty sure others will agree with me that while you may be rushed in this game, you will still at least have some form of fun.
As I said, it was still a fantastic game, just like the Classic, but if you do not like being rushed, then this might not be your kind of game. Of course you can find that out for yourself and either keep or refund.

I really like this game. It looks and sounds good, the mechanics are interesting and character progression is well designed. For the most part, it's a fun strategy game with heavily random elements. There's nothing quite as frustrating as failing on a check which you had a 98% chance to succeed, but on the other hand, there's nothing quite as satisfying as finally cornering the villain on the very last turn before the end of the game, throwing everything you have at it, and succeeding on a 50% roll to defeat it. That element of luck means you won't beat every adventure on the first try, but because the game lets you keep any cards you get even in failed attempts, you'll likely be stronger the next time around. You need a certain amount of patience to enjoy it, just like any strategy game, I suppose.
The only reason I'm not recommending it is because it is
buggy. The game itself runs fine on my computer, but so many things inside it don't work as they're supposed to. I felt like I encountered a new bug in every hour of gameplay. Here are a few of them: playing and cancelling a card does not cancel its effects; a location can't be closed when it's supposed to be; scenario-specific rules don't trigger; a card can be played but it does nothing; playing a card soft-locks the game; and some dice rolls have to be repeated for no apparent reason. To give you an idea of just how bad the problem is, there are close to 3000 (three thousand) bug reports on the official forum alone, and the game has only existed for a year and a half. Some 50 of those threads have been active in the past
, and that's only the bugs that people are actually bothering to report on the official forums - there are more to be found in the discussions here on Steam, and many go unreported, I'm sure. It seems like every patch fixes old bugs and introduces new ones. The game was in closed beta for the first year, and in my opinion, it should still be there.
If you're interested in this game, my advice would be to save your money and come back in a year or six months to see if the recent reviews have picked up, because right now it's a seriously flawed game. Not recommended.

***Another Note: I live in North America. If you live elsewhere, there may not be a server that ensures you have a decent connection. Considering that this game requires reading other players animations and split second desicion making, you may want to wait to buy this until you are sure there is decent server access for your area***
As a single player/co-op campaign game, this game is like a condensed souls game. You walk around gorgeous, delicatley designed worlds filled with enemies until you die and respawn or eventually kill everything that needs to be killed. Overall, as a $30 dollar product, I think this experience is worth it. You add PVP with a ton of depth and customization (both style and play style customization), this would become a killer product. At the moment, the servers are in a state where when I tried I was not able to get into PVP matches, and before I start to heap praise on this game, let me be clear that I think the server issues really SUCK. The Absolver team and Devolver will need to act fast to fix this or else this game will be dropped like For Honor (which I loved, but eventually stopped playing because problems with the game were not being fixed).
But, I find this game similar to DOOM 2016 in that the campaign makes this worth the price point alone. It is stellar, and here is why:
Let's start with the visual design... It's increadible. It's a really good mix of clean textures and shapes with just enough detail to make the individual items in the game feel unique and the environments not just all blend together. When you add to the mix really well executed animations (and lots of different animations), this game ends up being one of the coolest looking games ever. The beautiful environments mixed with the stellar animations make the fighting look so cinematic, but also really easy to follow for the player. It is impressive that the game manages to make fights look so good yet also feel really good.
To say more about the feel of this game, I honestly believe this is where it differs from the souls games the most and really becomes it's own thing. It feels like a fighting game (which is probably why I suck at it) rather than like a souls game. This game is about stringing together combos and building the perfect combo set (more on that later) rather than learning how to maximize the same three hit pattern for every enemy over and over again. The thing that makes this game more about stringing together combos is that on the fly you can switch your stance in game which then allows you to access a different set of moves that you can hand select. The set of moves you select is called a "deck" in game and can be changed through meditation (a menu option). The "deck" building combo system allows you to really change up the way your character feels in a fight, akin to changing what weapon you use in a souls game but with more chances to make subtle change ups rather than sweeping changes. But I am not really a fighting game guy, so I don't really think I can speak knowlegably about the depth of the system other than that I feel like it offers many possibilities for fighting styles and that it is very satisfying to use and edit. Another reviewer can probably do this more justice.
Finally, I just want to talk about some of the social aspects of the game. What I mean by this is that players will randomly enter your game often and in large numbers. It sounds familiar to the invasion system in souls, and it can be if a player enters your area looking for a fight. But the cool thing is that other players who enter the game are not automatically your enemies, or friends. It almost feels like Day-Z in that there is an inherit tension to finding a real person in game that is as likely to befriend you as they are to try and murder you, or maybe completely ignore you. You have the option to turn all of this off, but I really think it adds a lot to the game.
Also, you have the option to join friends games and play this completely co-op. I ended up playing the campaign the entire way through with my brother. I would say playing this game with a friend is a really satisfying way to spend a saturday (5-7 hours of a Saturday depending on how much you like to explore). This of course relies on having stable access to the servers which I luckily did.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game, which is why I decided that I would recommend it. Of course, I am biased in that this game largely worked for me, but it does not for many others. Hopefully this recommendation will someday be one with less caviates. But for now I only recommend this as a game that you should buy with a reminder that if it does not work for you... steams refund policy is pretty good and maybe come back for it when the server issues are hopefully fixed.

I've played close to 45 hours of Absolver at this time, and I can say this game is very solid and a lot of fun. This is also coming from someone who had to deal with no servers for the first few days of release. (I'm Australian). Despite this Absolver still managed to hold my attention for those first few days.
Pros -
- Combat is fun, and the deck building allows for a lot of customization, meaning people can have their own unique fighting styles.
- The game has a very high skill ceiling.
- The campaign, while short is servicable, and the different zones you travel through allow for enough variety for it to not get stale.
- The different fighting styles in the game (Forsaken, Stagger, Kahlt and Windfall) also throw some more complexity into the combat of the game, meaning not everyone will have the same abilities.
- The shard abilties while sometimes cheap, are useful and have their own place in combat.
Cons -
- The servers are very unreliable, while they have been getting better since launch it is still a glaring problem in the game. This also means you will ocasionally get stuck on loading screens, meaning you have to Alt + Tab and task manager out of the game.
- It is quite buggy, mostly due to the servers, but none the less i still encounter a few bugs while playing offline.
- At the moment in the game there isn't a whole lot of variety in modes, there is Campaign and 1v1. That is it. However the devs have planned to release more modes further down the track.
TLDR; Absolver is a very fun game with fluid and in-depth fighting mechanics, however the game gets weighed down by server issues and lack of content.

I wanted to love this game and for the majority of the game I did. It has a lot of the right elements, done the right way, which result in a great racing experience, very playable.
Then you get to the difficult end of the spectrum.
In the dictionary, under the term "nerfed" should be a picture of this game. Regardless of whether you manage to get the top cars, the level of AI, physics and performance changes that occur during the highest races drops the playability level down to all but unplayable. If you have learned the way to properly play and control your car through the various races and levels to get to the end races, you understand the elements around you and the other cars, how they behave. Unfortunately most of that information will do you no good, as the laws of physics suddenly stop applying.
Enemy cars will go from wrecking as you pass them to rocketing past you at 200 mph+. Pieces of paper in the road transform into massive obstacles able to flip your car high into the air on impact. Your car begins to perform like a ford pinto missing a few cylinders: One moment, it handles fine, the next it has no throttle response, no turning control or no brakes, or slides radically sideways if you so much as look as the hand brake button. Step on the gas pedal....it might respond, it might not. If you are really lucky, the wind from a passing car will make yours veer into that oncoming building corner or tree, stopping you instantly.
Don't worry, however, as things will revert just as quickly back to how you have come to understand them, once 3 or 4 of the opponent AI cars have passed you by, leaving you wondering just what the heck happened. You will have time to think about it after you lose the race again.
In playing this game, or any game, it is understandable that things get progressively harder. However, the "playability" of this game goes way down when the changes that make it harder are such that they are so readily apparent and unfair. You end up thinking "whoa, what the heck just happened?" a lot. Things happen which are beyond explanation and which are beyond you have any effect on whatsoever. There is no counter move you can do, no way to affect change in the situation at all. The outcome just changes, and the only thing you can do is keep the gas pedal down and watch the other cars pass you by.
The advantages given to the environment and AI cars in this make it a very different game at the end. I loved it up to that point, but there is no way to play against what you know about the game being useless to you when you are playing it. How do you race if gravity or the laws of matter change instantly for a few moments here and there, but never in your favor? There is no way to fight that. If you win, it will most likely be because of some freak bit of luck.
I don't expect it to be easy, but making it seem impossible by yanking victory from your grasp unfairly, and very visibly so, earns it a bad review. NERFED HARD, YO.

This is such an amazing game! In my opinion, it's underrated and not as popular as it should be. The game is fun, action-packed, and so addictive! It's is similar to FlatOut 2, however, this game has more game modes and updated graphics comparing to FlatOut 2. And surprisingly enough, the online servers in the game are still running in Ultimate Carnage! The thing is that you will need to download the Games for Windows Live client (remember GFWL back in the days?) because the online servers are run by it. All you need is a Microsoft account, and you can play online. There are a few people playing the game, but I've never come across a time where there was no one playing at all, so there's always a lobby to join. Any who, the game is tremendously fun! It's like Burnout, but different in a few aspects (more realistic, but it still maintains the massive mayhem that it contains) It's an action racing game, and the crashes and wrecks are what the game are great at delivering. There is also stunt mode, which is familiar to FlatOut fans as this mode has been around since the first instalment in the FlatOut series. You are in a huge and vivid stadium, and you are to send your driver flying through the stadium and hit bowling pins, dunk slam them into basketball baskets, hit them with a gigantic baseball bat, and so much more! The stunts are so fun and addictive, and absolutely hilarious because the way the characters move like ragdolls and fly around are funny! There is also a derby game mode, where the cars are parked on the edge of the arena, and they are going to drive and wreck each other, which is fun and addictive too. If you are a multiplayer type of person, then I'd still recommend this game to you, because it's so awesome when it comes to multiplayer (servers are still online). You can do demolition derbies, races, and even stunt modes in online. And the best part is doing stunt modes with other people, as you can see each other flying like ragdolls XD
The areas and tracks are also nice and interesting. You can drive on off-road tracks, or race on oval tracks... or even drive through trolleys in malls! The tracks are fun and entertaining!
If there was a bad thing about this game... it would be that the cars are too sensitive and slippery comparing to other racing games. They can be brought to a halt by simply hitting traffic cones and chairs.
But any who, it doesn't bother me at all, as there are simply too many pros. Brilliant game, brilliant franchise! I'm excited for their next game: FlatOut 4!!! :D :D :D

Pajama Sam: No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside is a point and click adventure game for kids with a few educational aspects thrown in. The plot is based on a comic that the main character, Pajama Sam, reads. He is on a mission to venture into his closet and defeat darkness so he won't have to be afraid of the dark anymore. You mainly click around to go to different screens and explore. You can talk to other characters, pick up items, and click on various parts of the environments as well for reactions or clues. And key locations of items are changed between playthroughs, giving it a few different ways to play. There's a lot of voicework in the game, with many characters having multiple dialogues for continued clicks. There's also a good amound of music and lots of sound effects to help go along with the colorful, cartoon style. You'll need to use a bit of problem solving for getting items and figuring out where to use them. There are even a few minigames to try out. Plus, there's a side quest for the more adventurous players to try and collect 10 pairs of socks. The socks are hidden throughout the game so you'll have 20 to try and spot as you search the screens of the game. It's a nice little touch for some extra challenge. Oh, and some of the humor is actually pretty good.
However, there are problems with this game. While there are many things to click on in any given location, a majority of them are simply there as goofy asides. There are typically a variety of different reactions for each item, but all they do is distract you from the main game. They don't really add much atmosphere, instead generally being there to keep kids entertained. It makes sense, sure, but it's not really something I'd call good game design, regardless of the target audience. There are even a few parts that don't have any real point to them, depending on which random set of circumstances the game gives you on your playthrough. Sometimes areas will have things to interact with but no reason to do so. Not that the extra bits aren't nice for a little more world there, or possibly an area to house a sock or two, but they don't feel necessary enough to include without looking at it as padding just a little bit. There also doesn't seem to be much reason to get all the socks. Not that there NEEDS to be a reward, and possibly there is as I missed a few, but it seems like the game just ends and doesn't really give you much incentive to go get them other than just wanting to do it for yourself.
Overall, it's a surprisingly solid game. I just randomly won it in a giveaway and figured it was going to be some lame kids' game. It actually isn't too bad. It could do more, do some things better, and be more challenging... but I understand its for kids that would probably spend more time figuring it out as it is. I didn't grow up with this game. I'm not blinded by nostalgia. I just thought it was genuinely a nice little experience. My only gripe is that it costs 7 bucks. That's a bit steep for this game, unless you're actually getting it for a kid. If you're getting it to check it out and you're not a kid, especially considering it's on Steam, then you're better off waiting for a sale to get it for only a few bucks. I wouldn't say it's worth full price, but if you're curious, it IS worth checking out. Pajama Sam: No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside gets a 6 out of 10 for being an older game for kids that has held up over the years, even without the nostalgia.

The game has a bunch of positives. It's fun and has a lot of potential as well as a lot already for it.
The only one criticism I had for the game that I can think of before the strike update is that, after logging in 7 days in a row, you get a weekly capsule. This used to give diamonds to people who had spent money, while kudos to those who simply didn't spend anything. It wasn't even that many diamonds. But, the developer greed really started to show when they made the weekly reward give you kudos no matter who you were. Keep in mind the diamond capsule was once a week, and wasn't even that great. Cumulatively, you would get a lot, but that's how weekly rewards work.
Besides this, read below about the Strike update... my main reason I am leaving a negative review.
The negatives have arrived very recently, with the new Airmech Strike update. I'm not saying it is entirely bad. I love the new layout. It's very intuitive and there is a lot to be said about it.
However, that's about it. Apart from that, there are extreme negative features found in this new update. Mainly how they streamlined the game into a solely pvp focused experience. Before this update the game had many features that appealed to players. PVE elements and the ability to fight against bots rather than players, especially good when matchmaking was bad, or when you wanted to hone your skills. And they didn't force you to do this in practice. I decided to spend money on this game because of the diverse content it promised.
They completely removed the diversity of the game, with the 'excuse' that they always intended for it to be a "pvp centered experience." Personally, I don't care what they envisioned the game to be. They gave us a product that appealed to us, and then stripped it down to make it incredibly simple and streamlined. Why didn't they do that from the beginning? They put out a specific product and then completely changed it. And a solely PVP based experience is complete bullcrap in my opinion.
Instead of adding on to the game, giving the new layout, improving the PVP features, they completely stripped the game of all other features and solely focused it on PVP. Who decided to do this? Where's the sandbox editor? That's right, they removed that feature, one that you had to pay for. They stripped the game of most of its content.
Though if you ask anyone in chat, they'll disagree with you. Probably because they're the only few people accepting of the new, horrible update who will stick around.
Wasteland promises to bring most of these features back. But my question is... Why would you remove all the features and put it into a separate gamemode... That's not even done yet? Even though the games will be linked, it would be much better to simply make wasteland a new, different experience, and not strip away from Strike for this.
I could be wrong about this, they could possibly pull of Wasteland well. But... I'm not holding my breath. I'll take a look at it, but I've got sincere doubts.
Yet another negative... is how they are handling these changes. Instead of waiting for Wasteland, they completely remove the aspects of the game and put out an unfinished product. As a result, you can't access your base and get rewards from your structures, because they removed them. So they removed one of the sources of daily income from the game, giving you no compensation for it. So you are stuck without the moneymaking structures, until Wasteland is released, so they say. They tell you to wait for Wasteland. Why would you just not release Strike and Wasteland at the same time? Why completely remove the aspects of the game and put so much doubt in the minds of the consumers? I can't fathom how they thought this was a good idea. Streamlining the game to solely PVP and then promising a PVE experience "later."
They could pull of Wasteland as a miraculous game. And if they do, I will change my review. But right now, things are looking bleak.
Though a major thing to consider, is how I said before, how poorly they are handling this. Instead of waiting for the two separate gamemodes, they just strip the game of all its content and promise something with actual content for later. They were too caught up in showing off their work to the public, that they competely forgot that Strike was void of any content.
I still think they could have ADDED on to the original game, adding more PVP elements rather than making it solely PVP, at least until they could actually prove to the public that Wasteland was a PVE experience to be desired.
I will keep an eye out for Wasteland. But Strike is a huge disappointment in my opinion.
Edit: Did they remove the daily quest? I think they did. Like, the one where you just log in and get it. I don't see it.

Watchmen: The End is Nigh Part 2 is the sequel to the horrible first game, but will the sequel fix the first ones mistakes ?
Watchmen: The End is Nigh Part 2 takes place right after the events of The End is Nigh. Rorschach get's a video film a girl so he and Nite Owl team up to get her back from her captives.
Gameplay wise the game is the same thing as part 1, nothing is changed. There's nothing new to change up the gameplay.
Graphics are the same. Very bad textures and nice comic style cut scenes. The levels do look nicer this time since they added more colors to the game.
Audio design is still as bad, the games audio cuts out and only comes back a few moments later, and the soundtrack is reused from the first part.
The game is way harder than the first part. They added new female enemies and they spam attacks that take away your health incredibly fast and the checkpoint system is messed up, the checkpoints are very far between which means dying is not an option. So your best chance of survival is to let the AI partner go in the battle head first while he takes out everyone and you just run around trying to avoid taking damage.
Level design this time is abysmal. The final level by itself is a confusing mess, really sloppy level design and everything pretty much looks the same.
Game is even shorter than part 1, only three chapters. all about 30 minutes long except for the final chapter which is about 45 minutes long. This is a tip for people who will have to play this game later on. Complete the level before exiting the game cause when you quit and return it's back to the start of the chapter. The game is also not buggy, apart from a few texture pop ins and character models spazing out and not to mention the  incredibly stupid partner AI.
The game is even worse than Part 1, This is not worth your time or money. Skip this no matter what. There is nothing good about part 2, awful level design, garbage combat and insane difficulty spike at the final chapter. Not worth the money. I give Watchmen: The End is Nigh Part 2 a 2/10

Oh jeez, where to start. I really enjoyed the first Watchmen game, and I went so far as to recommend to anyone who enjoys punching things at all. (And let's face it, most people enjoy punching things) The sequel is... a problem. The biggest issue here is that the game design left the building. The original End is Nigh ended when the game got done exploring its design. I would expect the sequel to add new elements, such as more combos, different enemy types... no, it did not. It's the first game, repackaged into new environments with three times as many physics objects.
So the gameplay is a let down, let's talk story. The original End is Nigh had a noir-esque narrative centered around the watergate scandal, and this one tells a more personal conflict. The city is up in flames due to a police strike, and in the midst of it all, Rorschach is most concenred with the well-being of a kidnapped girl, who was forced to star in underage pornography. Now, Rorschach has a problem with sexuality. A big problem. He seems to outright hate sex and anything sexy, probably due to his previous experiences.
His crusade to find and rescue the girl is justified only by the fact that she's underage, and Rorschach and a reluctant Nite Owl tear their way through a strip club and a brothel to get to her. Then, as it turns out, the "kidnapped" girl wasn't underage at all, and was instead there of her own volition. Nite Owl attempts to tell Rorschach that there's simply nothing they can do, but of course, he isn't having that. This culminates in a battle between the two of them on the rooftop, which ultimately ends their partnership.
It's actually a pretty neat story that dives deeper into both of their characters and motivations. You always get the impression that the two are an explosive mixture, and the way they do eventually break apart is realistic and interesting.
As an animated short film, this game's narrative would've been a blast, but one has to suffer through atrociously boring and uninspired gameplay to even get to the good parts, which are around 5 minutes total of the two hour experience.

Even though this is called "Part 2," it really has nothing to do with the first one at all. This was somewhat confusing since part 1 left you on a cliffhanger.
This game is not nearly as good as part 1. It is even shorter, having only 3 chapters, but this time they are much longer, but also very, very repetitive. All you seem to do is beat on a bunch of guys, then the reinforcements that come after you beat them, then open an annoying door that requires both characters and takes too long to open.
Then you do it over again...and over...and over...This is tolerable for the first two chapters, but the third chapter just seems to drag on for an unnecessarily  long time. Part 1 seemed to do a much better job at fleshing everything out.
The story is not at all interesting, if you can call it a story at all. But what would you expect from a 2 hour game I guess?
I would say to anyone looking to buy this, stick with Part 1; this isn't even worth the money.
