This is an extremely fun game, but you have to know what to expect beforehand. For people who have not played the tabletop version by Mike Selinker which this is based on (and of which this is an outstanding port):
* This is not a PvP-type of game. You do not play against other players. You play against the game.
* This is not a collectible card game in the sense that you are building a giant library:  you cannot freely add cards to your decks. It does contain a card viewer to check which cards you can encounter. There's a ton of them.
* This is game IS dependant on RNG. The trick is that the entire gameplay revolves around managing RNG. Nonetheless, you WILL get unlucky a few times. On the plus side, even when losing you get to keep some of the cards you won.
Having said that: the game is a lot of fun. You pit a team of adventurers against villains in different scenarios. The villain is hidden in one of the locations in that scenario and you have to flush him out with your party, corner and defeat him in 30 turns. Locations are made up of cards which you encounter and can sometimes acquire for your own decks, making your party stronger as you progress through the scenario's. Add in a barebones but clever level-up system with different roles to choose for your party members and you get some replay value out of it too.
What makes the game design so smart is that you have different playstyles depending on the size of your party. With 2 party members it revolves around acquiring the best cards, making the most optimal choices even at the cost of a few turns. With 6 party members it turns into a frantic race against the clock, forcing you to think differently about your deck and party composition.
The graphics are good, it stays true to the original art by Paizo and the backgrounds are vibrant showcases that are nice to look at, even after many hours play. The dice rolls are nicely animated too, it is almost as good as rolling actual dice, plus you get to unlock different dice sets to give each party member their own set. This way dice rolls become colorful displays as characters add their dice to checks, and you get to see which character's dice made you win a check. The menu music is very well done, the music while playing does get rehashed a lot but it is not very intrusive so I did not mind it much.
The game comes with 11 characters of 11 varying classes. The max party size is 6 characters, so you easily get two playthroughs out of the game if you want to give each character a go. You can buy or unlock (through play) different kits for each character, shaking up their abilities a little and adding some extra value, plus you get to do each scenario at three different difficulty levels. Needless to say, this game gives you dozens of hours of playtime. Excellent value for money.
Some tips for maximum enjoyment and challenge: if you buy the Obsidian Edition (which you should, Obsidian is a great developer deserving of support), refrain from adding in cards that are above your level if you encounter them in chests. It takes away a lot of the challenge and you will encounter them naturally as part of the story anyway. Also, even though it is tempting, try to not use the stash. The tabletop version didn't have one either. This way you stay as close to the excellent tabletop version as well. Which you should also get, because this game sadly lacks multiplayer but it is a blast to play with friends.

Whatever the reason, be it the sense of the unknown, the dulling of the sense we tend to rely on most, or some other more inherent instinct, at some point we've probably all shared a fear of the dark and what might be lurking in it. My solution to this was pulling the covers over my head and sleeping with the lights on, but I suppose I didn't have a surreal world living in my closet like Pajama Sam so I couldn't very well head out and attempt to capture darkness in my lunchbox.
Pajama Sam: No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside is the blanket garbed, flashlight wielding protagonist's debut and one of the few Humongous games I never got a chance to play as a kid. And that's a bit of a shame as it might possibly be the best written, most logical and entertaining series the studio put out in their edutainment boom.
Characters are lively and over the top, with clever writing and a lighthearted sense of humor that makes them delightful to interact with. The twisting art is somewhere between a haunted house and an Escher painting and still looks fantastic even with the original low resolution, clearly distinguishing between items you can pickup and packing a lot of charming little touches into almost every nook and cranny.
This certainly isn't the most challenging (or possessing any challenge whatsoever for that matter), but its simple puzzles are no less fun to solve and helping Sam and his friends overcome their feels is all kinds of heartwarming. Perhaps I'm simply biased toward all of Humongous's catalog, even those I never played, but whatever the case the hour or so I spent with NNtHWIDO (oof, that's some acronym) was a rather surprisingly entertaining bit of breezy adventure gaming, and I'm now eager to see what Sam's future endeavors have to offer.

While I would not reccomend it to anybody else in it's current state, I will continue to play this game as it is incredibly fun until you forced to restart due to the issues I talk about in my review.

Summary

Incredibly fun game that is infuriating to play due to horrific Quality of Life, atrocious ally AI, and many poor gameplay features. It feels like a solo indie developers first game ever made, covered by incredible pixel art.

TL;DR of Explanation

The difficulty of this game seems to come from an inability to decide what your allies roles are, rather than actual gameplay. Poor world generation in any of the islands you choose to play makes it impossible to win due to specific mechanics of the game, and punishes you for trying to learn the game aswell. Enemies are significantly faster than everything else and have a gigantic leap (which can render defenders useless if it bugs out which happens not too infrequently) causing them to punish you for not having a strong enough economy, and also punish you for trying to increase you economy at all.

Explanation

Note: Defenders refer to either Knights, Archers who follow Knights, Archers in towers, or people who man Catapults. Due to the inability to switch Villager jobs and un-queue build options you are punished for trying to learn the game. Your entire run can be completely ruined by upgrading or buying a single new building, as your builders will suicide into the enemies endlessly and you may be unable to recruit more villagers without them dying before reaching the base where you can choose their job. However not only does your run get ruined entirelu by this single mistake of trying to learn the game, your building does not get finished and you do not get to discover what it was. The enemies are so much faster than recruited villagers that if the camps they inhabit are too far away it is impossible to recruit them as the enemies outrun and kill them (even with a full day advantage of trying to make it home), making it impossible to progress and forcing you to restart and pray that you don't get that again. Not only is this a terrible mechanic, it makes no sense. If you live in the middle of nowhere and somebody offers you money and a place to live you'd probably be excited and want to get home as soon as you can, Not slowly waddle your way over there over the course of 1-3 days. The other main mechanic that severly punishes you for no reason is the inability to change what role and archer holds. I can appreciate the "pick their job and they're stuck with it" mechanic of the game, but if you upgrade a tower or get a knight your hunters (who are a large source of income) will automatically either follow the knight or sit in the tower accordingly, and no longer provide you income. This is another example of trying to learn the game and having your run ruined. Without the ability to decide which Archers are Hunters or Defenders(follow the Knight or are in a tower) you cannot distribute your archers evenly. Now you might ask "well if towers can ruin your run why bother getting them?" well since if an archer lands its shot is random, you can increase your chance of the shot landing by having them in a tower which is incredibly important for defending against multiple enemies. Another QoL issue is the inability to change what side of your town townsfolk (excluding Catapults which are decided on creation and builders whose jobs are unaffected by the side of town) the majority of your defenders and hunters can be useless as they do not protect against enemies, or seek out animals to provide income. This also means that because the enemies beat ~20-40% of your defenders (or bugged past them) they destroy most (if not all) of your hunters, builders, and defenders (not in tower) aswell.

Conclusion

In it's current state the game is nowhere close to worth the $16.99 (CAD) price tag it has. While the core gameplay is great (albeit flawed), the player experience is awful. The gameplay flaws and player experience have many issues that you would expect from a first time solo game developer who does not know what they are doing, which is very dissapointing to see in a sequel. Many of the issues are easily fixable if the developers choose to do so, and hopefully they decide to patch this game with them instead of only including them in the next installment of this game.

Amazingly simple yet deceptively deep settlement sim.
I purchased the original (I say purchased, it was free for a day) and thought the simplistic controls and aethetics are very well delivered. But dont let that fool you, it has a lot of depth
At its core its a coin and management sim. Your King or Queen must spread their money throughout your living village to ensure it doesnt get overrun on each side by the Greed, who approach when the sun sets.
In the day, you must venture right and left to discover what lurks beyond. It seems to be procedurally generated, but usually you will see the same things in each game i.e. Upgrade post, shrines, rivers, camps etc. Camps are vital and are where you obtain new villagers by dropping coins
Once villagers make their painfully slow walk back to the village you can then employ them to help build, defend or work in your village. Some jobs generate coins (farming, archers by day) some defend (archers by night) and some work (builders repair the onslaught of the Greed from the night before)
Its all a case of management. The Expansion does what all good expansions do, extend the lifespan of the core game by adding alot of elements and items.
so far (1 day in) I'd give it 8/10.

As a avid player of the tabletop mordheim and a player of Games workshops other games (Warhammer, W40k ect.) I find this game is a true homage to one of it's first true tabletop experiences, without (Well mostly) the obsessive power creeping that has come from it's latest instalments of tabletop games
Mordheim, as the name is stated, is played in the once great imperial city which is now just empty corridors and frigtening manisfestations of chaotic energy. And Mordheim the video game doesn't dissapoint. The city itself is well presented and offers the true tabletop experience, baring a few things that tabletop players are farmiliar with such as a birds eye view of the battlefield and no fog of War.
In a way this makes the game feel more like a discovering city fight than the all omnipotence view we as tabletop players come to expect, that is there are no way of knowing where your oponent is unless you take the energy to find them. I was genuenly surprised when my character walked out of a door to suddenly come face to face with a Rat Ogre. Boy did that make me a bit paranoid for open doorways and back alleys.
Overall The setting is what you would expect from this game, it hits the spot with not only a pinpoint nail, but also the flying hammer behind it.
Let it be known that the games i enjoy all have one thing in common, and that is not how pretty or how vibrant the world is, I am not a gamer who thinks of such trivial things so zealosly. Instead i find that the games i enjoy all have mechanics that are both easy to pick up and hard to master.
Mordheim is no different, it's mechanics very farmiliar to my knowledge of the tabletop game, with a few good exceptions. The Combat sequences do feel like they have that tabletop feel to them (Such as the no guarantee of doing a stance such as dodge or Parry), this is a good thing. It shows that the developers reseached their source material well.
However I did notice other things in game which vary way differently than their tabletop Counterpart. These features were noticeably different and feel more on the side of a computer game than a tabletop. And result in things that are rather alienating compared to it's tabletop counterpart (Which is a suggestion of you shouldn't believe everything that is being portraiyed in this game as it's tabletop counterpart) other than the few things that felt like they didn't feel right I had no quams with the system as it was hitting pretty close to home
Mordheim doesn't really feel like mordheim until you add the one core component from it's tabletop edition into the game, if it didn't have this it would just feel like a city fight of Warhammer Fantasy, and i would say as a person who has playedc both, they are SOO not the same
Instead the introduction of the persistant warbands and the campaign system trully make this a very well made recreation of the tabletop game and make every fight and every warband that much more investing to the player. It's not a simple matter of making a dream warband and proceeding to curb stomp every opponent out there but rather seeing your characters become the warriors they are from every bloody battle you encounter. You as a player pour your time and effort to make your characters an extension of yourself, which makes it all the more harder when those same characters lose vital parts of themselves or even perish from your roster permanently.
Mordheim the tabletop game was unforgiving to it's players and made them that much more invested in the survival or their warband, Mordheim the PC game delivers the same hit, time after time.
Overall, I feel  that this game is truly a great extension of it's tabletop counterpart and it makes due of it's promise to give you that genuine tabletop experience. If you are a veteran of the tabletop game i would highly invest in this. For those who haven't played a tabletop game i would suggest you try this out. The concepts and mechanics can help you get through the trial stages of learning this remarkable and addictive game.

Mordheim is hard, think Dark Souls. There is a sharp learning curve to it and even with my brother and I playing and sharing information I still couldn't get a lvl 10 warband decent enough to beat the last mission until I remade it 3 times. This was not as frustrating as it sounds though because there are plenty of options and variations to try, and each on has a particular niche that it works best in.
Lastly, I have had this game since early Beta and the team working on it is one of the best I have experienced. Currently the game is only lacking in a few quality of life tweaks like the touchiness of shooting through windows or ambushing through dorways. But in the short time I have owned this game these problems are repidly disappearing
My point is, the game is too hard for the people leaving poor reviews and I highly recommend it

Red String of Fate is very cute, first of all, as you'd probably expect.  It's also surprisingly deep at times.  I'm not saying it goes way deep into philosophy or anything, but there are moments that will make you stop and think.
Both of the routes are well-written and will leave you with that happy, warm-and-fuzzy feeling.  I would definitely suggest playing both even if you think you aren't interested in one of them.  I thought I wouldn't like Aaron that much but he turned out to be my favorite (though Luke was great too, of course).
The art isn't ***amazing***, but it is absolutely adorable and it illustrates the story very well.  Actually, I've seen the artist's work online and it's improved very much since this game, so if you're thinking about buying Ebullience Games' next visual novel, I can tell you for certain that the art will be/is even better.
If you don't already like visual novels, this one probably won't be the one to convert you, but if you do enjoy them, this one is pretty great and I would wholeheartedly recommend it.

I'd like to start off this review by saying that I, personally, effin' hate the concept of soulmates, or at least the notion of it that most people (and media) seem to have. So, when I first stumbled upon this game, I had zero expectations for it. I decided to play it anyway since I do so with any free VN I get my hands on, but I honestly thought it would be just another cliché thing that would have me rolling my eyes at stupid idealistic notions of romance the entire time.
So it was a lovely surprise when I found myself constantly laughing at the humor and smiling at the cute scenes rather than rolling my eyes at sappy overused ideas. The way the "red string of fate" issue was handled was also unexpected due to how down-to-earth it was. In the game, Valerie starts off obsessed with the immature ideas usually associated to the concept of fated lovers, and rather than fostering her delusions or including some plot twist that would prove them right all along, the game crushes all of them down by making Val realise (either the "easy" way by noticing it herself or the hard way by chasing her soulmate to no avail) that not everyone has/needs a perfect predestined relationship to find love and be happy. It is, overall, a surprisingly realistic take on such an idealistic topic.
The characters are funny and endearing. Rather than sticking to heavy stereotypes, you just get an extrovert with a light route and an introvert with a deeper story, and both are well-written. I like how the guy whose route you don't go for still sticks around as a good friend, and rather than a good or bad end, you basically get a romance end and a friendship end. Furthermore, instead of relying on how much you appease your guy of choice and whether he will stay with you or dump you, your choices only shape the way that Valerie herself handles her (and the guy's) already existing feelings. After the first choice, which is the one to set the route, you are the one to choose whether Val will move on from the red strings and embrace her love, or wallow in her obsession and refuse to acknowledge what she feels for the guy of choice. And even when you don't achieve a romance end and make Val turn down the guy, they still stay as very close friends, which also shows that (unrequited) love doesn't need to be the end-all-be-all and friendship is just as good
Despite its simplicity, I found this otome to be very innovative in that regard.
The technical side doesn't disappoint either, despite the art being a little subpar. There is a good amount of choices, most of which are intuitive enough, and a good number of CGs placed just in the right moments (although narration mentions changes in characters' poses/expressions that don't always reflect on the CGs, which may get kind of weird). The GUI looks cute, the music is pleasing and you can check a gallery with 2 extra illustrations besides all CGs.
Despite its flaws (the start was too fast for me and there were minor inconsistencies in writing), I liked this novel a lot. I recommend it without a doubt, whether you're into the cheesy fate thing or a more realistic person who still enjoys some cute romance. Looking forward to more from these devs!

This is an interesting visual novel which blends parts of East Asian lore and western romantic traditions. The main character is a young woman with the ability to see the red strings of fate that bind soulmates together. Valerie can see how stretched they are, or if they are broken and frayed (because that person's soulmate is no longer with us). The only string that she cannot see is her own. At least at first.
In one of her college course she meets Aaron, a person one year younger than her but in her same class (he's a gamer with high intelligence, so he finished high school a year early), someone she knew at her high school. His red string is frayed and broken. She also meets Luke, a student a year older who does not have a string of his own. Because he too can see them. They work together on a project that has significant ramifications for their ability to pass the class.
There are four paths. The choice of who to pursue is made in the first decision, and then there is a series of choices that eventually decide whether you go searching for your soulmate (which because you can't see your own thread you think they are on the other side of the world) or whether you will pursue a relationship with your chosen beau. One could say those seers who can see the strings might be wild cards who can pair with someone who's soulmate is gone, or with another seer. One does wonder if the ability might be passable through genetics, though.

Alliances don't mean anything in the game, I would go as far to say I don't want them, because if you break one everyone gets mad at you. Generally battles are on a much grander scale.

A board and card game based around adventuring solo or in a group, collecting loot, saving the town, and defeating the bad guys. Dice rolls and fun abound.
The Good:
+ Fun, addictive, "one more turn" gameplay for hours
+ Balanced and open to various playstyles and class combinations
+ A fair amount of replayability and challenge
+ Lovely art throughout
+ Can be played as a single character, or in a large party
+ Really comes alive when played with friends through Skype's screen share function, or in person
+ The story, while fairly cliche, keeps you hooked well enough
+ A mix of races and genders that frequently bucks trends and cliche
+ Finding and collecting new cards is a real treat
Worth Knowing:
/ This is not a digital version of the Pathfinder roleplaying game, and it doesn’t play much like it either.
The Bad:
- Menu bugs can occasionally require a restart
- No built in multiplayer at all
- Doesn't support the 3440 x 1440 resolution
- Music is entirely forgettable
- Fairly lackluster visual effects
The physical game itself is a blast, and while far from perfect and lacking built in multiplayer, its translation to the digital format does nothing so wrong as to ruin a great thing. If you're a fan of the roleplaying niche, enjoy the Pathfinder world, or just love a good board game, get your party into Skype, share your screen, and play for hours.

If you are like me and fancy a good adventure/shooter/RPG style top down view game in the vein of the Alien Breed, Space Siege (probably not the best example), Subterrain and similar games, Crash Landing will look quite appealing to you (especially when it being sold for $0.50 on a Groupees bundle).
The game is supported by decent graphics as shown on the trailer videos and screenshots but unfortunately suffers from many development issue that becomes quickly apparent after 0.2h of playing:
-  Control scheme that does not support running.  It might sound weird, but pressing left shift and not going for a sprint is, at least to me, highly unsual and quite disturbing in term of gameplay.  The absence of any kind of map which is replaced by a light spot moving around to show you where to go also points to the developper taking shortcut to go on a quick release.
- The absence of a game logo in your library (you can see the Unreal Engine instead) as well as the voice over in the game also reveal that the game was probably done on the cheap.  There is nothing wrong with that, but with the quite visually appealing graphics, there is a big clash between what you see and how the overall game really feels making not one that you will be willing to spend hours on.
- Additionaly the game misses a tutorial.  I generally don't like tutorials but since some of the controls here are unusual, a tutorial will be quite handy (possibly using the first sort of useless level to indicate what keys do what...).
- Dying at your first monster encounter (I don't think I spoiled anything here) because you are in a dark area and nothing told you to press F for the flashlight brings too much frustration on my side to keep playing.
In short, Crash Landing could have been a good game without necessarily bringing anything new to the genre but some bad development decisions make it an average game.  Will I give it a try again? Probably yes... But I am quite sure at the moment, I will probably never attempt to finish this game unless the developer does major upgrade...Simply because I got better ones in my Steam collection.

Update: I requested (and received) a refund for this game.  This is honestly the first time I have ever requested a refund on anything.  I sincerely hope the developer works to patch this game and make some much-needed improvements.  My original review follows:
When I read in the description that this game "follows in the footsteps of...Alien Breed or Shadowsgrounds," I was super-psyched.  The two Shadowgrounds games and three Alien Breed games are my favorite top-down shooters of all time.  However, my excitement quickly gave way to disappointment and, after about 70 minutes of play time, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game.  There's a lot of potential here but the game feels like an unfinished late-alpha or early-beta release.
The setting is good (if unoriginal) and the beginning of the story is somewhat intriguing (if uninspired) though I don't think I played long enough to evaluate how any of that pans out.  Even so, it's hard to care much because of the horrendous voice acting.  The ship's AI seems to have more emotion than your character does - you seriously sound indifferent that the ship has crashed and the rest of the crew is likely dead.
The controls are clunky from the get go and movement is terribly slow.  There does not seem to be a way to run - the control for "dash" causes you to roll forward, like an evasive maneuver.  There is very little to interact with in the environment - what you can interact with will be glowing, including pickups, computers, door controls, etc.  Not sure what to think about weapons.  You start with just a pistol but you find weapons components along the way, yet there's no indication what they do, if anything.  I did not play enough to find and try any other weapons.  There's no inventory management at all - the few items you can have are displayed in the HUD.
Another criticism is the save system - you have one save slot, regardless of which difficulty level you play.  There's simply no excuse for that in a modern game.  I should also mention that, in just over an hour, the game froze twice, forcing me to kill it and restart.  I could go on and on about everything that's wrong with this game and how disappointed I am but I think I'll cut it short.  In conclusion, this game has a ton of problems.  It's a combination of being unfinished and bad design decisions.  The game most definitely needs some severe patching but even that won't fix some of its issues.  And it will certainly never rank up there with Shadowgrounds or Alien Breed.  NOT RECOMMENDED.

Before you buy: (I bought this on sale and was still disappointed).
Minor spoilers ahead.
In Kingdom classic which has the same graphics, gameplay etc, you are given all features in one game. This means you can keep going and keep expanding. In this one you are given a few of them every level. The game then revolves around building a boat to move to the next level.
You have to recruit people. They are recruited in camps. Those camps are very far away and your horse will run out of breath way before getting there. Meaning a lot of the time you're just running really really far away to one of these camps, and then running all the way back. This is boring. Theres nothing to explore on the way either. On the way back to camp, your new recruits may encounter the enemy. If hit once, your new recruits are not your new recruits anymore, and the gold you paid is gone. Also, you ran your way to the camp. Your recruits will slowly walk to your base. The chances of them reaching your camp is therefore low. This means:
Run far to camp
Recruit
Run far back
Recruits have 50/50 chance of coming
Repeat
The game is also about expanding your base. If you expand past a camp, the camp will disappear and stop producing more people for you to recruit. And recruits happen to be the most important thing in the game.
You have two fronts: left and right. As you expand, left and right goes further and further apart, meaning just to do general logistics and upgrades, you have to run back and forth a LOT.
These two concepts ruin the game.
Kingdom Classic I enjoyed for a while. It should have ended there.

I've read and heard many criticisms about this game and do not quite understand them. I will try and address them and give my opinion as to why this is probably one of the top three Double Dragon games.
**Graphics:
Solid art design, although some of the enemies are a bit more cartoony than previous DD designs, the colors, backgrounds, animations and effects are pretty solid. The game mixes 3D models with the occasional 2D background object, The alley level is particularly nice. Varied environments and enemies with vibrant colors.
**Sound:
Great remixes of classic double dragon tunes and some new additions. Music and sounds are near flawless in this game. Some may loathe the voice acting, but for the tone they're going for, it's appropriate.
**Controls:
The game controls solidly for me. A lot of "Double Dragon veteran" players have criticized how slow and heavy the Lee brothers move, but I think they haven't played DD for a while. DD was always a slower, more methodical game than other beat 'em ups. Neon is actually a little bit faster (go check youtube, watch Super Double Dragon, or DD II). The dodge button is responsive, although you're vulnerable if you execute some moves. The dash is not instant unlike DD Advance and DD3, and that can be a cause for some headaches.
**Gameplay:
The game has a lot of moves, and some combos . Clever players can find ways to juggle opponents multiple times and incorporate grabs and special moves while doing so. The Lee brothers have mixtapes that grant abilities and special moves like fireballs, hurricane kicks, etc. You can't steamroll through waves of enemies thoughtlessly though, as enemies have some moves with "armor", not many, but it does require some recognition on the player. Players who dodge attacks correctly get a temporary buff. It's a nice addition, though not as satisfying as Super Double Dragon's parry and grab mechanics from blocking.
**Verdict:
For Insider: 8/10
I've played every iteration of Double Dragon, even the three fighting games (if you count Rage). I knew exactly what to expect from this game. I give it an 8/10. I've beaten it in normal and Dragon difficulty, working on replaying it again to do so in Double Dragon difficulty (which is quite hard).  Highly recommend it.
For Casual: 6/10
Don't even listen or Read IGN's super ignorant review of this game. It's a solid game if you like slower methodical beat' em ups. My wife is an RPG, Strategy game gamer and was able to beat this game a few times with me. She enjoyed the humor and although she doesn't always play beat 'em ups, she really enjoyed this one.  6/10

For newer fans to the genre: 3/10 to 5/10
These fans will probably hate this game the most. If you're used to the speed of Castle Crashers and want to blow through enemies with fast attacks and screen clearing moves this game is not like that. Watch some of the youtube videos for this game, but approach with caution.
** Extras Info
Game's tone is different from prior DD games, at first I was frustrated by this as I wanted a serious DD game, but the game did get more than a few laughs out of me. There are plenty of easter eggs and references to 80s-90s games and culture.

Mordheim: City of the Damned is a Tactical Squad RPG based on a tabletop game of roughly the same name set in the  Warhammer 40K franchise. It's a roguelike game somewhat similar to darkest dungeon in its roguelike mechanic. There are no savestates and your squadmembers can get permanent debuffs or permenantly die outright. The objective of the game is to collect wyrdstone at the request of the faction leader of your warband (party) and to do this you fight against other warbands of the same or different faction.
I love this game. I really do. It's been a while since I played a game for as long as this. That said it certainly isn't perfect by any stretch of the imagination.
My first few warbands were hell. My henchmen kept dying and my hero's kept getting injured to uselessness. I rage quit at least three times, but for whatever reason I kept getting back into the game. To be honest this is the very first warhammer game I've ever played and I can see why people are so into it. The grimdark atmosphere and the pure hoplessness of the whole world makes for a refreshing change. The opening cinematic reflects this beautifully.  It has a atmosphere to it that just spoke to me. The music and sound assets make the game feel so alive.
Which brings me to the first problem with the game. The RNG in this game is not the best. With that I mean the random number generator itself is broken. Its too streaky. If you have a 80% chance to hit you often hit either 4 out of 4 or miss 4 out of 4. Its weird like that. That said it also works the other way, if an enemy has a chance to hit of 80% they often have the same problem. It has gotten better with the RNG patch but it still happens too often to make mathemetical sense. I know programming true RNG is impossible and good RNG is rather hard but when it is such a huge part of your game you better have it as flawless as possible.
The second problem with the game is the lack of info it give about its mechanics to new players. A lot of information will need to be stumbled upon or found out be reading forums or a wiki. For example: dodge and parry are two stats that negate an enemies attack if they trigger. You can find that out without to much trouble. However what they don't say is that first the game will roll to see if the enemy will hit you. If they do they will roll to see if your parry or dodge works. If it works or not, your parry and dodge roll for that turn will be used up. Each attack after that won't have to go through you parry and dodge chance. Next to that is the fact that some stats and skills will lower your parry and dodge chance so that your 95% chance to dodge almost never reflects your actual chance to dodge. Which brings me to the fact you can't even have a 100% chance to dodge. While this is all information you will find out if you keep playing the game, it can get frustrating when you are just starting out. This is just one of the many mechanics that I, as a newb to the franchise, did not understand in the beginning.
The last problem with the game I would like to point out, like so many did before me, is the horrible loading times. Getting into a game takes upwards of 3 minutes of loading for me, with a SSD and a roughly 2 year old system. While I understand that my setup isn't the newest that is still a rather long time to load a map. Not something that really annoys me too much, as I'm usually watching something while I play games, but it is a problem.
The AI isn't the greatest. They hardly care about objectives, always know where you are and target your weakest units without fail. Its not a big problem, as this does provide a challenge, but 'smarter' AI would have been better. If only because it would have sometimes changed the tactics you'd need to employ for a battle.
With all the negativity out of the way lets get to the positive. The four warbands are amazing. They each have a unique flavor and playstyle. The sisters are awesome spellcasters, the mercenaries are fantastic range units, the scaven are fast and deadly and the possessed are brutal in melee. Their individual style can really be felt in the available leaders, heroes, impressives and henchman and the racial skills and spells. I love the fact that my whole playstyle changes each time I play a different warband. Its easily one of the best points of the game.
Surviving in this game early on is hard. Which makes it so much fun when you start leveling up the members of your warband. The number of skills available are amazing. Each one could change your whole playstyle. I'm a min/maxer by nature, so the amount of hours I spend on theorycrafting alone would easily double my playtime. The amount of max level heroes I threw away because I found a better build that required me to change just a few stat points or one skill number in the dozens. Its what keeps me going and is one of the things I love the most about this game. There's just so much customization. It's the best.
I enjoy the game a great deal, that said I can see how people might not. Still I would certainly recommend it to any fan of Tactical Squad RPGs.
tl;dr
Pro
- Great Atmosphere
- Great music and sound assets
- TSRPG
- Each warband has a unique playstyle
- Lots of potential to min/max
Con
- RNG
- Hard to get into
- Leaves a lot of important technical information hidden
- Long loading times

I have enjoyed this game since early access so to me this game has only gotten better but i'll break it down into positive / negative things there are to look out for so you can decide on your own if you would consider the same things positive / negative.
Negative:
- Still has some optimization to do
- There is a chance you will find an invisible wall or an invisible wall will be created because of something in the map
- Has a relatively high learning curve if you have not played anything like this before which can be overwhelming and may need to be taken in more than 1 session.
- Has no multiplayer unless you find a friend to set it up with or get very lucky some random person around your warbands lvl is looking for a game.
- A total of 4 races -> humans, Chaos, Skaven and Sisters of sigmar is a big issue for some even though i once again am fine with this number since i don't jump between races a lot.
- Most common complaint i can think of is the variation in missions (all missions are optional. Main objective is always to beat the opponents warband or make them rout before you lose or rout)

-> Wyrdstone Rush where you collect typically 45% - 60% of the wyrdstone in the map to complete the OPTIONAL      objective
-> Marked for death where you have certain targets from the other warband normally between 1 and 3 specific people you need to kill and take an insigna from
-> Crush their will where you are tasked with retrieving the opponents idol and bring it back to your own cart
I completely understand why some people would consider this a too small amount of missions even though i am completely fine with them.
Positive:
- They have done a great job at making your warband feel like they matter giving you that classic fear of someone getting killed or sustaining a permanent injure like an arm or a leg that has been severed.
- The insane number of different abilities both passive and active you can gain through the lvl up system
- The ability to equip your mercenaries with different weapons and armor to suit your playstyle not to mention the rarity difference from common to epic quality
- The depth they have put into the lvling. You are able to lvl up your warband, your mercenaries and give them stat ups, the different wyrdstone collecters and you can in a way lvl up the game with their veteran system.
Some of these make very little difference but make a nice surprise sometimes while others will be looked at as a goal to obtain after 1 - 2 missions
Summary:
I think the game has things to work on and i completely understand some of the concerns some might have but the most importent thing to me is the fact that the game runs well and provides a lot of things to do when you are not on a mission and a great tactical experience when you are in a mission.
It is very easy to look at the game at first and think of it as unforgiving and very hard but once you get the hang of it the game becomes very interesting and i will absolutely recommend this game.

The concept of a horror game from the perspective of a young child that does not fully understand its surroundings is definitely a good one. The weakness and slowness of a baby adds to the feeling of helplessness that drives fear, so it seems like a perfect match. And it may be one, but I don't think Among the Sleep uses it to its fullest. Very quickly, the game leaves its initially grounded setting in favor of something a bit more fantastical, and it does nothing but make the game feel weightless. The entire game is a few short levels of walking around and collecting things, which I suppose isn't out of the ordinary for a modern indie horror game, but that's exactly the problem. Among the Sleep takes a very interesting premise and uses it in an uninteresting way. The game isn't really bad in any particular way, but nearly every aspect of Among the Sleep is what a horror game should never be: predictable.

Among the Sleep is a first-person horror atmospheric adventure game developed and published by the Norwegian Krillbite Studio.
The game focuses on exploration, puzzles and horror, seen from the perspective of a two year old toddler.
The game starts when the toddler is having his second birthday party at home with his mother when the party is interrupted by someone at the front door.
When the mother walks towards  the front door, a man starts talking and a muffled conversation starts.
Suddenly the mother raises her voice at the person at the front door.
The toddler is frightened by the angry tone from his mother and the blurred vision will come up, indicating the fear of the toddler.
Then the mother returns quickly to the toddler with a present, a teddy bear but she doesn't tell from who the present is.
During the night you are awoken by a strange force that turns over your crib and Teddy is lost.
At this point your are completely alone, you must look for help and your adventure starts.
During the game you are most of the time accompanied your teddy bear, Teddy and together you two start searching for comfort.
Most of the time you are solving puzzles, navigating through the labyrinth of levels, dodging monsters and collecting memories of you mother to find her back again.
When traveling through the dark areas you can hug Teddy who will temporary emit light that helps you navigate.
You enter various dark and strange areas such as the interior of your house, expansive closets, the Gingerbread house, tunnels, an abandoned playground, forests, swamps etc.
When you are chased by monsters, you can hear them nearing by the increasing grating sounds and the more becoming blurry vision.
What I really liked about this game is the idea that you play as a two year old toddler but having a more developed brain/mind to solve these puzzles trough these surreal environments.
If you like adventure horror games or just want to wander around as a two year old toddler (again), I really recommend this game to you, certainly when it is on sale!

Among the Sleep is atmospheric and at times spooky, with a wonderful art style, and it's different from run-of-the-mill horror games in that you play as a toddler, but sadly that is just about all there is too the game. The puzzles in game are easy and there is little challenge to be found here. I had high hopes for Krillbite Studio, but while the game was good, it fell short of being a great game and a good scare.

Horribly F2P model badly ported to a paid game with most of the baggage still attached. Wost of all, it's a CCG in which you can't actually collect cards at all, decks operate on a "1 in, 1 out" policy, and you only have storage for 10 cards that aren't part of a deck. So sure, the game advertises having over a thousand cards, but it's impossible to actually have most of them, all you can do is endlessly collect gold to pay for random booster packs and hope you get something you can use right now. And as if the F2P-style booster packs aren't bad enough, you're also expected to buy a variety of time-limited bonuses to help you during quests - yes, it's good old pay-to-win nonsense in a single player paid game. The game constantly nags you about playing online and linking your actually F2P mobile version to share gold and such nonsense, as well as bombarding you with adverts to other games and even the game you're already playing - the first thing I saw on loading the game was a full-screen splash screen telling me I should buy the game. Perhaps worst of all, despite costing £20 the game doesn't even include all the available content and forces you to grind your way through the F2P nonsense exactly as if you were playing the mobile version if you want to actually play the whole game.
As for the actual gameplay, it's OK but no more than that. You click the "explore" button, roll some dice, and then either beat it or are forced to discard some cards. Beating a monster gets rid of it, beating an item or similar puts it in your hand so you can discard it to get a bonus on a future roll. And that's pretty much it. There are no animations, no voice acting, no characters or story worth speaking of, everything in the game is utterly generic fantasy. While that's pretty much expected of Pathfinder, which was created essentially as a fork of the already generic D&D, but the point of both games is to provide a world and basic framework on which to build your story. Unfortunately all this game does is say "Here's an elf rogue fighting a goblin" with no effort give you any reason to care why.
The tabletop game can be fun to play with a group, but there's really little point in buying this for PC. If you really want it on a computer, the mobile version (Android and iOS) is free and allows you to unlock all content through gameplay, which you'd end up having to do anyway even if you pay for it on Steam.

As someone who has played through the box version of this game, I would say the conversion to PC is excellent and immersive.  The added dialogue between party members and villians rounds out the traditional card game experience nicely and the earning of coins to "buy" card packs, dice skins, and boosts is a nice touch which also helps make additional playthroughs and party builds more entertaining.
If you have not played the box version this is a great party and deck building card game which diverges nicely from all of the Magic/Pokemon/Hearthstone/"insert-favorite-vs-deck-builder-cardgame-here"  This is not a one deck faces another deck type of game.  You pick characters which have different abilities and can hold certain types of cards and you play them against a card driven adventure.  You "explore" locations by drawing cards from their deck, you fight minions, henchmen and bosses, and you get LOOT!  Find a great piece of loot and you can use it in the next adventure by adding it to one of your character decks.  So as you play through the game you level up your characters, your characters' decks, and even the adventures get more challenging.
If you have played the box version this is a nice version to own, not only does it take less space to play, it also makes it easier to play solo while maintaining larger parties.  Half the fun of deck building card games is choosing your strategy and building working combos and this version makes trying whole new party builds very easy.

Pajama Sam: No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside - Raymond KT
I loved Pajama Sam growing up; I and my brother would just adore this classic. Beat it again and again and made us smarter in a way. Pajama Sam: No Need To Hide When It's Dark Outside is the most cleverly written children's game I've ever played. It also looks charming, has a great soundtrack, and three different routes each time you start from the beginning. It's enjoyable for kids and adults, and you won't regret giving it a try.
A key element for any children’s adventure game is voice acting – if the performances aren’t engaging, it’s likely that interest will be lost quickly. Thankfully, every moment you spend with these characters is a delight thanks to the brilliant and varied voices. Ranging from Sam’s high and chirpy voice to Otto’s hesitant and slightly wary style to the quiz show door’s enthusiastic zeal, each actor injects a highly distinctive personality into their respective roles. The music complements this perfectly, with upbeat tunes keeping the mood light while mixing in the occasional chime to add an unearthly air. Music even takes part in the game itself, with furniture dancing in secret and kitchen appliances singing about their functions.
The trees are just a sample of the unusual characters that will make an appearance. Sam is the only human (if you can call him that) in this world, an innocent and friendly young boy who is keen to assist others. Along the way he’ll encounter a toaster, a coat stand and a fridge, to name but a few of the everyday items that have come to life. The most memorable are Otto the boat and King the mine cart, both of whom you’ll help out with their troubles. They act as modes of transport, and thus you’ll spend more time connecting with them than anyone else. It’s a shame other minor characters don’t play a bigger role, because everyone has a unique personality (such as the carrot trying to rescue his friends from being used in a salad and the over-worked water well) and I’d have liked to interact more with this colourfully assorted cast.

This is a really decent game, with a simple to play and interesting mechanic to boost it.
However, the stupidity of the AI killed the enjoyment out of it for me.
Here's the mechanic,
You recruited town people with coins,
You then buy the tools with coins,
Open villagers will automatically go and get the nearest tool, and do their work.
Here are some of the ways for you to gain coins.
Hunters go out Hunting Animals.
Farmers Plow the Field.
Engineers cut down trees.
And here are the issues.
In order to Hire those villagers and buy tools, you need money,
Which mean that if you ran out of money and lost those villagers for whatever reason,
it is impossible for you to recover.
You cannot manually switch villagers occupation, they are stuck to what ever job they are.
There are the Left and Right sides of the Castle, You cannot assign which villagers go to which direction.
And most of the time, they will go to the one you don't want them too.
Hunters have proximity radius, and will not go out hunting beyond their range.
So, they are pretty much useless if there are no Animals nearby and you cannot expand your border.
Which is a problem, because you need them to go out hunting in the 1st place to get the coins to expand your border.
The Villagers do not retreat behind the next wall after there is a breach.
So, unless you build Layers of Walls beyond your Farms,
a single breach is more than enough to annihilate your villagers,
spelling game over for you due to inability to recover.
In one of my play through, I did a missed that destroyed all of my Farms and Farmers on the left side.
I would be able to recover if the Archers & Hunters on the right side won't just stay in their place and go out hunting.
I understand that the developer wanted to make the gameplay as simple as possible,
But the lack of adequate AI to support the system just simply ruined the experience for me.

This game is an amazing revival of the beat em' up genre.  It brings the Double Dragon Series into updated graphics and adds tons of unlockables and moves that add to the strong gameplay.  The music is half remixes and half new.  The new music is mostly 80's style vocal stuff, and it's not that great.  Its purpose is to add to the overall charm of the game.  DDN is an over-the-top game by far, with you destroying tanks with your bare hands, ripping apart biological weapons and then riding the remains down a cliff.  The voice-acting is also hilarious at times, with the "Bad Women" saying suggestive lines like "On your knees, please!" and "Punish me!".  Also notable is Skullmageddon, the new antagonist.  He has a high nasal voice and constantly  gives orders to his goons throughout the game in the most cocky tone imaginable.  His entire purpose is to add to the "So bad that it's good" vibe that this game gives off.  I noticed a considerable amount of slowdown when playing the game throughout, but it isn't horrible.  It's by no means fast-paced, and I recommend the Ps3 or Xbox 360 version if possible, but this version is still very enjoyable for a Double Dragon fan.  If you haven't played a Double Dragon or Beat-em up game before, you won't understand most of the inside jokes within the game.  If you like the genre and/or series, pick this game up, otherwise you just won't enjoy it that much. 7/10 Overall Score.

Double Dragon wasn't a game that needed revisiting. It's an old classic that, while time hasn't been kind toward (slowdowns are almost unbearable in the original), it's still highly regarded and considered a classic in the genre. The game has been released on a wide variety of systems, and even saw a faithful arcade port released to the XBox Live Arcade (slowdowns fixed). In other words, you've had every opportunity to own this game in some form or another.
When I first saw screenshotse for Double Dragon Neon, I immediately cringed and thought of the abomination that was Turtles in Time Reshelled. Upon firing it up, it was a relief that graphics were the only thing it had in common. Double Dragon Neon is a fun take on the series, with the 80s style turned up to 11 and an engine that actually makes it enjoyable to play. It's nothing ground-breaking, but it's still A LOT of fun to play.
You have a system that revolves around mixtapes, which grant you a boost to certain stats (such as power, defense, magic, etc), or allow your character to use special abilities, such as throwing fireballs, healing, or summoning dragons to crush every enemy on screen. You level up your mixtapes by collecting any that fall from enemies, or you can purchase them in store with money you collect from enemies. Once you max out your mixtape, you will want to visit a tapesmith to upgrade how many you can hold, which will further develop your stats.
And you'll need it. The game, while not terribly difficult, can be unforgiving for players wishing to play it like the 1980s classic and just mash out buttons. You have new abilities, such as duck, dodge, and rolling that you MUST learn to use in order to evade enemies and set yourself up to kill them without being hit. If you successfully dodge an attack, your character will gleam, which grants a bonus to your attack. Learning how each enemy attacks and what the best method of disposing of them keeps the game fresh, and fun. You may want to switch your mixtape stance to offer more defense in a particular area, or you may want to boost your magic to fight at a distance. Half the fun is figuring everything out and grinding to upgrade your stats (although non-RPG fans may not find the latter very fun).
Is Double Dragon Neon the best in the series? I think so (although the GBA versions are very good). Is it ground-breaking like the original? Not so much. But it's fun. Grab a friend for even more craziness.

So, let me get started by saying, due to the season, I was in the mood for some horror games.  I went from the Evil Within to this.  I did the Evil Within first because I assumed this to be a better game.  I really loved that game, ultimately.  This one... not so much.
Get the good out the way:
The graphics were generally really great here.  The faces had that slightly odd too realistic look to them which only added to that creepy factor here.  The color pallette was bland, but it fit the game perfectly.  Not too many chances of popping color when most of the game takes place in dark enclosed areas that are poorly lit.
Overall, the creep factor here was really high, though I wasn't expecting so many jump scares at the beginning, but they teetered out pretty quick and then it evened out. At points it really did feel like a haunted house experience which is what I was really going for.
Also, the game is optimized really great at this point.  I didn't play it on release and I never heard anything bad, but everything here was butter smooth.  Not single FPS issue the entire game.
Some of the bad:
I have a few criticisms here that are highly person.  The first is the overall size of each area.  The areas in this game are tiny.  I wasn't expecting huge open areas or anything, but each area is really miniscule.  I also feel the areas you go to are kind of derivative at this point.  You start in a tiny abandoned house.  You go to bigger (but not by much) house, then a boat house, then a boat, then a min....  The boat which is probably bigger than all of them and it felt noticeably bigger.  One of the reasons it feels that much bigger though is the enemy count.  You have to take it slow, check each room, watch out for enemies.  But once everything is dead and you take a run through, you find out that the areas can be almost entirely explored in about a minute and half when you aren't searching for items or being attacked.
One of the ways they extend these areas is the use of tapes, which at first I really liked.  You get to play as another character going through an area with slightly different events happening.  But then I realized that all they really did was utilize an area you were about to go through as Ethan.  In one section, they have you solve the puzzle on a tape, only to have Ethan run through and know the solution already.
Gunplay is terrible.  I wasn't expecting to come here and play a shooter, to be clear.  I wasn't looking for a first person shooter.  But, when you put guns in a game they should feel right or you should not have them.  First, no matter what I did, it always felt like there was a noticeable delay between me clicking my mouse and the gun shooting.  I would also like to point out that I was running the game just fine, I wasn't suffering from any FPS issues anywhere in the game, as previously mentioned.  Also, I have no idea what is going on with the enemies hit boxes.  I used my beginnig handgun on a mold, 4 shots to the head and it was done, bang, head exploded.  I thought, it makes ammo tight, but I can handle that.  Well, they must have decided later that 4 wasn't enough and left players with too much ammo to keep the suspense high.  So soon, it's taking no less than 7 headshots with that gun for the same enemy.  And by that I mean with actual hits, not shots I wasted that went wide because of the delayed feeling in the mouse click to gunshot ingame.  I get a shotgun, but I'm told that you can one shot these guys with a close shotgun blast. Alright, ammo is even tighter here since you can't craft any shotgun shells in the game, so I lure them in close.  BANG!  I see splurge come out, the mold goes down, I'm happy... then it starts to move and get up.  I had shot it basically point blank in the face, the animation where it covers it's face with it's arm wasn't happening, and yet I blew it's arm off.  So, now, the weird hitboxes and what I assume is how they change the second an animation likely begins is costing me ammo.
Next up is the fact that you are spending this entire game as if it takes place in a giant pool of molasses.  You are so slow, which is one of the ways I assume they also use to try and make areas seem bigger than they are.  But that translates to you aiming your gun.  More than one of my deaths was due to me essentially getting stun locked by a crawling mold.  These guys are fast.  You can outrun all the other kinds, but these guys will run you down quick.  I learned that early on, so I would purposely save shotgun ammo for them.  But on several occasions I would wait for them to get close with my shotgun aimed, I click, they somehow attack me first, my shotgun doesn't shoot, and ethan has to recover from being hit before he can aim his gun again, but the enemy now has me stun locked between recovery and pulling out my gun, the mold recovers faster.  Sometimes I could get it off, but it was nearly impossible not to waste ammo like this.  Some enemies feel like they were placed to simply make you waste ammo and take unavoidable damage.
I read in several places, "sometimes it's best to avoid combat and just run".  That is great, I like the idea that maybe I can run away and recover or get my bearings.  Only, the vast majority of locations in this game are constructed in such a way that you can't just run around enemies or avoid them.  For instance, there is a part in the main house that you have to go through a series of basement corridors and molds spawn in the corridors.  Sure, you can run back the way you came, but the molds follow eventually disappearing, meaning you can't kite them to larger areas where they can be avoided.  Then, when you continue down the corridor again, they spawn again.  I found very few sections of the game where I was not stuck in unavoidable combat.  I expect that from boss fights, but from basic shambling enemies it was more annoying and frustrating, which was then compounded by the fact that you spend the entire game in molasses.
I beat the game, but it felt more like a personal financial obligation by the end.  You start the game underpowered, then 3/4 of the way through you are stacked to the teeth with guns and ways to kill enemies.  It felt very uneven.  At one point I found myself confidently striding down hallways not afraid of what might come.  I had gotten my hands on a bunch of these remote bombs that I could place, run back and set off to kill groups of molded.  And if I ran out my inventory was full of other weapons.
Inventory management was back, but often I found myself weighed down with things that I never found a use for.  For example, I never used the psychostimulants once.  When you take them it makes it easier to find items laying around, which might have been useful for more Magnum ammo, which I had about 10 rounds of the entire game, which I didn't use till the last boss.  But it was never worth useing them I thought because I could thoroughly search rooms myself.  But, the caveat here is I couldn't really just leave them where I found them.  You don't have the option of picking an item up when you hit the action button, you pick it up.  Sometimes due to the frantic nature of the game I was running around trying to avoid enemies where I could and picking up everything I could see with little time think on it.  So your inventory fills up with things that you may not find useful and you may not have easy access to your storage container without a molasses run to the trailer.
For me, this game was more of an exercise in frustration.  The shooting mechanics were bad.  A good portion of my deaths felt cheap like the game had cheated me somehow.  One time I got caught between enemies when I hit two with my shotgun at close range, one fell to my side, but I got trapped between a wall and two fallen still alive molds.  The game plagued with moments like this.  The overall world was tiny.  I got it on sale, but it still kind of feels like money wasted.

As a long time Resident Evil fan I was initially very skeptic of this new approach to the series being first person but somehow Capcom managed to make a competent game out of it, which mostly doesn't fall victim to many modern horror game tropes that many other modern games fall into. RE7 mixes both classic and modern RE formula as one package, at times leaning towards one bias more than the other and vice versa, which creates both really good and really bad moments.
Let's talk about the bad moments because these are the most jarring moments of my playthrough and most of them are either easily fixable and/or avoidable. The first, major and most occurring flaw in this game is its unfair difficulty spikes both in and out of combat. It seems the game's only way to kill me in combat is to either outnumber and/or overpower me with sudden and unexpected strikes. In previous RE games, enemies that come within boundaries of you will slow down and walk towards you to give you time to react, but in this game the times that they relentlessly strike at you they not only stunlock you but they do it at the same time making for an almost instant kill at full health. Outside of combat, the puzzle room where you're trapped in with Lucas results in a forced death right after solving all those puzzles - that's your reward - a death and having to reload. Capcom thought it was a good idea to force "optional" content in order for you to solve that puzzle.
That's another weakness of RE7, the VHS tapes and the story/pacing. The "optional" VHS tapes really are garbage and don't add much to the already weak and dumb story. The one involving Mia is just avoid the scripted trigger box, the Happy Birthday tape is some crappy backstory for Mr. Nobody who has little to do with anything, and the only tape that's worth something is the one you're forced to play with Eveline. The story though, while it isn't bad or garbage, it's dumb and just not the game's driving force for me. The limb detachment mechanic is incredibly dumb, even for suspension of disbelief purposes, and the game attempts to explain this away by some white cell regeneration crap that conveniently only applies to Ethan and Jack. What Capcom could have done to improve the story is make the other characters as fun and interesting as Jack and Lucas, more related backstory, more logs to read, more iconic encounters with unique bosses and to do make the Baker's story more fleshed out in cutscenes. The moment when Ethan was talking to Jack about Eveline's virus disaster was probably the best moment in the story, the game needs more of that!
Other weak areas include the pacing of the game is too quick, the game is too short and it feels like the game doesn't want you to stay in one area for too long - despite the backtracking. You're being constantly pushed forward, sometimes literally, and there aren't enough moments where you can just explore some creepy locations and do some time wasting puzzle solving. It seems all the "puzzles" in this game are fairly straight forward A + B = C, with little room for me to use my imagination on how to find a solution. The only time I became stuck was trying to find more Corrosives in the Ship, but finally remembered about the 2F safe, which was guarded by a puzzle easier than singing the ABC song.
So what're RE7's strengths? Thankfully, they are gameplay and presentation related. The limited inventory, save room with transferable item boxes, RE1/4 style of presentation throughout the game and the variety and surprises that each scenario presents is surprisingly refreshing. The bosses were fun albeit with obvious weaknesses, except for the pit fight, which I really hated because of the stunlock crap. Jack is probably my favourite character and it was good to see him persistently used as the sort of "comeback stalker". During the early encounters, he scared me once when I saw him charging at me with an axe down the corridor, but he breaks out into some genuinely funny dialogue that helps break up the seriousness of the situation.
So I mean yeah, the combat is fine, headshots are satisfying, the variety in guns is okay, there're secrets, collectables and  extra game modes. No Mercenaries Mode sucks hard but the DLC has variety in them. I clocked in 7 hours first try on Normal mode, which is half as long as I expected the game to be. Playing as Mia was cool, I wish it was longer because the Ship segments are probably my favourite in the game, and she has more personality and reasoning for being in the story than the literal faceless Ethan.
Overall, I actually like RE7, I think it's the best RE game since 4 but that isn't saying much since the modern RE games are all garbage anyway. Capcom can do even better by making a longer game, more fleshed out story, revise their design decisions in terms of difficulty, make more challenging puzzles and keep the classic RE systems in. I don't think I'll be replaying the story again but the DLC content should keep me abay for a few more hours.

Great game. A quality TBS, but not for the feint-hearted. This game does not pull any punches, if you are easily frustrated by RNG sometimes going bad on you then you should probably steer clear for your heart's sake!
For everyone else though this game offers a great and intuitive combat system, built on the in-depth character customisation system, which ensures the combat gets more involved as you continue to grow your warband. All your characters have enormous potential for growth and customisation, no red shirts here.
The different warbands all play very differently from each other, which unique strengths and weaknesses that need to be played to if you want to last long on harder difficulties. This makes for some some nice variety in gameplay and enhances the replayability of the game.
Only two major downsides:
1) The predictability of the AI, after a couple dozen hours you will be able to fairly accurately predict how the AI will react to things, and accordingly it becomes easy to manipulate and destroy them by constantly swarming them.
2) The load times. This game has the worst load times of any game I've played in the last decade, no exaggeration. We're talking 5mins+ to load a level on an SSD.

I want SO badly to like this game.  Against my better judgement, I can't stop playing.  A WHF game where you can PLAY as SKAVEN!  Woah!  Despite a very long early access, there are a ton of balance issues.  The game advertises itself as hardcore.  It is riding the wave from the dark souls "difficult games are good" bandwagon.  The problem is, it isn't difficult, it's unbalanced.  Percentages don't mean anything.  You'll have a 90% chance to hit an enemy and never hit them for the whole battle.  You may have a 90% chance to dodge, but the enemy will hit you 3 times in a row.  With 2 of them being crits.  I bought this game when it was first released in early access on steam, and it wasn't this bad back then.  A recent patch says it "fixed" the rng system.  Since the patch, I've just noticed getting critted more often and hitting the enemy less often.  Supposedly the unbalanced RNG system is put in to counter how bad the AI can be.  I'd rather have a smarter AI. There are also so many ways for a warband to get screwed to the point that they become unplayable.  Permanent injuries happen often.  Miss 4 payments of wyrdstone and no more single player mode.  If you get rid of a warrior because of an injury that makes them basically useless (severed leg on an already super slow warrior) and you can't afford one of the overpriced hired swords, then you have to hire a new guy at level 0.  He won't help at all and will just die because the enemies will still be leveled based on your warband's level.  Ok, I've ranted enough.  I'll still be playing this game occasionally because I am a skaven fangirl, but this game really needs some fixing.

I've played the whole Flatout series, and this one is by far the best. Best graphics, more cars. Race grid went from 8 to 12 cars. I prefer the racing modes over the "novelty" stunt or demolition derby modes, but to each his own I guess.
The cars all have unique characteristics as far as speed, handling, nitro, etc, and are nicely modelled. The crashing and environmental destruction is satisfying. The ragdoll physics are amusing and sometimes hilarious. Quite a fun game overall if you like racing and wrecking.
My few beefs with the game are as follows:
-Car customization could be a bit expanded. I think you get a choice of one of six colors of the same basic paintjob for each car.
-Car upgrades are a bit primitive and limited.
-Multiplayer is dead, I've never found an online game
-Could use more variety of tracks.
-Object physics are a bit unpredictable and can be frustrating. You can sometimest plow right through a steel beam with no problem, ten seconds later you hit a potted plant or a lawnchair and it launches your car 10 feet in the air.
The biggest problem I have with the game is the following: Once you have earned and upgraded all the higher-end cars, it's not much of a challenge to beat the competition quite easily.
I often run the crappier cars just to have some challenge involved in winning races, with the better cars it's just way too easy. I wish there were a way to adjust the AI maybe 5-10% faster in order to get some closer racing.
In spite of the negatives I have listed, I still rate this game quite highly for fun factor. Learning the fast lines around the tracks and working your way up to earning enough money to buy better cars and upgrades is an engaging challenge. (although some cars can only be unlocked by winning special events).The problem is that once you've got all the cars and upgrades, you kind of reach a plateau and there's really nowhere to go from there, it becomes too easy.
Bear in mind that this review is focussed on the racing aspect of the game, others might have a lot of fun with the derbies, stunts and special events.
Despite my review including a lot of negatives, they are overall minor in nature. The game is very fun, and can be quite humorous at times. I guarantee you will get some good laughs out of it. It includes easy arcade style car handling, enjoyable drifting, jumping, crashing, ragdoll physics and environmental destruction. It's crazy good fun, in spite of it's few relatively minor flaws. If you enjoy high speeds, crashing, explosions, and sending your competitors through their windshields headfirst into a concrete bridge abuttment, this is for you. I recommend it highly.
Edit: I've seen a lot of reviews bashing this game due to GFWL causing the game to not run. I simply downloaded the latest iteration of GFWL and have never had a problem with it since.
