I believe Empire: Total War is the greatest Total War game of all, with a few qualifications. Of course the undeniable
TW game for me was Rome: Total War the First, which revolutionised the series and whatever genres you might want to identify in the wider title, a game which I have dumped huge amounts of hours into - amounts which grow even to this day by the occasional intense, weekend-long binge.
That opening paragraph may sound a bit contradictory - to begin with I call Empire the greatest TW title of all, then I immediately state that RTW is of course the
, but I am trying to work on a distinction, here.
What I'm trying to say is that ETW was a perfect storm, if you will, a game which came at just the right time, featured just the right shift in scenery and era, brought in just the right technologies and got just the right feel of UI, interaction and general gameplay. I said before that some qualifiers exist and they do - the game is not a perfect TW title - but it gets certain things very, very right.
To elaborate then, I start with the game's position in the series. If memory serves (and really how wrong could it get) the game came after Medieval 2 and the Kingdoms expansion thereof and somewhat logically endured an advancement through the ages to the Age of Empire - but it also came at a perfect technological moment that allowed it to be a true quantum leap over it's direct predecessor in many ways. The upgrade in graphics, UI, gameplay (the introduction of smaller settlements and such on the map) and the addition of naval combat - not to mention the introduction of guns, en masse (more on the flaws of this system a bit later) - all went together to make this game feel many years ahead of the earlier titles in the series, and usher in the later era that we are now enjoying.
The Age of Empire just seems to perfectly lend itself to the Total War idea. Warefare by gun is just that bit more tactical, that bit more impactful and rhytmic. The battles - especially the open battles, far from fortresses and the select range of infuriating consequences to trying to breach walls - have real breadth for elaboration and intrigue...
My lasting memory of a battle in Empire: Total War occured when my Dutch army, emboldened by the easy capture of Norway from the Swedes, marched on their home province only to be met by all the soldiers that should have been guarding Norway on top of the standard garrison. My army consisted of a general's body guard, two run down groups of Cavalry, and three groups of riflemen - we were up against at least twice that number - and many of those units were perfectly respectable, dangerous foes with little militia riff-raff mixed in.
I had retreated from battle once after blindly commiting my army to a seige and pulling out - but that very turn the Swedes marched out to put me to the sword. Terrified, I put my troops to the rear of my deployment zone, on top of a shallow hill with a small but dense wooded forest crowning it, a vague crescent of extra-steep terrain, halfway from the crest and facing towards where the enemy would come from, and another scattering of trees further down the slope but quite a way off to a flank. I arranged two groups of cavalry - including my captain - in the dense forest, and a third group off to the opposite flank behind the scattered trees, while I lined my riflemen along the top rim of the steep section, as best as I could - the rim wasn't wide enough for one group, let alone three.
The battle commenced, and a broad force of enemies set off towards my small group of men. Hanging on by the seat of my pants, I noticed a group of cavalry making a run for the flank of my riflemen that was overlooked by the dense forest, and instantly shot out both of my hidden horse groups to intercept the charge, resulting in a very quick sortie between the advancing lines and my steady riflemen. The banner of the enemy horse group flashed, marvel of marvels, and I took that as a sign to instsantly wheel around and send my horsemen back to the dense forest. briefly pursued, the opposing horse group wheeled away at the line of trees under pot shots from my riflemen, but the battle had only just begun as I sent the horses right back out again more or less instantly to counter-charge into the flanks of a huge unit of footsoldiers who had engaged my left flank. In the mean time I had done more or less the same manouver with my other flanking horsemen, breaking into the flank of a group of riflemen before wheeling away for a second charge to counter the opposing captain as they attempted to augment their advancing rifle troops with a charge by the general's bodyguard. The battle would see-saw mightily as my riflemen gamely held the high ground, wheeling this way and that to stave off probing groups of gunners, while my ragged cavalry units darted this way and that, charging, extracting themselves and charging again, trying always to lock units in pincer movements and circle around behind them to force them to flee.
Miraculously, with only medium losses to ground troops and only about 50% losses to my cavalry units, I eventually forced the entirety of the enemy army to sound a hasty retreat, barring their captain! Noting that I only had one enemy left on the battlefield, I threw everything I could at him - all of my remaining horses charged his larger group from two sides,w hile up the middle charged the remainders of my three groups of riflemen, swords drawn, for the kill. A heroic victory was won that day, and with it my everlasting affection for this title.
Of course, as I have hinted at, this is the greatest and grandest of the TW games in my estimations - mirroring the pomp of the setting - but it is simply not the best because of a couple of isolated by serious flaws.
A) Battle Bugs
Sadly, this game suffers from a few bugs in battle situations.
At one point while I was trying to mop up some pirates in the Leeward Islands my dutch riflemen refused to open fire on pirates crouching behind a wall, despite being well in range and themselves fired upon - a group of natives who I had sent creeping around behind and sprinting along the interior of the wall likewise refused to fight the 'dug in' enemy troops unless I simply told them to run through the enemy position, forcing them to automatically swing swords at them. Likewise a group of horsemen - I love me some flanking - who had circled around the
way had to sweep through and jump over the wall in question, heading for an empty space in the middle distance, in order to finally extricate the enemies from that wall and open them up to uninhibited, bug-free slaughter.
At another point, funnily enough also against pirates but this time at Port Royale, my troops of the Maratha Confederacy (I was trying to carve out some trade routes in the Caribbean) turned up with five groups of cannon and laid waste to the city walls - but not until I had lots two cannon and crew to invisible walls which forced them to walk in mid air, and this was just a prelude to the catastrophe that would be my attempt to enter into the town through the breaches in the walls - my riflemen just about struggled through in a completey buggy way, as did my elephants and such, but then half a platoon of elephants was cut down by the enemy captain, who despite being the last surviving member of his bodyguard was enjoying some kind of god mode bug as a result of being wedged between the invisible wall of the city gate and that of a section of ruined wall. I ultimately won that battle, but the unmitigated annoyance of trying to seige that settlement put my off seige battles for the remainder of my campaign - autoresolving any town that boasted fortifications.
B) Unplayable Factions
I must end now, word limit, but the fact that you can only play the 'major factions' available at the start of the game kills my inner completionist.9/10

Some of my fondest members are completing the Rise of the Runelords and Skulls & Shackle campaigns in the Pathfinder Adventure Card Game. It's a brilliant system, and lends itself well to solo play.
This is a very faithful adaptation whose main effect is to significantly speed things up (playing this physically, you will spend SO MUCH TIME shuffling) and take away the mental-math component, letting you make informed decisions and risks. The art is straight out of the game, but delightfully high res, the music and ambient sounds are much better than the digital version's mobile origins would suggest.
The move from F2P to B2P is a succesful one; this version gives you more than enough cards (in fact, it includes cards from other PACG sets, so much more than just the ones in the RIse of the Runelords campaign it's based on) and throws gold at you on top of that for regular treasure chests.
The one weird part is that treasure chests can give you cards that are well 'above your level' but nevertheless equippable, and thus make the game easier than was intended. I strongly recommend not using any above your current adventure deck number if you want a balanced playthrough. Alternatively, you can just hoard goal and not touch treasure chests until you want to do the higher difficulties (which are there to give the game additional replay value).
Overall, Obsidian has made an excellent platform for the game, and I look forward to them releasing other campaigns for it!

I have never met a game that captures the feel and flow of combat so well. You're fragile, healing potions are few and far between, and there are dozens of monsters between you and your goal: therefore you have to weave a complicated path through killing everything before it can strike, dodging or blocking those strikes, or just plain getting away from your enemies for a few turns.
Card Quest is fast, thrilling, and quickly stealing my evenings since I bought it. It is a card game, but there are no individual cards to hunt down, it wouldn't work in multiplayer, and it's more like the devs replaced typical turn-based rpg combat with cards. Instead of hitting attack, you choose an attack card from your hand. To dodge, use a dodge card when the enemy attacks. There are cards for drawing more cards, for restoring your limited resources, etc.
Okay. The skinny: you pick a class, wizard, fighter, rogue, ranger. Every class has different sets of cards that you mix n' match to build your deck. You can add equippable armors or amulets in your slots that augment different decks. Then you pick your campaign - there are three - and go right into combat. Every campaign is lavish, with short written segments to set the stage, with tons of varied enemies with darn good art, and bosses at the end of every gauntlet. Once you beat a specific segment's boss, you can choose where you go next, unlocking more story and fighting a different set of monsters. Rinse, repeat until you hit the final areas - I can't comment on them, because I'm still back in the catacombs or trying to kill a king.
Which is to say: this game is tough! Once you start getting hit, unless you can turn the tables and wipe out your enemies, you're going to die. A lot. Which is fine, the game is fun!
Play the tutorials first. They're not just good at teaching you the flow of the game, they're good puzzles in their own right and they give you handy equipment you can bring into the main campaigns. I particularly liked the rogue one, where you have to beat up an entire thief gang before they'd let you join.
To sum up: I love this game. I love playing as a wizard who surrounds themselves with electricity that roasts the undead as they swarm, who creates intricate illusions so enemies keep whiffing, who calls down the heavens to zap a towering mountain of corpses. I love how lovingly crafted this game is, with details built into every monster and encounter.
This game is incredible, and I highly, highly recommend it.

Also I wondered if it really would have been that much more work to generate some random background graphics in the enemy display.
Aside from that, I love this game for what it is: An atmospheric Indie treasure!

Great game! Start off with basic classes & decks, which as you unlock others, turn into a wild variety of play styles.
Amazing fun to see what you can cobble together, classes literally change their entire playstyles depending on equipment and accessories. For example, turning the usual glass-cannon mage into a pyro who does huge damage, but has to manage a overheat mechanic, or a necromancer who throws out bigger spells more often the further he goes due to his bodycount, but is almost helpless if he runs out of souls entirely.
It can be a bit frustrating to begin with, as your tools are limited, but this game is definitely designed to be replayed. Eventually you will end up creating decks to specifically defeat certain bosses to unlock others.
As far as RNG / AI goes, it's nicely balanced. Most deaths will come from your own poor choices. Such as bad decks, resource management, or deciding to try and draw one too many times instead of playing safe.

What I expected was a pleasant time playing a Magic: The Gathering clone. What I received was a ravenously-addicting card-based, turn-based RPG that feels like a great game of old thirty years after successful games of its genre have been mastered. I've become so fond of the game that it becomes strange for me to consider that I've played the game for a combined twelve hours—it only felt like a few, at most! Its design is simplistic and challenging, yet so phenomenal in its execution that a lack of adequate storytelling or accompanying music almost doesn't matter. It may be my bias for fantasy RPGs and pixel graphics, but Card Quest has become an easy choice for recommendation. The potential is certainly there for bigger and better content, and if the game's current state is anything to go off of, these developers are ones to watch in the gaming world. They may just make your next favorite game.
+ Challenge encourages learning
+ Simple, but effective
+ Great variety in enemy design
+ Great replayability
- Very limited story
- Lost potential in artistic integration

For anybody born during the 80s, the themes and quirks of 80s cartoons and video games will certainly show brilliantly as you play through this game.
It's important to start by saying that if you think this is going to be a complete faithful remake to the original Double Dragon, you're going to be disappointed- for a short while. Once you start getting into the swing of the game and its eccentricities, you'll know exactly why certain creative decisions were made. This game was clearly designed as a reboot which emphasizes on the martial arts craze during the 80s and 90s, the toy-advertising cartoons with cheesy villians with even cheesier voices, the prevelance of synthesized pop music and the visuals of 80s neon lights. Everything from the visuals, the music and the dialogue are brilliantly done to the point that you'll feel more than a touch of nostalgia from it.
The controls are solid, with the slight delay in attacking a nod to the original game's attack-lag, meaning combat needs to be thought-out. The old system of exploiting patterns to win battles is still there, but the difficulty is still intact, particularly for Double Dragon difficulty. The RPG system of building up stats and powering up special abilities and attacks is a great touch which gives players a few extra options in how they want to approach combat.
I would highly recommend this beat 'em up to anyone looking for an entertaining jaunt through the 80s.

TL;DR:
- Servers are currently very laggy.
- Don't buy right now, if you're a battle-hungry PvPer, because of heavy lag.
- Do buy, if you're here for the fighting itself, and the game's difficulty.
- I still recommend this game, regardless of the lag, since there's an Offline option, if lag is too much.
At the moment, the servers are quite laggy. I saw a tweet that Oceanic servers are up, but regardless of that, heavy lag spike is still ever present. (I live in AUS)
There is, however, an offline mode option in the main menu, if the lag is too much to handle. So you can still learn moves and build your combat deck, and wait for servers to become more stable.
With that said...
I still like the game.
Yeah, the lag is pretty unbearable at times and yeah, 1v1 PvP is, right now, out of the question, since both you and your opponent teleport everywhere every few hits... (Although, you do sometimes get some pretty stable games)
But the devs are working on creating more stable servers.
If you're only getting this for the open PvP and 1v1s, then, as of right now, just refrain from purchasing it until the servers are very stable.
But if you're getting this to experience the core gameplay, creating your own fighting move set, and the game's 'dark souls'-y-kinda difficulty, then, by all means, buy this game. This game will test your reaction time, skill and patience.
The game isn't very long however, so just take your time and explore. (I haven't finished it myself, but a friend of mine told me that he finished it in about 9-10 hours.)
Despite the short length, the areas in this game are very beautiful. Although practically every area is in "ruins", they all still differ from each other.
On that note though, since you'll be exploring quite a bit, you'll also run into the 'bosses' of each area. They'll have a much larger health pool, compared to the normal enemies, hanging around everywhere, and will usually have a unique set of moves. In some cases, some bosses will pull out a set of 'war gloves' or a sword on you. So be aware of that =P
Speaking of weapons, there are 3 types of weapons for you to use:
- Bare hands (Obviously, and you'll be using them for basically the whole game)
- War Gloves
- Swords
While War Gloves are basically the same as Bare Hands, Swords are more unique, as they have their own set of moves. But you can still use bare hand moves, alongside your sword moves.
War Gloves and Swords do share some features though:
- They both have a durability limit. So if it breaks, it's gone. (But if you 'own' a sword/war gloves, they'll still break but you can always 'resummon' them.
- They both can deal damage through guards.
I would explain more, but I think it's best if you experience it for yourself and learn more about the game through your own playtime. Explaining the 'combat deck' would take a pretty long time haha =P
But overall:
Despite the current lag issue, this is still a solid game. Challenging, beautiful but most importantly: FUN!

Short: If you're in this for multiplayer, and a HUGE fan of the TTG, then -maybe- this is for you.  If you're looking for something to fill the space XCom, Valkyria, or other great TBS games did then save your time and your money.
I was so excited by this that I bought it full price as soon as I found out about it.  That was a huge mistake.  I've loved almost every GWS PC and iOS game that's been released.  I've seen other reviews comparing this to XCom and Valkyria, and that comparison is so off base I'd swear they have to be friends with the devs.
Haven't experienced load times like this since Crysis.  But Crysis let you play for an hour after it loaded for a couple minutes, this has load times just to enter menus.  It's rare that a PC adaptation of a TT game is actually slower to set up than the real thing.  Maps are full of fake obstacles (eg: doors don't work, some ledges can be jumped off of/climbed and some can't, despite being the same height and looking the same).
The AI is poor, so they compensated by always making the AI teams stronger than yours.  This means there is one and only one strategy: team up on the AI as they arrive individually as you always lose in a fair fight.  This is not a deep strategy, it's a joke.  Imagine if the only way you could win at XCom is if the enemies came out single-file.  The AI is also sooooo verryy sloooooow, so don't think you're done excessive waiting just because the game's loaded.
The hardcore nature of the game, like roguelikes, is what drew me in.  A lot of players like that aspect, but it was built on top of a game that just isn't that good, and execution that feels half done.

I wanted to like this game, I really did since I'm an avid player of the tabletop game. Mordheim: City of the Damned has all the elements that make a tactical game fun. Campaign play, character advacement, varying scenarios, tough tactical decisions, and I could go on.
However, the game fights you at every corner. The random happenings completely upset the freedom of movement of the game as it locks in your current movements. The AI just ignores the sub-objectives and groups up into murderballs. The RNG elements are just too strong (numerous times I simply had crit-stun-out of action happen against back to back to back). I could sense the fun to be had with this game, but all I ended up with was more frustration than fun. With limited gameplay time, this game is getting uninstalled and downvoted.

This is a tough one. I've given it a fair crack and there's a lot I like about the game, but in the end I've decided that the negatives outweigh the positives.
It has the worst case of RNG♥♥♥♥♥hattery I've yet encountered. It makes bloodbowl look even handed and fair.
Routinely expect to rack up failure after failure at apparently simple tasks. (Writing this, I have just failed 13 sequential attempts to climb a wall that apparently had a 67% chance of success). It's also common place for you to miss a swing at an almost dead opponent who promptly turns around and kills your hero, while tzeentch strikes down your spellcasters at random. There's not enough men in a warband to compensate for these failures, so each battle quickly becomes incredibly frustrating and a few bad luck failures in a row cost you the battle and theres nothing you can do about it.
Crappy map work with lots of inexplicable cant-go-there spots.
Bugs. Many and various bugs. Ranging from graphical glitches and some twitchy camera work to it being completely random whether or not your guy in ambush stance actually attacks people moving into his range. Also I'm damned if I can figure out what conditions you have to satisy to make "charge" an option. Sometimes its' there, sometimes its not.
Gameplay is slow and drawn out. I've played for about 15 hours or so and only completed 1 story mission. Exciting it is not.
Battles have optional objectives which are intended to shake things up, however the moment you come into contact with the enemy you quickly become tied into a series of small fights and the optional objectives are forgotten. Since the enemy will rout and the battle ends as soon as more than 2-3 guys go down you never get a chance to go back to them.
The RPG elements dont appear to have much affect on the gameplay. None of the skills you can learn are really significant, most add a couple of % to a few RNG tests which, as previously stated, are utter bolloks anyway. Certainly they're massively outweighed by the effects of injuries.
Obscenely long loading times. I mean it. Go get a drink and do something else while the levels load.

I've been obsessed with all things horror since I was a kid, so it generally takes a lot to creep me out, but this game did. I know a lot of folks will disagree, but for me this was probably the creepiest game I've ever played. I think a big part of that is the shadow creatures you encounter, a lot of horror games (and movies) often lose that creepy atmosphere for me once the monster is revealed because I often find them too cheesy, but this game really plays on the fear of the unknown in that and many other ways.
This game also did an amazing job of making me feel like I was the character, which is not easy since you play as a 2 year old. The atmosphere it creates had me on edge the whole time, so I was hiding under every bed and thinking just about everything was the legs or feet of a creature while I was under there. On top of this you crawl faster than you walk, you have to drag and climb on objects to reach door handles, hugging your teddy bear companion provides a light source, etc.
A must play for anyone into atmospheric horror in my opinion. 10/10 and I really hope Krillbite will expand on this game further and/or release more survival horror in the future.

All opinions have been made after reaching level 60 in-game (current cap)
+ Combat system is as intricate as it is satisfying
+ Open-world aspect allows for fluid and unpredictable player interactions (whether that be fighting/teaming up with another player)
+ Diverse map locations showcased in a beautiful yet minimalistic aesthetic
+ Many different martial arts styles/moves to learn (everything from Capoeira to Zui Quan)
+ Boss fights that actually require your full attention and proper strategy
+ No Pay-2-Win aspects or ‘Cash Shop’ microtransactions
+ Very intense 1v1 PVP deathmatches (when the servers are actually online)
+ Includes the option of dynamic swordplay that seamlessly flows with the overall pace of the game
+ Knocking your opponent out with Calbot
- Very steep learning curve
- Matchmaking can sometimes pit a level 15 with a level 35+
- Severs are currently unstable and are offline most of the time
- Players outside of the US have too high a ping to be competitive
- Learning new moves requires a heavy amount of grinding
- Lack of diversity in enemies
- Offline saves allow for the modifying of user files that can lead to exploits/unfair advantages
Final Verdict:
If Sloclap fixes their server stability issues this game will be much better.  Learning new moves and perfecting your strategies offline is fun; but the game alone cannot support itself on just its singleplayer aspect.  That being said, I would still recommend this game to the hardcore beat-em-up fan who is looking for a fresh new perspective on the genre.  Considering the game is less than a week old, I am hoping that Sloclap will hastily fix their server instability; otherwise I will be forced to change my verdict to a thumbs-down due to Absolver's lack of overall longevity.
TL;DR version:
Absolver is an extremely difficult, yet satisfying, fighter that suffers from a lack of online server stability and hard-to-access content.  Only buy if you are willing to wait for developer Sloclap to fix their server issues, otherwise this game will be a mostly linear singleplayer experience.

Mordheim: City of the Damned
I’ve always loved table top games and played a little Warhammer 40k back in the day, and I’m a huge fan of 40k themed games, but I never really got into the classic Warhammer setting.  This was my first real experience both with the classic Warhammer setting and Mordheim, and I love it.
The gameplay feels like how a tabletop conversion with great graphics should, and at first there isn’t a whole lot to fights – knock them out before they knock you out.  As the game picks up you gain levels, new units, items, skills, and enchantments and things start taking off.  Skills and items sets, along with unit placement and scavenging, becomes a huge part of every encounter.  If you get far enough, you can even unlock some units from another faction for more diversity and options.
As many people have discussed, the game is brutally unforgiving.  Think XCOM on Ironman and one of the hardest settings – as much as I wish I had the option to turn off “Ironman” in this game, it’s built in.  The Random Number Generator (RNG) is more forgiving than it used to be, but people who are “perfectionists” will quickly find themselves stressed at all the things they cannot control.  You will miss with a 95% chance to hit, either because you rolled a “1” or because they dodged.  You will also get hit when your guy has “135%” chance to dodge incoming attacks.  And that’s the beauty of a true table top conversion.  Even gods have brain farts.
The weakest aspects of the game, at this point, is balancing and AI – and they Venn diagram into one another where the weakness of the game is concerned (for me, at least).  While each faction does something a little better than the other, the units are mostly the same across the board with the only real exception being Impressives and the Chaos faction’s large number of Fear/Terror/Alone immunities.  The AI also leaves something to be desired.  I often find that 1 or 2 of the enemies in a fight get stuck on walls, in doorways, or on stairs – especially common for the larger Ogre, Rat Ogre, and Chaos Spawn Impressives.  This is great for the player because it means less to manage, but it is also frustrating – it makes victories feel cheap, keeps you from fulfilling optional bounty objectives (as it is often the bounty targets who get stuck!), and you never know when that guy is going to decide to stop derping into a wall and join the fight.  Another problem is the way the AI will often bee-line for you - which means that Heroes, Leaders, and Impressives (that don’t get stuck) are the first you run into, which also means they’re the first of the enemies to go down before the henchman can support them if you’re patient and set up proper ambush points.  The way the game “balances” the poor AI decision making and pathing is by simply making them stronger than you.  In a “normal” fight, the easiest on the map, enemies have more wounds (hit points) and hit harder.  It scales up with difficulty; the hardest missions simply have units with 40% more wounds and damage on top of their guys having more skills and better stats.  What this means is that you will never have an even match-up against the AI; you’re always expected to out play them as you’re never on equal terms.
Despite the issues above, the developers are intent on polishing their game.  They are already working on improving the AI and making other adjustments as/when the community brings up issues.  The game has a lot of potential for growth as the Warhammer world is huge, with tons of units and factions that could be included, as well as more cosmetic options for people who are really into the customization aspect.  I look forward to seeing what the developers do and I hope to see more games like this, especially a Warhammer 40k type!

Thoroughly enjoyable. Not a deck building game, in case you were wondering.
You pick a class and, to start with, have no choice in character setup beyond that. As you progress through levels, you unlock permanent choices in character setup for that class. Those choices are set unlocks, eg "Unlock the xtreme four swords and belt pouches fighting style for Fighter by beating the forest, level 2-B".
Your choice in where to go is branching, so you want to ideally beat everywhere as everything to unlock all your options.
What do you do with those options? Each character class has three slots for card packs, which contain a preset group of cards per pack. Those cards build and consume various resources, and so you want to have a fair balance of build and consume for things. You also have three equipment slots that augment certain playstyles by drawing, generating, or damaging.
The art is not "great", but very much has the "oldschool RPG" charm. I enjoy the art here more than I'd enjoy something generic and bland.
The gameplay uses a few relatively simple basic mechanics for the monsters you encounter, with a good variety of tools for dealing with them, and you're made to consider what to do. It's not super duper deep, but it's also quite beyond the bland fare of clickers and very basic RPGs. You're at the mercy to some extent of RNG, but card draw and cycling is common enough that having the right type of deck matters a lot more in the later areas, and earlier areas are more a case of learning to use what you have.

Half a year ago I stopped playing Card Quest out of frustration, as it had one of the best tactical card-based combat systems I'd seen, which felt squandered for me as the fights were mostly scripted encounters, becoming almost puzzles to be solved. Coupled with the requirement of going through all the previous fights after every new death, it just became a chore to do the fights I could win with my eyes closed just so that I could get to the one I was struggling with.
Now a lot of things ghave changed - the encounters are still mostly scripted, but there is much more variation within them, you can finally choose how to level up your character, and there's a lot more items and subclasses to give the game some much-needed variation. You don't feel like guessing the designer's intended path anymore - instead you're solving emergent issues on the fly. And you don't have to do the early fights for hundred times anymore (although the requirements for it  are still a bit too restrictive, in my mind).
So yes, Card Quest is now making full use of its combat system, which relies on fighting-game like combos and careful management of very limited resources. There's no CCG element (although you can unlock decks, which are basically subclasses), so what you see when you start a stage is more or less what you will have to get by. There's never a point where you feel invincible, as it's often enough to overstretch yourself for one turn to receive a kicking, from which it'll be difficult (but not impossible) to get back on your feet. So Card Quest one of the more unique roguelikes on Steam, but despite being different it doesn't feel experimental - as of now, it's a fully realised and well thought out game.
Strategic, interesting, different characters have very different playstyles - if you like card games & turn based RPGs, this is the game for you.

This is a tentative recommendation. I enjoyed the game, but not quite for the reasons I expected.
When I bought this game, I expected it to be something of a 'deck-building' game, when it's really more of a resource-management game. That is to say I expected to theorycraft some overpowered decks by finding hidden synergies between card packs, but the way the game is designed causes most card packs to only work with a few others, and it's fairly obvious which ones go together and which ones don't.
In mechanics: You have three slots that can hold a card pack, and put together they create the deck you draw from. Most of the card packs will also use or generate a secondary resource, so if you try to combine packs that generate fire and use arcana (for example), you won't be able to attack or defend yourself for very long. Now there's usually at least two to three card packs per slot that use or generate this secondary resource, but that also means there are very few combinations that work together and it's pretty easy to see which ones will drain resources faster than they can be replenished.
Also on the negative, you unlock these sets one piece at a time, so the early part of the game is extremely difficult and grindy until you've unlocked enough packs or equipment to put together a new playstyle.
And finally, the endgame is pretty boring because there are a few easy-to-find deck combinations that are overpowered and will let you destroy pretty much anything before it can fight back, just because you end up generating more resources and cycling more cards than you use.
So why do I recommend it? Well, I could say that many card packs have special effects that aren't explained until you start using them, and they often force you to play the class differently. I could also say that the game does include a large enough variety of enemy mechanics that you'll need to keep a strategy in mind even by the end of the game. But really, I'm not sure. Maybe I just enjoy the rhythm inherent to a late-game character when I know which cards to chain to keep my resources strong. I'm hesitant to recommend Card Quest since I have more complaints about the game design than praise for it, but I had fun and I don't regret buying it at all, and that's the bottom line I'll judge a game by. Hence, the tentative recommendation.
I wouldn't recommend it to people who don't play card games, can't handle a difficult earlygame, or don't enjoy resource management, but I would recommend it to those who are looking for something interesting and different.

This game is a weird combination of good and complete♥♥♥♥♥♥
The story is really great. Writings on point, you come to care about characters, and even though most of what happens in the story is predictable if you're familar with this formula, it still keeps you on the edge of your seat wanting more.
This of course is countered by the gameplay being incredibly sub-par, and in some places, bad.
Taking cover and shooting feels fine I suppose, as good as it can for a third person shooter, but movement feels really floaty and just bad.
And the in between parts of missions, i.e. driving around since this is "open world", is waaay to overloaded, and this isn't helped by the fact that checkpoints are really punishing. Driving to and from missions becomes really obnoxious to do really fast, and it really makes me wish it was just a mission based game.
Speaking of that, I really wonder what happened to this game during development, because it seems like tons of content was cut. It's an open world game, with no open world elements. Sure you can go sell cars to a guy for cash to grab clothing or guns, but that's it. There aren't any side missions in the world, which is strange because you can go find npcs and prompt them for a mission, to which they'll say "I don't have anything for you right now", and they never do. But, there also isn't an in between time, so to speak, between missions. Its just one mission after another. It's really strange.
Also, if you want to enjoy yourself in this game, slap it on easy. The amount of times you die in absurd situations is many. I played through this game once back in the 360 days, so when I picked it up on here I decided I'd go ahead and play through it on hard, which is damn near impossible.
You get shot from every angle, enemies just run up to you when you don't expect it, and only some enemies are marked on your mini-map, so you often don't know if you're about to die or not.
I'd still recommend this game, because it IS good, it's just really janky. I'd say it's probably about a 7 or an 8 outta 10, and that's really just because of the story.
Also, skip the DLC, it's rubbish.

To their credit, Obsidian has finally bucked the trend and released a game with only a small number of game-ending logic bugs and crashes*. Good job guys. Took you long enough.
That said, they have made a really beautiful** port of an incredibly mediocre board game. Pathfinder Adventures is a very straightforward card game. There are so many location decks filled with a certain assortment of either helpful or hurtful cards, as well as a boss character somewhere within. Could be at the top, could be at the bottom. You flip a card and then must roll a die to either acquire the good card or defeat the bad card. And naturally since it's a co-op card game on PC, you're gonna be playing four different people at once which still will not be enough to require any thought or planning.
That's the game***. There's no real excitement or sense of adventure at all. You have a certain number of cards in your hand which you can use to boost the die or get better dice by discarding them (Or sometimes keeping them, if it is a weapon you are qualified for.). But beyond that there are no real choices. Always flash your best weapon, throw the best spell you can afford to lose, and chuck some dice. At least when classic RPGs are throwing dice, they at least show your dudes shooting or slicing at each other and the dice is behind the scenes. Here it's precisely the opposite.
This is a perfect game for turning off your brain and just relaxing. Move your dude, shuffle some virtual cards, chuck some virtual dice, and once you win, you get to pick up and shuffle around cards that give a minuscule +1 compared to the ones you already have to make you think tweaking your deck is fun. This is not a bad loop at all. It can be brainless, but still fun in a skinner box sort of way.
Brainless skinner box fun, huh? I guess that explains why Obsidian made this a F2P mobile game before porting to PC. Makes sense. Suddenly your board game has daily challenges with gold with which you can buy extra "cheat" cards to throw into the campaign stash or rainbow colored dice or alt characters or whatever. Luckily, in Obsidian's defense here, if you buy the game, you get the game. You will have free access to the entire box set of the first season of the PACG card game if you buy in at the base price, no BS there, and you are free to ignore it, play offline, and just play a pure version of this trivial game.
I'm mean to this game. I'll probably still play it because it's gorgeous, but it feels as flashy but insubstantial as most F2P mobile games when it is supposed to be a card game.
That said, having the game handle the shuffling and the dozen little fiddly effects (Oh this is +1d8 melee buit I get +1d4 Strength, but this uses dex for melee which is +1d12 instead and since the check is undead I get +1 and since it's divine I can roll some dice rather than throw away the card and...) certainly makes it more useful than the card game if you didn't have enough alcohol handy to trick your friends into suffering through this.
But compared to something like Sentinels of the Multiverse, this is only barely a game.
*EDIT: lol I just researched the history of the mobile release of this, apparently it released with one whole mode, the randomly generated quest mode, so bugged as to be unplayable. Unable to salvage it, Obsidian ended up cutting it. THERE'S the Obsidian we all know and love from way back!
**EDIT2: When I say beautiful, I mean all the art and assets and UI design provided by Obsidian. They did their job well here. The card game itself? Eh, the cards are ugly as sin. Plain solid backgrounds with really cruddy bug-eyed Pathfinder brand art; because apparently to Paizo a fantasy adventure is a carnival freakshow of increasingly uglier things for you to fight or befriend.
***EDIT3: In fairness, I have been told later scenarios break up this gameplay loop by a gentleman in the comments. I have not gotten that far.

I played this tabletop and on IOS so I knew a bit about the game before buying.
There are some bugs, which are annoying and I'm a little annoyed that they didn't give us the game for free on steam if you bought in moble like they said, but we did get some free goodies so I'll deal with it.
Anyway, the game is a nice implementation of the tabletop with extra cards, alternate chars and some bonus features. If you know nothing about the tabletop game, it's a semi-deck building adventure. You pick heros, they get a deck and they 'level up' (Gain new feats, skills etc) and collect new cards.
The objective of most scenarios is to find the villain, which means going though locations. Locations are decks of 10 cards with either a henchmen or a villain. When you find a henchman and defeat it, you can close the location. The object is to close enough locations to be able to tap the villian so he can't go into an open location and win the scenario. Locations contain cards that can be boons which are items that can go into your deck, or banes, things to keep you from winning. Each sceanrio has a timer of 30 turns, which you must defeat the villian by then.
The game has normal, hard and legendary mode allowing you to challenge yourself after winning, so there is a lot of replayablity.
Overall a good game if you are intresting in a different type of rpg.

I'm going to skip right to it, the only game I have been compelled to write a real review for.
For starters it is not the longest game it personally took me about ~3hrs to finish the campaign, however that's not the end of the boss encounters though, its replayability is tied to your level in pvp (which I have no problem with) that allows you to fight harder versions of the bosses you have already beaten changing their habits, attitude and abilities.
...now the important part of any fighting game
If you have a good connection online paired with another person that also has a good connection, boy o' boy does it feel nice, the hits feel like the hold weight, they feel heavy when they need to, they are fast when they need to, in a evenly match game it is palm-sweatingly intense duel.
The classes feel balanced and the variety of attacks feels refreshing.
I went into pvp without the knowledge of what is called a
hit only to realize I had been performing them and succesfully chaining them unintentionally purely because the input and the way it chains felt natural.
In saying that, with a poor connection online the game becomes a diceroll of luck, delaying inputs and magically teleporting enemies that don't stop hitting you frames earlier than the animation knocking you into a new dimesion.
This is solved however with the addition of being able to completely play offline with the only issue being that you obviously cannot play pvp.
The
landscape paired with the
tones span the world effortlessly with the only problem I've seen being very small texture clips on few cliffs and walls, the transitions of areas are well done creating a seamless world that feels alive.
The camera can be cause of a lot of problems when it comes to being too close to walls in a fight, somewhat breaking immersion and forcing you to look in very strange angles losing the flow of combat.
The UI especially in inventory can be annoying to navigate once you start getting a lot of different pieces of equipment but that is nothing but a personal annoyance.
I've yet to experience any major or noticeable fps drops running ultra on a i5-6600k and a gtx1070.
Overall I love this game whether it be online pvp or offline grinding, I was skeptical that it wouldn't feel right using a Keyboard and Mouse but it's something the team at Sloclap have made feel second nature, it has it's lag issues and to my knowledge that is one of the top priorities of the team to resolve, I highly reccommend this game to anyone that enjoys fighting games and hope the developers expand the game further because of its almost limitless potential.

TL:DR that's stolen from this thread
but sums up exactly how I feel:
"There are many situations you can get yourself in that there is no way, with the unit AI, to recover. Sure a 'verteran' player will know to avoid these situations; but this isn't SC2 or something were talking about here. This is a mobile-level clicker game for PC with pretty graphics. No one apart from a few masochists are gonna spend the time to learn in depth a game which they're only going to play for a few hours anyways.
To that end the AI really needs to be much better. Certainly you can work around it, but an unintuitive and stupid AI that requires micromanagement, in a game that makes micro near impossible, is just frustrating. There's nothing 'challenging' losing 4 hours of gameplay simply because you built a wall a little too far out. Sure, you won't do it again, because most likely you won't play the game again."
Now for my actual, personal review:
Honestly, I'm not sure how to feel about this game. I kinda wish there was a meh button. I have 2.2 hours in Kingdom: New Lands and 2 hours in Kingdom: Classic as well (comes with this purchase, basically it's an older version of the game). Having gotten it in a bundle, I'm satisfied with it, and I actually do think I will keep playing it some. But I don't think I can recommend it for someone to actually buy, unfortunately. It is fun, and the graphics are nice, but there's one fatal flaw that makes me give this game a negative review: you have very little control over anything. As an example, check out this thread, which is not by me but presents a problem that I've run into and tried to find an answer to:
The person responding to that post basically says "That's how the game works, so it shouldn't be changed." That commenter makes the forum seem pretty toxic, and it seems that many other people defending the game give this same argument. "That's not how the game works and it's not changing so deal with it." Good game design isn't "This is how the game works so this must be the best way to make the game." The game developer is not always right.
Pros:
+ Nice graphics
+ Simplistic gameplay
+ Easy to run (my graphics card is busted right now so I have to play on my laptop with integrated graphics, so this is a nice plus)
+ Comes with two versions of the game
+ There's a wiki that explains things, probably isn't official but it's helpful
+ Interesting concept
+ sense of exploration
+ save files
Neutral, depending on your perspective:
o The game doesn't really explain anything for you. This can be nice, but I think the game handles this poorly. It's possible that if the other flaws were fixed though and they left this alone though that I wouldn't think this, so I'm going to leave it as a neutral.
o The horse gets tired when you run. Can be annoying since you have long distances that you have to traverse, but is also realistic and makes you think about the best way to use your stamina, so up to you whether this is a pro or con
o Games can be pretty long for a permadeath game: see the last of my "fatal flaws"
Cons:
- Trying to figure out the game seems to punish you. See the last of my "fatal flaws" for elaboration
Fatal flaws:
-- No unit control. This means that all your archers may end up on one side and you can't do anything about it. You also can't convert people to different people, send knights to the opposite side of your fort, etc.
-- Can get into stagnant scenarios: I've had a couple times where I haven't been able to really do much of anything, but I also wasn't losing, so it was really just trying to figure out a way to just do at least something for a long time. One of them I'm currently stuck in and it's making me not want to go back to the game as much. Maybe you don't have any archers and you only have carpenters, maybe vice versa, maybe all your archers are stuck with knights that are useless, but there's a lot of times where you can't make much money but also aren't dying. The first time I did this, I built too many archer towers and all my archers got occupied and stopped earning me money. The second time, I saw a boat wreckage in the forest so I thought "oh cool let's build this" and then the majority of my people boarded the boat and I didn't have a way to make money. The third time, I hired a knight to destroy a portal (after checking the wiki, because I had had enough of trying to figure the game out only to lose all my people), and it died, so I decided to try again with two knights. I got two knights, and the majority of my archers joined them, but it only sent one knight to the portal (so I'm not sure why I was even able to hire two?). They destroyed the portal, but now all my archers are sticking with my knights and not hunting, so they're not making me any money, nor are they defending my base because all the enemies are now coming from the other side. This is where I'm currently at, and it's making me not want to go back to the game
Overall, this game can be fun, but it's flaws can be severely irritating, and I'd say it's not worth a buy. If you find it in a bundle though, go ahead and play it and see for yourself. It's at least fun for a little bit, but definitely not worth $15

I came close to liking this game. Its main ideas are pretty neat: Use a simple interface and control scheme to build up a kingdom/town that will keep you alive long enough to repair a ship to sail to new lands. The mood is really nice and the game itself works as a great podcast-listening game. Unfortunately, the RNG in all aspects is obnoxious.
The gameplay is a mixture of some light strategy, tower defense, and Minecraft/Terraria night defenses of your town. You earn and spend coins to upgrade defenses, recruit townspeople, build an economy, purchase upgrades, and build the inevitable ship to escape the current "level." It's all done with no menus and with a side-scrolling 2d control setup. The core of the game is very sound.
Every time you get to a new land, the layout is randomized. I've actually been screwed a few times because the game put enemy portals between me and recruitment camps, and since recruits slowly saunter to your base and get easily killed, I was screwed unless I could use the one night after a Red Moon to recruit two or three dudes, which isn't really enough to keep up with hordes.
it's also about a 50/50 crapshoot that your townspeople are useful at all. I've watched 6+ elite archers unleash on a wimpy single enemy vanguard unit just to have all of their arrows sail overhead, allowing the enemy to bumrush and instantly wipe out my walls. I've watched farmers hang 10 feet out of walls every night just to get whacked by enemies instead of just getting behind the wall. Catapults prioritizing single enemy units instead of clumps. Volley after ♥♥♥♥ing volley of the majority of my arrows hitting my own walls instead of the glob of enemies tearing away at them.
I found myself having to work around clunk just to get things to work right. For example: When you buy a catapult to defend your left flank, the catapult will automatically defend the furthest-left wall you have. Since the siege shop is right outside the first left wall, you are required to build up a second wall or that catapult and crew will just sit in the open until they are killed, flushing 12+ coins down the drain. So this creates a situation where you're at an advantage if more enemy spawn points are on your right flank because it just means you can have a catapult on your right without having to build extra walls, while you're in a bit more of a pickle if the enemy spawn on the side that your siege shop is on.
It bothers me because I feel like I've had very little to do with my failures in this game. Even RNG-laden games can make the player feel like every death is their fault, but I rarely felt like any game over in K:NL was the fault of anything but awful friendly AI and bad randomization rolls.. If I could have my way, I'd have combat abilities of villagers upped a touch, design the RNG so it won't give players bad level layouts, and require all recently-recruited peasants to sprint back to base, or at least increase the distance from which they sprint back to pick up equipment. The game also NEEDS the ability to deconstruct buildings so I can do things like tear down a tower to free up an extra archer or be able to tell my townspeople to defend a different wall (I suppose that's to keep you from just building a million walls so that enemies don't have enough time at night to attack you, but be reasonable). I'd also like to see the stamina of the basic horse upped a bit, but I could see that unbalancing things.
There's the layout for a great game here with some frustrating elements that really hamper getting in the way of something I could genuinely love and recommend.

It is with a heavy heart that I write this review. I bought into this game while it was still just out of alpha, and in that raw state, I could easily see the potential. I loved the tabletop version of Mordheim, but when people complained that this was not that game (which was a true statement,) I could defend it on the grounds that this was a different good game, as long as the devs fixed a few problems with it.
The biggest offenders during early beta were:
Poor RNG
Poor deployment
Unbalanced warband ratings (the AI always had higher ratings, sometimes significantly so,)
An impossible midgame (survival rate at warband level 5 was practically 0.)
Navigation difficulty (can't see the map except with a largely useless overhead view.)
I watched as the devs tweaked and tweaked. I continued to defend the game because they were trying to fix it. Eventually, I left the game for a while. I figured I would come back closer to release to see how it had changed. I did not get back to it until tonight, a little under a month after release.
I jumped back in and discovered some very beautiful new splash screens! The visuals had all gotten a touchup, including my warband models. Things were looking up!
Then I started the gameplay. My warband rating was 440. My opponent's rating (on regular difficulty) was 500, a 13% difference. Still, I could do this! It would be challenging, but what game worth its salt isn't? I started to play. Within 2 turns, my warband (which had been randomly deployed despite the fact that I wanted to manually deploy them) were being 2v1'ed. I had 2 henchmen that I could not get to the skirmishes because I could not find the right set of stairs. My engaged warriors did about 10% damage to the opponents' healthbars, who then one-shotted one character and stunned the other. (This was in the second round of the game, first round of combat mind you. I did not engage the enemy models because I knew I needed to gang up - I just could not find my way around the map (or even find a way to escape the enemy's close proximity.)
By turn 3 I had lost 2 units, one of whom was my hero, and routed. I then had both die in the after-action report.
I know that a good game should be challenging, but this level of stupidity is just...well.
I cannot recommend this game. I really want to, to validate my choice to buy in during beta, but in the interest of integrity, my advice is don't. Just don't. Find some other challenging game, one where the RNG doesn't kill you instantly, one where you can find your way around the levels, one where you do not lose because two warriors randomly die after only your first battle.
Find some other challenging game. Find a good game. Not this one.

Short version? it's fun, and a definite buy with friends to play it with.
Long version, Mordheim is a game that really tears me up, on one hand, the emotional side of me gets attached to each character, you can customize each one with a flurry of options and even write your own biography for them.  On the other hand, if you actually use them and they are put out of combat (happens pretty often by the way, even if you're experienced a bad RNG for a match can still ruin your day.)  then they could get brain damage, lose a limb, an eye, get a permanent wound, or even straight up die, which really breaks my heart when I spent so much time making them into a real character and then firing them because they got hit so hard they don't even remember where they are in the next battle.
So, if you like emotional heartbreak and aren't afraid to use a little imagination, definitely a game for you.
While the RNG can be a real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times, its usually fairly balanced and you'll get an extremely good game for each extremely bad one.  The game plays A LOT like XCOM, just in a very different setting.  To make things even more fun, it plays like XCOM does on ironman mode, with autosaves aplenty and no save scumming (or at least minimal) so what you do actually means something.
So, if you like XCOM, and want a challenge, go for it.
But maybe you really hate the fact that there's no progression in XCOM, that every game means you lose all your previous progress, well well well,  Mordheim's got you covered.  They put in a "Veteran System", which basically means the more you play, the better each new warband you make gets, crazy stuff right?
So if you like progression throughout an entire game and also through each one of the warbands you create. you know what to do.
You like choices?  Well, there's a few.  Sure, four warbands may not be a ton of choices, but like the rest of the choices in game, they actually matter.  Each different warband actually has an entirely different storyline, that's baller!  I mean, that makes the game like, 4 times more replayable, at least!  Not to mention each warband looks and plays distinctly differently.  You may play your sisters of sigmar like tanks, and your skaven like rogues, or you could do it the other way around, I don't judge.
So if you like choices, yup, this game is the way to go.
Maybe you hate difficult games, well then this is tough for me to recommend, but I'll do it anyway!  In fact, you should recommend it too!  Grab a friend, name a warband "The Salvation Army" and feed your friends to your heart's content!  Easy mode has never been so, well, easy!
Want something easy? Yeah, mordheim even has that.
Or maybe you wanna show off the greatest warband that has ever existed.  Can't get enough of rubbing it in your friends faces that you wreck everything, but don't want all your grade A units to come back from a battle beaten and bruised? Oh man, guess what?  Yeah, morheim's got you.  In exhibition mode you can crush your friends warband without actually destroying it for real, proving you're the king of the city of the damned (for whatever that title is worth.)
Like to brag?  Do it.
I guess it wouldn't be a review without a bad section though, I'd like to see coop 2v2 warband matches, I think that'd be cool.  Then you could mix up your strategies and build warbands around support, I'd love to see some straight healers supporting another warband, it would bring a whole new perspective to the game.  The item interface is mildly annoying, the fact that you can't drop items and cant get rid of anything unless you put it in a chest is really inconvenient, especially on missions where you have to pick up certain items, but I suppose you could always just consider it another resource management tactical choice "should I pick up this nice item? or use this character to go get the quest items?" Finally, impressive units are insane, I have to push my whole team on one to even attempt to fight it, and if its friends are nearby they wreck me.  It's not even about luck at that point, they are just entirely too good at both offense and defence.  My whole team can barely take one out (relatively early game) and then they get to have 3 swings on my characters?  It's like the game is trying to wound my warband.
So, get this game, and also, if you don't have friends, just add me, I'm game to feed you whenever.

I will levy one bit of criticism against a particular RNG element in the game.The smite or "magic kill debuff" is really unecessary. In the game using any spell has a chance of giving your spellcaster one of a variety of debuffs or negative actions. Some examples are:
-turn ends immediately
-reduced accuracy for a couple turns
-other stat debuffs like hit chance
One of these negative actions in response to ANY spell cast could be a smite which deals 9999 damage to the caster and thus insta kills them. This can happen to your casters or the NPC team casters and I've seen both. Ultimately it's too strong a penalty and I think it stronglty discourages using casters. The other debuffs are one thing, but the insta kill is too much. Why have a caster when you could just recruit another melee hero who has no chance of dying on an arbitrary action? It already takes a ton of money just to teach them spells so why bother?
This is the games biggest weakness in my opinion and I wish they would remove it. Even when it happens to the opposing team it's usually not a big enough deal that it changes the tide of battle and if that is the point of it, an RNG mechanic that can change the tide of battle, it can be done in a lot of other more interesting ways.

Resident Evil 7 is a masterclass on how to reinvent yourself in todays modern survival horror genre. The story manages to drag you in and drop you into this visceral experience seen through the eyes of a newcomer to the series. Following a distress call from his missing wife of three years, Mia, you take on the role of Ethan as you step onto the Baker Property and beyond. Mainstays from the series return in excellent fashion as the game also returns to that familiar feeling of dread last seen nearly 20 years ago in the Spencer Mansion (which interestingly was built by the same contractors that are to credit for the Baker Residence.)  Do yourself a favor and pick this game up, especially if it's on sale - I myself grabbed it during a Capcom sale.
Personal ratings:
Graphics - 9/10 Some prerendered backgrounds are very noticeable when a majority of the game is rendered beautfiully.
Controls - 8/10 Some aim assist issues and general clunkiness (which apparently is lessened in vr) are present
Story - 10/10 I absolutely enjoyed the main story of this game and appreciated its pacing. While there is some slow-down towards the final portion of the game I found that the story didn't skip a beat.
Sound - 8/10 There are several sections in this game where the sound design places the sound behind or around you than rather where it is coming from. Notably in the Old House section.
Replayability - 10/10  While I haven't completed this game on the Harder difficulties, I have completed a second run for several achievements. There's enough beckoning you into returning to this title and dredging through the harder difficulty modes that give this a perfect replayability score.
DLC - As of posting this review I haven't purchased the dlc for this game.
Rating - 9/10

Long version.
This is a PvE single player card based RPG. There are currently 3 scenarios each with different areas. Each areas also mean different enemy with different dangerous things.
There are 4 player classes and each has their own subclasses.
Each classes has its own card set and item. Each classes also play completely differently.
Example,
Fighter offensive cards has higher stamina thus attack less often. But this is compensate by Fighter is the only class with 0 stamina defensive card, with actually stronger effect to boot.
Rogue offensive cards has low stamina cost and can kill so much in 1 turn. But defensive card is pretty expensive, and Rogue will dead fast if has insufficient stamina for multiple enemy attacks.
Most items in this game are not better/worse than any other. Each has different play style and suitable for different type of encounter. Player should always experiment and make own sick combo.
New update also let player choose level up perk. Each classes has it own set of perks.
Since there are so much play style within a class, you will choose different perks for different card/gear setup.
Each scenarios has multiple routes and bosses. It can only completed by 3 runs in order to unlock all items.
This actually give a lot replayability. Some combo might work in this route/zone, but more useless at another area.
Developer actively listen to forum post and try to improve the game. The balance might not perfect yet but is getting very close. Most item/card give unique gameplay for all classes.
The game offer a lot of gameplay value and should be loved by strategic fans.

A highly recommended spiritual lovechild of DreamQuest and CardHunter. If you disliked either of those titles this probably won't float your boat either, but if you enjoyed them or have never tried them this is worth giving a shot. Don't be turned away by the graphics it's all about drawing cards and murdering monsters.
What is the Game?
Essentially the game is about unlocking and equipping new equipment and loadouts, which give you abilities and access to different sets of cards. Ex- You can make a Berserker / Longsword / Spiked Shield combo for your Warrior which would create a deck for you on Berserker Style defensive moves, Longsword attacks and combos, and Shield Blocks that harm the enemy.
After you set your character you go out into the dungeons which are a series of fights leading to a boss battle. Kill the boss and unlock a new item for your character class! There are 3 dungeons each with 20ish floors total so there is a ton of content to fight through as it's a pretty different experience with each of the 4 classes. The better content does tend to live near the end so as you progress you do tend to become more powerful in addition to simply becoming a better player.
Overall - The class variety, the replayability and overall gameplay make this is an easy sell for the pricepoint. I've sunk a ton of hours into this game and still plan on playing more. At this point the devs are close enough to full release it might make sense to wait for the official launch but it's very playable currently and basically all the game content is present, so don't let that stop you if you want to jump in. The core design on the game is really well executed and the classes and weapons and styles all play and feel surpisingly unique from one another.
The Devs are super active so despite a few balance issues both across classes and within classes I'm very excited to see where they take this and support them moving forword.
Definately give this game try.

This crazy physics destruction derby arcade racing title provides more evidence that its developer, Bugbear, might hate cars almost as much as it loves making games about cars. The numerous ways the vehicles in this game can be dented, smashed, crashed, crumpled, and shredded may well make petrolheads weep tears of dismayed sadness, but then, that's the fun of it. The entertainingly visceral physics engine, that sees cars and environments alike torn apart violently at the slightest touch, provides a fascinating look into what the Burnout games might be like if cars were continued to allowed racing after the otherwise fatal takedowns.
It refines and expands on Bugbear's previous FlatOut game exponentially, which makes it slightly infuriating that there are unforgiveable surface blemishes on an otherwise impeccable arcade derby racer. The inclusion of Games for Windows Live has basically all but guaranteed that the online community for this game is dead as a doornail, but perhaps worse, in my opinion - and certainly more invasive - is an absolutely wretched soundtrack. Seriously, I don't think I've come across a worse use of licensed music in a videogame. The cheap, faux-metal pop-rock that found its way into this game's soundscape is utterly painful, and I had it switched off almost immediately. I don't quite understand how these music choices were made, save that they were the only they could properly afford. At any rate, the music is abominable, and while I must stress that, that is my opinion, I will also stress that my opinion is, in the case, unquestionably correct.

Bringing the Total War series to the gunpowder age, Empire really nails the "line of battle" style of warfare. It had the biggest map in the series to date, with three massive theaters to conquer and several small trade areas ripe for naval control. Diplomacy was massively overhauled, bringing much-needed improvements and making negotiating actually viable for once.
It also introduced several completely new features, including epic playable naval battles and a tech tree to progress through the campaign, both of which have become staples of the series. The historical battles, while great, are less polished than normal and lack the intro cutscenes that are usually featured.
There's a mini-campaign included that allows you to play as the USA through four stages of history - Jamestown, French & Indian War, American Revolution, and finally as the USA on the Grand Campaign. It's a special version of the Grand Campaign that starts at 1783 and is incredibly challenging.
The biggest downside to the game, by far, is that the DLC unit packs are more or less required to have rosters that feel complete. This was CA's first game to experiment with DLC packs and they left many elite units off of the vanilla rosters, to be included in the DLC. If you get the DLC packs, then the game is amazing, but I fear for the experience of anyone trying to play it vanilla.
The Warpath DLC is interesting, but a rather disappointing expansion campaign when compared to the others in the series.

Among the Sleep is both beautiful and tragic at the same time.
The story unfolds in such a way that it leaves room for your imagination to run wild as you explore creatively designed areas, solve fun interactive puzzles, and hide from the monsters under your bed.
I was very impressed with the controls and the detail put into the game, from the cute pajamas right down to the stitching in the rug that you crawl across. Tons of items are intractable and it is surprisingly easy to lose yourself in simple things like stacking blocks or piling toys into chests.
The monsters in the game are unique and tie very well in to the story – no spoilers, you need to play to the end! There are several moments in the game where the monsters can come after you, but if you are patient and hide well then they can be avoided to some extent.
I really enjoyed this game, I even came back and played it again for the achievements and the prologue. The story is incredibly touching and will leave you with some pretty heavy emotions by the time you reach the end. Among the Sleep is a gem, don’t miss out on this one!

text:
It has top notch customization. You can modify almost every element of most of your firearms. You can modify a gun's receiver, barrel, muzzle, stock, sight, bullet types, and colour. You can also throw on trinkets on them. The customization doesn't stop there: you can also modify your character. There is a wide variety of helmets, body armours, and leg armours to choose from. You can equip different gears in different slots. You can even modify what you can buy at the depot (a "store" that is found within games where you can buy things such as hardsuits with the points you've gotten from kills, assists, objectives...).
It has superb optimization. It is also very friendly towards free players. Essentially everything can be bought with free currency. It also is not plagued with RNG elements like many F2P games (and even paid games). In BLR, all guns are very quick to kill. TTK is superb, although this makes all guns feel the same. Combine the fast TTK with essentially no recoil and you get stale, boring weapons. The skill ceiling is pretty close to the ground.
The gameplay is really fast. In BLR, you are forced to fight or die. HRV is a unique gameplay mechanic that definitely adds to the uniqueness of BLR.
That said:
The game has a dead community and what is left of it is scummy people. There are updates (and bug fixes) every century. There is virtually no depth to the game. There is almost no story. It comes off as "just the casual F2P FPS", which is sort of strange considering how much customization there is in the game.

Card Quest is the trading card game you wanted to play without all the hassle of min-maxing your deck with all the random drops. Each character has a specific subset of equipment they can use (and collect during the game), with each piece of equipment coming with a pre-selected array of cards - in other words, you select three mini-decks that together create your overall deck. I find it a welcome change of pace because while I can appreciate the hardcore fine-tuning of your deck with specific cards, sometimes you just want to focus on the tactical aspect of the battles.
You'd think this would make this game a walk in the park, but nothing could be further from the truth. The tutorial will kick your teeth in as you learn the basic synergies and possible combos you can string, and then the main game will shower you with more options, more challenges and more headscratchers.
The best aspect of the game is that it never feels as if the game simply decided to screw you over. When you lose, you can always pinpoint your defeat to a mistaken discard, stamina overuse, poor target selection, lack of foresight, etc. There's always a way, and that way is never dependent on buying a legendary card pack with your hard-earned money.
If you're casual about card-collecting, but you love a good challenge (and what a challenge it is!), then look no further.

Thanks to the popularity of Hearthstone, which built upon the success of Magic, the PC games market has seen an explosion of card-combat games hitting the market. Within the genre are many different varieties of games. What Card Quest has accomplished gives it a strong sense of uniqueness while maintaining traditional values of card games and dungeon crawlers.
The combination of presentation, high level of challenge (to the point of a healthy level of frustration) and the significant diversity in the gameplay make Card Quest one of my favorite games in the genre that I have played.
As it continues through its development cycle and closes in on graduating from the Early Access program, Card Quest, has the potential to be one of 2017’s sleeper hits. It already represents tremendous value at just $7.99 (the prices will likely be increased upon release).
As I find it illogical to provide a review score for a game that is not yet officially released I'll score this game on the hype meter. With that in mind, I score the game a well-deserved 8/10 on the hype meter.

The Windows Live thing is nothing to concern yourself with. When the game starts, it logs into Windows and then the main menu appears without a hiccup. The achievements you receive are actually recorded through Windows Live. So again, there's no problem here, you can play with or without it.
The graphics are NICE, man!
MUCH better, shinier and sharper than I would've imagined.
I have it turned all the way up on every setting. It looks gorgeous; much like the hi-res screenshots you see up top (not that video or any YouTube video you come across). It'll leave tire marks on the road when you turn sharply or burn rubber. When the gas station gets ran over, the fireball blast is really sweet. The car models were done with care. I love the junkyard body and paint jobs. Excellent lighting and visuals that can compete with any ENB+SweetFX modded Grid game. The collision damage is NOT on par with Grid, let's make that perfectly clear; but it does get the job done.
The framerate is spectacular.
There are no FPS drops and the game runs smooth as butter. Even Grid has a problem with this from time to time on the best systems (google it). Not this Flatout version, though. Every race has been nothing short of fulfilling track drama at the highest of speeds. Only Gas Guzzlers races are faster...and more...insane!
Customizing your ride is awesome.
Every upgrade has its positives and negatives; but I didn't realize that at first. I tricked my first ride out with all the upgrades, thinking it would be able to just drift to victory with ease. Nope! It was too heavy and beefy to carry all the speed upgrades. So it turned out to be a general ride instead of the General Lee. It gets me 4th place with consistancy. Thank of it as an M1 Abrams in a muscle car frame...with speed enhancements.
The Tracks!
Here is where the game comes alive. The tracks run more like Gas Guzzlers Extreme; so you have variances throughout the race. I don't think I've ever made the same lap twice in a single race yet. Almost everything is destructible like in GGE but even more so in this game. I also like the fact that they incorporated ramps to lauch off of. There are times when I really do feel like Beau & Luke Duke in the General Lee. My ride is flying 50 feet off the ground with my confederate flag license plate hanging on by a screw and mud spewing from my undercarriage. We race (and crash) through dirt, asphalt, water...highways, lumber yards, farms, back roads, suburbs, cities...with a combination of each at times. It's awesome, man.
Flatout: UC is what racing should be. Just a few good ol' boys & gals racing cars meant to be raced!
