TLDR; This game could be so, so, SO good - better than Civilization V - if the ground combat didn't suck so, so, SO bad.
The city-building, trading, politics, etc. are all great. The problem is combat. You get two options. Option 1 is "auto resolve", but the math behind the "balance of power" scale (which determines who wins and by how much) is way broken - I've pitted massive armies against tiny ones and the "balance of power" was sometimes shown as even, so auto-resolving meant I lost as many units as I killed despite having triple my enemies' forces (no significant difference in troop type, i.e. I wasn't fighting strong units with weaker ones). Even with the horrors of option 2 I still always got better results doing it that way instead of auto-resolve.
Option 2 is "play the battle yourself", which is what drove me to write a bad review. At first it seems like the coolest thing ever. You get thousands of little troops and the graphics are gorgeous (especially considering this game is 7 years old). HOWEVER, the control over them is ridiculously clunky. There is no attack-move - they run until they reach their destination, then they have to form up in ranks again, then stop moving, then they can start shooting, but they only attack in a cone, so you have to point the cone towards the other troops. Your guys won't turn on their own to face enemies, so if the other troops try to flank your guys, you have to manually turn them by holding down a button, or just repositioning them entirely (which takes 15 seconds to do). This means that every unit in the game behaves like fixed artillery instead of sentient people with legs holding muskets. Many times even if you are mostly pointed at them (enemies within attack cone but not centered), and in range, and BEING SHOT AT, and your guys are dying, they will stand around and do nothing until you point them at the enemies better, and then they still have to finish repositioning to the new orientation and getting into formation before anyone will shoot. I have never played an RTS where your foot soldiers will stand there and take it while being shot at without needing a very specific "do nothing" command. Since they have to be in perfect formation to shoot (you can't just stop them mid-move and let them fire at nearby enemies), this means that the 100-200 soldiers in a group don't actually attack as individuals but rather as members of a whole, so really you only have 15-20 units that act like mob artillery instead of 1000 individual foot soldiers. After hundreds of hours of Starcraft and Starcraft 2 this is painful to experience.
Think you can paint your whole big army and tell them to move somewhere in a giant 1000-strong advance? Nope! Since there's so damn many of them, and they can't overlap while moving, giving 1000 units a concerted move command on anything but a salt-flat-esque open area just results in them confusedly (and very, very slowly) jamming up together and standing around doing nothing (while being shot at and dying) so each of your 15-20 squads have to be moved individually if you want anything reasonable to happen. This is as big a letdown for me as the previous paragraph, as I bought this game because it seemed like less micromanagement than other RTS's but really you have to micro MORE because you can't leave a squad alone. The best solution I found was to form my troops into a giant horseshoe at the beginning and leave them, and wait (minutes) for the enemies to walk into the attack cones.
Sea combat is awesome. The satisfaction of flanking a ship and catching 'em in the crossfire (send 'em down to see Old Hob) of 48 broadside cannons and watching chunks fly off before they disappear to the crushing black oblivion of Davy Jone's Locker almost makes up for the ground combat.
Overall 5/10, would maybe play it for the Jack Sparrow Simulator portion again.

After retrying the game today, for some reason, I decided to remove my previous review which had a very strong focus on the context of the game rather than the game itself. The recommendation remains negative though.
The first thing you'll be asked to do when starting a new game is to choose a mode (career - which means you start with limited resources and have to acquire more to build bigger ships - and creation - which means you have access to nearly an infinite amount of parts). Sadly for the career mode there is only 3 starting option, start with a small fighter or a freighter and the last being no ship but with some random part in your stock which sometimes produce quite awkward results. You will then set the size of the galaxy and how many factions inhabits it as well as name it (this is actually your save).
The core of the game is the ship design/building. You have several parts of several types which you can use and they come in various sizes (with some blocks shapes that are specific to a size or another). Once you build your "hull" and depending on how many parts of this or that type you set, you have space to put subsystems. Weapons are set on hardpoints which you also set by placing those weapon mounts. Overall the system is nice and as long as you remain in the hangar, lighting and controls are manageable.
The UI is sometimes a bit annoying as you can get menus overlapping each others. To give an example, when you have the parts panel open and go to the shop, the parts panel has priority over the shop one which does not make much sense as obviously when you open the shop you ain't going to build your ship. Another example are the pop up windows when you place modules which may happen partially off-screen. Those are details and are easily sorted (as you can close the side panel of part directly or drag the windows) but it shows an unfinished or unpolished state of the game.
Once you launch your ship, that is when the state of the game really shows. The first shocking thing that struck me is the lighting. While lighting is kind of realistic (light source = sun) and background is pretty dark (nebular clouds are also pretty dark) it often leads you to barely seeing your own ship or which direction she's headed.
There are several promising features in this game, although it is difficult to get involved. Mining is the first thing I tried to do and while it is easy to grasp and do, it is not fun. You select an asteroid, warp to it at range, bring the context menu again to mine and then... well, you wait till either the asteroid is destroyed or your cargo is full. I returned to the station I came from by warping to it and hoped to find a docking option in the contextual menu while having it selected, but you have to manoeuver manually in the "docking line" first and then on approach you get to confirm you want to dock.
Once docked with your cargo you of course hope to sell it. So first you need to transfer the cargo from your ship to the station and then you may trade it. When trading, you click on each goods and then select a quantity you want to sell. There are little option to accelerate this process like "shift-click" to sell all of a good.
I won't detail combat or faction interractions here, although my overall experience of those features was that they were pretty bland. Of course I did not play enough in career mode to fully appreciate the content of late game like having tons of parts and a huge vessel for example. You can surely experience that directly with the creation mode, although my feeling is that if you're not solely an avid ship builder this will kind of work like a cheat and chances are that you will roll over everything else in the game once you launch your masterdesign and subsequently loose interest in doing anything else in the game very quickly (there is no story to uncover and generally speaking nothing that gives you a real sense of accomplishing anything anyway).
As I said above regarding mining there is this feeling that the game does not make the player participate actively to the things he can do and at the same time make actions available to him sort of chores. It is not a that much of a bad game, but the unfinished state sadly end up with this product being mediocre (this is apparently explained by half the studio workforce, 2 on 4, having left the project). I would like to see it updated and apparently that is also the opinion of the remaining employees, but everyone's got to eat and I can't blame gamers for not buying this leading to the makers having to work on something that is actually economically sustainable.

This is the only game I have ever played that has a warp drive of sorts (except star trek online). You can build your own ships from scratch, and make truly any design you desire. NPCs will also have these ships available, meaning you can give them ships that equal your own in terms of power (so the game changes as you become more inventive). It is tricky to manage the subsystems along with the space of the ship, but once you know what you're doing everything should be fine
The worst thing about this game would have to be...the repetitiveness of placing weapons. You have to select your turret each time, and place it so it looks right. The mirroring isn't as finely tuned as the mirroring in Kerbal Space Program. Additionally, once the turret is down you must go into the weapons subsystem and select what each individual turret should be equiped with. Making large ships with lots of subsystems can get tedious and/or confusing, especially if you want everything to look even (which I do).
A good point, the galactic relations allow you to make enemies and allies, which can be fun. Trading is something that I haven't yet figured out, which leads me to believe that it's poorly explained, however overall this is a fun game if you want to build your own ships and fight others in space.
The main thing that would make this game a massive improvement would be multiplayer, better controls, better graphics, simpler mechanics to build ships, and getting rid of a few mission scripts that don't work.

This game is a combination of 80s nostalgia and all the weird nonsense we associate with 90s nostalgia in 2014. Where do I start with Double Dragon Neon?
If you're familiar with the glory days of NES and Arcade gaming, Double Dragon is a legendary side scrolling beat 'em up. It reallly paved the way for the genre as a whole, and is definitely a standout in the realm of retro gaming. It's a must play for anyone interested in classic games.
That being said, Double Dragon Neon begins with an HD recreation of the original game's first level which is almost completely faithful to the original, with the exception of the game's much newer gameplay mechanics. Then you blast off in a pagoda rocketship and fight a skeleton in outer space.
I have mixed feelings about this, because the original Double Dragon did not have space skeletor or rocketships. However, the game is good enough that I can forgive this bit of poetic license. The game includes standard beat em up mechanics, but with added modern features of active dodging - hard to get used to but incredible once you get the hang of it - and upgradeable special abilities. The fresh take on the old visuals is great, with comic book inspired rendered models that really look like updated versions of the classic characters. Standing out above everything else is the soundtrack, an 80s inspired mix of rock and new wave that really sounds like something that you'd hear on the radio in 1985.
I strongly recommend this game to any fans of classic beat em ups. It's a trip, and while it takes its liberties with the source, it really does feel like a labor of love.

The game I chose to play for essay 2 was called “Among the Sleep”, its great qualities were it was scary and was very detailed. In the game the mother is portrayed as a scary lady and she screams and grabs you at random times and the only way for her not to get you is to hide, which keeps you scared the whole time. Also the detailing throughout the game is very good like giving off hints to show hoe the mother really was to the child. For example there was drawings on the walls that shoed the mothers actions towards the child and alcohol bottles were thrown everywhere showing her addiction. The down side of this game was how it ended and it was very difficult to see and move around sometimes since it was in the dark. The game ended by the toddler just opening the door to his father and his mother was left in the kitchen crying.

Among the sleep is a first person game where the player character is a baby. You play as a small child and along with your trusty Teddy Bear side kick you must search for your mother, solve puzzles, and get through the horrors present in your own imagination. It is a curious and frightful nightmare for the toddler. The narrative goes to some nightmarish places, but it ends all too abruptly, and technical issues apply the sleeping cap to an already mixed release. The story behind the game is a well-written script and the ending is just a little heart warming. One problem the player might have is the control part. If the player does not have a mouse, it would be a hard for them to get through the game. The player would use the trackpad, but it would take some time to move things around and open doors.

Among the Sleep takes you to a whole new dimension. You start to believe you are really living in this child’s shoes. This video game has ton of interesting visuals which hold important clues most of the time. I absolutely love the creepy feel! The vibe is amazing and really creeps you out, the whole atmosphere is eerie and just plain SCARY, including the music. It’s crazy to think this game actually gives you some emotional attachment, you start to think carefully in order to help yourself (the toddler) out. The storyline behind this game is chilling! You have many ideas of what themes are involved and the ending provides great closure! Not everything is what it seems in the game. Overall, great exciting game! I really enjoyed playing. It was incredibly fun; and very creepy at times thanks to teddy. I would recommend this game for any creepy adventure video games!

In Absolver, you will fight a handful of random goons in the tutorial, and then be given access to the combat deck.

ATTENTION: IGNORE ALL NEGATIVE REVIEWS TO DO WITH SERVERS AND PERFORMANCE
This game had just recently launched and did not expect the sheer quantity of players it had recieved. More servers and servers in different locations around the world are still rolling out, be patient. There are a few bugs which are to be expected from a completely new type of game. chill fams.
THE REVIEW: When it comes to actual gameplay, absolver is a solid, solid PVP FOCUSSED FIGHTING GAME, something those who leave negative reviews about a lack of PVE content do not understand. If you do not like hardcore, deep pvp, you will not enjoy this game, THIS IS NOT DARK SOULS, despite the many, inaccurate comparisons.
When you enter the world of absolver, you are in control of a starter character, eqipped with a heal spell, a basic move deck, a special ability, and some starting armor. The PVE content of the game is meant to teach you the controls, as well as give you some levels, moves and equipement to start PVP with. Other players will be present, along with npcs in your world provided you are connected to the internet, of which you may befriend, or fight. Moves are learned through blocking, dodging or using your special ability on said move, as another character, npc or player, attacks you with it. Armor and other equipment is found in loot staches hidden around the PVE world, as well as from fallen npc characters and bosses. lastly, spells, which apply buffs, or debuffs to you or your opponent are gained upon defeating boss characters.
Character customization in absolver nears endless posibilites, I am still unsure of how exactly the loot system works, but it seems you can find the same pieces of armor in different states of decay, colors, weight, and stats. Combat decks are fully customizable, each of the many moves starting in in either the 2 forward facing stances or 2 backward facing stances (left or right) and ending in one of the 4 stances, flipping depending on which side the move started on,
ex) if you start your front right combo with a roundhouse kick that finishes in the back left, starting your front left combo with the same kick would leave you in the back right stance.
Combos are mixed up with an alternate attack, which can be activated at any time durring your combo with your alternate attack button (ps cont: triange, xbox cont: "Y"), these alternate attacks will reposition you to whichever stance they finish in, allowing you to easily switch between and mix up combos. combining this with the use of feints, blocking, special abilities, spells and weapons, makes for a nearly endlessly deep combat system, which differs greatly from other fighting games which are most likely 2 dimentional, and have characters with preset moves, combos, stats, and abilities.
Weapons are another interesting feature which can further spice up combat, in the PVE world, players are able to find weapons on the ground, or take them from npcs which spawn with them or pick them up of the ground before you. Like with armor, Swords and "war gloves" can be found and equipped to your character as a spell, and can be summoned using shards (mana) that is gained through dealing and taking damage. "War gloves" are armored gloves which increase the damage of hand based attacks, such as punches, and as such, you may use any of your empty handed moves to make your "war glove' deck. Swords are a different beast, they are equipped in your right hand, and have their own unique moves to learn. Empty-handed moves can be used in your sword deck, however it is best to learn as many sword moves as possible to maximize use out of said sword.
Each move has damage scaling with either, strength, dexterity, or mobility, the first 2 are improved with stat investment, the latter by wearing lighter armor. the scalings of each move COMBINE into an overall deck scaling. once you have a deck you are happy with, look at the overall scaling of the deck, and build your character around that, not the individual moves, something I discovered a little bit late.
Many for-honor-like and souls-like labels have been unfairly attached to this game, neither come close. Absolver is entirely new, aside from the souls-esque open world and bonfire like "altar" checkpoint sytem (which is very good). As long as the developers stay attentive, and add more content targeted towards longevity, such as a ranked pvp system, and a single player, or coop dungeon, the mechanics of absolver are solid enough to keep it alive and well for countless years to come. If you like fighting games, PVP, character customization, and the satisfying "THWACK" sounds that come from beating someone senseless, this game is a NECESSARY BUY.

Absolver is a fluid, martial arts inspired, non-linear, semi-open world figting game. It has a complex system of attacks and skills that can be polished to perfection with regular practice and a simple, but effective gear system. But more importantly this is the best looking game you will ever play. The beatifully stylised graphics leads to an experience to be reckoned with. The art style and art design is pitch perfect and the stunning enviroment design seals the deal.
This game takes the idea of game and runs with it, there is little in the way of detailed exposition, and nothing that is explained to you feels forced. The fact that for some of the more complex concepts in the game you must work to understand them really makes this game feel rewarding.
There is no mini map in this game, just one large map that can only be obsered occasionally, this means you must explore the game in detail and learn your enviroments. This means that after only a short time you have come to learn the world around you, a process which is often hindered by mini-maps and waypoints.
All of this combined leads to a game where you really have to learn, like a martial art, and that makes this game one of the most rewarding you'll ever play. Practicing a new trick or combo until you get it right in the practice zone rewards you with a real, tangible skill which you can aply to your gameplay experience.
The story is a bit vague and shallow, but the game makes up for this with expertly crafted atmosphere. Also due to the absolute non-linearity of the game, the story is forced to be unintrusive. SO, if you're looking for a story driven experience, this game doesn't really supply this. However, the game does form a story, through your unique journey.
The game is, in terms of completing the story, very short but the rich and immersive gameplay outside of that is far more expansive.
So, in terms of ratings:
Art: 5/5 - Spectacular and breathtaking at times
Music: 3/5 - Fits the game well enough
Gameplay: 4/5 - Unique and immersive
Multiplayer: 3/5 - Interesting but underdeveloped
Co-op: 4/5 - Fun with friends
Requirements: 3/5 - Quite heavy
Length: 3/5 - Short
Functionality: 2/5 - Often buggy
Personal enjoyment: 5/5 - Loved it
Enviroments: 5/5 - Great
Tl;dr
Total Score: 37/50 - A unique gameplay experience with brilliant art design, interesting combat and spectacular enviroments.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike conducted by the Imperial Japanese Navy against the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on the morning of December 7, 1941 (December 8 in Japan). The attack led to the United States' entry into World War II. The attack was intended as a preventive action in order to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from interfering with military actions the Empire of Japan was planning in Southeast Asia against overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States. There were simultaneous Japanese attacks on the U.S.-held Philippines and on the British Empire in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong. The attack came as a profound shock to the American people and led directly to the American entry into World War II in both the Pacific and European theaters. The following day, December 8, the United States declared war on Japan. Domestic support for non-interventionism, which had been strong, disappeared. Clandestine support of Britain (e.g., the Neutrality Patrol) was replaced by active alliance. Yeah, ok...for half a buck I can't really ask for much, right? :-\
You basically get what you see: a simple physics game: remove blocks in such a way that a block hits Romans but not other characters (like that Christ guy). I could talk about graphics style (standard), the storyline (100% tacked on), but again: half a buck.
Still...I downvoted because the levels just aren't very well made. There usually isn't an "aha" moment when solving things, but rather a series of trial and error.  This complaint is diminished a bit because the level at least isn't expecting a perfect solution (it uses the three-star-system for this), but it doesn't hold my attention.
So...there you have it. I'd say it's a good effort in learning how to make a game (probably worth pointing out that aside from perhaps a controversial theme, this game doesn't do anything wrong either...it just doesn't stand out in any way whatsoever).

Being a veteran from tabletop Mordheim I just had to try this game. Like most games I feel this game has its strong points, oddities and areas with room for improvement.
Yay!
- I like the graphics and the field of view when you run around the city with your warriors, at no time did I get odd camera angles or lost sight of my warrior.
- I like the movement system and the option to retrace your steps when you realise you ran the wrong way (This ofcourse is not possible if you get ambushed/ step in a trap/ pick up loot.)
- Once loading is finished the missions are smooth going.
- I like the campaign system. The missions in itsself arent too varied but every battle is hugely differant anyways.
- customization is quite nice. Some more wouldnt have hurt at all but you can give your warriors fairly uniqye appearances. I like it you can see on a model which sort of armor it wears and what weapons it holds.
Undecided:
- Some more information would be nice at times. The tutorial is quite informative but a little more explaination about how combat works would have been apprechiated.
- Loading times. Pretty darn long. I guess this is where refills and bathroom breaks come in. Mitigated by the lack of loading once a mission starts.
- Difficulty settings: I like it when I can decide myself at what difficulty I play. Yes, you can (ussaully) decide to stick to 'normal' missions but it'd be fun too if you once in a while were the stronger gang on paper yourself.
- I am not in too far so maybe this still is to come but I'd be neat if there were engagements with more then 2 gangs involved. 2 weaker gangs ganging up on a stronger gang? Yes please.
Nay
-Only four types of gangs! I realise the studio is small and adding new gangs costs a lot of time but I for one wouldn't mind paying if some gangs were added as dlc's. Gimme orcs! Undead! Elves! Dwarves!
-All games being Ironman can be heart rending when you lose a valued member of your gang. Not seeing what your taking out members of other gangs results in is a bit dull. Why can't member be captured?? I'd be nice to have some sort of league idea where 64 gangs slug it in Mordheim in a Blood Bowl tournament style. Then it's fun to cripple an opposing warband.
Despite some nays I still think all in all the game is quite worth the bucks you pay for it. If you like turnbased strategy and warhammer fantasy then Mordheim is defenitely a game you should try.

The game features a good story overall, with a lot of deep and hidden things that have to be put together, as it is not spelled out to the toddler protagonist. Loved figuring out the child's issues and real problems behind this Alice in Wonderland-type exploration. The controls and mechanics are a little strange. They make sense, with them being a toddler, but the game features a slow waddle in the up-right standing position and a faster crawl. I found myself almost bugging out the game switching back and forth too quickly so I could move around at a faster pace. If you just slow down the animations get laggy, but as long as you let yourself fall into the game this shouldn't be an issue for you. Other than that has pretty good overall controls and mechanics. In closing, I definitely enjoyed Among the Sleep and would recommend it to anyone to give a try to, but good game overall.

*SPOILERS DUH*
Among the Sleep is a horror experience trauma that gives a perspective of a young toddler going through an adventure with an imaginary talking teddy bear to find the child's lost depressed alcoholic mother. The visuals and effects the developers interpret on how the gamers witness the young child's point of view of the environment surroundings, figures/toys, and the monsters are all a horrifying imagination. Overall, the game has a very unique idea, an original concept, and a wonderful short storytelling experience, but the only downfall is wanting more out of the game. Personally I wanted a little bit more out of the game, more to the story, perhaps what happens next after the father takes the child. Will the mother ever come back? Will she regain strength and fix her issues with alcoholic? Questions left me to wondering on what could happen next. Sequel or without, I enjoyed the overall premence of the game and will give my rating 4/5 stars.

In its current state, this game is barely playable. An average turn takes several minutes to process (around 5 minutes most of the time), the game is very buggy and unstable, and the AI is laughable. It really, really pains me to say this, but please, stay away from this, even on discount.
1. There are a lot of different units, and those are quite accurate.
2. The OOB is pretty well researched.
3. Map is pretty large and quite beautiful.
1. Oh boy. It's harder to say what works.
2. The game runs really poorly, even when other games on the same engine by the same studio work well.
3. It's very unstable and CTDs are way too common, although it's still much better than on day one.
4. AI is laughable. In the Grand Campaign it spreads its units a lot so you can beat them apart. It makes it way too easy to win. Russians have sent Kutuzov with a small force to Vienna when I was approaching it. Two perfectly good armies remained close to Poland and very far from Vienna. Defeating Kutuzov and what remained of the Austrian army was not hard at all.
5. There is absolutely no coordination between AI allies. I know, the Napoleonic Era is famous for examples of allies not cooperating too well, but there is nothing here. They won't fight battles together at all unless by coincidence.
6. Diplomacy is very buggy. Asking Austrians to give Bavarians their lands back missed most of them with no option for me to change it in any way - there was no way to give them Regensburg or any other lands for that matter, just Munchen. I was also unable to ask for some cities in Italy causing a terrible Austrian enclave in Padova. The Pressburg Peace chain of events is broken for me - it doesn't grant me any new territories like it's supposed to but reverts everything to status quo which is game-breaking. So far, I've received no response from the developers.
7. There are too few decisions and events. It would be nice to have some peace options as decisions where you have to decide how far you want to go in your demands, depending of course on how badly beaten your opponent are.
8. Sadly, years after release this is still not good and according to forums, it probably never will. It's a shame because they managed to fix the Pride of Nations which is actually a pretty good game now, but cannot give this one any love.

I feel that a large number of the negative reviews about this game has to do with the crashing, while I have played it for a little over four hours I only had one crash. I visited the forums and saw some very helpful tricks to fix stability of the game and it hasn't crashed since.
As a long time wargamer, but not entirely familiar with the AGEOD engine, it was surprisingly easy to pick up and understand without having to dive deep into the players manual.
Pros;
-A massive amounts of artwork for portraits and other unit cards.
-All of mainland Europe was modeled, hundreds if not over a thousand regions.
-The UI might seem or look a bit outdated, but it's extremely streamlined. It's easy to see data, and the tooltips are in fact helpful. (As a new player this was very important to me).
-The battleplaner is a very way to make an impact on battles, and if it works out, you will be rewarded for choosing the correct plan.
-It's also very nice to see that naval warfare is in the game, as I haven't actually engaged in it yet with my Austrian campaign, I can see that the British and Spanish are duking it out over the high seas every turn :)
-Diplomacy is pretty well done, as it is possible to craft alliances and other diplomatic relations with all of the nations of Europe and elsewhere.
-The game does have scripts so that things are somewhat structured, however there is leeway in that so the player does have the ability to flex theire strategic creativeness.
Cons;
-I wont' add stability / crashing as a con, as I believe the community has this issue using newer cards on an old engine. Using the forums and contacting their tech support is the best approach.
-Tutorials are somewhat helpful, but it can take a bit of rereading to pick up minor missed details. I recommend visiting youtube, and the forums for more information about the game.
-I think the largest con I see is that it can take a while for the computer to process turns, even gaming on a HPC it can stil take several minutes to get through a turn. (However once a turn is complete, depending on what nation you're playing as, you might need to take 15 minutes or more just to get everything done during your turn!)

Kids of Hellas : the fifth game of the Hercules series. The concept still works : a real-time casual game with resource management made of several levels with specific goals (collect x gold, save x kids and open x gifs, kill the minotaurs, etc.). Let your servants gather wood, food and gold, build some constructions such as farms and mines and help them remove obstacles thanks to Hercules, Megara, Cerberus or even Medusa. Fortunately the portal system is back, there are hidden objects to collect again and puzzle pieces to unlock additional levels.
The story is about creepy kids this time, as Ares decides to create a zombified army by using enchanted toys. Your goal is, as always, to foil the sinister plans of the Gods by destroying the factory and saving the children in the process.
This fifth game feels a bit easier than its predecessor, however, it remains enjoyable if you're familiar with 12 Labours of Hercules. If you're looking for a casual and mostly easy game, yet entertaining with a relaxing soundtrack, or even just to kill time, Kids of Hellas will do the job, especially given that the game is regularly on sale. There are 23 achievements to get and trading cards to acquire by playing for collectors and achievement hunters.

First of all, this isn't GTA, so get that idea out of your head and you'll be OK. It is a linear story driven game based in an open world environment. The story is outstanding if a bit tropish, but tropish in a good way, it is well executed in every way. It is believeable and the charactors are believeable. The writng is excellent and the voice acting superb. There was no point were I wasn't completely immersed in the world of Vito Scaletta, aspiring wise guy and WWII Vet.
The atmosphere is filled in with the era's music and what's on the radio changes as you move forward in time with each completed chapter. The cars change with the year and conversations people have on the street are remnicent of what you might expect two people to be talking about at that time, although the variety isn't very broad.
It took me 17 hours to finish and unless you really like the story offers very little replayability. For these reasons and the fact that it's not a new game I wouldn't buy it for $30. I bought it at 75% off, although 50% off would be well worth it IMO. The DLC offer very little to the game, I wouldn't get any of them unless they are at least 75% off.
In 2017 the game's graphics hold up very well and the game isn't demaning on modern hardware. I played it in 4K and although it clearly doesn't have 4K assets it looked pretty fantastic. The controls and physics are very good, I would argue better than GTA V in many ways. Auto aim on the controller isn't as good as in GTA V, but this made me play it with a keyboard and mouse when I wasn't driving and it is hands down the best way to play this game.
All in all, this game is a true gem and comes highly recommended by me. It'd be a real shame to miss out on this treat.

The Good:
If you actually know what Resident Evil used to be (and was supposed to be) then yes, this is in fact a great RE game
. I won't lie saying this is the perfect "return to roots" nor the most amazing Survival Horror experience I've ever played, because it's not, but the elements of a proper RE experience are in fact right here in this game: Exploration, backtracking, managing limited supplies, key hunting and puzzle solving in a tense and horrifying situation, with the occasional enemies getting in your way.
If you remember, that's how RE used to be before it turned into casual horde shooter with piñata enemies, badass indestructible agents, infected merchants, and QTEs and explosions everywhere. In RE7 you do have access to various fire weapons to fight or just defend yourself against enemies, but combat is not the main aspect of the game, this is not a typical shooter that throws dozens of enemies at you one after the other so you can just gun down everything in your path because "it's cool and fun".
The Bad:
The first person view combined with the Average Joe main character sadly does make it look like a quite generic first person horror game at times, and the occasional cheap jumpscares just reinforce that feeling (though even that is still more fresh than 'yet another over the shoulder action shooter').
And I must also tell you that it lacks of enemy variety and has quite a drop in quality towards the last section of the game, when it suddenly turns into a corridor shooter with a terribly scripted final boss battle and a shoehorned fan-service ending. So basically you'll realize there's pretty much nothing new or interesting to see once you reach the last third of the game. Hopefully, there's the "free" Not a Hero chapter which hopefully will make up for those mistakes the game does towards the end but, guess what, it's not out yet.
Should you buy it?
If you want Survival Horror (adapted to modern gaming conventions that is, don't expect literal old school survival), definitely yes. Now if you just want an horror-themed "zombie" shooter, then better think twice, this might not be a game for you.
If you have doubts, wait for a discount. For a survival horror fan this is a step in the right direction for sure, and a very good game overall, but it has some flaws and it's quite overpriced for the amount of content you get. Don't bother with the Season Pass unless you played and really loved the main story and want more, or wait until all the content is finally released. The game is still not complete as of today since there are two extra episodes yet to be released.

The Early Access phase of the game is over, with the game making tremendous strides since then. This game is a hardcore experience, which players often forget before purchasing the game. You will lose warband members, RNG will not go your way sometimes (as with any RNG based game), you'll be scraping to get by with your wyrdstone shipments, and many other frustrating experiences. But the game is worth, oh is it worth it.
Pros:
- The city of Mordheim is beautifully rendered. It really captures the feeling of exploring a haunted city. Each map is randomly generated, so no match will be exactly the same.
-Each warband feels different from one another, with different skills and strategies being important for each one.
-You are able to progress your character through leveling up characteristics, purchasing skills, and equipping different sets of weapons and armor.
-If you're a warhammer fan, you'll love this game.
-Permanent injuries make you feel a connection with your characters, since you don't know when it'll be their last session.
-In depth tactical experience with positioning, stances, and environmental advantages being crucial to victory.
-Rogue Factor is an amazing company. They value player feedback and have sculpted the game through Early Access in response to the community input. They are very quick to fix bugs, and bring out updates.
Cons:
- only four warbands (witch hunters are being added, so more warbands are on the way)
-The AI can be really annoying. Their pathfinding isn't the best and they can make silly tactical choices that cost them the game.
-Loading times (fixed, only 20-30 seconds now).
-Needs more multiplayer support.
-Could use more warband customization.
I would suggest this game if you like tactical RPGs or the warhammer universe. There will be times where you are frustrated, but that comes with any game. Rogue Factor deserves another round of applause for being extremely responsive to player feedback. There will most likely be DLC down the road (warbands, customization, maps, etc).

Load times- Yes they can be long. probably averaging around 60-90 seconds for me. But if i remember correctly the developers have said they are working on it and have already reduced them quite a bit compared to beta.

I've never typed a Steam review before, but this will be my first. Why?
I really enjoy Absolver. It may be short, the servers sometimes fail me, and I wish there could be more meaningful online encounters with players. Your experience is basically isolated to you and your friends. However, the combat, the highlight and foundation of the game, is addicting if you're willing to sink your teeth into it.
To me, I take the simplicity of the overall game as a means to focus on your character, YOUR journey. You are the most important and attention-grabbing..."thing" in the world, and you'll meet many people with different philosophies and styles. What I love about this is that the game then forces you focus on the individuals, which results in an overall experience that involves self-improvement. If you don't have very good moves, get more and experiment. If you can't get used to your class' ability, practice. If you get beat by someone with a better combat deck, observe them, emulate, and adapt. You're essentially giving an identity to your Prospect, who has none. Are you one who gives up? Or are you one that rises from a nobody to a well-known mentor and Absolver? That's what makes it most enticing: making your own mark in the game.
Which leads me to my point: why am I writing my first Steam review for this game? While I'm fully aware that this game isn't for a mainstream audience, and many won't like such a focused and "incomplete" game, that DOESN'T mean this game deserves bad reviews that lowers its status from "Positive" to "Mixed." This niche community NEEDS to attract more like-minded players that can appreciate Absolver for what it is.

Anyone who's ever played early access games knows (or should) that this sort of thing is a possibility. This particular game? If you're nosy about the awesome ship builder, and it goes on sale, sure, might be worth poking. Just don't expect a game. A turn-based strategy game set during the Napoleonic Wars. The game was developed by AGEOD, a developer considered to be an able strategy game maker. The game offers four different scenarios set within different periods of Napoleon's rule. These include the so-called Grand Campaign (1805-1815) and a few smaller ones: Austerlitz (1805), Battle of Jena (1806), and Waterloo (1815). The battles are fought on the strategical level, so the player controls entire armies instead of individual soldiers. Apart form being able to control French forces, the player also has access to the British, Spanish, Russian, Austrian, Prussian, and Ottoman armies. The gameplay requires the player mainly to effectively lead their military forces, but also take manage supply lines, military improvements, and diplomacy. Similar to most of the previous games from AGEOD, this one also focuses on faithful recreation of historical events. However, the creators also allow the players to create alternative versions of history, providing the option to manipulate the outcomes of certain events.

Well, I know that many have reviewed and have said their fair share about this game, but I guess I will share what I feel others should know if there were to think about buying this game.
Do I think this game is a good game: Yes, I do. I don't think its the holy grail of the DMC series (not counting the reboot here since I havnt played it as of yet.) But I do find it a great addition to the series. It took me a while to play it merely due to time, but as a vetren of the series of old, I would say that I did enjoy it.
How did this game compare to the others: I would say that it would be ranked 2nd out of the 4 main series in my opinion. It is a close first for sure, but there are minor details that just draw it away a little. I havn't gotten a chance to play the Special edition, but this one just did things that went CRAZY! For one, I like the addition of Nero, I did have fun playing as him, and after upgrading alot, loved his devil arm. But I did not have fun with his lack of 'power'. When I say power for Nero, I mean, you remove that devil arm of his and he loses alot of skill. And when you play as Dante for the later half, you realize just how much you rely on that thing for all of his moves or power. Thats not a bad thing, but I feel they could have done a little bit more skills with it besides something like "hold" which just allows you to hold an enemy. Maybe something like combing it with your gun or the Yamato more often. Say for example they included an ability that allowed Nero to use his devil arm to grip to the walls, allowing you to be more strategic but perhaps allowing for more skills or combos with it.
Dante isnt perfect either though. I love that they allowed all four styles this time around. It was so releaving having those so I could switch from the four at will, instead of having to decide what to use before each mission. His weapons were...okay. I did like to use them, but...some were just more common used from me then others. Lucifer could have been improved more, and Pandora needed to be downgraded to me. It was powerful, but confusing at times when I didn't want something to happen. That and the game didn't explain it that well I feel, (or I was being dumb! Wont question it here XD). The final thing with Dante that just hurt his playing style to me was his actual styles. I feel that they were so much better implemented in DMC3, but got downgraded in this game. Being able to move 3 times in Trickster was my favorite thing, but once, it annoyed me and I felt I could have gotten around situations better without it.
Still, the negatives aside, I would recommend this one. Great gameplay, very smooth, and it was just overall fun as heck. Be ready to die though if you think you could play this after coming from DMC3, cause your going to have one hell of a ride!
Bit of interest though, I will say, characters were spot on.
So yes, if your a fan of the series, or want to get into it, I would say start here, or with DMC1. Then go to 3....2 is questionable.
P.S. BUCK THAT FINAL BOSS! I HATE YOU FOR THOSE ATTACKS! <:T)

Solid and fun beat em up, though not without a few flaws.
Comparing it to other coin op beat em ups, it's pretty decent. Combat is fairly intuitive and rewards you for using strategy and dodging attacks instead of just mashing. It's a bit sluggish however, even compared to many older coin op brawlers. Your move speed is slow, you attack slow , and even your run has a pretty lengthy delay on it. It's definitely not the smoothest combat engine out there. The game also uses way too many buttons, throwing and dodging could easily have been inputs instead of dedicated buttons. The slight rpg/leveling elements are also pretty unwanted, not doing much beyond forcing you to replay early levels to make end game stuff maneagable. Overall it's fun if you have an appreciation for beat em ups, but I would personally rank games like Alien Vs Predator, Knights of The Round, DND: Mystara, Sengoku 3, etc. a bit higher in terms of gameplay design and fun factor.
Co op is fun but...the netcode is perhaps the most unstable I have ever encountered in a game. Enemies and even the players constantly teleport, sometimes to an absolutely absurd degree. It's often extremely choppy online. And even when these issues are not acting up, co op had horrendous input lag for me that made dodging and timing basically impossible. My connections with games are generally decent, and I've heard very similar complaints from others, so watch out if you're buying this to play with friends. If the netcode doesn't agree with one of you, it could be a traumatic experience.
In terms of aesthetics, the game was pretty charming for me. It may depend on your tolerance for wacky voices, but I found it amusing and quirky. The music is also pretty great, parodying the 80's aesthetic while being legitimately awesome in its own right. Character designs (courtsey of Genzoman) are solid too, and come to life pretty well in game.
Definitely some enjoyment to be had here, just make sure you're down with coin op brawlers, like the aesthetic, have a good connection, and don't mind one or two quesitonable design choices.

Resident Evil 7 pays homage to where the original crafted the survival horror genre that so many fans know & love. A true modern survival horror done extremely well, if you're looking for that next title to do that genre justice look no further. The gameplay is a mix of old school with new school elements that takes the player on a thrilling and horrifying journey.
PROS:
-Graphics are jaw dropping. Sharp, detailed, and extremely unnerving textures & lighting.
-The various creepy sounds you'll hear throughout this game will keep you on edge the whole way through. The soundtrack is extremely well done I feel, and was very subtle yet powerful in regards to enhancing the experiences and scenarios.
-The game play is actually extremely fun. Killing enemies is actually extremely satisfying despite the fact that the best option in combat scenarios often at times is fleeing.
_****THE STORY***** literally the best part of the game in my opinion. The whole time my cousin and I played this game we kept theorizing what would be the situation or what would happen next and we could not pin it at all. The fact that this story leaves you in complete mystery compared to Resident Evil 5/6's painfully obvious story arcs was a very pleasant surprise and quite the thrilling experience to unravel.
-Had some Resident Evil 4-like gruesome deaths. I didn't experience nearly the amount that was in RE4 but the few that I did see were pretty......intense.
-There is some replay value in regards to a key point of the story. Not going to give spoilers so take my word for it, especially if you care about the story then it would be worth going through again for this point alone. Also to try again on a harder difficulty setting because why not. I mean I guess you could just YouTube it after beating the game to find out what the difference is but that takes the fun out of it!
CONS:
-Puzzles are fun and neat but not that challenging in my opinion. Slightly disappointed in regards here.
-game is kinda short

Now, before we get started I am usually pretty harsh on games and RE7 will be no exception, so lets cut to the chase.
The first thing I noticed was it crashed and crashed and took me a while to figure it out, but got it solved in the end. So if you do have issues, there are ways to fix it, though it is never a good start.
To be honest it's good but it's not that good, graphics for this day and age are pretty average but it takes a lot of grunt to run it, the coolings fans on my graphics card have been working overtime while playing this game which it's not common for them to run constantly. It does leave me wondering why? It's not the graphics are bad they're just not spectacular not what I was expecting for a AAA game now days, I mean what is with their hair? I have seen better, more relaistic hair in PS2 games.
The game play does run smoothly though, it's your average trudging slowly around style, but it flows well, no stutter, even going from a slow walk right into quickly drawing your weapon and gunning down enimies then back to walking it all works really well.
Sound effects escpecially early on are great with random squeaking floor boards and closing doors, does build some good atmosphere, unfortunately that doesn't last, the effects do, well the sound effects do, the effect they have on you don't as it eventually becomes background noise and you realise enemies have their own background noise, so no need to worry about squeaking floor boards.
Now to the game itself.
Story is.. thin... very thin, there's not much happening, which is good and bad a straight forward plot is often much better than a thick convoluted plot with ridiculous twists, but there wasn't enough to keep me wondering and engaged, audio dialog, though well spoken is pretty light on content as well.
But it's RE what about the scares you might ask?
Well it starts off good, few decent jump scares here and there and while it is atmospheric, it just didn't suck me in. I almost played it casually a few hours here and there, not something that I was glued to in the zone. The sound effects like I mention earlier probably played apart as does getting further into the game the enemies rather than changing types or getting stronger just become more abundant, so you start to expect them around every corner. Out of actual types of enemies there seems to be just the 4 main ones, besides bosses and weird one offs for one zone. So they get very easy to learn.
Overall I rate it 6/10
Average, more like a well polish indie title than something I'd expect from a major publishers flagship product.

Great game with some bafflingly stupid design decisions. The developers have done an admirable job imitating the feel of the classic Mordheim miniatures game. The systems work well and there's some interesting decisions to be made once your warband gets past the first couple of missions and gain a few skills. Persistent injuries, forced ironman and your main income being what you scavenge in the middle of combat makes the campaign compelling even though it's mostly random missions. If you wanted a 50-50 mix of Blood Bowl and X-COM, this is it.
What pulls the game down is 3 things:
- Less-than-stellar (read: bloody stupid) AI. A big no-no in a strategy game
- Obscene waiting times. Maps take ages to load and if 3-4 enemies have a turn in succession you may as well tab out and watch a youtube video
- Godawful 3rd person camera and WASD movement. The game is practically begging for an isometric/eye-in-the-sky view.
If you can live with that, this is a solid game. Especially if you play it against people instead of the easily cheesable AI.

A good friend of mine bought this for me, despite my resistance to the idea. Simply put, the game is good, but might seem too short if you're playing alone.
More elaborately put, I was honestly shocked by how much I enjoyed this game. Its by no means a perfect game, but I've always hated action RPGs like Dark Souls, the last fighting game I enjoyed was Tekken 3, and the graphics looked pretty bland at first.
For starters. the fighting deck is a genius idea for combat, and makes every fight unique. Sometimes you steamroll, sometimes you get steamrolled. But, a surprisingly large amount of the duels I was engaged in felt tense, and engaged me. I'll admit I'm pretty bad at combo's and what not, but if you can learn the games combat, you'll find yourself in an incredibly deep and complex system.
Then there's the art style. What at first seemed like extremely ok graphics turned out to be heavily stylized, but borderline photorealistic beauty. Every screenshot of this game(barring some bugs) looks like a painting.
But, there's one thing that I have to warn the potential buyer of; the game is somewhat short. It took me about 5 hours to complete the main quest, and there were only three bosses in the entire game. Although, if you're like me and obsess in every video game about creating the most effective way to play it, then the combat deck will definitely provide you with at least 20 or 30 more hours of theory crafting, move learning, and memorizing your setup. And, the endgame provided actually rewards players who build insane decks. Once you've completed the 'Combat Trial' mode, you can found your own school, and teach other players your way of fighting.
Now for some negatives. I played this game with 5 other people, and I found the online services to be extremely lacking. Only 3 players, friendly or otherwise, can share a lobby at one instance. I'm sure there's a reason for this balance wise, but it made the game feel very secluded. Additionally, there's no way to toggle off friendly fire, which would be fine if the lock-on system didn't automatically shift towards other players at random. Connection also seemed to be an issue, and rubberbanding wasn't uncommon.
Overall, I'd give this game a 7/10 right now, and maybe an 8/10 if the devs fixed a few of its issues. If you think you'' enjoy this game, you definitely will.

I don't recommend this game to anyone in it's current state.
Pros-
-It's eye candy. The world and art style are great to watch and explore despite so simple.
-Tons of moves that you can sort in any way you like. If you want to use only kicks you can do that, if you want to use nothing but heavy attacks you can do that. You don't pick a character in this game like in any traditional fighter, you make your Siegfried, Akuma, etc.
-Really cool and diverse classes. The game gives you the choice of three starting classes with a fourth secret unlockable class through the games story. All in all the two classes that I tried were really fun to mess around with.
-Lots of items. At the start you get your standard clothes and as you beat enemies or rank up on the combat trials you get more and more clothes. Even if you get the same pants, shirt or shoes twice, chances are that you get it in a different color or even in a better condition.
-Beating the "bosses" in story mode is pretty fun. Not too difficult for the average person but not too easy for the veteran fighting game enthusiast.
-All in all the game has a ton of cool mechanics that make it a blast to play.
Cons
-The game crashes........ a lot. I understand that this game was made by a small company and it's only been out for a bit. But why are people so quick to forgive a game not being up to par? If you went to a restaurant that's family owned (a diner) would you be so quick to forgive for the food not being cooked well?
-The servers. The servers are god awful. I have never once opened up the game and logged in succesfully in the first try. At one point I kept retrying for half an hour straight with no news on the companies twitter or anything to indicate that it was on my end or theirs. AND EVEN WHEN YOU? DO LOG ON............... the game is laggy or it crashes when you try to go for combat trials. I have a 200mbps/20mbps connection. I shouldn't lag. Ever.
-The game is full of bugs. Ive clipped under the map, outside the map and sometimes I've gotten stuck inside barrels. It's just not finished.I would be quick to forgive this too but everytime it happens I have to close the game (sometimes even after you close the game the game doesn't really close) and try to log back in or just give up entirely
-The game rewards lagging and spamming fast attacks. Sometimes you face a challenge you could never hope to beat and that is the lag spam combo. Players will take advantage of the lag they posses and just destroy you with fast elbow or fast jab until you die. You can't block forever and you can't dodge it cause of the games tracking.
-The classes are unbalanced. As it stands now people should really try to get good with the parry class. Absorb is a joke, you can't win against a serious player while using that class, granted it is stated to be the easiest class to play as but it's no excuse. Windfalls main ability is to dodge......... and pretty much every other class can dodge. Why would they make a class based on an ability other classes have?
-There's no ranking system and no way to track your wins and losses. This one isn't as big of a deal but most players want to keep track of how good they're getting.
-The level cap is idiotic. Why did they add this and why does it extend to combat trials? You feel cheated after losing to someone 10 or 20 levels higher than you and can't help to feel frustrated and angry at the level gap. There's also no way to redistribute your stats. So if you mess up and put a point in a stat you didn't want to you have to just live with it or make a new character and start over.
-The school system doesn't make an impact. If the school system weren't there it wouldn't make a difference. It's a feature that sounds cooler than it actually is.
-Lack of communication from the devs.
-The "story" is so irrelevant. You just do it to pass time and it's forgettable. It quicly becomes boring to play free roam and you spend most of your time trying to connect with laggy players in combat trials.
-You can't add people you randomly encounter. Sometimes I would actually like to add some of the random players I find but I can't. Your ingame name isn't necessaraly your Steam name.
-The targetting system is trash. I play on an xbox 360 controller and most times trying to change targets doesn't work and it gets you killed.
-There's only 1v1's available on combat trials. I get the feeling they're going to add 2v2's and 3v3's because there's some locked/greyed out modes we can't get to yet but it should have came out on release.
-There's a frame cap. This one I get but I would still like to make use of my 144hz monitor :/
-Snape killed Dumbledore.
All in all this game feels the same way Minecraft did when it was in alpha. It's innovative and has great mechanics but it doesn't have as many features as you would come to expect. I understand the game is only 30USD (half the price of a game like For Honor). I understand the game was developed by a small studio. I understand that the game can only really stand to get better with time. I understand that there's ways to play around lag spammers. I understand. I can't recommend this game to any sensible person. It isn't finished yet. Buy it when it gets finished and all the issues get worked out or buy it on sale if you really want to play.

WoN is a true Grand Strategy title of the Napoleonic Wars starting from 1805 till Waterloo in 1815. Very ambitious game with a *very* emphatic NOPE. The website still sells it as early access. Last update was over a year ago as of this writing. It states:

This week’s patch includes an early implementation that should give you a basic idea of where we want to go with it.
So basically with the final release, we have an "early implementation" of a "basic idea" for the economy. I'm certainly not trying to be antagonistic here, but that just seems blatantly wrong to me. It feels pretty deceitful to sell a product as complete when it has clearly not been finished. I really wanted to like it. It was one of the first early-access titles I've purchased and I admit, the ship builder is pretty fun. Flying your ship, or interacting with the universe on any meaningful level seems non-existant. Combat is boring and janky, the economy sim is incomplete, and the whole thing reeks of alpha. For clarification, alpha as in the pre-beta stage, beta meaning the game is feature complete and only requires bug fixing, optimization, and testing. In essence I'm saying that things are missing. Overall, once you finish building your ship, you may as well just quit the game; it's peaked. That was the high point, that was the single most fun thing that you will ever do in this game. It's just boring. Obviously, no developer sets their sights on making a boring game. I'm not mad, I understand money and motivation don't last forever, but this game really should have been *so* much more than what is offered. The procedural random galaxy and shipbuilder alone must have been truly momental tasks to overcome. I don't know what happened with the devs (the forums are malfunctioning or have been removed as of this writing), but it's genuinely as though they just vanished. If and when they do return, I hope that they will learn from their mistakes and move on.

Empire is a true Total War game and one of my favourites. It is all about historical gameplay in the 18th century.
It is worth every penny and it really deserves its positive reviews.
It is time for my own review after I got the last achievement in Empire:
+ Although the game is from 2009 the graphic ist still good
+ Interesting and nice battlefields: Take cover in buildings, fields, hiding behind walls and fences etc.
+ Unit detail is good and the animations are well made
+ Naval battles need a bit exercise but once you know how it works they are great
+ Huge map (You can fight in North America, a bit in South America, Europe, partly Africa, Russia and India)
+ Trading routes in South Africa, South America and in the Asian regions to boost your income
+ There is a Pirate faction (Caribbean)
+ Fighting with firearms, cannons etc. is a great experience
+ Huge battles
+ Units talk to you in their own language
+ You can place "forts" on the campaign map
+ Technology research is made in universities and divided in more branches
+ You can steal technologies
+ Religion and diplomacy
+ Weather effects
+ Native Americans
+ Armies can destroy important villages etc.
+ Great sound, ambient music = great feeling
+ Revolutions (can create a new faction with its own flag etc.)
+ Historical background information
+ A high replayability due to the whole feeling of this historical era, captured in this detailed game
+ Friendly fire!
- The AI is sometimes gamebreaking bad. It is passive and has a bad pathfinding. Simply, it has often no strategy...
- There is no multiplayer campaign or a co-op mode
- Sieges are, how can I say it... boring, nearly everytime the same sh...
- No general or admiral speeches. I mean, it's an era for heroes and you have nothing to say to motivate us?
- Generals are weak and have no real skills
- Although the naval battles are great, I wish they were more polished if you know what I mean
- Pirate faction unplayable
- The drummers play always the same "marching" sound
- I wish there had been partly a real soundtrack with music of the era
- I miss expeditions in South America and Native factions on that continent
- I'm not sure but slavery in colonies or in general is not existing at all
- Diplomacy is good but it really could have been more than what it is now...
- Friendly fire!
All in all, Empire is a great game. The 18th century is a fresh and interesting era to play. There is a lot to discover and to conquer. Also, there are a lot of interesting mods to install. If you ask me, the game is a must have!
Have fun!

I'd recently played 'Outlast' which I also enjoyed despite being a 'horror' game, but I think the main difference with the scares in Among the Sleep is that they are unexpected, whereas a game like 'Outlast' is quite tense the whole way through.
The way the story unfolds throughout the game through clues and hints makes you pay close attention to what's going on around you without getting in the way of the game itself. I've been playing this game for years, and its predecessor. This game makes no pretentions, it is a stripped down RTS, but it is stripped down in a good way. The map is divided into territories, holding territories increases your income, denying territories to your opponent denies them theirs. It's all about moving tactically between these zones and defending your command centre. You have land, sea and air units, it's all quite simple and that is basically the  (very addictive) game.
As for the story: it is very zany, comic book style and darkly humorous. It's a sci-fi storyline which is told between levels in cutscenes (and also via radio chatter while you're playing). Now the game is story driven in a very simple way i.e. cutscenes set up the level and your objectives form a part of the overall storyline. You could skip all the story without really affecting the game, but it's worth watching if you get the humour.
This is a remastered edition but don't expect AAA graphics, it's the simplicity of this while remaining challenging is what makes it an enduring classic for me. You can just pick it up and play, you don't need to invest time in learning how to control it. An absolute classic, great for scratching a quick strategy itch. Well worth getting this remastered edition for this sale price.

I'd like to say, first of all, that most of the negative reviews for this game are very out of date; most are from 2014, immediately after the game was released. Most of the complaints about the cinematics/cutscenes have been addressed; you now have the good old, funny, comic-styled cutscenes in between chapters and briefings again.
The original Z: Steel Soldiers was released back in 2001. The version that has been released here on Steam is a remaster of the original. While there are a few lacking features from the original Z: Steel Soldiers (a game which I loved), such as multiplayer, I am glad that this has finally come to Steam as my old copy had broken some years ago, and that the game is now easily accessible to purchase and play. I am also glad that , despite this game not being that popular on Steam since release,  they are still working slowly on re-implementing the skirmish mode and improving the gameplay, as seen on the news section. It shows that the developers truly are dedicated to delivering a good game experience.
The graphics in this game have been improved considerably since the old version, mostly for the better, as it is no longer looking so out of date at first glance, especially to someone who has not heard or seen the game before. However, I will admit that I feel some of the visual charm has been lost from the old game due to the graphical changes; colours are less vibrant and the sense of scale on the units has been skewed a bit through the changes, but that's just my opinion.
The game unfortunately does have issues with its user interface and its controls. For example, the mini-map is sometimes replaced with a PIP-window, so sometimes you won't be able to see your map, therefore taking away some of the control and situational awareness for a short period of time. My suggestions, to make the game that much better, would be to see an improvement to the things I mentioned above; return the original visual style for old times sake to preserve the work the original developers had done on it, and the user interface could be made to not be so clunky and slow by making the UI transitions instant to speed up micro. The controls would benefit from having the option to use WASD to pan the camera up/left/down/right. The PIP-window, alerting you about certain events, needs to have its own window, or at the very least have a toggle on/off option.
Despite these issues, it is still pretty fun and presents itself very well; the voice acting is top quality and the cutscenes/briefings in the campaign are hilariously well written. Some of the missions do present quite a challenge at times. There is a sense of satisfaction in wreaking havoc across the battlefield; infantry, vehicles and buildings all cause explosions. The bigger they are, the bigger the explosion.
If you are looking to kill a few hours in a strategy arcade game, I highly recommend you buy it. At this price, it is dirt cheap and well worth it for what it offers. If you're still not convinced and slightly wary of parting your money, buy it during a sale.
Skirmish has now been implemented, rejoice!
The devs have listened to the players and there has now been some changes to the balance of units. A bug with the Disruptor unit, which was present even in the original version, has now been fixed.
Massive update has added quite a few new features which were not a part of the original version:
• Visual FoW system added - Previously, you had to click on units to see how far they could see. Now, at a glance (as in most RTS games), you can see the extent to how far all of your units can see portions of the map without having to click on each one.
• Higher resolution options - Some resolutions were not working before, now they do.
• Cinematic Mode - Can press F12 to enter a cinematic / no HUD view mode (good for capturing videos / screenshots)
I struggle to play with awkward mechanics and unfortunate troop selection options. You fight more with the camera and troops selection than you fight the enemies.

Z and Steel Soldiers are among my favourite RTS, so I was a bit wary of this "remake".
After playing a few hours, I must say I am pleasantly surprised. The new gameplay and UI need some time to get used to, but I believe it's actually smoother than in the original and brings Steel Soldiers closer to the simple, arcade, fast-paced gameplay of the first Z, while retaining all the new buildings and units.
The improved graphics are a mixed bag for me. I appreciate the improved textures and FX, but the bots have been redesigned and have lost much of what gave them personnality in the first place.
My biggest complaint is the absence of skirmish and multiplayer modes. The campaign is cool and has a pretty good story, but sometimes you just want to play a map with the full toybox.
All in all, it's a pretty decent port of a great game, that only lacks a few game modes to become a good port.

10/10 An awesomely bodacious 1980s experience.
This game is both a Double Dragon game and a radical love letter to the 1980s. Stuff ranging from the background music being rich with 1980s styling (courtesy of Jake Kaufman, a.k.a. DJ VIRT), to the attire and character designs (Billy and Jimmy talking like Bill and Ted while dressing more in the style of Fist of the North Star, for instance). The first is basically a remake of the original game's first stage, but every stage after is an awesome tribute to what people liked in the 1980s and surrounding years. Whether it is a boss who happens to be a blue combat robot with a Capcom style theme tune, a main villain who looks like samurai Skeletor, or just the songs that play on the second stage of an area... it's like an entire decade and the years surrounding it in one game.
Oh yeah it plays well too, having taken all the improvements of every Double Dragon game before it, improved upon them, and added it's own as well. It also has multiple difficulty levels and a growth system for upgrading the capabilities of Billy and Jimmy, which fits the difficulty levels perfectly.

Classic side-scrolling beat-'em-up gameplay, elevated by outstanding visual design, a highly memorable antagonist and one of the best game soundtracks in recent memory.
I only played single-player - which offers a stiff challenge at the highest difficulty level - and had terrific fun with this title.  But I imagine co-op would be even more of a blast.

Do you like 80's style arcade action with radical music, intense combat, amusing and memorable characters, great boss design and one of the best endings ever made? Then you owe it to yourself to play the hell out of this game.

This game is a 8/10. And needs much love for fans who love Double Dragon, beat'em ups, and nostalgia trips of the 70s and 80s.
The Good: The game has a vintage feel of controls like a blast from the past. The music in this game features remixes of classic theme music from past Double Dragon games, and some new original music thrown in as well that is up beat and awesone to beat down. Making you wish there was a sound track seperate to the game. Graphics is smooth and the art style and theme of the game with "Neon" fits perfect of 80s throwback. The game now features some RPG elements, such as power tapes that can increase your stats and powers as the levels start to get slowly harder with tougher enemies. There are a veriety of weapons for you to pick up and use. The bosses have predictable partens in this game, but provide challange. Most of the game has a lot of pop culture references of the 70s, 80s, and even 90s. Unlike the console ports, the PC version offers what all Double Dragon fans wanted in the game, which is online bro-op, co-op. So there is a lot of replayability with this game featuring co-op online or off.
The Bad: The controls can feel a little awkward to handle at first. And can take time to get used to. There isn't really a lot of attack veriety in the game such as different combos or different attacks that can be performed to add in depth of gameplay. The game feels short and can be done in about less than 2 hours. The game also has a few difficulty spikes in some parts. So going back to previous levels to grind is an option if you can't progress the next level.
Above all, this is a game that deserves recognition. It's been a long wait for those who are Double Dragon fans and beat'em up fans alike and feels like a breath of fresh air. As it's the classic story, the evil syndicate steals your girl, you go out to kick their head in with your one true weapon that is your fists, and save the girl. And the evil leader who is behind all of this is...a Skellator wanna be. Who cares if it sounds out of place? This is Double Dragon, and I hope to see more of the brawler/beat'em up style gameplay continue for future games to get better and better.

Save Jesus is the newest installment of the Bible series. You play as God and your main goal is to protect Jesus from the soldiers from hell. THIS REVIEW WILL HAVE SPOILERS
Story: 5/5. The story was well made. After the annexation of Serbia, roman forces have been cracking down everywhere looking for the son of God, Jesus Christ. Jesus, is crippled and injured after the bombing attacks, and asks for the help of God. God realizes that it is not Jesus's time yet so he comes down to help his injured son. He and his son are attacked and are surrounded by the Romans. Throughout the game, Jesus and God make the hardest descisions any man could ever make, in order to escape from the Roman's wrath. Once Jesus is at the gates, the future Jesus, Jesus 2.0, is sent back in time to kill his past self in order the fix the chaos brought to the world. God is left paralyzed as he is there to watch his son kill his son. Once Jesus 2.0 pulls the trigger, he noticies the future has not changed. He then comes to the conclusion that this was a clone of Jesus. Throughout the rest of the game, you play as Jesus 2.0, who had to cut his own toe off in order to find Christ. Christ 2.0 grabs the cross and fights Jesus, once Jesus lies weakened, he understands that his fate has come and is crucified by 2.0. But then jesus is knocked off the cross and then Julius Ceaser comes in, and enters his true form. Jesus 2.0. sacrifices himself in order to save the world. Jesus is then crucified and the future is saved. The story, as you can tell, should be concealed in a time capsule so the future civilization can see our achievments. The story is the best video game story ever.
Gameplay: 5/5. The gameplay is original and innovative. The physics in the game feel realistic, the controls are amazing, not too stiff and not too floaty. The graphics are also stunning, as you can see, this was their main focus. This is next gen times a gazillion. Truly in a league of it's own
Soundtrack: 2/5: The soundtrack is forgetable, but, you're given the option to mute the music so it's okay.
Verdict: The game has skipable cutscenes, an excellent story, great graphics and gameplay, and deserves a 9.5/10. Truly game of the year.
