This is the best Survival Horror game that I've played in a while, the graphics are gorgeous, the attention to details is overwhelming, the narrative is engaging and the mechanics are amazing.
Resident Evil VII manage to rescue the main elements from most classic horror movies, and put them in a cohesive story line. You'll have bits from The Exorcist, The Evil Dead, The Shining, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, The Ring, Blair Witch Project, Saw and even Se7en, all set up in a "beautiful" Louisiana environment that resembles the first season of True Detective in the most elegant and respectful way.
The First Person Perspective has been refined from previous games of the genre like Outlast or Alien Isolation, to put you right in the shoes of the main character, making the jump scares and the psychological terrors even more intense. This game have some of the most memorable moments in the history of the genre, moments that will accompany you and haunt your dreams, long after beating the game (Mia and Eveline are giving me a hard time sleeping).
The combat mechanics are by far the best of the series and manage to keep you by the edge of your sit at every moment and the boss fights are creative are ever changing (My fight with Jack in the garage was completely different the second time around), same for the stealth sections of the game.
The story surrounding your missing wife Mia and the insane Baker Family is fascinating to say the least and the pay off is extremely well constructed and satisfying, opening the door for a new chapter within the Resident Evil mythos and at the same time paying homage to the old premise.
For the last couple of years, the horror survival genre has been driven by the indie industry (Outlast, Amnesia, Slender Man) with a few exceptions, but Capcom just proved that the AAA companies still have a say in the matter. After the cancellation of Silent Hills (way to go Konamy), Resident Evil VII is something that all the enthusiasts of the genre desperately need it without knowing and manages to deliver beyond my wildest dreams in every single aspect.
I can't wait to see where the franchise is gonna go after this, and I hope Capcom don't forget about us PC Gamers.

If you like the war hammer universe, small squad tactical (x-com style), challenging game that is still very reflective of the tabletop then this unknown game is great.
I have played from early beta throughout early access until launch. This is a great small studio that deserves the support.

The game has a learning curve and the RNG can be a little annoying at times but also adds some suspense to the game.  Sometimes, you have a great plan but your warband can't execute and sometimes, a lone soldier holds the line against the odds.
Unlike a game like X-com, even a novice henchman has pretty good chances to hit but they have shakey morale.  Don't let novices get surrounded or they might rout and get themselves killed.
Remember that collecting Wyrdstone is your primary goal.  Killing the enemy is secondary.  Of course, if you spot a lone enemy, kill him/her and if a bunch of enemies engage, they send in all your warband to fight, but in the beginning of a skirmish, try to gather some loot and wyrdstone before hand.  This will help you greatly after the battle as you need the wyrdstone and loot to pay for the treatment of your wounded and salaries of your troops.
Overall I have had a lot of fun so far.  Challenging game but satisfying as well.
The multiplayer scene is not great, but I think it will get better over time.  Regardless the AI is challenging enough for me.

I suspect that like blood bowl it will really shine in muliplayer.
Still its a great game, roll on the DLC for additional warbands (there is only 4 flavours to start with), oh and can we have a Necromunda game next?

It is with great sorrow that I will use the "thumb down" on this one.
Except a addict wargamer, I am also a Napoleonic fan so I was more than happy to purchase when I got the newsletter from Slitherine that Wars of Napoleon is now on Steam.  First impression quite good: A LOT of game depth, tones of units and statistics, fog of war and proper army/corps displays and move with a per day/week system, quite interesting. The essential Napoleonic atmosphere was there, as well as the historical accuracy that history geeks like myself enjoy. There was a first dissapointment - no "tutorial game" to guide you through all the mechanics, something that I consider essential for "deep" tactical games, but what the hell - I simply watched all the tutorial videos instead, taking notes like a proper wargaming geek.
The first scenario (Waterloo) went well, if we exclude the fact I got confused a few times with organisation of corps and movement, its a different thing to watch and to do it. I got there eventually and played through, but by the end of it another dissapointment emerged: Knowing almost nothing of the game, I easily won as France; the AI seemed to comprehent even less about the game than I did.
So is that the reason of the thumbs down - hell no. It is the fact that upon starting the other scenarios, the game crashes begun. At first I think "ok its a crash, it can happen". Then the second crash a turn later starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off and you change the Austerlitz scenario to the Prussian campaign. Then a third crash happens with the Prussians, so decide that I should no longer play the allies because with the French it did not crash during the first scenario. So I take the French in the Grand Campaign, taking 20 minutes to do a proper turn and it crashes again... twice.
It is somewhere here that I stop trying. I do not mind the 30 euros, I would buy even if it was 50 because its my type of game. Nor will I ask for money back, hoping that later patches will fix it. But until then... the game is not ready. I sincerely hope the developers do something about it, because its evident that there is a lot of effort and love into this game and I want to play it. So I am waiting and hoping, but currently not recommending it unless people don't mind crashes every 30 minutes or so.

Premise: I really wanted to like this game, and I still do to some extent. Bear with me this might be a long text (if you're bored just skip to tl;dr down below).
I have bought the game on 2 December 2015, the devs have the tendency to publish on historical dates (December 2 is the date of the battle of Austerlitz) adn they did it again with May 5 (Napoleon's death) although it was delayed a bit. This may seem a trivial thing BUT they release this game in an unplayable state regardless just because the date was historical.
I love Napoleon and his Age a lot, every time I hear about the Napoleonic era I get proud like it was a tale about my grandfather. I have bought and played every single napoleonic game in existence, board game and \ or card game. So it came natural for me to buy this one, despite the fact that Pride of Nations, another title by AgeoD, didnt suit my taste, but then again, that was probably because it was very complicated and hard to get into. The devs have a history of good games on their shoulders, despite being in very small number. I was confident that historical accuracy was their aim and they would deliver, but the game was absolutely broken.
Foundamental elements like the UI, the buttons, the saving system, everything was either not functioning, or missing, or prone to crash every turn. It seems that the Steam release is still under development, because the last patch didnt fix all the bugs and spelling errors and silly scripts that undermine the game. I have complained on the devs forum and it was told to me that "they are a small team and they have a very tiny budget". Well then, that excuse doesnt work: let me tell you this: if you know that you are a small dev team, and you are not confident in a product of this magnitude being released, because you know that you need more time and tests to run, then dont release the game in a "beta" state. It is as simple as that. Instead, players are treated as beta testers and even now the team is asking for feedback and support because there are a ton more people like me that had problems in the past and still do to this day. In my case, the game crashes at random times between turns very early on, or gives strange error messages in the option menu. The frame rate is atrocious, even for an i7 CPU; in the text messages which are describing currency in the game, sometimes they refer to "dollars", sometimes to "pounds".
I just dont understand the developers' behaviour. Quite frankly, AgeoD needs to pull their stuff together and get it done properly, and learn from their mistakes. To the potential buyers I say: dont buy this game in its current state. Wait several months until you are absolutely sure that the product is worth the price. I paid 40 Eur to be a betatester, dont make the same mistake.
tl;dr - The game is still an "under construction" beta and if you buy it you get to be a beta tester with an empty wallet. Wait for this game to be finished properly. Also, it is apparent that this is not a finished game as the devs didnt even bother to get rid of the debug log.

Sorry in advance for the long review. TL;DR if you like fighting games this a unique experience
Most of the negative reviews surrounding this game have to do with network issues, people using spam decks, and hackers.
1. Hackers are going to be an issue in every major online experience (look at battlefield 1 and COD). I've ran into one maybe two hackers, and even then I was still able to beat them. I just view it as another challenge, but that's just me.
2. Most network issues have been resolved on my end, and I've had an easy experience linking with other people in co-op for the most part
3. Spammy decks ruling the field is not an indication of poor mechanics, just that people don't know how to counter them. Lots of spams use repeated moves over and over, which means as a Forsaken or Kahlt, you only have to get one parry/avoid correct in order to interrupt their flow, then turtle into a block because fast attacks don't drain ANY stamina. Only harder punches/kicks/ guard breaks etc. Windfall has the easiest time against spam decks because you can just sidestep people or duck, jump whatever. It takes practice.
As someone who has played this game almost everyday since it came out, practice is essential to maintaining your timing and chops. Contrary to what a lot of negative reviews say, it IS ACTUALLY a very high skill game. You have to plan your deck, make necessary strategic adjustments if something isn't working, and make tactical adjustments during fights. The game is a mindgame and I LOVE IT! Warning: you will get salty in this game, its just going to happen. People who have been playing for 60 hours are going to beat the crap out of you, but take it as a learning experience. You can make some great friends in this game if you're respectful and bow to eachother after each encounter. People will offer to teach you moves you don't know, you can teach them moves. Its basically about as close as being in a wuxia movie as you can get: lone hero travels, meets other martial artists, learns skills, makes friends, makes enemies, tastes defeat, smells victory.
My advice to new players: Don't take losses personally, just attribute it to your deck not being well rounded enough. For the first 30 hours, I'd recommend experimenting with your deck as much as possible. Don't get complacent with one style if its not serving you. Also, take advice from others who critique you. And get salty. its ok. it happens to all of us.
Again, TL;DR buy if you like fighting games

Here's a really good example of why Steam GreenLight usually doesn't work as planned.
Originally I invested in this game for the idea, knowing full well it would be a while before development finished. However, the stunning slowness and absolute lack of proper patching didn't even remotely keep me interested to boot up the game. The few hours I messed around with it showed promise, especially in the ship building aspect. Unfortunately, this is real life -- developers get lazy, lose motivation, perhaps funding gets cut.
This is exactly why Steam GreenLight was a failure. In retrospect, it's a good idea -- sometimes developers need help or the extra customer funding to push their game to the max. Keen Software is a good example of how to do it; they engage in their community very often, an update is out once every 1-2 weeks reflecting some sort of desire or functionality customers wanted, and it is well-recieved and fleshed out to be a game of its own. Badland Studio had promises, but fell short; a disappointment of a company at best.

Kinetic Void started off as a really good idea for a game. 100% open world, pure 'do-as-you-wish' ship construction and exploration.
That's about all the good I can say about it.
The dev team was really small, inexperienced, and although they were pretty active in the community and media, the game itself fell short by many expectations. There are still a lot of bugs, no actual tutorial, ship building in itself is pretty complicated, and the game overall is not really well optimized.
When it boiled down to release I started to regret my purchase as despite the fact it's no longer Early Access, the game itself still feels largely incomplete. Buggy, no tutorial whatsoever, still not well optimized to run, and the ship building, although the interface is better, it still is really complicated a workflow overall. Not even the missions would work correctly. Which was a pain.
Of course, having already purchased this game I decided to cling on and hope for the best, but then suddenly, the game went quiet on all mediums: forum, update schedule, and youtube.
The entire dev team dropped out of the KV project, pretty much leaving only 2 behind. While it's more of a lack of interest than a 'take money and run' scheme (funds went to dev salaries), the 2 developers that DID stay behind, as much as I'd like to applaud them, can't do much either, not when they are also trying to work on a side project to make ends meet.
I bought the game with high hopes that were never repaid. If you're here looking for a space sandbox, there are other, much better games that haven't been abandoned and left to rot in the pits of Steam. Don't buy this. It was never worth the $20, and never will be.

So at the moment I can say that the game is ok but its not something thats totally blowing my mind. WIth that said though I'm definitely willing to go back later if they make improvements later on down the line since I see this as a game that has some serious potential here to be great. So i'll just do some pros and cons but keep in mind though that this is an initial reaction to the first few hours of the game:
Pros:
-Beautiful game. Lovely 2d art style that compells me to move forward and explore. I especially really love the water reflections as I move through the world.
-Building up a small encampment and seeing it grow larger can be satisfying.
-The perspective of just being one person on a horse.
Cons:
-Way to simple.
I do not mean this as saying that there is no depth but as a way of saying that it compromises the ability to actually adapt to your surroundings around you. Buildings can only be placed in fixed spots and though you can upgrade defensive towers, you can't choose where to place them. I think the best way to improve this is to give players more choice to be able to choose where to plop down towers and walls and your starting area. I think it's reasonable though to have certain things fixed in place like mills/farms however.

-Limited choices in terms of commanding others.
It bugged me that I was not able to tell my subjects to come follow me and follow my orders. Especially when there were moments were I clearly had tools that needed to be picked up but the villager just idled there. I should at least in some capacity be able to command my subjects and tell them where they must go. I would prefer to have the ability to command my subject in some way to follow, attack or be assigned to something specific, but at the same time also be able to let them go and do what they will.
-Roles are permenant.
Considering the limited number of units you can recruit I would like to be able to reassign roles to certain units so as to have greater level of control over my characters. I feel that with too much automation I do not have the control that I want to be able to reassign units especially in the early game when it especially matters.
-Too much emphasis on deliberate minimalism:
From what I can tell this seems to be a deliberate design choice that doesn't seem to work all that well entirely. The initial tutorial doesn't seem shy about telling you what to do at first with dialogue but after that it all just seems to go away and you're left to figure things for yourself without much feedback telling you what to do. When I first started playing the game I had no idea you were to build a boat and sale for new lands and i only found out about that after a third playthrough. I think it would benefit this game to not be afraid to use dialogue to tell you what you need to do and what roles your subjects and buildings play in the world.
Just to continue on the minimalism point its especially frustrating to not be able to manage and control your steeds stamina meter. Sometimes I'd be sprinting across only to have it unexpectedly stop with no idea why and worst yet with no idea as to when i'm able to run again. This is especially frustrating during encounters when I run into those night raiders who are royally messing up my face. I'd like to be able to see my stamina bar in this case or at least have better visual cues from my horse as to how much stamina i have, when i can run and when i should tell my horse to slow down.
-Lack of rebindable keys:
I have a personal preference towards being able to set my keys to whatever i wish. Its just a personal choice in this case but I don't like having to double tap keys to run and holding shift too often in my case tends to cause my game to minimize and a window popping up about shift keys.
-Enemys are kind of boring.
They don't really do anything interesting aside from bum rushing you in the night and are honestly kind of visually uninteresting. Some more diversity in terms of enemies would go a long way to keeping players interested in what they are engaging with.
So what it essentially boils down to is giving players more choices in terms of what they can do so at to keep them engaged especially in moments when theres down time but also better communicating to your players what needs to be done in the game as well.

It’s hard to know how big an effect a parent’s actions can have on children, until certain mannerisms start to materialise in that child’s behaviour. In Among the Sleep, you’ll be confronted by such scenes that might bring a tear to the eye of parents who play through. I’m not a parent myself, but at the end I couldn’t help staring at the screen in bewilderment of what I had just played through. Read more in our Among the Sleep review below.
Having just finished watching the film “Room”, I was reminded just how much an adult’s behaviour can impact the lives of their children. Among the Sleep touches on quite a lot of issues that parents face, but more importantly, it takes you on a two-year old toddlers journey through a world of imagination that depicts just how different a child’s perception of their surroundings is.
There is so much about Among the Sleep’s story that I’d love to talk about, but unfortunately that would involve spoiling the majority of the game. I’m going to do my best to touch upon certain aspects without potentially ruining the experience of those who are yet to play it.
The beginning of Among the Sleep starts with the toddling protagonist downing a glass of drink. Because of the way you are first seeing the world through the rounded walls of a drinking glass, my first impression was that I might be witnessing a birth scene. But as I moved my mouse around, more and more of the world became visible. Eventually I was left looking at the beaming face of the toddler’s mother. It was the two-year old’s birthday and the mother was preparing a cake.
As you wait for the cake to be presented to you, you’re given the opportunity to look around the kitchen, and even play with an abacus. Finally mother comes back with the cake and cuts a slice for mister toddler to eat. Unfortunately, before we got to sink our teeth into this tasty looking cake, we were interrupted by a knock at the door of the toddler’s house.
Here’s where the strangeness begins. Distortion lines start to appear around everything and the sound becomes muted. A growing feeling of unease pierces the atmosphere. Just as you’re starting to think you’ve fallen into a scene from Paranormal Activity, the distortion dissipates when you hear the mother shout “NO!”, and slam the door.
Back she comes with a present in her hands and a face conveniently disguised with a big smile. But before you’re allowed to open it, she picks you up and takes you and the present upstairs. You get placed in a playpen and the present is set down upon a chest of drawers. When the mother leaves the room, you gain control of the toddler.
The usual ‘WASD’ keys control your movement while the mouse is used to look around. Also, ‘left-click’ allows you to interact with objects. Obviously toddlers aren’t known for their jumping prowess, so instead of jump, the ‘space-bar’ allows you climb onto platforms such as chairs and open drawers. Holding ‘shift’ lets you sprint for a short period of time, but instead of being presented with a stamina gauge, you’ll simply fall over when you can no longer keep up the pace. The ‘control’ key drops you to the floor and allows you to crawl through narrow nooks and crannies.
Eventually you come across Teddy. A loveable soft toy who accompanies you on your adventure. In the toddler’s mind, Teddy can talk, and informs you that by pressing ‘F’ to cuddle him, you’ll feel safer. What he really means is that he’ll light up and allow you to see in really dark places. To be honest, I was constantly pressing ‘F’ because it gets quite creepy in the dark… Not only is Teddy a provider of light, but he also acts as a guide to the toddler.
The gameplay in Among the Sleep mainly consists of solving puzzles. Each puzzle rewards you with a memory that’s required for progressing to the next area of the game. The puzzles are relatively simple and won’t require a lot of thinking to solve, but the journey involved in solving each puzzle takes you through some incredibly imaginative environments; from dark, creepy playgrounds, to mazes of bookshelves haunted by a tall, crazy-haired, lurching monster.
Speaking of monsters, you’re not going to find as many of them out in the dark as you believed you would as a child. However, in later areas of the game, the tall monsters will appear more frequently. If they catch you, you’ll be in trouble and have to start again from a previous checkpoint. Thankfully the checkpoints come around often, and you won’t be replaying certain parts of puzzles over and over.
Among the Sleep incorporates a great physics engine that allows you to open drawers, cupboards, fridges and interact with pretty much anything you can see. Some puzzles and achievements require you to pick up certain items and throw them. This gives things an extra injection of realism and also lengthens the overall gameplay experience.
An extra little incentive when playing Among the Sleep are the many toddler-like drawings scattered around each area. The drawings depict some scenes we can only imagine are events the toddler has lived through.
All throughout Among the Sleep, you’ll be followed by a feeling of unease. Teddy will whisper to you that things look dangerous and you should be careful. Creepy sounds and crescendos in the music add a feeling of panic to your journey, and when you first encounter the creepy, tall, crazy-haired monster, you’ll be looking over your shoulder every time you hear something out of the ordinary.
From the moment you are taken upstairs and witness the introduction credits apparate before your eyes in the form of glowing lights, you can tell that you’re in for a visual treat. The graphics have a cartoony feel to them, resembling something you might see in a Pixar film. Everything in the real world is drawn with such bright, vivid colours. Each colour stands out the way you’d imagine a toddler to see them. In contrast, the imaginary world is dark, full of shadows and incorporates creepy distorted shapes to the overall design of things.
Playing as a toddler, you would expect their movement to be quite wobbly and Krillbite Studios certainly deliver in terms of wobbliness. It definitely injects an extra bit of realism to the character you are playing. Otherwise it might just feel like you’re playing as any FPS character in an overgrown world.
The soundtrack is eery and coats everything with an unnerving sheen. Sounds and effects raise goosebumps on your skin, especially when the monsters commence their pursuit of your tiny form.
Among the Sleep is truly a masterpiece and tells a story we’re all too familiar with. This could be confronting to some, but the way it plays out through the eyes and imagination of a toddler, portrays it in a different light. Those of you who aren’t parents might stop and reflect on the adventure you’ve just played through. Parents might shed a tear or go and give an extra hug to their children.
The entire game is so smooth to play, and although it only lasts for around three hours, you’ll feel like those three hours just flew by. Krillbite Studios have added Steam achievements to the game, so there’s a bit of replayability in terms of collecting everything and unlocking each achievement.
If you’re looking for a game that relies more on telling a rich story rather than throwing you deep into an action-packed shootout, Among the Sleep will not disappoint. It’s story will leave you speechless but you won’t be able to help yourself from wanting more.

If you enjoy a challenge, beware: this game is horribly, horribly ADDICTIVE.
Reading through the reviews, you'll find lots of common threads: you will come to care deeply about your warband; you will curse the RNG (and the entire lineage of anyone who created it); and you will be pulled deeply into a thematic, immersive world.
In the end, narrative will be a key factor in your experience — not just the narrative of the game's campaign but, more importantly, the narrative of your collective experiences. That will include tales of victory snatched from the jaws of defeat, frustrations due to unforeseen events (likely combined with minor mistakes), pyrrhic victories, and even fortunate defeats.
I once had a relatively inexperienced character hold against, and severely damage, a massive Rat Ogre, long enough for help to arrive. In a later game, when facing the lethally quick Skaven (rat people), he stuck his neck out to help two fellow warriors get to a safe position, delaying the Skaven leader and tying up three others for two turns, before paying the ultimate price (perma-death).
Through it all, you'll be challenged, and likely have to restart with a new warband or two. But once you get a handle on the gameplay, you'll be rewarded with a nuanced tactical and strategic challenge. For instance, I spend several minutes at the start of each game (against the AI, mind you) looking over the game's map, planning my deployment and strategy for that mission. You'll benefit not only from such planning, but also from careful use of tactics, such as adjusting your formations to ensure shooters have clear shots of incoming enemies, and ensuring that your fighters are in ambush stances to prevent access to your soft targets.
Oh, and friendly tip for fellow lovers of ranged combat: set melee weapons as your primary weapons for your shooters (you can have 2 sets of weapons), and their ranged weapons as secondary. You'll be able to switch back during the game, but (most) melee weapons give you far better initiative, which can buy you time to get into position. And for this purpose, stick to initiative-boosting weapons, like spears, daggers, and swords.
Enjoy!

Finally, Capcom returns Resident Evil to it's former Survival Horror roots. This game plays exactly how a modern Resident Evil game should. It has all the hallmarks of a classic Resident Evil game but streamlined to make it a bit less frustrating or confusing for new players.
Everything here is high quality, from the voice acting to the locations in the game, the music and the graphics, the combat and the bosses. Everything just works well here and fits together nicely. Emphasis has been taken away from the action and focused more on it's horror elements. This is immediately noticable with the decision to go 1st person which I think is for the best. 1st person allows for a more immersive experience versus the cinematic experience of the last few RE titles. Additionally, there are few cutscenes that take control away from the player, no QTEs and no co-op so there is nothing to take you out of the zone in this game.
In terms of pacing it nails it down perfectly as well. A good horror game knows when to get silent and let the player explore a new spooky area. Tension rises as the player becomes skeptical of the safety of the area until finally revealing the enemies. However my only complaint here would be the enemy variety, I wish just a few more were added into the mix. Especially considering the weapon arsenal is larger than necessary.
Difficulty is another important aspect of a good survival horror game. I only played on Normal so far so I can only comment on that. I think the balance was just right for a first-time playthrough on Normal. If you are very careful, thorough and accurate as well as avoid taking damage as much as you can, you will find more than enough to get by but not so much that it feels too easy. So in other words, you will always worry about your supplies but never exactly run completely out of them so long as you have some level of competency. Take this comment with a grain of salt though considering I have been playing Resident Evil games since 1996.
I will be playing the game again on the harder difficulty and will update my review if anything unexpected should arise. Overall, I think Resident Evil 7 is a great comeback for the series and a step in the right direction for survival horror as a whole. I would love to see more games like this and to see Capcom continue in this direction while thinking of new ways to innovate the genre. For classic RE fans or horror fans in general, this is a must buy.

Extremely surprised at how good the game was. I’m really specific in which survival horror games I choose to play. I generally only like survival horror games that are similar to the first Silent Hill games.  RE7 turned out to be a pretty honest game to be specified as survival horror, considering that most games labeled survival horror nowadays are just a first-person game in a spooky setting with nothing but jump scares. RE7 has survival horror roots such as limited ammo, the option to run or fight from enemies, and “stiff” controls (not in a bad way, but in a way that makes certain points of the game more intense). While the game has good original survival horror elements, it also takes place in First-Person view which is a change from the RE games, but it’s not used as a gimmick so much as it makes the game very atmospheric, and a good combo of classic survival horror with a more modern twist. RE7 also has a very good inventory system similar to RE4 making item management something important, and makes it feel slightly more realistic as your character can't hold every weapon given to them throughout the game. Overall this game is very good and has replay value, and I hope can inspire other game developers to make survival horror games more like RE7.

Is it perfect? No, not at all. Weapons like the Burner suck, the game itself is relatively short, and the final parts of the game starting from the ship have a noticeable drop in quality compared to the first section of the game.
However, is it a bad game? No. It's closer to the original spirit of Resident Evil than Resi 4 was, it being standalone is an amazing saving grace (seriously after the garbage crossoverfest that was 6 I think we needed to get away from the rest of the Resi universe for at least one game.), the game itself feels great and it has a LOT of replay value as is to be expected from a Resident Evil game- You can get at least 3 playthroughs out of it.
Don't buy if you're looking for a dollar to hour ratio (I mean, you shouldn't buy horror games period if you want a dollar to hour ratio, they're a genre that inherently benefits from being short and sweet), but do buy if you want a decent, but not necessarily classic, Resident Evil game. Here's hoping the free DLC is good, and that the best influence this game had is on Capcom's business philosophy, though looking at sales compared to Resi 6, prospects of Resident Evil returning to actual decent games as opposed to blockbuster Michael Bay-esque garbage seems bleak. At the least, we can enjoy it while it lasts.

I've always been fascinated by the game concept, to be introduced to the world through a child's eyes. Where everything and anything is possible. A world so full of life and colors, danger and adventure, fear and magic. Nothing your plain adult life could bring you close to. A world where you can be the hero of your bedtime story. You begin your adventure at night, the time when we rest after a long day, time where nothing mostly ever happens. But not for a 2 years old!
Among the Sleep, introduces you to a terrifying experience, which is completely insane and traumatizing on a basic human level. Takes place on a stormy late night, your mother is missing and you're a helpless little infant who sets off on a quest to rescue her. While he faces his fears of being lost in the dark, monsters lurking in the closets and every dark corner, worlds shifting, objects stretching which gives the illusion of hellish presence in the most clever ways I have ever seen, that you begin to imagine things and jump at the slightest noise. A psychological masterpiece.
Many recent horror games, such as Outlast, Amnesia, DreadOut and more, have been aiming to achieve making the player feel helpess in the face of danger or supernatural exsitence, by stripping away any means of fighting back. Which is probably the scariest feeling of all. But I can't imagine what could be more helpless than a little toddler, who can't yet talk and can barely walk, so you're basically forced to cope with your surrounding.
A big thank you to the Devs for releasing an update with new achievements. Being an achievement hunter, I had to replay the game, and it was even more rewarding than my first playthrough. It opened my eyes and made me realize what a special little game it was. It also added a Slenderman feeling into it, only a toddler version.
The game runs perfectly smooth, haven't encountered a single problem, still has its amazing visuals and physics and I noticed a greater update in the ambiance and sounds, which creates a much better horror atmposphere.
I strongly believe this game deserves a lot more credit, as it leaves a strong impact on you that a lot of big titles can't do. With its provoking story and innovation to the horror genre, I urge you to try it.

Among the Sleep Review -NO SPOILERS!-(except for the part about the footie pajamas)
Among the Sleep is a unique game that is played in the innocent eyes of a young child. I enjoyed this game - not only because of the horror element, which was very well done - but also because it told a valuable and emotional story with only a few words. In the minds of toddlers, many things and situations that happen in their lives sometimes don’t make sense. This game did a great job “translating” what was really happening into something that a toddler would see and understand. Moreover, it was absolutely terrifying. Many things make this game unique and different from most other first person games. First of all, the only way to transport yourself is toddling or crawling-which can make running away from certain death quite tense at times. Second, you play only two feet from the ground making everything around huge and curious. Third, you can see your body if you look down! You’re not a floating head bobbing around! Also, the baby footie pajamas are very nice. There will never be a dull moment when this incredible game is played and it may or may not make one speechless for a few days. I recommend it for anyone who is looking for a clean and eerie game that has good morals and lessons to be learned - including not making a single noise. There is one thing all must know when playing this: don’t break a bottle.

I loved Among the Sleep! Gorgeous and delightfully spooky atmosphere. Excellent story - I loved trying to figure things out as the game went along and still winding up surprised! I hope more games try to whole 'perspective of a child' thing, it's brilliant.

Among the Sleep has a very impressive affect on the player. It shows the great idea that only a genius could think of - using the perspective of a baby. Throughout this baby perspective, we can clearly notice that the baby has worries over many things like their mother's scream. At the beginning of the game, the character's mother goes to answer the door that had just had the doorbell ring. The mother then screams which queues the music and visual effects to give a dramatic effect. This happens to show that the baby feels stressed and panicked as though the mother is giving a distress call - an in-danger tone. I find this is a very creative idea and the creator really understands how emotion is built up in a game.
After seeing the monster, I have a slight lust of disappointment, for as soon as a monster is shown in a game, that ruins the horror element of a build up. No studios are able to create a monster that is more horrifying that what we, as consumers, create in our head from mysterious build-ups, such as lighting effects and creaky floorboards. As soon as a monster is shown in a game, it automatically drops some tension and makes the player less scared of the monster. This game has lost the horrific momentum by showing the monster, and the monster doesn't look very scary, but I guess there are limits as to how scary you can make a monster look. And to be quite straight... what is a monster? A monster is a horrific creature or person that is created IN OUT HEADS by dramatic effects and noises. Making a monster be shown in a game really doesn't make it a monster anymore.
The teddy bear's voice acting and sounds are very good. The sound effects successfully create tension and the teddy bear successfully sounds like a
- I mean a nice friend.  In addition, the animations of movement in the game are very smooth, however are a little slow and... the opposite of slick. Whatever that word is.
As far as I can judge on the game mechanics, they are quite simple and not all that amazing. Animations for the things the character uses are very simple and could be improved through more time in development.
I do believe this game has a really good story line, really good twists and successfully shows the in-depth perspective of a baby in every-day situations. Among the Sleep shows a definite prime example of what a baby would think about as they go to sleep on a dark, windy night. It shows how the baby is petrified and shows how simple things are over-exaggerated in the baby's mind, such as a wardrobe.
Overall, I think this game really is worth the play and if you don't play this game, you'd be missing out on a lot of interesting perspective.

They nailed the atmosphere on this one, and the story is really good.  The toddler movement mechanics were a nice touch as well; I kept getting frustrated when I would run and fall down, but it wasn't frustration at the game... it was the frustration of walking around as a cumbersome 2 year old.
There were only a few drawbacks.  The graphics are dated, but I didn't really notice.  Also, the game is a bit short for how much it costs (maybe a couple of hours long), but it was still a very satisfying experience.

***REVIEW EDIT- months have gone by since I bought this game expecting that the developers would patch the errors and engage more in the community (specifically regarding missing content, things not working, etc) and there has been very little on this front. Aside from one patch that helped with animations, very little has changed since my initial review. Therefore, I can't say that I still recommend this game, and would instead recommend tracking down a copy of the original. It hasn't aged well graphically, but the gameplay is superior to this port.
First thing out of the way- the only thing in this game right now is the campaign mode, the same from the original SS.
It's definitely a work-in-progress. I just popped my old copy of SS in and played it, and then played this version. It's much more touch-friendly for touch devices since it was just released on Google Play (and maybe the App Store?) very recently. This is very evident in the UI. Being able to scale the size of the game would be very helpful, as for having a 1080p monitor I should be able to zoom out far more.
Keeping in mind it's a work-in-progress, here are my observations after having played through the first world of the game:
---
Pros:
+ Same great gameplay from the original.
+ The cutscenes are back, as are the original voices. None of that has changed.
+ Campaign now "rates" you out of 3 stars (a la Angry Birds) for your performance. It has no effect on unlocking campaign levels.
+ Textures look much nicer. Not all of them, however (see below)
Cons:
- Skirmish is not here (but coming, as the developer has announced)
- not optimized for large displays (the icons are huge, perhaps for touch device friendliness?)
- No MP (yet)
- Can't customize controls as far as I've seen so far
- Music has very noticeable looping
- Can't use Build Repeat on buildings
- Too many unnecessary animations in the menus (hiding loading times, perhaps?)
- Textures are updated, which means a very different art style. Others have likened this to looking like "crash dummies" and for some parts I would agree. I personally prefered the older art style because they looked more like off-the-line robots rather than things with personality (which the hero units should have!) but to each their own.
- Units run on the air. Or at least, that's what it looks like. Their feet and shadows don't line up and it looks really odd.
Other thoughts:
= I would really love it if the developer could also include the nice build animation from the original (or something like it!) because it was really cool to see the lines slowly build and the "walls" slowly form on buildings. It's a much more jarring animation now but is still in stages. A decrease in the animations for "right-clicking" on units would be great, too. It just seems like it makes it take more time than it needs to.
= The menu background graphic is kind of odd- I'm not sure why it's there, as it doesn't really have a lot to do with the game's setting.
= The globe is nice for giving a sense of perspective for where the battles are taking place in the campaign, but it's HUGE. Seeing all the levels/making the transition better would be cool.
= PLEASE try to find a way to bring back the old economy UI! Being able to see your income differential was much better than just having a ticker with how much money you currently have.
Bugs so far- Bunkers having HUGE amounts of health/it not being hit properly; units climbing up cliffs when they should not be able to jump that distance; Units not being able to be hit when standing next to (but not blocked by) a building.
It's also hard sometimes to select certain units in a group. At times units will clump up and then you can't ever select one, it selects all.
----
That all being said, I still do enjoy the game. Is it as enjoyable as the previous incarnation? Not yet. Hopefully it will be! I'm looking forward to seeing how things turn out. I don't regret purchasing this *yet*, but I'll check back in a couple of months to see how it's progressed.
Recommendation: YES, though be prepared to be disappointed a little, especially if you expect the exact same game with a facelift. The developers are sincerely looking at feedback and that's reassuring.

Before 'Command & Conquer' and before 'Dawn of War' was an impressive RTS style game on the Amiga called 'Z Steel Soldiers' It was developed by one of the most popular and most sort after developers on the Amiga.
Thankfully it's made the transition to Steam with a new HD look without losing it's original gameplay qualities. Nostalgia is strong with this one and I've had a blast. if ever a game was ahead of its time.... this is on of them.

, i'd reccomend this game to people who are hard-boiled Z:SS fans or Z series fans who don't mind having Early Access game. The keywords here are
Yep, this game does feel a bit like Early Access. There are some bugs and glitches here and there, most frequent of them are invincible bunkers (protip - bring some Pyros, their attacks ignore terrain at all) and targeting glitch, which makes your cursor think it's still on enemy building (it made me fail mission 12). Other bugs include units being stuck in buildings, units being unable to enter buildings (makes mission 18 unwinnable), untis reacting weird when under attack (I once had psycho running halfway around the map to retaliate to a guy who just popped up from nearby bridge), and minor non-gamebreaking bugs.
Compared to original, graphics have been improved (original units looked like voodoo dolls of low-poly models; i could count polygons on those on my fingers), howerver there is a problem with bloom sometimes, plus bump mapping on some models look a bit over the top. Some units have been changed in their look, like Toughs now represtent robotic heavy weapons guy from TF2, only armed with homing missile launchers instead of machineguns, and mobile radar jammer now wheeled vehicle instead of tracked one it used to be. Generally, robots look more human than they were supposed to in original game concept-art, and some buildings feel like they've been enlarged and rescaled (worst case with robot factory and air hangar - the former feels a bit bloated, the latter has huge control tower).
My major complain so far is the interface. It's horrible, feels console-ish, and does not present some vital infromation, like balance of income and expences, timer in timed missions, unit count and upgrade levels.
But as far as gampelay goes, it still feels like i'm back in original ZSS: grab a handful of psychos, take as much of the flags on a map as you can, build up a strike group and go wipe the map with your enemies. Or, watch them wipe map with your troops, if you've miscalculated something. The latter however right now is entirely your fault, since there are no difficulty setting, and AI is somewhat clueless on what's it doing (however, on mission 14 AI tried to drop a light tank and two pyros on my command center via transport heli - never seen AI doing that in original).
Multiplayer and Skirmish modes are missing so far, and i can't get clear understanding if devs will impliment them anytime soon/late.
Finally, the sounds are taken right from original Z:SS, as wel as music tracks (and projectile models, save for Laser's - it's much brighter than original one was). However, currently there is a problem with music: it stucks in a loop and never ends. Even "mission successful" music. So, i dunno, pop your favorite epic techo playlist while you're at it? :D
So, as i said: get this if you're either hard-boiled Z:Steel Soldiers fan, or if you're Z series fan and don't mind game being a bit raw at the moment. Or if you like buying raw games and then complain on forums. Otherwise, wait.

First off, this version of the game has been made obselete by the Special Edition, which has more playable characters, a couple new modes and more content for your buck. That said, I happened to buy this before the Special Edition came out...and I'm actually surprised that they released an updated version of this game in 2015, because some parts of it are dated as hell. All the standard tropes of PS2-era Japanese action games are on full display, ranging from fixed camera angles, obscenely annoying special missions, arbitrary puzzles (this was always Devil May Cry's schtick though) and a story that's like reaaaaaallly anime, and not in a great way (also Devil May Cry's schtick, with the exception of the third game).
But the actual meat and potatoes of DMC4, the stylish combat, is still really good. You've got a crapload of weapons, including my favorite - the Pandora, a transformable suitcase that changes into 666 different types of gun - and switching between Dante's styles or using Nero's devil arm on the fly to throw foes is grand. Only thing is, I would've liked the game more if it had just starred Dante, especially because Dante's levels are a backtracking paltry amount compared to Nero's. Nero reminds me too much of a Final Fantasy protagonist, and part of the joy of DMC is watching Dante take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything because he knows he's an outrageous demon hunter. Nero just doesn't have that flamboyance, and I get that he was created to draw new players into the series, but because his design is so similar to Dante, you can't help but compare the two. Dante always comes out on top...so it's like, what was the point of putting Nero in there at all?
Anyway, still a solid game, though DMC3 remains the king of the pre-reboot titles.

Since there seems to be some controversy about why this game is short in my opinion, here's some clarification:
The biggest time sinks in this game are fighting completely optional enemies and finding items required to advance the story. Especially at harder difficulties you'd be a fool to actually engage combat and waste ammo that you'll certainly need for the next boss encounter when you might as well just run past the enemies. There is no punishment to skipping the vast majority of enemies in the game.
The time spent in order to find quest items like cables, fuses and so on drastically decreases on your consecutive playthroughs as you already know their locations.
Combining these two realizations actually leaves you with very little game left, as the story in itself is very short. The best multiplayer tactical turn-based strategy game I've ever encountered, bar none. As a lifelong devotee to the turn-based classics like XCOM, Jagged Alliance and Silent Storm, I've always wanted the beauty of Necromunda's consequence-laden multiplayer skirmishes brought to the PC - and this game delivers.
After two days of owning the title, I've accumulated 17 hours of multiplayer-only battles, and the matches I now have under my belt are without doubt the most memorable strategy gaming experiences I've ever had - even better than playing Necromunda with miniatures. Hell, I'm terrified this game will distract me from my own programming work!
As everybody will tell you, the third-person movement and control scheme will seem strange at first, but they serve to immerse you more; like how Firaxis' introduction of cinematic shots for dramatic moments did, but better. Warband management is the real-deal Necromunda/Mordheim experience; defeats and victories don't feel so black and white, as even a victor might walk away worse for wear, or - as is the case against a friend - economically poorer for not focusing on resources.
This is the first time I've ever felt compelled to write a review for a game, but as somebody who's been trying for years to find a multiplayer strategy experience that captures the nuances of the Necromunda/Mordheim systems, and as somebody who's programming a TBS myself, I desperately want this developer to succeed with this product and consider releasing a DLC for some of the fringe-factions.
I implore you to buy it, harass your friends to buy it, and start a small tourney where each of you has a warband that you only pit against each other in multiplayer. You'll have more fun than any other TBS game can offer you right now, at least in the multiplayer aspect.

The fifth instalment of the 12 Labours of Hercules series feels more like an expansion pack rather than a new game, but it manages to deliver the fun time management gameplay this series is famous for.
As all longer series, 12 Labours of Hercules has its ups and downs. Lucky for us, even the downs result in enjoyable time management games, including the current subject, Kids of Hellas.
Similarly to Girl Power, this one didn’t touch the game mechanics too much: you still use 2-4 servants to gather resources and spend them on clearing obstacles, with Hercules and Megara helping out every now and then.
Whereas all games up until now asked the player to find the best order of actions to meet the level goals, Kids of Hellas decided to simplify the level layouts considerably: conveniently placed production buildings, the almost total absence of thieves, or the removal of cost on the actions performed by Hercules and Megara are all there to make the player’s life easier.
…And the re-introduced stockpile limit makes sure that all these changes mean nothing when the player constantly has to manage the resource levels, making sure to not gather more than it can be held, nor to spend them faster than they are acquired.
While this new focus on micromanagement possibly will alienate some of the returning players, Kids of Hellas is still enjoyable enough for anyone already familiar with the series to give them a try.

TLDR: Recommended if you're in for the challenge.
The 5th installment of a series is rarely a peak achievement, generally we can be happy if "more of the same" is done decently. And on the surface, T12LoH V perfectly conforms this trend - the visuals and the music tread the same old (although pretty good) ground, there are no gameplay improvements to speak of compared to the last two games, and the story is even sillier than before. If you play time / resource management games for relaxation, then part V is definitely the weakest of the series.
However, the only reason I play these games is that reaching gold times are decently challenging, forcing the player to think up strategies and work around resource or other constraints. This aspect was getting rather stale in parts III and IV, but part V is a much welcome improvement. It's much harder to hit gold times, and also most of the levels have multiple constraints that need to be unraveled in the correct order, sometimes with rather exact phased timing. As a result, I'm enjoying this installment the best since the initial game.

I must say this is the toughest 12 Labours of Hercules compared to the other four series. You need to practice your moves several times in order to beat the Gold and the Developer's record. All in all, this game is frustrating but enjoyable once you beat the score.

This game is really fun if you can deal with the learning curve and some of the games downfalls. The story itself is pretty short and can be beaten in around 2-3 hours if you've already done it. My first run was around 4-5 hours to beat the story. The PvP gives me mixed feelings. The PvP can
be rewarding. Doing combat trials rewards you with good xp and new gear after you level up. The one aspect I enjoy about the PvP is that you can still progress even if you lose. The aspect of PvP that I don't like is how easy it is to abuse the game. Fast decks are really easy to abuse as all your opponent can do is guard until their stamina is spent or attempt to do their stances defense ability. The thing that sucks about that is there is huge risk with little reward in my opinion. Also you fight anyone in PvP. There is no rank system or ELO or even a skill based system, it is just you against anyone. This does help you learn as you can see what style of combat is the best and how to improve in combat. But it gets annoying when higher levels beat you senselessly because of stats, more available moves, gear, and experience. It is very possible to outskill your opponent however. Since there is a lack of a "smart" match making system, I always go against higher levels. Because of this I have gotten better and can deal with them even if their sword or stats is better.
The thing that keeps me playing is the growth and progression that most games don't offer. You can constantly get better and improve your character. You also get more skilled at doing combos, avoiding attacks, and positioning yourself too. Lots of skill involved when the game isn't abused.
Overall a great game to play. A lot of skill involved which makes the game very fun and intense at times. Can't wait for new updates. Only thing I would like is for fast decks to be balanced a little more, maybe less damage or more stamina spent? I will update this review the more I play to see if my outlook on the game ever changes.

I'll let others review the scary aspect of this game. I wanna focus on the toddler simulation aspect.
Holy cow. I wish there was a way to just have a toddler simulator based on these mechanics. After I played through the actual storyline I went back and started over again and just played around in the playroom and was blown away by the attention to physics. Drag a stool across the wooden floor, it slides okay. Push it across carpet and you're in for a struggle. You can't lift a pillow above your head but you can toss an inflatable ball a few feet.
You can pick things up, put them down, open and close things, climb and even fall. There's no health bar so spills don't really matter. You wobble when you walk and make appropriate sounds as you move around. And it's interesting to see the world from the perspective of one so small (again). In all I would love to see more done with just the simulator side of things. It would be a riot to run around the house and interact with the environment without having to worry about the 'bad guys' getting you.
After a long hard week of adulting, sometimes I don't want my gaming to give me puzzles or enemies to deal with. I just want to unwind. but I'm not into the farming or app-type games. This is just my style! I'd love to see more walking simulators like this.

This is a brilliant game.  Instantly addicting.  I've never played a snow plow game and at first I was confused how they would make such a small game board into a plowing game but sure enough, it's perfect.  Don't change a thing.
You are given a tiny world with cars going from one side to the next, and they need to drive on the roads to get there.  It snows endlessly creating roadblocks which you have to clear.  The longer you play the crazier it gets until you eventually crash into a car and lose.  I haven't lost by any other means in that time period but I'm assuming they would also fire you from your job if the people got too upset.  As you play through and get 10 points (10 cars made it through) you unlock the medium sized board, with the exact same rules but on a much bigger surface there is so much more going on.  It took me a good dozen times to get that 10 points in one run.
The controls are really weird, but it has some great controller support and after awhile you get the hang of it.  Basically you press left if you want your truck to make a 90 degree turn, press left twice if you want to do a 180, and you can cancel a turn at any time by pressing the opposite direction.  The first 10 minutes will be confusing to you but it's smooth sailing afterwards.  Or actually smooth plowing.  Hopefully.  Anyways, I really enjoyed the game and I will be putting it on my favorites list, definitely.  Kudos.

This is a great pickup-and-play game.  It satisfies a primal urge that we, as humans, have to move large mounds of things.  If you find yourself lying awake at night wondering what it all means, this game is for you!
At first I was having a lot of trouble controlling my plow (I've never driven a plow before), but once I started driving on the roads instead of through the snow I had a much easier time.  I think I'll apply this lesson to my real life driving techniques as well.
Love the music too!  Good variety of tracks to keep your ears happy.  The humming of your beastly plow motor can be a bit harsh at times, but not so much that it ruins the experience.
10/10 would plow again... wait, that's not how I meant it... I- ...  I will play this game.

While it is not going to be for everyone, I had quite a bit of fun with Dawn of the Plow. It is not really a game that I would play for hours at a time but it is a game that works well in 15-20 minute increments.
The one thing that people might have some issues with are the controls. The controls aren't the most precise but this appears to have been done on purpose to help simulate driving on slippery roads. I usually hate imprecise controls but they work in Dawn of the Plow since the whole game is centered around slipping and sliding around. If the driving controls were really precise the game would just be boring since it would be too easy.
How much play time you get out of the game depends on how much you like chasing high scores. If you are the type of gamer that just wants to beat a game and then move on you aren't going to get a lot out of Dawn of the Plow since you can "beat" the whole game in less than an hour. If you like trying to beat your own high scores though I think you could get a lot of time out of the game.
While its' not perfect, I think Dawn of the Plow is a pretty good game. If the concept interests you I think you will enjoy the game.
Note: I received a free review copy from the developer but received no other compensation.

And due to its controlls I could barely get past the first boss, which I in the end did beat, and never get past the second. Thus far this game is my only exposure to the
(
) series, and it’s left solid enough of an impression on me to want to play the others. A friend of mine was kind enough to gift me this game, so thanks again, mate! (Not sure if he wants to stay anonymous or not).
The game’s combat is focused around fighting off hordes of enemies, using your gun, your sword, and your Devil Bringer, which can be used to grab enemies, throws, and other melee based attacks. By playing well (string together combos of varied moves against enemies without taking damage) you can fill a gauge, that can be used to activate your Devil Trigger, which grants you extra damage and some health regen.
About halfway through the game you’ll switch playable characters from Nero to Dante (from previous
games), and he boasts a different play style. He lacks the Devil Bringer, and has 4 different styles of attack, which can be switched between at any time during gameplay. He likewise can activate the Devil Trigger for added benefits.
Now I’ll be honest, it’s been awhile since I’ve played the game and I can’t remember the story all that much (I usually write reviews within a few days of finishing a game, but I played through this one long before I even started writing reviews). From what I can recollect and from skimming over the plot on Wikipedia, it’s some cluster♥♥♥♥ involving demons, a religious order, and Dante and Nero. It didn’t really stick in my mind much, so it apparently isn’t all that memorable.
While the game is a lot of fun, it’s not without its shortcomings. There’s a fairly significant amount of backtracking through old levels, and just recycling old parts. I have no problem with some slight use of backtracking, especially when it’s done to further the story and features some new gameplay, but here it just feels lazy. The camera for the game can sometimes be annoying, but isn’t ever too much of an issue.
The music for the game is frankly abysmal, sounding like the sort of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hard rock you’d get from some godawful band like Disturbed. With the same damn song playing constantly through the game any time you enter combat and the action heats up. A hard rock or metal soundtrack could probably work really well for this game, if we were given some decent tracks. But sadly, we’re not treated to Slayer.
When I originally played through this game I had to use a keyboard, as I didn’t then have a controller to use. While I normally prefer a keyboard and mouse, it really doesn’t work at all for this game (though I should note it uses a keyboard only). I did a lot of remapping just to get things to a workable state, using WASD to move, and some combination of JKNIMO for attacks, and some other keys for switching styles as Dante. It took a looooong time to adjust to, and it was always far from ideal, but I managed to make it work. I gave the game a quick 15 minute test run right before writing this review with a controller, and it plays substantially smoother. You could play
with a keyboard, but I highly recommend a controller, you’ll be much happier for it.
From poking about online, it seems most people complete this game on normal difficulty (Devil Hunter) in about 12-16 hours. I took quite a bit longer than that, but that’s most likely just me being bad at the game. (It should be noted that
has a very high difficulty, and it’s all the better for it).
I’d also recommend playing it on Devil Hunter, even if you’re new to the series. The game will tell you to try the easy mode first, but after 2 levels of that, I realized it just wasn’t enough, and I switched over to playing it properly. There’s some bonus difficulty modes once you complete the game, but I haven’t bothered with those yet.
As of this writing,
has a Special Edition on Steam, which gives you a few more characters to play with, and I think some other bonus content (I don’t have the SE, so I’m not certain). As of this writing, it’s only a $5 price difference at full price, and probably about the same on sale. I’d say pick up the SE instead of this version if you plan on getting this game.
can be a bloody hard challenge at times, but it’s damn good fun. Certainly worth your time and money.

You would think that the Gods learned their lessons to let Hercules in peace. But Ares had to ask our hero to help him in a war. And as Hercules refused, the God of War decided to turn all the kids of Hellas into an army of zombies. Hercules, Megara and all their friends will have to save the children and to return them home... with the servants doing all the work as usual.
It's already the fifth episode in Hercules's life. Nothing really changed in terms of gameplay. Allow me to paste a text I've made for the profile of the previous games on Neoseeker (inspired mainly by my reviews).
The game has three difficulties: Casual (without timer and without score kept), Normal (with a timer and with score) and Expert (with a timer that goes faster and with score).
The goal is to finish the level by reaching objectives given (in time if you're playing in Normal or Expert). You're sending workers to clean or repair the road, to gather ressources (food, wood, gold) whether they're outside or being produced, to build buildings (farm for food, workshop for wood, mine for gold, outposts for expanding the inventory and to stock faster resources). During the course of your adventure, you may be helped by other mythological figures like Pegasus. Generally, before being able to use them for specific tasks (Pegasus can make rocks fall down, the Lion is taking pieces of meat, Medusa is scaring Minotaurs and Cerberus is doing the same task but for ghosts for example). You can also exchange gold for floating ressources with Charon.
Also, you can get favors from Gods by building poles in their honor: Demeter will make ressources being produced faster, Hephaistos that will make your servants work faster, Apollon will scare every robber, Hermes will make your workers run faster, etc.
Robbers are also returning: if you leave your ressources unattended for a certain period of time, thieves will steal them.
Hercules and Megara are still there: the former for moving boulders or other specific tasks, like saving the children, the latter for growing fruit trees and clean the soil. New allies are also revealed as sellers: for example, they can sell 2 gold for 3 wood.
The search for puzzles pieces is also included, to unlock a jigsaw puzzle that will do the same for bonus levels.
While the first levels can be done easily without bonus, later, you can activate some if the energy bar reachs it: work faster (ressources appear faster and workers are doing their tasks faster), run faster (workers see their speed increased when running from a task to another), stop time (timer is frozen), more ressources (each ressource gathered is giving one more), temporary worker (one more worker will help). These bonus are limited in time and are resplenished. Their place in the bar is varying from a level to another.
Children can be used to retrieve more energy for the bonus bar.
Are you still with me? Ok, I'm just checking if you didn't run away from that long description. Let's focus on the other points.
The graphics didn't change at all, they're still colorful and nice. The soundtrack is also identical.
As usual, 12 Labours of Hercules isn't a big surprise: apart for the children and the new allies, nothing is really different. However, if I'm writing a late review, it's simply because I was waiting for a fix for an achievement that didn't work. Indeed, the only level with thieves was impossible to realize the anti-theft achievement because ressources were at the other end of the map, with rocks and bridges to repair. Now, since two days, they've added thieves in other levels (like 4.4) and since then, everything is working fine.
Should you purchase this game? If you're a fan of the series, you're not going to miss it. I'm recommending it to every player out there that wants to try casual time management games. But, true, while the rest of the series is cheaper, the five bucks I've spent are five bucks well spent. I've still enjoyed greatly this new episode and I'm pretty sure that many people will keep it like that.

A TLDR at the bottom of this review to summarise my points.
I really enjoy this game, though it is anything but a 'pick up and play' game for when you have ten minutes to kill. The graphics are beautiful and illustrate the lush environments of a seedy and damned city. The gameplay is challenging from the outset and learning curve (if you ignore the tutorials) can be steep. I chose to play through as Skaven, and haven't tried the other races as yet, so my opinions may be invalid or void with regards to their gameplay. The customisation of characters is adequate, it's not an integral part of the game, and seems to be purely asthetic, though it is a nice touch, as is the injuries, for example; if a character maims a hand, their hand on the character model is mangled.
The story missions, character progression and warband management are all solid, on the whole, the game is well made and fun, whilst having a high level of strategic gameplay. However... and this is my only gripe about the game thus far, the load times are ridiculous! I have a high end machine, and yet sometimes I can go away boil the kettle, make a cup of tea or coffee and return and it still hasn't finished loading the map. This is the main reason I have yet to try any of the online features. Also, it is annoying when the voice overs from the mission and the narrator fight it out trying to talk over eachother, resulting in a garbled mess of voices and leaving you to read the mission objectives etc... for vital information you need.
TLDR:
+graphics
+voice acting
+ gameplay
+story
+ challenging
- load times
- voices overlapping

Kingdom New Lands is one of a kind game. Initially, I was skeptical and the game looked downright easy. However, as the game progress, the challenge increases manifold. The best part is the game tells you a story without a word or tutorial. The nitty-gritty of the gameplay is taught through nicest subtleties.
I really like how forest disappears making way for farming land and pastures, how light and snow gleams through the water. The environment and art direction execution are flawless so are the music. It enthuses the player in a spellbinding force.
Granted the gameplay is repetitive but its applicable to even AAA games, same old chores side missions and whatnot have always made the game benign. I managed to 100% complete the game with all achievements and unlike the palpable fear I managed to do it ease. Had it been not for the achievement I could have pushed it past 120 days.
Overall its a nice twist on strategy game and it's not for everyone. I really like the game and I highly recommend it, the game asks you to put your best foot forward and teaches you a very important lesson in life - making the most with the least. I am eagerly looking forward to the sixth island and the next iteration, however, I wish the developer make substantive changes in the next version unlike they had made in the earlier and current version.

A majority of projects never achieve the features promised during the founding phase and run away with everyones money, leaving the game in a bad condition. This has to stop.

OFP Cold War Crisis was a childhood game for me, but I wasn't particularly sold on ArmA so I had to give this a spin. Overall, there's a negative for every positive, but if you're willing to look over the negatives, you'll be rewarded with a pretty cool experience. It's a bit more streamlined and casual than ArmA, so it was easier for me to get into. Story was more interesting to me than the ArmA campaigns, but had its downsides as well (lack of character, more than anything). I had quite a bit of fun playing the challenge missions in co op with friends, felt like I was actually in the thick of it as I yelled out enemy positions from behind cover while being shot at, hoping my friend would be able to flank them. If you're a diehard MilSim fan, you'll definitely find something of merit in this game. Totally worth splitting a $20 with a friend and trying to beat the challenge missions. Really is a bit of a hidden gem, floundered mostly by publisher decisions.

This game is good. Not bad, not perfect. Has its own charm.
The things I liked the most were the immersion in the missions. You must prepare you attack and take advantage of your environment with your playmates who will save your back before you know it (or the contrary that's said). You have to be patient and listen to your environment. Adapt your tactics and never attack in front. A single bullet can kill you and it's all over. Your squad is precious but you can also play alone against the world. Play in hardcore mode if you want greater challenge with no hud.
But the game has been better now with the Island War Mod, improving the AI and graphics giving fresh air to the game while giving you the opportunity to take on all the map (a big one) and retake capture points one by one against the PLA, adding many and many hours of gameplay.
Check also the editor. It's always a pleasure to play a game with a tool when you can use your imagination to create your own content. Check the missions online, there is a ton of them. And for it's price, this game deserve its attention.
Now the worst points of the game :
- Sound : the environment sounds are good. Not the warfare ones which sound pretty synthetic to me.
- AI (vanilla) : the basic AI of the game can be brillant some times or a total mess. Some stay stuck in a truck whereas your squad is firing at it, some goes in front of you without noticing anything, some seems to see you behind your cover...It can be very annoying some time. A reason more to prepare carefully your approach. You'll nerver know what you meet.
Last words : see what goes good for you in this game. Surely not the game of the year but clearly a good one. Not the most beautiful but you don't notice it has 8 years old now. Thanks to modders and the open world scale of the game, it can be very enjoyable for those who don't want to spend time and money for better sims.

Just a note to all you readers, I don't like traditional fighting games.  I absolutely suck at them and I always end up button mashing. Smash, Tekken, Street Fighter, etc., I've played them all because my brother loves those types of games, but I don't.  Now, that being said, this is possibly the only fighting game I have thoroughly enjoyed and can see myself continue playing.  The combat feels fluid and just MAKES SENSE.  Some attacks flow well into other attacks, and it's your job to figure out how you want to fight.  The single player aspect is very short, I finished it in one day, but consider the single player "campaign" as an extended tutorial for the PvP aspect, which is where the game truly lies.  Mastering your own fighting style and making it as you go seems like it would be a chore, but in reality, it's actually quite a lot of fun, and lends a whole lot of replayability as you strive to beat yourself (and others in PvP, but you have to master yourself first.)
The reason the ratings seem to be so mixed is that the game is having server issues.  I will admit, I have had these issues as well, BUT, the devs have reached out and are in communication with us, the players.  They keep updating us on their progress, and have been pushing updates far faster than I thought they would.  So kudos to them for such hard work.  Once those issues are fixed, there is no reason to not give this game a try if you are interested at all in a RPG/Third person fighting game.  Even with a few issues still in place, and I emphasize a few, this game is still worth your time and money.
TL;DR - The combat is fluid, polished and fun, and the developers work with the players to get things done.  Worth it.
