Absolver is not a souls-like. It's not a hack and slash, it's not a button masher. The closes thing you could compare Absolver to is For Honour. That being said, I have never played For Honour, so Absolver is entirely new and fresh for me.
From the outside, you see the gameplay as normal beat 'em up gameplay but with some fancy kicks. But, your eyes are drawn down to the bottom of the screen and you notice the ever changing, ever confusing quadrant system. This is where Absolver shines. It isn't just hitting X a few times, then Y and dodge. Each quadrant,  (controlled with the analogue stick) can have up to three moves and one alternative move. These can be quick punches, strong kicks, or anywhere in between. Every move is different, and cannot be repeated. Some moves can dodge attacks, for example a low spinning kick can avoid high punches, or an elbow strike can dodge a sword thrust. Each attack having individual aspect and traits makes every action vitally important. You can't just mash buttons, because all of a sudden you're in a different quadrant (because a lot of moves transition you between them) and then you're doing heavy kicks when you're out of stamina. All of a sudden, your guard is gone and your getting smacked in the face. This game is a lot more strategical than it first appears, and can only be experienced to its fullest with trial and error and practice in the online mode.
Online combat is vital to this game. The single player (if you can even call it that - it's really seemless multiplayer) can be completed in about 6 hours. By that point, you should have a decent combat deck, and it's time to jump into multiplayer. The single player is essentially a long tutorial. Only by playing multiplayer can you truly realise how terrible your combat deck is. And that isn't a bad thing, it's far from it in fact. This way you learn how to improve, learning new tactics from your opponents. And, of course, you can learn attacks from your combatant, further increasing combat deck possibilities. In all my hours of his game, I'm still learning, progressing, and getting better in every way possible.
One part of this game that is comparable to Dark Souls is the plot. And by that I mean, there is none, unless you look for it. Weapon and armour descriptions, NPC dialogue and other very minor parts of the game are your entire source for the plot. This might seem like a downside, but of course the game isn't focused on the story aspect. It also leaves so much room for intrigue and theories, I've spent a long time reading and taking part with people discussing lore over the last few days. Like the plot, the music follows suit. Along the lines of the old Tomb Raider games, it's quiet. Eerily quiet. Music only is in this game when it's required. It builds tension and drama. It perfectly fits the gameplay to the point where you don't even notice the subtleness of the soundtrack.
On that topic, the community is amazing. Very few times have I felt like I was being overpowered, assaulted or any such things when playing the game. If someone picks a fight with you in the world and you lose, they almost always revive you, bow, and continue on their merry way.
As for the server issues, I haven't had too many problems. Sometimes I can't connect to the server, and there might be a little bit of input lag but very, very rarely. I can't say anything about the Australian servers, but I believe Sloclap have / are working on a fix to the issues.
In summary, this game has a lot more depth than first appears. Sloclap have done an excellent job making a deep, intricate system of fighting along with a world that sparks community intrigue. I look forward to seeing what they add to the game, whether it's new moves, new weapons or even just a new pair of boots. I recommend this game to anyone who wants a strong, online experience filled with trial and error with an incredible, friendly community to become the best fighter you can.

Point-defense systems, cargo, salvage and mining are options for a "career" play to build up resources however the grind is long and boring. Ship movement is your typical thrusters and a hyperspace system to jump from point A to B faster, however when jumping you loose your perception on distance and its an annoying wait to see when the ship feels like ending the trip near the target. The shield is a more literal "kinetic field Generator" to protect the ship from damage, but limits movement. You go faster with it off, but take damge to the hull without a shield to cover your rear.
To complicate matters the ship construction designs are done impressively free, able to freely rotate and adjust segments any combination you desire without distance restrictions or locking points - but it comes back to bite the design mechanic in how over-use of too many blocks can kill the gameplay performance. Some moderate limitations have been done to limit weapons and design, but it falls back to an inherit issue with the firepower and accuracy. There is no need for thinking small here, bigger ships, more power, shields and weapons will always do better. It makes any ammount of small craft obsolete and limits the gameplay feel - and punishes you for it as the ship becomes more sluggish with its size increasing. It makes the gameplay drag on in a rather negative way.
I admit its a fun way to loose hours in it, crafting a unique ship - but you'll be so drained when done and after flying it for only short distances you'll not want to actually play with it much after.
The game itself remains largely shallow in its build. No real story, gameplay or function - just create a random set of stars and factions/corporations and choose who you blow up basically. The faction loyalties shift freely with each fight, but it lacks heavily in the substance department for the actual game. No kind of character exists outside nameless portraits and your own nickname. In the basic Career mode you start with a small ship and grind up, but can just kick off in Sandbox to build whatever then just fly faster without the tedious grinding spree to build up to the big ship.
It is a great concept, plenty of heart in it to be honest - but its end application feels lacking, and in a really big way. Pick it up if your really interested in its unique way of doing things, but be wary there isn't much here.

I bought this game during Early Access because the game looked hugley promising.  This seemed to be the game that would fill the void left in the absence of Elite, Escape Velocity, or a good X game after the abomination that is Rebirth.  Unfortunatley as development trucked along, much more slowly than originally promised at that, features in development began to be cut.  First the scale of the universe was reduced, then the Newtonian physics that were one of the huge selling points of the game were cut in favor of a "simplified" traditional flight model that has ships slow down when engines are cut, turn like atmospheric craft, and have velocity rather than acceleration limits (and these limits are VERY small, measured in triple-diget KPH in the enormity of a solar system).
The robust mission and faction system never materialized, leaving players with very little more to do than in alpha stages.  Basically you can trade legitimatley, or pirate and sale.  The universe offers almost nothing else to do.  There are no indications of where one can buy and sell items let alone how the prices will fluctuate nor what ship modules will be available until you reach a system in the tiny galaxies generated each new time you start a game.  Even then what faction controls a star system (the number of which can be ajusted when you create a galaxy, but they are nothing more than interchangable names and their influence almost never changes for any reason).
The one good thing that I can say about this game is that the ship editor is fairly large.  It was reduced in features since the alpha, again in an attempt to simplify which they failed at anyway, but still offers many options in terms of ship design.  The wide range of vessels both original and copies of famous ships from sci-fi series does attest to this.  Unfortunatley there is nothing to do with your ship other than mindlessly shoot other ships.
If you think that Elite: Dangerous doesn't give you enough help in the universe nor enough interaction with the economy, NPCs, or factions, then stay away from this game.  The tutorials, to the VERY limited extent they exist at all, teach you nothing and somehow saying you recieve no guidence manages to be an understatement.  Even the graphics are nothing to write home about.  Actual old games like X3 or Escape Velocity Nova manage to be better at this, and if you want less story and more trade and exploration with a game that looks beautiful check out Elite: Dangerous or keep your eye out for the (as of time of writing) unreleased Star Citizen or No Man's Sky.
Was I wrong to be under the impression that getting this game on early access came with a price break?  I paid $19.99 for early access and the game is now $19.99 on release?

Yes, it's finally a version of DoDonPachi Daifukkatsu that you can easily purchase and have work and be more or less playable and no, the port isn't a perfect 1:1 of the arcade/xbox version - particularly in terms of slowdown. To be specific, slowdown had to be emulated for PCs since hardware is different across systems where the Xbox could throttle the processor until it more or less matches the arcade performance. This causes a few issues, but my biggest problem with it is that situations where I'd expect slowdown to ease in/ease out the transition can be almost instantaneous, so in some situations you're slow-mo weaving through bullets and then suddenly the game's back at regular speed and you're dead or farting out one of your autobombs. Not a good feeling, but you can still play around it.
So if you want the best way to play it, this probably isn't it - that's the Xbox version. But if you just want to finally be able to play it because you can't or don't want to spring for the Xbox version for any reason, it's perfectly acceptable.

Dodonpachi is an anime game that has been constantly recommended to me by a few friends. Dodonpachi this, dodonpachi that; they'd rant and rave about how long they've waited to play this game. So when the time came and the game was finally finished, I purchased it.
Does it live up to the hype? Read on, fellow gamer.
If you're unfamiliar with games like dodonpachi, it is what is called a "galaga" style game. Galaga was a commodore 64 game that was very popular in the early 90s, if you are old enough to remember. The objective is to survive long enough while an onslaught of aliens slowly crept up in front of you all the while you try to kill them with your lasers. Obviously, dodonpachi has better graphics, and a japanimation style, but unfortunately not without problems.
I own a very nice 50" 4k HDTV and I'm used to being treated to masterpieces like Watch Dogs 2 and Horizon: Zero Dawn, so when I first started up dodonpachi I was expecting comparable graphics. For a game that was made in 2016, it unfortunately disappoints. CAVE (the creators of this game) try to fool you into thinking it is a 4k game by filling the screen with hand drawn oriental cartoon art (me so sneaky!). Unfortunately, the actual play area is confined to an oddly shaped area in the center of the screen. I really don't get it, you've got all this room and you can't figure out a way to use it? Anyway, to top this off I spotted many jaggies and pixelation so the 3D rendering engine must have some bugs or they're not using much anti-aliasing. The 2d inspired graphics look nice, but are far inferior stylistically to the indie artgame masterpieces such as "brink" and "fez".
The story is underdeveloped (or perhaps abstruse to the "gweilo" mind?) and I don't understand it. There are no cutscenes or anything to explain it. Instead you are thrown directly into thousands of bullets without a why or a what-for. No effort is made to tell you why they are shooting at you, why you are shooting at them, and the story behind it. I felt sort of guilty slaughtering so many enemies without knowing if they were russian or something first. There was no philosophical underpinning- no exploration of deep themes in seminal art games such as gone home or the stanley parable. You have no choices in the game that unlock different endings. You just shoot from your little spaceship, and get to the ending 20 minutes later. Is this really an acceptable level of content?
The gameplay is slightly more redeeming. You pilot a ship in a 2d plane of movement. This allows you to move along a y axis unlike previous galaga style games, squaring the possibilities. As this was designed for PC (us master race, right? seriously, check out /r/pcmasterrace on reddit), it was built for a keyboard and mouse, allowing great precision compared to, say, a controller, or arcade stick for this style of retrogame. However, my mouse must not have been set up correctly as it did nothing considering this is a pc game. I think you are able to change the yaw or elevation of your craft with your mouse, but I could just not get it working. I use a razer chroma deathadder, as a hardcore gamer and e-sports enthusiast, and perhaps it had too many DPIs for the primitive engine of this game.
As far as soundtracks go, it is surprisingly quite good. The music fits the levels, and seems to be a form of japanese dubstep. It has a lot of synthesizers, like an 80s style song. It has not caught up to electronic music on the level of skrillex, but for a videogame, it does not disappoint and is great ambient noise for your space battles against the large robot schoolgirl bosses with anime powers (which were a bit offputting, objectifying, a bit misogynistic, and made me sexually uncomfortable, but I can forgive the cultural gap).
Anyway, I easily completed the game in 20 minutes on my first attempt. Besides promising gameplay this is just not the kind of thing for hardcore gamers such as myself. Although it has much artificial difficulty like a game such as dark souls where you constantly die, you immediately are revived by pressing 'continue' right where you left off, making all those deaths pointless, and even rewarded by the game! There are no checkpoints and you just continue indefinitely until you reach the final boss. Where are the alternative endings, or replay value? Where is the extra content that rewards skilled players? Something like a secret level or boss after you beat the game would have been nice, but make no mistake- this is a credit feeder for sure- much like the old arcade games that preceded it. In addition, there is no online multiplayer besides a primitive arcade-style leaderboard for those who try to play the mathematics minigame that gives you higher scores by increasing the numbers on your screen. I barely passed algebra 2 in highschool, and am a sociology major, so I don't find mathematical puzzles in my games to be worthwhile or exciting to pursue. Sadly, I am not a japanese math PhD that can do integrationals and sign/co-sign, and this kind a of contrived form of difficulty is not for me.
All in all - Dodonpachi? More like dodonpasse. Super Nintendo quality games just don't live up to their contemporaries anymore, and it's time to change. Maybe CAVE should start making mobile phone games, or arcade games, instead. When I am on my pc or console, I want a game to deliver. I want fast paced action oriented multiplayer of a game like overwatch or call of duty, not slow old primitve ones such as quake or unreal tournament. I want the cinematic cutscenes and story of something like watch dogs or jordan peele's postmodern masterpiece "get out", not planetscape: tormentor or those black and white snoozefests by that old fat italian guy (felloni? fullani? I can't remember). Some things are better off left in the past. It's time for the japanese to come out of hiding in their caves and accept they lost the war- the videogame war- and incorporate western technology and engrossing stories into their AAA titles.
Overall, I give dodonpachi 7/10 gameplay, 6/10 soundtrack, and 3/10 hardcores, for a cumulative score of 5.85. Thanks for reading my review. Be sure to rate and comment down below, and subscribe to my streams on twitch and youtube.

We had to wait a long time for a North American release of Dodonpachi Daifukkatsu (DFK), but it was worth it.  You really get your money's worth with Resurrection.  Not only are you getting Dodonpachi Daifukkatsu 1.5, you're getting 1.51 (previously Europe-only paid DLC), Black Label, and 3 arrange modes.  1.5 and 1.51 are fairly similar, but even discounting those (and the Novice modes), you still have 5 distinct shmups in this one package!
Add onto that the built-in variety of ship types and shot types for those ships, and you have a crazy amount of content and ways to play.  You've got your usual (well, except for Daioujou) Types A, B, and C here.  You can choose between Bomb Style, Power Style, or Strong Style, similar to the Element Dolls system of DOJ or the dresses of SDOJ.  Strong Style had to be unlocked in the arcades, but here they just give it to you.  Bomb Style is your usual "shot" type, Power features two modes to switch between with their own properties and is good for scoring but you can't manually bomb, and Strong Style has the best features of Bomb and Power, but your hyper builds very slowly.
The main gameplay of DFK revolves around bullet cancelling.  When you use your hyper, your shot will cancel enemy bullets, increasing both your score and your chances of survival.  This mechanic, coupled with the unusual 4-button layout, makes DFK a very accessible game for newcomers to the series.  In fact, on my first time picking up Novice mode, I accidentally 1CCed it.  Normal mode does present a number of interesting challenges even for veterans of the DDP series (I'm looking at you, stage 5 laser rings).  Another unique mechanic in DFK is the ability to "push back" enemy lasers with your own laser, which is pretty cool.  This is one with both a low skill floor and a high skill ceiling, and it's very satisfying and feels good to play.
Arrange A of DFK is "daioujou" style.  Instead of building a meter for hypers, you get hyper pickups like DOJ, though you're locked into a particular ship type.  Arrange B is an infinite lives score attack mode where the color of bee pickups and using shot or laser (as well as replaying stages) will determine the strength of enemies and the speed and density of their bullet patterns.
Black Label introduces the "RED" mechanic, where holding down rapid-shot and the laser button at the same time will do a ShotLaser similar to the 360 mode of Saidaioujou.  In that game, using the ShotLaser drained your health.  Here, it increases the RED meter, making enemy patterns more difficult at certain thresholds.  Black Label also gives you the ability to turn off auto-bombing if you like.  Selecting Strong Style in BL will give you the harder Loop 2 patterns from 1.5 right off the bat, making it similar to Expert dress from SDOJ.
Black Label Arrange is the wonderful "ketsuipachi", where you play through Black Label but using the Tiger Schwert ship from Ketsui, complete with lock-on laser and even scoring chips.  The OST is also an arranged version of the Ketsui OST, done by the very skilled Virt.  It can't be overstated how good the music in Black Label Arrange is; it even outclasses the already amazing Black Label OST, in my opinion.
In most of these modes, you have a 2nd route through each stage (the "hidden" or Ura route), featuring more difficult patterns and some throwback midbosses to tickle your nostalgia.  You also have a 2nd loop which can also have 2 routes, as well as a grand total of 3 or 4 TLBs.
I really can't recommend this one highly enough.  If you're a fan of the Dodonpachi series at all, this is a must-have just for the sheer amount of content on offer here.  If you're unsure about whether or not you're a fan, this is an excellent game to cut your teeth on, with its beginner-friendly 4-button layout and bullet canceling mechanic.

I was so taken away by this game, my whole life had been taken away from me for 3 hours, I became a new man, I became Erwin Lemmor. Seeing through the eyes of this character, I couldn't help but melt in my chair, as the backgrounds and histories of the tanks were revealed to me, never once has my heart gone so soft.

I wish it could last forever.

Double Dragon Neon tries to pay homage to the original Double Dragon but fails miserably; the combat is half broken, animations and graphics are poor, the upgrade system terrible and the bonus levels uninspiring. Let me try and explain:
The combat is broken because you'll be punching air sometimes, even though you're absolutely certain it was a direct hit. There are difficulty spikes that don't make any sense. Low life thugs will be hitting you from all sides without once allowing you to hit them back. And those are some of the easier enemies. And if you lose all your lives you have to start all over again. There are no checkpoints. Grrr... Rage building up.
The graphics are poor; the 3D models of the characters look bland and have no personality. The stages look alright, though, but they can't save this game from looking terrible. The characters lack animation which make them feel sluggish and unresponsive.
The upgrade system is a nice addition, if it was properly executed. You'll be collecting cards to upgrade your abilities, which works, but the upgrades, in addition to the combat, are useless and not worth the trouble of executing. There are a couple of moves that might you out in tight situations but after having tried several of them I decided to stick with just one that seemed to be working alright. So, good idea, poor execution.
Same goes for the bonus levels, which are bland and just don't make any sense. There's nothing else to say here.
And that goes for the entire game. I don't know why it exists but this game never should've happened in the first place.
Avoid at all costs.
[Rating: 51/100]

I've played The Mystery of the Druids through to completion on an older computer before it was released here on Steam, so I know more about it than anyone would ever want to.
Without giving away too much about the plot, all I can say about this game is that the cutscenes are utterly ridiculous, the puzzles are obtuse and violate pretty much every ounce of common sense the average person possesses, and the main character, Brent Halligan, might just be the worst video game protagonist of all time (yes, even worse than Darkseed II's Mike Dawson). Being that this is a point-and-click adventure game, a genre well-known for having ridiculous puzzles and, at times, even more ridiculous characters... I do, in a twisted sense, sort of recommend playing it for yourself.
Alas, the game was originally designed for computers running Windows 98/XP, and Nordic's attempts to get it working properly on modern systems haven't quite been perfected yet, so you will most likely experience crashes every five minutes or so. Until the day this becomes more functional, I'd say just hunt down a copy of the original retail game and fire up your old XP computer instead.

This is an odd review. The game plays fair, but the mechanics are not for the faint of heart. The quick anwser is that I would not recommend it to other's as it's particularly niche and unforgiving. Frankly if this fits someone's niche perfectly I doubt they even will look at the reviews, however I can see casual players being burned.
My beefs:
i) Pacing is slow. This includes playing/fighting on the map, but also the time investment needed to progress is quite large. Almost into the grindy realm.
ii) Unforgiving. You can literally spend hours honing your character, picking spells and skills, spending alot of your gold on them, only to have a rough few hits lead to an injury that truncates that character.
iii) Playstyle becomes defensive. Largely due to the previous point, your effort to save your character's from any hit means you constantly are trying to swamp any resistance, which can lead to long games adjusting for position which just exasterbates the drain on enjoyment.
iv) Repetative. The leveling system is beautifully detailed, however the large number of games you play to level your characters tend to not diverge much from one to the other. This game is more enjoyable in short sessions as long one's tend to become monatonous.
v) Frustrating. The game is successful at getting you to grow attached to your main characters, however there is some maps that put you in a difficult position that often leads to a rout of your men as you fight to stay alive. When such things happen, it is needlessly frustrating as the punishment onthe loss can be quite huge, from loss of all your hardearned weapons, injuries dimishing the characters, to permanent deaths of your characters. Frankly this game is not for the faint of heart, nor the easily discouraged.
So personally I'm the typical audience for this game, and I'd pass it off as a 6/10 for other's of a similar mindset. However I'd mark it just 4/10 for the general player. As the points above will have a much larger impact on their playtime.

After the successful Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis or now better known as Arma: Cold War Assault, comes Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising which aims to succeed its predecessor with enhanced visuals, gunplay, and realistic elements and for the most part it does, but at the same time it’s a step backwards in some areas. Instead of Bohemia Interactive Studio developing this sequel, Codemasters has continued to develop the Operation Flashpoint series and unfortunately, the franchise has taken a wrong turn as the many enjoying elements and overall support from the last game are lacking. While the single player campaign and single missions are up to par with many other shooters for its time, multiplayer is a limited option which is strongly going to influence whether you buy this game or not.
The story is set in 2011, where the Chinese government becomes aware in their shortage of oil during a national economic crisis and discover that a neighbouring island in the Pacific Ocean reserves an oilfield. Since this island belongs to Russia and that the nation’s desperation grows as their essential resources diminish, China makes a daring decision to go to war and attack the island which America, who have an allegiance to Russia, respond by organising an invasion to seize control of the island. Alike other open world games, Dragon Rising is one large map that can be played on all modes. Although it doesn’t have nearly as much land to explore compared to Cold War Assault which had 5 relatively large maps, the textures of the environment and overall visuals are majorly improved. Distant smoke rising on the horizon and dirt smacked onto the screen from incoming shrapnel successfully delivers that feeling of being in the boots of a soldier in real-time warfare which is important for character development. The story plot however is generic and with no cutscenes except for a prologue and no relationship between characters, there is little motivation to keep players hooked and instead makes it feel like a boring grind. On the other hand, the gameplay and realism invigorates the campaign. Codemasters have really tried to develop Dragon Rising as an accurate depiction of contemporary warfare especially by making players aware of how mortal their character’s life is unlike other first-person shooters that belittle the power of your adversaries especially on lower difficulty settings, which offers little to celebrate over after accomplishing goals since there is no real challenge. This is not the case at all in Dragon Rising and it works effectively to keep players aware of their surroundings and take necessary precautions in order to be successful in their undertakings. The easiest difficulty is deemed ‘normal’ hinting that this is by no means an easy game. Even more experienced players will have to manage to subdue the hardships throughout the campaign and it’s quite evident that Codemasters wants players to become completely involved and immersed in an open world adventure and playing on hardcore is not discouraged here. On hardcore difficulty, there is no confusion that Dragon Rising is seen as a simulation before it is seen a game. There are no checkpoints, minimised HUD, and teammates will not respawn if killed for the rest of the mission and all progress can be lost in just one shot. This keeps players intrigued long enough to explore all the diverse weapons, vehicles, and other features that the game offers. Each weapon including the attachments feel distinguishable and each are suited to different environments and missions whether it’s using a mounted machine gun to defend your position from being overwhelmed or using a sniper rifle with an infrared scope and suppressor that’s ideal for a night operation. Every mission accomplished gives you a relieved sense of achievement but upon completing the final mission, you wouldn’t know if you were proud of yourself because of the effort you invested into the difficult campaign or if you were proud of your tolerance for enduring several hours of the faults in the game. It may be both, but these drawbacks pull back its potential from being one of the most, if not the best military first person shooter to date.
Engagements with enemy AI can be intensive yet exciting but there are some bugs that can spoil these moments. You can also expect to randomly be fired upon by allies for no apparent reason, even if you are out of their line of fire. It’s understandable that friendly fire is enabled in the game to give a more realistic approach to warfare, but couldn’t the developers program friendly AI to not shoot the player in the back? During gunfights, your teammates may also break formation to stand in front of you, typically resulting in their demise or they might not take cover and rather stand out in the open. Introducing players to some game features like vehicles is not done well either. Aside from a review of your control setup within the first mission, there is a lack of tutorial missions which many other shooters like Arma have many of and these make an important first impression on the game and gives players an understanding on how to utilise different in-game features. What hurts the gameplay is that players are inhibited from adjusting their field or view. Considering that many of the weapons take up half the screen and essentially diminish the player’s peripheral vision, it can be frustrating since the game’s main motive is realism. A lack of certain animations can put players off as well. Simple animations to heal yourself by applying dressings or to enter and exit vehicles would add to an immersive experience. There are however, noticable animations such as reloading an anti-tank launcher on the ground which deserves credit. While these problems range from minor to major, the multiplayer is the prime concern.
The multiplayer servers have shut down and there is no way to join public games. I didn’t have the chance to play multiplayer and from what I’ve read, there are mixed comments made about it. From what I’ve seen in the menu, you can still organise a private match using LAN if you have a few friends willing to play. You can also play co-op in campaign which is a great addition and is not seen enough in other games.
While Dragon Rising captures many of the fundamentals of being a realistic military shooter, it suffers from a lack of polish which is strongly evident in both the story value of the campaign and the multiplayer’s current state. Ultimately however, there wasn’t enough devotion put in from the developers to earn the reputation of being a shooter to remember for years to come which it could have been had they have done that. A positive which future games can take from this, is the realistic elements that are done well such as the restrictions for each difficulty and weapon variations and also improve on the elements that the game suffers from like the lack of animations and unsophisticated AI. Since Dragon Rising’s release, many successors like Arma and Battlefield have done this and as a result, have developed a larger fan base and received great acclamation. I could hardly recommend this game with the reason that there are many shooters that do most things in this game better both older and newer but at $2, there is little to be upset over with the value you’re getting. This game deserves a higher rating and it could have one if the developers hadn’t abandoned the key element that depends on most first-person shooter’s lasting appeal: the multiplayer. With all being said, there are still many fun and yet rewarding moments to be had but the lack of attention to detail and multiplayer really butchers the Dragon Rising’s longevity.
6/10

Fantastic game, satisfying gameplay, has a few problems.
The gameplay is very well tuned for even numbers of combatants and feels very satisfying when you successfully block an opponent's move and punish their predictability. When you find yourself fighting against the odds, even against the basic NPC enemies, the game becomes much more difficult. I can't really complain about that too much though, since that alone makes the game feel much more realistic. In real life it takes a much bigger skill gap to defeat two or three opponents single-handed than to defeat a just one.
As far as problems, the game is often somewhat laggy and has crashed on me a couple times. However, I believe a patch last night should fix some of the crashing and they are working on improving the game servers.
PVP and PVE is great, I just don't like how many bugs and crashes there are, also connection problems are common.

Honestly, the combat system is the only passable part of this game. While extremely promising, it feels like a dangerously premature release. Even forgetting the fact that the infrastructure still can't handle the game (I regularly can't play because I "can't connect to server"), the mechanics for joining (and remaining in) parties, camera controls, ledge mechanics, and nearly every other part of the gameplay experience feels unpolished at best, and downright broken at worst.
For instance, when partying up with friends, it's easy to fall out of the party by accidentally knocking them a bit during a group fight. At that point, they become visually indistinguishable from enemies by color, and it takes two menu actions to get back to party status (Request Stop Fight > Friend Accepts > Request Party > Friend Accepts).
The game lacks a jump button, which would seem to be something really core to a robust fighting game. I'll forgive that as a premeditated limitation to focus the game experience, but the way the game is built doesn't make you slowly forget that you don't have one -- all of your attacks contain heavy forward momentum such that it feels nearly impossible to knock an opponent off a ledge (even from a good striking distance) without following him off of it, plummeting to your death in a way that feels silly and avoidable. At the very least, if you propel yourself off a ledge rather than being knocked there, you should be able to grab a ledge and take a few seconds to recover -- a mechanic that would allow you to be punished by enemies, but gives you a chance to continue playing if circumstances allow.
When you die, you're given a prompt that you can "Hold A to revive," but doing this will revive you onto another server, leaving your party and forcing you to wait until your friends find another altar to invite you again. Instead, your friends must find and revive you within 60 seconds. That's fine, but the UI should make the distinction and consequences WAY more clear, and when your party is not in a combat situation and you're sparring among friends, you should be able to revive yourself.
The game doesn't feel straightforward in terms of target switching, either. Complex fight scenarios with multiple allies and enemies require you to hold one button and manipulate a joystick to change targets, rather than a one-button solution to cycling through them or re-targeting. In addition, allies can be targeted as easily as enemies, making it easy to target and wail a combo on your friends before you can see what's happening.
The UI doesn't show your shards (used for abilities), you kinda just have to check your leg.
All-in-all, this game feels like an alpha. I requested a refund, the first time I've ever done so on Steam in nearly a decade of buying and playing games on the platform. I don't recommend the game yet -- the fighting system is promising, but the game has a long way to go before it's actually fun.

The classic horror franchise is getting a new perspective in this sequel/ soft reboot. Hopefully the game turned out as well as the fans hoped and provided some horrific tension to experience. I will be reviewing Resident Evil 7 with a pro/ con style and finish it off with my conclusion.
Pro:
The game has amazing music. The game has so much music and how it influences mood and atmosphere. One of my favorite has to the be saferoom music. Resident evil is very notorious for having a well made saferoom music. The idea is to make the player feel safe but constantly aware of the lingering threat behind the door. The other songs are splendid to listen to.
The new perspective allows to new opportunity of experience. Yes lets get it out of the way that Resident Evil 7 is also on VR and how it is natural to play a vr game in first person but there can be a deeper meaning that adds a level of fear to the game. The idea that you as the player are Ethan. You see the experience through his eyes and its a bit easier to become immersed in the world. Soon as the player the enemies feel like they are not attack Ethan the but you as the player.
Welcome back old mechanics. Long have i missed the time of item boxes from the earlier Resident evil titles like 1 and 2 and it is nice to see them come back for this title. Item management was a pretty big deal back then so it was great to see that come back with the idea of limited item space. It always makes the player worry about picking up an item and using the space and later learning there was medic supplies a little further down. So there will be the struggle of do i need more health items or ammo or need the space to have my shotgun or other key items.
There is a new difficulty. The new difficulty ironically named "Madhouse" is in all sense of the word madhouse. It is very challenging since enemies are obviously more bullet spongey and supplies are limited but there is a new twist added to it. Items are moved around to different locations than their normal difficulty counter parts, enemies are in relitively newer locations than they were in previous difficulties such as now an area has 2 fat guys than 1 or now there is 3 crawlers than 1. It provides a definite challenge to those who seek it but a newer and unique experience than their previous experience.
The story is very nice. The story is held together with cliche's from other horror icons like texas chainsaw, fear, saw, ect. It is not unqiue to its horror is what i am trying to get across but the story of how Mia is tied in with it and how the infection works really is an interesting topic to learn. Learning how the bakers were before the infection was nice.
The atmosphere is amazing. Yes resident evil is finally back at a residence and there is evil among the character. Jokes aside, the atmosphere created is amazing with how old and unkept the areas are and the cliche of a backwater family in the middle of the woods raising horror on intruders is something that was in a few movies but this game lets you experience it as the character. Truely a horric experience.
con:
Late game gets very challenging when you play as mia and the first area you get to explore has those annoying 4 legged crawlers and a handgun that give you just 2 bullets. I get that challenge is important in a game but that is just annoying. It could have been better but it came off as slow and annoying.
A choice leads to unreasonable expectations. You get to make a choice to see who live and dies when if you chose the one other than mia she dies regardless which makes no sense since you cure her infection and Mia gets angery at you which is rightfully so since she is your wife for 3 years but on the flip side if you choose to save Mia the other girl gets angery because you didnt save her even though you dont really know her that well so her expecations that you would choose to save her over your wife of 3 years. This story elements felt kind of forced and really if time was taken could have fixed it so it doesnt feel like some teenage drama than anything rational.
Conclusion:
The game was a blast. It wasnt scary but it did hold some really nice atmosphere moments that were unsettling to a degree. The game play was very classic but with the new twist of first person which was always a welcomed change in my book. I am a massive fan of the Resident Evil series and it was good to see how the tides of how crappy the franchise became after 4 are now back to its normal enjoyable experience. Resident Evil 7 is a game that can compete agains the likes of Resident Evil 4 in my eyes so I fully recommend Resident Evil 7.

I have unusual feelings about this game.  I've played most of the Resident Evil games, and this one is definitely much further into the spooky atmosphere than the last few, making the action less of a focus.  This is good and bad.  The normal enemies are mostly just annoying, but you always feel vulnerable and cautious.
Honestly, on my first play through the game on normal mode, I didn't like it all that much.  I didn't think it was bad, but there are parts (in combat and otherwise) where it can be confusing.  The camera swings all around, leaving you disoriented.  The enemies seemed to have lots of life, but were not particularly dangerous.  I thought the game got better as it went on.
Being a big fan of hard games and hearing that the hard mode (Madhouse) was much better, I decided to try it despite my first experience going through the game.  Oh man, it is SO much better.  It seems like the game was designed on hard mode, then they played it down for the main game.  The combat against normal enemies is better, you have to actually sneak, resource management becomes a important and the boss battles are incredible (about on par with RE4).  However, I felt that, contrary to my feelings in the first playthrough, the game became less fun as it went on.  You start to get overloaded with resources and the best parts of the hard mode lessen in importance.
Overall, I enjoyed the game (on hard mode) a lot and would rank it as follows with the other Resident Evil Games I've played:
Best =RE4 > RE5 (Co-op only!, single player is lame) > RE7(Madhouse) > RE1 > RE2 > RE Revelations 2 > RE7 (not Madhouse) > RE Zero > RE6 = Worst

Given Capcom's more recent entries in the franchise being more heavily oriented toward action gameplay I have to say that RE7 was a very pleasant surprise. It's hard to disclose everything positive about the game without treading into spoiler territory so here's my attempt at doing so and explaining my reasoning behind my recomendation of the game.
The biggest factor for me was the return of the atmosphere. I was skeptical at first about the perspective change to first-person as it was clearly done this way to make it VR compatible and I don't subscribe to the belief that VR is a worthwhile investment in its current iteration. However upon actually playing the game I found that the shift in perspective was actually pretty well executed in terms of the gameplay and horror aspects of the game.
Walking down hallways and turning corners is suspenseful, the audio plays a huge part in this like it did with the older entries of the series. Like any good horror game the audio is key in predicting what you're up against and isn't just a tool to add cheap jumpscares into the mix. There were a lot of genuine moments in my first playthrough where I would hear footsteps or moans that indicated an upcoming threat which gave me the freedom to choose how I engaged the situation.
Because of that last point I soon realised that not only did the atmosphere contribute to my enjoyment, but the freedom to choose between fight or flight did too. A large part of why I bought this game in the first place is that I had heard about it paying homage to the older games in that regard. I simply adore the first three games and Code Veronica because of that aspect, in many situations you don't even need to fight if you know how to avoid the enemies.
I will say though that the variety in threats does feel a little underwhelming compared to the originals and that does somewhat detract from the scare factor. That said, my first encounters were all still just as memorable to me as they were in the older games. I wouldn't necessarily say this is an entirely bad point though, the first game also suffered a similar flaw afterall.
In terms of combat I feel that they did a fantastic job of blending the old inventory management aspects of using items and weapons extremely well with the hotkeys and action aspects of more recent titles. Your inventory space is very limited like the old games, but you can hotkey your weapons and there is a dedicated heal button that removes the need to navigate the menu mid combat. Admittedly I have mistakenly hit the heal button without meaning to which has caused me to waste items, but that's my own silly fault.
That about sums up my thoughts on the game in terms of spoiler-free critique. There's a lot that I love about the game that I feel should really be experienced blind though. I love this game and I recommend it because of that, though the DLC options leave a lot to be desired.
Here's hoping the upcoming free DLC will be just as engaging and thematically fitting to the source material.

The game is absolutely amazing. This is definitely a Devil May Cry game. If you enjoyed 1 and 3, you will like this one just as much. Even if you didn't enjoy the other DMC games, you should still give this a try, whether it be because of the games being too hard, the simple control scheme, the fixed camera or the backtracking, this game improves on all of those making it a good game to start with or play even if you didn't enjoy the classic DMC games.
For those who haven't played a DMC game, they are hardcore action games notorious for their difficulty. You fight demons throughout the whole games and you also fight bosses and solve puzzles. The combat is very solid, responsive, satisfying and is also very challenging to master. However being able to master the games mechanics will cause some absolutely beautiful combos and moves that your character will do which will look awesome. The games are also known for playing heavy metal music during the fight scenes and also some fairly irritating backtracking, which thankfully, has been toned down a lot in this game.
The PC port is okay. The game works fairly well with keyboard and mouse (despite lack of camera control with the mouse) but the game works better with a controller. Not just because the mouse control doesn't work, but because games from this genre are just better off being played with a controller. The PC version doesn't include any overintensive features so it is also very easy to run on any machine with a high frame rate. While not the best looking game in the world, it still has enough PC specific features. There is also a Directx 10 mode. However, at least for me, this seemed to make the game a bit more unstable causing it to crash more. There also didn't appear to be that much of a difference between DX9 and DX10 modes. The PC version also has a mode which was not included on the PS3 and 360 versions due to power restraints - Legendary dark knight mode which spawns way more enemies on screen. This makes the game a lot more frantic and enjoyable and could maybe also appeal to fans of the Dynasty Warriors franchise. (Update - This mode is also included in the Special Edition of the game and may also be included on the console versions of the Special Edition)
The game fixes a lot of problems that the original games have and makes the combat a lot better. It is  a little slow paced and clunky at first and the game is by no means as brutally challenging as DMC1 and 3, but it is still good. Also, your first playthrough may take you some time as you do have a few annoying puzzle sections and a few moments where you may be unsure of where to go, however it is all easy to remember so your second playthrough will be a breeze (in terms of the travelling).
However, the game still has it's problems. The level design is a bit weak. The second half of the game is just all of the levels you have played through in reverse with no puzzles included. You even replay the same bosses but in reverse order. Also, for 2/3rds of the game you don't play as Dante. You play as Dante for the second half of the game and only the second half unfortunately. You cannot go back to previous levels and play as Dante which is dissapointing. However it does make the game much more enjoyable when Dante is finally playable. That may sound annoying for die-hard fans of DMC, however Nero, Dante's replacement is still fun to use, even though he feels a little slow and basic at first.
Even though the level design is a little weak, that does not by any means the game is not fun to replay. It is just as fun to replay as the 3rd game. As for difficulty, easy mode is like Devil May Cry 2, however Dante must die (very hard) mode is comparable to Devil May Cry 3 on harder difficulties which, in my opinion, is spot on how they should have done the difficulty. I like this because experts get their challenge, however the game is also noob friendly. This DMC game is a good one to start with, actually as it is not so forgiving. The combat isn't amazing at first, but once you start unlocking upgrades and slowly get better, the combat begins to get amazing.
Overall, DMC4 is a brilliant and worthwhile entry to the series. Despite not playing as Dante, the core is still DMC. Some could argue the combat is not as good as DMC3, however in some ways 4 is more enjoyable as it is not so brutally hard. It also does not include as much backtracking or mapless wandering around like in 3. Even if you didn't like DMC 1 or 3, you should still give this one a whirl as it might be more your thing in terms of difficulty, mechanics and level design. If you are a hardcore DMC fan, you should also give this a go, but don't expect it to be too much better than the original games.
That said there's almost no point to getting this when the Special Edition is supposedly better aside from it being somewhat less optimized to this.

Ahhh Cave. They are the masters of bullet hell. And this game... DoDonPachi Resurrection, or DoDonPachi DaiFukkatsu as it's known overseas, is pretty much their magnum opus. As per the norm for the genre, as soon as you start the game you'll be wading through bullets as you fight your way to the end of the stage to the final showdown with each stage's main boss, which always comes in the form of a transforming giant robot girl.
If that sounds weird, then you've obviously not experienced the signature weirdness of Cave's games (which I for one find quite charming TBH). Cave consistently makes great games with bizarre settings that definitely are not cliche by any standard, and that just adds to the appeal in my opinion. Add to that the high production values and replayability of the experience and you have a damn sweet package. As always the artwork is amazing with massive sprites that fill the screen (the giant robot boss girls are pretty cool too!), and the soundtrack is nice all around.
On top of all that is a deep scoring system that will take quite a long time to master the intricacies of, as well as the fact that EVERY revision of DodDonPachi Resurrection is included in the package, from the original all the way up to Black label Arrange for a total of 8 versions. Each one has multiple ships and multiple playstyles per ship, so there's enough variation here that you won't get bored of blowing the clothes off giant robot babes. So what are you waiting for? Get out there, and kick some metal butt!

Launched initially in 2008 for Arcade, then ported for Mobile Phones and Xbox 360 in 2010 and finally launched in October 2016 for PC Steam, DoDonPachi Resurrection also known as DoDonpachi DaiFukkatsu belongs to the genre shoot 'em up (aka shmup) and is the fifth game in the DonPachi series created by Cave, a Japanese developer with prominent role in the development of the so-called "Maniac Shooters" also known by the the expressions "Bullet Hell" or "Danmaku", a sub-genre of shoot'em ups characterized by a gameplay fast, intense and frantic with the enemies "urinating" bullets all the time, defying dexterity and motor skills of the player who often have millimetric spaces to dodge the bullets and hit your enemies.  The first game on the series, DonPachi (1995) was the kickoff, but was the second game, DoDonPachi (1997) who really made the series famous, having been one of the main responsible for the rise and popularization of the "Maniac Shooters" in Japan. After DoDonPachi, came the sequences DoDonPachi II: Bee Storm (2001), DoDonPachi DaiOuJou (2002), DoDonPachi DaiFukkatsu/Resurrection (2008) and DoDonPachi SaiDaiOuJou (2012). Returning to DoDonPachi Resurrection/Daifukkatsu, this Steam version contains eight different modes and arrangements: Normal 1.5, Normal 1.51, Arrange A, Arrange B, Black Label, Novice, Black Label Novice e Black Label Arrange, each one with certain peculiarities, for example, while the Normal 1.5 mode corresponds to the normal game, but with refinements, Normal 1.51 presents a different punctuation system and controls and the Black Label Mode presents a new attack method and also a new Final Boss and so on, bringing a really interesting variety. The plot of the game is totally  focused on science fiction and unfolds six years after the events narrated in the previous game (DoDonPachi DaiOuJou) in which anomalies are detected in the fabric of space time and after an accurate analysis is discovered that a powerful virus with evil intentions to destroy mankind infected the computers of the  Headquarters of DoDonPachi's Squadron and is using time travel portals to send large amounts of materials and informations to the past, thus the DoDonPachi Squadron is sent into the past to fight the threat and they are surprised by the attack of the Element Daughters, enormous bosses that are evolutions of the Element Dolls (cybernetic artificial beings in female forms which were connected to the ships for the purpose of providing tactical data and improving maneuverability of the DoDonPachi's Squadron in DDP DaiOuJjou). The gameplay of DoDonPachi Resurrection is intense and exciting. The player will face thousands of enemies, besides facing challenging middle and final-stage bosses. You must hit enemies while dodge the bullets fired by them and the player can also cancel enemies shots under certain conditions such as through the use of the hyper counter (activated when the hyper counter gauge is full), for example, or through the use of the concentrated laser that can also block the concentrated laser fired by enemy ships. Hitting enemies in sequence increases the "Hit Combos" counter which has strong influence on increasing the score. The game offers to the player three different ships, each with its own characteristics and also three game modes: Bomb Mode (when you get hit and when you have a remaining bomb At your disposal this is automatically triggered devastating enemies around you.); Power Mode (you have two sub-modes here: Normal and Boost, in the first you have a higher speed when maneuvering the ship, but the shots are weak with a smaller width range and in the second you have much more powerful and wide shots, but the ship's displacement is slower) and Strong Mode (combines the advantages of both Bomb and Power modes). Speaking of the controls, I can tell that they respond very well to the commands and in this video I used the analog stick of my Xbox 360 Wireless Controller. From a graphic point of view, the Cave certainly did once again a great job, because the game is beautiful and full of flashy effects. At certain times, especially when the action is more intense and there are many bursts happening at the same time the frame rate usually drops and the game presents some slowdowns, but I noticed that this is a feature also present in the original arcade, so I believe that a part is intentional to leave the game more accessible, however, another part may be associated with the original arcade hardware limitations. The sound department of the game is very competent, both in terms of the quality of the musics, as well as the sound effects and the digitized voices. DoDonPachi Resurrection is another great chapter in the series and one of the best additions of the genre to the Steam library! To see me playing this game, please check this video:

Empire: Total War.
This game is, beyond a doubt, one of the most uninspiring games of the Total War series that I have had the pleasure of playing.  It has so many bugs, you'd think of calling your local pest control.  The portraits for the characters in the game are..lackluster.  They didn't even bother to give the people in the portraits a background, at least in my experience with the game.  The Battle AI is absolutely random, having some brilliant moments of high-stakes deployment, but other times losing a battle they should clearly win.  I myself survived a nasty battle, playing as Sweden.  I had four regiments of line infantry, and was attacked by nearly a stack of Austrian militia and line infantry, yet I still won because the Austrian soldiers actually refused to press forward and engage me.
That last bit is the heart of the issue; this game, as incredible as the potential was for a world-wide, 18th century-based game, it is seriously undercut by the odd decisions that were undertaken. For example, I don't know who's idea it was to make every single siege battle on a city with walls look identical, but that was lazy work.  Even as far back as Rome: Total War, cities had varying shapes and sizes to their walls.  Yet things are identical, here, in the 18th century?  A time marked by decidedly huge differences in everything from one cities' religious tolerance, to troops per unit, to the ideals of the local monarch?  Creative Assembly, please.  We would rather you take longer and give us a better experience, than to hurry up and weaken the magic of your earlier works.
But, you may be reading this, and seeing that I still recommend this game.  Why is that?
Because this game does many things very well indeed.  When at 'ultra' settings, this game is very, very beautiful.  Crisp uniforms, detailed smoke clouds from mass musket volley fire, the reflective water on the campaign map.  I find it all very much a step into a new era of Total War.  And the audio is impressive, as well.  The sound of hundreds of men running and shouting in combat, the sound of cannon barrages firing and then the thumping clash of the shells landing upon the enemy, the officers' barking orders, to which a drum plays the command to the men.  As a fan of history, I can't help but find myself fully immersed in the sounds of the battle, despite the lackluster AI ability.
There is, however, a much larger reason to play this game.  A reason that fits nearly every single game since 2000.  What am I talking about?
Modifications.
The community for this game have made hundreds, if not THOUSANDS, of modifications for this game, ranging from changing the accuracy of the men in each regiment, to a complete and total overhaul of the game...including ridding the game of most of the issues that it was saddled with upon its release.
So yes, this game is far from perfect.  It does have many issues.  But, in the end, I will gladly recommend this game to any fan of historical affectations, or even simply those of a curious mindset.  Because despite this game not being perfect, it brings enough to the table to keep those that are willing to work through the issues entertained.

As a big fan of the Total War series, I have spend more hours playing this game that I would like to admit. When I bought it as it came out in 2009 (I can't believe so much time has passed!) it was a good game that brought freshness to the series from the Ancient World of Rome Total War and the obscure Dark Ages of Medieval 2 Total War to the era of Enlightenment of the 18th century. For the first time one could engage in naval battles and the map was expanded to not only Europe and the Near East but also the American Continent and the Indian Subcontinent, bringing even more different game styles and strategies. A technologial tree was introduced that makes you feel like an Enlightened Despot trying to pull your country out of the darkness and superstition of the 17th century into the light and reason of the 18th century.
That was long ago, and now I think hat every new Total War title (except Napoleon) has surpassed Empire Total War by a lot, and that is good because it means that somehow the developers strive to make the series even better even though lately they've perverted themselves by selling bugged games that needed much patching and delivering the rest of it through senseless DLCs.
The battle style sure is different than in other previous titles, now having to accomodate to the battle lines of fring troops and cannons, where muskets and cannons reigned ever more over swords and cavalry. A fun game to play where the campaign map is immense and evermore tactics and strategies can be executed.
Two of the complains I have are that one, you cannot repair any forts built in your cities, meaninf that as they are breached and damaged, when the next battle is fought, the enemy won't have to bother to storm the walls or breach them again with artillery as the holes remain. So your best (and most expensive option) is to demolish the fort and built on again, jet you may have no time to finish it on time for the next attack, and honestly it's better to fight a battle with some protection given by your partly destroyed fort than not having any protection at all, especially if you're heavily outnumbered. I can understand that forts usually take a lot of time to repair as they did in reality, but the fact that no repair button is given in the first place just doesn't make any sense.
The second complaint I have about the game is how easy it is foer the enemy to raid and damage your buildings. Let's say you utterly defeat an enemy army that had invaded you country and only a hundred or so of them survive. You'll expect them to retreat shamefully back to their borders but no, instead they'll start sacking and damaginf every building in their vicinity, which impairs you of their benefits. That type of strategic warfare makes sense and adds spice to the game, but the fact that these buildings supposedly built in smaller cities and towns which have thousans or tens of thousands inhabitants can be overrun by a hundred or so of enemy soldiers just frustrates me. One time playing as Prussia I had an enemy cavarly platoon of 20 men destroy my buildings and depreiving me of their benefits, only to come back after I repaired them. Certainly you'll expect that a town of a couple of thousand inhabitants can fend off 20 cavarlymen right? Not in this game.
Anyhow if you get past this two most frustratin issues you'll have a good time.
Defiently one of the top Total War games.

A beautiful 2D side-scrolling adventure with heavy elements of tower defence, strategy, and survival.
It's deliberately vague when you start, and your monarchs WILL die at least the first few attempts as you learn through trial and error rather than having everything spelled out for you, which can make for a challenging and frustrating experience to begin with.
But with learning comes the thrill of figuring out better approaches and succeeding, rewarding you for patience and strategy, and surviving long nights and hordes of enemies at your walls. Your subjects are simple-folk, and will do as you command, but you have to be clever and thoughtful in how and where you use them as they can’t change jobs once assigned (unless they lose their tool in an attack). This is all part of the challenge.
Once you figure out a strategy that works for you and see everything there is to see in the game there is little replayability, but you’ll get a solid 15-30 hours of entertainment and challenge from both the Classic version and the New Lands expansion which come bundled together. I think that’s pretty good value for an independent game, however it might not be quite worth it at full price unless you’re looking for a fun adventure with a pretty clear end-state (although you can keep going forever after clearing the final island if you wish).
It’s a definite purchase during a sale though. I highly recommend checking it out if it sounds even remotely like your type of game. Great fun!

Quite a nice tackle on one of the gems of the pre MMORPG offline gaming epicness.
What I expected: A somewhat DoW2 influenced brawling game looslely tied together by the mordheim theme.
What´s actually in the game: A careful adaption of the tabletop game. The one thing that I imagined beeing a flaw in gameplay was the Action point system, since I´m quite a diehard fan of the tabletop I feared that it wont "feel"like mordheim. Boy was I wrong :D
Short explaination: Your fighters can use their AP to move arround, reclaim AP´s by simply going back the path you used. So you are able position them tactically and set up traps, find nice sniping spots... But be careful of the chaotic infestations on the ground, walls and in corners, they will interrupt your movement if a charater gets too close and set´s it off. This will end a movement substep, and a char cant reclaim the AP´s he used till he hit the trap.
The experince system is a bit different, as well as the attributes. It´s heavily influenced by the Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay system and it works really great!
The procedural map generator is really cool, and the campaign special scneraios bring a lot of flavour with them, and you´re able to field the dramatis personae of your warband to the skirmish.

This game is definetly NOT for everybody, in fact it is very niche. All you 30+ gamers will like it a lot. I have grown up playing turn based strategy games, which were very popualr in the 90's and been waiting for a good title for years.
Playing this game will require careful planning and a lot of patience. In exchange it is a very rewarding experience and a serious time sink.
After playing for some hours, my advice:
take only easy missions for as long as you can. Be careful to keep the deadline with your shipments -though i don't know what is going to happen if you don't, i did it so far, but based on the rest of the game it will not be good for you.
Gather the green crystals during missions, you have to produce a given number after some battles, like a tax.
When engaging on missions, keep your group together, always use ambush stance and charge as much as you can. Avoid being charged is essential.
All of your enemies will be evil scum who try to kill your soldiers. You must keep them alive!
Your hero will become a terminator.
If you loose a battle nothing punishing happens, in fact you won't have a flawless campaign.
Don't get too attached to any of your soldiers, they might die during any mission.
If you play recklessly, your soldiers will get knocked out. Be patient or you will be angry. Luck is not on your side vs CPU, but not unfair either.
On low level, don't bother with scavenging, don't make detours for a chest. Stay alive and gather crytals instead.
You can visit your wagon during missions and put items in the chest, making room on your solder to pick more stuff up.
Your soldiers dont necessarily die when they hit the floor in a battle. After the mission you will get to know if he died, needs some days to recover, got some long lasting negative state, or recovers fully.
The loot your soldier is carrying is lost if he gets knocked out on a mission (very frustrating)
If the enemy warband is loosing, they tend to flee the battle, making the goals of the missons very hard to complete.
Be careful using the shop not to buy items instead of selling (menus look like made with consoles in mind sadly), i spend half my gold by mistake when i tried to sell my junk.
Pros:
If you play it correctly it can be a very enjoyable and rewarding experience
Art direction is very well done
Solid rules and well executed gameplay
Bug free and very stable (Win10x64)
4 factions

Mordheim is a turn based strategy game with some vague similarities to the XCOM series but set in the dark, gritty fantasy world of Games Workshop's Warhammer Fantasy setting.
This game is an adaption of the classic tabletop game Mordheim (which was itself the fantasy reskin of the excellent TT game Necromunda) and it captures the setting extremely well. The graphics and music evoke the right atmosphere and look damn good, especially when you realise what a small team it was working on this game.
The game itself is hard. Like, really hard. Particualrly at the beginning, where the learning curve is like an overhanging cliff (and the wide skill selection is an avalanche that starts when you're part way up). The tutorials are good but they don't cover everything, they're definitely worth going through though. It does get easier and you'll find that you're able to do Brutal and Deadly missions and generally win, although that doesn't mean you won't lose people to going Out of Action during those wins.
Ah yes, out of action... This game has permanent consequences for your actions. There's no save scumming, although there is an ironman style autosave feature in case of crashes, etc. Other than that you have to live with your decsisions and, due to it's TT roots, the roll of the die. Yeah, sometimes RNG can screw you, it's just that sort of game. Your mooks will go down and out and, when they do, they will end up picking up injuries or straight up dying. That part of Mordheim and, at least for me, part of the fun!
So the purpose of the game? You've been sent to Mordheim by a baacker who is funding your activities in the city. Their exact nature and reasons for sending you there vary from faction to faction but suiffice it to say you work for them. And what you're doing for them is collecting warpstone, a resource that's scattered throughout the maps. You will periodically have deliveries to fill for them where they require a particualr amount of warpstone. Failing to make those deliveries will eventually lose you the game so try to make them on time. Other than that you will be levelling up your warriors and your warband, as well as you as a player via the Veteran System whereby you get perks like additional starting gold and access to Veteran Skills. Your warband will gain stat increases, more strategy points and offence points, as well as gaining skill points to spend on the bewildering array of passive and active skills available (warning: they aren't cheap, especially when you master a skill). Some of your guys will gain access to spells, and as you level up new hero types (and eventually the mighty Impressives) will be come available to your warband.  You'll also loot more powerful equipment and begin discover magical formulae that allow you to place marks on your weapons and armour, that do a variety of things.
All in all I would definitely recommend the game. I very much enjoy it and can't wait to have a try at multiplayer (I've only done single player thus far), where I think the game will really shine. Just be aware that it is a hardcore exsperience. You will lose matches, you will have people get injured and die, your equipment will be looted from their bodies, you will struggle for gold to pay your warband and buy skills and replacement warriors. That's an integral part of Mordheim and might mean that the game isn't for you, which is fine. It is for me though, I absolutely love it!

I bought it in early access ages ago as I played this tabletop game as a child and loved it.
I waited until it was out of early access before playing it as I didn't want to ruin it (just like I don't watch trailers for movies).
I am loving it. The game mechanics are very different to the original game but they work very well as a video game. Amazingly well in fact. This is the best designed game I'm played in a long time.
I love the open-ended, rogue-like nature of the game. I got brutally slaughtered in the first game (before I realised not to split my band up) but still enjoyed it as I was immediately spending XP and changing my choice of weapons.
Losing is common, but it's not so bad as your warriors don't die (some get injuries, usually 1 max). Just keep grabbing Wyrdstone on the matches.
I've had zero crashes in 13 hours, of playtime. It is slow to load the matches (~40 secs) but once they start it's fine.
If you like tactical combat and open-ended gamepleay, I can honestly say this is the best game like this that I've ever played in the last couple of years.
Edit after 150 hrs:
Still enjoying the game very much. The main flaw, and it's a big one, is that the AI pathfinding is pretty poor. This means that sometimes the AI warriors get stuck and essentially waste their turn. I hope they fix this in a patch as this game could otherwise be a classic.

Pros:
+ It's a survival horror game similar to the style of the original Resident Evil in that there is a house full of monsters to explore and escape from, but the camera is now in the first-person perspective.
+ It isn't a first-person walking simulator or clone of other combat-less horror games. This game has GUNS (and knives)!
+ Being actual survival horror, ammo and health must be found (or crafted/mixed).  Enemies will NOT drop items.
+ It's not a reboot.  It's an isolated incident away from other existing characters, but it exists within the established Resident Evil canon.  I'd say these new characters are likely going to meet some fan favorites sooner or later...
+ The game genuinely surprised me with things I didn't expect to see, like a ridiculous situation involving chainsaws. :)
+ I don't think it's too short. My first time through was around 11 hours. That's long compared to a classic RE game. (I do a lot of exploring and searching.)
Cons:
- Some people think it's short. I disagree, but I'll put it here to be fair.  I'm not sure what those people expect, though.
- The lack of multiplayer may turn some people away, but that doesn't apply to me or some others.
- While I like the game's narrative or plot, I think some aspects toward the middle and the end could have been handled better.  Maybe there was no time.  I still enjoy it, though.
- Enemies can be kind of dumb in some ways, but this can be used to the player's advantage.  I'm not sure this is a con.
"Resident Evil 7 is the most 'Resident Evil' Resident Evil since Resident Evil." - Me
People looking for another action game to play with a friend, like RE5 and RE6, may find this single-player game harder to love.  It really is for the survival horror crowd. I'd say a fan of classic Resident Evil that isn't turned away by a camera perspective change should love this.  It's classic survival horror brought to life with current technology.  Back in 1996, we could only dream of a Resident Evil that looked this good.  As a RE fan since the beginning, it's right up my alley and has quickly taken a place among my favorites in the series.  I think it's an easy 8-8.5/10. It's a great game in my book and I'd recommend it to the Resident Evil fan who truly knows what it means to say, "I got a shotgun!"
...But if that quote was too obscure for you, I will leave you with, "It's really powerful, especially against living things!"

I feel like there is a good game in here somewhere, but at present, I cannot recommend it yet.
Why have I been playing it so far?
Offline, the 1v1 combat feels great. I love the feeling of learning and anticipating enemy attacks, and it's incredibly satisfying both to land hits and to evade enemy attacks. You learn to recognise the wind-up, or just learn the attack sequence.
Learning new moves from NPCs might seem boring - you block or use your combat style's special evasion (absorb, dodge, parry) enough times and you learn it.  But this helps you as a player to learn the move, and learn the appropriate timing.
So all that is great.  But at time of writing, the multiplayer is garbage in Australia. Even just running around trying to defeat NPCs is awful because all the positive stuff I wrote above goes out the window when both you and the NPCs are teleporting around in a dizzying manner, and all you can do is watch your HP drop down until you die.
And as you might imagine, it's also not terribly fun playing against other people when the same thing happens.
Furthermore, as much as I've praised the feel of the 1v1 combat, fighting against more than one enemy just feels like an exercise in frustration.
Honestly, if I can just get a solid 1v1 experience, that would be worth a thumbs up recommendation.  The lack of polish in everything else wouldn't even matter to me.
