Remember the Godfather game? Enjoyed it decently, maybe wanted more?
This plays a lot like that, in a sense, buuut:
+ Cars look better and more variation
+ You have a garage you can store cars in
+ You can change clothes
+ Much better voice acting and more dialogue to the story, way more
+ More characters, and character development
+ Generation ahead in graphics, more detail in atmosphere and setting, presentation is nice and well executed
+ Optimized well
+ Your character has a backstory
+ Songs on the radio change to reflect the times, as the game moves forward in years
+ Cars also change to reflect changing times
+ The map is easier to read
+ Landmarks like The Empire State building, Brooklyn Bridge, China town etc. are awesome to drive across & see in the background
+ Cinematic dialogue sequences
+ You don't just talk with other characters, they actually join you on some missions which is awesome
+ Sometime it's snowing, you might notice npc's slipping on ice, the roads/tires are affected.
+ Much more detailed environment, some limited interaction with it, could've been more interaction but there is some
+ Nice lockpicking system, more simple rather than as advanced as Skyrim, but different and fits in nicely
+ Assortment of rifles, machine guns, pistols. Only one shotgun. Weapons are powerful and accurate though.
+ Characters dialogue reactions to your actions on the road, or elsewhere, like hitting cars, driving too fast/slow, hitting pedestrians, are often very funny,
- No Crouch!? ... makes taking cover difficult/limited, especially in open world streets
- Shooting system is fine, nothing wrong with it, fun, satisfying, accurate and realistic, but could've been developed to do just that much more with; being able stick your crosshair to an enemy and move it around to select to shoot in the kneecap for example or head or hands to disarm would've been so fantastic in this game, seriously (that is the best aspect of the Godfather that would've fit and be really great to use here; it's what you miss the most, almost everything else is better) Someone let me know if there's a mod that enables that
- Could've been a third level of 'epic' nature of the weapons, like in Godfather, the golden Python magnum, street sweeper shotgun and uzi, etc.. The only one of these is the silver 1911 pistol with the extended clip, which is awesome but the others are missing. The thompson I guess is fine but why not have a more powerful shotgun and thompson at the end like Godfather did? Lol. At least the weapons are powerful, accurate and varied. ('cept only one shotgun)
- It's still open world, but it often feels like there is little to do beyond going to the next mission. Gas stations, bars you can drink at, and clothes stores are cool and awesome additions, but there's no reward for interacting with the open world that affects your effectiveness in combat gameplay, or pay, or weapon unlocks; having stores to knock over for the family you're working for is missing here
- Can't pull out weapons in apartments and therefore have awesome shootouts with cops whenever you want in said open world through a 2nd or 3rd floor window
I know they're different games, but Mafia II probably took a few cues from the Godfather, you can kind of tell; and it's a good thing. (this has way more interaction between characters, sometimes you meet them at the bar for a cinematic, etc.)
Perhaps too many in some areas, (playing safe) and not enough in others, but still, pretty solid, well written and immersive. The soundtrack is presented better in Mafia II through the radios in the cars.
Story and characters are very well presented and likeable, especially your partner Joe, who is very humorous and fun loving throughout the game. You feel more connected and drawn into these aspects than running around knocking stores over, though that was fun too. This is obviously a significant step up in graphics from the Godfather.
I never played the first Mafia or Mafia III, but I hear less praise for those than this game.
Mafia II, I can assure you, is pretty damn good, it's worth completing. If you like Mob stories/settings /the 50's time period style, and/or enjoyed the Godfather game and want more; I would definitely recommend this.
On the whole I would say the Godfather is a grittier game; this one illicits way more emotion, since there is actually character development, story/plot, and voice acting; the only thing it's lacking is the "Lvl.3" type weapons of Godfather, the lock-on aim feature, and maybe a few more things to interact with in the open world, the way Godfather had stores to knock over for the Corleone family. Lol if you can't tell already, those features fused into this is what I want and would make it "the" greatest Mob game probably; maybe someone can make that a reality in the future, using this, or in another future title of a similar inspiration. The two need to have a baby.
It's not gonna overwhelm or blow you away. But it's received due praise for its writing and the gun play is pretty satisfying. And like I said, some moments in the plot will really throw you for a loop in a nice unexpected manner. I don't have nor have I played any of the DLC.
Lots of things letting you feel and believe you are really in the time period, good sound/music, the music changes to reflect the times as the story moves forward in specific years, so that's cool. Cool cars, great character dialogue and writing, nice presentation overall, fun and pretty smooth gameplay.
Don't ask me why, but in games like these two, more shootouts where you are firing from a window with a tommy gun or what not, is always very satisfying and mob like; a few more of these would've satisfied one often voiced complaint that the game could've been just a tad longer.

Probably the worst FlatOut of the series.
It feels like a fail Burnout clone without any of the things that make Burnout fun.
The music consists of maybe 10 tracks of completely bland, forgettable rock music.
The challenge mode was ok, but it consisted mainly of boring time trials with a couple of the ejection challenges. Unfortunately most of the best career cars were only unlocked from from getting first place in some of the challenges.
In the carreer mode, you can get boost from jumps, ramming into debris (sort of), or other cars, but strangely enough, not drifting or near misses.
The problem is that ramming into things obviously makes you slower, with the chance that you can randomly fly off the road for each thing you hit. The physics are pretty bad sometimes, and combined with the stunning no-steer effect from hitting items or other cars can make things really frustrating.
When there's loose crap littered all over the road, do you drive through the large boulder, or the small cardboard box?
If you chose boulder, Congratulations! Boulders usually plink harmlessly off the car, while small cardboard boxes can cause you to fly up into the air and flip several times before landing you in a nearby field.
Because boost is only gained in so few ways, it can make it hard to catch up to first place when in second if there are few jumps on the map. If there are no cars to slam off, and all the loose junk has been knocked out of its initial position (and therefore gives no boost when you hit it agian) and there aren't any jumps, it becomes amazingly hard to catch up to the Designated Winner (the suspiciously fast AI car that rarely gets touched by other cars and can go through most debris without losing any speed)
Now, I understand that stunning (hitting another car with yours and temporarily disabling their ability to steer) is pretty much a given on battle racing games that don't use weapon pickups. What I don't understand is why in this game, you get stunned as well when you hit them first. I can't count how many times I would tap another car, and we would effectively be stuck together, as we couldn't seperate unless either I hit the brakes (the AI never did) or we both flew off the road together. This happened with the AI as well, if they got to close to me, they would not try to turn or follow the track, they would just follow me off the edge of the road/into the wall/field/whatever. At one point I had 3 cars stuck to me, one to the left, one to the right and a car that was sideways in front of me that couldn't or wouldn't move until the whole mass just crashed.
Even runs on maps I knew well and was winning would be ruined if I hit some random thing like a trashbag in the road the wrong way.
Another problem is that "Reset Car" only worked when it wanted to. Sometimes I could reset right after getting spun backwards or flying into a pole, other times I would have to sit and watch my car flip 20 times in the air for 10 seconds because I ran into a tiny bit of debris.
During the final hours when I was truly getting bored, the game consisted of driving a bit, getting completely jacked by the AI cars or some random trash, and restarting the map. Over. And over. And Over.
It felt like the debris added lots of randomness without adding any fun.
The game is probably more fun with people, unfortunately, the MP is dead.
Combine all that with the fact that the game is infected with GFWL, earns the game my final score of:
STAY AWAY!

From the other reviews I read it seems the game idea was good and it had good potential, and I say that as someone who did make a simple top down shooter (I do a bit of programming)... the fundamentals are not executed well. Bad reviews suck and my goal is not to offend the developer - I don't know if the dev will read this but here's my advice to you: Practice doing a simple top down shooter with just 1 weapon, fixed movement speed (no sprinting/walking) and add 1 to 3 enemy types.
Play with making one enmy fast, slow, high health, low health, many of that enemy type (100 at once), few of that enemy type. Play with this and once you're able to make this really fun, those are the fundamentals. Then you can work on adding more aspects to the game that will make it more challenging, strategic, whatever you want your game to be.
Unfortunately I cannot recommend this game in this current state.

Gun-play is what you'd expect from a top down shooter with good weapons which includes a mini-gun, flamethrower and grenade launcher etc.
Throw-able objects are there such as the frag grenades and the ones used in the grenade launcher as well as land mines, proximity and pressure.
You do have air support, it's the dropship.
Armed with an HE auto cannon and missile launcher, it does save your♥♥♥♥♥a lot if you use it correctly.
Squad mechanics are simple but not too simple as you can direct your squad individually or as a whole to move to one place or to follow you.
You also have an APC.
It's armed with an auto-turret with 10000 rounds I think and a good bit of armour till it explodes.
It does show damage depending on its durability which is quite nice too see but might have contributed to the FPS drops here and there.
Do note that the marines CAN repair the APC IF it's damaged enough, below 10,000 or when it's smoking on fire.
The enemies are aliens with princesses instead of queens and regular drones and some have blood on their claws.
The AI is, meh to say the best and the least. Not that good but it's passable.
An interesting thing I found about it, is that if you get captured (that can happen) the marines will charge to your position to save you and unest you. All the marines. They may or may not leave the APC.
They also move away from grenades that you may accidentally throw at them.
The missions are tough enough with perma-death as a thing. It's too much trial and error but you get the hang of it soon after but it will take time.
Mission 1:
You're going to a base where meteors are falling down all around you. Complete and objective the objectives and evac. Long but it's an odd start to a game but it's straight into the mission, no briefs other than the one you get when you select the mission and
Mission 2:
You're in a city, you gotta do some tasks, and the aliens are there to kill you and capture colonists.
Your job is to evac as many civilians as possible trapped in certain locations. This is the part where you get to command marines and it's with the APC as well. The aliens keep coming and
you have LIMITED ammo, I repeat, LIMITED ammo. The marines take ammo from the APC and the amount there is the amount of magazines they can use. They only take their specified ammo type so they ain't taking any of your fancy big guns.
Survival mode:
Exactly what it means.
That's all I'll say to prevent as much spoilers.
So would I recommend it?
At its current state. It's okay but not that okay. It lacks content of extra missions and is tedious to get past the first mission but it's neither the best or the worst. It's just good if you like a challenge.

The game is crazy hard, but I like the lack of forgiveness.  The 2nd mission is a ton of fun just getting past the first is a chore though and the tutorial is a desert of information.  Also, there are stability issues, I haven't had many but they are annoying.  There are a lot of bugs that need to be worked out (particularly getting scientists to stay in the police station, game crashes).  The command UI is ARMA2 complicated but once you've worked with it you can get things done fairly fast.  The screen effects are pretty annoying (wish they had an option to turn them off);  and for the meteorites, there is a method to avoiding them consistently.  In fact I almost never get unless I forget that they aren't just for ambiance.
That being said, the premise is really cool;  it's like AVP2 but what if the main compound wasn't overrun before you got there.  There are also a lot of cool little mechanics like your squad have limited ammo, but can resupply at the APC (but if the APC stock runs dry your done).  Most of the games worth comes from the 50,000 ways you can approach the 2nd mission and survival.
Overall, the game needs more polish and more content wouldn't hurt;  it is however a ton of fun.

An oldie but a goodie. Set in an alternate 2011, you play as various U.S. Marine fireteam leaders, part of a USMC task force dispatched to liberate the fictional Russian Island of Skira which has been occupied by the PLA, aka the Peoples Liberation Army, aka the Chinese. If you have played this game's sequel on PC (Operation Flashpoint Red River), you will be happy to hear this title escapes the windows live integration with which it is burdened. Thank God! I remember playing this when it first came out on the XBOX 360 and even though I may be a little nostalgic over this title, I think it defiantly holds up and would still thoroughly recommend it, even at non sale prices, if you are looking for a solid tactical shooter. Though keep in mind you will pretty much be buying a campaign at this point as the multiplayer is dead.
The connection to and comparison with the ARMA series is kind of unavoidable and while this game lacks a lot of what made up even ARMA II, it also excels in many respects too. Compared to the ARMA series, the multiplayer was never really heavily populated and lacked some depth. The other major point of comparison is that of mod support. Something which has kept the ARMA series going strong throughout those games' life cycles has been the ability to mod the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of those games. This is something Operation Flashpoint Dragon Rising (OF DR) lacks and so its replay value is greatly diminished, something which contributed to its sharp drop off in players. Though there have been some mods developed for the game since its release, these have been somewhat limited in scope compared to many mods you can find for ARMA.
However it is unfair to characterise this game solely by its negative aspects compared to the ARMA series. There are many elements in OF DR which were done very well and are still better that the ARMA series even to this day (ARMA III). One of these elements is the AI. I am sure many of you are familiar with the frustrating AI in the ARMA series and while the OP DR AI is not perfect, it achieved in 2009 what we can only dream the AI in ARMA was like today. They use cover, support each other, as well as you, make intelligent call outs and assault buildings very effectively to name a few things. The only major downside I found with the AI in this game is that they often do not seem to be able to engage enemy infantry past 200m, though this is rarely a real problem. Other aspects in which OP DR surpasses ARMA include the better modelled vehicle interiors and fantastic character animations. I particularly love the reload animation for the launchers which I have never seen anything which comes close in any other game.
Releasing in 2009, though a little dated, its graphics still hold up. The character and weapon models are very good and the terrain is beautiful. Throughout the campaign you are given a number of different weapons with various different attachments to play with and the sound design for all of them is quite excellent. The campaign takes place on the fictional island of Skira (a faithful recreation of the real Kiska Island) and features a wide variety of missions including; platoon sized assaults in the day as well as the night, infiltration, rescue and assassination/sabotage missions all of which are very fun in their own way. Despite the game being on console it plays perfectly on PC and the need to adapt the control scheme to consoles resulted in smooth and intuitive gameplay. The highlight of which is the command wheel. This command wheel is how you command your aforementioned AI and is very simple to navigate while at the same time, offering a lot of depth to the player in commanding how he wants his squad to act. This includes; movement, fire discipline, formations and spread to name a few.
I did however have a few other issues with the game though none are major things and some had been in hardly any games in 2009 and so could be considered unfair criticisms but this is looking back from today’s tactical shooters. One issue I had was the limited weapon handling the game gives you regarding ranging and aiming your weapons. What I mean by this is that when using iron sights, there is no way to adjust zero and the game doesn't tell you your weapon’s zero with any sight or scope. Though this is less of an issue with scopes as there are often mil-dots to adjust off. When using some sights like the ACOG, it is also impossible to use the backup iron sights on top of the sighting system, making it tricky to engage targets close in. The last complaint I have with the game is that it is only possible to change the weapon/equipment in your hands or give an order using the command wheel while stationary. Although you can give a limited amount of orders on the map, this often put me in the position of having to stop dead while under enemy fire to execute an action or issue an order.
Despite the small number of criticisms I have of this game, it is one of my all-time favourites. Overall as I said at the top, I would highly recommend this game if you are interested in the tactical shooter genre and want to play an interesting and fun campaign outside of the ARMA series.

TBH, I was kind of on the fence with this one, then I read the review section and made up my minds that I've got to thumbs down this one. For one thing, it certainly got some lousy fans. At a glance any negative review quickly get hit with unhelpful grading even if the comments were valid. But not to dwell on that. I'll talk about the actual problem of this game.
The good news is, compare to classic, this installment introduced plenty of new content/mechanics, such as new mount and new statues. If classic have even a few of those elements included I'd probably give it a thumbs up. Unfortunately, most of the statues, new mount and whatnot is locked till you completed new island. Which means that even though there are new contents, the game itself is also severely watered down and you'll pretty much do the same thing to complete an island just to work through another island to get something else. On top of that, even island 3 feels huge and traveling on the horse back and forth gets old real fast.
But the biggest problem I've been facing is still the buggy AI, AI walk/run with lousy timing, and sometimes they will flatout ignore objective because somehow that task is assigned to another builder half way accross the world or something. Which brings me to my next point.
The size of the map is huge. That on it's own isn't too bad but unfortunately this game introduced a timed mechanics that is also the weather. Your current island enters a neverending winter after a certain periods of time. Which makes it that much harder for your horse to recover by eating grass. But with the introduction of mother portal, you can never secure an island and have to move to a different island because the approaching winter kills the grass and makes it that much harder to traverse your kingdom.
All in all. I would say that kingdom is an interesting experiment but ultimately failed to deliver. It's certainly a fairly beautiful game. I'm just not sure if it's for everyone. Unless you're fairly patient when it comes to games.

Darwinia is a game developed and published by Introversion Software
The retro, polygonal graphics, (tasteful) chiptune soundtrack, and overall atmosphere are really interesting to experience. The gameplay is fun in a non-frustrating way - it's hard to get into a position where you lose, and even if you aren't employing the optimal strategy for a level, given enough time, you will be able to beat each stage in different ways
I rarely got frustrated with this game and never really felt bored, even though a lot of the gameplay isn't necessarily that complex. The story doesn't dominate the experience, but the brief sections where you learn more about Darwinia are definitely rewarding
Overall, all these little details don't really matter in the face of the fact that I constantly was entertained while playing this game and never really felt bad, something that even modern games don't necessarily provide
If you're expecting a complex RTS, this is not that game. Think of it as more of "digital weeding", as you slowly and carefully purge the viruses through each stage using a variety of tools

A great game to kill a few hours with - I got it in a package with Uplink as I wanted that game, but I've ended up liking this game just as much.
Briefly, your task is to kill a virus infection on a server where some guy has been running a digital life simulator.  You have 3 basic programs at your disposal - Squads, Engineers, and Officers.  You use Squads to kill enemies, and engineers to capture nodes (for spawning) and collecting digital "souls" of the things that die.  If the engineer goes to a repository, it can transfer the souls in there, and friendly "Darwinians" will gradually come out.  These aren't directly controllable, but can be directed with the "Officer" program to go to areas, and they'll automatically performs tasks like manning equipment or combat.
The gameplay is good, but what really makes the game stand out is the philosophy - particularly with the AI Darwinians seeing the programmer as a sort of "God".  It's very tastefully done in a way that makes you think, without underestimating your intelligence and ramming the point down your throat.
It's got about 3hrs worth of play - it's not massive, but it's worth the price it is, and more.  It's the sort of game to play if you fancy something a bit different for a while.

So I'm going to start off by saying I'm not a guy who plays OG arcade ports of these games so I am not going to compare them to that seeing as how it would be freaking impossible for these guys match slowdown from static hardware to that of dynamic hardware.
You ask most people who have bought this game who aren't elitist diehards who own PCBs of the originals and they will tell you that this is an awesome game. And THAT is all you need to know. You have people who don't want others to enjoy a different version of DoDonPachi, because to them it's some kind of sacrilegious act since scores from this version can't be compared to scores from other versions.
I sort of had this mindset with Cave's first release on STEAM with Mushihimesama and I quickly learned to just look at these releases as stand-alones. It causes less stress and it helps me enjoy the game. Cave is releasing these games so that they can hopefully bring in thousands of new fans instead of pleasing a handful of grumpy elitists. They need to continue going this route.
DoDonPachi Resurrection is a fantastic package offering up numerous modes of play that I still need time to explore. Each mode brings different dynamics that require the player to put in more time to master. Patterns are different, ships are different, scoring mechanics are different, speed is different. You're basically getting thousands of dollars of arcade games in one neat bundle for around $26 (during the sale).
You've got fantastic art direction with all the designs of the enemies, backgrounds, player's ships, bullet spreads, sparkly bonus items, and debris/explosion. Every thing is just a joy to behold while playing the game. It's pretty destracting, but in a good way. I'll end up losing concentration and getting destroyed because I just want to take the time and enjoy the hard work that went into creating these wonderful designs.
Music and sound design are also top notch. The music helps me focus while the sounds from attacks and explosions help me feel like I'm an unstoppable force of complete annihilation.
Technically this game does have it's issues in terms of a boss disappearing on stage 5 of BLA and some unwarranted slowdown (this I don't care about because I never played the original releases and could care less). But if you've bought products from Degica before they are quick to release patches. Hell, they've already released 3 patches since the game's release YESTERDAY. Even on just now as of writing this to fix the sound tracks. When you buy from Degica you know you're going to get support for your software. Unlike other companies like Koei Tecmo.
If you're hesitant about buying this game don't be. Don't listen to the elitists. They are just angry people who don't want others to enjoy a different version of their precious games. Hopefully Cave releases something brand new on this platform so they can argue about nothing.

So this game....
Well before I get into anything about it let me warn you potential buyer that this game is HARD (with a capital H,A,R and D for emphasise) and that there are bugs (both the type you kill with a shotgun and the type you kill with coding changes)
Permadeath is a thing in this game, lose all your Marines and it's back to the menu you go, lose the APC, your pretty much ****d and back to the menu you go, get backed into a corner - menu time, rock falls everyone dies, yep you guessed it, back to the menu you go.
As another review said, this game is almost Dwarf Fortress levels of hard and is about as forgiving as a Elephant (the bain of Dwarfs) who you've just whipped in the love spuds with a wet towel.  Let alone the fact that the tutorial is actually a manual and the first mission throws you in the deep end, while your high on drugs, without a floatation device and screams "Swim boy, swim" at you while your being pelted with orbital based death (rocks fall and YOU die)
But then it all starts to make sense and little by little you progress through the map:
You make it the base without being squashed (pro tip, those items on the ground at the start CAN be picked up and used)
You knock out some turrets and blow a hole in the wall (F8 is your friend here)
You figure out most of the controls and manage to complete your objective (one way or another, it's amazing what a liberal application of C4 can solve)
You make it to mission 2
You crash the APC
You get owned by everything in sight
You try again
And again
And again
You finally have everything down that you need to know and become a lean mean killing machine.
You feel like a total badass.
You get cocky
Something new comes along and kicks your♥♥♥♥♥sending you back to the menu crying like a b***h
So yeah, be prepared to stare at the menu screen a lot while playing this, your going to become quite good friends :)
Right then onto the rest of the game, the graphics are meh. Which for the most part is not an issue although the Marines could do with a serious touchup to make them actually look like space marines and not brown haired clones.
The sound is ok, motion tracker is nice and sounds similar to the one from Aliens while the guns are your generic [Insert gun firing sound here] affair.
UI. Very unfriendly and until you tame it will attempt to bite your hands at every chance.
Gameplay... I'm not gonna sugarcoat this, it has a LOT of backtracking, you go to colony building 'X', fight through alien hoard,  pick up survivors, run like frak back to the APC, depending on how many survivors there were (APC has limited room) go to another building and repeat or go back to the space port to drop them off for evac. This game has as much backtracking as Metroid.
AI. Does the job, nothing more, nothing less.
Atmosphere. Captures the feel of Aliens perfectly. Hell, the only way it could be more Aliens is if a modder came along and redid all the Marines to look like Colonial Marines and the APC and Dropship to look like the ones from the movies (hint, hint modders)
Motion tracker sounds great (even though it picks up your marines and APC which gets anoying)
You can weld doors shut (or cut them open/blow them off their hinges)
C4 is fun and has a nice countdown effect.
Weather effects and lighting help raise the tension and make it feel like LV426 from Aliens.
The monsters (Aliens) are fast and can come out of nowhere very quickly if your not careful.
Overall I recommend this game for its pricetag. It's not the best game ever, it's not the worst. It is a better Aliens game than a certain other game made by a much larger professional gaming studio i know of *cough* Box Gear *cough*
and while as I (and others) have said, this game is HARD and very unforgiving (so be prepared for frustration) it does have its moments where the Awesome dial gets turned up to 11. So if your looking for the best Aliens Colonial Marine simulator in well.... forever, then this might just be for you.
P.S This game has been named wrong, it should have been called Marine Commander simulator 2015, seriously, it's that hard.
p.p.s, Ignore the hours played... Steam dun goofed and hasn't regestered them for some reason.... might be because I was offline at the time and the game crashed :(
p.p.p.s Seriously, any good modders out there who want a great Aliens game, were waiting for you. I'd do it myself but I shudder to think of the horror I might release upon an unsuspecting public.
EDIT: Turns out it's even easier to mod than I thought, 10 minutes of google fu will net you a modified dropship and APC that you can edit into the game with just
to bring home the Aliens feel (warning can cause some graphic issues)

So the game has been released. How does it fare up?
Overall pretty well.
To make this short, sweet, and lazy: if you fall into any of these catagories, you'll probably find this game worth the price:
-fan of the original mordheim tabletop game
-fan of warhammer
-constant progression marred by varying degrees of crippling injuries suffered in battle
-don't mind a bit of RNG goodness
-like the idea of being able to customize a warband and watch as they grind themselves into the ground hunting for precious green rocks admist the horrors of a dangerous trap filled battlefield.
Did those interest you? if so, you might enjoy this game.
however, there are some things to keep in mind:
-graphic/animation quality is quite low for a title priced as such, especially when compared to the incredible graphics of also recently released vermintide.
-1v1 matches only. No options (balanced or not) for multi-player. Considering how long each match takes, this might be for the best, but still something to mention that the option isn't present whatsoever.
-rng injuries/battle system is fun for some, but not fun for others.
-not enough customization options to make the warriors truly feel like "your own". Presets can be quite annoying to work with.
-LOOONGG loading times. even on SSD and cranked up computer.
-Occasional multiplayer D-syncs which makes playing contest matches a bit risky.
keep in mind, at this point, for those more focused on the narrative, there is a "contest" mode which allows injuries and such to take place in multiplayer, but no way to set up leagues, multi-player matches, or other features one might expect when trying to do those old-classic crazy matches like you can when huddled around a mordheim tabletop.
for 40 bucks, the quality of the game is a bit low. I recommend it if those bullet points interested you. If they didn't, then perhaps look into vermintide for a AAA production game at a 30 dollar price tag set in the warhammer universe.

I bought relatively early into Early Access, And I was super disappointed - the game was sluggish, unbalanced, boring and the multiplayer battles without consequences.
And then I started again with the last patch, after taking half a year off.
Boy did this get far. Mordheim is brilliant now. It's still a bit sluggish, a bit slow with the loading, but it's so, so, so much fun. While there's only four warbands, there's plenty of opportunity with different weapon styles and skillings to build your own unique troop. And every battle counts, every engagement could end badly for you.
The AI isn't very good, but it gets lucky every now and then and manages to outflank you, so there's still a considerable risk. Mordheim teaches humility - like when your Matriarch tank loses her shield arm and can't enter Parry stance anymore, rendering her completely useless as a tank. And replacing her from the scratch will take a lot of time and training you might not have, as your commander expects a large delivery of warpstone soon!
My initial disappointment is completely gone, and I'll be the first in line when new DLC featuring more warbands hits the store. It's so good, and so exciting.

There isn't a whole lot to be said that hasn't already been said. This game is good. Really good. It's a hack and slash that bases itself in ridiculousness. There are more ways to take out your foes than French restaurants have ways to say, "Your taste in wine is atrocious." Excellent combat, great soundtrack. The cutscenes are actually enjoyable to watch and are not prerendered; They use the in-game engine, which is as detailed as it is colorful, a refreshing change of pace from other games of its generation. In terms of port quality, it's beautiful. Even on my absolute toaster of a computer, the game manages to stay at around 85 frames per second, even when the screen is crowded with baddies with the PC exclusive Legendary Dark Knight difficulty. The keyboard controls won't do you well, however. I'd recommend getting an Xbox 360 controller, which is nearly perfect, except for two points I'll get to later.
The game has a ton of replay value. Aside from Bloody Palace, there are a plethora of unlockable moves, difficulties, and artwork/biographies, but I have to note that the latter is stuff that anyone can find in a quick search on Google. Really, the most rewarding part of this game is the game itself, and overcoming the increasing challenges it throws at you by practicing and mastering the combat. Even after beating everything the game keeps track of with an S rating, I still don't feel like I'm as good at it as I could be, and this is a welcome feeling to have.
Cons: Aside from fewer style moves than in DMC 3, the biggest issues I noted were
- The camera. It gets stuck on scenery and can get jammed into places that make it impossible to see what you're doing (especially during boss battles). The targeting is also a pain. It seems that no matter which of the targeting modes I choose, I can never lock on to the enemy I want. When the camera and targeting issues combine, combat feels much harder than it should be.
-The length. The various difficulty options are a blast, but the core game is just too short. 20 missions, okay, but 3 of them are only boss battles. Dante is fun to play as, but he only gets 7 missions, and most of them are backtracking. The one unique boss fight he gets is its own level and can be completed in about 10 minutes. It feels like two halves of a game are slapped together here, with Nero missing a big chunk of missions and Dante not having much of an opportunity to show off his insanely large moveset.
- The controller. I know, I know, it's not really a criticism of the game, but I know that most people are going to be using an Xbox 360 controller with this, and while it is the best of the controllers I tried, it has issues which negatively show in the game. The D-pad is horrid, it makes instant style switching with Dante touchy to the point that combos will be screwed up. Nero is another problem. I found myself doing "the claw" with my right hand many times during combat, as I was charging the exceed meter, charging the gun, adjusting the camera, and dodging attacks at the same time. Changing the controls only helps so much; There is simply too much going on at one time for the few amount of buttons on the controller.
It's pretty fun, and this is where I'd crack a joke about it being like Dark Souls with less anime, but it's interesting I should bring up Dark Souls, because...
I got this just before DMC 4 Special Edition was announced, which is set to come out this summer, and is going to be offered as its own thing. If you pay for this version now, you're not getting the full deal which comes out in a matter of months. As such, I have to strongly suggest just waiting for SE.

Devil May Cry 4 is an amazing hack-and-slash game that is easy to learn and hard to master. The combat system is very in depth and there is always more room for improvement, even for the greatest masters of the game. It also has many different difficulty levels that will keep you busy for HOURS. You get to play as either Nero, who has a very interesting combat system because of his grab ability, and Dante, who has a variety of weapons and fighting styles to choose from while in game, giving an indefinite number of possibilities for combos. Plus, the game is very pretty, even on the lowest graphics settings, and for a PC port, it is not that bad.
Now here's the part where you yell at me for stating my opinion. My main criticisms of the game lie heavily in the story, which I honestly believe was bland and tasteless. Dante isn't the main character, but instead, it's Nero, who in my opinion, acted too much like a whiny ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (though his combat is very unique). A majority of the characters are completely one-dimensional and don't really serve any purpose other than being the damsel in distress or the power-hungry bad guy or the envious rival . I pretty much only enjoyed the parts of the story where Dante was included because at least he was cheeky in an enjoyable way. Although I liked Nero's combat style, it got old for me pretty quick.
Other downsides include the camera problems (which I am pretty sure is typical for a Devil May Cry game), a lack of costumes, the hideous amount of backtracking which puts Dante's role in the game to shame (I am talking you're backtracking for almost HALF THE GAME), and the lame final boss whose attack patterns are very predictable. Plus there's not much innovation put into the level design, which brings me back to the backtracking issue. I honestly felt like I was playing a somewhat incomplete story.
Overall DMC4 was a mostly fun ride from start to end. It does bring back Bloody Palace as well as has a couple fun bosses. What it fails at in areas such as level design and completeness, the game makes up for it with an awesome combat system, beautiful visuals, and long playability. It wasn't as good as Devil May Cry 3, but better than DmC Devil May Cry.
Overall I give Dante May Backtrack 4 an 8/10

The much awated port of DoDonPatchi has at last arrived, and it's quite the package at that.
Released back in 2008 for arcades, DoDonPatchi DaiFukKatsu (DDP DFK for short), also known as DoDonPatchi Resurrection, is one of CAVE's most notable STG's to date, while chances are the largest fan favourite of the series at that. DDP DFK builds up from it's previous installment by pushing a more understanable scoring and chaining system, far more bullets on the screen, and a more easier to grasp and use Hyper system to give the player more tools and options to survive and score large. This installment comes with the notable 1.5, 1.51, Arrange A&B, and then the long desired Black Label and the fan nicknamed "Ketsuipachi" arranged with Jake "Virt" Kauffman's soundtrack fully intact, a first for oversea players to obtain without importing!
While it is a first for the entire DDP DFK experance to be together at last as a single package, there did come a lot of current issues in turn that hopfully will be fixed in the future. As it stands, the Arrange A suffers from the lack of slowdown period, leading towards it being far harder then ever intended, while in turn the "Ketsuipachi" suffers from FAR more slowdown then it should have at all, making it's experance far easier then it should be. Add onto this that the Stage 5 boss might not even show up visable, andd the OST currently corrupted with static, and the package feels almost rushed in many ways. Given it's somewhat steep asking price, and the fact that most people buying the will more then likely find theirself only playing Black Label/BLA, it might be best to hold off buying till fixes are applyed. Otherwise if you're willing to look past these flaws, this is the most complete DDP DFK package to date, and it's PC release ensures that you'll not need to hunt down a JP 360 ever again.

In short: This game plays like the unholy lovechild of
and
.
Gameplay:
The primary controls are simple; you use WASD to move the camera. Scroll up and down to move along the Z axis. The camera centers on your mouse cursor, which is an unusual design choice, but it fits perfectly in this game--because you directly control your most important combat units.
When you select, say, a Squad (basic infantry, armed with lasers and explosives), you can left-click to move them, right-click to fire, and
to fire off the currently-selected explosion-producing device. Similarly, when you unlock the Armor (which acts as an APC/turret) you can select it and manually aim the guns once it's been converted to a turret.
The other primary combat unit you'll work with are the Darwinians themselves. You can't directly control them like you would a Squad or Armor, but you can create Officers who can then issue goto and follow orders to nearby Darwinians. They start with no weapons, but putting some time into researching them leads to giving them lasers or even grenades (now that's a scary thought). Further, you need Darwinians to run various structures in the world, usually either your turrets or key objectives.
It's particularly key to learn how to use Darwinians to your advantage, because instead of requiring resources to build units, you have a
at any given time. You start with the ability to have 3 units at once, and can upgrade to 4 or even 5. Thankfully, Armor only counts as a unit as long as it's not turned into a turret, but you're gonna have quite a bit of trouble fighting with so little room for reinforcements, especially if you're trying to run your resource-collecting, building-capturing Engineers at the same time.
Story:
So you're connecting to this virtual theme park--the titular Darwinia. But, as you finish connecting, the data stream begins popping errors left and right, and when you go to the entrance, the owner of the 'park'--Dr. Sepulveda--messages you, irritated and confused. He doesn't know how you got in, but he would appreciate some help; his park is overrun with a terrible virus, and it's destroying all of Darwinia, along with the most advanced AI known to man: the Darwinians. An entire culture, born and raised within a mainframe, hundreds of generations old...brought to its knees. Dr. Sepulveda has a request for you: help him save Darwinia from the virus. It's not like you have anything better to do, right? And if you fail to save the Darwinians, the loss in AI research alone is priceless...
Problems:
There's a few glitches here and there. Sometimes, units will try to move "onto" a building, and start spazzing out around it.
There's also some enemies that are just a pain to deal with until you figure out how to work around their strengths. Pro tip: The game expects you to take direct control of your Squads when they're facing something nasty. If you leave a Squad to face something like a Centipede or a Spider, or even big clusters of regular Virii, they'll take hits.
Overall, I just plain love this game. It's got a few rough spots, but the charm drew me in, and the gameplay kept me there.

Note: I'm Australian, so before a couple of days ago there were no servers around me, which made the game super laggy unless you play in offline mode. Sloclap are very dedicated to fixing bugs and server issues, and the servers get better every day as they fix things on their end. So now with OCE servers the game is very enjoyable.
• Unique even to the fighting game genre. Robust and intuitive fighting mechanics, Absolver doesn't leave a lot to be desired.
• Very fluid controlls, IMO best played with a controller
• Copious amounts of customization, including being able to re write all of your attack strings, and wear any combination of (or no) clothes/gear
• Great art style, the game looks exactly how it does in the screenshots and trailers
• When the matchmaking works, it works very quickly
• Sizeable playerbase, especially for this kind of game
• Very pretty soundtrack that compliments the environments well
• The game is difficult, which makes every fight, even fights against NPCs in the world feel like a real fight. with nearly 20 hours I still come across a strong NPC when I'm not paying attention and get outplayed by the game's AI. Challenging but fun.
• Dedicated dev team that are constantly fixing the server issues, and are in the process of opening more servers worldwide
• Skillfull balanced PVP
• Incentive to keep roaming the world fighting enemies and learning new moves
• The story seems to have set itself up for future updates and extentions to the single player experience. Hopefully Sloclap capitalizes on this and releases more playable content.
• The game will somtimes get stuck on a loading screen or stuck trying to find a match when you enter a 1v1
• Frequent lag when you enter a new area
• Occasional laggy 1v1s because the game favours quick matchmaking over quality connection
• Occasional crashes, but never enough to become annoying
• Lack of PVE content, with the single player game acting more as a large tutorial for the multiplayer game
• Fighting multiple enemies can sometimes be awkward, and switching targets is the only problem I have with the game's controls.
Absolver kind of exceded my expectations. I wanted it to be this good, but I was scared it wouldn't be.
If you don't want to spend 30 dollars on this game, I would definitely recommend picking it up in a sale, as it's one of the better fighting games I think I've ever played.
Lush combat and engaging environments make Absolver a must play. 8/10

A 3D, 3rd-Person, Turn-Based, Tactical, RPG set in the world of Warhammer Fantasy. Mordheim: City of the Damned has everything that I love in a game: a grim-dark universe rich with lore, simple controls, procedural encounters, customizable characters, and a difficulty that cannot be altered or lowered.
This game is hard, not because it requires skill but because every action taken by your characters, (walking is mundane and requires no actual roll), will be resolved randomly based on a percentage of your characters' skill; this percentage will be bigger or smaller from how high the skill is required to perform that action is. This means, you, as the player, have no actual control in how well your characters perform, the most that you, as the player, will be doing is moving your characters to an enemy and telling them to attack or up to a wall and telling them to climb it, all you can do is watch and hope they succeed. The player is soley responsible for strategy on the field and building up your warband to get better percentage rolls.
So let me reiterate, this game is hard, and you will become frustrated when you fail but the replayability for this game is extremely high and I advise playing as each of the available factions because they each require different types of mindsets to play them, and nothing feels better than settling with a race or faction that just speaks to you on an emotional level.
Anyways, I recommend this game to anyone who is a huge fan of unforgiving turn-based random number generators, meaning if you really liked Darkest Dungeon you are gonna enjoy this. I have been playing since the Cult of the Possessed were first added during Early Access so I am very pleased with how this game has evolved.
Oh and I highly recommend looking up the official lore and fluff for Warhammer Fantasy, you'll be suprised at how vast the universe can really be.
Thanks for reading.

This is a seriously good game and very addictive, especially if you are a fan of the Warhammer Fantasy Universe.  The controls are easy to pick up and combat / movement both simple and advanced are fully explained in the excellent tutorials.
Here comes the inevitable 'but'part.
1.  Even though the game is centred around the collection of Wyrdstone there is little opportunity to hsrvest any once you make contact with the enemy.  You simply have to pile all your warriors in to prevent isolated warrkors from getting splattered.  It seems like the only time you can collect any is if you deploy near to a deposit or come across some on your way to link up with your warband.
2. The acquisition of loot is impossible once the enemy warband routes. This means that even though you may have put OOA some enemy with really good items that you have no chance to loot them. Also, even if you win the match standing 2 meters away from the huge Wyrdstone deposit you were on your way to you get no chance to collect it and therefore do not benefit from your victory.  Maybe a victorious warband should be given 1 final turn to collect any nearby loot/wyrdstone but made to ignore and be ignored by remaining enemies.
3.  At certain times you have no say in the deployment of your warriors and they end up at isolated spawn points.  Then on the very first turn, some enemies can sprint across half the map, home in on them, stun them with their first blow and OOA your warrior with the next 2 hits...and there's nothing you can do about it, you're just a spectator at this point. I dont mind hard games or getting a bashing if I make mistakes, in fact i relish the experience of playing my way back out of difficult situations. However, in my opinion, no game should arbitrarily place you in a position where you literally have no chance to influence (for your benefit or detriment) the outcome of that position.
I realise that this game is still early access so my aim here is to inform, not to rant.
If you like turn based strategy games and / or the Warhammer Fantasy Universe then buy this game immediately because it's one of the best you will ever play.

This one hit me on a personal level.  Had a few tears at the end of it.  10/10

Among the Sleep takes the horror of helplessness a step further by putting the player in the footie pajamas of a small child. The first person camera wobbles and drags on the ground to simulate the perspective of a child that hasn't quite mastered walking yet, but somehow I still found myself trying to translate the distorted reality the child was seeing instead of living it. The unraveling of that mystery is engaging and I was always left wondering. I didn't manage to sort through it all until everything was properly revealed. But other mediums are just as good if not better at keeping the audience guessing. What games do so well, and what Among the Sleep did not succeed at, is dropping the player in a situation and asking how would they react. As the game itself is as simple to play as it is short, the understanding born of that process never has a chance to come about. Shortness isn't a bad thing though. The game doesn't wear out its welcome and it doesn't take more than it gives. It does have an interesting story to tell, and tells it well, just not better than a movie might.

As an old-school twitch gamer, one of my better memories was consistently beating the original Double Dragon in arcades on a single quarter. It was one of the first arcade beat-em-ups and arguably one of the best of its time. Now WayForward has finally brought their reimagining of the franchise to PC after a console release in late 2012.
Pros:
-----
- Neon introduces a few new concepts to the genre such as Gleam, which doubles your attack power for a short time after successfully dodging an attack and an upgrade system for magic attacks and passive bonuses in the form of mixtapes. The more of a mixtape you have, the more powerful that attack or bonus is. Enemies drop them, but you can also buy them from shops. Tapesmiths allow you to pick up more tapes in exchange for mythril, which you get from defeating bosses.
- (Note: I played with an XBox 360 controller) While there are more button commands to get used to than the original, the controls feel very solid. Nothing seems janky or off. I suggest a quick glance at the Help screen to see all your available standard moves.
- There is a good variety of enemies, some requiring a specific way to finish them off quicker than just mashing your punch button. Abobos are freakin' huge now!
- Effects and voice acting are passable, but what really stands out is the soundtrack. Virt has done an amazing job making original songs for the game that have that definite 80's vibe and the remixing of the original game's tracks are very well done.
- ONLINE CO-OP. It took the PC port of this game to get what console owners were promised over a year ago and never received, online co-op. Beat-em-ups are always 10x more fun with a friend, and with team powerups like sharing health that you can activate almost anytime by high-fiving your partner, it makes traversing the game easier as well.
- Unlike the dark, gritty visuals of the original, this game goes for a brighter, cartoony aesthetic. This game knows its audience and opted for a campy, offbeat feel, almost making fun of the era it wants to copy, and it mostly works.
Cons:
-----
- All these attacks at my command and NO BACK ELBOW? Anyone who played the original Double Dragon knows that move is your bread and butter for making progress in the game.
- Graphics are alright and the game has a cartoony vibe, but nothing really stands out. Also, apart from resolutions and windowed/full screen mode, there's no graphical tweaking. I'm not saying a game like this really needs those options, but when you see them in nearly every PC game, it's noticeable when they're missing.
I feel this is one of WayForwards best games to date. Much like with DuckTales Remastered, they have honoured the source material while adding a modern flair. Join up with a friend and go save Marion!

Ahh, the 80's. The golden era of pop culture. It brought us many wonderful things such as the NES, Ray-Bans, Transformers, and bigass hair. It also brought us an arcade classic, a 2-player beat-em-up known as Double Dragon. It got everything right, from smashing gameplay to perfectly executed co-op mayhem. And now WayForward has stepped out of the DeLorean to hand us their throwback to the past: Double Dragon Neon. This magnificent tour-de-force blows the 80's head off with a rocket launcher, builds a cyborg out of it's corpse, and then puts said cyborg on a surfboard to the future to kick modern gaming convention in the cojones. All while listening to hair metal on a boombox. It has been a long time since I have seen a game that has this level of insanity taking itself with a gospel level of seriousness.
And what would Double Dragon be without the twin heroes, Billy and Jimmy Lee? WayForward has brought the original dudebros to life with amazingly detailed cel-shaded models. All the classic enemies are here, from the lowly street thug cannon fodder, leather-clad whip-cracking bondage babes, and the infamous Abobo. Add to that the main villian, Skullmageddon, who could easily be described as a skeletal version of The Shredder from TMNT. That is if The Shredder was batsh*t insane and on LSD. This guy is pure evil though, and he makes no bones about trying to pun you to death. On the music front, Jake Kaufman (AKA Virt) has brought the sound of the 80's back to life with a massively awesome mixture of vocal pop and hard rockin hits. The complete soundtrack is downloadable at his Bandcamp page for the low low price of NADA, so check it out!
The gameplay in Double Dragon Neon is largely unchanged from the original game, however there are a few new addons that change things up considerably. As you make your way through the game, defeated enemies will drop mixtapes. These audio treats come in two flavors, upgrade tapes that add to your stats, and Sōsetsuken tapes that add to your special attacks. Be sure to grab as many as you can, because you can stack each tape to further upgrade your stats and moves! The special attacks are quite varied, ranging from a classic cyclone kick to a hadouken-inspired fireball. Be sure to listen to each mixtape as well, the lyrics are quite funny.
I started out playing Double Dragon Neon expecting to play a decent remake of a beloved game. And what I got was an experience that far exceeded my expectations as WayForward has ripped the 80's a new one, and yanked this glorious beast out of the void. I honestly cannot find a single thing to complain about with this game. So if you are pining for the days of big music, bad puns, and beating the ever-loving crap out of big dudes named Abobo, Double Dragon Neon will NOT disappoint. And it's only gonna take up $10 of your hairspray budget!

Alright, so let's see what all the fuss is about...
It seems like the kind of RTS someone who had a vague idea what an RTS was but had never actually played one would make. There's less focus on massing units or build trees. The closest thing to gathering resources is the spirits you pick up from dead "virii", which are... floating arrows, mostly. There were these snaky things too and this giant egg-laying spider.
I guess that brings me to the graphics. They're awful. I get that the blocky low-poly was an aesthetic choice, but everything looks so... bland. It kind of reminds me of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, where everything's pee-and-poop green and yellowish. The units are all pixel blurred like they're hentai genitals or something.
There's... no music as far, as I can tell. I certainly didn't hear much of anything while I was playing. I apparently bought the soundtrack along with the game in a big bundle. I imagine I got a big empty folder for my money.
Pathfinding is nonexistent. Everything tries to travel in a straight line. If something gets in the way that's intraversible then the unit moves straight into it and stops. If something gets in the way that's deadly then the unit will move straight into it and dies. I lost engineers and spirits that way. When some of your units are described as "AI decades in development", being unable to traverse a simple landscape is a little ridiculous.
Well, order queueing is a thing, right? No. I don't know what it is with Introversion games and not having the ability to select multiple things or queue up actions with shift clicking but it's just not there, and that makes the lack of pathfinding even more infuriating. Games in the 90's had pathfinding and order queueing. Come on!
I'll tell you why I quit. I was in the second level, and I was expected to get 150 darwinians under the tree. To do this I needed to reincarnate them in incubators by gathering spirits. The problem with this is while you're gathering spirits they drift away and then you can't pick them up. This leaves you with the very likely possibility that you'll not have the minimum 150 by the time you've scoured the map, killed everything, captured all the buildings, and painstakingly escorted these little dudes all the way back to the start of the map. I happened to have 138 by the time I was done, with a stray darwinian stuck on the wrong side of a deadly fence surrounding the starting area. Considering this all took me an hour, this is infuriating, and it's the second level.
When a game starts to feel like a chore or work, then I stop playing it. I feel kind of bad giving it a negative rating based on two levels, but I really don't feel like I screwed up hard enough to warrant failing the level. The second level. A level where I'm still getting the grips of the mechanics of the game. Something that shouldn't take very long to get through. Something that shouldn't have ESCORT MISSIONS.
Or, well, I didn't fail the level, since it didn't even bother to check if the objectives were completable and tell me. Nice.

Late to the party writing this review, but it's still good for people wondering about whether this game is worth it.
**TL;DR: It abso-♥♥♥♥ing-lutely is.**
Not gonna give spoilers, but your experience may vary depending on whether or not you're fine with or know of all the cliche tropes in most games nowadays ("lol plot armor", "lol good guy evades danger 2752767891 times"; best example I can give is the♥♥♥♥♥♥that happens in, like, Dead Space 3). I'm not using the term "cliche tropes" in a negative light at all.
DO NOT PLAY ON EASY FOR YOUR FIRST RUN. Even if you do have a different version of the game that gives you the option to play on Madhouse, I still wouldn't really recommend Madhouse for a 1st run. I think I got more out of this game on a Normal run than I would have had I picked Madhouse.
Gonna break this game down in halves, again doing my best to not spoil. That said, I love this game so much that I'm probably going to sound like I'm overhyping it. Leave any and all expectations you may have on the ground floor when you first play this game.
1st half: 12/10
Ho-ly♥♥♥♥♥♥ In my opinion, RE7 has probably the best first half of any video game I can ever think of. First off, this half made me feel something I rarely feel in video games: fear. A lot of the♥♥♥♥♥♥that happens enabled me to establish a new-found respect for any horror movie protagonist I've ever thought was a complete retard for doing something exceptionally dumb (or not doing something at all) when faced with the bad guys (more on them in a bit).
There is another thing I haven't seen other games do as well as this half did: create an actually compelling, immersive environment (though I could still argue this somewhat tapers off towards the finish of this half). Obviously, the environment is scary, and is still done exceptionally well, but I would have probably gotten bored with it if it was strictly just scary. The timing of adding interesting dynamics to the environment was absolutely PERFECT. Each time I would have  probably started to get bored/numbed/jaded about my surroundings, they throw in something that enabled me to sort of restart or recycle my ability to really be able to take in the environment and feel compelling fear once more. My favorite part of this is that many of these instances have absolutely NOTHING AT ALL to do with the story, and were so ♥♥♥♥ing great I didn't give a ♥♥♥♥ it didn't play into the story because I was at least entertained. I felt extremely rewarded for actually taking the time to pay attention to details, keeping otherwise trivial parts of dialogue in mind, and exploring.
As an aside, another thing this game was great with in terms of timing was finding the inventory upgrades. Every single time I felt like I would be absolutely ♥♥♥♥ed by a lack of inventory space, the next room had a backpack.
I feel the first few encounters with the more "common" enemies added to the atmosphere of this game, and were fairly symbolic of the struggles of the game, but this kinda runs out of gas as you progress and figure out how to block. The first few can kinda give you a swift kick in the balls in some not-immediately obvious ways, but once you're done with the sort of feeling out process in how to deal with (or, more specifically, fight) them, they're not too bad. Still, at any point in the game, getting hit just once by one of them, even if it was a fluke, usually opens the floodgates that lead you to the "YOU DIED" screen.
Last but not least...
The boss fights. Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing God these boss fights. I loved these boss fights so much, I feel I need to break these down in parts, too. Again, I'll try to not give too much away.
1st fight - Remember when I said I have a new found respect for dumb horror movie protagonists? And the tropes? It starts here, both in their unique way. I found it easy to forget certain things when faced with such a threat as this boss, and it was "only" the first one. Normally, I'd probably class this as an average tutorial-like boss fight with typical hit and run strats,  Great opening fight.
2nd - THIS. MOTHER. ♥♥♥♥ING. FIGHT. This is among my all-time favorite boss fights, especially the first time I tried it because I could not believe I made another dumb horror film character mistake, and it was probably the dumbest one of all time, and I ♥♥♥♥ing loved it. I was entertained. This fight is possibly also the craziest and most entertaining boss fight I've played in a long, long time. That is, until...
3rd - ANOTHER AWESOME FIGHT. I generally preferred the fight before this one, but I know many others who preffer this, and for damn good reason. It was this fight where I knew I was in for something special with RE7.
4th - I honestly don't know whether this was a good fight or a bad one, or a middle-of-the-road fight and am still debating it with myself to this day. Quality aside, I'll just say I will forget the other fights way before I forget about this one.
5th - Still pretty crazy, still pretty good, but is probably the weakest of the bunch so far in terms of actual combat. Perhaps also the least remarkable of the boss fights, but it certainly fits in. Works great for a conclusion of the first half.
And it's downhill from here. Not a sharp decline, but I don't think they could have topped the first half.
2nd half: 7.5/10
Early parts of this half retained some of its fear factor, but quickly turns from a horror game into much more of a shooter, and the game seems more confused in doing so. Many of the subtleties that brings everything together for the first half is pretty much gone, and tries TOO hard to get jumpscares, as opposed to radiating a feeling of fear or impending doom, again, as found in the first half. By this point, you know how to deal with enemies, and no new ones appear for the rest of the game, with the exception of a variant of an enemy after a long gauntlet-type pushing uphill fight, and you will have the most OP weapon in the game (not the magnum, if you could believe it) at your disposal, but is/was still at least a reward for exploring thoroughly.
A couple decent ambushes kinda save it, but it's just generic shooter 3436257 at this point. A certain revelation could have been done far, FAR better, but is still uplifting enough to not really get considered offensive as far as the characters go, and gives you motivation so you can soldier through the rest of the game.
In true RE fashion, the final boss is an absolute pushover. No real creativity, just a dump your mag, lolcutscene, gg sort of boss taken from Dead Space 1, but without needing to contend with wacky aim or small weak spots. It didn't help that the path to said final boss is probably the most annoying sequence in the game.
Overall: 9/10. Definitely take a shot with this game.

I’ve had this one in the backlog for a while now and only recently got around to playing it. Resident Evil 7 is the 7th main entry to the popular survival horror franchise. After receiving a lot of negative feedback for the past few Resident Evil games, Capcom decided to reinvent the franchise and switched the game’s perspective from the traditional 3rd person action gameplay to a 1st person game with a larger emphasis on horror. But were the changes enough to save this classic franchise?
Well… yes and no. Resident evil 7 does bring back the survival horror aspects from the original games along with the tight inventory management and puzzle solving, but the new 1st person perspective brings its own issues, and fans of the past few resident evil games may not appreciate the slower pace.
The game’s story starts off with our main protagonist, Ethan driving out to some swamp looking for his girlfriend. It’s not very clear how Ethan managed to figure out the exact location of Mia but whatever. Once you reach the old rundown house, you’ll immediately start encountering cliché scary things like balls rolling across the hallway and little girls appearing down hallways. Within the first hour, you’ll meet the family and the game’s main antagonists throughout the story. There’s Jack, the deranged redneck father who will continuously pop up when you least expect it. Then there’s his wife, Margerine, a crazy insect lady, and then there’s their son who isn’t really a scary character at all, but does make it possible for the developers to throw in a clever “Escape Room” segment later on. The game’s broken up into a few distinct chapters defined by these characters and each character has their own boss encounter. Towards the end of the game, the game’s setting will change drastically and the story will start to piece itself together, but it feels shoehorned in and I can’t help but remember the final half of Metal Gear Solid 2 where you take control of a different character and the story and gameplay starts to get ridiculous.
Resident Evil 7’s gameplay is much more focused on puzzle solving and horror. You’re given weapons, but ammo is extremely limited and I never felt like I was prepared for encounters. The weapons themselves all feel incredibly weak and most of the enemies in the game can’t even be killed. Because of this, running and shutting doors behind you is often the best tactic for escaping conflict. The game’s enemies will occasionally roam around the narrow corridors of the house requiring the player to sneak around, but the map design never really lends itself to this type of hide-and-seek gameplay and you often just need to wait for the enemy to walk from one spot to the other before you can move to the next segment. If the enemy spots you, you can awkwardly slow jog down the hall away from them and close the door behind you to slow them down. Once they lose sight of you, they start roaming their same scripted path again. After a few encounters, you’ll start to have a better understanding of how the game’s designed and the horror aspect of the game doesn’t have as strong of an impact as it does in the opening hour. You’ll realize that you just need to bypass the person hunting you, find the key to a door, turn around and go back, then crawl through a small confined space that the enemy can’t follow you into until they inevitably jump out at you in a scripted scene that sets up a boss fight.
The game’s boss fights really highlight the weaknesses in the game’s core control scheme. Trying to fight Jack in a tiny arena was incredibly frustrating because of the slow player movement and painfully slow turning speed. The game requires that you make precision shots often and they’re difficult to pull off in such small areas. Couple that with the game’s incredibly slow reloading mechanic and stupid slow sprint speed and it’s easy to see the flaw in the game’s controls.
The game also features some basic inventory management, but it felt like more of a hastle than it needed to be. You not only need to manage ammo and weapons, but you also need to make sure you have enough space to pick up important quest items like keys. There were several instances throughout the game where I was stuck backtracking to pickup a key I had placed in storage to make room for ammo. I never felt like this inventory management added to the experience, you could always just carry a large amount of ammo for each weapon and kill all of the enemies in the area, then backtrack to pick up all your keys from the storage container and walk around opening locked doors without any threats.
And finally, let’s talk about visuals and performance. Resident Evil 7 runs great completely maxed out with framerates ranging anywhere between 100 to 160 fps at any time. The game’s visuals look phenomenal but I did feel that some of the character’s speaking animations felt off and didn’t look that convincing. Aside from that, textures, lighting, and sound design are all top notch and the best this series has to offer.
And that’s all there really is to say about this game. Resident Evil 7 abandons the action oriented design of the past few games and instead borrows elements from the original Resident Evil while also taking elements from modern horror games like Outlast and Alien Isolation. But unfortunetly, it doesn’t seem to be better than any of those titles. The redneck family simply isn’t that scary, even when they jump out at you, and the game’s awkward slow paced controls that try to make you feel vulnerable just don’t feel believable and it makes for more of a frustrating experience than a scary one. The story is decent enough, but I couldn’t help but notice that it borrows a lot of elements from FEAR which came out over a decade ago. Thankfully the graphics and performance are excellent and the overall product feels very polished. The game by itself is a great experience with a few scares here and there, and a decent story (albeit incredibly copy-paste).
I recommend picking this one up, but at a good discount. There's better games in this franchise, but this is a step in the right direction for Capcom and hopefully they'll learn from mistakes made in this game for their inevitable Resident Evil 8.

Pros:
- complex and responsive combat that feels very satisfying
- fun and competititve multiplayer (both PvE and PvP)
- charming environments
- minimalistic yet appealing character design
- mysterious story and lore
Cons:
- often unstable game connections for multiplayer matches (about 1 of 5 matches result in crash or disconnect)
- game is quite short for the asking price (finished the main story in about 6hrs)
- lack of variety - the world itself feels more like a multiplayer hub in an MMO rather than a single player game world; not enough items to loot, not enough enemy variety; very few interactions with environment
Despite all its shortcomings, Absolver is an incredibly addictive game with lasting appeal far beyond it's short storyline. That is, if it manages to get you engaged in its competetive multiplayer.

Having said that, Flatout 2 was one of my favorite games on the PS2, so I am enjoying the view as I replay a treasured memory. I recommend this game to racing fans who like to rub fenders. The addition of leaderboards adds to the replayability. The stunt challenges are difficult but addictive.
The tracks look great, and have lots of destructible objects to ram through in order to gain boost, but I wish the tracks didn't overlap on each other so much. Farm Valley 1 and Farm Valley 2 will share sections of track, for instance, which doesn't really work for me.
On the bad side, the soundtrack is short, repetetive, and, unmemorable. Sometimes objects will intersect with cars in an unrealistic way. Like any game we love, it's too short.
Overall 8/10
