This game is the epitome of easy to learn, hard to master. Move left and right, drop coins, that's the only stuff you can do, but it Works. With each run, you will either improve in terms of skill or unlock new content in the game, but you have to not be afraid of failing.
A big complaint I've seen is that this game seems to be the same game over and over. It's a game in the ilk of FTL, in that with each playthrough, you can do more, and unlock more things for future runs. If you are not a fan of games that are essentially iterative new game pluses, linked together to form a bigger game, this is not the game for you (and that's a-ok).
Another complaint I've seen is the inability to undo actions, e.g. you can't destroy buildings you create (at least not easily). That's part of the design, in that you need to be intentional with your actions. This is a very tight game. This is not Age of Empires II on easy mode (a game I love, especially on that mode). This is a game where all your actions matter. If you waste your gold, it's on you. This is not a button masher. To beat the game, you need to think about what you've done in a run that worked and didn't work, plan, and follow your plan...which is hard when the world is as enchanting as the world of this game, in terms of graphics, music, and even the little animations.
If you like a mix of tower defense, planning, kingdom management (I don't want to say it's RTS? but it technically is real time strategy, in that it requires strategy and is not turn based, etc.), new game pluses, simple base mechanics, exploration, and aren't afraid of failing, this is the game for you. It's a game that's hard to put down for a reason. I would get this full price, not even just on sale, but I got it on sale for a Very Good Price.
But whatever you do, don't get it on your phone, unless you never want to sleep again. ;-)

This is a very complicated game that needs a softer introduction for inexperienced players.
Right now the "tutorial" presents a firehose of useful information without any experience using that information interleaved. That means it goes in one ear and out the other. Thus the "tutorial" system is extensive but is not actually suitable for true beginners. A better way to hook beginners would be to rapidly show them a quick-and-easy barely useful build without going into every detail of that build. Then get the player launched, guide them to another system/whatever and dock. Travelling to the other system should show some of the features/drawbacks of the build. Then enhance the craft. Launch. Script an easy Skirmish and guide them through it. Guide subsequent repairs. Return to dock. Buy replacements, upgrade, etc. That is a true tutorial -- what exists now is more akin to a one-time hovering tooltip.
The graphics look good and the complexity revealed thus far hints at greatness. Unfortunately the time and rote memorization it takes to get initially acquainted with this game keeps me from truly playing it. I've never truly gotten out of the hangar before I had to quit and at that point there is nothing exciting about the game that makes me want to return to it any time soon. Once out in space the game can get a little empty. There are missions to do which give you an immediate objective or you can go out and sort of do your own thing. There is mining for resources and diplomacy which allows you to go into a hostile system and hunt enemy ships for bounties. It can get a little old though. In my opinion, more diverse missions should be added as well as an option to select mission based on what kind of playstyle you have (maybe a mission interface at space stations?). This would allow players who want to play as a pirate to do raid missions, miners to do resource gathering, etc... I also think smaller stations should be implemented that do not have shipyards, but rather some sort of other funtions (ie. Smugglers' dens, military instalations, trade centers, etc?).  One more thing I would hope to see is more interaction with friendly faction ships, because as of now, friendlies just sort of drift around space and don't do much. I'd like to see something like, escort missions for friendly factions, or the possibility of hiring wingmen to fly around with you and assist in combat.
I think the game is deifitely on the right track, it IS a fun game as is but it still needs some work, I hope a DEV gets the chance to read this review and think about the suggestions I've made. I think implementing  some of them would make the game feel fuller once the fun of ship building wears out or you've run out of ship ideas.

I am a big fan of this series. Devil May Cry 3 is probably my all-time favourite console game, but I missed this one in my transition from console to PC gaming.  Seeing DMC4 cheap on steam, I had no choice but to see what I missed.
Essentially, this is a lot like DMC3, not quite as good, but still a worthy addition to the series and well worth picking up if you like console hack n slash games.  As you would expect, the combat is fluid and responsive, although a little boring to start with as you need to upgrade yourself with new combos.  New hero Nero isn’t nearly as bad♥♥♥♥♥as Dante is, and sadly only has one melee weapon, but he has his devil bringer hand-thingy which lets you perform grappling attacks, which can be fun.  It still looks pretty good for an old console game, runs at about 70FPS on my crappy laptop, and the environments are colourful, diverse and well designed, with platforming and not too simple puzzles thrown in to pace things out.  And the pace is good.  The game really comes alive in the boss battles, which pits in some epic confrontations against some ginormous hulking behemoths for some true power fantasy.  They would be nicer if Capcom didn’t shamelessly recycle the bosses though. It’s also got a kooky anime style storyline that some will love and some will hate.  For me it was a bit on the silly side, but then again this is Devil May Cry.
On the flip side, this game forces you to play through on the easier difficulties before unlocking the harder modes, despite the fact that the two default difficulties are easy enough for a monkey to get through.  I’m the kinda sadistic wretch who feels unchallenged if a boss doesn’t kill me the first few times.  I’ve no problem with easy modes, but having to play through on an easy mode first cheapened the ride for me.  Secondly, half way through the game, SPOILER ALERT you get to play as Dante for a few levels.  Dante plays much better than Nero in my opinion, and I would have rather just played through the whole game with him.
All in all, DMC4 is the pure, unadulterated power fantasy that we’ve come to love about the series. It might not be quite as good as DMC3, ad it doesn’t have the ridiculously amazing combat of the reboot DMC: Devil May Cry, but you still can’t go wrong with DMC 4 if you’re looking for a good looking hack n slash game to lose yourself in.

It's an action-packed, testosterone-fueled game.  Most of the time it gives an impression that it's an horror game due to its creepy atmosphere and level design.  That is, until the monsters show up and the music amps it up in several levels.  It's a horror game alright. but's in the opposite perspective.  It's you, the player, who is the horror in this game.
As far as mechanics go, it's quite surprising that several combos can be done in only a single button.  It's all the matter of timing and precision in order to be able to pull these combos off.  Before I started getting this game I've been hearing that Devil May Cry is a masher's game.  There's a lot of mashing alright, but the rewards are higher if the presses are timed properly.
As for the stages, it's pretty straightforward and the "puzzle" elements are more into proper timing of using the Devil Bringer than anything else.  Some design flaws like bad camera angles can make the game more difficult than it should be.   I'll be updating this once I get to play more missions and unlock other characters.
Overall, the game is fun and it's a good respite from games that you take seriously, particularly the competitive ones.

8/10 An Unfinished Masterpiece
Let's get this out of the way: This has the best combat I've ever seen in an action game, even better than my favorite action game, Devil May Cry 3. I like playing as Nero. I think what other people have categorized as whininess, I categorize as having a character and humanity other than pure snark. His combat is unique from Dante's, and I enjoyed every second of this game.
Why 8/10? Because, as great as Nero is, he sure isn't Dante. You do get to play as Dante, but only for 8 missions, all of them backtracking and featuring the same bosses that Nero fought. And all of these bosses feel weird when fought with Dante, as they're all built around Nero's moveset. And Dante's combat has received a huge upgrade from the greatest action game ever with the much needed ability to switch styles at will! It's great that he's in here, but it feels like such a fully featured playable character had much more unique content planned for him than none at all! I'm convinced that he did, and they ran out of time to build more than just a handful of stages to be recycled over 20 missions.
This makes the DmC reboot so tragic. I actually like it a lot, and Ninja Theory made one of my favorite games: Enslaved. But Devil May Cry was far from stale enough to deserve a reboot. 4 entries (3 of them the most solid actioners you can find) was far from the milked bone dry state of Resident Evil. But if they progressed with Dante as the main character of a true Devil May Cry 5, imagine the sheer awesomeness that would unfold!
One thing to note is the high quality of this PC port. I'm running a laptop with no dedicated graphics card, so I'm pretty used to low-to-mid settings and 30-40 FPS. Imagine my surprise when a Japanese console game gets 60 FPS on max settings, all the time. I've never seen something so well optimized besides maybe Half-Life 2. This game looks amazing, and it makes me wonder why Ubisoft games that look nowhere near as good require triple the horsepower. Maybe Capcom felt sorry for the horrible state of DMC3 PC, so they made this as good of a port as possible. Really impressive.
The graphics are amazing. My only gripe is a small one, about very large ones. Seriously, you Japanese pervs. Boobs do not behave in that way!
I highly recommend Devil May Cry 4, but not as much as I would if the game were built around Dante.

Really fun old-school point and click game. And by "old-school" I mean it is appaently a remaster of the original game released in 2005.
Yep. It is a 12 year old game. So don't expect it to run well on a PCMasterRace Windows 10 Beast rig with a 21:9 or 4k multiple monitor set up.
It runs great on a Windows 7 toaster. Which actualy surprised me, being that it was developed for Windows 2000, Windows XP. I did not need to set Win 7 to XP compatibility, but newer rigs than my 6 year old one may need to run the game in XP compatibility mode. The game does not have settings to adjust like modern, next-gen games. Because the game was developed in the early 2000's.  When most computers were so similar, they were not needed. So, stop complaining if you can't get it to run well on your $6000 Beast Rig. The game was made to play on Legacy machines.
That all said, the graphics show their age, but for gamers from "way-back-when", they were an amusing, colorful trip back in time. For me, at least. A classic point and click game from a decade+ ago.  When many Steam gamers were still toddlers. Or not even a sparkle in their parents' eyes yet.
Great humor and music from back then, may be over the heads of younger folks who aren't too familiar with how things were back in the 90's and early turn of the cnetury. Older gamers will *hopefully* appreciate the feeling of playing a game from our "younger" days. (I was 39 when this game first came out, lol!)
It won't impress you with anything new, it isn't going to be like playing a newer next-gen game. But it is quirky, charming, bright, colorful, casual, and amusing for some of us "old fogies". At the time of this review, it is 90% off. If you play on a toaster, and have a few (or more) grey hairs, I think it is something you shuld get, just for the nostalgia and chuckles.
For you kids... yeah, yeah. It has Trading Cards, but no achievements. The Trading Cards are currently listed on the Market at prices far higher than they are worth. You won't make profit, if that's all you are looking to do.
I thoroughly enjoyed it. Your Milage May Vary. Widely.

Magic Potion Destroyer is a much refined version of Magic Potion Explorer, though depending on your perspective the games' style might be too dissimilar for this to be true. Regardless, while Magic Potion Explorer was more of an idle game, Magic Potion Destroyer is more hands-on.
The other review here is pretty spot-on as to why that is, so I'll instead just say this makes Magic Potion Destroyer a much more involved experience - you really need to juggle those stats and know when to end a run, so that you can progress as much as possible in the shortest amount of time possible. It's way too easy to get suckered into reaching Wave 100, and at first it'll be near impossible without spending ungodly amounts of time on a stage, but at the same time each cleared wave gives you one point to spend on drinking potions which raise your stats by a ton.
It's still a somewhat idle game as is par for the series, so you might want to play this one while keeping an eye on the TV or something.

I personally like Magic Potion Destroyer after playing it for awhile, I like how the game flows, and while it definitely starts slow, from the 2nd stage on it begins to pick up and starts to feel very fun! I've begun playing it for some videos, so you can check those out here! :)
Magic Potion Destroyer is a sort-of Auto Battler where you fight waves on a stage by stage basis, fighting tougher enemies until either you reach wave 100 or you clear the stage by using a certain spell which requires a certain amount of MP depending on the stage. You use MP you gain through battling to purchase upgrades for that stage and strengthen your character, but it all goes away after clearing the stage.
Though there is a form of permanent progression in the form of Potions that you unlock by fulfilling various requirements, like clearing stages or reaching certain levels of stats, and you unlock Dose Points to equip potions with by pushing to the furthest wave you can on every level. The potions are extremely potent and can easily change how easy/hard your game is based on what you have equipped, like Double Max HP/MP, Double Attack/Regen, MP gained multiplier increase when you increase your Max MP, and Elemental Attacks.
Da Moosic is also vurry good. 8/10
I'm not extremely far into it (currently at stage 9), but I've greatly enjoyed progressing and going back to clear wave 100 on older stages. Overall I would definitely give this a positive, though I could imagine if the game had too many stages, the repetitive nature could become boring, though I think the in game speed ups of animations help this perhaps.

Alright kids, uncle Mexican is gonna tell ya somethin'. I am a max level forsaken class and this game has got to be one of my favorite fighters. The combat system is so unique and flexable and gives loads for creativity within your playstyle and generally what you want to do. The story isn't the longest, but it doesn't actually take away from the game too much. Almost everything about the fighting is satisfying. Every hit, every dodge, every parry is so good to get and the flow of the game is fantastic. Nothing feels overpowered and it's mostly based off of reaction and reading opponents. Every fight is a new experience, literally, because everyone has their own quirky style so for the most part, it doesn't get old. For some problems, the server issue has been funky and not the most stable, but is getting better by the day. There is a grind feel that the deveolopers very strongly show. Just about every move must be learned which takes some time and dedication. If you find someone with a school however, you can join and use the school moveset to get an advantage. You can also learn abilities earlier on by staying in a school. This game is great, and should only get better with time and I strongly suggest you pick it up. For the price, it's definetly worth it.

Note, this is coming from someone who hasn't played many fighting games.
Cons:
- Still glitchy, still server issues.
- Small dev team to fix issues and provide new content
- Limited gameplay. It's a game about fighting others and it doesn't offer much else.
Pros:
- Fun. I figured I'd be bored by now, but learning combat moves, trying different combat decks, and learning how to go against different opponents really keeps your attention.
- There's a lot of room to adapt against an opponent. I originally was annoyed when I got placed against an opponent much more experienced than I, but then one of those experienced players stayed around for a few rematches, and that's when I really enjoyed this game. It became my goal to kill him just once and I eventually did; I did well enough for him to change things up on me a few times, so it took a while.
- I can really see schools / dojos working in this game, with a really good player not only sharing his move deck with players, but teaching them to play. And that's what's great about this game; there's not only so much to learn, but there's also so much to teach. It's a game where a good player can have fun teaching casual strangers, and casual strangers can have fun against an overwhelming opponent.
Hold-Ups:
- Some people will like this game right away, but for others, know that the developers have promissed to continue improving the game. At the moment, I think the game is worth between the actual $30 and a $15 price tag, depending on how much fun an individual has in it. If the developers deliver on new content and continue to do so, I'll happily change that to being worth the full price tag for most people.

After 18 hours of play time, I can safely say this is the best $35 I have ever spent on Pre-ordering a game. The story is a little short but the way the decks are customizable makes this game go to into a whole new personal level. I have not unlocked even 2/3 of the total amount of moves yet and there is still a lot more customization I can add to my deck. Over all, I highly recommend this game. If you do but it does not give up in the first 2 hours keep playing and see how much more fun and challenging this gets!

I really do like this game, and want it to succeed.  That said, there are some problems that need to be adressed.
After having played the game to completion a couple times now, with more time under my belt,and in endgame (I think), I feel more equiped to make my case not not buy. The loading screens have been almost completely taken care of thanks to the devs, so that's not my point anymore. Unfortunately, it's something more to the core of the game, and what keeps people coming back to play again and again. Content.
As I said in my previous review, I love the looks of the game. I love the combat, the progression, and even what little story there is. It has it's own special tone that the relaxing music in the background helps to achieve, and the customization has me constantly wanting to make improvements to my combat deck. The game even has a low cost of just 30 bucks, incredible value these days, with most new games being 60 or more, with no sense of refinement. This game has it's own feel and place in the market, and does something truly different from all other fighting games. Totally worth a look.
With all that said, however, it just isn't enough. Having beaten the main story, grinded in 1v1 PvP to combat level 60, and beaten T3 final boss, I have to say I'm looking for a reason to keep playing this game. I guess I could go farm a couple enemies to get ALL the moves, but I already have the vast majority, and my deck feels fine without that one drunken sword move. I have plenty of clothing from pvp drops, so I don't really feel the need to grind for more of that. Which brings us to the final reason to keep playing: PvP.
Now don't get me wrong; I like fighting people with their own decks and playstyles, but if there's no real reason or reward other than, 'that one piece of clothing you never actually wanted,' or just to tell the other person 'I won, git gud scrub' I just don't know if it's worth it. My experience has been mostly good, with just a few frustrating match ups, due only to the opponent's deck being almost counter to mine.(good on them) But it had very little sense of meaning or purpose other than getting to level 60 to finally beat Risryn. It just feels a bit like running in a circle.
Now I know that this may seem bit too negative, since the dev team was so small, yet did so much. I don't want you to think this is a bad game, because it's not; it just isn't complete yet. As it stands the endless PvP just doesn't feel rewarding enough to keep me playing for more than half an hour. If you actually managed to read this far, I thank you for your 5 min. You will never get it back :)

I good start, a fantastic theme, and it was exciting when it came seemingly out of the blue with a very responsable use of computing resources for it's time achieving a really good look.
Sadly by now it's probably just run it's coarse, and this is a cautionary tale in it's self about how much one should spend extendedly into the life of a game with this kind of payment model, and more so when the focuse is PvP and nothing but. So how could've all this gone better? Well, lets go over some thoughts.
Games like this need to keep feeling fresh, giving people something new to do or at least to see thinking they're doing something new. When you finally stop doing regular updates of content for this sort, it's like when a shopping mall loses it's last food place. You know things are not doing well, you know you lost the coming content you crave that keeps you going between even bigger things, and then even what you have starts to leave. You know, like customers and even the keeping shops, aka the other customers that keep the other customers coming in themselves.
Lets face it, part of what keeps these free to play models going is that they allow for people to volonteer themselves as foder for those who spent money to catch up on some of this gear. No new content, more people get the same gear, and less creatively new feeling things to try, so the big boys leave and the newer kids as they both lose the symboitic relationships that keep players playing further.
That goes well into the point of less people playing, less people to make money from, and the buzz is gone. Why? Well, there's not much of an experience for a game that's multi player only with no campaign or focused PVE content.
With that said it's not like this game could NEVER do something again. The answers are actually staring them right there in the face, hell, even OVERWATCH tells some lessons on this, because even OVERWATCH, a game that ptiches as a pure hero multi player shooter, even though it's not the first to do it, they're often credited for such, well even they have co op events. Giving people an objective beyond just killing fellow players. It changes the experience.
And all the more, co op, PVE, making MISSIONS, could very well save the game. The universe is fantastic looking. Sci fi is in, some good writing can add a lot of purpose, as can people's imagination when you give them fuel to do it. Missions, Co Op for people to KNOW they have something to do with the game even when others run off, new things to see and experience, even prompt your community to make some writing adventures sharing their experiences. There is a LOT that could be done here. Overwatch showed how powerful it's simple little story on the side, with hints durring game play, can make a huge bolstering move for it's community, and so people are all the more invested as they build their own story to charachters as these dialog and other hints in stages continue to push the lore, and then they further push that with these CO OP events.
I will mention PvE and Co Op time and time again because it's a lesson that one, should've been learned by now, two, something we shouldn't have abandoend to simply feed off of PvP alone to be fueld by natural instinct of mutual irradication to be E sport pro. It's over saturated, and you can still go for it, but it shouldn't be the ONLY thing you go for and do. As a video game, you can be many things, and you should realize there's more than being a tool for competition when everyone else is doing it too, and has all the more backing and resources. A lot of these games with their newest age graphics, to show someone something new, it's a crutch. A powerful crutch, but it's not what keeps things going as new visuals and graphical power comes.
This game has some great art design for it's ideal, it should be pushed, the theme can be grown, give missions to let people know there's game to be played even without all their friends on other games. Either way, it needs content, a game like this can't just sit there without more content and survive. When you're a free to play model, that's blatantly the name of the game.
For all that is good here, it's indeed feeling kind of obvious that the team is coasting now. Not putting new work in, just collecting on what can be collected by keeping it up and running till it further burns down, and it's very much in those late ashes.

Darwinia is one of my favourites. Your goal is to conquer 10 maps, and you can do it at your own pace, which is unique for a real-time strategy game. It's also forgiving, if one strategy doesn't work out, you can try another one. I've played it thrice, each iteration took me about 20 hours (though you may be able to do it quicker).
The game has a very nice storyline, dealing with artificial intelligence, and seems to pay homage to Sir Clive Sinclair, a British entrepreneur and visionary who created the ZX Spectrum home computer in the 1980s, without explicitly mentioning his name.
The game is relatively old, I got my first copy in 2005. (Tidbit: Darwinia was also released on Steam in 2005, as one of the first 3rd-party games. While Mac OS X and Linux version of Darwinia existed since 2005, it took Valve till 2010 to release a OS X client, and till 2013 to release a Linux client).

Virus busting simulator to the max. You are a hacker who helps an awesome informatic doctor who created Darwinia and has viruses everywhere on his world. With the simple programs he gives to you, you can control them directly and bust viruses as you upgrade the researches you have and what you have found.
Introversion Software is best for their technologic indie games such as Uplink, DEFCON and the newer game Prison Architect, which instead it bases off the daily prison life. Consider getting this game and the other games by Introversion for your maximum enjoyment.
Story: 10/10 - The story is intense and quite heartwarming, the writing of the story is best having a story about the Darwinians and its locations are different. There's also a Prologue level in where you can get to be teached how to play.
Controls: 8/10 - The controls for the game are well-prepared, but sometimes when you get to move with holding your cursor you'd sometimes get swapped off with another unit. But its use of Keyboard & Mouse controls are good enough the same.
Graphics: 10/10 - From what i have saw, this game makes clever use of pixellated shaders for the unit models (Squad, Engineers, enemies, etc.) and aswell the 2d sprite entities of the Darwinians. Their frame rate of the model turnings have a excellent take, the HUD looks like as a futuristic PSX game design and it reminds me if this game was made in the 1990s with great graphics.
Music: 9/10 - It has some music, and it is especially intended for cutscenes. None music is intended to work when you play the game, as to face with the atmosphere of the 1980s technology setting. But in the intros you'd laugh that some are took from the amiga cracktros for the cracktro-styled intros. I have even heard one which is a remix to Thunder Cross by Konami, a obscure space shooter arcade game.
Gameplay: 9/10 - It has a different genre of strategy in this game, you can find research cubes in some of the locations to obtain more stuff such as more weapons for your Squads, new units, and more. Sadly, you have few units like Squad, Engineers and Officers for the Darwinians, but it's good the same because it would be ridiculous to have like a team of different units. :P
Total: 4.6/5
You might also check out Multiwinia, the multiplayer-driven sequel to Darwinia. It has the same gameplay but with 6 different game modes for greater enjoyment with your friends. ;)

I first saw this game in 2005, after someone told me there is an RTS with decent looks which only weights 1.5MB. Indeed it was so small, due to absence of textures and usage of "procedurally generated" graphics or something instead, which look stylish and very original. Unfortunately my experience at that time ended right in the first mission because I didn't know how to complete it and the "help" system gave no clues.
10 years later, in 2015 I got this game inside a bundle together with Prison Architect from the same dev (Prison Architect is a very good game btw). So, now, again, I almost got stuck in the 1st mission. Luckily I then guessed that you need to capture some satellite dishes (or something, the graphics are pretty low-polygonal) by placing an engineer next to it. And to go to a different island - since you can't send squads there because they don't walk over water - you need to delete a squad, then create a new one near a satellite dish on a different island. And - engineers walk over water and get to that dish... ok. This time I completed the first mission and got stuck in the second one because I don't know how to transport a flock of darwinians over water. And I ran out of patience because it took me half an hour to guess why red snakes keeps respawning (you need to kill a big red egg-laying spider with grenades or something - normal shots don't seem to hit it? the presentation was very unclear). That basically sums up my experience with the game.
Pros:
- great unique graphical style
- pleasing music
- nice intro scenes at the beginning of the game (one of them is a "game of life" simulation well-known to programmers and mathematicians; another says the game was cracked by a hacker which it's not since I got it on Steam..)
- intriguing story
Cons:
- terrible tutorial, nothing is explained -> which alone makes the game unplayable for the vast majority of players and would actually make this game worth 0/10. Yet, judging from other reviews, also ones I read on professional websites, I still think that's it's me who is dumb and there is tons of gameplay which I wasn't patient/clever enough to get to. I'm pretty damn sure I represent the majority though
- non-existent pathfinding (basically, units can only walk in straight lines, and if there is something in the way which they can't walk thru - they will keep pushing into that obstacle forever)
- awkward camera system, with mouse wheel zooming in/out working in reverse (!), with no way to reconfigure that
- unique but awkward unit selection/creation/ordering/combat system
- units walk too slow over huge landscapes, no way to speed up the game
- no save/reload
Overall, this game is more of "look how much we can stuff into 1.5MB" rather than a product for real people. I doubt they even tested this game on anyone outside their office. If you get it in a bundle for $1 or less - fine, it's worth a look for its originality. But most likely you won't be able to play it due to the described issues.

Still in early access, but they seem to be making pretty good progress with it.
The progression (Campaign) is already in the game a bit and takes the form of running what amount to skirmish missions (Kill or route the enemy team with some optional objectives) with story missions placed in that you have to run skirmish missions to rank up for.
The game is a tactical RPG, instead of both sides taking turns, each unit has an "initiative" score that determines when it is it's turn to move.
Movement is free flowing and controlled by WASD keys. You can move a certain amount of points in any direction, with unlimited backtracking (As long as you aren't overwatched/ambushed/trapped) until you confirm the movement
A loot system is within the game, and before and after each battle, you will need to deal with the warbands equipment and stats/skills.
The setting is pretty neat, it takes place within an Empire city that was destroyed by a Chaos meteor that has strewn valuable Warpstones all over the city.
Each of the current 4 warbands has a neat play-style and reason for being within Mordheim.
Sisters of Sigmar: Heavily armored nuns that lack ranged weaponry. They are trying to purge the city and destroy the Warpstone.
Reiklander Mercenaries: Medium to heavy armored humans that have an abundance of ranged weaponry. They are trying to collect the warpstone to sell to other Human nations.
Cult of the Possessed: Mutants and Demons that are fairly medium to heavily armored, they lack good ranged weaponry, but make up for it with a variety of neat mutations and mechanics. They are trying to collect all the Warpstone to appease their god.
Skaven douches: Light armored mostly, dodge everything, and moves all the ♥♥♥♥ing time. They want the warpstone cause they are greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s or something.
The persistent injury system is very unique, a unit going down in a battle is not the end of the world, and very easy to recover from. Often they may not even die, but can be effected by a variety of injuries that alter the way they play.
And example is my Chaos Magistrate who originally started out as a caster...well..a blow to the head has convinced him he is actually a god, and only ever uses melee weapons now...thought I should fire him, but damn, he is making it work.
Any-who, I enjoy the game.

To properly review this game I think it's worth that I explain  a situation that occurred in one of my latest games as Sisters of Sigmar. My warband was battered during a story mission and I was certain I would lose the battle and pay dearly with tonnes of injuries, probably ending my run as this warband. Instead the Mercenary Ogre who was about to kill the VIP I had to keep alive missed three time in a row against her whilst she was stunned. The level 0 henchman Novice I had with her managed to land a critical hit, stunning the ogre, which led to my spellcaster calling a comet down from the sky and crushing the ogre where he stood, winning the battle for me.
Now, this game is a beta. Like all betas, it comes with the "don't buy if you rage easily at faults only a game can do." Case in point: three quarters of my game time so far has been with my Mercenary Warband. I go into their fourth story mission and the games bugs out, the enemy I was facing never ends its turn, probably a unit I cannot see moving about  endlessly trying to reach one of my guys. I was forced to abandon the mission, and all of my warband was injured. All three of my heroes died, two archers lost their arms and would have to be fired, and my leader became a simpleton. Needless to say, I wasn't too pleased.
Despite this, the game is immensely fun and satisfying if you can get over its rocky starting out phase. The interface tells you nothing on the surface when in-game, requiring you to be out in warband management or to go into a seperate menu to find out what "Righteous Fury" actually does and why it always misses. The payment and treatment system gets in the way a bit too, you will often be forced to fire and replace henchmen and heroes to keep your warband at fighting strength. However this can often be wasteful, the game seems to force you to pay for treatment and upkeep before you can fire any warrior in the warband, which seems utterly bizarre to me.
Despite these negatives, the game shines on premise alone. The way characters are controlled is similar to turn based tactics games like Valkyria Chronicles. With the RPG elements of the tabletop Warhammer Fantasy Battles game, like the original board game was intended to be based around. The amount of customisation, stat variance, spells, skills, weapons, armours and trinkets in the game at present allow you to make your warband however you desire. This makes for some great innovation as people try to find the best possible set ups for your heroes and henchmen, but due to the diverse choice of loadouts, you can very easily counter these "metas" of soldiers should you want to play online.
Multiplayer is not why you will buy this game mind you, the game's AI is not stupid, but can be exploited once you have figured out pathing, who it will target, etc. You will often find times when your spellcaster is near to death and hide them behind a shieldwall of heroes, and the AI will sooner run the length of the map for another attempt at that spellcaster than fight into your men. Ledges and cliffs are often exploitable too. Sisters of Sigmar come with no ranged weapons besides their spells, and the AI will refuse to use shortcuts like climbing and leaping, this results in very easy missions that are labelled "brutal" just because you stacked 5 archers on a cliff and put your captain and hero with a high parry chance in the way of the stairs up, leading to a Turkey shoot for your men.
Overall, I would say this game has btrought me hours of fun already. I've been frustrated with how the game can♥♥♥♥♥♥you over sometimes, but that's just how these games go. XCOM fans who enjoy the iron man difficulties will find a passioniate love for this game. As it takes XCOM's "lose a man and that's it" style of gameplay and turns it up to eleven, with a whole host of mental and physical injuries that can steal your level 7 Champion from you in the blink of an eye. Needless to say, I do love this game.

PROS:
+ Good story.

+ Loveable characters.
+ Nicely modeled cars and weapons.

CONS:
- Very linear.
- No sidequests.
- Checkpoints are few and far between.
- Due to there only being three radio stations, music can get repetitive.
- Lots and lots of driving with no fast travel.
- The Wanted Posters are a pain to collect.
- Achivements that require you to have two of the DLC packs.
- No multiplayer (something like what GTA5 has would have been nice.)
- Due to events in the story, you constanly lose all your guns, some of which you spend your own money to buy.
- Civilian Driver AI is terrible and will constanly swerve into you, which in turn makes the police come after you.
- There were some glitches that happened due to me skipping cutscenes too quickly that ended up with me being stuck in the floor and unable to move, leading to me having to restart the chapter.
- Cliff hanger ending.
----------------------------
Although it may seem like I gave it a lot of cons, which I did, I still adore it. I like how I can mow down a crowd of civilians but Joe will still get mad at me for running a red light.

First of all, let me be clear--IMO all positive and negative reviews on Steam stand CORRECT. Yes, this game is just as good as people claimed, and as aweful as some have criticized.
Skip to the end for TL;DR
This game is the bad brother of ARMA, but good enough to truly realize what CoD MW1 could have been on a next level of size, depth, and lethality. And I think a few things should be covered so that those who read on will know what to expect. note* I still have not dived myself into mission editor and not enough players for PvP, so no comments on these.
Missions--Campaign is similar to CoD, the missions do cover some of the most basic of types: ambush, night raid, charge and hold town, diversionary strike (support)...etc. Each mission would be a blend of these, so expect some time to be invested, especially if you do take things carefully. These missions are quite standard and relatable to what most contemporary armies would do, and yet both CoD and newer Battlefield doesn't quite capture the size and freedom that OFDR offers. The enemy do go on a patrol path, with another patrol that overlaps to provide constant oversight. It is a very reasonable design that challenges one to think "how can i approach this defense before 12 men start stacking grenades on me?" I truly appreciate this design work, but more on that on the AI behaviour.
Size/Gunplay--Since this game is loosely similar to ARMA, semi-open world travel is a key feature. All missions range from medium to large area of terrain. players must travel most of the time on foot to get to objectives. Luckily, the designers have put enough enemies along reasonable key points, hilltops with machine gun nests, and ammo crates to make things more interesting. Pick you routes, plan ahead, use your binoculars to SEE WHERE THINGS ARE, and proceed to walk your own path. No restirctions other than enemy fire, and you will be ambushed if you make a bad move.
See the issue is that camoflage in this game works. I am both impressed and traumatized at how enemies can sneak right into your face and shoot your at point blank range. And that is because there is no minimap, no Friend/Foe tags (need this more in shooters), and the bushes are such a well blend of colours especially if the graphics are set to low.
While this game is not as hardcore on the simulation side, the sway of the gun when moving, lack of jumping mechanics, and recoil system does give a very hard time to aim, if only I can see. While this may turn some of you away (door on the right, please help yourself), I certainly loved it because i actually felt like firing a gun for the 1st time. Granted, I still have yet tried ARMA 2, but at least OFDR gave me my first time. Taking the stinger from your shoulder also requires loading time, cuz no one ever puts an explosive near their head during bullet fights (do these things blow? if anyone knows plz inform), nd the same goes for putting it back on the shoulder.
And to fellow soldiers: please LOOK, then DO. if you don't know what to DO, stop and don't panic, LOOK MORE.
AI--their designs can go from baffilngly stupid to insane manhunt machines. They will duck if suppressed, alert if bullets fly by, flee if crushed, and will run a circle to catch you in the back 10min later. They will always spot novice players (like me) before you even see their muzzle flash. And yet, AI teammates will also stand in one spot and receive grenades while you, the leader, try to heal yourself. Im not too experienced in AI mechaincs, so I can't give a full analysis, but just bear in mind that they are very good shots over 300m+, your health doesn't count much across the various difficulties, and they will nail you when given the chance. Try to keep moving in unpredictable directions and keep far away from imminent danger; works alright for me.
Multiplayer--please, for the love of God, either hate it and don't play it; love it and Google how to fix it. There are pinned Steam forum posts on how easy it is to register and setup Tunngle. No knowledge on hosting servers, just install, launch and login, find the right OFDR server, and all your friends will be in the same public room. one of you host a LAN game, and everyone just jump in. My experience with coop is delightful--me and my bud had so much fun killing fellow PLA soldiers, getting bullet skinned by PLA soldiers, sneaking around in forests, and hiding behind bushes while the magnificent AI takes care of the rest. Think that says enough?
Guns/Characters/Vehicles--When entering coop and single playergames, you get pre-assigned by the game to a 4-men squad. The only thing you can choose is class: stand. rifleman, Spec Ops rifleman, grenadier, engineer (explosives), AT,  sniper, medic, and squad automatic. It covers most classes like Battlefield, but no weapon choices like Battlefield. Quite sad, but I guess Defense budget got cut again. The first player/host will always have to be team leader, thus limiting player weapon choices even further. Luckily enemies do drop standardized weapons from the PLA side, and you can use that method to switch weapons if no ammo crates in the vaccinity.
Vehicle numbers and types are also very much lacking: jeeps, APCs, ENEMY tanks, choppers. This is a major disadvantage for OFDR, and I will not smooth this one because it is just that lackluster. Also, since Codemasters have quite deserted this game, it is ironic that the very 1st original OF (later ARMA CWC) has more available mods than this game. Shame...
Conclusion--I LOVED this game. My AMD HD6450 can actually run this pretty smooth at 900p (windowed), I had hours of blast on coop with my buddy, and completing the missions are actually a worthwhile experience. I am a diehard coop fan, and this FPS has provided me with enough assets to make a game challenging, walk a whole lot, plan ahead, fail my plan miserably, and try new ways at how to deal with crazy AIs.
As for others, please don't buy if the gun sway, heavy recoil is not your type; I understand, after all every boy wants to be laser-aimbot spec Ops. Also, this not not truly open world, lacks modding, very little ingame assets, and bascially no LAN players unless you have friend(s). Since Tunngle is basically hazzle free, please no further b*tching on that, or just be honets about how much you hate CodeMasters, which I won't mind.

Kingdom is a triumph in minimalistic but brilliant design that's both dripping with atmosphere and an absolute joy to play. Make sure you get it with the New Lands expansion and prepare lots of coffee, food and a stress ball.
The goal is simple, you play as a monarch to gather resources, hire followers, build and expand your kingdom, then repair the boat to get off the island in conquest of new lands.
This game has one of the best and intuitive UI design I've seen in a while. Every interaction is done with only three keys but don't be fooled by its simplistic design. The mechanics are very tight and beneath it are many little layered elements that you only notice as you play the game through over and over again, but that's where the game really shines.
The game throws you right into it at the start with a very basic tutorial. Not much will be revealed at first but that's the beauty of it. Unlike other rogue-like survival games where you get a little stronger with each playthrough, the focus in Kingdom is more of gained knowledge and experience.
With every playthrough, you learn more and more about the finer details and subtle cues to help you survive each island. I highly suggest NOT consulting a FAQ when playing this game for the first few times and just make your own mistakes to slowly peel away the layers for yourself.
Replayability comes in the form of unlocks which change how you play the game and since the land is semi-procedurally generated, it's up to you to adapt and manage your resources. Timing is very important in this game and there is no undo function to every command you make, so plan properly as even a poorly placed tree chop can spell the death of all your builders.
Get this game. It's sublime.

While I myself haven't played it in a while (I have more hours put into the original than this version since I started playing well before this came out), I can still recommend this game to fans of tower defense or base management games. It has one of the simplest yet most effective control setups (only uses 3 buttons for movement and interaction) and the gameplay mechanics are very easy to understand. The only thing you need to remember is that you need enough gold, and that's that. No advanced combat mechanics. No deep array of classes or powers to memorize. Just the need of gold to upgrade and purchase buildings and units, and learning how to effectively spend that gold to guarantee success.
I will also say that this sprite work is gorgeous, and the ambient sounds and music really help emerse you into the game, so those looking for a game to relax to may find enjoyment with this too.

This game manages to combine easygoing input (just 1/2 buttons + directional input) with some nice strategic depth. Other big plusses are the immersive atmosphere, the music/audio, and the way in which all the gameplay elements combine perfectly.
I always play this game if I don't really feel like doing anything else, because somehow it's always challenging enough, without being too complex.
Also, +1 for the original concept of being an RTS that you control through an ingame character. I know very few games similar to this!

Game is always a joy to return to.
Essentially it's a city-builder with elements of surviving. Your goal is to last as long as you can, all while trying to progress to new 'Islands' [Levels] in means of experiencing a harder challange.
The game will take a few runs to get the hang of, but once you understand how gold works, which direction the enemies are coming from the most, and where to build up your defenses? You want to keep going, over and over again.
Might I add, the visuals and music for this game are stunning. The way the reflections work off of the water, the sky, the various weather-conditions from fog to rain... it makes it truly feel like you're progressing your kingdom through a series of patches.
Yes, the game has its problems, with confusing AI and all of that, but I feel once you understand the true core of the game and how it works, you can easily play around that and have yourself a worthwhile experience.
Highly recommend it, and overly recommend it when and if it goes on sale.

2016 Update: Game is in stasis as the lead dev is now alone on the team and is looking for help to continue the project.
TLDR; game has one awesome ship builder and ship workshop collection that lets you pit your builds against other player made ships you add to the game (PvE, not PvP), but not much else in the way of features. It has given me over two hundred hours of playtime, which when compared to my playtime on bigger titles, makes me feel that it was still worth my money despite my disappointment that further development did not continue.
---
Warning #1: If building ships and then flying them is not your thing and you're looking for a more linear/on-rails type of game, then this is probably not your thing.
Warning #2: This is not a space dogfighting simulator or a replacement for Star Citizen.
Warning #3: This will let you build a great many types of ships and then fight in them. Don't expect much else. Due to the lack of other games that let you do this as extensively as KV does, I will still recommend this game despite many of the flaws. Edit: I have Starmade and my playtime on it versus this game should tell you what I prefer.
Warning #4: Get player made ships off the Workshop. Seriously. It is not modding per se but more an intended aspect of the game. Pit your designs against that of other players and all in all make the galaxy a much more varied and interesting place. :D
---
Disclaimer: I see a lot of bitterness from people who were following the game for a long time, so I should say that though I was following it, my own purchase was recent and I am free of any negative bias or expectation in that context. I was never a backer. My review should help new people looking for a different sort of space game experience.
---
The 'Build' here means the ability to build your own ships. As far as I know (so far) you can only build your own ship, not structures or anything else.
The 'Battle' is you against everything else. I have seen no sign of being able to have NPC allied ships under your control in a 'fleet' (so far).
The 'Explore' depends on how big you make the starting universe. However, it's only space travel. I don't believe there is any planet landing involved. Edit: However, you can enter the atmosphere of the planet and fly over the surface. Devs plan on bringing in working cities and such on the surface and possible even space to ground/ground to space exchange of fire. :-D
---
Early hours impressions: having a blast making ships! :D
Yet to actually leave the shipyard. WIll update as I play more~!
===
Update #1 (12/7/2014): I have left the shipyard and blown up my first space pirates. Hmmm, I think my ship's too strong.
Essential impression: This game is basically the developers providing you with the tools to start your adventure. How you want it to be will depend on you, it seems. For example, I made my ship too strong so wiped out enemies without feeling like I was in any danger. Unfortunately, it's impossible to assess what I can do to have a fun experience at this point. Work need to be done to give some cues to players to be able to intuitively assess how strong they are compared to enemies, etc.
There appears to be a lot more to this game, and I've barely begun to scratch the surface. Still would recommend at this point.
Update #1.5 (12/7/2014; later in the day): found strong enemies. Almost died. Fun fun. Seems the preparation a.k.a. building your ship is 95% of the fight. If I hadn't built my shape they way I had (out of pure dumb luck) I would've died. Me gusta...
Again, no real way to assess what can happen. You could say this is more realistic. :-P
Also, The missions just scroll and don't seem to be tracked per se. Not sure I'm a fan of this system. Seemed weak.
Seriously huge annoyance when you are trying to crawl within range of the station to dock in a big ship... Maybe I'm missing something? The 'Warp to within 10' doesn't always work... I often end up 50+ away when warping to a station.
Update 2.0 (2/10/2015): still playing this game. Like I have said before, this game gives you the tools to make your own pew pew experience. Highly recommend getting fellow-player made ships and populating the galaxies you generate. Just subscribing will do. Meeting and then fighting said ships will let you pit your design against that of other people. Getting the workshop ships is, imo, essential to enjoying this game, and isn't 'modding' in any way but intended.

I really do like this game, and want it to succeed.  That said, there are some problems that need to be adressed.
After having played the game to completion a couple times now, with more time under my belt,and in endgame (I think), I feel more equiped to make my case not not buy. The loading screens have been almost completely taken care of thanks to the devs, so that's not my point anymore. Unfortunately, it's something more to the core of the game, and what keeps people coming back to play again and again. Content.
As I said in my previous review, I love the looks of the game. I love the combat, the progression, and even what little story there is. It has it's own special tone that the relaxing music in the background helps to achieve, and the customization has me constantly wanting to make improvements to my combat deck. The game even has a low cost of just 30 bucks, incredible value these days, with most new games being 60 or more, with no sense of refinement. This game has it's own feel and place in the market, and does something truly different from all other fighting games. Totally worth a look.
With all that said, however, it just isn't enough. Having beaten the main story, grinded in 1v1 PvP to combat level 60, and beaten T3 final boss, I have to say I'm looking for a reason to keep playing this game. I guess I could go farm a couple enemies to get ALL the moves, but I already have the vast majority, and my deck feels fine without that one drunken sword move. I have plenty of clothing from pvp drops, so I don't really feel the need to grind for more of that. Which brings us to the final reason to keep playing: PvP.
Now don't get me wrong; I like fighting people with their own decks and playstyles, but if there's no real reason or reward other than, 'that one piece of clothing you never actually wanted,' or just to tell the other person 'I won, git gud scrub' I just don't know if it's worth it. My experience has been mostly good, with just a few frustrating match ups, due only to the opponent's deck being almost counter to mine.(good on them) But it had very little sense of meaning or purpose other than getting to level 60 to finally beat Risryn. Kingdoms: New Lands is a 2D sidescroller with elegantly simple pixel art in which you play the leader of a small community under attack by monsters who want to steal all your stuff including, finally, the crown you wear as leader. By day you must gather resources to recruit and supply villagers and assign tasks to defend against the escalating waves of monsters that will attack when it grows dark. Your ultimate goal in New Lands is to clear a path to the coast and construct a ship to take the crown (and you) to safety. The game is a bit buggy, especially concerning the AI of your villagers; sometimes this can be fixed by saving and reloading your game, but often I have lost half a village because I assigned a tree to be cut down in an area that was then overrun by monsters. This is fairly normal for resource management games, and the fix I would recommend would to have in-game options to both unassign tasks (possibly by simply reaching up to grab the coin from it) and to reset the game state internally, maybe symbolized as the player/leader barking orders at their people. I find this game very addictive in the short term, but I suspect once I've hunted most of the achievements my interest will wain. Well worth the money.

You play as Vito Scaletta who's just returning home from the war. Vito finds out that his mother and sister is in debt. To make some quick cash, Vito asks his best friend Joe Barbaro who has mob connections.
Positives:
+ The story: Really engaging. Feels like you're watching a gangster movie.
+ The setting: Empire Bay is beautiful and has a real retro vibe. The city changes as you progress with the story.
+ Graphics: I'm playing in 2017 and i think its decent for a game released back in 2010.
+ Cars: Based on real vehicles of that time.
+ Sound: Great voice acting and hits from the 40s and 50s!
+ Playboy centerfolds!
+ Shootouts: Satisfying and very action packed!
+ The cops do their jobs! They bust you for speeding, fighting, carrying weapons, hit and runs. They report your license plate and give a description of you.
+ You run out of gas!
Negatives:
- No manual save.
- Most people wear the same type of clothes.
- Doesn't really feel open world.
- The game feels linear: You only have one mission at a time.
- Nothing much to do in the city.
- No real use for money other than upgrading your cars and buying drinks or suits.
- Can't ride the bus or a taxi.
- Certain buildings are accessible only during certain missions.
- No real reason to explore the city other than collecting wanted posters.
- Wish the cops bust you for beating the red light.
- Though you can die while driving, you're never thrown out of your car no matter how bad the crash.
- Can't go around the city after the ending. Continuing after the ending just takes you to the final shootout.
- Ending is too short.
- Enemy AI can be bad at times: You can just aim and wait for them to pop out.
Score: 7.8/10

This is a tough one. The original Operation Flashpoint GOTY game was one of the greatest 'realistic', tactical, sans-health bar FPS games of all time, with two fantastic expansions which both added huge amounts of content to the game (in much the same way Morrowind was improved by Tribunal and Bloodmoon) and a wonderful gameplay style that gave the game tremendous replayability and gave the player tremendous scope to imagine the world around them.
Of course, after that original title the companies that were responsible for the game split up - Bohemia Interactive making the ARMA series (eternally disapointing in kind of the same way Gothic was: just not refined, polished, bug-free or fun enough to match the technological ambition) and Codemasters making this game.
Dragon Rising was many years in the making, and while you can say that in certain ways it was a better shooter than the ARMA titles, you can say that it was nevertheless dissapointing and an inferior title to the original OpFlash in terms of how it contrasted with the titles already available.
If we are to compare this game with ARMA then you might say that the game is a bit more stable, the missions a bit more cinematic and well paced, the guns a bit more realistic and satisfying to use. These advantages are real and enjoyable, but none of them represent industry leading iterations of the features - the original OpFlash lead the industry in map size, replayability, freedom, difficulty (if you so desired) and scope, but Dragon Rising doesn't really set the world alight in any one way.
This does have to do with the bugs that, while not as annoying as in ARMA 2, for example, are still present. I once played a mission where a tank somehow got stuck to my soldier by an invisible, 10 meter pole. no kidding, I walked around the map with a many tonne tank spinning wildly ten meters above my head, smacking and clattering into the ground incessantly whenever I tried to get in a vehicle but, somewhat disapointingly, refusing to crush the squad mates that I tired to hard to splatter. Another time I had to give up on an entire playthrough as a certain mission bugged and was simply impossible to complete.
The zones are still big, the soliders still responsive to orders, the enemies still reasonably deadly, but the island of Skira fails to burst into life in the same way the original OpFlash island of Everon did, largely because the game is let down by instability and unconvincing scenarios. It is a huge shame that this game failed, and while some admirable advertising almost convinced me to give Red River a go it was apparently even worse than DR, and as such sadly I fear we must lay this game to rest.
I am reminded of the classic xBox shooter BLACK. Quite forgotten now, it had a really polished feel and really immersive, solid missions. It is perhaps where the ingredients that would have made Dragon Rising a really good game snuck off to.
I still recommend this game, because it is better than ARMA 2 for as long as it lasts before it bugs out, and it just has a better title, let's face it.

I don't even know how to get started with this game.
The story is totally cheesy over the top madness. You play as two demon hunters and guess what? You fight demons and save the world, big surprise. The story is narrated through unbelieveable cutscenes, where the characters get impaled and yet survive, do impossible stuff like deflecting bullets with other bullets, punch a giant stone wall into smithereens, transform a suitcase in a gunship and so on. Big explosions, action and stuff spiced up with crazy music. I was laughing hard during most of these cutscenes. The characters are totally crazy and over the top. There's this guy who wears a red coat and cowboy boots, who would get laughed out of any bar, that's totally crazy. The word is about to be destroyed and he acts all cocky and makes fun of his enemies. The dumbest hilarious cutscene involves him drawing a heart in a hell gate with blade-mines and then make it go boom, while flamenco music plays.
The music is terrific, loud and sang with a weird growling voice. The lyrics are beyond redemption and listening to some tracks would make any normal human being flee in terror, and its speed it's well known for causing tachycardia.
The gameplay is totally unrealistic. You have these two guys who wield swords as tall as they are and shoot unlimited bullets out of oversized guns. You can do physics defying stuff like launch an enemy in the air, follow it, swing your sword at it a few times, then hover on it showering it with bullets, then hit it some more, then kick its face a few times, plant a few blade-mines on it, then pull out a katana and slash it, then land in a crowd of enemies punching the ground causing an explosion and flip your shotgun at them like a nunchaku while shooting. On top of it, the action is so fast you can't really understand what's going on unless you're pro or someting.
There's this kid that's like the sheer power character. He can "act" his sword to make it ignite and spinning through the screen covered in fire, charge up gun shots to make groups of enemies explode and has the ability to execute high damaging grapples on foes. Than there's this other guys that has five "styles" that you can switch on the fly and every stile changes the function of your "style button" according to your equipped weapon. And speaking of weapons oh boy, this guy is a walking army, he has 3 melee weapons and 3 ranged ones and one of them has 4 normal firing modes. All of this stuff makes this guy incredibly complex to use. I mean, who needs all that variety? The combat system let's you pull out some infuriatingly complex combos if you are skilled enough but who cares?! Why can't I just spam Y and get SSS ranking?!

For almost daily streams of Mordheim and FAQ dialogue, catch my stream at
Mordheim: City of the Damnit will make you break your computer.  Your dice will always fail.  Your best fighter is gonna go down HARD in some of the most gut wrenching ways.  And after you piece the broken parts of your computer together, you will realize just how much you love it!
In Mordheim there is not just you and the opponent, there is you, the opponent, and the map.  If you are not careful, the map of Mordheim will slap you around (or help) and put an end to that uber strategy you were just gonna pull off.  The need to improvise, the need to make the best of a worst situation, these elements are actually fun.
"But how the hell can losing my characters in defeat be fun?!"  Glad ya asked.  See, if one of your characters goes down in a fight, they don't die, they do an injury check.  They could lose an eye, a leg, they could be rendered useless, or they may even have a "Near Death Experience" and gain extra XP!  Also, for every injury, a warrior recieves a negative rating on their overall rating meter that contributes to the strenght of your warband.  Long story short, if your rating meter is lowered on a specific warrior and that warrior does not lose a vital statistic (such as his Intelligence is harmed, meanwhile he is a Strength based warrior), the warrior just made your warband stronger.  Also, some injuries are just fun and they really add flavor and character to your mercenaries.
Every mode in the game feels incredibly distinct.  Such as, the random battles which fall underneath the catagories of "Capture the Flag, Wyrdstone Rush, and Marked for Death" are fun and exciting fast maps to play (relatively, battles can go upwards of 2 hours.)  Campaing maps are rich in story and objective and feel like a Dungeons and Dragons table top game brought to life.  On-line versus play is constantly being tweaked and perfected and strategy certainly helps.  It is VERY fast paced with options to have count down timers till the turn is ended for each player.  These times can be adjusted to fit your convenience.
And to touch on customization, this system is incerdibly deep, from the character progression skill trees to the ability to customize each individual body part skin on nearly every warrior and give custom color sets as well.
The amount of progress this game has had since the release of Blood Bowl 2 is staggering.  There are positives, there are negatives, but ultimately, this is a title that will please big fans of Final Fantasy Tactics, X Com, Disgaea, and Total War.
I feel like I only scratched the very very tip of the iceberg when talking about this game.  Again, please check out my stream for any and all questions, I love talking about Mordheim!

I purchased the early access game on Halloween after reading some pretty great sounding reviews. Just a little bit of background I don't write reviews on video games EVER as I haven't found any that stand out to me enough to warrant a review (please note I'm 21 and have been gaming since I was about 6). I am a fan of strategy games such as xcom, civ 5, galactic civ, Dawn of War 1 & 2. Mordheim as an early access game has already managed to push them out of my mind. It is challenging but not ridiculously like dark souls (which is important as at that level of challenging the game is no longer fun). I find myself attached to the characters on my team and worrying way more than I should about my characters surviving.
The things I love about this game
- Warband team style play offers customization for play style ergo you can use 1 hand weapons, 2 hand weapons, archers, magic all to your play style
- 2 resources gold and wyrdstones which can make for some extra complexity as you have to ensure you have enough of both otherwise you'll tick someone off (not enough gold and you can't pay for treatments or pay your soldiers not enough wyrdstones and you won't be able to make your quota to your employer)
- Have yet to find any really overpowered units. using 1 hand weapons for example you lose damage if you compare it to a 2 hand weapon but you gain dodge chance or you can equip a shield and be able to parry.
- Magic abilities have the chance to backfire or curse characters as you use it so you can't train your mage up to be as ***kicker and use him to kill the whole enemy team (atleast from what I've seen so far).
- It's only early access which means they are actually looking at reviews and bugs and game suggestions and actually fixing them and modifying the game so it can only go up from here!
Things that I feel should be addressed
- I say addressed as it's in early access still so most of these are just things that need to be tweaked as they're still working on the game.
- the percentages for tasks appear a little skewed to me. what I mean is I'll have a 75 percent chance to hit someone I'll attack them 4 times and miss all 4 times. This get's a little irritating when you have your havy hitter who has a big 2 handed weapons that does but loads of damage but can only attack once per turn and he constantly misses. Or when you are trying to climb a wall and you have a 70 percent chance and you use all of your moves falling and injuring your character who is wearing cloth armor and is an archer (near killed him doing this).
If you ask me archers are a little underpowered making them reload was a good check and balance however they do very little damage and can only attack once per turn (keep in mind they're just hitting the first skill point for me so I may be able to upgrade them down the road to be better)
Ergo just off of the campaign to the first act this game is awesome! I haven't even touched the multiplayer yet!

With the new update introducing the campaign mode and proper warband managment the game has much more content, it's fun as hell but has some issues. I honestly don't trust the RNG, anything below 80% is a guaranteed miss in my experience, maybe i'm unlucky but it definately feels off. The camera angles can be extremely frustrating, if you're using any of the large creatures like the Ogre you'll get a great view of it's♥♥♥♥♥ and thats all. The game as a whole works well though, and it's got enough content to keep you occupied for many hours. I'd like to see more item variety, more item drops and more rune recipe drops, in the 40 or so hours I've played the game I've only seen one named magical item.

First of all, if you like tactics games, you will like this game. Valkyria chronicles, War of the lions, Fire emblem, XCOM, if you have favorable memories of any of those games then you will know the drill here and have a good time.

The basic concept for most matches boils down to that. Many people will complain that deployments can decide a mission before the game starts, but those same out of position characters are usually the ones who gather your resources. And honestly, if your deployment makes you lose the game your doing it wrong, since you can always turn on the option to personally deploy your forces. And at that point you can either do hammer and anvil scenarios (which will always favor you) or retreat and gather scenarios (where you pull back to a defensible location first before moving back out to collect resources)
Also, there is a large degree of verticality to this game that doesnt really have an equilvalent in those other games i mentioned. Mobile factions (or factions that make themselves pseudo mobile) tend to do well simply because they have an easier time navigating the world. Ranged weapons are critical in many of these vertical locations as they allow you to get in damage when your opponent cant.
That being said there IS a faction for which only the bravest and manliest among you will play. The sisters of sigmar. My faction of course :p

They are the least mobile faction with the worst ability to climb, leap, or generally cover ground.They are the only faction that is completely incapable of using ranged weapons. Sound awesome? Thats because they are also the best faction in straight fights. 1 on 1 they will beat their equivalent in other factions....but if your opponent lets you be 1 on 1, they are doing something wrong :p
Hope this helps, cheers!

I typically play grand strategy titles but picked this up on a whim. I am glad I did. The game strikes a very good balance between challenge vs. playability, emersion, risk vs. reward, progression, etc.. I absolutely love the 3rd person point of view and feel of the game play. It gives you the illusion of playing out a mini adventure, each time you start a new mission. There are quite a few naysayers out there who exclaim that the game is too hard or unfair. This is a thinking man's game. You must plan out your actions carefully and execute. Do I risk splitting up to gather more reward or play it safe so that I have strength in numbers? If you like a challenging game that affords you the opportunity to imagine yourself as the leader of a small band of brothers (or rats, sisters, etc..) and enjoy advancement and progression, you will like this title. I am not crazy about the Warhammer universe, but the gameplay has me addicted...there is always one more thing I want to do before putting the game down...good mix of tactical play, overall strategy in mission deployment, warband management, etc..
Pros
Immersive Gameplay: You identify with your merry band of warriors
Nail biting: Many missions will come right down to the wire
Challenging Gameplay: Rewarding to those that want a challenge. Feeling of accomplishment. You earned your victory!
Varied Maps and Mission set Ups: Every mission will be a bit different than the one before.
Point of View: Refreshing 3rd person perspective that plays out before your eyes. It doesnt seem turned base...you are almost watching an action movie.
Fog of War: What's in that house across the street? Should I risk going in and getting cornered? What about that treasure chest that's in there?
Customization: Moderate character customization options. rename and tailor the look of your warband.
Pick and Choose: though not really a sandbox game, you have some flexibility in picking the missions you want to play.
Fun: I just enjoy playing the game. I cant put it down.
Cons
Iron Man: No combat saves. For me, this adds to the game tension (risk vs. reward) so is not an negative, but the game is unforgiving. You will live with your mistakes (or die by them).
Finesse Required: You must learn the tactics and how to play the game to get good at it. (Hint: Stay together!)
Luck: There are some situations that amount to dumb luck (good and bad) that no amount of tactics will overcome. This hasn't occurred too often, but it does happen.
Customization Options: what is available is good but wish there was more.
Repetitive Missions: though I have not tired of the missions, they are similar in scope and style, save for the four story missions. Could become "grindy" for some.
Review based on the solo campaign. I have not played the mulitplayer portion of the game.

Introversion is a small development house that deserves more attention than it gets.   The team makes modest, beautifully conceived, games that are compelling to play and darwinia is one of their best.
The gameplay is challenging enough without, save perhaps one small exception, being frustrating. This allows you flexibility in play so, whether you are the aggressive type or slow and methodical, you should find a satisfying game.  I never felt forced to find the trick to advance forward and the game never worked against my approach to the maps, as often happens in other games.
The graphics are simple, as you would expect from a group that isn't cranking out a million dollar blockbuster, but beautiful and enhance, rather than detract from, the experience.  At first it might seem offputting, but you quickly realize that it isn't something that requires tolerance but actually fits the game's story and design. The story doesn't feel like an afterthought.  It is well written and has a strange emotional pull for a video game.  The lovely music changes to help drive this emotion  but is never in your face and never becomes tiresome. It all combines beautifully, and doesn't feel slapped together, but has a spare, elegant quality.
I found myself amazed at how emotionally attached I became to each little stick figure and its survival.
This game is well worth the modest price.  It isn't a throwaway, have a look during a sale, type of game. I never felt that I was having to overlook flaws or that I had made a donation to an aspiring developer.  Although relatively short it has great replay value, especially the later missions. I finished the game and have played it numerous times through and I go back and replay it every so often.  This should tell you something, in an age where we have steam accounts bursting with games we play for a few minutes and never glance at again.
