I really wanted to love this gime. I like the concept of economy based only on gold, player's purse with limited space, conquering new lands with hard labour of people and monsters attacking every night. It's simple but effective premise. Unfortunately the execution is frustrating, tiresome and mostly boring.
I do not have a problem with basic base builders. I like more complicated games, but can see the appeal of something simpler. What I have problem with is the fact, that after losing or moving to another island I have to build my base and economy from scratch. Which is very slow and very time consuming process, considering that you have limited amount of gold and time everyday, your horse do not have unlimited stamina and everything needs your attention. 90% of the game is traveling from one side of the map to another, either exploring or gathering gold (untill you build portals, but to do that you need a lot of gold and an army), 5% spending that gold, and 5% waiting untill dawn (har har har...), cause in darkness monsters can easily steal your crown. Get ambushed with tired horse, lost crown, lost three hours of progress, start from the very first island.
And because your purse is limited you can't explore too far, unless you want to lost some of the gold from treasure chests (surplus will fall on the ground, later to be picked by monsters, or into the water). You need to constantly spend, but not too much, cause there is always new recruit that needs bow, a wall that needs repairs, shrine that needs some money et cetera. And because you need to spend cash personally, you either have enough gold to build something, or have to go back another day.
I could endure that - after all I am Dwarf Fortress player and losing is fun! - but rewards for moving from one island to another are ridiculously small. By changing location you unlock new things on the islands - shrines, a dog et cetera. What are they purpose? Dunno, check on Wiki, cause game don't have that info. You know what their purpose is? Good, now ignore half of them cause they are useless. Like dog. Barking at the side where enemy is attacking? Neat, untill both sides are attacked. Oh and every island have more than one reward, but those are unblocked one at a time. You want another one from that particular island? Play the game again, mate!
Did I mention that AI in this game is terrible? I get it, archers will defend only one side of your base, ok, but why farmers don't get behind walls sooner? Why archers can't stand a little bit more behind walls, so they would not be attacked? Why they aim is so terrible, that about half of them can't hit enemies? I can have 40 archers and still loose the wall cause half of them are basically blind. And when the wall fall every one of your men will run to the next one, even if it is half a map away, and get massacred while doing that. Which means you sometimes can not expand, cause walls spots are placed randomly and moving to the next one is just too huge of a risk.
On top of that builders are slow as hell, which is frustrating when you want to build wall far away from your town. And upgrade it, which is mandatory, since enemies hordes grow bigger and bigger every night. And do not get me started about builders, that end their work and just stand there, even if they are far, far away from your town.
Basically if you want to have some fun with this game you need to play it its way and do things in correct order. You need to very slowly gather cash, very slowly expand your town and very slowly gather army to protect it and attack enemy portals. Do something wrong and you will end up with not enough resources and too many enemies to deal with, which means restart from the beginning. If you like that sort of things, then go for it. 15 dollars will give you a lot of playtime. Otherwise don't bother, this game is not worth it.

In between development of Azure Striker Gunvolt and Mighty No. 9, Inti Creates developed this short retro throwback. The story involves a crossover with the characters Gunvolt from AZS, Beck from MN9, and Ekoro from GalGun teaming up to save...love I think, doesn't really matter. For Mighty No. 9 Kickstarter Backers or early buyers of Azure Striker Gunvolt this game was free. For everyone else $5 seems a fair price. There's 8 levels each with a Mega Man style boss fight plus a 9th final boss. Like Mega Man the bosses emphasize pattern recognition and timing your attacks to win. The controls feel as good if not better than any classic Mega Man with each character possessing a unique movement ability and charge ability. Ekoro can briefly float and convert enemies into familiars. Beck can slide and perform charge tackles on the ground or in midair. Gunvolt can double jump and fire a powerful beam not unlike Kirby's Beam power-up however you must remain still to perform it so it's mostly useless except for some hard to reach places. If you're experienced with Mega Man titles or the like then the levels themselves should be fairly easy to beat. Most enemies can be bypassed faster than fighting without taking damage. The bosses though are fairly tough in places but with patience can be mastered. Overall I'd say the game feels like a homebrew Mega Man of the highest quality and getting all the achievements are reasonable and satisfying.

Fair warning, I don't remember paying for this game; I think I got it as part of the promotion for Kickstarting MN9.
Having said that, I've been a fan of Megaman for a long time and grew up on Megaman 2 in particular, since that was one of the few cartridges I had when I was a kid.  My reflexes have gotten worse since then, since I haven't been constantly platform gaming - it's not something I've kept up on - so while the controls are very tight, I end up taking a lot of damage simply because I'm not very good.  Whether this is a function of my poor skill or the difficulty of the game, well, I'll leave that to the individual.
The concept itself is fairly simple - there are a collection of stages that you're required to beat for 'the ending' (which is a text roll - sorry if that's spoilery), plus extra stages on the other side of the warp that you can challenge for the sake of an achievement or two.  But like most retro 8-bit style games, the fun isn't necessarily in beating the game - it's in playing it.  And in that respect, I think, Mighty Gunvolt does the job and does it well.
There are three selectable characters, who move slightly differently; because of that, the stages have layouts where some parts are only accessible if you're a certain character, which reminds me of Rockman & Forte/Megaman & Bass.  All three characters are complete in themselves and don't feel too derivative of each other, which is nice.
The game as a whole seems well-put-together, but somewhat lacking in depth because of its short length.  The gameplay is still very solid though, and the stage bosses range in challenge from 'reasonably easy to no-damage-run' to 'ragequit if you're on the wrong character'.  Again, take that with a grain of salt because I'm not a good platformer player.
Overall, I had fun with this one all the way through, at least when I wasn't screaming obscenities at the bosses.  I'm not sure I'd pay $5 for it if I hadn't known about it first, but for me at least, the experience was worth at least that much.

Having bought this in early access a while back, I saw a great potential in Kinetic Void that I hoped would someday be realised. Sadly, with it reaching its milestone v1.0 just a few days ago, I cannot in good faith recommend this game, for reasons I'll outline below.
First and foremost, this game still feels very, very unfinished. Going purely on the surface aesthetics, the visuals (which I remain a fan of) may be reasonable, but the interface remains a chore to interact with and there's something distinctly offputting about the cumbersome text windows used to introduce you to the game's mechanics. Overall, it's adequate. But that's all.
In terms of gameplay, Kinetic Void has changed in a few subtle but relatively significant steps since the early access builds of a month or two ago. The economy system seems to be in full drive, and the updates you receive regarding loss of cargo et cetera definitely maintain the connection between you and the big wide galaxy. In terms of the ship-to-ship combat, however, I find that even in its supposedly finished state the controls are unintuitive, with a host of keyboard bindings to memorise which, while I could get to grips with, might not be everyone's cup of tea. There's also nothing particularly inspiring about the combat- you lock on to a ship, then let your guns auto-fire on them until either you or they explode. You can try and manually fire your guns with the handy target-leading reticule now implemented, but it's still painfully monotonous and generally a wasted effort. That, and with the drastic reduction in flight speed that was implemented a while back, the game still plays very slowly and dogfights, which used to be relatively intense, are now relatively lacklustre.
Regarding other aspects of the game: the music remains the same as it's been since I first bought it, and is for the most part adequate. It's occasionally repetetive, and the game possesses no facility for contextual change, so combat will sound basically identical to drifting aimlessly through space. Of storyline there is essentially no sign, but then this was never supposed to be a story-driven game, so there's no discredit meant by that. What could have been a well thought out and richly populated universe, however, has been sacrificed for the sake of customisation.
This is indeed my problem with this game. Yes, you read that right. My main problem with Kinetic Void is the degree of customisation. Normally, I love games that include vast and excessively complex levels of customisation. What Kinetic Void offers, however, is a deceptively shallow amount of purely aesthetic customisation. Sure, you can build whatever shape ship you want and put whatever guns you want on it. But essentially, what do all those guns do? They're essentially reskins of the same gun, with different 'on-paper' stats. There's no distinct feel to it. As a game intended to be played more than once, Kinetic Void has little to involve the player and prompt different playthroughs. That lack of distinction is where I feel the game really falls down, and it's a problem I've seen with several games offering the same degree of customisation as Kinetic Void. The developers have clearly made a conscious effort to give the player a unique experience with plenty of options, and I respect that. But that breadth comes at the expense of depth. The universe of Kinetic Void is as harsh and barren as space itself, populated with empty, identical ships that maintain a visual pretense of being different. It's a very specific issue I have with the game, and I realise that many people might not feel the same way about it, but as someone whose expectations were built up significantly by the early-access hype, I cannot help but feel disappointed with how Kinetic Void has progressed.
On a positive note, the developers intend to continue adding features, meaning that there may be a little light at the end of the tunnel for us early-access buyers. For the most part, however, I feel that with significant overhaul now a recently dead prospect, Kinetic Void is and will always be simply an 'adequate' iteration of a dream that could have been great.

Mordheim: City of the Damned  is a  Turn-Based Strategy Game that´s based on the Rules of the Games Workshop Tabletop Game Mordheim. Mordheim: CotD offers the Player the possibility to explore the ruined City of Mordheim with his Warband to scavenge for wyrdstone and treasure and  of course to battle rival warbands. Mordheim offers a single player mode as well as a multiplayer mode. The game looks fantastic and can be both great fun and highly frustrating due to its Games Workshop typical randomness.  The tactical fights in Mordheim are, especially during the first half dozen or so fights, challenging, not so much because of the brilliant AI, but in Hard, Brutal or even Deadly Maps the AI Units get buffed to the point where unskilled warbands are very likely to perish.
The more strategic side of the game (levelling your warband and picking the right skills) is fun and rewarding, but due to the lack of a save game option your faults will be permant and that might proof to be very frustrating for players new to Mordheim.
The developer decided to make the game a permanent "hard-core" mode, meaning there is only autosave and closing the game during a battle (or the game crashing) will leave your warband in a devastated condition (wounded, missing equipment,probably even dead).
So IF you allready play the Tabletop game and like it: buy Mordheim:Cotd.
But as for now I wouldn´t recommend Mordheim: CotD to casual gamers because of the formentioned "Perma Hard-Core Mode", the game might proof to be to frustrating and time consuming to build up even your first warband.

While unpolished (and currently not entirely finished), Mordheim is a tense, thoroughly entertaining strategy game.
If you like hardcore, turn-based strategy games, definitely give it some serious consideration.

You gotta hand it to Capcom, at least when it comes to Resident Evil. This is the second time that the series has been on the brink of death. Right when you think it's over, you feel teeth sink into your ankle as it pulls you down for more. A cursory glance might give the impression that it's an Amnesia or Outlast knock off, but there's so much more in RE7 that the comparison seems forced. The combat is focused on resource management and spacing. The antagonists are hideous and remarkably unique- you simply haven't seen bad guys like the Baker family. The story is threadbare at first (gotta find muh wife) but by the end I wanted to pour over all of the documents I found again. Even the black goop monsters (which have been in vogue for the past 10 years in the most random games) have had some serious work put in their design and animations. And the setting! The swamps of Louisiana are an absolutely perfect location for a dilapidated old house. Which is good because you're going to be spending a lot of time exploring said house. Combat, resource management, exploration, and story? Sounds like a good ol' fashioned Resident Evil to me- do ignore the smell though.

Photo-realistic graphics and awesome gameplay, with shooting that feels real and non-gimmicky. Boss battles and enemy encounters are a blast and the game is a ton of fun all the way through, especially since it's scary af. The story is mediocre at best though, definitely something that could be improved in the next one. All in all, 100% worth the purchase.

After Resident Evil 6, I didn't buy 7 at launch, having lost a significant bit of faith in the franchise. 6 was the inevitable result of the developer taking 5's too-heavy action leanings (I love 5 but acknowledge it's a poor direction for the series), and turning everything up to 11 until it's just an ear-bleeding din of too many playable characters, no horror, and a giant boss that just felt desperate how big it was, and another that was just a face-palmingly non-sensical Transformer. It took me 3 different attempts at getting through all of RE 6 before I finally forced myself to finish, and I honestly never plan on touching it again, so 7 was something I just wasn't interested in...man, I'm glad I took the plunge and finally gave 7 a go.
Graphically, if you don't have a video card that meets the recommended specs, certain things in the game will look a little weird, like hair, and certain things will be a little blurry (even without motion blur), but the game looked good enough on my GeForce 770 for me to get by. Artistically, however, my video card didn't hold things back at all. The visual design itself of the game was great, with characters who looked more like real people and less like someone went down an anime character trope checklist like the series seemed to be going for previously. I would dare say only one character was a massive trope, and there's a very cool late-game twist that I didn't see coming until a few minutes before the reveal. The decrepit southern home and other locales were disturbingly creepy to be in from a visual standpoint, though there's more to these things than just how it looks...
Working in concert with the look of the game, the sound effects are excellent, and they round out the spookiness of the environment. The look and sound of the locations had me nervous as I went along, inching forward, listening carefully for sounds that might signal impending danger. The voice-acting was handled well. I'm from the American south, and the voices sounded believable and not like silly cartoon versions of southerners, which is nice for immersion.
RE7's plot has more twists than I've ever seen before in an RE game, which i found to be very fun. There are some nice clues that typically don't give too much away, but might help you figure something out and be surprised at your own revelation a few minutes before the reveal, or the surprise will completely blind-side you. Both of these happened to me, and I loved it each time. I only have 3 complaints about the story: 1. You are viewing what your main character views, but the game cuts out an entire scene which he has no excuse for forgetting, and it vastly changes how you should feel about certain characters. 2. There is a choice you have to make which determines your ending, and I think it was handled poorly because you aren't given enough information to make a good decision and doing the most selfless thing gives what most consider the "bad" ending. 3. Regardless of your choice, one character just drops out of the game completely, despite being quite important. I'm hoping upcoming DLC or a sequel will address it, because that character is probably my favorite character in RE7. These are pretty minor complaints, though. Over all, I think this is my favorite RE plot to date.
This is the meat of the game. People sneer at first person shooters, but it's an excellent perspective for immersion, and your own character doesn't block the view.  This means tank controls are gone, though it's compensated sufficiently by having your movement speed cut down while you're aiming guns, and ammo, though not terribly scarce, is in short enough supply that I found myself resorting to the knife in most fights (though I wish I hadn't in retrospect...there really is enough ammo). You get a new knife late-game, and it's glorious, allowing for easy kills, but the early-game knife is just terrible. My favorite weapons were the shotguns, and they feel quite powerful when you land a perfect headshot up close.
The opening hour of the game (your first run if you're not going fast) might be kind of a drag. It has little to no Resident Evil gameplay (weird puzzles, gunplay against slow-moving monsters, inventory management, etc., and mostly consists of wandering around a creepy environment designed to milk jump scares out of you. I found myself getting drowsy until nearly the climax of the opening, at which things get good and stay really good until you complete the game, so I definitely suggest sticking with it if the very opening is dull and doesn't feel very Resident-Evil-y for you.
RE7 features sneaking, which is only in very specific locations and very, very, very few enemies will not notice you immediately, meaning you will be running away or fighting almost everything in the game. If you hear "RE7 has sneaking," don't go thinking that this is a stealth game, because it's not, and the stealth is just kinda okay.
Puzzles are back, baby, and so are the locked doors you'll get themed keys to unlock. Nothing is terribly complicated, though one puzzle was rather awesome and I think Jigsaw would approve. You can watch an interactive video tape and use what you learn from that to change the outcome of your own dealings with that puzzle, which felt incredibly satisfying for me.
This game had less bosses than some RE games, but that's a good thing. RE6 had piles of boss fights and more combat than you could shake a stick at. This game is a return to form for Resident Evil, feeling closer to something between RE1 and RE4, with 1's map design and puzzles, and 4's sensible combat without going full-on action game.
Some folks take issue with the game being short. There's an achievement for finishing in under 4 hours, though it took me over 14. Granted, I did only heal 3 times because I was such an item tightwad, and kept getting killed. I honestly prefer shorter games that last a handful of hours to an experience that drags on for the sake of padding out run-time, so RE7 has won my appreciation in that regard, having great content without stretching it out and diminishing the well-paced structure of the game.
Not everyone will love the game, but I really enjoyed it and I feel like Resident Evil is back and fun again. As an entry in the series, I recommend it alongside great stuff like the REmake, 2, and 4. It feels a little weird, especially during that first hour which just feels like a horror game with jump scares and nothing more, but when the Resident Evil locked doors and map exploration starts up, things got
fun for me, and I hope it will for you as well.

Never before have I played a game so simultaneously enjoyable and frustrating. I'll skip straight to the meat, details to a minimum.
Pros:
1. Fun, reactive hand-to-hand combat with occasional weapon 'power ups' (though there are NOT many weapons in the game at the point of me writing this - or at least, I have found very few. Maybe there are more as PVP rewards, which I'm just now diving into.)
2. Optimization-emphatic movesets that allow you to customize your own combat techniques.
3. Graphics are generally good - occasionally a bit off, but mostly pleasing.
4. Smooth transition between combat and exploration.
Neutral:
1. Duplicates of dropped items/equipment with no shop or way to get rid of them - annoying to cycle through them if you grind for a while.
2. Move deck demos show some moves as faster than then are - not very helpful in the long run.
3. I'm not sure armor does anything as of yet, since I seem to take the same damage completely nude (underwear) as I do in full heavy armor. Maybe bugged.
Cons:
1. The servers (or server, as circumstance and quantity may have it) are garbage. Wow. Seriously, shame on you Devolver - releasing a combat game that thrives on split-second decisions and combo chaining and alternating, and you play directly into the main reason other games in the genre (See: For Honor) die off before their prime.
2. AI is either pathetically easy or annoyingly good - never feels quite right.
3. Bugs galore. Just played my first PVP game, and decided I didn't wanna rematch the guy (his moveset was annoying and I was a tad laggy, a la con #1). I go to press 'exit', and it just sits me at the same screen instead of exiting. I did not get put into a new game, couldn't leave, had to alt+f4.
4. Short. Short short short. I get it, the main focus is on the PVP, but come on man. All the in-game hype about becoming an Absolver and it's over in, what, less than 10 hours? At the time of writing this, I have 9.1 hours played - and at least 2 of those are running around because the map is slightly confusing or just grinding and not doing story stuff.
5. Last one. It honestly doesn't seem... Well, finished. I'm gonna explain what I mean, so if you care, read on - if not, skip ahead.
Absolver feels like a game that was rushed, due to hype or need for some cash or literally any reason - it just doesn't feel done. The core mechanics are in place, yes, and they play like a charm. However, much of the game feels like it frankly lacks content. For exaample, you can be mentored in 'schools' by various NPCs.  Except... Your only options are one man (Raakio, who you will inevitably meet, and who teaches you the only style not available from the get-go) and other players. That sounds cool, right? Other players, teaching you moves - except, you could just as easily go out and find whatever NPC uses them and learn them yourself with a little patience. Or, another one: in the trailers, players (or enemies) are shown using things like polearms, which is badass! . . . if they were in the game. Again, disclaimer, I'm not very far in the PVP, so they may be locked behind PVP rewards. Finally, even the item amount is... Sparse, or feels like it is.  The Masks, one of the most iconic parts of the game, only have about 5 (or 6 if you pre-ordered) in the game that you can acquire through the story mode. On a similar note, there are only 3 weapons in the story mode (2 swords, 1 war-gauntlets). Even in articles written about the game, it's mentioned that much of the content will be added post-launch. Why? That's like putting meat back on the bones, not garnishing the roast.
TL;DR this game is buggy, feels unfinished, and the server sucks - but honestly, it's fun and I like it a lot. Despite its flaws, I would recommend it and I am hopeful for the future due to how much its blown up so far. I can only wish that Devolver fixes the server issue soon. I can do with bugs, as long as I can hop back in just as easily.

I've played a few hours of this and "completed" the game. TLDR at bottom along with edit
Lemme start off with the bad.
Really short game. Really short, unless you're into pvp. Then it could probably go on indefinitely for you. I also found it sad that the world was really small and mostly empty. Purely superficial eye candy. I found the move set learning system to be slow, and really grindy. It takes a long time and you must have immense patience. There had been a couple times where I had tried to grind out some exp to learn enemies' moves only to get the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of me by an npc to seem to have auto-guard on. That said, the enemy difficulty is somewhat inconsistent. The fact that at any point you can get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked because you were slacking isn't a bad thing however, it's slightly offputting to have wild variance in a single group of enemies. Which leads me to my next point. With as much depth that this game contains in its combat model, group fights are a ♥♥♥♥ing pain. Which is another point of inconsistency, and if the lesson is power in numbers, then this game repeatedly beats the dead horse with iron fists. The camera angles and lock ons are wonderful for 1v1 fights but very limiting when fighting multiple enemies which leads to some somewhat frustrating fights on your own.
Now for the good.
This game is fun, at its core design aside from the flaws mentioned above, and it's very saddening that it is so short. As you're going through the story, they are upfront for the most part. SPOILER beat six bosses, then head to the tower. It's like a wonderful prologue to an epic story. I'm not into fighting games, but this one is fun. There is a lot of depth to be had through it's combat. You can mix all the combos, and really make a unique fighter. It's just unfortunate that the use for your character pass a certain point is only useful in pvp. The enviorment is lush and beautiful, it very much looks like a painting. The universe it takes place it sounds really interesting as well, I hope they add dlc to develop the story more. I think this game deserves to be more than a brawler. The customization is interesting, although you don't get to really customize your fighter, you do get to choose from a fairly wide variety of gear, and some even come in different colors should you find duplicates. Overall, I am enjoying this game though, it's misleading to say for how long. I hope this game gets the development and attention from its creators that it deserves.

Darwinia is really great. Perhaps not the best "game" or RTS out there, but there are some really unique aspects to it, if you can get past the frustrating and confusing first missions.
This is very clearly an indie game, but it's one of a kind we don't see too often, nowadays. Everyone can make some kind of game, so our focus has shifted and broadened from what it was back then, when mainly programmers and computer scientists could make a game on their own. And this game shows that perspective a lot.
This game is you trying to clean up an accident that happened with sentient AIs that downloaded a Spam e-mail's virus. And the way that the story is presented is clearly from a more technical point of view which is not all that common, nowadays.
I'd think of Darwinia more as a Sandbox than as a game. Honestly, the campaign wasn't all that good. The game hasn't aged well (suprisingly, the graphics still looks fairy modern). It doesn't explain its mechanics well at all, and I was stuck on the first two levels for completely different reasons.
For example, the missions don't end. You'll get a message that your objectives are complete, and then you manually leave the level. It's... strange. And if you miss the message, good luck finding what's wrong!
Also, a lot of the missions boil down to "wars of attrition", while you figure out a decent strategy.
I thought of dropping the game after the first couple of level.
By the end, however, it gets really good. Once you get past the micro managing a squad with a very awkward path-finding, you get to spawning dozens and dozens of Darwinians, and exploding dozens of the enemies at once. Then it gets really cool!
It's mostly a Conquest game, where you try to spawn as many Darwinians and move them to a ConqueredPoint to spawn even more of them, and eventually conquer the whole map. But something about the way its done is really charming, and it's just fun to see the AI do their thing.
I didn't enjoy the campaign, for the most part. But certainly something to try out!

This is one of those games that manage to feel poetic, beautiful, and touching, while actually offering really interesting gameplay. In itself, this makes it 100% worth playing.
The game is also impressive in its gameplay simplicity and elegance. You can actually perform only 3 inputs in this game: go left, go right, and throw a coin. How can this lead to a real-time strategy challenge, you ask? Well, you activate specialized workers and militia men by giving them coins, you upgrade buildings and defenses by investing coins, and you make sure to be at the right place at the right time to manage the two fronts of your kingdom and get intel on what to do next. Brilliant design work, really.
Now, replayability is not one of Kingdom's strong points. But that's ok. You can just play a few maps and spend maybe 5-10 hours in its world. It will have shared with you a whole new strategy experience, while sweeping you in the character's personal journey through hope, beauty and melancholy.
Definitely worth 15$.

Let's start by saying that my hour count isn't representative. I bought the original retail version of this game 4 years ago, and I've played it for days.
Do you like shooters? Do you like them little bit tougher and more tactical, but are you scared of ArmA's complexity and bored of Battlefield's simplicity? If you answered yes to all the questions, then I've got a game for you.
Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising, along with its slightly hotter sister Red River is basically a "revival" of sorts of the old series Operation Flashpoint. The concept stays the same since the first game. A tactical military shooter, which throws you into a big, open world and gives you goals. You can either complete them to advance the campaign/mission further, or you can just ♥♥♥♥ around in the big open world with vehicles ranging from jeeps to helicopters.
Graphics are really pretty for an open-world sandbox that came out in 2009, albeit a bit brown, the shooting is solid, vehicles handle like real vehicles, albeit a little simplified, enemy AI is actually smart (I've seen enemy soldiers laying supressing fire on my squad, while the rest of them flanked us and attacked us from behind), your AI companions follow your orders well and are capable of handling themselves quite easily (seriously, for the first 30 or so minutes, you
depend on these guys, they saved my♥♥♥♥♥♥multiple times even as an experienced player) and the story is quite interesting for a military sandbox.
Sounds good? Because it is, but it's
perfect. Not at all. My first major gripe with this game is the tutorial. Or the lack of it. The game throws you into a mission without any explanation of the basic controls, and you better have Google opened on the Steam browser, because you will have to look up controls for yourself.
The second big problem is the artillery support the HQ can give you. It makes the game way too easy sometimes. Seriously, you can just call in a barrage 90% of the time and it will solve your issues instantly.
Third (more of a nitpick than anything though) issue I have with this game are the aforementioned team-mates. While their AI is good, they sometimes do nothing until you give orders. Which can be a huge problem if you get downed, because the medic
not help you by himself sometimes.
Over all, I recommend this game. It's dirt cheap, and great fun when you get used to the strange controls, harsh weapon physics and brown-ish graphics.
8/10, this game along with its sis is a great sequel to a masterpiece of a game.

Underrated game in my mind. I played this originally on the Xbox 360 back when it released, then later on purchased it on PC within a Codemasters Bundle that was on sale.
A lot of people like to say negative things about this game, but honestly, I really enjoyed it. I thoroughly enjoy realistic tactical shooters and milsims, and this game ranks high on the list of available games. That's not to say it doesn't have its problems. The AI isn't the best (although there is a mod to remedy this), and the resolutions are restricted to 1280x1024 as the highest option. To fix this, you'll need to download another .exe and replace the one in the game installation folder. The guides section has this fix explained in detail with links to the file.
The game has a great campaign, and in fact, it's easily one of the best single-player campaigns I've experienced; very enjoyable and expansive missions that feel very immersive and challenging in a very unforgiving manner. Screw up just a tiny bit, and it'll cost you greatly. There's a few side missions available independently from the campaign, plus you can download a ton of mission packs off of modding websites to further enhance the single-player longevity.
Multiplayer is no longer officially supported, which is unfortunate, however, there is a very simple workaround. Simply use Gameranger and host LAN games and you'll be completely set.
Now onto my gripes. These two issues are single handedly my biggest problems with this game, and if they weren't there, this would easily be one of the top military tactical shooters out there, and would be something I'd put a LOT more time into. These issues are FOV (Field of View) and mouse acceleration. Absolutely unforgivable to not have proper support in these areas. The FOV is locked at around 60, which is horrid. There's no way to change it, at all, by any means. Now, I did get used to it, and didn't let it ruin my experience too much, and I'll get to that in a second.
As for mouse acceleration, once again, no fix available. You're stuck with it, and it sucks. In this regard, playing with a controller is actually superior, although your aim will undoubtedly suffer from it.
Now if it was one or the other, it wouldn't be that much of a problem. For example, if you could increase your FOV to around 90, but the mouse acceleration was still present, it would still be annoying, but it would be
annoying. If there was no mouse acceleration, but the FOV was still locked at 60, once again, less annoying. But the two combined.... just, it's terrible, and as I said, unforgivable in a PC game.
Aside from that, this is easily one of the most optimized games I've ever played. The performance is outstanding, especially on any PC stronger than an Xbox 360. I mean think about it, last gen consoles could run this game. Naturally people would compare this game to Arma, and in the realm of performance, there's no comparison. The EGO Engine is outstanding, and the visuals still hold up well even today.
In fact, I'd compare the visuals to the newly released SQUAD, and in some ways, it even looks better. To be completely honest, after playing this game through again just recently, I'd say it's
similar to SQUAD in gameplay style, and even the HUD elements (compass, weapon selection menu, etc.), only it has a very detailed single-player experience.
To rap things up, it's an excellent game, hampered down by two glaring issues that can be mitigated if you play this game the way it was designed... as a console game. What I mean by this, plug in your Xbox 360 controller, sit back farther than usual, and the FOV will be somewhat more tolerable, and mouse acceleration will be a non-issue since you're not even using a mouse.
If you can get past those two issues, you're in for a great military shooter experience. Calling in artillery and mortor fire is easily one of the most satisfying things you can do in this game, among many other things.
So with that in mind, given its price, I'd recommend it. Plus with Steams ability to refund, you'll be able to experience enough within 2 hours to determine whether or not you'll want to issue one.

There’s no reason to beat around the bush here, the game wants to be an old school Mega Man. So in that respect how does it hold up?
Well when it works it’s quite enjoyable. But a number of issues, mostly a lack of polish, really hold it back. As long as you like the genre you’ll get some fun out of it and its short length means you aren’t in for a serious time sink either way, but the next Shovel Knight this is not.
The issues primarily stem from the lack of variety in tactics here. Jump n’ shoot, jump n’ shoot. Classic mechanics but the lack of alternate weapons really hurts your ability to handle things tactically, instead sometimes it just boils down to slamming yourself against a wall enough times until things go your way. Add to this some spotty hit-detection and you have a recipe for aggravation. This is most prominent in the boss battles, some are well built and like a classic Mega Man game can be overcome with careful observation and reaction. However too many of them are cheap, with several of them possessing attacks you simply have NO way to dodge unless you were moving before they even began telegraphing the attack. This means far too many boss battles devolve into you jamming on the fire button as quickly as possible while you pray it doesn’t use one of its undodgeable attacks too many times in a row and you can damage it faster than it can you.
With all that said you’d think I’d be giving it a negative review. But several of the stages and bosses are just too good to do that. Like I said, when it works it really works and feels just like those classic days of yore. But if you do pick it up prepare for the fact you’ll have to deal with the less interesting/cheap bosses along the way.

Never before have I played a game so simultaneously enjoyable and frustrating. I'll skip straight to the meat, details to a minimum.
Pros:
1. Fun, reactive hand-to-hand combat with occasional weapon 'power ups' (though there are NOT many weapons in the game at the point of me writing this - or at least, I have found very few. Maybe there are more as PVP rewards, which I'm just now diving into.)
2. Optimization-emphatic movesets that allow you to customize your own combat techniques.
3. Graphics are generally good - occasionally a bit off, but mostly pleasing.
4. Smooth transition between combat and exploration.
Neutral:
1. Duplicates of dropped items/equipment with no shop or way to get rid of them - annoying to cycle through them if you grind for a while.
2. Move deck demos show some moves as faster than then are - not very helpful in the long run.
3. I'm not sure armor does anything as of yet, since I seem to take the same damage completely nude (underwear) as I do in full heavy armor. Maybe bugged.
Cons:
1. The servers (or server, as circumstance and quantity may have it) are garbage. Wow. Seriously, shame on you Devolver - releasing a combat game that thrives on split-second decisions and combo chaining and alternating, and you play directly into the main reason other games in the genre (See: For Honor) die off before their prime.
2. AI is either pathetically easy or annoyingly good - never feels quite right.
3. Bugs galore. Just played my first PVP game, and decided I didn't wanna rematch the guy (his moveset was annoying and I was a tad laggy, a la con #1). I go to press 'exit', and it just sits me at the same screen instead of exiting. I did not get put into a new game, couldn't leave, had to alt+f4.
4. Short. Short short short. I get it, the main focus is on the PVP, but come on man. All the in-game hype about becoming an Absolver and it's over in, what, less than 10 hours? At the time of writing this, I have 9.1 hours played - and at least 2 of those are running around because the map is slightly confusing or just grinding and not doing story stuff.
5. Last one. It honestly doesn't seem... Well, finished. I'm gonna explain what I mean, so if you care, read on - if not, skip ahead.
Absolver feels like a game that was rushed, due to hype or need for some cash or literally any reason - it just doesn't feel done. The core mechanics are in place, yes, and they play like a charm. However, much of the game feels like it frankly lacks content. For exaample, you can be mentored in 'schools' by various NPCs.  Except... Your only options are one man (Raakio, who you will inevitably meet, and who teaches you the only style not available from the get-go) and other players. That sounds cool, right? Other players, teaching you moves - except, you could just as easily go out and find whatever NPC uses them and learn them yourself with a little patience. Or, another one: in the trailers, players (or enemies) are shown using things like polearms, which is badass! . . . if they were in the game. Again, disclaimer, I'm not very far in the PVP, so they may be locked behind PVP rewards. Finally, even the item amount is... Sparse, or feels like it is.  The Masks, one of the most iconic parts of the game, only have about 5 (or 6 if you pre-ordered) in the game that you can acquire through the story mode. On a similar note, there are only 3 weapons in the story mode (2 swords, 1 war-gauntlets). Even in articles written about the game, it's mentioned that much of the content will be added post-launch. Why? That's like putting meat back on the bones, not garnishing the roast.
TL;DR this game is buggy, feels unfinished, and the server sucks - but honestly, it's fun and I like it a lot. Despite its flaws, I would recommend it and I am hopeful for the future due to how much its blown up so far. I can only wish that Devolver fixes the server issue soon. I can do with bugs, as long as I can hop back in just as easily.

I've played a few hours of this and "completed" the game. TLDR at bottom along with edit
Lemme start off with the bad.
Really short game. Really short, unless you're into pvp. Then it could probably go on indefinitely for you. I also found it sad that the world was really small and mostly empty. Purely superficial eye candy. I found the move set learning system to be slow, and really grindy. It takes a long time and you must have immense patience. There had been a couple times where I had tried to grind out some exp to learn enemies' moves only to get the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of me by an npc to seem to have auto-guard on. That said, the enemy difficulty is somewhat inconsistent. The fact that at any point you can get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked because you were slacking isn't a bad thing however, it's slightly offputting to have wild variance in a single group of enemies. Which leads me to my next point. With as much depth that this game contains in its combat model, group fights are a ♥♥♥♥ing pain. Which is another point of inconsistency, and if the lesson is power in numbers, then this game repeatedly beats the dead horse with iron fists. The camera angles and lock ons are wonderful for 1v1 fights but very limiting when fighting multiple enemies which leads to some somewhat frustrating fights on your own.
Now for the good.
This game is fun, at its core design aside from the flaws mentioned above, and it's very saddening that it is so short. As you're going through the story, they are upfront for the most part. SPOILER beat six bosses, then head to the tower. It's like a wonderful prologue to an epic story. I'm not into fighting games, but this one is fun. There is a lot of depth to be had through it's combat. You can mix all the combos, and really make a unique fighter. It's just unfortunate that the use for your character pass a certain point is only useful in pvp. The enviorment is lush and beautiful, it very much looks like a painting. The universe it takes place it sounds really interesting as well, I hope they add dlc to develop the story more. I think this game deserves to be more than a brawler. The customization is interesting, although you don't get to really customize your fighter, you do get to choose from a fairly wide variety of gear, and some even come in different colors should you find duplicates. Overall, I am enjoying this game though, it's misleading to say for how long. I hope this game gets the development and attention from its creators that it deserves.
TL;DR Game is short, fighting is fun. Masks are the new hats, and bring friends.
EDIT:  After putting a few more hours into this game and the hype and initial fun wears off. This game is a patience tester. I would not purchase this game again. Combat controls are unresponsive, I dont know whether that's intentional against certain fighting stances or my location in comparison to the world. I know it's not my internet or my pc as I have the best package of internet from my provider and my computer is a beast.
Builds are unbalanced as it stands right now. Basically, just put on fast, interruptive, difficult to dodge moves. Basically Eddy from Tekken. Which again reiterates the (un)intentional, difficulty of dodging moves in this game. I may have picked the wrong character, but of the four classes windfall is definitely at a disavantage, not only do you have to time your dodge but you must pick the correct direction as well know each of the moves you're up against. The windfall moveset is trash also, because the space bar dash is even more effective and all classes can use it. So basically, every other class has two damage avoidance techniques and which puts windfall at a disadvantage for minimal gain.
Also this game's grind is worse than a Korean MMO, for even less variety. Equipment and moves sets are painfully slow to grind out and occur as random drops, you'll mostly be fighting 2 v 1 at the minimum for such sets. This game is like Dark Souls, but without any smooth ability to take on multiple opponents.
Even with all that "fixed", the server issues are out of control. It has been down most of today and yesterday. With this games main pull being online pvp, you're stuck fighting the annoying NPCs, in a tiny little area. Essentially castrating this game and any remotely interesting part of it.
You can chalk it up to salt, that's fine. This game is ♥♥♥♥ing annoying.
Save your money, or wait til this game's server issues are resolved. There is not enough content to justify 30 bucks for offline mode only. They could've added some offline mortal combat esque battle tower thing which would've saved this whole server debaucle.

The short story-
I've been following the company on twitter/discord. They seem to be on top of their bugs, and consistently bringing more content, I don't see why this game wouldn't thrive later on. So far they are looking good, but it's still early. Not quite enough game modes for a buy just yet. Pvp wise, all they have is 1v1.

The longer story-
This card-deck style strategy game, mixed with reflex and skill-based timing, is a well-crafted piece of art and visual effect. The martial arts aspect is very real, meaning the fighting moves are all actual real-life moves. No teleporting, DOA style ninja fighting in this one gents.

If this game is to survive, they must keep the community in the loop. They can't be cryptic about "free content on the way", and then not tell us what's coming.

Discovery 1: After beating the main game, or the "tutorial", PVP is pretty much all there is left to do. As of now, all there is for competitive PVP is 1v1, and random duels that can be initiated exploring the already explored area.
Discovery 2: The game's 'learning' system, makes for unlocking moves through playing against other players or AI. But mostly PVP.
Or in other words, take your beatdown from players who have the moves unlocked.
Or, in other other words, jump into a fight with a dude that pulls a double barrel role handspring that somehow ends up with a heel in your face, while your arsenal consists of an exaggerated hand slap.
Discovery 3: The game has the fighting style, 'drunken fist'. I think it's pretty cool.
Discovery 4: You can't switch between styles or moves while in a match. So, if someone's deck completely counters your deck, you have to bite the bullet until the match is over. This game is brutal, it will not babysit you. The beginning gives you the basics of combat, drops you into an open world and thats it. No guidance, no map, no objective points, just good luck. For the first two or three hours you play this you will just be wandering around trying to figure out what to do. And while all this is going on you will be getting killed over and over again by the npcs, thats right the npcs are actually difficult on this game and there is no way to lower the difficulty. This game will kick your butt over and over. But despite all that I recommend trying it, for three main reasons. First reason is the combat, best melee combat in ANY game. This took what For Honor tried to do and made it better, with so many different moves and fighting styles everytime you fight another player they will be using a style you probably have not seen before. not in game styles necesarilly but their rythim and how they respond to your actions. And when you finally start to develope your own personal style and get these great exchanges, you feel like a badass. No game can make you feel cooler than this one, it makes you feel like you're in the middle of a kung fu movie. The second reason is because of the community, this game is similar to destiny in that other players are constantly in the game with you, and pvp is always on. This may sound like it'd be cancerous, but it's just the opposite. Players are constantly working together in order to advance, you can even do boss fights together. I was running around the map lost as hell and bumped into another player. We naturally started running around lost together and before I knew it we had been playing for two hours and defeated 4 bosses, all without saying a single word to eachother. The mentor system is amazing as well, it gives novice players a chance to try out high level players moves which just encourages you to grind harder to reach that level. Which brings me to my last reason, The Grind. As I said before, the game doesn't give you any guidance, so you are left to explore, grow, and discover yourself and it's done beautifully. Hours are spent wandering the map looking for the bosses, which can be fought in any order, and even more are spent just trying to get better. The boss fights are tough but fair, all of them can be done solo, but i recommend finding a buddy for the first couple.
In conclusion, this game will make you frustrated, you will want to tear your hair out....but you will also love every moment of it. For some reason even though the learning curve is so steep, I never rage quit once throughout my play through. There's something about the challenge that just kept me asking for more. This game is far from perfect though, there is no fast travel which is frustrating, the load times can be long, the servers are either perfect or none existant, and honestly I want more boss fights and more areas to be explored. A few things to mention though are that the servers have improved dramatically since launch which bodes well for the future, and it is confirmed that more content will continue to be added to the game. all in all this game is amazing and I recommend it to anyone that wants a good fighter or something to just grind away in.
If youre still reading, thanks for listening to my rant.
Good luck Prospects!

This game is dire beyond measure. Avoid. Really avoid.
I can see what they were trying to do. Visually the game looks at first glance like an improved version of Rollercoaster Tycoon 3, and some care and attention has gone into creating a single park and a single design of coaster. Do not be decived by these superficial similarities.
This is NOT a rollercoaster building game, it is not a park management game, I'm not sure what exactly it is if I'm honest. The closest thing I can compare it to is something like Temple Run, only with rollercoasters and a first person perspective.
Each level, you are given a few segments of rollercoaster pre-built. Your job is to link them together, in the pre-set (but not shown) order, and that is it. You are asked to add various elements such as barel rolls or corkscrews in between each element, and there are gems to collect which basically show you exactly where your track should go (except not every section has gems, and then you're left circling round looking for the next segment of track). This all sounds quite fun so far, and would be a good game mechanic in a game like Rollercoaster Tycoon any of its rivals. But this game doesn't share any of those games mechanics.
You cannot place track with any kind of sensible interface. You cannot undo your track except by restarting the level. You cannot see your ride from any perspective other than first person, riding in the front seat. I don't just mean when riding it, I mean all the time. You build the track by piloting the first car through the air like a flight simulator, aiming for the next section of pre-built track, and hitting the space bar in a kind of quicktime event to try to connect to it. This really isn't much fun at all, and leads to hilariously awful coasters with curves that would be impossible in real life and really not fun. Then by the time you get to level three, the game starts to feature pre-built segments that involve jumps and you realise that not even it takes itself seriously any more.
Couple this awful gameplay and lack of realism with a terrible interface, bad colision detection (most of the time if your track collides with things the cars fly through the air and disintegrate, but sometimes they don't, and then you can have coasters going right through trees, buildings, and other bits of track), and you end up with a truely awful game.
Run, run far away from this awful thing and never look back.

TL; DR: Good game with really fun gameplay and mostly tight controls but that can be a little frustrating at times. Over-the-top fun characters, story and cutscenes. Disappointing lack of additional playable characters.
Finally got around to beating this game and I have to say, I'm sorry it took me so long (due to technical bugs corrupting my game saves and such). The gameplay is as strong as it's been in the long-standing franchise, better actually as you get to play as new hero Nero as well as Dante later on in the game. They both play very differently but offer equally compelling modes of fun and over-the-top signature DMC aerial & ground combos mixed with guns but I was partial to Dante's gameplay as I found his ground combos, 4 styles and additional weaponry to offer a lot more versatility and enjoyment. In fact, Dante sports some of the most creative and badass weapons that I've had to joy to play with and for them alone the game is worth getting.
But I digress, aside from the incredibly fun, tight and varied combat the game takes you through cool-looking environments typical of the series that are are both grand in scale and that offer neat platforming elements and hidden collectibles/missions that round up the game nicely.
However, as it also typical of the franchise there is a fair amount of backtracking as you need to go back and unlock certain areas once you gain the appropriate new ability (which is fine) but this is further compounded by the fact that you revisit the same exact areas when you later play as Dante. I find this to be shame and a sign of the development team cutting corners and saving time & money, but it ultimately cheapens the quality of the game. What's more is that you fight the exact same 3 bosses as Dante that you did as Nero which just feels like a let-down and a missed opportunity to have turned a really good game into a fantastic one.
Next, the story. There isn't anything really original about it as it's your standard corrupt organization-turned-zealots-who-try-to-remake-the-world-in-their-image-and-the-hero(s)-have-to-stop-them fare. Despite this I really enjoyed it thanks to the playful & devil-may-care (lawl, see wut I did there? :P) attitudes of both main characters although it's a lot more pronounced and entertaining in Dante's case than it is with Nero. The story is also filled with over-the-top HILARIOUS cutscenes such as a back & forth theatrical soliloquy between Dante and one of the game's bosses that is one of the funniest moments that I've experienced in a game :). Coupled with this are lots of extremely stylish and badass sequences that really help to further set the tone for the game and give you an appreciation for how powerful these characters really are.
As for the shortcomings of the game I found the use of fixed camera angles in many locations to be rather frustrating as it's easy to have your character come to a sudden stop or start running in the opposite direction when you enter a new area where the camera angle is different from the previous one. I also felt that 2 of the more difficult moves (for Nero) were overly complicated to perform as they require incredible reflexes and timing which I and I'm sure many other gamers just don't have and so I never really used them. This is in contrast to similiar combo-heavy games like God of War, Bayonetta and Castlevania: Lords of Shadow that have as complicated a move and ability set but where all the controls are accessible and aren't an exercise in frustration.
It's also rather unfortunate that despite being able to unlock 2 additional harder modes (and 2 even tougher after that, h.o.l.y.c.r.a.p.!) after having beaten the game there is no further option to play as Trish/Gloria or Lady which is another missed opportunity, Team Ninja :(. I say this because you could unlock Trish and Vergil as playable characters in DMC 2 & 3, respectively.
Furthermore I find it disappointing that the devleopper resorted to over-sexualizing their female characters in order to help sell the game, giving them unrealistic exagerrated curves and bounciness that they didn't possess in previous games in the series. I'm all for sexy models but only when they make sense and aren't objectifying.
Finally, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the game's intrinsic difficulty: the game is HARD (especially on the 2nd default difficulty available at the start) and will kick your♥♥♥♥♥♥and challenge you to play better, which I loved. But if you're the type of person who shies away from demanding games that test your reflexes and coordination then you may want to try the easier setting yet still expect to struggle.

I'll be honest, when I first discovered this little gem, it was a bootleg copy.  But I loved it so much that I had to give the devs their due.
The game is short and sweet, but that doesn't mean it's not fun.  Darwinia drops you into a virtual world inhabited by Darwinians, A.I. programs that are the result of a 10-year research project.  Unfortunately, a virus has gotten loose in the system, and it's up to you and Dr. Sepulveda (the world's creator) to eradicate it.
The game plays like an action/RTS hybrid, with a look-and-feel heavily inspired by TRON.  Your main "programs" (read: units) are the Squad, which can attack the virii directly, and the Engineer, which can recapture buildings taken by the virus and collect digital "souls" for reprocessing.  Most levels consist of the having the Squads and Engineers clear out an infected area, converting the dead virii into new Darwinians, then sending in the Darwinians to work the various buildings that are central to Darwinia's operation.  Later on, you get some upgrades and new programs that allow the Darwinians themselves to join in the fight.
The control scheme is interesting; you create programs by drawing gestures with the mouse.  Once you master this, it's a snap to quickly roll out whichever programs are suited to the task at hand, especially when it comes to switching between the Squad's secondary weapons.  You can switch to a menu-driven interface if you prefer, but I personally think the gesture system is more fun, if a little finicky at times.  Maintaining your composure enough to accurately draw a gesture while in the heat of battle is part of the challenge!
If I had one complaint about Darwinia, it's that it's just too darn short.  You can reasonably finish the game in a weekend, but it only leaves you hungry for more.  Guess I'll need to check out Multiwinia next...

Ok, so i know what you're thinking.
"What's this guy doin'? He's only played the game for two hours! Why's he writing a review about it?"
Well, the problem is... two hours is pretty much all that was needed.
So it's pretty obvious from the get-go that this game is trying to be a callback to Classic Megaman, but with a little bit of a twist, by adding multiple characters with different abilities. While it's an interesting concept, this game is really lacks the energy needed to bring it to life. The levels are short, and the bosses are extremely easy. The only really hard part is the final boss; here, the game spikes up drastically in difficulty, which is rather jarring.
There also isn't really anything to keep you invested, either. The gameplay is kinda barebones, which isn't a problem in itself, but the level design doesn't really do much to challenge you. It almost feels lazy, which is disappointing, considering the legacy it's attempting to live up to. You also don't really get anything for beating the bosses except passage into the next boring level. The only remotely engaging thing(not counting the achievements, which are mostly just there as a courtesy) is the points system. As you defeat enemies and collect candy and fruit(?), you have a multiplier which goes up steadily. However, the points don't do jack sh*t, and there's no leaderboard, so you don't really have any motivation to perfect your play.
And on top of that, the game is incredibly short. Even if you're not really excellent at this style of platformer, you'll probably be able to beat the game within the hour. And while there are a few bonus levels, they have pretty much the same issues the main levels have. In fact, they're almost worse; they feel sort of empty, as though they're just there to make the game a little longer.
Overall, this game just feels slapped together. There's no soul in it, and nothing in it is memorable or even really that fun. The only reason i ended up playing this game was because i got it bundled in for free with Azure Striker Gunvolt(which is a fantastic game). I don't know if they're still doing that, but if they're not, then don't waste your money. Even considering how cheap it is, it's just not worth it unless you can get it for free.

This IS the continuation of Operation Flashpoint, to a degree.
So when Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crises was released early in 2001, the developers of it Bohemia Interactive had a bit of a falling out with the publisher, Codemasters.
The title remained operation flashpoint, and the engine that was operation flashpoint 1 was redeveloped, Bohemia Ineteractive then went in the direction they did with ARMA 1 2 & 3, Take on Helicopters, Take on Mars I also believe. The Arma franchise went foreward and Codemasters put money into other products as after a few more OFP titles they didn't make the haul in cash they were looking for- probably for the best actually, the later titles were no better then this if that.
This is almost a Battlefield meets Arma 1.5/2 engine, it still is very much like Arma or Operation Flashpoint in terms of controls, 'jankiness', try-hard realism, but some aspects of the game were made a lot arcadey, forgiving, and catering to the players action packed experiance instead of getting sniped from hard to see soldiers in fields at dusk (though thats still likely to happen in this engine).
If you do enjoy campaigns in the Arma engine, or you enjoy playing with the mission editors- Mission Editor is pretty much the same it was to Operation Flashpoint if memory serves me right-, and you have a few bucks to blow, this game can give you some more arcade like hours of fun then arma can, though for content it really is no replacement!

I started following this game more than a year ago. Back then, it wasn't for me, because Mordheim is all about the progression of warbands in my opining. Now, however, since they added progression, it is my mostly played game, and it is still in Early Access!
This game is a shining example of how an Early Access game should be produced:
1. The developer listens to the community, reads the forums, and responds, not only in writing, but in the game. Some of the updates have been as a direct result of player feedback.
2. The updates are wonderful. Their contents are extensive and the rate of updates are regular (at least one per week).
3. They do their very best at developing the balance withing the game in a logical manner. Add something, wait for feedback, and if needed tweak it. Add something else, repeat. It is like watching some one paint a painting; each stroke with the brush is based on the previous, and the picture emerges ever more beautifully.
Sure, I don't agree on everything. Some decisions seems strange to me, like the way the warband teleports around the city, and how they are perfectly safe in their "virtual" home base in between missions.
The game itself is loads of fun, though! It is really hard, and sometimes frustrating, since it is in a permanent state of Hardcore (permanent injuries and death may happen to characters, and NO saving and reloading). It's got fantastic graphics, and wherever you are there is a palpable corruption in the air; very reminiscent of the remakes of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre in 2003, and The Hills Have Eyes in 2006. The bits of information that are lying around are great for encouraging the player to explore the setting to uncover the story of what happened gradually. The VHS tapes are a great idea. While the stealth isn't perfect it seemed to fit the atmosphere. After all you're playing a terrified Average Joe looking for his wife, not a ninja. The jump scares work well and there a couple of moments in particular which stood out for me.
I found the combat and boss-fights somewhat detrimental to the atmosphere of the game. An approach where you have to set up traps or simply escape would've felt more in line with the atmosphere. The boss-fights only succeeded in stripping away a lot of the horror and tension. One particular boss-fight successfully placed me in an attritional mindset more at home in Dark Souls. The molded are little more than stereotypical monsters and are lacking in comparison to the well crafted malevolence of the Baker Family. It felt like the molded encounters should've been a far rarer, and a much more dangerous, occurrence.
A greater focus on the Bakers hunting you would've made this a perfect horror game. As it is it's "merely" a good game and well worth buying.

Throughout the playthrough, my surroundings in real life smelt more like fart on every jump scare. These are not your usual obviously scripted Jump scares... They catch you off guard, and they don't take away player control, so if you are the type to through your controller when scared, you better get it back quickly, or you gonna die!

Absolver is about improving yourself as a player through combat.  WIth a very detailed customizable combat set,  you can create your own combos to perform on your enemies.  You choose from 3 classes in the start: Forbidden, Kahlt and Windfall.  The Forbidden style can parry incoming attacks and stun your enemy, the Kahlt style absorbs an incoming attack and the Windfall style can dodge and slow down incoming attacks.  Your proficiency in utilizing your ability for your respective style can mean the difference between winning and losing.
Pros:

Cons:

Despite the cons, you'll still enjoy this game if you value skill in 1v1s because that's what Absolver is all about.  I would still recommend this game to you because I still like it and if these issues are fixed then it would be even more solid.

It's rough, but it's a gem for sure.
This game boasts an incredible intricate system for customizing fighting styles and combos - you could spend hours tweaking your combat deck until its something finely tuned and just for you. But more than that, this game definitely relies on more than just a knowledge of its mechanics, an idea of what builds are popular, or a hinge on some predetermined meta. It's honestly surprising how much honest to goodness fight sense you need to take an edge in this game. Even with the perfect build - if that sort of thing even exists, hell, I don't think it does - each 1v1 demands that you've got a good handle on when and when not to pressure your opponent, how you tackle the pace of the fight, making sure you don't overextend your own reserves...it definitely goes beyond just mashing x with the fastest moves equipped.
Granted, there's a lot wrong with the game right now - lighting bugs on lower graphical settings, constant freezes, infinite loading screens and ctds, horrendous lag during the occasional matchups - if you want a detailed list, all you really have to do is go on the game's subreddit to point out the gripes that players are having right now.
But I think this game has more than enough potential to make those mechanical issues more than worth putting up with while the devs iron out the kinks. With the arena as addicting as it is right now, and the promise of more content on the way, I really can't recommend this game enough.

As of this write up I've played about 6 hours of Kinetic Void, according to Steam.
The main draw to this is obviously going to be ship building and customisation.
There seems to be a fair number of parts to mix and match between and the editor, once you get used to it, is fairly intuitive. There are some bugs with the mirroring tool that desperately need to be worked out – at times the game will not recognise that the mirrored part is positioned in a perfectly valid location, despite registering the original component as being fine to put down. You can pretty much attach whatever you want to whatever you want. Go nuts – it’s not going to stop you. The basic shapes are generally quite blocky, but there’s enough manipulation to go around that you can, with a little innovation, make some interesting ships and they won’t look like a spruced up Minecraft creation.
Combat, despite being a central focus of this game, isn’t particularly mind-blowing. It’s mid-way between EVE and X3. You won’t get straight up X3 style twitch-based dog-fighting, but you won’t be forced to watch your ship auto-pilot in circles which you hit hotkeys 1-9 to fire your missiles. It's a bit clunky but it works and there's some room for skill involved, alongside some tactical considerations to think about.
There's an economy. Who knows how it works, but it does. And you start to realise how essential non-combatants are in a universe. Games like X3, Vegastrike, etc - you see so many random little shuttles and traders and civilian craft trundling around the universe from station to station. For the most part they aren't actually doing anything, but it's nice to have them there – they add a bit of flesh to the skeleton. In Kinetic void, you don't have that. There are only military grade ships. This is tied into, and probably because of, the way the game determines what class a ship is - procedurally based on various factors. But it also means that everything is flatly centred on combat. Feasibly you could populate the universe with your own cargo tugs and passenger shuttles and so on and so forth: but everything seems to be classed as a combat vessel, and so you don't want to run up against a fleet of unarmed cargo tugs that the AI has pulled out of the background because it thinks they're fighters.
You can mine in this game and you can trade, but you are the only person mining in the entire universe, and you are the only actual trader in the universe. That makes it feel very lifeless, despite the fact that there are usually a fair number of ships flying around. The economy runs in the background, and events occur and things change it, but none of it happens in front of you. It doesn't appear to be as fleshed out as it should be. As far as I can tell there are two stations in the entire game: the ship station and the mining station. The mining station appears to be for visual effect only. You can't dock at it and it doesn't do anything. So you mine an steroid for about 5 different resources, trade them for credits at the all-in-one station, and upgrade your ship. There really doesn't appear to be an on-the-surface economy and that’s really disappointing because it’s only logical to conclude that you can’t actually affect the economy through the economy. If you can, you are the only one capable of doing it, when you should be just one more ship in the universe. Where are the other mining vessels drilling into asteroids? Where are the other scavengers going after scrapped vessels? Where are the merchants trying to make a profit from the uncertain wartime market? What are these resources going towards? Why do they exist? What do they build? Who knows.
The universe needs more persistence. Enemies will show up in your sector, usually accompanied by mission markers, and you can run or fight. They'd be more of a threat if they could affect things if they could harass trade lanes, kill merchants, and affect the economy underlying the various wars that sprout up. Or if they just stayed in system after you've docked. Because they instantly de-spawn the minute you dock so the system gets reset to 0, which means that anything that looked like it could be interesting, could potentially produce emergent scenarios, etc.... well that's gone. This really needs to be fixed, because it undermines everything that a space sim should be about.
You don’t feel like you’re immersed in the game – just skimming the surface of the under-lying calculations. Wars happen, sectors are taken, but there’s no apparent war. Someone desperately called me to this frontline battle. I expected to be way in over my head, but I thought it would be worth the view, so I jumped into the conflict. Nothing. Concerned that I had got the wrong system, I checked the map. Yep - active war zone designation. I was in a war zone without a shot being fired. The faction holding the zone lost, and were eradicated, but nobody saw them fighting an enemy.
Planetary flight is fun to have. Not much more to say.
Kinetic Void just doesn't feel like it has the depth that you expect from a space sim. It doesn't seem to know whether it wants to be a universe simulation or a combat simulation, and ends up in this strange space between. I honestly wouldn't say it's at 1.0 status. It feels like space sim lite. The ship building is good fun, the fact that your own ships start to populate the universe around you is brilliant. But the universe itself just doesn't feel very alive and that undermines the whole experience.
The game will run on a potato: with everything turned down to very low it runs on a mid-2010 Macbook pro with 320M chipset at a decent clip and doesn't stutter much.

Dreadful. It is really hard to say anything else to be honest. It is also equally hard to find the motivation to spend time writing a proper review for something that certainly is not a proper finished game. It is not a matter of it simply being in an unpolished beta or alpha state, it is the matter of it being, well, not a game yet. There is barely any gameplay to be had, core ui functionality is completely absent, and the gameplay on offer barely qualifies as more than a tech test.
This would be fine, if said tech test was something new, something revolutionary, such as the Swarm tech test or if it had dynamic visual damage on the ships. If there was anything beyond the most barebones physics and graphics engine tech that has already been outdone 10 years ago or more, by games such as X2: The Threat (yes, i said X2, not X3).
That is how antiquated this game already is, it is released in 2014 with features, gameplay and tech that has been outdone by games released 10 years ago.
Then, on what basis could i possibly recommend this game? On the basis of it being an indie kickstarter project? No, it isnt good enough. If one starts to recommend and promote any indie project just for the sole reason of "supporting the little guy", we only betray ourselves as gamers and customers with basic consumer rights.
There is nothing on offer in Kinetic Void that is better, or even equal, to games already on the market, indie or AAA.
Many of the competitors even have a lower pricepoint, or have been in the bargain bin for years!
This is not just about making games. Its about basic supply and demand.
If other games have existed for 10 years that do everything this game wants to do, better, then there simply is no demand for this game. If there is no demand for this game, what was the point?
The development time would have been better spent pursuing something else, because as of right now i cant possibly claim that Kinetic Void has anything of value to bring to the gaming scene what so ever.
