There are two types of players that will play this game; those who played Kingdom previously and those who just jumped into Kingdom: New Lands. Two very different reviews depending on this.
For those who played Kingdom; this game is a fantastic "2.0" update to the game. It takes the whole game and turns it up to eleven in terms of replayability, adventure, exploration and challenge. In the original game, you had one island to clear at a moderate difficulty. Now there are five islands that are structured around difficulty. The first island you land on will be tiny and trivial to conquer. The last island land on will be 2x or 3x larger than you have ever seen before and blighted with the Greed. After you cleared an island in Kingdom it was the end of the play through. In New Lands, it is only the beginning. Now when you are done, you can prepare yourself a small cushion to make the next island a little easier such as bringing a full purse. All in all, Kingdom: New Lands makes the game just better in every way than just Kingdom.
If you have never played Kingdom, Kingdom: New Lands is going to feel like a difficult resource management rogue-like. That's about all I want to spoil. The whole point of the game is that Kingdoms rise and eventually fall. Do not be afraid to try something, learn from your mistakes and you will be on the path to glory soon enough.

If Fantasia and Fix-It Felix, Jr. had a baby, Drip Drip would be it. You must manage your resources and weather the storm in this casual strategy game.
Each of the 24 missions lasts a predetermined amount of time. The objective is to last the full duration of the storm without the basement flooding or the building collapsing from water damage. You buy different tools and containers with your money to catch all the drips, and then you dump the containers out the open windows to earn more money. Random events can occur that must be dealt with immediately, or they can destroy your tools and cause damage. The storm also varies in intensity which gives you some calm periods to recuperate from any damage that may have occurred.
I completed the game in about 3-3.5 hours on Medium difficulty. I thought the characters were cute, and I liked the gameplay a lot at first, but it felt repetitive later on. So, I tried to up the difficulty to increase the excitement, but I couldn't change it without starting over completely. Overall, it was a well made game, and it accomplished what it set out to do. It's worth playing if you enjoy games with real time disaster prevention, and resource management, but with the lack of replay value, wait for a sale price.

"Yet another World War II game", you might say... but Brothers in Arms is a World War II game with a difference. Rather than the lone-wolf approach of Medal of Honor, or the uber soldier approach of Call of Duty, Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 places strong emphasis on tactics and teamwork, with particular focus on historical accuracy. Many man hours were spent pouring over old aerial reconnaissance photographs, in order to recreate the landscape as accurately as possible.
In this game, you play as the leader of two squadrons, of which you need to make use of in order to prevail. In order to progress, you need to make use of suppresion and flank tactics, i.e. using one fire team to suppress, and the other to flank and eliminate said enemy. Given the focus of the game on tactics, a run and gun approach will generally end badly (side note: the historical and realistic focus means it is difficult to hit shots - the sway and recoil take some getting used to). The mistake most people make is trying to play this as a normal FPS: it is not, and you will get frustrated.
Unique, with a strong focus on historical accuracy and showcasing the bonds fomed in combat, Road to Hill 30 is well worth your time. Recommended for anyone looking for something different and/or challenging, outside of the normal genres.

This is a unique and interesting theme for this game, I can see why people compare it to the likes of Tron etc.
I have given this game a not reccomended stamp, do not let this say that I do not appreciate it and I will try to give it a short and fair breakdown.
Firstly this was part of a bundle and free games are always a welcome distraction and even if you buy it, the price is very cheap, this defianatly gives it a plus point as too many really bad games get waya with charging far more than this. This is not a bad game, not by any stretch.
The first thing I would say is that I absolutly LOVE the soundtrack! the mix of old 8 and 16 bit music with a modern twist is greatly appreciated. I can acutally see me listening to some of this outside of this game it is definatly good enough.
The theme of the game being set inside a network that has been invaded by a virus,and you have to help restore systems and giving personification to the systems and AI is a wonderful touch. I also like the progression it is tied into finding upgades via research that your enigneers have to scan in order to upgade your capabillites. The graphics are pretty simple, and this works in its favour, almost like a visual representation of something much more complex.
The unlocking of new areas is tied into the opening of ports in the maps you visit, this is wonderful as it both plays on the theme, keeps within the story and makes you push to the ports in order to open up more content.
You can clearly see the effor that has been out in here and as an indie title the has definatly got some wonderful features and a little bit of a story to carry it.
Now the bad, Firstly the tutorials are awful, they simply do not explain things enough, I am not asking for hand holding here just it is kind of like;
to do this... go in that direction.... meh figure it out yourself.....
I spent a few hours playing around with it, and a lot I had to figure out myself, some people said oh its a learning curve, no a learning curve implies that you actually are told what tools you have at your disposal, and you have to learn how to impliment those tools, that is not the case here, the tutorial is just to sparse. In order to progress any further I would have had to look up how to get any further outside of the game, that should never have to happen with this type of game in my opinion.
Secondly there are a few little annoying glitches and bugs, like when selecting a unit to build, often I would not always get the one I chose, and so had to dismiss the unit just built and give the build order again, its annoying the first time, by the tenth time I was actually getting into the habit of automatically holding down the unit menu [TAB] in order to cancel what it was going to build... thats not a good thing. And a number of troops would happily walk into force feilds or danger despite having a clear path they could have took, meaning micro management is compulsory.
Thirdly there is no way (that I have figured out, forgive me if this comes a little later in) to group up multiple units, this makes micro management even more annoying and takes away from the flow of gameplay as you cannot split tasks easily.
Overall this is not a bad game at all, the theme is enjoyable the story is alright and for the price you definatly get a good few hours distration, and the soundtrack it as I said earlier really good.

As you probably have read from various other reviews: It's a short, sweet, game. I don't think I need to reiterate the same point, so I'll focus elsewhere, namely gameplay, on why the game is all right. Also to suggest some ideas for improvement.
Honestly, the game is nothing great or really memorable, but it is fun. You could save your money for other 2D sidescrollers or get this game without remorse as the three playable characters ensure some replayability.
If you are interested, I would recommend purchasing Azure Gunvolt, which comes with Mighty Gunvolt for free.
The main incentive for replaying this game is for the playable cast.
Ekoro from Gal*Gun, which is the Easy Mode character, will probably take you about thirty minutes, at most, to beat all nine levels. Beck, who I think would suit speedrunners, and Gunvolt, average guy , will both take you around an hour each.
In total, you'll probably get the amount of time put into an NES game back in the day. Your experience depends on how well you can adjust to each character's abilities as well as which one you choose to first encounter the bosses.
All three characters play similarly: You can jump and shoot a projectile weapon.  Each character has a unique ability and a different manuevering mechanic that helps them get around the levels.
However, both of these aspects are heavily underused that my main problem with this game is not its short length, rather it's unfinished execution of both level design and each character's abilities.
For example, Ekoro can possess an enemy to fight for her with her charged up attack. Immediately you might think of Kirby's Copy ability from the SNES Dreamland days. However, it doesn't matter who you posses because they all simply hover and shoot a single projectile every now and then. The only noticable difference is the size of their hit-boxes.
Beck, on the otherhand, seems given the most attention when it comes to his boss-fights as you have to use all his abilities in battle. In the School level, you fight a plant-boss where the vines are out of Beck's normal reach.  But if you dash against the wall, Beck gets knocked back a little higher, letting you hit the vines.
More of these boss-fights needed this kind of synergy for every character. They are not bad; they leave a lot to be desired is all. Some will feel difficult only because of the character you chose. The first level's boss for Beck is much more difficult compared to Ekoro's battle with the same boss in stage four.
The level design is also very basic, and you can generally tell when one character has a certain route to go through the level compared to another character's limitations. If there's a narrow path, it's for Beck; if it's a much higher jump, Gunvolt can only reach there; and if it's a long distance jump, Ekoro is the only one for the job.
Again, sometimes you can use Beck's abilities to explore other routes but this happens far less than expected and other characters have their own paths. Health pick-ups are abundant, so you can really rush through the levels to get to the boss-encounters at the end. And the enemy variety is small, carrying several types over all stages with no new challenges to fit a different stage.
Like I said before, the game doesn't do anything different, but I think they could've better implemented each character's abilities to traverse the levels in challenging ways. Or they could've implemented a party system like Castlevania 3 where you can choose two partners (sharing one life-bar) to change things up.
Since there is no story or end-game reward or incentive, I think breaking-down, briefly, the pros and cons of each character will be more useful to expand upon each character's faults. (FYI, you won't learn anything about any character from their series, and unless you are familiar with the games you won't know which bosses are tie-ins.)
There's nothing that says this game isn't worth the $5 for purchase. But, on the other hand, I cannot think of much to get other players to try this game out immediately. It's for die-hard fans looking for some light-hearted fun.

I got this game for free for backing Mighty No. 9. It looked like an old-school Mega Man game so I figured if I could get a game on about the same level as an NES Mega Man, that's a great deal! Unfortunately this game falls far too short.
The other reviewers here have done a pretty good job explaining what you can expect from the game, though I can't for the life of me understand why a large majority of them are giving this game a positive review. 3 characters, unique movesets between them, 5 main game levels, 4 extra levels etc etc. That's all fine and good. However, this game lacks any depth whatsoever. I'll elaborate.
You pick your 1 of 3 characters, go through your 5 levels in about ehhh... 20-25 minutes and then you're done. That's it. Credits roll and you've finished the game. IMO, it was a disappointing experience and there was basically no legitimate story to speak of. This review will probably take longer to write than it takes to complete the game and with a better story! I have 30 minutes played and I'd say at least 5 minutes if not more was just selecting the other characters to see what they did differently. You get no new abilities, no power-ups at all, just 5 generically cliche levels with 5 relatively easy bosses. I played one of the extra stages and it's just more of the same that you get from the initial 5. There was very little challenge at all.
You collect fruits and candies throughout the stages that award points and you have what I can only assume is a point multiplier that goes up as you collect more. These points serve no tangible purpose in the game and I can only assume exists for those that wish to perfect their runs and achieve high scores. Even then, it's a poor attempt to add replay value to an otherwise short and lackluster game.
So, if you're like me and was hoping for a game that could measure up to NES Mega Man games made nearly 20 years ago, I think you may find yourself disappointed.

Mighty Gunvolt is 8-bit throwback on the old-skool 2D action/platformer. You get 3 playable characters: Beck (Mighty No 9), Gunvolt (Azure Striker Gunvolt) and Ekoro (Gal*Gun). Each having their own movesets with strengths and weaknesses that differ from one another. There's 5 main stages, each with a boss at the end. The stages and bosses are mostly from Gunvolt. There's also 4 additional stages that were originally DLC stages from the 3DS version, but they are now included along with the full game. The stages and bosses are mostly from Gunvolt, but theres a small handful of stages and bosses from Gal*Gun and MN9.
Pros:
-Playing the 3 characters gives a bit of variety in running through the stages and fighting bosses
-The 2-D sprites look clean, yep simple
-8-bit music helps to bring out that old nostalgia from the NES days
-Easy enough to pick up the gameplay but can be challenging to fight the bosses
Cons:
-Game length is lacking, even with the extra stages
-No resolution or even a windows options
-Controls felt slightly sluggish but responsive
-Loading screens ( Seriously....theres loading screens in an 8-bit style game at this day in age of gaming)
-Could of used more stages and music from Gal*Gun and MN9
Overall: For the little time I put into the game along with its mostly minor flaws, I say wait for a cheap sale. The game does offer some variety and replay value with its old-skool gameplay, but it just doesnt last for long. It's a decent distraction for those waiting on MN9, but there are other games of this specific genre that do it better. If you got this game free when buying Azure Striker Gunvolt I'd say give it a try. But I wouldnt reccomend buying Mighty Gunvolt at its current full price. Also i think this game could use some optimization.

All in all it is a good game, but it is not a good Total War game, in my opinion.
If you think that Total Wars should be all about real time strategy, then be my guest, this is the game for you, and I would definitely recommend it. However, if like me you think that Total Wars should be less about taking an army and smashing a lot of heads, and more about taking a country and leading it to create an empire, then steer away from this game.
First of all, I feel that the great improvements made to the RTS part ended up emptying the TBS part, while Total War games before this one always pursued a balance between the two aspects. Now, the campaign map is simply too easy - in particular because the other factions don't even try to really resist to your invasion, but counteract with a small-scale guerrilla in your conquered areas. It would be a great idea, if it wasn't for the fact that quite soon you get so rich you don't really care about them burning down some buildings, when you can afford to rebuild them every single turn. No matter how awful your faction is, you are going to conquer the world on the campaign map, unless you really wanna play all the battles and lose them all spectacularly (generally, even auto-resolving battles works well enough to ensure your supremacy).
Then, the disappearance of the family tree - it might be more realistic and historically accurate (since when do Total War games care about that?), but suddenly your head of faction is just a name, and your generals are just a special unit you need to create an army; no traits, no marriages, no fidelity, nothing really has any influence on your gameplay.
Finally, the cities - once upon a time they were living entities, which had meaningful unrest, visible growth, different needs and different buildings, peculiar to the faction, the historical period, the culture, and even the region. Now, you have five slots, with a limited choice of buildings. Trust me, you are going to build EXACTLY the same buildings, in the same order, in every city and with every faction. What's the point of having a technology tree if you only have a bunch of buildings to build?
But they gave us ship battles, that makes up for everything, right?

UPDATED REVIEW:
In spite of my initial review of the game being rather negative, especially with regard to the random number generator and other random aspects of the game, I have to say that the game kept me playing.  I've been playing the last couple of days, steadily working through a new campaign, and I am absolutely loving the game now.
One thing that isn't very apparent when you start out is the fact that, in the early stages of the campaign, the game is brutal.  This is largely because your warriors don't have any skills, gear, or money to acquire new gear.  Similar to other campaign-oriented tactical games, like Darkest Dungeon, X-Com, Blood Bowl, etc., if you persevere with the "darwinian" nature of the early game--and simply understand that warriors will die--the game eventually 'opens up' as the warriors that do survive slowly acquire the skills and gear necessary to become even better.  As additional hero/warrior slots and types unlock, and the money starts flowing, things get better and better.
The RNG can still be frustrating at times (most tactics games are like this), but as your warriors become more skilled and powerful, the chances for really bad streaks of 'bad luck' tend to be mitigated somewhat.  More than anything, with the right gear and/or stat increases, your warriors don't seem quite as fragile.
At this point, if I could change anything about the game, I'd perhaps add a little more information to the in-game tutorial.  While it goes through the motions of showing you a handful of common things you can do, it doesn't really expalin why you would want to do said things.  For example, learning how to disengage from battles and drawing the enemy into ambushes is extremely important, especially in the early part of the campaign, when your warriors are weak and can't trade blows for very long without being knocked out of combat.  Keeping your warriors 'alive' is also vitally important, as rout tests are based on the morale/number of warriors you have on the field of battle.  Therefore, if you have a deeply wounded warrior, sometimes its best to run him back to your cart (or some other safe area), and just let him sit out the remainder of the battle (instead of being knocked out).
The other thing that the tutorial doesn't really explain very well is the smuggler's den.  This part of the campaign game is extremely important, as it funds pretty much everything you do wtih your warband.  Without a fundamental understanding of how the smuggler's den works, you simply won't have the gold necessary to buy additional heroes/warriors, or pay for training, treatment, wages/pay, scouts, etc.
All in all, I'm having  a lot of fun with the game now.  The initial hurdle of getting through the first few battles, and coming to grips with how each of the game's campaign systems work may have taken more than a few hours, but I have to say now that the game is really fun.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
This game has a lot of potential, and I like a lot of what I am seeing--however, that said, I can't find myself recommending this game (yet) for one simple reason:  The hideously random nature of the game is just too ridiculous.
Now, don't get me wrong, I'm not just saying this in a "kneejerk" kind of way.  I understand perception bias (that sense that you're ALWAYS getting bad dice/percentage rolls, when you really aren't), and I can appreciate the fact that the game is difficult (sometimes brutally so).  Having played many games in which the RNG is a major factor to your success, I am well aware that streaks of good and/or bad luck happen.   But the RNG is just the tip of the iceberg, and when combined with all of the other randam "elements" of the game, it just makes for an extremely frustrating experience.
When you're not getting a string of bad rolls (say, five or six 75%-83% success failures in a row ... while the enemy team seems to never miss), you have to deal with unlucky positioning and/or creature spawns as you move your team around the map.  Because all movement is turn-oriented, and based on an initiative order, you're commited to your movements when you have no idea what's around the next corner.  In a general sense, this is fine, as it's all part of city-fighting.  But frustration sets in quickly when nearly every other mission spawns neutral creatures (like horrors, daemonettes, etc.) that utterly rip your team apart.  You make one unlucky move, and *bam* two of your warriors are dead.  You can't disengage.  You can't flee.  You're just dead.  And these aren't even "Hard" or "Brutal" missions--this is on "Normal".
I played one mission where a daemonette murdered nearly the whole enemy team (they had two members left) as I strategically outlanked both the enemy team and the daemonette, while I raided their wagon.  Pretty cool.  But even with only two members left, the enemy team would not route.  And then the daemonette, apparently wanting to "share the wealth", ran all the way across the map to where the rest of my team was, and proceeded to murder one of my warriors.  After which, my team suddenly routed, even though I still had my leader and one more member than the enemy.  I instantly lost the mission.  While it was kind of 'interesting' and cool that I could "play" the daemonette to kill the enemy team, in the end, the totally "artificial" way in which the daemonette just ran across the map to murder my team and randomly cause a route was highly annoying.  Which leads me to my next issue:  routing.
Routing seems completely random.  I can kill the enemy leader and half their team, and nothing happens.  But if my leader gats taken out, it's almost a certainty that my team will be instantly routed.  Route tests seem to happen without any kind of discernible indicator, too, besides some text.  One turn, everything is fine-and the next you simply lose.  LoL.  The concept behind being defeated by route testing is fine, but the implementation is poor and rather unsatisfying from a gaming perpective.  Which just about sums up the entire experience of this game.
On its own, the RNG is fine.  In other games, like Blood Bowl, or Talisman, it's an integrated part of the gameplay--because you can either strategize around the randomness, or the game is simply driven by the randomness and centered more on making choices.  Mordheim is neither:  you can't strategize many outcomes because positioning, encountering and randomly spawed creatures of ridiculous strength ruin any "game plan" you might have; and at many times the combat does seem very driven by the randomness while not providing anything even resembling an interesting choice to make.  More often than not, you have to just sit there, selecting the same thing you've selected for the last three rounds, while you slowly watch your team get ripped apart by unlucky circumstances and dice rolls.
I really want to like this game, but it just really seems to be missing something.  The only feeling I have while playing this game is one of intense frustration.  Which is really strange, because I absolutely love randomness and replayability in games.  Mordheim just doesn't have the right "mix' or synergy yet between randomness and game mechanics, and it's for this reason that I simply cannot recommend this game at this time.  That is not to say, however, that, in the future, this game will not be good.  As of now, the game is still in early access and many of the balancing and/or frustrating aspects of the game may still be tweaked.

In 1999 I was 14 and very much an impressionable nerd. My friends were interested in Warhammer Fantasy and one of them got the 3rd Edition 40k starter box. I had a look at his White Dwarf magazines and Mordheim jumped out to me. A role playing games based on end-time conspiracy theory set in the WHFB universe. Of course in 1999 we had the whole year 2000 prophesy nuts going beserk.
My first warband was the Cult of the Possessed, followed by the Witch Hunters. My friends played Skaven, Undead and Orcs, the last of which was released in White Dwarf magazine. My friend who played Skaven let his brother use the mercs from the starter box, and my own brother got the starter box and used mercs as well. On top of this, the table-top club we went to had about half a dozen guys also buy the starter box. In up, we had at least 12 people playing all different warbands every weekend for about 3 years.
Around 2003, I moved away from my home town and stopped table-top gaming for a while. I picked it up again however in 2009 and started playing Mordheim again until 2011. Life was a lot faster and I couldn't play as much as I used to. When I heard about this game coming out, I immediately jumped on board the band wagon because of my teenage passion for it and rekindling the fires of my youth.
Now for the game itself.
I feel that the game could use a little spit and polish to improve a few graphical and sound issues (as well as some dodgy camera angles), but overall this game captures the feeling of playing the tabletop game. The music and visuals are incredibly atmospheric and the turn based nature of the game works well as a translation of the table-top to the PC. Would I change any gameplay elements? Not really. The only real thing i'd like to see added is the ability to play a multiplayer campaign against friends or with jump-in games to mix things up a little bit.

A beautiful and atmospheric management game which ironically squanders its own potential through poor management. Fantastic art, animations, visual effects, music and general atmosphere. With a simple system of building, protecting and expanding a settlement while trying to construct a boat to escape the island. At first, it was one of the few games that genuinely feels exciting to return to.
However after only a few hours of playing, the promise is quickly lost. After running left and right as far as possible to survey the land, there is virtually no reason to explore anymore. The only activity that requires the player to leave their base is recruiting new helpers from camps around the map. Which requires tedious and exhausting amounts of time spent doing absolutely nothing but riding to their camp everytime you want and can afford new recruits. And this is indeed a commonality.
Because everything runs off currency, the player only has anything interesting to do; when they have currency. And so during those many, many moments when the player does not have any; they simply have nothing to do but sit around waiting for their helpers to get more for them. There isn't even that much to build, the game is actually lacking a lot of diversity that it needs to make expansion even interesting. There's literally barely anything to build or advance.
In the end, the game is sixty percent riding around to recruit more people, thirty percent waiting to get more currency, and ten percent buying things. And so ironically, the developers poor management of their resource management game mechanics makes it honestly, boring. Because so much time is spent grinding instead of doing anything interesting. The game looks and feels amazing, but the balance of the mechanics and the lack of activities ruins it completely.
Players cannot attack or fight, they cannot perform any unique activities, they have no reason to explore after the first sweep; as the monarch of the land the player spends almost all their time literally doing grunt work.
If the grind nature of the game itself and the lack of proper things to occupy the player is not bad enough, the game itself is fundamentally flawed to the point of potentially being unplayable.
There are three sources that players can get coins from consistently; farming, hunting and trading. The trading camp will despawn if players clear the trees around it while expanding their base, so if the trader camp spawns near any important points of interest; you have to choose between having it or destroying it to make use of that point of interest. The only consistent and reliable creatures you can hunt are rabbits, which only spawn in places you naturally have to raze while building your base. So you have to choose between hunting, or having an undersized base lacking primary buildings. Finally you have farming, which takes a long time to set up; costs a lot; and even better, during winter it doesn't work anymore. Every single primary method of getting currency, which the entire game runs off of, can be rendered null. And borderline will be rendered null if the game generates a map in the wrong way, so you can basically end up having your game become unplayable because in order to progress you had to destroy everything that you need to progress because the game spawned things in the path of your destruction. This includes the places where you recruit people, they too will be destroyed if you remove the trees around them to progress.
The ally programming for the game is also, poor. They automatically choose one side of the base to defend, you cannot choose or change this for yourself. So if the threats on the island are only coming from one side, all the defenders on the other side are useless. You cannot reassign them, and they assign themselves automatically so some archers you recruit will automatically be useless because some will always go to the side you don't need them on. And if your base is being destroyed from one side, all the defenders on the other side won't come to help even if they aren't busy. Sometimes allies will linger outside of the base walls even its night when the monsters will come, you cannot choose what buildings your builders prioritize. If you mark some trees in the wilderness to be cut down or something in the wilderness to be built and it happens to be near night or turn night, the builders will run out to do the thing and get themselves killed by the monsters. You cannot tell the builders to wait until day or retreat, and they like all the other characters in the game are very slow even when running.
The programming for the game itself is sub par and amatuerish. Players have to move onto a coin to pick it up, if a coin spawns on them they will not pick them up after the first coin because the game is not coded to check for a coin if they are present; it is coded to check for a coin on impact with one. Catapults will not be pulled back to the wall behind them if the wall they are set behind is destroyed, defenders will crowd at walls that haven't even been built yet over ones that have. Defenders will not change sides to fight off threats even if one side is not being attacked and all the defenders are there while the other side has none and is being attacked; and you have no control over this. Even the deer are badly programmed. The deer are coded to run when they are attacked or approached, but they continue to run in the initial direction they were scared towards even if something new scares them from another direction. Because the deer are not coded to change their direction actively when they are running, they only do it after they stop running. This makes it much harder to hunt deer because when your defenders shoot them and the deer runs, you have to wait for the deer to stop running before you can scare it back towards your defenders to shoot it because it is not coded to change its direction based on where the threat is when it is already running from one.
The game doesn't even have that much content, there's some randomization to the maps but barely any, and unique points of interest are actually more of a bother because you have to travel to them anytime you want to do something with them. It takes only an hour or so to reach most of the maximum upgrades on your base, and that's not because you get currency so fast; it's because there's that little upgrades you can make. Technically, this game only has an hour worth of unique content. Yet it's being sold for the price of some indie games, especially Rogue-likes, which offer double digit hours of gameplay.
The beautiful graphics, the atmosphere, everything artistic about the game itself is phenominal ten out of ten. But everything gameplay oriented about it is simply just bad. The lack of content, the grind, the lack of diversity, the bare bones poor design of all of the systems, mechanics and programming of the game itself.
It's fun for the first hour when everything is new, then it's just boring and subpar on every functional level. This is worth a few dollars at the most, if only for the effort that the artists and sound designers put in. And this is the updated re-release of the game, and it's this generally bad. This game was originally sold for the same price with even less content and polish.

This game does the TT origins justice. Even if you never played Mordheim for hours on end in real life, this modern day adaption is downright excellent. This is how an Early Access should go.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEVED FIRSTLY ON 20th OCTOBER 2015. (Update 8, Patch 4, EA rating - 95/100)
This is an updated review after full-release. Changes are written with capital letters. (Release 19/NOV/2015, v. 1.0.4.1).
My overall rating for Mordheim: City of the Damned: 100/100
Another adaptation from Warhammer universe, this combines elements of real-time strategy and RPG genre. Decent atmospheric settings full of horror and merciless battles, that is what this game promises you. Add a management of your warband, improvement of skills and a decent portion of strategy with luck and you have, what it is really called. War over cursed city, which we will look into further in details.
GAMEPLAY
+ Good design and performance
+ Strategic map
+ Variety of actions and reactions (most of them are responsive)
+ Good tutorials
+ Warband management
+ Commented objectives, stories before and after the mission
+ VOICED STORIES AND INTRO ADDED
o Complex control
- Four factions only (may not be negative at all)
Gameplay is a decent part of the game and it is very well balanced. Now there are only four factions, but tactics, randomised elements on map and also important luck factor are creating a formidable game experience. Turn-based strategy is very well combined with RPG genre, so you have to improve your warband, change the position and disposition of the troops, after that, you have to fight your battles on the battlefield.
Battles need another strategy guidance, you have to rely not only on your warriors, but also to environment and luck. Everything is possible in war, so also here, even the weakest unit can disable or rout the strongest enemy with the right conditions and events happened.
Commented objectives, intros and outros to the mission are adding a great impression to the atmosphere of the whole game. Player can feel himself/herself like the biggest general and strategist in the world.
VISUALS
+ Excellent graphics
+ Art style
+ Cam view
+ Wounds have influence on characters' appearance
Visually is Mordheim stunning. Perfect set of backgrounds, various part of Mordheim, nice details on units and many features have a wonderful impression on a player. Also your warriors may suffer wounds and injuries, which are visible then, so you can tell, who is a novice and who battle-toughened veteran.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Well composed
+ Theme for each faction, map
+ RELEASED AS AN EXCLUSIVE OFFER FOR ALL PLAYERS
Soundtrack adds points for Mordheim: City of the Damned, themes are adequately changing, underlining both nature of each faction and sinister atmosphere of cursed city of Mordheim. After full release it was added and automatically downloaded to game folder (link specified at store page).
MULTIPLAYER
+ Balanced
+ Various mods
o Seeking by rating (adjustable)
Multiplayer also provides another possibilities for your warband to perform, you can choose of plenty modes and community is fair and friendly. There is also "Exhibition" mode, where no penalties will remain after ending. For other, experienced units are recommended, because loss can disrupt your precisely build warband in one unlucky mission. Though you can seek the enemy just to suit your rank, so it is compensable and you do not have to have an elite unit at all.
SUMMARY
This title is a very wonderful adaptiation of Warhammer universe, yet in the process of perfection through Early Access. Also turn-based strategy and RPG combination seems very promising, though there might be some bugs and people should be aware of that and considering this during their reviews, written or spoken, does not matter what. Developers are working fast, communicating with community and releasing patches regularly, each with huge balance.
About the price, game is complex, replayable, I understand that 39,99 EUR might be expensive for some players (Early Access costed 31,99 EUR), but it is worthy, singleplayer for sure, multiplayer experience are giving also points to this title. Though it is very similar to late Early-Access phase, it has those improvements, which exactly were needed to be done.
The game is recommended for Warhammer fans, turn-based strategy, RPG players and also players outside this genres. Each of us has a bit of dark fantasy within us.

I don't write reviews, ever; but this game warrants so much more than a simple review. It warrants our thanks.
The main draw of this game is its combat... and it's done incredibly well. It's pretty much the quintessential martial arts fighting game. Sloclap really outdid themselves. It truly is hard to describe how well done the combat is done in this game, but i'll try.
The combat is easy to learn, hard to master. There are four stances, Front L/R and Back L/R each with 3 attack slots and an alternate attack slot. There are over 150+ moves in the game that you can learn and your 'Combat Deck' can be completely customized to how you like to play with different moves you learn throughout gameplay. I have yet to meet someone that fought exactly like I do. There are 3 Styles: Windfall, Khalt, and Forsaken. Each one of these starting styles begin with a basic moveset and a unique ability. Windfall players can avoid attacks, Forsaken players can parry attacks, and Khalt can absorb attacks. There is also another style in-game that can be unlocked that is in the style of Drunken Boxing. All players can feint and dodge attacks. Utilization of these mechanics along with the customization of your unique moveset is really what makes this game great.
I can tell the development team worked a LONG time on the combat in this game. It is the exact opposite of clunky. Most moves flow together seemlessly and effortlessly. With a wide-range of moves to collect, dozens of hours can be spent to hone your martial arts prowess and develop your very own style. You can even become a Mentor in-game, which allows you to open your own school to share your movesets with your students. Amazing.
The PVE aspect in this game is short, but fun as hell. The world map was designed similarly to Dark Souls. All of the different areas connect together to a main hub. When you begin, you can choose to go any path you like, and it's not invalid. From what I can tell, the NPC's scale to your level.
The main draw to this game is the PVP. Currently, there is only 1v1 arena matches, but I think they will release new gametypes as the development continues. Fighting other people in this game is truly a unique experience. Each match is different and engaging, because everyone's style of play is different. Some people like to play deliberate and defensively, others like to play aggresively and wild. Each of these has their weaknesses that can be exploited if you utilize all of the tools that the game gives you. After playing this game a while, you really start to feel like a martial arts master.
The community in this game is amazing. There is no chat function, akin to Dark Souls, which I think is great. But people communicate through emotes and context clues. I met a lot of really great people that have helped me in this game; it's really comforting to know that the community is non-toxic, because that could really destroy a game like this.

First thing's first. I enjoy Kinetic Void a lot. I've had this game for over a year now, and in that time I've seen it progress remarkably far, with most of the work going into the Shipyard (by far this game's most impressive feature) and the general usability. The game is in a very playable state, but make sure you read at least some of the tutorials and give it some time to get used to the way the editor works - it's a great tool if you give it time.
The shipyard, where you build your vessels, is almost at completion (I think they mentioned more parts were to be added), but mechanically it's there and it's very robust. There's a working galactic economy, and factions will vie for control of star systems.
Yes, the game's got lots of features to come - some more ambitious ones rely on good sales -  but then what other game allows you to choose almost any given space ship from any game/movie/series that someone has built and fly it around in a sandbox galaxy. You can also change the game files so that, say, one faction uses all Star Destroyers, while another has ships from the Halo universe, Mass Effect or whatever you like.
And this is without mentioning the hundreds of stellar, original, designs created by players and uploaded to the workshop (early workshop integration was an excellent decision by the devs). Most 'Space' games will give you the choice of a handful of ships to pilot and own, whereas KV's 'build your own' approach means that aside from as many as YOU can build, you can tap into the creative output of hundreds of other players, many of whom have written backstory/lore for their ships in their workshop descriptions. These can be used to populate your universe.
The Devs are very open about how the game is progressing and I think that they are helped by a strong community. You get responses to any feedback or bug reports you leave very quickly and the direction in which the game is headed is very clearly layed out.
I spend about 90% of my time on this game in the shipyard, so I should make it clear that unless you plan to immerse yourself in the ship creation aspect, you probably won't get the most out of Kinetic Void, but if, like me, you get sucked up into the whole creative process of building a ship from scratch, you can't go wrong. A big thumbs up from me! :)

Fantastic concept, will never be worth $20 dollars in it's current state.
The game has a unique ship building system which is sort of unique. Otherwise, it's nothing special.
There appear to be quite... 'variety' of things to do, and events that unfold througout the.. 'galaxy,' like wars, and what appears to be something similar to a stock market of sorts. Otherwise, that's it.
I tried to see what this war thing was all about, only to find nothing different (in the few hours that I had spared after slowly traveling to it), heck even the spawnrate for hostile ships seemed the same.
You can mine asteroids, salvage destroyed enemy ships, and fight enemy ships, follwed up by crashing into very badly textured planets, which you can't really do anything at, as of yet (I would think it might work as some sort of psuedo space station-asteroid that you could both mine and trade at, or whatever).
The developers developed the system to be overly complex, only to supply extremely minimal explenations. Experimenting is almost a must, just to get a complete handle of how to do stuff. At some points, I even found myself pressing every single key on my keyboard, just to see which button did what, as there were no other ways to finding out, until maybe recently.
The space flight itself is incredibly boring, and you may as well be running around in your room, holding a car in your hand, squeeling "Vroom!" like a child- although only moving your ship at a snails pace. In otherwords, the ships handle with an unnecessarily complex system (which about half is redundant/useless), and fly like toys.
The combat is not much better, depending on how you do it.
Most of the time, you will be just sitting there, either blasting your lasers/rockets/whatever at the enemy, whittling down their shields, and then their hull. Then they go boom. Then you move on.
Sometimes, the ships even crash into your own, absolutely obliterating you.
The best way to earn money is to just grind the asteroids away, and sell the ores you get at the stations. (which are now incredibly ♥♥♥♥ing hard to find, since they made only one every 2 lightyears spawn compared to the usual 10 or so in small groups you used to be able to find).
The only problem with selling is that you need to first take your ship's inventory, move everything into the station's inventory, and then go to the shop, click on your inventory, then click on the checkbox for your cargo, then the ore/water you collected, then finally.. sell them for a measily price of what might as well be 2 cents.
This might be easier if it were in a better GUI, and the redundant stuff being removed. (EG shops being able to buy your stuff directly from ship inventory).
The exploration aspect is ok, but bassically once you'd seen a single system, you'd seen them all.
the different faction ships are not really much different from the other faction's, even though the factions are random gen, which I understand- making randomly generated ships as well would probably be a bit too much for these devs.
Regardless, there's no point in exploring, beyond trade (which combined with the slow-paced travel system = you tearing hair out).
Rating?
EDIT:
1/10, minimal to no work has been done. Very little has been added, fixed or changed. Presumably, the project has been abandonded.
Dont buy it, it will just be another game to taunt you with regret in your steam library.

With the knowledge that it is an early access game, I am going to hold my tongue, or fingers a little. While I love space sims especially with that sandbox aspect I have a few complaints.
I started a career mode game so I could try it out. I hadn't played the game in a few months and wanted to see what was new... Not much was for starters, but that is to be expected, a lot of Early Access games don't have a lot of updates (Except for something like Space Engineers ). I picked the random parts and started building my ship. After 1 and a half hours of fumbling around both because of player error, and because its a little weird... I press launch only to have to put in subsystems. (no I couldn't read the tutorial, the UI freaked out and overlapped the words) Once I figure (sortof) that out, I launch it... The game loads, and within 5 seconds.. not anymore or any less, I was destroyed... So I tried again... and again... Only to end with the same result. Then I go to the main menu, and decide to try and load a 65 part ship from my workshop... It loaded, and a warning popped up saying that I had to many parts and it might crash... 65 parts, and I hadn't even added the big shiny hanger doors and millions of hanger control modules I wanted to.. So I decided to launch it (and after some more subsystem fumbling) got it launched. I fought off the army outside, and then got up to my max speed of 57. In space. In a simulation game. Then I look at the directory, and find out if I press T and turn off a shield thing that stops me I will go faster... So a top speed of 83. Way to go for the USS Gweepo... A new speed Record. Then I point it towards the nearest planet hoping I will be able to use the new mining laser thing I put on to mine stuff off the planet. I watch as the numbers slowly decrease from 202.1 to 202 to 201.9 and so on. After seeing that I did the only sensible thing. Tried to warp towards the planet... Only to warp into it. Ten minutes later I spawn again and warp (correctly luckily) to the planet and try and land on it. Only to die again.
Overall, I think this game CAN have potential if the devs iron out the bugs that it has. They (he\she\it, I dunno) seem to be very interested in te steam community so I give them points just for that.. Also, collision, and speed especially when it says that if you press the "T" key it activates Newtonian flight, should mean I have a fixed acceleration, up to an infinite speed. Not just a faster speed. Big ships need a boost, the AI needs help, Weapons need balancing, People need a little breathing room at spawn. Along with that comes the good stuff about it. You can (at the risk of crashing) build masive ships that destroy entire fleets (it was fun, until the game engine died) You can also build little fighters that reach 800 (units of speed and distance needed) While it may not be the #1 space sim on my wish list (Limit Theory is so awesome :3 ) It has a fighting chance. I can't wait to see what comes of it!

PvP needs some major changes. The game Airmech tries to be isn't very enjoyable. The matches are long and boring, and sit at an unreasonably high skill floor.
Airmech tries to be a Mix of MOBA and RTS, but ends up playing like a MOBA that wants to be an RTS, with large masses of units that obselece the Airmech to be nothing more than a clunky RTS cursor, and with upcoming changes to re-install "command mode" that enables almost full-blown RTS controls, the Airmech will drift more in the way of being an overglorified RTS camera.
Maps are built like MOBA maps, with outposts acting similar to lane towers, being lane-centric, and movement being focused on mech movement, rather than unit movement, but with RTS unit controls, you end up with the tankiest units being dominant over all units, resulting in very static, un-diverse unit usage and very mirrored gameplay, depsite the very large and diverse base unit roster in the game. Games play out almost the same every match, with a small skirmish for the middle post, using nothing more than Tanks and artillery units, and then a slow snowball for the side that wins the midfight, slowly building up Early-game, and then Later-game Tanks supported by Anti-Air units, limiting the enemy mech from doing anything except copying the unit composition thier enemy is using.
Many units are blatantly useless and overshadowed by others, not at all helped by the high-tier group of players taking issue with every balance change or new mechanic that doesn't allow Tanks and thier beloved " skilled micro" gameplay to be the dominant meta. These high-tier players don't understand that keeping the gameplay bland and the skill floor high will not allow the game to grow, somehow expecting a niche inde game like this to grow into an e-sport overnight with the gameplay it has now.
The developers have pushed some very interetsing changes that look like they'd go in the direction that would be healthy for the game, such as the previous "arm mechanic" much despised by the high-tier community, or shifting power balance towards Mech abilities, to better allow mechs to fight against units, which was not recieved well on a high-level either.
At the same time, the developers push changes that conserve the current game's state, such as Command mode, which, as I stated, serve to trivialize the role of the mech on the battlefield, or add new, but unecessary units to the roster, that either serve to become uselesss due to thier supposed role not being viably present in games, such as new Light units supposedly used for harass or flanking roles that are never used due to tank dominance, or units that are hurtful to balance, such as a new Late-game Anti-Air unit that is heavily armed and armored, and so hurts the mech-to-unit balance further that it was in the late-game.
This game a huge potential, and is great for messing around. The community at large is wonderful, and the game, at a low level, can be fun to play with friends or against bots, but at the higher level, where the depth of the game should be present, Airmech Strike just doesn't hold up in it's current state.
I would strongly recommend you try the PvE derivative game, Airmech Wastelands, if you're interested, however.

After all this time Capcom finally did it. Ok, after RE5 and probably one of the worst games I ever seen: RE6, was not difficult to do something better, but this game is really good, one of the best of this year without a doubt. If for you Resident Evil is all about zombies, Wesker and T-Virus... just avoid this game, if for you RE is about survival horror, exploration and avoiding enemies, solve puzzles, be in an state of tension every single time you need to come back all the way with a new item on your inventory... this game is a must have.
This is RE back to its roots, and feels so good, and this is so bad for us because you'll have a hard time while playing it.
At the start the game show a total chase for Outlast's style (that's great), but when you move throught it, the game reveals its true form: a traditional Resident Evil adventure, more than one might believe.
Its story hoocked from the beginning (with its minor plot flaws) but it's far more interesting than tipical RE history, has some unbelievably scary moments, exploration, puzzles (not difficult ones. But there's one optional puzzle very much clasical and intrincate), that tension when you open a door, even if you already entered in that room many times, the weird things, the cryptic notes throwing some info, run out of bullets...
The game takes successful elements from contemporary horror games and mix it with the classical elementes of the saga. If you don't like RE maybe you find some things odd but if not, this is RE, every bit of the game. Graphically it’s beautiful to look at, has a good sound and music, the soundtrack has two or three good themes (Go Tell Aunt Rhody is great) and the rest are just anecdotal ambient, has characters with personality (one of them with an awesome interpretation) and the game it's filled with some totally unexpected awesome moments, the plot is very interesting (it's the deepest and more rich story on RE and the best narrated) the story is a crescendo, a big one. Even the end credits are awesome!
The "bad" things are that I really think they should called the game Resident Evil with no number on the title, and like I said before this is not Outlast or Dead Space, Dying Light... and there's some things odd, like the controls, ponderous (the character has probably the more slow sprint in history), that the flashlight automatically turns on and off in concrete moments, cannot hide in places or peek around a corner... but all that is because it has clasical elements but even so... it feels weird sometimes. But overall, a great game and a great experience.

Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 offers a unique world war 2 experience centered around squad tactice, movement, and suppression. The game is by no means perfect, but the positive aspects far outweigh the negative aspects.
The squad system works very well, and most levels are designed to support it. Each squad has a purpose and their weaponry reflect that. The players is naturally guided to use each squad as they are intended. The AI is also solid, for the most part. The level design is mostly linear with a few alternate routes that mostly serve as flanking routes. However, when the level does open up and the player is free to complete objectives as they wish, the game really shines. One particular level involves the player clearning out a town with an assault squad and tank. The player must maintain complete awareness of their surroundings, as well as understand the weaknesses of each part of their squad (eg. assault squad is weak to fire in open areas, and the tank is weak to panzerfausts and AT guns). This blend of open ended level design allows and squad-based mechanics allow the players to immerse themselves within the environment whilst planning a stregic approach while adjusting their strategy on the fly when they need to. These are the most fun moments of the game.
While I still definitely recommend the game, the flaws are incredibly noticeable and become exacerbated in the mission involving the industrial sections of Carantan. Throughout the game, some minor pathing issues and bugs can arise, resulting in incredibly stupid friendly AI routines when given orders. The game's utilization of auto saves can also get inferiating when placed 10+ minutes apart, especially when the player has to fight through mutliple tough enemy squads. These are mostly minor and don't hinder enjoyment too much, but are compounded with the above-mentioned level. Many bugs and pathings issues arise, making AI movement difficult and costly, especially when trying to flank or move out of fire. The worst example of this is a curb before the player enters a warehouse. Friendly AI, including that in another squad not lead by you, will get caught on the curb and unable to advance after some gittery movement and a bit of player-assisted jumping and pushing. To make this even worse, this occurs right before several tough enemy squads enter the warehouse. The auto save distance is also terrible. In order for the player to reach the first auto save, the player must wipe out about 20 enemy soldiers. In an arcade-style shooter like Call of Duty, this wouldn't be a big deal. In a game with realistic ballistics, weapon movement, and damage, this can take upwards of 15 minutes on harder difficulties, and with the AI problems present, it is infuriating beyond belief. In fact, I am writing this review because of this level. It is ridiculous. I am a perfectionist trying to get through without any friendlies killed, an it's almost impossible to do so with these issues present. Despite the bull**** in this mission, the game's still a lot of fun and very unique compared to other WW2 shooters.

Review updated on 10-29-2015,
Pros:
- Mordheim on the PC
- Graphics, loosely bringing to life the grim world of WFRP which is the setting that specialist game's Mordheim takes place.
- 4 Races to choose from.
- Uses names, items, archtypes, and warband classes we're used to from the Mordheim rulebook.
- Uses its own unique turned based system (re-read that please) that is trying to mimic XCom:EA. So if you guys liked XCom:EA, you'll feel at home here more or less.
Cons:
- Developer -easily- manipulated by a few hardcore members of the community.
- No Alt-F4ing. Driver crash? You're screwed. Game crash? You're screwed. Game bug that requires you to Alt-F4 out or abandon the mission? You're screwed. They add a new feature that has a bug that requires you to Alt-F4 or abandon mission? You're hosed. Power outage do to thunderstorm? You're screwed.
- NOT Mordheim. If you were expecting a recreation of the table top miniatures game, like Cyanide's Bloodbowl 1 or 2, forget it. The developer has stated they lack the experience and funding to do that. Additionally they've stated they have no interest in doing that and that in their opinion "it wouldn't work". Suggesting the developers are inexperienced and a lot of it shows throughout the game.
- Arcane Spell failure on armor? In -MY- Warhammer? WTF? Again, its own rule system hacked together by an inexperienced developer.
- Frustrating gameplay; be prepared for AI with artificially inflated wounds (think 200+ while yours are 100 or less).
- Be prepared for Demons who've been artificially front loaded with skills and hitpoints because NOT HARDCORE Enough! to randomly appear in your missions and annihilate your warband.
- Camera locking (that's right, camera locks in during AoE casting).
- Camera not designed for a turned based tactics game. For a game modelling itself similar to XCom, it lacks the 3/4th isometric camera that worked for that game.
- Turned based gameplay similar to Valyria Chronicles, in that it's third person.
- No symbols or signs to denote what effects a friend or enemy has. Is an enemy on overwatch? Is an enemy about to ambush?
- Pretty much all of the tools you've come to love from games such as Wasteland 2, Shadowrun Returns, or XCom, are gone. The developer decided to reinvent the wheel dispite lacking funding, time, man power and enthusiasm. Chock up to another IP rental from GW for quick cash based on the name only.
- Warband model customization (what made Specialist Games "special") is non-existant. Be prepared for all of your model's faces to look the same.
- Additional races will potentially be released as paid DLC.
The dev claims things will change over time especially nearing release. However, the more glaring issues, especially the core gameplay will remain. A lot of their responses seem unenthusiastic, claiming lack of funding or time. Lack of experience shows both in the gameplay balancing, art design, and animation.
When asked why certain features, staples of the table top are missing, the developer claims: "we lack funding, and we didn't want to settle for just ok", in reference to weapons on skaven tails or Sisters of Sigmar whips. You then look at the in-game animations and they look awful. If those pass for "better than ok", I'd hate to see what "ok" must mean to these guys.
Mordheim was never really about the rules, rarely was any Specialist game. It was about modelling and the hobby, allowing you to customize the looks of a warband and have some backstory, something you normally didn't do for rank and file troops. This is something the developer totally missed.
Here's hoping the game improves by release.
Updated on 10-29-2015
- Although I feel like this was a wasted oppertunity for a game that mirrored the table top, on its own without the Mordheim tag, it's decent and improving.
- The developer seems pretty open to community feedback and is willing to implement changes within the framework of what they already have. That can be a good thing, but I'm also seeing a bit of "design by comittee" going on which can be bad. And currently there seems to be quite a lot of design by comittee to cater to a vocal but extremely hardcore (think Alt-F4, or crash, or power outage and you can lose your entire warband) group.

What can I say about this game?...  Well, it’s fun.  It’s frustrating.  It’s simple.  It’s small.  Did I mention it’s fun?  That said, it's not worth $10, and I'll tell you why;
Roller Coaster Rampage is pretty different from every other roller coaster game I’ve played.  The coasters in this game are virtually “created” as you ride them.  Trust me, it’s a very unique experience, and often that is where a lot of frustration comes from.
There are 2 modes you can currently play in Roller Coaster Rampage.  There’s the Campaign mode where you basically try to collect as many gems as you can while linking your on-the-fly track with already pre-constructed pieces of track.  Then there’s the Free Ride mode, in which you just make a coaster any way you like.  You'll find yourself spending most of your time in Free Ride, as the Campaign mode is rather easy and only has about 30-ish challenges to finish.
I found quite a few things dissapointing about this game.  One disappointment with this game was the content seemed to be drastically lacking.  It’s virtually impossible to build the same coaster, but you only have one location so the scenery all around you is always the same.  The location is rather small as well, leaving you struggling to build any ride that lasts longer than a minute or two.  The coaster itself was also always the same.  You couldn’t change to a wooden one, or a hanging one, or any other coaster than the standard metal one.  The starting station was always the same, however in Campain Mode it was sometimes rotated a bit to make your launching and landing directions different.
Element impacts (crashing into objects) were random as well.  Some things like the coaster track legs would get out of your way as you crossed them and other times you would ram into them and your hard work would come to an immediate and very violent end.  Occasionally when legs did move they would interfere with a part of the track you already built, leaving you to sloppily go right through a track leg when you went back and rode the coaster after it's built.  It was impossible to know if it’s safe to cross under another track or not.  This made most of my coasters climb as they progressed and then dive back into the station at the end, instead of having a large hill at the very beginning.  It also kept me from doing several cool maneuvers, like having a loop run through the center of another loop.  Scenery was also touch-and-go as well.  It was hard to tell what you could safely pass through and what you couldn’t.  On occasion, sometimes an object would be deadly to your coaster one pass and safe the next.  It was a mix that made it hard to do the quick decision making that the game requires you to make.
Another thing that brought frustrations was the control layout.  I found the controls really awkward, especially since you have to really think fast while playing.  Your acceleration/breaking and “roll” was controlled by the WASD keys while the arrow keys controlled left/right and up/down movement.  You also had the numbers 1-3 for “stunts” like left/right corkscrews and looping.  It probably would have been a much better setup with Q and E for the corkscrews and maybe R or F for looping.  That would be more common, and easier, for those who are practiced in FPS games.
It’s not all bad though.  I really enjoy this game as a simple time waster.  It’s fast to load and you can quickly get yourself into the “Free Mode”.  Even if you’ve only got 10 minutes to waste you can get a few rides in before you have to shut it down.  I often find myself firing up this game in those few minutes before leaving for work, just because I know it’s a game that you can be satisfied with only playing it 5 minutes.
The purchase price of $9.99 is very high, and it's the main reason I'm not giving my recommendation for this game.  There's just too much lacking.  A lack of content makes it nothing more than a quick time waster.  The controls are frustrating.  The unchanging scenery is just lazy game designers.  It's not worth $10.
I bought the game as part of a 4-game bundle for $5.99 which makes my purchase worth it.  If you can buy it like that, or on sale for no more than $2, then go for it.  Otherwise you're just paying Cadillac prices to own a Ford.

I know that sounds harsh but it's something that has to be said.
A lot of people aren't recommending this game.
I see why. Roller Coaster Rampage is simply a game about Roller Coasters. That's it.
However, This game delivers everything that it promises. (I haven't seen much destruction in my playtime though.) The graphics for this game look 2007-ish, and not up to modern specs. The Coaster Creation is an innovative idea, although it takes a bit of getting used to. Most players would feel more comfortable playing this with a controller.
The campaign (as it's called in game) is merely a set of simple challenges that can be completed quite easily, and they seem very repetitive. There is only 1 park available in Roller Coaster Rampage, and it gets small and boring, fast. If you could walk around the park and visit other attractions, the game could be reasonably fun. However, you cannot.
Free-Play mode is where the game shines. The track can be easily created and then you can ride the insane monstrosity you've created (But I couldn't find a save button). It's pretty neat, but construction can get messy with lots of rails and support beams everywhere. When you hit high speeds the track seems to get choppy (even though the game renders at a nice 60 fps), and the railcars seem unable to follow physics.
Workshop support is 'Coming Soon!', but I have no idea how long that's been there.
But why do I recommend this game? It's simply a fun little time killer. I bought it for $2.50 during the Holiday Sale, and that's as much as this game is worth. If you're thinking about dropping $10 on this, wait for it to go on sale for $2 or less.
tl;dr
Graphics: 7/10 - looks cartoony, but a little on the low-def side.
Overall Gameplay: 6/10 Needs fine tuning, and a controller greatly helps.
Campaign: 5/10 - Average challenges that add little to mechanics and design.
Free-Play: 8/10 - Fun, but you cannot save tracks. Physics and Construction seem a bit wonky.
Overall Score - 6/10. Average, but definitely not worth $10. Wait for a sale.

This game is enjoyable, but it's not worth $10. The premise is amusing enough, and was executed adequately. I loved all the historical references, especially the more obscure ones (such as the speculation that Panzer was in Mädchen in Uniform), as well as the irreverent (to put it mildly) sense of humor throughout. And the military-related jokes were spot on.
But the problems were present, and quite jarring. For one thing, the game is chock full of grammatical and spelling errors, and rather obvious ones at that. Then there's the bugs: Skipping in one place made my game crash so badly that only the Task Manager could close it, and even then, my Steam client thought it was still running, so I couldn't restart it or play a different game. Even using the Task Manager to close Steam didn't help here. The only thing that helped was restarting my computer. Also, there's a line of dialogue in the kitchen that is attributed to Panzer, no matter who's actually saying it, and under some conditions, the school music plays throughout the rest of the game, even when you change scenes, and even while other music was playing. Such basic errors are inexcusable, and indicative of rushed, sloppy work.
Then there's the adult content patch. It hardly does anything, other than adding a risqué drawing of whatever tank you manage to win over. The drawings are nice, but they're really not much, and the patch itself is even bigger than the actual game. But perhaps this is due to the fact that this game was made with TyranoBuilder (hint to the creators--RenPy is much better in this regard, and many others).
Overall, I give this game a 6/10. Fun to play for the most part, but the bugs and bad grammar really bring it down.

Over the years, Resident Evil has gone from horror to more of a action focused game, this is undenialbe. But with the release of Resident Evil 7, the series has finally gotten the balance of the two it desperately needed as of recent.
Unlike other Resident Evil games, this one is always in first person and while some die hard fans of the games that came out before this one may be a little miffed about it, I feel like it adds to the immersion of the character a lot more.
And immersive this game is, every action is in first person and you can interact in situations where other horror games wouldn't allow you to. For example, in the early part of the game, you have you hand pinned to a wall by a screwdriver. The game will prompt you with a QTE where you try to screw the screwdriver out of your hand, but no matter what, you can't. You can try all you might, but either way, that hand is going to come off when the chainsaw comes out. You block it with your hand once you get it free, and the blood practically rains on you, and after its all over what can you do? You can pick up your severed hand and put it in your inventory.
And for fans who want a bit of action in there, don't worry, you can have a cheesy-yet-awesome chainsaw fight with one of the big baddies of the game. Even before that you can drive a car around a garage and ram into him a bunch, why? Cause it's awesome thats why. It's small moments like these that make people remember the game even after they stopped playing it.
Another thing the game has going for it is the absolutely amazing realistic graphics, the use of real photos as textures for the game made it a lot more scary when it seems so real. For people who worry about it hurting performance, fret not, for the game is optimized so that it runs good on almost all computers. Resident Evil 7's soundtrack is quite good as well and deserves a listen.
Further more, for players who wish to have more modes for the story/game, the DLC's are worthwhile purchase. From the addicting migrane that is Ethan Must Die mode to the story focused Daughters, the Banned Footage DLCs are very good. As of writing this, End of Zoe, which is said to be a story DLC focused on Zoe after the events of Resi 7, has not come out yet. The same applies for Not a Hero.
Though, it does have some bad in it like all games do, for one being the small amounts of jumpscares there are, and some of them feel not scary at all and more like the original Evil Dead's cheesy close ups to the faces. Particuarlly with Mia when she turns in the beginning of the game, her close up does look gross and creepy, but her "creepy laugh" comes off more as a witch's laugh in a kid's halloween special.
All in all though, Resident Evil 7 has breathed fresh air into a series thats been drug through the mud the past couple years and I have good faith that this will continue in future installments of it.

The one thing I didn't expect was that there were genuinely tense/scary moments that I rarely feel when playing RE games, and I even jumped a few times.
The puzzles could have been more difficult, and the tension was mostly near the first part of the game, but it was still a really fun game.  Whenever I finish a game and feel a bit bummed out that it is over, I know that it was a good one!

Devil May Cry 4 is an excellent PC port. I am not a hardcore hack and slash fan; DMC games are the only games in the genre that I've really played. I first played DMC4 when it was released on the PS3 and used to play it almost exclusively. I always felt the game was very fair in how it treated the player. Enemies telegraph their attacks and, in most cases, at least, will not initiate attacks if they are off-screen, so there should be few frustrating surprises for most players. Most bosses are a lot of fun to fight.
Both of the playable characters are fun to play, and they are different enough from each other that mastering both of them will likely take a player a solid amount of time. I do feel that Dante is much more complicated than Nero, but newcomers to the series will be playing as Nero, so they will have time to get familiar with the game playing as him before they start playing with the more complicated Dante. Nevertheless, I felt that they are both rewarding to play. Creating stylish combos is extremely satisfying and rewarding.
The campaign itself suffers from severe repetition; nearly half of the game is made up of backtracking. The story is lackluster and has glaring questions that were not addressed. However, the weak story is forgivable due to the game's focus on action, and it is perfectly fine to ignore it entirely. The backtracking is a problem that I cannot ignore; the latter half of the campaign feels very repetitive even if I'm playing as a different character with a vastly different moveset. Many of the bosses have to be fought multiple times, and, unfortunately, the variety of bosses is not as great as it was in DMC3.
I don't feel that DMC4 is unpleasant to look at, but its age shows. However, the game is a good port; it runs very smoothly and I did not feel like I was lacking options. The level design is suitably dark and the atmosphere is appropriate. Some enemy designs appear to have been reused from older DMC titles, but it's fun enough to beat up enemies that I hardly mind. The scoring system and the unlockables add replayability to the game.
Turbo mode and Legendary Dark Knight mode, which are both exclusive to the PC version of the game, make the PC port worth purchasing over its console counterparts, especially considering how well the game runs on PC. I feel that these features make the PC version worth buying over the console versions. Turbo mode speeds the game up, making a fast-paced action even faster. Legendary Dark Knight mode spawns hordes of enemies. Both of these features make the game so much better and more enjoyable, even as someone who played a great deal on the PS3. Playing the game with a controller is imperative; this game was not made with a keyboard and mouse in mind.
