This is if the HBO Band of Brothers miniseries was turned into a tactical FPS game. You are Sgt. Matthew Baker of the 502nd PIR of the 101st Airborne and you command 13 men. You are dropped behind enemy lines and find yourself surrounded by only a small handful of fellow paratroopers. It is hours before the landings would begin and you must clear and secure key roads, bridges, and towns against outnumbering odds with only a handful of men and limited ammunition. For eight days, you and your squad would slowly regroup and begin to fight their way to secure key towns such as St. Come du Mont, Viervelle, and the prize, Carentan. Gearbox has replaced the familiar gameplay concepts of both Call of Duty and Battlefield with a very realistic, authentic, yet simple gameplay. Focusing on trying to fight your way through overwhelming odds and doing your best to keep your men alive.
Now, I enjoyed this game and its series just as much as the HBO Band of Brothers series. Not only does it feel authentic, but it plays realistically and smart as well. Instead of facing dozens of spawning enemies like in Call of Duty. You would encounter small German fire teams that try to outsmart you and your men. It makes it nearly impossible to go charging blindly at fixed positions like you would do in Call of Duty titles. This game has enemies that not only are deadly and difficult to fight, but very smart as well. A single burst from an MG42 would kill you instantly if you are not playing smart and quick on your feet. Fire and Manuever tactics are the key to you and your squad's survival. The AI in this game are SUPER smart, if your squad takes fire, your men will automatically respond by taking cover and returning fire. Brothers in Arms also allows you to direct your fireteams, using the most common US Airborne tactic (the Four F's) FIND them, FIX them, FLANK them, and FINISH them. Use one fireteam to provide suppressing fire to pin down the Germans and flank around them with another fireteam as an Assault element.
Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 is an absolute MUST-HAVE for any WW2 Gamer Fan! Provides a great story, strong characters, and very smart and realistic gameplay. You feel the value of your squadmembers, because it is nearly impossible to pass any mission all by yourself. With a great historical research team at Gearbox, you actually will find yourself in the boots of a Squad leader in the 502nd PIR on DDAY. Very fun, very challenging, and above all, very smart! A flat-out 10/10!

I did come very close to giving this game a thumbs down, if only on the basis that the storefront (in fact, all the storefronts, also on Android, Xbox, PS4) is deliberately misleading about what Funk of Titans actually is. The short and narrow of the issue: if you're looking for a traditional 2.5D platformer that lets you explore levels, this isn't it. Funk of Titans is an autorunner, of the same ilk as games like Bit.Trip Runner and Rayman Jungle Run.
That means that your character follows a pre-determined path and you are given the opportunity to perform actions at the right moments. The simplistic nature of the controls for such games makes them ideal fodder for mobile stores, and indeed, FoT started out as a mobile game whose premise - taking the myth of Perseus and turning it into a Blaxpoitation parody, complete with a version of Zeus that has a little more than a passing resemblance to Samuel L. Jackson. It doesn't take itself particularly seriously - the game is littered with nerd gags in the form of collectables and unlockables.
So, with that being out of the way now, what are we looking at. Three worlds, 42 levels in total, you're looking at around 2-3 hours of playtime if you breeze through without trying to get all three medals, around 6 hours of playtime if you're a completionist and call for all three medals on each level, try to level up to the maximum and get all 21 achievements. It isn't a challenging game, even for the most casual gamer, and relies a lot more on blunt memory recall than skill. The secrets (in each case a Pegasus statue that gives you one of the requisite medals and grants you access to an end-of-level minigame) are pretty much signposted - you might miss them on the first run, but you'll know where it is by the time you come to your second run-through. Said minigame, which involves Perseus riding the game's version of Pegasus (a jet engine with a horse's head mounted on it) is funny the first time, fun the next few times, and teeth-gnashingly tedious and monotonous once you've had to go through it the 50th time.
Controls are responsive enough, although combat doesn't require a great deal of skill, with some very generous collision detection.
Graphically, it's a straight mobile port of a Unity Engine game, so you're looking that's par for the course with this type of game - PS2-level geometry, texture and shadow effects combined with some very in-your-face lighting effects. The music, which appears to have been licensed from an external composer, is top-notch, and it's a pity that there's no separate soundtrack available.
Knowing what you're getting, Funk of Titans is a fun, functional little casual time-waster that'll give you a few hours of entertainment. But it's also painful to witness the potential of such an imaginative principle being wasted on such a banal principle, and I hope Crowd of Monsters revives Funky Perseus at some point to give us a fully-fledged platformer one day, because goodness knows, the imaginative story and style deserves better than this.

So I am going to try and be as informative as I possibly can with this game.
The game has four factions each one with unique units that can wield and use varieties of armor and weapons. To start the game you are going to choose one of four factions, the choice of faction is crucial to your play style. Once chosen you are going to begin leveling, and yes you level everything, even the poor little meat shields you hide your damage dealers behind. This entire game is based on leveling, accept that fact and youll be perfectly happy with the game. Now the key detail of this game in my eyes is going to be resource management in the warband screen. EVERY MEMBER of your warband must be paid, and you must send wyrdstone to those who request it, miss four shipments and its game over. Inside your camp you can almost fully customize your characters (this is a detail of the game that i want more improvement on) by changing the styles of their gear and equipping them new armor and weapons, also training them over days in spell casting and skill use.
now once outside of your warbands camp youll be placed on the campaign screen (the newest update added this finally!). Once on the screen youll be given a variety of missions to choose from, all with varying difficulty and loot. Once you get your warband high enough you will be given an end of act mission. These end of act missions have objectives that must be completed such as placing sanctified hammers on statues, and cleansing the corruption from holy artifacts.
The actual gameplay is a turn based strategy format. Units take turns based on their initiation, this is lowered by heavier cumberson items and armor/weapons. In many ways I have found that the weaker glass cannon units go first most of the time, and depending on your faction you may or may not have any of those. Now one thing this games combat does very well is its implication of stances. there are many stances in this game including ambush dodge and parry, being the primary stances. Combat can be very difficult at times because your units move spaces may not get you in a proper postion to attack, and often leads to bottlenecking through doorways or over bridges. Each mission you recieve has a primary objective of killing all enemies or causing them to retreat. Retreat is caused by you forcibly removing morale from an enemy by either surrounding them and causing fear, or the killing of their units. (im not sure about this but it seems like killing enemy heroes and leaders causes a deeper impact on morale)
One thing to be wary of is any kind of % chance, as this game is still in Alpha I will go back and change this review as needed but as of now a 78% chance of climbing over a wall seems to have only a 30% success rate, and yes I have tested this by losing over 3 units to trying to climb one wall.
All in all this game is amazing, definitely a must have for any warhammer player, and a must try for any strategy enthusiast, this game will punish you through crippling soldiers or even permanent death though. So if you do decide to try it watch for ambushes, and stay away from charging Daemons! Enjoy!

This is a rather short, 6 hours tops, VN, telling a story of a guy, who was sent to the school, where all the girls are anthropomorphic version of tanks, and this fact is the main seller of the game. While this idea sounds interesting enough to buy the game just out of curiosity, after completing one route and starting the game anew to finish another one, you begin to see many problems it has.
You are Erwin, a cadet who was sent to Japanese Tank School as a part of his training. After arriving to the school however, you find out, that all of the students are girls, and they are actually tanks. Five of them can be dated. So you choose between:
- Sherman the Tomboy
- T-34 the Tsundere
- IS-2 the Yandere
- Panzer IV the Ditz
- Tiger I the Himedere (I think she's more like dandere though, but who cares)
So after choosing one, you start to work your way to the good ending, through some usual anime stuff, like school life, dates, hot springs and beaches.
Doesn't sound too bad so far? Well, for the first hour and a half you can get some enjoyment from it. Panzermadels got a heavy focus on comedy and using anime related stereotypes, and while jokes and references aren't always that funny, sometimes they can make you smile a bit. Also it's interesting to find out how things will work out with the girl you chose.
And when you get to the ending, you start to see the first problems.
First off, the endings are pretty much bad and very bad. After doing everything right and even getting a chance to visit the insides of a tank (kinda like the favourite joke of the devs) you are
, or, if you screwed up in some way
. You know, I kinda believe that there should be a way to win in any game, even if it's VN. Getting somewhat immersed and then recieving an ending like this is pretty much a slap in the face.
But ok. Let's say you can deal with it. You start to hope there's some enjoyment to be found in completing other routes.
But no. As you read through the familiar intro stuff as you do in any VN, you start to see that nothing is changing, almost at all. And that's the biggest problem of the game:
It becomes worst when you get to the ending again and realise, that the only difference between routes is the CG of the girl in the final scene. As a result, the only reason to replay the game is to read through a date scene and unlock a sexy art. But is it really worth it? And that brings us to...
Talking about art in VN suggests discussing character CG, backgrounds and fullscreen art for especially important moments of the game.
Character CG is pretty much fair. It may be good or average, depending on your art tastes, but I don't think it can be considered bad. I do think though that the design is kinda boring, all of the tank girls look simply like girls, without any perks that can define what kind of the tank they are. I'm not talking about something mecha-related, like in Kantai Collection or Panzer Waltz. Hair clips, badges, hairstyles and clothes - all of that stuff could be creatively used for that purpose. And what can we see in the game? German tanks are blondes, and Maus super-heavy tank got huge♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bravo. Also there could be more variation in poses, since there's only around 2 or 3 for each girl.
Backgrounds are simply lazy. By the look of it, I'm pretty sure that every background is simply a blurred photo, there are even some random people in the place that's supposed to be a school caffeterria, and random 20+ aged guy in the kitchen where only our main hero is supposed to be. Come on.
And fullscreen art. The only important moment in the game, it seems, is the sex scene, since you only get one for each girl. And it simply shows your chosen tank girl in some suggesting pose. Also, while the game was luring people with promises of some hentai content, actual H-patch was released around year later. People in comments talk about it like it's goddamn miracle and best thing to happen in their life. In reality, only thing it did was removing pants and other stuff so you can see nipples and ♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Totally worth it. And it really bothers me, that those arts are done in different styles. I mean, what the hell? Even if different people done them, they should've tried to make them look at least somewhat similar.
Not much to say about it. Of course, it's not a voiced VN, so there are some sound effects only, which pretty much do the job. Same can be said about music, nothing out of this world, but nothing to complain about either.
While performance doesn't really matter in VN, I did encounter some problems.
- Game takes some time to load, at least a minute
- Skip button skips ALL of the text, there's no way to skip only previously read text
- Skipping text in the clubs related part of the game makes two music themes play at the same time, restart needed
- Loading saves in some parts of the game doesn't let you advance (you'll have to load different save)
As you can see, it's not very polished product, but chances are you won't encounter any problems at least on your first run.

Because almost everyone i've read in this review section has said most of what needs to be said, I'm going to keep this brief.
The game sort of coasts on the idea that it's a roguelike, which implies a degree of difficulty and death, and a high level of replay value due to procedural generation. At least for me this is what gives roguelikes their compelling nature.
So point by point, let's talk about the difficulty. The game isn't actually so much hard as it is obfuscated. There's no way to obtain the information besides trial and error or a visit to the wiki. Once you know the mechanics through trial and error it's a pretty simple matter to optimize. It's like a math equation really, interesting but only in a quickly passing and slightly frustrating way.
The deaths that happen are usually due to the same thing, and unfortunately starting over is not very interesting. It's not rewarding or even all that frustrating to die, you learn at most a kernel of information about what you did wrong and the nature of that mistake just usually makes me shrug my shoulders and go "well, okay." In addition, you will still eventually die despite not making any mistakes, and while this is somewhat expected in Kingdoms this isn't due to a steadily rising difficulty but instead is the result of the forcible removal of resource generation in a resource management game. Pretty weak.
Which is what gives this game a shockingly low replay value. There's nothing about the mechanics that are really interesting or creative in a way that makes me glad to start over, and in an expansion which mainly brings starting over to the table that's a really bad thing. There's nothing interesting about the battles because they're a one button affair, building each kingdom is exactly the same.
The horse is pretty though.

This is a good indie game with some good effort behind it, but I ended up being disappointed. The game feels slow and contemplative, and the atmosphere is quite beautiful. However, the game ends up being a time-limited rogue-like survival game. Time limited by an unending Winter, rogue-like RNG based mobs and map generation, survival game as you must escape every island before the inevitable game mechanics crushes your settlement's defenses.
The developer was clearly not interested in writing a tutorial or instructions, and relied on the community to produce guides (half these things you'd never know unless someone told you). It shouldn't be called "Kingdom" but rather "Nomadic" or something of that sort. You get punished for taking your time. Even if you build a very strong "kingdom" or fort the game mechanics will deliberately tear you apart at some point.
Frankly, the unending winter feels rather cheap, and unexplained. It makes me wonder if they were simply too lazy to program in a Spring transition.
The AI is sometimes frustrating in an unexplained way. Knights will run away with all their followers when a wall is at ~40-50% health and leave the rest of your defenders. I ask, why not at 10-20%? And they run back to your keep which can be a million miles away. Two knights with six archery followers can make up a nice chunk of your wall's defenses, and the knights can do some defending, but they refuse to. I'd rather they stand their ground or do some fighting. They actually weaken your defenses, unless you want to attack or leave on a boat. They are only good for that. The builders also have weird priorities when it comes to build queues. You have very little control over which units gets into the boat. Your villagers are also dumb and will put themselves in harm's way very easiily.
You lack real control in the game due to simplified controls, and you have to read guides to find out how to deal with the complex and unstated game mechanics (how does the Banker work? Can't get archers out of a tower once you build it, can't cancel construction, etc)

Game is quite fun the first few hours, but after a while the randomness of site locations makes the game unbearable. I am on the fifth island now, and there are no vagrant camps (necessary to hire new peasants) to be found on either side without crossing a portal very far away (a day's ride). Practically, the game was already lost, because no peasants means no archers, builders or farmers which means no income. No income means no catapults, which in turn means that the first blood moon (where a huge wave of enemies spawns) is most likely your death. The game doesn't have a comeback mechanic, so when you lose too many tools/weapons and peasants, it's over.
This highlights another key problem: Catapults are too important. If you lose one wall with a catapult, it's game over in most cases, and you can only have two catapults (one for each side). You can have very powerful ballista towers, but for those you need a special upgrade (a hermit found somwhere in the forest), which is again, random.
Additionally, I haven't found a reason yet why you wouldn't want a wall in front of your towers and why you should build further out than your starting location. It decreases your potential income (less rabbit spawns), increases walking distances, removes vagrant camps, and lonely towers are a prime target for floaters, that take your archers away. So, you are actually building a very small town instead of a kingdom. Outposts aren't really possible in this game.
Even more annoying, when you die and restart you will lose all progress from the last islands. Every time you finish an island, you can take some workers, knights and coins with you for the next island, which gives you a head start. However, if you die (which might happen quite often, see: randomness), you can't try again with the head start.
The game is also very finicky regarding the undoing of actions. If you build a water well a little too far out, you might as well restart because you are going to lose farmers constantly. Some people say it's a learning experience, I just say it's bad design. There's no reason why actions shouldn't be undoable, at least for a small fee.
Overall, the game is fun in the beginning, but the randomness destroys it. Completing an island is a huge time investment, that may be lost in an instant if you aren't careful enough. You can unlock certain "upgrades" for future plays, but those are also random - again.

So. FTL: Faster Than Light is a sort of action-strategy game in which you take control of one of many spaceships and embark on a journey beyond your wildest dreams.
Do you like Star Trek/Wars? Do you like strategy games? Do you like dying? Do you like having so many endorphins released into you as soon as you beat the game once that you go into a coma? Well, you're probably gonna love this game as much as I do.
Pros:
-Great soundtrack; tends to get stuck in your head easily >w>
-Great Gameplay, a very immersive and addictive experience that will keep you coming back for more. Deaths are a core mechanic, so don't feel bad if you get killed a couple of times!
-Satisfying progression system; the new ships all offer unique and fun playstyles. Some expand upon a prior playstyle, such as the Osprey with the Kestrel. Others are unique and innovative, such as the Torus.
-Challenging; Anything can happen, and even on the easiest difficulties, you will get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you the first few times.
-Satisfying final boss; builds upon everything you've faced in the game and is a true test of skill.
Cons:
-Difficulty curve is somewhat high for new players.
-Rougelike; This can be a pro or a con depending on how you feel about it. Your death means you're going back to square one, and this can be frustrating for newer players are well.
-You will die. A LOT. Again, depends on the player.
Conclusion:
I love this game. This may be one of the best games I've played in a long time. I recommend this game to anyone that likes strategy and/or sci-fi experiences!

This game is in Early Alpha stage. So I took that in consideration and looked in the long run. Not just as to what it offers at the moment.
Kinetic Void is a new genre of Spaceship Simulator. Having it's roots from the old freelancer and other games from the genre, it bring us new aspects of the game. Creating your own ship.
Kinetic void let the players create their own ships, the way they want. You are able to design and create the ships you want for any purpose that may suite you. Want a nice looking sleek ship? Go ahead and make one. Want a big though ship like the Galactica? Go Ahead. And when we talk about creating ship, the Devs have gone further then just looks. All of the ship needs, from the power to radars, to crew quarters are your to choice to decide where they go. And to protect these important systems is one of your goal. Having, technically, no limits, you can build any ship you would have though about.
But creating ships is not the only aspect. If this is something that is not your taste, you can simply take some of the default ship, or why not download some designs from the community workshop? Having over  thousands of community created ships, there is a ship for everyone out there... If designing is not your taste.
Kinetic void launches you in a Procedural Generation world where Factions of NPCs each struggling to survive and conquer the galaxy in their own own. You are sent in this sandbox word with one goal: Living your life how  you want it. You want to be a merchant, selling Goods around the universe? Go ahead. Want to be a smuggler and go past blockades? Want to just shoot at things and be a pirate? Or defend the innocent? All is yours to decide.
Kinetic Void aims to  be one of the, if not the space sim with the most opened up world, with the most customized game possible and it does it in a way that makes  you wonder: Why no one though of this before?
If you are a fan of any space ship simulator, Kinetic Void is a must. From it's amazing artwork, to the infinity of customization, to the hard work of the Team, there's absolutely no reason not to have this game.

Road to hill 30 is the first installment of the Brothers in Arms series. This game was released around 2005 so it’s dated by today’s standards.
Brothers in Arms is a tactics based first person shooter that puts you in the boots of Sgt. Mathew Baker during the D-Day air drop and the week following. The game focuses on battlefield awareness and suppression and flanking tactics. The problem with this is that we are so conditioned to the linear, fast paced, alone in the fight shooters like the Call of Duty or Medal of Honor games. With that, this game can feel rather frustrating at time, your accuracy is rather low compared to other titles, and there is no way to heal yourself during a mission.
All in all, if you are wanting a run and gun shooter this game is not for you.
So why is this game so good? Its and excellent example of a tactics based shooter that makes you think about your next move carefully. The story is also amazing as the characters feel more real than any other shooter of its time. I’m at a loss for words trying to describe how it feels, but it’s just not like other games where you just watched someone get shot. In other games it just felt like “oh, well. That guy’s dead.” in this game they feel like actual people.
Aside from the accuracy drop back, the game feels more realistic than some other games. Aiming down the sights of your gun is actually visually correct, recoil can be disorientating and you can’t really tell where your shots are hitting, your movement feels a bit labored (while it’s not widely excepted as a good thing, it fits with the authentic feel as those soldiers cared about fifty pounds of gear.), and you actually feel responsible for you squad.
For its time, this game was a rather authentic emotion experience compared to other games. While it lacked some of the shooting capabilities of popular titles like Call of Duty or Medal of Honor, Bothers in Arms focused less on being a video game about shooting Nazis and more on being a soldier and squad commander.
Trust me if you’re looking for some classic WW2 PTSD this would be the game to get it from.

Devil May Cry 4 is an amazing hack-and-slash game that is easy to learn and hard to master. The combat system is very in depth and there is always more room for improvement, even for the greatest masters of the game. It also has many different difficulty levels that will keep you busy for HOURS. You get to play as either Nero, who has a very interesting combat system because of his grab ability, and Dante, who has a variety of weapons and fighting styles to choose from while in game, giving an indefinite number of possibilities for combos. Plus, the game is very pretty, even on the lowest graphics settings, and for a PC port, it is not that bad.
Now here's the part where you yell at me for stating my opinion. My main criticisms of the game lie heavily in the story, which I honestly believe was bland and tasteless. Dante isn't the main character, but instead, it's Nero, who in my opinion, acted too much like a whiny ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (though his combat is very unique). A majority of the characters are completely one-dimensional and don't really serve any purpose other than being the damsel in distress or the power-hungry bad guy or the envious rival . I pretty much only enjoyed the parts of the story where Dante was included because at least he was cheeky in an enjoyable way. Although I liked Nero's combat style, it got old for me pretty quick.
Other downsides include the camera problems (which I am pretty sure is typical for a Devil May Cry game), a lack of costumes, the hideous amount of backtracking which puts Dante's role in the game to shame (I am talking you're backtracking for almost HALF THE GAME), and the lame final boss whose attack patterns are very predictable. Plus there's not much innovation put into the level design, which brings me back to the backtracking issue. I honestly felt like I was playing a somewhat incomplete story.
Overall DMC4 was a mostly fun ride from start to end. It does bring back Bloody Palace as well as has a couple fun bosses. What it fails at in areas such as level design and completeness, the game makes up for it with an awesome combat system, beautiful visuals, and long playability.
Overall I give Dante May Backtrack 4 a 7/10

For a runner game, this is actually pretty good. The levels have a nice flow to the them, the game more often works with you than against you, and it's not too long so as to feel stretched out but not too short such that ideas feel underdeveloped, and the game has enough distinct elements to it that the levels don't feel repetitive.
Adding to that is the fact that this game looks gorgeous, especially for the price point. A strong cartoony aesthetic with a pretty large variety of different level themes fitting into the three distinct worlds. The aesthetic almost never gets in the way of being able to see anything either and the rare instance it does is usually inconsequential.
The soundtrack is probably the weak link here... it doesn't strike me as actually that funky, it's very video-gamey with some elements of funk but none of the tunes really made me groove that hard. Ironically, I think the pop and rock spoofs of their respective boss battles fit their themes more than the actual funk, and there's not a whole lot of different tracks in this game either; only 4 total level themes and 4 variations of the boss theme, plus a miniboss theme and an overworld theme. It can get a bit repetitive, basically.
The game has 39 levels, 3 minibosses, and 3 bosses, the bosses being a pseudo rhythm game that basically poses no challenge at all. Not that the main game is that hard either; it's fairly easy but not too easy.
As far as casual games go, this is a pretty fun one, not something to write home about but I enjoyed my time with it. Maybe not worth its full price but on sale, definitely check it out if you're a fan of runner type games, I don't think I've played any other ones I enjoyed more than this one, so.

Why do I hamper myself with Glen Hobble? Because he has been with me since day one. He picked up his injuries in the line of duty and he lost a leg saving his captain. Buy this game. Help the community to make it even better. Do it for me. Do it for Glen.

Finished RE7 clocked in at 7 hours (My playtime is a lot of AFK time) and tbh, It was fun but there's a lot of disappointments.

The bad was pretty much everything else, I wasn't caring at all of the story, disconnected from the MC and didn't care about the other characters, rushed ending, dislikeable monster design and just not plain scary.

A decent horror adventure game that built up a good atmosphere and was at times genuinely frightening. It's "unique" slant was that you play through the eyes of a toddler making the perspective and movement very different to usual.
You play as a toddler that has to wander through your dreams, rendered in 3D, looking for four memories that will allow you a way out. You are accompanied of your travels by your teddy who offers advice and can cast light if hugged. You traverse the adventure in a fairly linear fashion, with a few of puzzles to solve, but nothing too difficult, and some monsters to avoid but death is a minor inconvenience in this game as you are restart at the last save and there are frequent background saves made throughout the adventure.
The initial section is played whilst you are awake and allows you to get the gist of the controls and understand the mechanics of the gameplay.
The are another four levels to make your way through, each taking around 30 minutes to an hour to complete. Each level has its own theme and all of them are hauntingly rendered. It is worth noting the ending is very good too.
I can't see any replay value in the game unless you want the achievements

Among the Sleep is an eerie exploration game with light puzzle elements.  The hook is you play as a toddler, embarking through a dream/nightmare world to find your missing mother.  The dev did a nice job with the toddler aspect.  For example you crawl faster than you walk, your companion is a teddy bear, and everything that looks interesting is maddeningly out of reach.  The puzzles are simple fetch quests, but they too are filled with things from the world of a 2 year old that make them endurable even though it’s a bit boring at times.  You will play shape fit games, search for jigsaw pieces, explore through playground equipment and perform many other tot friendly activities as you make your way through the adventure till the surprising ending.  While the toddler elements make Among the Sleep interesting and worth playing, the gameplay is little more than a walking errr make that crawling simulator without any real scares.  You will occasionally avoid the "Fear" that is chasing you, mostly by hiding, which can be creative at times, but other than that it’s a linear and simple affair.  More creepy than scary, a decent play when you have a few hours to kill one dark evening and want to try a different spin on a "horror" game.  Sometimes the real “fear” in life lies where you would least expect it.

Awesome game!  The "story," foreshadowing, unique gameplay, atmosphere and clever level design are all presented well in this game.  The only downside is the length, even though it feels appropriate given the lack of gameplay mechanics the  devs had to work with.
The cleverness to the scare tactics was genius.  Just like when I was a kid, it was the unknown that scared me the most.  So much of this game works on the player's imagination instead of cheap jump-scares.  In a lot of horror games, it is common to start predicting the scary section which can often soften the blow.  Not in this game.  The ambiance is done  well enough that the anticipation of a predictable scare actually makes it worse.  Kind of like being in a dream and knowing that it's going bad.
They did such a good job with the sound effects.  The bumps, creaks, groans, smashes, screams and cries all drive the unsettled nerves home.
The devs also did an excellent job making you feel as helpless as a two year old child.  The toddler can crawl faster than walk, he will fall over if he sprints for more than a short distance, his light source is a teddy-bear that lights up when hugged, water is a nono, everything seems much larger and daunting, he can't reach doorknobs without something to climb on, and his lack of fine motor skills makes the clunkyness of "click and hold" mouse interactions feel right.
The foreshadowing is great.  A lot of the clues you get to the story are in the environment or depicted as a two-year-old's scribbled drawing.
Though the  length is short but feels accurate for the game, it is hard to say that a 3-4 hour game with little to no replay value  should be $20.  The reason why I say that it has  no replay value is the fact that the game relies so heavily on the unknown and the imagination for the fear to work, that there will be nothing worth seeing again given that the gameplay is a little "slow"
If you really like horror games,  you probably already own this game, but if you don't, then you need to go get it.  It's worth the full price if you are a fan of the genre; otherwise, wait for a sale, but be sure to grab it when the price drops.
The game could be longer, but it's a nice (and sad) story.

Solid 6/10. Would be a 7 or an 8 if not for so many bugs.
***Update***
Actually going to lower my score to a 5/10. It's an average game with some glaring problems. More bugs have crept up, such as falling through the ground, areas not loading, servers seemingly getting worse. Not to mention little quality of life things like having to log in to quit the game? Not sure who thought that was a good idea. I'm on a pretty decent computer with a good wired internet connection and it's just inexcusable for a released game to have a lot of these problems.
And while a lot of others have said they've ended up enjoying the game more after a certain point I think I'm actually going in the opposite direction as it's more frustrating than fun for me now.
***End of update***
It will constantly hang when loading into or out of combat trials (pvp). As others have said, the servers are hit or miss and I'm in one of the better areas apparently (West coast of Canada). The content is also fairly sparce. Took me about 3-4 hours to beat, and a lot of that was just finding the bosses needed to open the final path. It feels like it should still be in beta to be honest and if you're on the fence, I'd say wait for a decent sale. You'll likely come into the game when it's been polished up, with some more content to boot.
A more detailed review:
A fun game, especially if you're a sucker for martial arts. That being said, the pace of combat is measured and fairly slow. Difficulty in pve seems to stem from having more than one enemy to fight at a time when the fighting system just isn't well set up for such a thing. I like that the enemies don't just wait their turn from an outside perspective, but in practice it's more frustrating than fun. Collecting/unlocking moves is a clever idea, but is a little tedious (block/parry/dodge to learn moves).
The hits feel meaty with real weight behind them though. Many a time I pumped my fist after a particularily nasty jumping kick sent my enemy to the ground in defeat. And pvp feels pretty good most of the time. You'll rarely run into a person with the same moves as the last person you fought.
Art style is...fine. They set up a semi interesting world that doesn't really go anywhere. Think a Dark Souls-like story approach, without all the lore...so basically just wandering around fighting folks for no real reason.
I've heard the combat compared to both Dark Souls and For Honor, and the former is definitely apt as you're managing stamina and every hit is deliberate. I haven't played For Honor, but from what I saw of the game it had a similar looking parry/block system, but this game could have used the actual indicators of where the opponent is attacking. Some moves you'll swear you've parried it correctly but you'll just get smacked and you're not sure if it was just the wrong direction you hit, or the wrong timing.
Customizable loot is cool, and I see a healthy variation from other players. That being said, the drops are RNG based (it seems) so again, it can be a little tedious to unlock that cool mask/vest/etc etc.
Final Thoughts:
I was looking forward to this game for a while, and it's not a bad game...But in a year like this, with amazing games slapping you across the face (in every genre, on every system) you're better off elsewhere imo. Lots of potential, with just enough weird quirks/annoying bits to keep me from really recommending.

This game is extraordinarily slow paced, especially if you're playing to win, but it is also extremely deep and immersive. And it realizes its concept very well--being in charge of the systems and crew of a whole ship in combat is cool, and the noncombat encounters really do make you feel like a scavenger trying to weigh risks to squeak by. It certainly oozes atmosphere.
Between the general roguelike nature, and the huge number of different ships with different loadouts and strengths/weaknesses, it also has a ton of reply value. Fortunately, with the exception of the final boss, just because you've played it before doesn't mean you can predict what will happen (in general, or in response to specific actions). Sadly the final boss is the same every time, and there's only a few viable strategies to defeat it that you'll repeat each time.
It's not perfect. Game balance is iffy--a few ships are just plain weak unless you get good RNG and find another weapon, while others have strong enough weapons to last the whole game with just common upgrades. The ultimate goal is to get strong enough to defeat the final boss by the time you reach the final boss, but the boss is the same every time and has some pronounced strengths and weaknesses that skew the game balance. And like I said, combat can be extremely slow depending on your loadout and how much you use the pause feature (which you need to win), and you're encouraged to explore as many nodes as you possibly can in each sector.
Also, about the RNG: "Bad" RNG that costs you resources can usually be avoided by actions with lower risk-reward, which is as it should be. But "good" RNG can make you much stronger (such as a free/cheap weapon, free crew, lots of resources, or even just finding what you need in a shop), and is very random. So RNG can swing the game's difficulty a good deal.
Still, this game delivers very well on a unique premise, and is both deep and replayable. I had a lot of fun with it, and if you're patient you will too. (Also, when you've got a few wins under your belt I suggest grabbing the Captain's Edition mod, and possibly a final boss randomizer mod).

Yes I review a game here everyone else had played years ago and I won't state anything new here, too. I left the series after the very first OF, my computer back than was struggling with the graphics but the game left a lasting impression on me- especially the mission editor was great. I am not a multiplayer guy, online MP is to tough for me, LANs just don't happen anymore. So I am just testing and reviewing the solo player mission here.
What can I say:
It is hard. Maybe I just suck, but I rarely have played a game that is so frustrating. The realism is good, although I think the ability of your team mates and your enemy differs a lot. My team rarely hits anything while the enemy snipes you from 500+ meters, whether you lie down or you run zigzag. I like the AI (they flank you when you camp or throw grenades) but all tactics on my side seem to be completely bugged or useless. Telling your team to flank or to suppress simply makes them act stupid (they advance but don't fire OR they start firing wildly but stand still). The team is great at spotting enemies, often long before I see them, but they completely fail at shooting/hitting them. Even a soldier standing still facing his rear side or non moving targets at 25m distance! Then it seems to be impossible to sneak up at someone. I tried at night, crawling through high grass towards an enemy outpost overwatching the other direction. At 25m he turned around and started firing at me. And this triggered the alarm for ALL troops in the mission area. How did he radio/set the alarm while turning around and shooting?
It is good that you cannot sneak/knife through entire missions, but the missions rely on stealth/avoiding contact or firefights. The game spils this everytime you try. It gets pretty annoying restarting missions simply because the game balancing is crap. Everytime you make a tiny mistake (although you did what was expected) combat helicopters show up and blast you to kingdom come. Or entire companies of enemies appear out of thin air and encirlce your position.
I play this game on a medium laptop with just ok settings. This does not work well. Zoom and vision are pretty realistic, enemies at 200m are a handful of pixels only. This game only works well on full resolution and large monitors. You should also be able to have good to max video settings at hand, otherwise the surroundings are rendered so roughly that it is almost impossible to tell enemies from objects.
This is not an action game. In large parts it asks you to crawl/sneak through forest or brush land, avoiding being seen. You advance a few dozen meters, then check area with your binoculars. Changing weapon to binocular and back takes awfully long, though.
You can not choose weapons/equipment freely for your missions. You will often wish you could bring a sniper rifle along, but you are not allowed to. You will run out of ammo fast, especially if you don't switch to single fire always. Calling for ammo resupply does not work. Your team mates won't share a single mag with you. Looting dead enemies only works if you get to them fast. They disappear after a few moments. Usually they only carry a minimum equipment set (often their rifle has a single mag left, no spare magazines). I wonder how they can shoot at you endlessly while alive, but when they die their ammunition magically vanishes...
Teammates in vehicles don't fight. They do mount the MG on a jeep while you drive, but don't expect them to use it. Regardless of commands you have given them. They are also not able to drive a vehicle while you mount the weapons... pretty much sucks.
It feels like this game was made for multiplayer and got a handful of bugged and annoying solo missions attached to it later.
It was ok for 10€ but I was pretty disappointed by it. I have to check out the editor options yet, but so far I could not find anything that compares to the easy to use and flexible editor from the original game.

The game unpolished in terms of the mechanics, but also in terms of the animations and voice acting; none of which are individually damning by any means, but together, they make this game very difficult to enjoy.  The biggest problem though, the one thing that just kills this game for me sometimes is the AI; that stupid, clumsy, indescrete, terminally dopey AI that gives away your position, and still manages to get into combat when you've told them to hold their fire.  Seriously, I'd rather have four Elmer Fudds follow me around with pop guns, because at least then they'd just hide behind a rock or something so I could do the mission myself.
The HUD system for issuing commands is also way too complicated and insanely frustrating at times. So i've played this game for about 40 hours or so and I think it's time to tell you guys my opinion of the game so far. I'll probably be updating this review the more i play this game, but this is my opinion so far.
This game donesn't have the awesome atmosphere, enviroments and music that DMC3 had, but it's still and awesome game. The graphics are great! They still hold up 6 years after its release. The voice acting is pretty average as well as the story. But you don't play a DMC game for that story♥♥♥♥♥♥ You play it for the combat! The fighting mechanics have been revamped since DMC3. Now Dante can switch fighting styles on the go and can hold 3 guns, and melee weapons at the same time which makes for much more possibilities. They've also added a new character named Nero who is actually the main character of the game. Even though he's not as complex as Dante, he's still got a far bit of depth to his combos and relies more on timing with his EX gauge. Nero is also more accesable to new players of the series. His combos are more simple in comparison to Dante, but he still plays great. There were also some new features added to the PC version of this game, the best of these being the new difficulty, Legendary Dark Knight mode. Legendary Dark Knight mode is a great addition to the game and it's pretty addictive as well. This game will also run on a low end PC just fine , there is also alot of replay value here and if you love the DMC series, you'll find yourself sinking plenty of hours into this game.
Now here comes the bad. My problems with the game would be that it doesn't feel as finished or polished as DMC3, and that's because it's not. The enviroments are kind of copy and paste (Except for the Jungle) and the music is mediocre at best. It is also alot more repetative than the previous games (I don't know about 2 because i've never played it). You fight the 4 same bosses at least 3 times in 1 playthrough and the chess sections are ridiculous. But that doesn't mean the game is bad. Overall it has great graphics, neat cutscenes and one of the most satisfying combat systems in any game i've played. If you can get over it's minor flaws, you will have a blast experimenting with new and different combos and enjoying yourself in one of the best action games of all time.
To me I liked Nero way more than Dante, his arm grab was just so fun. His motorcycle sword is just great.
It's pretty good, but the level design and combat is shallower than DMC3, but unlike DMC3 it's a good port.

Assault Suit Leynos was a cult classic on the Sega Genesis released in North America as Target Earth, and this HD remake serves as the ultimate way to experience it. For the uninitiated, Assault Suits is a small short lived mecha franchise from the 90s that wears its classic mecha anime influences on its sleeve without any shame at all, and are known for being intense and difficult with deliberately slow and heavy controls meant to really feel like you're controlling a massive metal war machine.
The remake brings the original Sega game into the modern age with some GORGEOUS 2D graphics that are extremely detailed and pleasing to look at. The original game's beloved soundtrack is completely redone with rocking music, sound effects have that retro sound and vibe to them, its just a fantastic game to look and listen to. Gameplay is improved from the original, taking in some carry over ideas from Assault Suits Valken from the SNES - namely the expanded control scheme giving the shield and boost dedicated buttons as well as a melee attack. There are eight levels of progressing difficulty, often with narrative driven objectives such as destroying enemy warships or protecting valuable targets as opposed to just reaching the end of a level. There's an arcade and classic mode, with classic being based off the original Sega game with no voice acting or extra features, and arcade mode offers slightly retooled levels with extra objectives and expanded story with voice acting.
The game is hard as hell, the original was known for its legendary difficulty and the remake retains that spirit with gusto. There are no lives and infinite continues at least, but that's just a small comfort for how much certain levels and bosses will beat you in. If you're into that retro-hard challegne that comes from repetition, memorization, and raw "git gud", then you'll find Leynos welcome, but it isn't for everyone. The game also essentially NEEDS a gamepad to be enjoyed, this is a port of a PS4 game, and while it supports keyboard that is not how the original or the remake was intended to be played. Be forewarned!
There are some technical issues, though. The game has some unfairly demanding system requirements (mostly due to each level loading all its assets at once which is STUPID), and even with a modest machine you can get some slowdown. Fortunately this slowdown is in the SNES style where too many sprites on the screen cause everything to move in slow motion as opposed to frame rate skips and choppiness, so its perfectly playable regardless, but beware momements where too much is exploding on screen at once.
All in all though if you're a fan of retro games or a fan of mecha games then Leynos is one of the best either way. The remake truly gave it love an adoration, the developers being obvious fans who made their own mecha action game called Armored Suit Gunhound EX, which if you've played can see the clear and obvious influences from Assault Suits on. Definite recommendation from me!

What this game looks like it should be based on the videos and screenshots would be pretty cool, unfortunately the controls, menus, and general game design does not live up to it.
-You get to customize your loadout every story mission, but in the first mission you don't have anything to switch out so it's just a waste of time as you try and re-try as the difficulty is ridiculous. This also adds frustration as you can't just hit a "confirm" button to continue, you have to scroll down to a "start" button and then confirm. Also, the stuff you unlock isn't available when you choose to play individual missions instead of a continuous story mode.
-Most of the difficulty comes from massive enemy groups that seem to be continuously respawning alongside time-limited special enemies who sometimes get a cinematic entrance and boss health bar, but mostly don't, plus the poor control scheme.
-Since this game is a remake of an older title its controls only account for one d-pad/control stick. As a result you have to aim and move with the same directional control. This is a big problem because, as mentioned above, there are huge groups of enemies advancing toward you so you will spend most of your time retreating, meaning you have to keep turning around in between bursts of fire, also your block only protects from attacks hitting your front side. There is an aim-lock button, but if your aim is slightly too high or low you have to stop, reorient, fire to make sure you're lined up, lock, and then continue moving, this method is arguably just as bad. This is frustrating on land missions, but in zero-gravity missions it is even worse as you need to keep dodging enemy fire by flying up and down.
-As mentioned above, unlocks seem to be either broken or highly specific. There is an overall levelling system which has told me that I unlocked weapons for customization, but I didn't see them anywhere. It turns out that after you unlock things you have to go into your options menu and switch them on for some reason. Also many of the unlocks seem to be a way of padding out basic content. In the little time I played I unlocked both a laser sight to show me where my shots would go and a meter informing me how much boost I have left. Those weren't special equipable tools or anything, they were universally "switched on" from that point on.
-Overall this game just reeks of incompletion. Basic enemy density and weapon power need serious tweeking, Character protraits look and animate like something from early 2000's Newgrounds flashes, and after finishing the tutorial I found my character jumping up out of the bottom of the screen during an ingame text sequence, apparently they forgot to disconnect my inputs from my character so as I confirmed the completion of a text sequence, my mech would jump. Oh also, after rebinding the controls and coming back to the game later I found that somehow up and down had been bound to "reset". I had to delete and reinstall the whole game as there was no way to move through menus to change this. Also the most recent update at the current time is a developer update informing game owners that you can't exit the game using a controller, you need to press esc on your keyboard.
Just don't buy it unless a there is a major update/mod some time in the future

Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic new entry into the franchise, which, let's be honest, has gone very stale in the past years. The developers did something really impressive: They took a step back from the previous games and tried to find a completely new approach for this one, without disregarding everything that made the older games good in the first place. They combined elements of different games  in the genre to create a fresh and interesting blend.
Read the story synapse on the store page, there is not much to be add. The Bakers are very interesting villains, but don't be fooled by the promo material and trailers: There is so much more going on and the game offers surprises all along the way. It caught me off-guard how much twists and turns they put into this.
The Atmosphere in this game is brilliant. They have balanced out suspense, action and exploration rather well and there are definitive peaks along the way. There are passages that are downright frightening and suspenseful, followed by some intense action (thank god not as much as in the previous two games), followed by some calmer exploration and puzzle-solving. The constant change helps the game to not get boring and to always feel fresh and interesting.
The redneck-Setting is also a welcome change. The Bakers are interesting villains with unique traits to each of them. One warning though: This game is bloody and in some scenes downright disturbing. So if you are kinda sensitive to violence, gore and Horror in general, you might want to reconsider playing it. Also: Jump Scares. Not too many, but they are there, and they are well done. I jumped.. more than once.
The great thing is, the game never relies on cheap jump scares. There is so much subtle horror spread in as well, and especially these subtle elements made this game frightening (That freaking old woman in the wheelchair, I swear...).
The Gameplay might have switched massive in terms of perspective, changing from shoulder perspective to first person, but the core is still the same, as you might know from older entries in the series: Explore a complex, but somewhat open area, try to solve riddles and collect items to open up new ways. The inventory management can get a bit tedious, but I think they deliberately made it that way to recreate the way, the older games worked.
The shooting works fine, although the enemy-types get somewhat stale after a few hours, especially since the main enemies aren't all that interesting to begin with. Excluded from this are the bossfight, of which there are plenty. Every single Boss fight has some sort of gimmick and creative idea and all in all they are plain fun.
This is where things get a bit rough. The graphics are fine, but nothing to write home about. The Lighting is very atmospheric and the use of color is clever in most places, but whenever you stop to look at details, washed out textures and rough edges, combined with some horrible smoothening effects will make your eyes hurt. The physics are also almost laughably bad, especially when it comes to the movement of hair. I don't know, if its because of the havok physics engine, but other technologies, like in Rise of the Tomb Raider do a far better job.
But when it comes to sound, Resident Evil 7 steals the show. The music is subtle in most places, but always fitting while the sound effects are the main reason you almost crap your pants every five seconds. The whole house is creaking, every object in the envoirement that would emit some sort of sound has a realistic sound made for it. The world feels alive and the immersion is therefore fantastic.
The game is not too short and not too long. It took me about 8 hours to complete for the first time which is nice and dandy, since it started to drag a bit in the end. Interestingly, there are different endings and since you have to settle on one ending way before the game actually ends, I am keen to replay it again right now to find out how the last third of game pans out with  a different choice.
Can't say much about the DLCs, havent bought them, yet. But for the main game, it is worth it's price tag.

Note that this review is written and submitted for a currently unfinished game(as of September 10th 2014), and that anything therein is subject to change.
Kinetic Void is a pretty decent looking space simulator with a lot of potential and a small but dedicated development team. I figure that the easiest way to review the game is to just list off a few of the more notable pros an cons as they are at the time of writing this review.
PROS:
-The game has a fairly robust ship creator/editor that allows you to make some really interesting and complex stuff if you sit down and practice a bit
-The player has a good amount of control over various aspects of both their ship and their way of spacefaring. Controls are fluid, weapons are responsive, and the game supports both keyboard and mouse control of the player's ship.
-It was interesting to learn that ship designs you save can potentially be used by NPCs, including enemies.
-The development team takes their time with updates, but is extremely consistent and dedicated in their work. New content might take a while, but I've never felt that the game has been abandoned by the devs like so many other early access titles.
CONS:
-Being early-access, there are still a number of bugs and other assorted issues to be ironed out. You're accepting that fact by purchasing the game in an incomplete state
-Space is almost realistically a bit too empty a lot of the time. I'd really like to see the number and variety of structures in each system increased
-Currently the variety of parts in the game is fairly large, but all parts are locked to one of five size classes, meaning that it can sometimes be difficult to make attractive ships, mainly smaller craft like fighters and interceptors.
-The game has little in the way of missions or goals. You're dropped in and expected to find your way around the vast expanse of space on your own. This will most likely be fixed later, but hey, that's life, you know?
Overall, I'd recommed this game to a friend if I knew that they were interested in a space sim that will eventually be very in-depth and detailed. Right now the game is still very lacking in features, but I have faith in the dev team to complete Kinetic Void, and the amount of content and bug fixes increases with every update.

“ I realize it's all random and occasionally, you get a run through where the game throws scrap and weapons at you and you breeze through and kill the boss but these games almost never happen.”
“From what I understand, there's tips and ways to increase the odds but with the pause button that just means there is a correct way to play and hopefully win “
“There is absolutely no decisionmaking on the map. Click merchant if you have money, fish on a blank empty sector if you don't.“
These are three excerpts taken from three negative reviews of the game and I can say with confidence that they are all false and I will spend my review disproving their points and offering my own anecdotes and thoughts about the game.
Firstly, while I concede there are underlying luck-based components to the game the negatives reviews have a tendency to strongly downplay the underlying strategical elements and complexity of the game. The game is not so luck-based that a couple stray bullets will end a run or a couple lucky hits will outright win the game.  Underneath its deceptively simple surface, there are many ways to minimize your risks and maximize your average returns on every FTL run, and to me, that is what makes the game so fun and enjoyable.
From weapons and room configuration to crew members' races and special abilities; from investments decisions to assignment of battle stations during a firefight; from the route you decide on to the exit beacon to the decision of momentarily reallocating your oxygen power block to the engines to increase your dodge percentage to avoid an incoming missile these there is a seemingly endless tree of decisions all of which are important to the survival of your alien crew. It is mundane but super important decisions like "Do you put that fire out with your human character or open the doors to let the oxygen out of the room at risk of when your doors get damaged not being able to close that to restore the oxygen?" and "Do I put that Engi or that Human on the helm?" that makes the game so complex and endearing to its me and the rest of its playerbase.
Beyond its decision making, the game is also a testament to mechanical skill. Being able to deftly maneuver your troops to effectively eliminate all threats provides a sense of internal satisfaction that only comes after hours of forgetting to turn your oxygen back on and having a crew member asphyxiate to death.
While there are certainly "wrong" ways to play the game (if we define wrong as strictly suboptimal), there are not a definite "right" way to play the game as there are a variety of different strategies, each with different difficulty levels and rewards. While not everyone may share my same enthusiasm, to me, the game is still as interesting on its 50th run as it was on my tenth. The game has a very steep but very rewarding learning curve and I feel many of the negative reviews were off-put by the polarizing extreme simplicity on easy mode or hair-pulling frustration on hard mode. For me, FTL is the perfect game – it provides a canvas for my creativity while also testing my own abilities to paint my vision on that canvas. And unlike what some of the negative reviewers suggest, an FTL run is the amalgamation of a player’s decisions and their ability to enact on those decisions and they will always be rewarded accordingly (most of the time).

Darwinia is a classic indie game, an RTS on a large yet microscopic level.  Very tron-like in it's intention and it pulls the theme off well.  I highly recommend it, and it's "sequel", Multiwinia.  The basic story revolves around you, a hacker, that finds a scientist's private server, that contains his experiment on creating a digital species (Darwinians).  But viruses have corrupted the majority of his life's work, and you need to command his creations to free themselves from the malware and virueses that are destroying the world that the scientist has created for them.  It makes you feel good when you have a victory, and mourn the loss when innocent souls are slaughtered on a mass scale in these epic battles.
Gameplay-wise, it has essentially no resource management whatsoever.  But that is a good thing, especially for those that are just dipping their toes in the RTS genre, and just want action.  You instead control the battlefield by initiating various programs and deploying them to fight the infection. as well as appointing captains of the local population of darwinians that rally those nearby to attack, move to a position, and such.  The programs you can initiate to help fight your battles include engineers that collect dead 'souls' to be revived, and capture important buildings such as spawn points and traffic lanes.  Then there are you direct combat commandoes, the squad.  The squad is a group of 3-5 heavily armored humanoid soldiers that you can command to directly move anywhere, and you can direct their fire yourself, like in a top-down shooter.  Upgrades can also allow them to lob grenades at your will, among other things.  As I mentioned before, you can appoint a Darwinian to be a captain of sorts via another command.  The final program is initiating an airstrike over a designated location, devastatingly ripping anything below (including your own troops) to pieces.
As you progress through the campaign, you can find boxes of previous research from the scientist, and tell him to research (essentially, upgrade) one of your commands, which takes some time but is useful.  Upgrades include adding more members to a squad, allowing regular darwinians to throw grenades, adding another bomber to your airstrike runs, etc.
No buildings that you can control ccan ever be destroyed, and there is no resource whatsoever that you have.  Darwinians spawn in waves, coming out of large buildings that you can take control of with your engineers.  Your engineers can also pick up the souls of dead enemies and allies that linger after they die, to deposit them into these buildings that resurrect them.
As you can see from the trailer, the battles are massive cluster#$!@s of friendly and not so friendly darwinians, other enemies lke snaking viruses and spiders, etc.
The story is inspiring, the gameplay is unique, simple, and fun - I would recommend it to anyone, even those that don't do the RTS genre.  To be honest, this a a gateway drug to the RTS genre.  What I have to say to the customer who wants to buy this, is that they should buy this in the pack you can see below that has all the classic games from Introversion (The development studio behind this) and two of their soundtracks.  Multiwinia is essentially the same as darwinia just without as much direct unit creation, but focuses on the aspects of using the darwinians in legions and using such strategies.  You can get power ups too, that allow you to do various things like in Darwinia, plus some more.  DEFCON is a good RTS that takes heavy inspiration from movies like 'Wargames' and the general Cold War scenarios that were hypothesized in the mid 20th century.  You control a world power with nukes.  You are just the general in the bunker, not any politician.  As the situation escalates, you mobilize more and more forces that you place strategically early in the game.  Then everything goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥as thermonuclear war breaks out.  It really is more complex than what I'm saying here, and you might as well get it with getting the other games.  Uplink is a neat, almost too-plausible hacker simulator inspired by the things you see in your average action movie.
So I would get all of their games for the value price when they are bundled, and it includes the soundtracks to two of them.

Back in 2002, a Czech game company known as Illusion Softworks released an awesome period action game: Mafia. Featuring a massive open-world backdrop with linear story progression, this chronicled the journeys of one young cab driver, Tommy Angelo, as he is unwillingly inducted into the Salieri crime family back in the 1930s. The game tracked how he found new best friends, a special girl and dangerous enemies, and eventually, how he turned stoolie against his Sicilian companions (the story he tells to a detective at the end of the chronology in 1938 is used as a framing element for a game-length flashback).
Gameplay was very similar to the modern Grand Theft Auto games; third-person behind the back, driving sequences, etc. But two things set this game apart and surprisingly, lowered it in some peoples’ eyes (though not mine): the linear story progression (you’re always pushed toward more story development instead of being encouraged to explore) and the rather realistic (compared to GTA) laws (speed, drive on the wrong side, run a traffic light, and you’re ticketed; fire a weapon out of a combat zone, run people over, and you’re arrested)
January 2008: Illusion Softworks is bought by the software giant Take-Two Interactive and renamed 2K Czech, placing it under the same distributive umbrella as Grand Theft Auto and BioShock. It would soon turn out a title that would find itself in good company with those venerable titles.
Mafia II, released in September 2010, continues the tradition of fine storytelling and gripping cinematic action started by its predecessor. This time, you are Vito Scaletta, returning from action in his native Sicily during World War II. Granted an extended leave of absence due to a little less-than-legal finagling by his childhood friend Joe, and looking for a leg up in Empire Bay (seems to be a fictitious counterpart to Manhattan), he begins to be courted by the underworld element which ensnares his fair city.
Graphics quality has improved quite a bit from the first in the series, naturally; it’s been eight years, after all. The sound is really great, from period tunes of the 40s and 50s to typically excellent car and weapon sounds. This game also really knows how to give a good first impression; stepping out of the cab after sharing a drink with Joe, shortly after arriving back in the Bay, you’re greeted by a wonderfully snowy cityscape and contemporary Christmas song (the game begins in January of 1945, and the wonder and magic of the season have yet to wear off).
Gameplay is just as solid as ever, with a cover system inherited from other modern shooters. There are collectibles in the form of Playboy magazines and Wanted posters, to keep you quite busy through the story.
Overall, I give this series five out of five! Check it out; it’s an offer you can’t refuse!

FlatOut: Ultimate Carnage is essentially a high-definition update of FlatOut 2. There are a couple of new gameplay modes and some technical improvements, but that's about it.
Still, the game is enjoyable. It looks a lot better and the physics have been beefed up, which leads to lots of big crashes. The FlatOut 2 campaign was fun, and it's still fun here. The minigames return intact, and they're more addictive than they should be.
FlatOut: Ultimate Carnage is a Games For Windows Live title (you can't run the game without it), and there are over 40 achievements to try and get. Some of them are pretty difficult to obtain, so if you like achievements FlatOut: Ultimate Carnage has them.
FlatOut: Ultimate Carnage is best-suited for people who never played FlatOut 2. However, if you don't have FlatOut 2 anymore and want to play it again, Ultimate Carnage will do the job.

I should sleep.  Somewhere among the sleep is me, half awake and bufuddled.  The barely awake dad who has to see what is terrifying my 2 year old at 3AM.  Those dark hallways with toys everywhere, been there. *You* try walking through that minefield of balls, dolls, and wooden blocks.  But I've seen the terror in thier eyes, tears falling and crying out frantically for someone to make them feel safe again.  And in no other game has it ever been recreated with such clarity.
In this game you are two years old again.  Toddling long.  Crawling is faster.  Exploring the hidden world that always seems foreboding.  Mundane objects take on a menacing appearance, unknown sounds all the more spine chilling.  And also in this game, there is a tone of something else.  Alcohol bottles strewn across the floor.  Refridgerator doors left wide open.  In the world of Among the Sleep you must traverse the completely believeable household universe of two year old terror.
Gameplay is mostly interacting with objects, some simple puzzles.  You travel through some toddler nightmare lands collecting items to fit in a slot, or solving a way to smash open a toy chest.  Then a bit of cat and mouse chases with a monster that looms nearby, searching for you.  Seeking you out all the time.
Visually, it's quite well done and a lot of attention to game detail with shadow and specific uses of color.  I played with both a KB&M and Controller, both work very well.  No in game crashes for me and I never got stuck on geometry or bugs.

I have to add, that although this is a horror game, you are limited the horror of a two year old.  It's not a gorefest of a demon infested graveyard waiting for you, it's a  playground with ledges and hiding holes, spooky libraries, or being chased in a coat closet.  These are familiar areas to most of us and it may or may not frighten you.  I would say for those who cannot endure most horror games, this is substanially less anxiety causing.  Perhaps with some, it may hit a few heartstrings which you will discover later towards the end.
The game is a story more than anything.  Not a visual novel or a game with lots of in-game dialogue, but a storytelling nonetheless.  And at the end, you'll see what the true terror is that plagues our little character.  The full game is a little short. After I was done I played the DLC which is also short where you save your plush toys from the cold, but a little scarier than the main game.  Among the sleep is a good game, a gamble really in this age of horror games.  And it's well done.   At $20 I personally think that it's pricey.  I got this in a bundle, though, and think it was money well spent.
Forgot to add - in the kitchen I spent a good bit of time destroying everything I could get my little hands on.  Wreaking the dishes and lobbing a coffee maker off the counter was bliss. Destruco-Toddler skill points +10.  Cheers.

Personally, I give this game an 8/10 with the following reasons:

Alright, so playing this game my first order of business was to edit the controls. Normally, people complain about the controls of every single game that was created for the console and put on a PC; this game was very simple for adjusting controls, but really wanted you to work for it when it came to playing. I could go on about the controls in the game, but let me say this: I got to a point where the way I adjusted my controls made the game better than what it was AFTER I got my PS3 controller to play it with. Yep. I made the game better on the Keyboard than on the Controller. In Dark Souls, that'd be IMPOSSIBLE; in this game, it's pretty easy. This game earns a 10/10 for controls on that alone.
Now, not to spoil the game with the story of it, I'm only going on the gameplay aspect; you want the story, use google. I played this game entirely for the gameplay. Nero is pretty simple to control, but if you're using an older machine, you're going to have serious problems. The lag extremely effects how well you react; most times you can simply press a button when a game a local-based lags on your computer and it will slowly move. In DMC4, if you press anything, the lag actually makes the game ignore your command entirely. Backwards compatibility, I label this a 4/10.
The biggest problem I had with this game is that Nero has limited weapons but does 3x as much damage as Dante, so killing as Dante takes a long time. Also, if you're new to the game, Dante will make you cry when you're fighting against him; this is coming from a guy who beat Heaven and Hell mode on DMC3 once. Dante will actually gain ALL of his weapons after you beat the game once; and believe me, he'll use them against you on the first stage of your next game. Dante also has a tendency to avoid whatever you throw at him unless you force him on the offensive and dodge his attacks yourself. Even then, he's faster than Nero, so good luck. And on your second playthrough, the first level turns out to be a major challenge. I didn't bother with Heaven or Hell mode for this exact reason. 3/10 on difficulty
After level 1, the game is pretty enjoyable so long as you play as Nero. However, when you switch to Dante, everything becomes a major challenge. The lag becomes real, damaging enemies becomes tedious and to replace the cool minigames Nero had, Dante has immediate danger and headache inducing puzzles 24/7; in one level, all areas that were connected are redone to have portals replace the connections between them. Basically, you're going to go through a new maze a la Silph Co. teleporters. Oh, but these aren't exactly connected to each other; you can go into one and then decide to backtrack and come out of a totally different portal then the one you walked through. If you're like me and get busy playing games, this is a struggle.
Aside from that, this game was good. I don't like to praise good games or attack bad games, more show a contrary side to my own opinion. If you want my controls, message me. They worked exceptionally.
