I had tried the free edition some time ago but it lacked mouse support and was a PITA to control and I quit. But I read many recommendations about the game so I gave it another try. Since recently mouse support was added its easier to control and is quite fun now. So I purchased the full version via Steam.
In general I can recommend the game.
BUT it still has many flaws and is definitely NOT for everyone:
- you stick with the ship you choose from the beginning. And this heavily determines the way you play and the equipment you can use.
- there is a little tutorial but basically you are on your own so I needed to refer to a guide to learn the ropes.
- VERY steep learning curve. You will fail ALOT and in most cases don't even know why. So this demands a little masochism from you.
- In most cases my ships explode within seconds. No time to react, gtfo or even analyse what best to do.
- It depends highly on randomness wether you find the right equipment and good trade routes for earning money. Every new run seems to lack something I saw in another run.
- Mining sucks. Seriously. Most rocks don't give ores. No way to find out what and how many.
- Radar range is pretty limited so you have to fly over the whole system to uncover everything (and you are never shure you got all). This way you often end up close to strong enemies when you are inattentive.
- Even the ship(s) with most cargo hold and module slots have too little for my taste. So you may need to make hard decisions on what to take with you and hwat to leave behind.
- When you die you have to repeat the whole system. So jump alot just for saving your progress in one system.
- Albeit procedural it looks always similar and familiar. No real surprises yet.
- This similarity also makes it difficult for me to distinguish different runs. I ended to write down where to find some module I can't afford yet and important (mission) stuff.
- Its pretty hard to make decent money for good equipment. Stations have limited funds so I can't sell all stuff I find right away for a good price (this sucks with limited cargohold). And often I have found a weapon or module worth
thousands of credits but the station only buys it for 10% of its value. This "paywall" (ingame money!) seems pretty artifical to me to increase difficulty.
- Many modules and weapons are just garbage. Stuff you would NEVER fit yourself. So in the end I always aim for the same upgrade path. This means lot of waiting until I find the item AND I can afford it!
- (escort) missions are sometimes hard and may fail. Even the main/storyline quests can fail!
- installing new and found equipment costs (partially serious) money. So its hard to just "try out" something.
- attacked stations spawn new ships. Lacking firepower you may not take them out because you are "disturbed" again and again.
- its pretty difficult to repair found equipment. So I was often frustrated when I found something good but it was damaged and I could only sell it.
- no interaction with planets and moons. They are basically only background. The game consists only of stations and ships (and their wrecks).
- friendly fire only for player. Means I can hurt my "buddies" but enemies don't hurt each other.
- no health bars for enemies so you can't tell how well you do.
- the game does not show a price indicator for goods. So I don't know if its a good deal or not. There too many goods to learn the prices for all or loock them up oog.
- finished a difficult and long mission and the game crashed before I could jump/save.
Why do I still recommend it yet the many flaws?
- Because of the high difficulty its also pretty rewarding to find equipment or make good money.
- Its not required that you don't die. Belongs to the learning process.
- Albeit 15 years old the game is still under constant (but slow) development.
- Highly modable (I did not try mods for myself yet). You can even look at the source code!
- You don't take a path the designers "predefined" for you. You search your own way. Interesting decisions have to be made.
- The roguelike elements offer a high replay value.
- Lots of content to explore.
So if you like spacegames AND have a high frustration tolerance -> go for it. If you are more the "casual" gamer look for something more polished and streamlined. Or try the free demo first.
Note: I play with Steam Client in Offline mode. So the displayed game time is incorrect. Currently I have at least 30 hours.
Some tips:
- read the guides!
- money, energy/fuel and cargo space are precious resources. Don't waste them! Look at the value to weight ratio.
- go for solar armor and solar panels. Beeing energy independant (in the beginning) makes exploring more relaxed and inexpensive.
- sell the right stuff to the right stations so you get max money out of it. Learn the prices!
- green glowing wrecks will contaminate your ship. Know BEFORE looting where you get rid of it.
- use sniping and hiding behind rocks to not get hit.
- when you find something good (100 MW reactor) jump through a gate and back to save it. Just incase you die so you can keep it.
- note where you find good equipment and how much it costs to come back later when you can afford it. Plan your upgrades!
- Don't fight every pirate you see. Often its better to fly around, explore and sell stuff you loot from wrecks (this also prevents buying something expensive what you can find for free). When you know your surroundings and have better
equipment then kill every pirate.
- Wait with storyline missions until you are prepared. They don't go away.
- try NOT to get demotivated by difficult and "unfair" things. See them as challenge. Everyone can play an easy game!

At its heart, Transcendence is a hybrid of Escape Velocity and Rogue. If that concept excites you, no need to read further; just buy it!
The game meshes the story of a galactic pilgrimage at the behest of the God Domina, with real time, 2D top-down combat across randomly generated star systems (effectively serving as “dungeons”) and a healthy dollop of loot. The star systems always follow a standard progression in terms of the factions and events you will encounter, so they are not entirely random. However, the implementation still ensures that no two games are ever the same.
The background of the various factions that populate these systems is hinted at through dialogue on stations and occasional missions, but is still rather nebulous. However, there are many intricate interplays and relationships between the factions that really grant the game depth and strengthen its similarity to Rogue. Finding secret trading or loot opportunities, making allies or enemies and just plain exploring all have surprising depth and provide a great balance of risk and reward. If you manage to avoid spoilers, you will still be discovering new aspects to this game even after years of playing!
Again in common with Rogue, the gear available throughout the game is extensive and varied, usually presenting specific qualities or quirks rather than simply incremental upgrades. There are also a number of different ships on offer with various strengths and limitations. Together with the numerous loadout options, this will greatly impact your experience and play style. Unfortunately, some of them are significantly underpowered and so they can be considered almost as difficulty levels rather than equal alternatives. Regardless, this feature provides Transcendence with even greater longevity.
The meat of the game is combat and it involves both twitchy action skills and tactics, a la Escape Velocity. Battles can also be chaotic and brutal, with death by friendly fire or a single lucky shot a common possibility. The variety of enemies on offer and their varying tactics and abilities are generally engaging and challenging. Unfortunately, it feels that cheesing encounters is sometimes the only way to survive. Often, you are hideously outgunned and unless the RNG God has smiled upon you, will frequently lack the appropriate gear to manage every encounter. It seems that I commonly spend the final third of the game playing hide and seek around neutral stations and cowering behind planets waiting for shields to charge, while my foes circle aggressively... Abuse of the powers granted by Domina are often the only way out. At times, this can start to sap the fun out of the experience.
Although the game technically has perma-death, it does allow you to continue playing after dying, at the cost of losing your score. Players can also purchase insurance during their travels, which can prevent a single cheap death from ending your glorious run to the center of the galaxy. However, as the cost of each subsequent policy grows exponentially, you are always concious of your vulnerability. Its a great balance that caters for the hardcore while still offering a degree of accessibility.

Of all the reviews I read, good and bad, after I played the game I only have this to say: This is an old school Hidden Object game.  This is how they all used to be when actual storylines were first being introduced and being refined.  The games centered on the Hidden Object scenes, with the occassional pick up of inventory items to be used later or to solve some puzzle.  The games were not as strictly linear as they are now, but had a more "open world" feel with "bottle necks".  The games were also not nearly as "hand-holding" as they are now.  The gamer had to think and OMG guess about what had to done, plus click everywhere.  Yes it was and is annoying and frustrating but that is partly what made the game challenging, out thinking the game/developers.
Being a fool for old school this was a really refreshing game for me to play.  Very different puzzles and needing a completely different mind set compared to more recent and HD graphic "hand-holding" games of today.  One of the complaints centered on the half-completed objects in the hidden object scenes.  Well all I can say to that is you got what you clicked (Do remember this game was made before 3D was standard, so the objects were drawn in, not overlayed.)
The actual puzzles of this game include suduko, logic, slide, matching, "minesweeper" among many other types.  This game includes a vast and usually unseen variety of puzzles compared to the color, sound, and match fare of today.  So no crying about how hard the puzzles are, expand your repertorie.
If you want a challenging game and are bored with the standard fare of today, try yesteryear (in game time 2 years is like 2 centuries).  This game overall is quite challenging.  No penalties for hints which I had almost forgotten about being so used to today's games where there are penalties for hints, map use, and misclicks.  Hints were standard fare in old school and the gamer was expected to use the hint button... a lot, as well as be click "happy".  Guides and YouTube did not exist then like they do now.
Old school games did not have (or require) achievements, in-game or later the all important steam achievements.  They especially did not require trading cards to even be considered playable.  So if as a gamer one is looking for those things, this game has none of that.  So welcome to the adult version of "Highlights" and enjoy what made the games of today what they are today.

Darwinia is hard to describe. It's part RTS, part god game one could say. You are in charge of protecting and restoring the Darwinian population, however you can't directly control them. Although the officer tool does make up for that fact. Instead you spawn in several programs to assist the little guys in order to destroy the red virus that has infected their world.
The gameplay is pretty solid, and becomes massively fun during the fights where you get to utilize your Darwinians. Having two massive forces collide and duke it out while you influence the battle field with your programs is something not many games capture too well.
Speaking of the Darwinians, they are the stars of this game. They are important for manning buildings, turrets, and eventually the main fighting force at your disposal. They have a few things they do that adds a nice little touch, such as jumping into the air when a mission is complete, or mourning over the loss of a fallen comrade. The story brags about how smart these guys are, but they don't do much that isn't scripted. They really come to life in battle however, their digital screams, panic, and blaring war trumpets and marching tunes give them character.
The story is servicable, although nothing groundbreaking. They thankfully allow you to skip through it if you aren't that interested, although I soaked in as much as I could. If your a sap like me, you'll grow fond of the little guys, otherwise the gameplay should suffice.
All in all, the game is great fun and a blast to play. It took me around 6 hours to beat on one playthrough. Beating it will give you a level editor to muck around in and another profile with all locations enabled, so you can edit to your heart's content. Some would argue it's a little short, and I feel like it could have a few more levels, but what it does offer is more than worth it's price tag.

It's funny, I have owned this game since it came out, somehow, and I'm not sure how I got it. All I know is it was on Steam when Steam was brand new (i.e. used for Half Life, TFC, CS) and since Darwinia was on it, I assumed it was made by valve. Haha, silly young me.
Anyhow, this game is an interesting take on the RTS genre with some "lemmings" functionality built in; in other words, there are units in this game that are friendly, that move around, and that you cannot directly control.  They fit into the story because they are the artificial life forms that you need to protect.  You do so with a couple "squads" so to speak of programs you can control directly.  Together with these not-exactly-helpless, but non-controllable "AI", you must navigate the campaign and complete various objectives. There are some extremely large-scale battles that seem very chaotic due to the lack of direct control the player has, but overall the game is fun and challenging despite being a little raw.
What I really must add in is that the game kind of made me, the player, believe these sprites were, in fact, "living" beings. The game, in its simplicity, is actually very immersive, and it's easy to project "soul" onto these sprites you are trying to save. When they die, you feel sad, when they are happy, you're happy. It's a fascinating combination of storytelling and gameplay mechanics that created an unexpected sense of emotion for me while playing.
Naturally the trailers and screenshots don't do that last bit justice. But Introversion is a stellar developer and Darwinia meets the high bar they set for themselves and their games. I would definitely recommend.

Darwinia is one of my favorite games of all time. So it gets an obvious reccomendation from me. There is a lot going on with Darwinia and I've never played anything like it. It's one of those types of games that is really hard to describe, and you can only really understand after playing it for a bit. It's a weird game to get into at first. But once you get past the first two or so levels and understand what's going on it really takes off.
So basically what's going on with this game is your thrown into a level, and your given a few goals to complete the level. There are a lot of different objectives in the game, but most of the time your goal is to kill all the enemies on the map, and move your little Darwinians to key locations. What's really nice about the levels is all tools the game gives you tie in together in really clear ways. You make soilders to kill enemies and create souls, the engineers retrieve the souls and bring them to the soul collector to generate new darwininans, and the Darwinians interact with the map and you don't have direct control over them. It all comes together really well.
My favorite part about the game though is how much freedom you get. It sounds weird but let me explain. Darwinia perfectly lets you experience it at your own pace, and in your own way. There's so many ways to handle each situation in the game, and you're encouraged to handle it any way you want to. You can be super effiecient and try to carefully mine every enemies' soul, or you can do things more crazy and charge in with air strikes. Both are valid strategies in Darwinia. You can try spam engineers to take over a semi-hostile base and raise hell from inside the enemy territory, or you can enter from the shores and work your way in. The game doesn't care which way you do it. Nothings timed, nothings scored. And I love that. Because if you had a score, or a time limit it means you'd have to play the game in the most effient way, but without those things I felt more encouraged to try out crazier ideas, or ideas that I knew were just stupid, but its ok because it's fun. And that's what Darwinia encourages. It's all free. But it's more than just that. The game let's you jump into and out of levels at anytime and it you'll be able to jump right back into exactly where you left off instantly. You can acess more than one level at once so if you get bored or stuck on one level, you can jump out and start working on another level. It's great! Probably my absolute favorite part about Darwinia is how free the camera is, and that's a really weird thing to say, but lemme explain. The camera in Darwinia is very free. You can move it to any location, and look at anything from almost any angle. It's almost like a camera you'd see in an editor of some sort. But it really really works in Darwinia. Because the camera is so free it really makes the game feel like a world that's actively happening, and you're just interacting with it. Almost like a little toybox world, or at least that's how it makes me feel anyway.
With the camera, and entire game giving you so much freedom, and a lot of the units do things on their own in this game, ontop of the very simple art style(which is perfect for this game), and the great ambience the sounds create, I felt like I could get really immersed into game. I liked to put the camera at dramatic angles and imagine all sorts of adventures and stories as things were happening. I've taken more screenshots in this game than any other. So basically what I'm getting at, is if you like to imagine weird stuff or like to get really immersed into a game both strategically and artistically, then this game does the trick.
And the game has a level editor and mod creator. Yeah. ♥♥♥♥in sweet. This is one of those games that I have NO idea why this isn't more popular. And the story is really weird and cool. And it's really existential and you are an active part of the story... like you the person sitting at their computer, not you the player in the game. It's a bit weird, and I didnt really understand what was going on for awhile. But I really like that kind of stuff so the plot I really really liked.
So final reccomendations: Definity get this game. It's amazing. It really really appeals to what I like personally, so you probably wont think it's the most amazing thing like I do, but I think you'll definitly have fun. Don't get it if you don't think you'll be able to handle the controls. Darwinia can also be really weird difficult to understand at first so if you're not willing to do that, then you probably wont enjoy it either.
Anyway, love this game. Personal favorite. And it's $10. So no excuses. That's less than a movie, or dinner at a nice restaurant.

Absolver in a nutshell as of right now:
Pros:
* Somewhat interesting combat and deckbuilding for your fighter. This is sadly however brought down due to the fact that fast move decks are basically 100% better than slow move decks. Period.
* Graphics are ok. Decent amount of looks customization
* New concept, novel idea.
* Feint system works nicely, as does the countering... when it works.
Cons:
* Horrible connectivity issues. Thought For Honor was bad? Wait until you can't even play the game online. Then wait until you can, and then the game decides to migrate you to some new host while you're fighting a boss you spent 10 mintues or so, trying to learn moves from. Then the boss dissapears, and so did your progress. Then wait until you get migrated to another session again and find out you can't fight anything because your character can no longer attack now. Then find out no other way than to quit the game to fix it. Then stop playing for the day altogether because you're annoyed and frustrated.
* Terrible matchmaking. Are you a new player trying to learn the game, level 5, no moves, barely able to move? You will get matchmade in 1v1 matches against someone who already beat the game, is level 35, has all the moves, fully geared out, and plays at the highest levels. Literally no matchmaking was put in place.
* Really short singleplayer/non 1v1 pvp content. You will beat the game probably within a day, maybe two if you spend your time farming every move you don't know. That is assuming you don't run into those other problems from before. There is literally nothing to do in the game after you beat it in 5 hours other than 1v1 combat with said terrible matchmaking.
* Customization of moves/combat appears to be endless... until you find out only a few moves and styles of play are actually worth using.
* Terrible level design. You will get lost. You will spend hours running around trying to find the next place to go (I guess at least that increases the amount of hours you get from SP). You will get frustrated. You will die endlessly to encounters designed around online play, which doesn't work about 90% of the time.
* You will fall off ledges all the time. All the time. Additionally there are some cancerous 1v1 arenas which have edges everywhere. Even if you push your opponent off, you will likely fall right with them as most moves move you forward as you hit and you cannot dash backwards easily after the fact.
* The worst camera in any game ever when you are in enclosed spaces. Seriously, who the ♥♥♥♥ thought that camera was OK to release like that? If you end up near a wall, you will eat a huge amount of free damage. Not because your opponent is good... because you opponent is likely spamming super fast moves and you can't even see what they are because the wall is in your way. Oh and then it will start spazzing out and spinning in the air. Seriously, I have not seen a camera this bad in a loooooong time.
* AI that runs back and forth MMO style when you run out of aggro  range. Said aggro range will sometimes seem consistent, but then you'll get into a fight with an enemy, they will almost die, then decide to run back to their spawn midcombat and regen a bunch of health. That wouldn't be so bad, except you don't regen your health. So then any progress you made to learning moves essentially is wasted. Yay more grinding due to broken systems.
* Cheating - Saves are apparently stored locally, which means they can be easily editable. Look around the net to see examples, you will find them easily. This is kind of important for a fighting game.
Would I recommend this game to a friend? No, and I recommended For Honor to them. That should tell you the current state of Absolver at the moment. Tons of online problems, lack of endgame content,  bad matchmaking, unbalanced movesets, cheating, the worst camera in any fighting game in recent years, developers who release a game and charge money for a region which they have no servers for (and therefore game is unplayable  in AUS region).
No, don't buy Absolver. Wait and see what happens. I'm past my refund period but you should save your money. This game looks better from the outside than it actually is.

Overly simple FPS with a little bit of tactical gameplay. This is basically a WW2 themed FPS but each combat can be planned by scouting the area and planning your approach. Sounds good and looking good with the screenshots? Unfortunately it is not but rather disappointing.
The dialogue is really lame like a conversation about what the German soldiers had for breakfast. Not funny and terrible. The dialog and voice acting naration by the main character made him sound whiny. The characters don't seem angry, afraid, agitated, motivated or anything at all.
Weapon aiming is terrible. The game started with crosshair display set to off and I think I know why. Because aiming without looking down the iron sight is so much better. Either way, ammo projectile don't fire within the crosshair area but it gives you more view without zooming down the iron sight. Maybe it is how rifles and pistols work back in the day but it really gets on your nerve after you spam the entire clip missing every bullet. Reloading changes the entire clip so remaining ammo is discarded.
Enemy A.I. is simple. Each battle, I simply run beside/flank them and take them off close range. Its much more effective his way really. Maybe it works for the first few chapters but no matter because my patient ran out sooner.
Now in the screenshot of the game made each battle seems engaging. This is simply a matter of angle the shot was taken. The maps are bare minimal. Each chapter is so short that the map might be smaller than a CS:GO map. There is only 1 route to take and it is blocked off with 2-D grasses or trees most of the time. Reaching a combat area, are some trees, branches, fences and probably a building. That is literally it. Imagine a flat area with a few props placed "strategically" for enemies to appear and how you can flank them. You cannot heal during chapter but automatically rearmed and back to business on the next chapter.
You can give orders to the squad mate following you but their deaths are permanent I think. Honestly, the story is so badly written I could not care less for these mates. They are simply there to be cannon fodder or distract enemies. Orders are issued by right clicking and directing them to another location. Depending on where the destination lands, action will automatically be executed such as taking cover, mounting the machine gun and etc. You can also get them to focus fire and supress the enemies as indicated with an icon over their head. Supressed enemies fires with a longer interval so you have more window.
All these I pressed on to play since people are claiming the story is good. The final straw is when I threw a grenade and it probably landed few feet away. I moved out from my cover to throw a second one to find it landing in front of 2 enemies covering behind 2 pieces of wooden fence with legs and torse obviously visible since the fence does not cover entirely from ground up. The grenade explodes without dealing any damage to the enemy.
So why the 2 in the score? For such an old game it actually supports native 1080 resolution.

Mordheim is a gritty and near to literal take on the original Mordheim system.  The emphasis in early access has been on balance and keeping to the spirit of its tabletop predecessor, and it has done that in spades.  Its color pallete and graphic design are ludicrously dark and forboding.  Every map is liberally painted with corruption and death, with every little bump or crevess hiding another way to get killed.  In this aspect, it is just like every game of Mordheim you've ever played on your high school buddies kitchen table.
Where the game differs is in its combat and warband growth.  The warband building system is difficult to master, yet varied enough to cater to quite a few different playstyles in one warband.  Half of the challenge right now is finding out what works the best, and I forsee it becoming quite similar to the tabletop game's tendency to rely on cookie cutter net lists, but this doesn't bother me at all.  Its something you can plan for and counter with ingenuity and skilled gameplay.
Combat is often initiated totally by surprise, yet can be flipped in just two or three actions.  While individual characters can shine, what really makes the difference is your follow up.  This is a great way to really do combat, as it makes you truly have to think out each turn before you take action.
All of these together come wrapped up in a very neat little package, a promise of things to come.  Its still in early access, but there is still so much more Rogue Factor can do.  The skys the limit...try it out..watch the learning curve, and you will be happy you spent the cash

A beautifully rendered, interesting sandbox/space fighter.
+ Has amazing graphics
+ Well optimized
+ Unique economical model
+ Option to switch between realistic (newtonian) and Kinetic Field flight (controls your velocity and direction precisely) modes
- Notifies you of missions, auto-accepts them and thereby sends in bad guys to murderize you (as of D13, planned to change in the future)
* Has built-in tutorial, but is not perticularly useful or userfriendly
Overall a good game, but still needs work; hence early access. If you are into space flight games and wish to build your own ships to shoot down your enemies, while looking absolutely beutiful at the same time, this is you're game.
EDIT: After letting it sit a while, most importantly after leaving early access, I feel like this game just does not live up to its potential. Unless the devs pick it up seriously again or give it to someone else, it will forever be a singleplayer sandbox of Elite:Dangerous with 60% of the features missing.
I really want to love this game, but the lack of content (which would be ok with multiplayer) really kills it for me. If you are considering buying this game, don't. To the devs I ask only one thing, please, please, please finish this game as it deserves to be! You guys are letting a game with so much potential die and be ripped apart by a now-hostile community that is so ashamed by the fact this game was not finished.
That being said I still like to just fly around in sandbox with a massive ship and blast everything out of everyone, but then I get bored and the economy is pointless in sandbox and quite frankly, with the limited information and lack of in-game tags of items to their economic counterparts, impenetrable and boring in career. I love the idea of a complex economic system, but there just isn't enough to do in it and the same with factions.
Aside from missions, that rarely work, all you can do is not trade with a faction you don't like or blow up all their ships and not affect the trade of that faction as all ships (except yours) are military, with minimal cargo and minimal reward other than a tiny bit of rep from other factions, which does not give you lower prices or more hangar space (which is just taunting me in the station UI, waiting to be implemented along with the scaning system) or any other reward for that matter, making the only good way to get money reliably is to go mining, which takes a ridiculous period of time to mine one asteroid, which give maybe two good minerals at a time and dosn't sell for very much at all, maybe getting you enough to buy half of a hull segment on your already tiny mining ship, that must be built from the 'random parts' selection when creating the galaxy, as the Oberon Freighter has no mining laser (although it has a salvage, with not enough cargo space to hold any of the salvagable items) and the fighter (whose name escapes me) has barely enough firepower to get into a fight with a ship its own size, much less one of the ships that the AI controls with aimbot level skills (to be fair, your turrets have the same ability to aim with rediculous accuracy) and are almost all made of size three and up parts that dwarf your tiny starter ship.
Basically, don't buy; devs, please finish this game. Great potential, but not enough to be considered complete. Sorry devs, I can't recomend this to anyone else although I would love to be able to. Please change my mind with a new update that can fix all the little things I have listed above, I know its hard to develop games, but please take another go; for your reputation's sake.

-The story is engaging, and is a refreshing change from saving the world/town/city.
The puzzles are fairly simple. The biggest problem that I had was finding my way out of a few dark areas. For the most part, the game provides light markers to show you which way to go.

Absolver is a fantastic game. I am bad at traditional fighting games, but have been a kickboxer for 20 years. I actually built in-game combos around my go-to combinations that I use in real life; nearly all the moves are built into the game. Fighting in Absolver FEELS like fighting. You build your combos, you get a feel for you opponents style, and you execute your combos in a system that is both simple and deeply complex at the same time. I have never feel cheated in a PVP fight. I have felt frustrated that I couldn't time my attacks, I have felt overwhelmed at an opponents brilliant deck, but I have never felt helpless. For every move, and every combo, there are numerous counters and options available.
The game had some initial network issues, but they have mostly resolved it. There are still some random time I can't connect, but I just use that time to accomplish whatever offline mode things I wanted, or spend a few hours trying to create a new deck.
The PVE content is pretty minimal, but the world is beautiful and intriguing. Enemies will sometimes fight you in groups. Sometimes they kick each other in the head and kill themselves. Its good. If you can't take down 4 NPCs attacking you as a group, I'd say you aren't actually done with PVE yet.
Let me put it simply: If you like martial arts, but have never liked how fighting games control, or how a quick attack button mash can cheese you to death, buy this game. Play it, build your combos, win some, lose some, and feel amazing.

-All those unidentified devices, AAAARRRRRGGGGHHHH!!! (more of a personal thing)
-Some people may take time to get used to the controls (they can now be rebinded in-game. Yay!)


GAMEPLAY

Transcendence is a top-down, roguelike, spaceship simulator. You choose a craft to pilot and fly around different star systems hunting outlaws, doing missions, mining asteroids, and trading goods. Pretty standard space stuff. The thing is, as you go to new systems the enemies and their bases become tougher, but so do you... at least you should be... you are upgrading your equipment as you go right? Anyways, you get the picture. Kill stuff, find stuff, sell stuff, buy stuff.

However, that is a woeful oversimplification of the game. There is a wealth of mechanics that are understood easily enough, but will continue to surprise you even after playing it for +300 hours.

The game is indeed quite difficult. Any number of things can go wrong in space and lead to your journey's premature end. Running out of fuel, getting thrown in prison, blown up by pirates, blown up by outlaws, blown up by slavers, blown up by drug dealers, blown up by pteravors, blown up by aliens, and even getting blown up by your own weapons. Suffice it to say that you will be blown up alot before you actually beat the game.

One of my only complaints would be that the AI is pretty stupid and can be exploited to do many weird and sometimes "cheaty" things. But I could also say that was part of the fun. Nonetheless, I think we can all agree that no one likes seeing the accusatory "Pirate!" message popup just because you had a stray Thermo-Cannon shot. I mean, it's not my fault that E-100 freighter was in the way! And besides, it's armor was paper thin... seriously though, who decided it would be a good idea to let a bunch of rose-petal-flimsy freighters roam a warzone without any protection besides that flimsy laser cannon of theirs? That thing can't even scratch an Ares Sandstorm class ship! Ugggh.

The game has had several expansions released. Though the core game is free and can be downloaded from Kronosaur's website, the Steam version has all the current expansions. If you buy the Steam version you are also given any future expansions. Like I said earlier, the developer has done a good job of steadily releasing updates and expansions. We expect to see the next one in the main story come out soon.


STORY

The story is relayed through short pieces of prose that you read, usually while docked at some significant station. It delivers an interesting tale that isn't totally fleshed out yet, leaving alot of unexplained things. However, the expansions have made great progress in clearing up and expanding the story's universe. The main story itself only has the first part of three planned sections released and ends on somewhat of a cliffhanger. Future expansions to the main story are expected to be released soon (hopefully).


GRAPHICS

The graphics are, from what I can tell, mostly 2D sprites with lots of them having multiple facings. Updates have drastically improved the eye-candy  to be quite pleasing. It now includes things like shadows, light-shading, more facings for objects, detailed thruster exhaust, etc. Rest assured you won't be disappointed. They serve their purpose and do so admirably.


CONCLUSION

Personally, I would put this game as #2 on my top ten best games ever. Right behind Cortex Command (no throwing tomatoes please!).

Personal opinion aside, this game has been wonderfully taken care of by both it's developer and community for many years and shows no sign of stopping. It has been refined over and over again to the point that it is easily one of the most worked on indie games there is. I highly recommend it and suggest you try out the free version on
if your not sure.

In this game, you play as some teenager who constantly throws away sharp objects and hammers as you investigate the mysterious disappearance of your friends from a Halloween party hosted at the most haunted house in the universe, and whether or not your immensely bitter best friend with access to mysterious occult artifacts is somehow involved.
The hidden object scenes are serviceable. Most scenes use the 'one or two items are arbitrarily hidden behind another item' mechanic, which is kind of stupid, but at least your mouse highlights whenever you hover it over such an object. One big flaw is that the list of objects only displays about half the total for that scene, and you can't 'click ahead' and clear an object if it's not on the visible portion of the list.
The puzzles are definitely the game's weakest point. Many of them are unintuitive (the fish/bathtub one springs to mind) and perhaps because of this a lot of the puzzles include a complete solution under the '?' menu, which if you find yourself reaching for it I don't know why you wouldn't just click the Skip button altogether. I also have a specific beef with the sudoku puzzle late in the game; I wanted to try and puzzle it out on my own, but turned the game off to go to sleep. When I returned to the game the next day, none of my progress had been saved. (An earlier puzzle, one of those beams of light/mirror deals, saved the positions of its lanterns even after quitting and returning, so this was a particularly boneheaded move).
Sometimes the 'take item to a certain location' puzzles were a bit obtuse, but fortunately the map highlights any place you can interact with given whatever items you have in your inventory. There really are a lot of locations, and as a result hidden object scenes are rarely repeated.
The plot is typical bananas revolving around a cursed board game and a bunch of dead losers whining about how they were personally responsible for sending the whole estate to Hell, despite it being out of their hands thanks to a big ol' curse. The more interesting plot, ironically, is the teen drama involving one of the protagonist's friends going bonkers enough to send the whole class to Hell, but sadly that's hardly touched upon.
I wish Steam let you rate games as mediocre, but I suppose in the end I'd recommend this game. Definitely not at full price! I'd say hold out for at least 75%, or wait for it to pop up in a bundle again.
Oh, almost forgot: This game had an awesome cat, an awesome crow, and three awesome owls.

I can't recommend this game, not at all. Why?
There are good things - a few. Drawings/scenes are quite nice, and there are some intresting cutscene animations (videos that resemble to the story about Death in  Harry Potter 7 ) , but after a certain point I just skipped them, as the game itself was too painful.
There is no voice acting to speak of.
There is little to no feedback about the interactive areas in Hidden Object Scenes (HOSs), this usually turns the game into a clickfest. Items hidden behind tiles of wall that looks the exact same as the other ones, but you need to find THAT one.
Quite a few items in HOSs are not even drawn correctly - only the visible half is drawn, so when it pops out because you found it you can eyeball a nice half watering can, for example.
Also, click detection is strange, usually you need painfully precise clicks to your actions be registered, especially while using items between HOSs.
The message window - info about your surroundings, about the story - if visible for a fixed, 5 secondish time. But wait! It's not visible for 5 second until your last click on an item - it's visible from the first! The timer doesn't get refreshed when you click on an item as long as the message window is up , so you quite often end up with flashing text that's only visible for 1-2 seconds.
And finally:
HOSs sometimes have invisible items. Once I had to find a peace sign and even the hint showed a blank place where the sign *supposed to be*.
And this is why I write this review now, instead of finishing the game. I think I'm at the Stables and need to find a floppy disk in the recect Hidden Object Scene, but EVEN THE HINT COULDN'T FIND IT.
Never, ever buy this game.  I've played with bad-ish HOGs like Theatre of the Absurd - but I enjoyed it all along. On the other hand in the case of Shadows: Price for Our Sins I only struggled, because of how bad and frustrating the game is at almost every point.

This is one of the best squad based first person shooters I have ever played.  I played this game many years ago when it first came out and it still hits all the right places.  The soundtrack is beautiful, listening to it might remind you of the soundtrack to Saving Private Ryan or the Band of Brothers series.  You get a real sense of the harrowing bravery of the men who fought in WW2.  I'm pretty sure all the characters in your squad are fictitous but they fleshed them out so well I felt they could almost be passed off as real people.  In normal difficulty levels I can't tell you how many times I reloaded a checkpoint because I'll be damned if I lose Hartsock or Corrion!
I haven't played the multiplayer, but I can say I was incredibly satisfied with the single player campaign. In terms of action it can ease you into it, throw you into a frantic fray of issuing orders to your squads in order to outmaneuver the Nazis, and there are times when you just♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants going up against a field of 88s or panzer tanks with nothing but your squads (hopefully they're alive), your rifles and your wits.  The level of difficulty that you play the game also unlocks some pretty cool "making of" stills and audio, not only do they provide some great insight to how the game was made (and how they replicated major battlefields down to the closest details of it's time.  They also unlock After Action Reports (used to figure out gameplay) and various bios (weapons, notable people you encounter, units) in the game.  The premise to the game mechanics is taking full advantage of the 4 "F"s (Find, Fix, Flank, Finish).  You're squad is pretty damn smart, they'll run and shoot, find the nearest cover (from where you tell them to go) jump out of your way when you're shooting and yell at you when you get in their way.  Squad management can be tedious on harder levels when you really need to manage your squads.  You have a definite health bar (no health regen) I believe the only way to possibly regain health is to beat the level or reach a checkpoint.
The graphics and default controls are dated, thankfully you can customize the controls.  Despite being dated I think the graphics hold up really well, animations can be a bit stiff but everything looks pretty good considering it's age.  I can still play this game and simply find a quiet part of the level and just enjoy the scenery.
Weapons handling is about a legit as a game can to this day in my opinion.  I get most modern shooters create this ease of use (EOTech/red-dot sight) interface where the bullet always goes where you point the reticle, but this game pretty much relies on you using iron sights (and at times scopes for sniper rifles).  Each weapon feels like it handles in a unique way, they each fire with different levels of accuracy.  Of course some people don't like this level of realism (which I can understand).
I really recommend this game, sale or not, it's some of Gearbox's finest work and really wish it would return to these roots someday.

My favorite part about Brothers in Arms is how they really focus on your squad members. It's not necessarily the best story I've ever seen nor is it the best WW2 shooter I've played (though it is both a good story and shooter). However I think this is the closest I've ever seen a game kinda emphasize the drama of war in a way shows like Saving Private Ryan or Band of Brothers do.
Overall, a decent FPS. Only a few drawbacks: Jump response is slow. Not much stamina-can't run very long and the bar takes too long to recharge. And third- swim function is slow.

I guess Capcom got tired of the series having two different titles in Japan and America so they combined the two names into one. Unimaginative name aside, this game is a return to form - Capcom recognized their mistake in turning the series into co-cop action games and returned to a single player horror experience, this time with a fresh first person camera perspective. While this is easily the third best game in the series after REmake and RE4, it's also one of the most frustrating entries thanks to some unfulfilled potential.
In a break from RE tradition, this game introduces a new main character, Ethan Winters. The basic setup is very similar to Silent Hill 2 - he receives a message from his wife who has been missing for 3 years, summoning him to meet up with her - but it quickly diverges from that template. This message brings him yet another mansion, only this time the mansion is a run down estate in Louisiana owned by the Bakers, a truly deranged southern family. They spend the first 2/3 of the game stalking you through the estate's many houses and outbuildings, the scope of which silently conjures a familial history of slave ownership.
The opening sequence in the guest house immediately shows you how serious they were about returning to horror here - this is BY FAR the scariest game in the series. I didn't this the RE series would ever go this far - this may be the first time a horror game has ever had me freaked out in the daytime. The claustrophobia induced by the odd camera angles from the early games has been wonderfully updated in first person with tight spaces and a flashlight which gives you a tiny field of view. The house is downright disgusting, and a lot of what you have to do to traverse it is quite nauseating (naturally including draining a mold-filled bathtub in a tribute to the original). The visuals are wonderful, and the music is used sply but effectively. The monster designs are great, and while there are a few reprised ideas, they feel more like a cute nod to previous entries than lazy recycling.
Mechanically, this game is a return to the core principles of old RE. Magically interconnected item boxes are back. Typewriter save spots are back in the form of cassette recorders (though you only get a limited number of saves in the form of cassettes in the 'Madhouse' hard mode that's unlocked after beating the game - otherwise it works like the RE4 typewriters). The core of the game is once again a key hunt in a big house. It's difficult even on normal, and you will run out of ammo frequently, putting you in hairy situations. Health and ammo crafting systems have been combined and streamlined - you can combine a green herb, gunpowder or solid fuel with a chem pack or strong chem pack to craft 6 different items. This isn't quite as much of a return to old-school design as the teaser implied - it holds your hand a bit more in the form of frequent autosaves and an objective list - but it feels like a nice compromise between the cruelty of those old games and the excessive handholding of modern ones. It hits a nice sweet spot.
Most of the game feels like it could have been a new IP or offshoot, thanks to a much more intimate story with a new main character, a new camera perspective, and a very different kind of horror. Unfortunately, it becomes much more uninspired once it starts trying to be a Resident Evil game again in the final act. Several plot twists feel like forced attempts to tie this unrelated story into the main series, transforming the story into an addled and incoherent mess of smashed-together tropes. This is primarily frustrating because for the first time ever, the plot of a Resident Evil game was almost good. It was probably silly of me to expect it to remain that way.
To make matters worse. the gameplay also declines in the final act. The Bakers aren't the only enemies in the game - there are also new zombielike creatures called the Molded. These creatures are quite scary and hard to defeat early on in the game, but once the game forgets about the Bakers and gives you stronger firepower, it devolves into another dull zombie shooter. Granted, it doesn't swarm you with enemies in a fast-paced manner filled with quicktime events (of which there are close to none), so it's still a step above the previous entries, but it's a big step down for this game. It doesn't help that the environments become rather mundane once you leave the estate - the salt mines in the final stage are particularly dull.
After the lengthy action trilogy, this game returned to being brief and tight - my clear time was around 7.5hrs. I feel like this is an optimal length for a horror game (though it seems a bit scant if you're paying full price, as there are no extra modes), but seeing as even this brief game had filler towards the end once they ran out of ideas, I would have preferred that it was even shorter and they'd just made the Bakers the entire focus. I can only imagine what the game would have been like if they'd brought in the history of the deep south a bit more. I haven't bought any of the DLC, so I can't comment on that, but not all of it has been released yet anyway.
The PC port is great - I can't remember the last time I could get away with running a new game on native resolution, let alone without turning everything down! It took quite a bit of tweaking to get to that point, but my GPU isn't supposed to be powerful enough to run this game at all and I managed to run it on high settings - while the initial release evidently had some optimization issues, they seem to have cleared them up incredibly well with patches.

Kingdom: New Lands is a simple survival sort of game. From what the tutorial, in the form of the previous ghostly monarch, tells you in small words, you have to "Build, Expand, Defend" It's fun at first, you have a couple citizens, you buy tools to make them builders or hunters, and you build, expand, and defend, and than you might just have doomed yourself already.
First off, everything in this game is done by the power of money, you use coin to do everything, and anything. If you don't have any coin, you can't do a single thing but wait. Through the final words, build, expand, and defend, your first run may have you do just that, build your walls, expand them, than defend at night. First wave comes, it's easy and you survive. All seems well unless you've fallen into a major mechanic the game hasen't told you. You realize your hunters arn't making any coin, which is because you may of over-expanded and now those little rabbit spawn points are behind your walls, which makes them despawn, therefor killing your economy. Thankfully there's some treasure chest around the map to give you more coin to do things, so if you thought to explore and find them, you can play a little longer.
Besides rabbits, a common resource gathering thing in these sorts of games are chopping wood, you use your coin to chop wood for coin, this is partially true as ordering to chop wood cost one coin and you may get one or two back. In the process of doing this however, you might end up overchopping to the "recruitment camps" outside your base.
Unlike most games like this where you spawn more units with resources, instead, new units pop up in these tent and campfire areas in the forest in the form of beggers, you give them coin and they become citizens who can than pick up tools you buy. If you cut down the last tree covering these camps however, they just disapear and cut you off from getting more units. The first island has atleast 3 of these camps thankfully, so you might be able to figure this out before it's too late, but by then, these pitfalls may of set you back a bit which makes things even harder as a begginer from what's to come.
A bloodmoon hits, a small army hits your walls, it's fairly early so you most likley should live, building/expanding should have made you build a couple towers where archers are safe to shoot enemies even if your wall collapses, but a breach in your falls will have alot of your archers on the ground hit, further sending back your economy for now you need to repay them if they lost their coin, and pay even more for their bows. You pick up the pieces and finally manage to get a stable economy and supply of recruits from the remaining spawn camps, all seems well so you upgrade things, explore, and find out you can get coin from farms. It's a survival game at first glance, so you block up the direction where enemies attack you from useing alot of coin the process, which might be a bad idea by this point.
On the way to fortifying your defenses, you may of notice this wrecked ship and payed coin for it to do something, and than find out you have to keep paying more coins, 2 at a time, to have small ship pieces pop out, it takes awhile so you ignore it for the moment, and upgrade everything else. Your defenses hold, everything seems well. This is the first island, so you take your time to find out what everything does. Since everything is done with money, you may be focused on making farmers to have plenty to spare. If you didn't finish building that ship however, you might already be dead.
The last begginer unfriendly thing the game throws at you, is one of those super lame events some survival games have. An absolute "game ender" in the form of winter, will hit if you have survived on the same island too long. At first, it looks like a cool mechanic, you have farmers, it's winter and they can't grow anything at winter, so you have to wait it out until spring. Than bloodmoons hit, your walls are collapsing, you may or may not defeat these big guys that are hammering your walls, and if you haven't finished building that ship, the last of your coin may of been wasted rebuilding your fallen walls. More days pass, your walls are all being chipped slowly, you wonder when winter ends, than you die, unless you have that ship fully built and moved all the way to the docks on the other side of the map, your dead, because, WINTER NEVER ENDS!!! Yup a totally messed up game-ending mechanic. It cuts off your only means of playing the game, it cuts off your only way to get out of the level, and it essentially forces you to sit at your base and wait untill you die because you ABSOLUTLEY CAN"T DO ANYTHING BY THAT POINT!!! If you're lucky enough to have realized the recruitment map thing sooner, you might have a chance with the trader giving you 8 coins per day for the price of one, but if not, there is no way to get any more coins by the time winter hits, let's just say... you're ROYALLY screwed...
So much time has passed, but if you like the game, you'll try again and finally build that ship. When you do, you will sail away on it leaving your "Kingdom" back on doom island, and than you proceed to the next level.
That was just about the experience you might run into on the first level. The next ones to come may be even worse. Later levels have multiple enemy portals that you have to fight to clear a path for the boat to reach the dock, but destroying these portals dosen't make anything easier, they trigger a bloodmoon, separate from the normal blood moon, which means they may stack with the normal one. The onslaught will be worse to survive, and by the 5th and final island, the game was just completley unfair.
I had to reroll the map 3 times because, you know those little recruitment camps all the way out in the woods that are your only source of new units? Well, they have a chance of spawning, not behind one, but two ENEMY PORTALS, making it near impossible to progress at all. Before I knew they can spawn normally, I tried my best running from one side of the map, to the other, having as much coin as I could carry with just the 2 starter beggers your base comes with, but running all that way takes so long, night eventually hits, I had to bribe the enemy to go away, than pay the beggers, than wait for them to walk all the way to base, which they may or may not make it to, since by than, night may hit again and another wave of enemies comes, which I have to bribe or be out of coin by than, or skip, which means my new recruits that are not in base yet can still get the coin smacked out of them. I managed to find, I kid you not, a magical unicorn that craps out 3 coins everytime it eats, which made the whole bribing tactic actually work. The long journey to get a few units made it difficult to upgrade my base though, and I wasen't able to build up an army to clear those 2 portals blocking the recruitment camp, and even If I was able to, the bloodmoons it would of triggered would be unlivable.
This game, oh man this game, I coulden't really decide If I loved or hated it for the longest time. It is fun, yet frustrating, SUPER FRUSTRATING!!! Yet something still kept pulling me back to play it everytime.
I'd finish an island I said, I'd try one more I said, I'll finish the 5th to say I beat it and than never play it again I said! Almost 24 hours later, I beat the 5th island + 2 more extra because.... reasons....
In the end however, my final thoughts of this game is that it's a pain, a ROYAL pain :3
I just can't reccomend it to be fun, it's really REALLY frustrating, but I surely will miss that magical coin crapping Unicorn.

I can never forget that day.
The day when my grandpa died.
I was only 8.
He called me to his bedside and whispered to me, in a voice feeble yet somewhat unsatisfied.
He said to me, "My lovely grandson, I have nothing to give you in this life, as I have been poor and unfortunate,"
"Money and fortune, women and sex, lush and class, I can give you none."
I wasn't feeling any bit of dissapoint, as I knew very well of him, of his life, of his potential, of the legacy he could leave to his descendants.
And then there was, as I remembered correctly, a short silence.
"Except for this."
My hand was tightly grabbed and, the next thing I remembered, was a 4-GB-flash-drive-like object being secretly put in my hand, so secretly that not even the people around me had noticed.
"Finish my life's work." Those were his last words.
After years and years of attempting to figure out just what that only file in the flash drive was, here I was, sitting in front of my laptop, Airmech was released.
The next thing happened can only explained by me as providence: I copied the file to Airmech save folder, opened Airmech arena, attempted to load the file.
It loaded.
It was a 1 vs 1 game, on its 132th minute.
There was only one Base left, and it was surrounded by enemies' Shooters.
The Base health bar was already at 12%, and I had 23 Tanks that were, even the closest ones, at least ten miles away from this Base.
........................................
Years have passed.
There is, like the beginning, only one Enemy Base left.
Except that one Base, is the only one not owned by me.
My right hand trembled as I reached the "Attack" button, never knowing the cause of the tremble being either years of non-stop playing, or the fact that I am now only one button away from fulfilling my grandfather's wish.
The tanks just reached the base and destroyed it.
I looked out the window, tears in both my eyes formed two vertical lines across my face.
Noticed the image in the window, the reflection of yet another old man with eyeful of tears, crying, yet satisfied.
I stared at the blue sky, whispered:
"I finished your work, grandpa."

Now, while it says I *only* have 82.6 hours in game, this only counts after the several hundreds of hours I acquired before I ever downloaded Steam.
In the time I have spent with this game I have bought a very large portion of weapons, gear and armor in the game with in-game currency, bought several gifts (AMRs mainly kek) for other players, which were the only things I ever spent Zen on, as well as join one of the top clans in the game and become an officer.
The game was pretty great.
The starting Assault Rifle was pretty baller, so it essentially eliminated the P2W factor.
Same for the armor, it was a balance between strength and speed, and any purchasable armor changed essentially those two things.
The HRV was one of the most unique things I have ever seen in a game, literally giving the player completely legitimate access to wall-hacks, and was one of the greatest separating factor between this and many other FPS.
It was all going well until corporate garbage sent the game to hell and back, but only being dragged out half as far as it was by a company that was tossed aside, essentially starving, trying to feed it's own starving child.
To hell with this corporate nonsense.
The parity patch wasn't too bad, but essentially I gave up on the game after I began recieving incredibly lag spikes, as well as being unable to find many players. One of the good things (in my opinion, because many seem to challenge this) was the purchasing system. Everything felt less expensive (again, it feels like this to me, even though several people had complaints about things becoming more expensive apparently). I was able to start filling in missing portions of my collection with Combat Points, but eventually I was forced to leave this game behind.
In short, this game is a perfect practical example of the phrase "Oh, how the mighty have fallen!", as it was an absolute stunner. Beautiful visuals, solid fast-paced gameplay and a very in-depth customization system.
Now it sits to die in my Steam library, as it does for many others.
I have recently made contact with the leader of my former clan, and he also believes the game is essentially dead, yet he continues to play it.
I would, too, had I not prioritized other things.
So please, this is a message to all devs and publishers: please, do not let this happen. Moving on from a game is one thing.
Leaving it to die, however is something entirely different.

this is probably the only multiplayer fps i play, and for good reason:
_______PROS AND CONS: i'll write a much more in depth review under these, but if you just want my opinion in short, here it is:
PROS:
great, visceral gunplay.
in-depth customization.
cerebral gameplay with a sort-of built it "wallhack" that everyone gets. (that makes highlevel gameplay more accessible for the deaf!)
great visuals, even on lower end machines
for the most part well-done microtransaction system that never felt pay to win.
CONS:
buying guns permanently can get really expensive, but there is also a rental option to try it out against opponents, and you can use any weapons attachments armor and gear you want in training and practice mode against bots,
not many servers and a medium sized community + no-longer active devs can make the game feel stagnant at times.
_______IN DEPTH REVIEW
the visceral shooting with great feedback makes the gunsplay feel awesome, combined with the variety of customization options for what your gun is, how you customize that gun, your character stats, your gear, in-round items and overall aesthetics gives a very solid and fun foundation with good gamefeel.
and the HRV mechanic is fantastic, letting you occasionally send out a blip to see through walls locating all players in the map, at the cost of being unable to use your weapon while its active and the short active time. everyone has this power, but based on how you customize your character you can use it very differently.
it lets more tactical players get an overview of the battlefield, meaning even after a few hours of playing you'll find yourself planning flanks, and if you really give yourself time to memorize maps much more complicated maneuvers can be used.
it lets CQC players always stay in the action, meaning matches never feel dull since if you're not in the action, you're heading for it.
sniping in blacklight is one of the more unique takes on it as a playstyle, and i love it. HRV means camping becomes muuuch more difficult, but it also means you can spend your time preparing shots at high threat targets and enemy warlords. the customization also means a dedicated sniper can use very specialized weapons and evade HRV and sight, but only if you use it right and know what you're doing.
in short, HRV leads to cerebral gameplay and freshens everything up about the game. and on a side-note, it also means that listening for footsteps is still useful, but by no means required for mid to high level gameplay. this means the game becomes instantly more accessible for deaf and hard of hearing players!
this isnt even mentioning the futuristic aesthetic which, if it's your cup of tea, is really well done.
and notice how i really havent touched on the free-to-play/microtransation part? because in my time playing i havent felt hindered by it or felt like my game was ruined by players who did purchase items. almost every time i've been killed by a player with much better gear than me they were also just much more skilled than me and higher level. the only items no purchasable with the in-game currency are some camo, weapon skins, and i believe a weapon tag that are all money themed. so as long as you're okay with not walking into the battlefield wearing dollar-bill covered military gear then the currency system wont be massively interfering.
in short: a shooter for people who love shooters and people who are picky about them. people who like charging in with a shotgun and people who like planning and sneaking and sniping, and anyone in between. people with fulltime jobs and a bit less time but more money, and people with more freetime and less cash.
9/10
p.s. my number one dream game would be neotokyo 2, made in cooperation with the creators and the BLR team. i'm drooling at the thought of it.

I absolutely recommend this game, it provides some unique experiences.
Playing a toddler is not only a unique idea, it is actually integrated into the game world - I really felt the vulnerability of the small kid when I played the game. The toddler perpective is also the "glue" that brings the otherwise un-relatable story layers together.
What makes the game very special is the "mind♥♥♥♥" aspect. The game starts with two layers of story -the "real world" and the phantasy world of the toddler where the main quest takes place. At the very end of the game, both layers are enriched by a background story (meta layer) which puts all events into a new - and very disturbing - perspective. To avoid spoilers I will not go into details.
I cannot name another game that made me think about its story that way - and especially, in what position the game puts me as a player. Enjoying the "main quest" as a toddler is the obvious purpose of the game, but things get uncomfortable when it is revealed what the main quest represents.
All this is delivered without being overly mysterious and confusing (compared to movies of this type) and without the usage of the ususal "tools" - very creepy environemtns, gore and violence - it only happens in your mind when you think through the different levels of the story.
This game is actually story-driven in the best possible way, but also still relies on traditional game mechanics - which differentiates it from walking simulators.
The only (mild) complain that I have is the short playtime.

I actually enjoyed this one. I actually cared about the story for once in one of these things. While the story wasn't the best it was still interesting and had a decent catch and conclusion.  I enjoyed the silhouette cut scenes even though all the cut scenes in this game had terrible resolution. The puzzles were decent. The difficulty went up and down a lot; some puzzes I found just plain difficult, others I found the instructions baffling, and others were very simple. The Hidden Object Game parts of the game were interesting. I liked and disliked that for some of the items you had to do some other actions first. I liked it when the actions made sense like taking other items, putting them together to make the whole item. That was cool. But I did not like it when it was an arbitrary "click on this RANDOM item to get it to move so you can see the item you need hidden BEHIND it!" Why the hell would I ever have thought "oh yes, that thimble is DEFINITELY behind that hat!" The item using puzzles were decent though sometimes the reason you needed an item was pretty stupid. Like the part where your character wouldn't put her hand in a fountain because it's dirty? Hello? People's lives are at stake and you're worried about a bit of algae on your hands? Please.
Overall, a decent Hidden Object, Point and Click game.

The journal is very detailed - it contains almost every bit of the plot - and the map is very useful as it can save you a lot of time by teleporting you to the desired scenes. The graffics and the sound are very simple but well-working and the voice overs are bad. There are some bugs and glitches throughout the game, but none gamebreaking. It took me 4 hours to complete. Recommended only for fans of hidden-object/puzzle games and only in a discount or in a bundle, since the original price is a bit high compared to what it gives.

If you like ghost stories, then this mediocre game should worth a few bucks for you, especially if it is on sale. It’s far from being the worst hidden object title on Steam, but even further of being the best.
Shadows: Price of Our Sins had a really sound idea behind it: a hidden object puzzle game featuring a ghost story about witchcraft, love, betrayal and tragedy. It’s the execution that suffers.
The game has no voiceover after the intro, so everything is told in large– and frankly, very boring– text dumps. Also, the main plot seen at the beginning pretty much disappears, and never gets a proper resolution: after solving the final puzzle, it just… stops.
The puzzles range from bad to above average. They are also repetitive, with an uncomforting emphasis on colour puzzles. Despite this it is recommended to play it on an easier difficulty, since they follow little logic: key items just turn up abruptly in the most unexpected places.
The graphic style fits well to the atmosphere, but it is also quite dated, which really shows in the meticulous pixel hunting of the hidden object scenes.

The nto confuse me even further are these completely separate cutscenes that are done with flash animation rather than CGI. It looks like as if this game was done by 2 completely different developers. It just throws you off. The voice acting is dull and emotionless like they weren't even trying. The gameplay was your standard hidden object play through. Nothing fancy. The puzzles were great as least but some puzzles were either a little too easy and some were totally cryptic. Do I recommend this game, no. Not unless you are a die hard fan of hidden object games or if it's on sale. It's a 5/10 for me.

The only minor annoyance I had is while all other pop-up/zoom-in windows close if you click out of the window, to close the board game you have to click on its icon again. Seems inconsistent.
The puzzles were mostly quite easy, which I liked, but one of my main problem with the game is that the instructions were often vague and in a couple of cases incorrect. (= It told me to solve puzzle in a different way than what later turned out to be the actual solution. Minor but important errors in wording.) Also the HO scenes are very junkpile-ish with many unrelated items (and what is a takeaway food box doing in an at least 100 years ago abandoned place?) and the scenes sometimes had wrong names for objects, like calling garlic onion and such.
kinda BS, the whole thing is just one boring and overcomplicated deus-ex machina, with very 1 dimensional characters (perhaps the only exception is the cook). Also the game seems somewhat racist to me, with 3 token minority characters, all based on racial & gendered stereotypes. Plus one HO scene mixed Native American and Japanese elements, which seemed quite culturally appropriative.
I don't know if I would recommend it, I'm really on the fence, but I picked recommend because for me it was still worth my time, even if just barely. If beautiful graphics and very good sound design make a game worth for you then go for it, but if the quality of the plot or the HO scenes are important to you or you are bothered by racist and sexist stereotypes then avoid it.

I can't, in good conscience, recommend this game. While the puzzles and hidden object parts of the game work just fine - the story is incredibly lacking. Which is saying something considering that most hidden object games have very weak stories to begin with.
The premise starts out okay. You're going to a friends party. This friend just inherited an old mansion. Starts out okay. It's after you find your friends that the story starts to fall apart. You don't really know what's happening because you step outside to take a call from your mom, but your friends decide to play a jumanji-esque board game which ends up trapping their souls. Standard stuff. But it's the 'why' they are affected by all of this, is what causes confusion.
I loosely think I understand the whole plot, but it's completely dreadful and definitely not worth the price. If you insist on getting the game, please save your money and buy it on sale or in a bundle.

The game starts out kind of interesting, you are invited to a Halloween party and then all you friends go missing. Once you start searching for them however the game shifts away from that current day setting and you end up searching through generic old kitchens, farms and churches and solving issues of some old ghosts. The story itself is just some generic love story with black magic and stuff and never manages to properly tie together with the current day setting at the start of the game.
Minigames are overall ok, hidden object scenes are solid as well. The item use in the game however feels pretty arbitary and requires far to much backtracking, which is fast thanks to the minimap, but kind of destroys the flow of the game.
Overall it's not a terrible game, it just ended up being far to generic after the promising start. I also had some technical issues with the game displaying a black screen instead of a cutscenes, restarting the game fixed that, but I lost a cutscene or two that way.

There are some issues, but overall it's got potential. The tutorial is nearly non-existant, but hopefully that will improve with time. Fingers crossed that is turns out as good as we hope.
6/10, for now.

I should preface this by asking you to ignore my hours in this game. I played quite a bit of it offline and apparently Steam doesn't track hours spent offline.
I've said it before and I'll say it again: One of the most damning words you can use to describe a video game is "potential". With almost all of the absolute worst games of the last generation, "potential" was the best word people could use to describe them. Duke Nukem Forever, The Walking Dead: Survival Instinct, X-Rebirth, these all had massive potential and that is part of why they were considered such disappointments. If "potential" is the best word you have to describe a game, that game has failed, Early Access or no. And sadly, that is the best word I can use to describe Kinetic Void.
I first picked up this game last year in May, actually getting it with a Steam card gifted to me for my birthday. I should've bought something else. This game barely had any content at the time, even for an Early Access game. Earlier this year Earth: Year 2066 was released in Early Access and was massively criticized for having next to no content and that's about what the game was like when I first bought it. You had access to plenty of ship customizations and...that was about it. Then you flew around in a very pretty screenshot area and then you stopped. That was about it. Rarely enemies would appear and then you would attack them in broken combat. Or maybe you went to a ship drydock (which it takes like 4 years to reach, more on that later) and found out that you couldn't dock. I get it, it's Early Access and things are gonna be buggy and broken, but when there's only 3 things to do in your game, you would expect those 3 things to actually work to some degree. So instead it turned into a pretty screenshot game and nothing more.
Moving around in this game in absolutely awful. It takes FOREVER to reach anywhere. I get it, space is big but this is a video game, you are allowed to cut down on size if it makes the game more accessable and fun. Even in FTL mode it still feels like it takes ages to move around, up until you stop paying attention and crash into a planet. Scratch that, you never crash unless you're shot down, so all you do is clip through solid landmasses, whether it's a planet, a moon or a space station, you just clip through it.
This could have been fixed by either cutting down on the size and scope to something more manageable or to include more things that happen along the way. Encountering Space Pirates (If the combat worked), seeing two fleets battling each other, encountering a stranded merchant ship, these all could have helped it not feel so empty and boring. As is, the exploration feels less like the magic and wonder of something like Skyrim and making me feel more like this:
I haven't checked up too often on this game since then, I haven't really felt like revisiting this slog of a space explorer but after a years worth of updates I decided to revisit it. It isn't that much better now, sadly. After a year of updates it still feels the same to me, a bit like the difference between the DayZ mod and standalone: Months and months of work and nothing seems to have changed. Things are indeed different, but nothing big is different. Combat is still broken to the point of being unplayable and exploration still takes several millenia to ever do anything at all.
Sorry kids, but until further notice, "potential" is the best word I can come up with for this game and "boring as hell" is the worst. Not recommended at all, only spend your money if you want to fund the development cycle. Otherwise, there's too many games for you to buy that desrve your money for you to waste any on this slog of a game.
