I preordered the game in July and I have to say it is better than i suspected it to be.
Wifi / Server problems:
You will see a lot of people complaining about the servers being crap and I have not had that issue very often. Sure there are some hours of the day where I can't connect online, but that doesn't mean I can't go and learn more moves and improve my prospects/absolvers.
A little trick I have found if you are having problems connecting with friends: if you have one friend online, have them invite you if you are offline in the start menu, 9 times out of 10 it will work. At least it has worked for me when I have done it.
If that doesn't work try completely closing steam and your game and restarting it. Sometimes updates get in the way.
All in all everything has been working out great, just some few lag issues due to the fact a lot of people have been playing this game and have unstable wifi connections.
Deciding on buying the game or not:
If you enjoy movement of martial arts, no salty voice or text chat, and the open encounters with fellow prospects/absolvers then you will enjoy this game. You just need patience with learning the moves, fighting other people and the servers.
The offline main "Story" isn't very long but constantly improving, learning new styles and moves will take a good while. When writing this review I have put in over 31 hours in about 4 days and I still haven't learned two of the four current styles that are out or all of the moves.
It is also great to play with friends, helping them improve, fighting together and doing a good spar every now and again.
If you are thinking about getting this game, don't let others discourage you. Try it out, test it, if it doesn't work or you don't like it, refund it under two hours.

Definitely, the best word to describe Far Cry.
If you're looking for a FPS which requires effort, look no further.
First Person Shooters are not usually my first choice of game genre, but I like to think that I can hold my own - at least in Easy Mode. Unfortunately, that was -not- the case this time around. 90% of the time I was face down in the dirt with a grenade up my bum.
The AI is surprisingly intelligent, and you will get your butt handed to you if you dash in guns blazing, that being said; checkpoints are well spaced and there are just enough health packs, armour and ammo crates scattered around to get you through each level if you plan carefully.
Each area map is huge, though you should expect to do a lot of crawling through the undergrowth, and the aesthetic variation is minimal - anticipate leaves in your hair, dirt on your pants and the occasional bug in your mouth.
While the gameplay is brilliant, the narrative is somewhat lackluster. If you're looking for interesting cutscenes and a tale to tie yourself to, this may not be the game for you. I believe each game is standalone, and so can be played in any order you wish without stories crashing into each other.
In all honesty, after many hours of frustration, I dedicated the rest of my time to watching (what must be a robot play) on Youtube.
If like me you feel you need to see this one through to the end before starting the next available in the series, here's the link I watched, played by
I tip my hat to you.
On the basis that I enjoyed enough to watch 10 hours of footage, I will rate it positively, but I found this altogether too difficult to play successfully, and ultimately did not enjoy it. If you are seeking a run and gun and are new to the FPS genre, I would suggest avoiding unless you live for long and arduous battles.

Disclaimer: I don't have the steam version of Far Cry 2, so I can't write a review for it, but I am SO♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the game that I said "Lets just include a Far Cry 2 Review with my Far Cry 1 review."
First off, Far Cry.
I played this game on either Easy or Normal, I can't really remember.
And I absolutely hated it.
Now, I enjoy hard games. I don't mind difficulty in games. But when a game is so hard that I feel like I'm going to have a nervous breakdown, I don't like it. I think games are supposed to be somewhat difficult, but still not so difficult you find yourself hating the game, This is how I felt with Far Cry.
The whole story for this game is you play some muscular pixel man named Jack, who found himself on the island because of vacation or whatever the hell. Because of such a vague and pretty much terrible starting montage, you really have no idea why you're on the island in the first place. You just know that you're in a hawaiian t-shirt EVERYONE recognizes you with, and every single living thing on the island wants to kill you.
Without spoilers: This game is so long. So so so so long. I've noticed many older games are usually extremely long, but this one takes the cake. When you think the story is going to end, it ends up putting a twist you don't expect in it. Then when you think the game is done, it gives you yet ANOTHER twist. I enjoy long games, but when its so long and repetative that it feels like you're doing the same level over and over again, it gets extremely boring. Not to mention its extremely hard. I had to actually edit code in the game just to be able to cheat so i could have the satisfaction of finishing the game, because the creators were sadistic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who couldn't make their game easier.
With spoilers:
In the end, if you like older games and you know what to expect with them (bad graphics, extremely long and eventually boring gameplay and ultimately the same location over and over again), then this game is perfect for you. We can talk all day about how this game was ahead of its time back in the day, or how it opened a great franchise; but in the end, its aged horribly.
Now for Far Cry 2.
God, do I absolutely hate this game.
This game is just like Far Cry when it comes to telling you literally nothing about whats going on. All you know is you were suddenly dropped off in Africa to kill some arms dealer named "The Jackal", and there are two factions fighting over the UAC (Unnamed African Country. How creative, Ubisoft). They don't tell you anything about the factions, who is good or who is bad. Pretty much your only job is to kill.
Without spoilers: Just like Far Cry, this game is extremely boring and repetitive. At first I really enjoyed it, but after the 80th jeep rammed into me, or I got another vague quest telling me to kill somebody who doesnt seem all that bad, I got tired of it very quickly. I understand its supposed to be set in Africa, so there won't be a lot of colour or variety in the scenery but holy crap. They could have at least put something in there to make it not so bland. The sky was pretty much the only colourful thing in the whole game.
With spoilers:
In the end, I would say, if you love incredibly boring and repetitive games; this is the perfect game for you. The only reasons why I manned up and finished it was so I could say I finished it. And you can totally do the same, but just keep in mind that you have to be extremely commited to this game to finish it.
All in all, I feel anyone who buys these games are often people who feel like they need to finished Far Cry and Far Cry 2 to play 3 and 4, and let me just say, you totally don't have to. Not only is every single Far Cry game non-related, but you can just watch someone on YouTube having to struggle instead of paying money to play it (and potentially never ending it)
Some people might have different experiences with this game, but personally for me, I hated both of these games and I hope I never have to look at their ♥♥♥♥♥ faces again.

This game was like crack to me: I couldn't take distance from it eventhough I wanted to stop. I eventually did stop playing after I unlocked the last achievement, because by that point any player would have seen more than enough of this simple but suprisingly deep game.
Kingdom is a sidescroller where your interactions are limited to the things you spent your money on: hire workers to build and upgrade, archers to kill, farmers to recieve more money. With the exception of one mount in New Lands, there is no other way to fend of the daily zombie-like army that attacks you every night (every 10 minutes in real time). The control scheme exists with a total of 4 buttons: left, right, shift (to run) and an interaction button. As you can imagine, you run a lot from left to right and back expanding your kingdom.
First time players might find the limited construction options questionable, like the fact that you can't place walls, towers and farms anywhere you want unless it's located on a randomly, pre-defined spot respectively recognizable with dirt, a rock and a small stream of water. This means you can't always have a good constellation of towers and walls. Instead, you have to make a choice: Do you cut through the woods to find a better spot, risking your base to be neglected for a night or two, or do you stick with what you have right now?
The simplicity has also a charm: the graphical design is calm and relaxing and the music and sounds go hand-in-hand with it. You mostly just run, time your attacks and think forward. Their are more mechanics going on than the developper will tell you about (in fact, they almost tell you nothing), which brings the satisfaction of discovery but also the frustration of trial-and-error with it. Let me start off by saying that this is in my top ten favorite games of all time. Darwinia's a cool retro-style game about a digital world populated by little people called Darwinians, who are under siege by a dangerous computer virus. Under the instructions of Darwinia's creator, you have to help get rid of the virus and restore Darwinia to it's fully-funtional self.
The whole time playing I thought I had the ending figured out, I thought it was going to end on some lame twist where Darwinia's actually Earth or something. But no, it actually ended very originally, and on an extremely bitter-sweet note.
My only complaint, and it's really a minor one, is that for a game called "Darwinia" it's not very Darwinian. I was expecting a lot of heavy symbolism reflecting Charles Darwin's Theories of Evolution, but there's only a few, very subtle, nods to evolution where you can upgrade the troops of Darwinia. In fact the game's sequel "Multiwinia" is more Darwinian, since the Darwinians are battling eachother for supremacy.
There's actually more symbolism for religion than anything else. But don't be alarmed by that, the symbols are very subtle. And even then the symbolism is actually really good, the symbolism helps the message it tries to convey, which I won't tell you, because it would spoil the ending. Just trust me it's a really good and interesting message.
I can't recommend this game or the team behind it enough. I've never seen anything like Darwinia, and I'd say you should check it out too.

Pros 'n Cons:
+Very atmospheric, puts you constantly on edge, even if nothing is actually nearby (which most of the time, nothing is).
+Great sound design, so much work went into creating the soundscape for this game, there's pretty much always something going on in that arena. MUST be played with headphones.
+Creative premise, though I'm sure it won't be for long (on steam, nothing ever remains original for long, I'm lookin' at you, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DayZ clones).
+Neat monster design (though I wish I'd have been able to get a better look at the second one at some point, you get plenty of chances to see the first one, the second one you only kind of see its bottom half).
-Definitely too short for something that costs $20. If you're thinking that the story can't possibly be over once you've collected all 4 memories, you are totally wrong, because it is, barring an epilogue scene (which I didn't see coming, though I knew there was going to be SOME kind of twist ending).
-Has a very slow ramp up for such a short game. While the atmosphere is incredibly thick, it takes until about 1/2 of the way through the game before you are in any actual danger (IE, there's a roaming monster chasing you that will game over you if it touches you).
-Only one real threat, and while it's terrifying, I'd have liked for there to be more. I believe technically the second monster CAN kill you, but I never had this happen because I've played Amnesia and know how to hide properly.
-Did I mention it's short? Oh my God it's so short.
Seriously though, wait until this thing is on sale for $5, buy it then, play it once (it'll only take a few hours), uninstall it, and never think about it again, but it's totally worth a playthrough. I hope to see more from this team in the future.

Bought this during the summer sale, figuring that it could be a fun point-and-click adventure.  The music and scenery are very nice, and at some points it's enjoyable to just sit there and kind of take it in.  The puzzles are challenging enough (the map tells you which areas are "Active", i.e. "it's possible to use an object here", however) and if you're a fan of "I Spy" type of puzzles (sit there and find all the hidden items), then you're in luck - because this game has plenty (to the point that I almost got a little tired of them).  I will say this game is pretty well put together, but does have its problems.  The voice acting was a little awkward in the beginning, but during the black and white animated "cutscenes" it was pretty good.  The story itself is pretty standard - ghosts trapped by their compliance in a curse, etc, etc.  The characters were fairly typical (and one of the ghosts was about every stereotype of a Japanese and/or Asian woman? Was that really necessary?), though most of them were likeable enough.  The story relies on a lot of outdated horror tropes - being cursed by "black magic" messing up a "Pagan Ritual" and using supposed "Voodoo Dolls".  And sometimes the search and find puzzle sections were a little ridiculous?  There was just so much stuff thrown into them, sometimes it took away from the puzzle.  At any rate, it's not a bad game, and was actually really fun at some points (The puzzles, art, scenery, and music made it likeable), but I'm glad I didn't pay full price for it.

First, don't let the time spent on this game fool you. The majority of this game I have spent playing offline, due to a recent internet outage, and this being one of the few steam games I had already downloaded.  Apparently Steam doesn't count offline time toward gameplay time.
The game is a fun WWII Squad based FPS. Normally, I don't like squad based games. I have enough trouble keeping me alive without having to worry about different characters too. However, this was highly enjoyable! It however doesn't feel very cinematic, which for me is a downer. However, there are some minor cutscenes between chapters that help tell the story along.
You can tell that Gearbox was inspired by the popular HBO series Band of Brothers(Which came out 4 years before BIA). Not just in name, but similar opening soundtrack, Similar titling colors..among other details. However, similarities aside, it's still very much it's own game, and I think has proven it's self to be one of the better WWII titles of that generation of games.
The graphics are very dated, but for a 2005 game look fantastic! Likewise, the voice acting isn't too shabby either! Much better than I expected from a game from that era.
Only a few negatives really, and those are:
I felt default controls for me were a bit of an annoyance, but that's all changeable in the games options.
A better cover system would have been nice. Yea, you can crouch behind walls/barrels/logs/ravines, but theres no Real cover system in place. That being said, Cover systems weren't common in 2005, so again...that complaint is easily forgiven.
Other than that, the game is a fantastic WWII title! I'm looking forward to checking out the rest of the BIA titles.

Thanks to the sale, I was able to buy and play this again for old-times sake. This was one of the first WW2 shooters I've ever played, alongside Medal of Honor. The tactics and the use of your team to complete objectives is what today's generation of shooters needs and not just rush killing, like CoD. The graphics may not be the best, but the mechanics make the game so realistic; for example, the suppression and flanking.

This is a series I missed when it first came out. I bought the entire pack and started with Road to Hill 30. If you're like me and don't have any nostalgia from the series, I would recommend skipping this one unless it's on sale. Even if you got it in a bundle, it's hardly worth installing.
There are certain mechanics in the game that are very interesting. You have to command two fireteams while battling German infantry and the odd tank through the fields and towns of Normandy. Suppression is very important and this is a mechanic I liked. It wasn't easy to shoot and it's very difficult to snipe heads poking out of cover like in most other games. This is on purpose, and forces you to try and flank your enemy. Some levels start behave as puzzles as you figure out the best way to move your squad.
But in the end, this game has aged badly. In 2006 it may have been great, but by today's standards it's all very dull. The writing is cliche and awful. The voice acting is bad. The story is completely unengaging. I won't judge this game by its graphics, since that would be unfair. But the environments are boring. You spend half the time ducking behind the same hedgerows and mounds of dirt. The towns are empty and lifeless, and the battles are quiet and not very exciting. The game of suppress and flank starts to get tedious after the first few levels.
By the last few chapters I was raring to get this game over with so I could just uninstall it. If you've never played Brothers in Arms before, I would recommend skipping this one unless you really have time to kill. I'm looking forward to moving on to the sequel - I'm hoping they've made improvements.

Dragon Rising is a case of developer and publisher apathy. This was a pretty solid tactical shooter at its core, but the inability for Codemasters to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥at the time has relegated it to an "OK"
To be certain, this game is *NOTHING* like the original Operation Flashpoint. That's ArmA. In fact, there was a lot of hope for this game since ArmA 1, as in Armed Assault: Combat Operations, was so poorly received.  However, ArmA 2 dropped and made this utterly irrelevant.
1.) ArmA 2 got a demo before it launched
2.) Dragon Rising got a demo after it launched
And, to top this off, the game's biggest drawback is that it suffers from consolization. The control responses for inventory management are painfully slow.
The AI, is also, hit and miss. At times, its competent. Other times it craps its pants and rolls in the grass. It always sees through cover, through brush, and through smoke.
In all, this could have been a great beginner's tactical shooter. But, it's just so gimped. For the price? Yeah, it's not bad, at all.

kingdom is a survival game of sorts. it has beautiful pixel art, and a nice relaxing soundtrack to go with it for the most parts, and some nice tense music during attacks. the controls are simple, and easy to work with.
the gist of the game consists of you starting off with some minimal gold, and you manage your resources, in terms of money and manpower, build up your kingdom, protect your kingdom, while plotting to escape to the next land.
for the most parts, it's a really fun game to get into, and as you try to unlock some content, it becomes more fun, as you'll end up having a bit more different stuff to play with. but in the end, the content does feel a bit lacking, as you'd notice the longer you play, it slowly becomes a bit more repetitive (more noticeable if you attempt to do the 100-day achievement, and overstay at an island, it gets pretty boring once snowfall comes).
regardless, i had a really good time with the game, and i do hope, if we ever see a sequel, that maybe the devs might want to consider having some 'random events' to spice things up, a couple more different units (for player and enemies alike), and perhaps also add a 'deconstruct' option, so we can sometimes switch up strategies, and move our borders, etc.

-- FIRST OF ALL --
Don't listen to those who are being cry babies about getting ganked. Some people don't know the features of this game. I saw a comment like "Not for solo players , if you don't have any friends to play with - just stay away from this game" Well that's not true my friend. There is an offline mode for you to play if you want to solo this game. if you want to compete with others, well that's an easy task because nothing (not just players) can harm you whlie you are at a shrine and that's where you que up for duels. if you want to gank you can do that freely.
Go offline if you want to play solo. it's under the options menu. (starting screen options menu)
-- For the review --
I have 30 hours on record and I am loving this game so far.
Combat deck is a good mechanic to customize your character.
You can spend hours into your combat deck and enjoy with the outcome of it. ( I really do enjoy that very much)
in my opinion , combat deck mechanic is better than the "most" pesky talent mechanics where you end up the same build with nearly every character.
Stances are good (every one of these stances has their purpose for real )
Move learning is AMAZING both in logical and fun way. You will find yourself spending a lot of time in a combat even if you are able to finish it quickly. This learning mechanic blew my mind for real. Guess what? You can freaking learn these moves from other players as well as mobs and bosses.
Multiplayer duels are good as well. I enjoy competing. A fighter game more than an rpg.
You plan your moves, you edit your combat deck (with the moves you've learnt), you adapt to your deck and playstyle, you will learn the other moves and their animations for quick responses (reflex dodges / parries /absorbs and the other special skill) and the most important thing is, you will enjoy doing all these.
Adapting to a new deck is alway challenging. Learning about which move leads to another, cutting your combos for another mixup, openers , life savers , quick ones and the strong ones. There are some different type of moves which can lead to a dodge/hit or parry/hit even an absorb/hit. Learning these and mixing up is amazing.
Another thing is, you can teach your moves to someone. That means you will be able to become a mentor! I am not talking about school thing which I will later. Well I guess I'll keep playing this game for a long time and I am sure I will enjoy every moment.

Holy crud this game is cool. Remember Escape Velocity? This is one of the closest things I've found to EV. Its an entirely keyboard driven (in a good way) top-down space game. Travel around, join factions, do missions, trade, fight etc. Its really fun.
Its easy enough to pick up and play, although deep enough that you can spend hours travelling around and customizing your ship. I havent found out if you can buy a new ship or if you have the same ship the entire game so make sure you pick what you want fropm the start. Theres a type of ship for every gameplay style. I prefer the Manticore Heavy Fighter. Its got enough gun slots to do serious damage, but also has a decent cargo space to carry stuff. Its a tank though, so make sure you get nice arnor, youre not going to be zipping around in it.
Theres a ton of different ships, armor, weapons, items. Graphics are what youd expect, little ships of all shapes and sizes flying around with a tiny comet of "flame" coming out of the rear end when you fire thrusters. Lasers are lines, and shots are little round blips. Typical top down space game graphics, but they arent bad. The music is awesome, lots of Empire Strikes Back style scores.
Do not, under any circustances run out of fuel. You use fuel to power everything. If you run out, game over. Literally. No floating randomly about or hailing a passing ship. (AFAIK there is no communication between ships, or maybe I just dont have the ship piece yet to do that).
The game does let you ressurrect by loading a save after death, although there is a notation for "respecting permadeath" on your charsheet, so it knows if you do this. Best of both worlds, IMHO.
The story's interesting and weird. I was doing a bunch of random sidequests, of the go blow up (x) or escort (y) vein. I was told to go blow up an anarchist space station. I did and docked to loot (always fun - docking to loot stations and ships I just blew up!), when suddenly.... a story plot happened on the station. It was an interesting story hook too. So there is more to the story than just the main plot.
If you like EV, you'll like this game. I just wish you could hail/threaten/communicate with other passing ships, and there was more faction subplots, but thats a relatively minor gripe. Its a good game.

Airmech is one of those cute games you pick up at one point and give it a try before you get so addicted to it that you need to limit yourself.
The game is simple in concept, really simple actually. But when it comes to fighting players for example, you need to think fast and have a good selection of units (Did I mention that you choose your own units?). At one point, the devs even made a troll unit what humps enemies. I wish I was kidding.
When it comes to items, you got a wide selection of items, hell, such a wide selection that the devs make literally anything an item. Even a damn teddy bear. A TEDDY BEAR. For example, there is a rare item which I believe you only get during summer and it's sunscreen. And by this game's logic, if you smear some sunscreen on your mech, you give it 5% more damage resistance.
When it comes to the main focus of the game which is the mechs, you got quite the wide selection. For example, I started playing when Ultimate Mechs were a thing, though during my break they were removed and I got full compensation for that by me keeping the Ultimate parts and skin of the ultimate mech I had (Ultimate Striker for those wondering). And I was satisfied cause the parts still made the mech strong as hell.
When it comes to mech choices you got a wide array of all sorts of mechs. There is the Angel for one, a sniper(If you focus on the rifle a lot it can be ♥♥♥♥ing OP, thanks airmech! <3) and you got the Osprey too which is a healer(Combine an  Osprey with maxed healing capabilites and a Warthog with maxed damaged, you get basically the unholy love combo of Heavy and Medic from TF2. BTW, FemPyro is bae). One of the best mechs I had the pleasure of using is the Helix, whose alt fire is the fact he spams rockets. So, with a Helix, you could be going insane if you focus on the rockets.
Then we have cosmetics, nothing much to say about them other than there are skins for every mech, trails for when you walk or fly and tracers which color your lasers. And it seems that Airmech is starting to pump out auras too.
So, now one of the main focus points of the game, PVP.
PVP is, as mentioned before, quite the fast paced part of the game. After my long break, I was in a PVP match because a person said in Zone Chat if they won, they would give the loser a pet, if they lost, they would give the winner a VIP ticket (which lets you buy past event stuff and whatnot). And I was about to be ♥♥♥♥ing destroyed because the dude got 2 squadrons of tanks built near my base. But his ping went through the roof and I won.
Anyway, yeah, the PVP is fast as hell. THOUGH  KEEP IN MIND, ULTIMATE MECHS AND UNITS ARE ONLY ALLOWED IN PVP MATCHES IF THEY ARE ALLOWED IN THE MATCH OPTIONS.
AND LAST, BUT NOT LEAST, THE COMMUNITY! (dun dun duuuun!)
The community is so ♥♥♥♥ing great I can't even handle it. The first time I started playing, an epic person gifted me the pack where I got my main mech (Ultimate Striker) and Prime Helix skin from. In addition to all the other mechs.
So yeah, the community is the icing on the cake and it's like getting a boob job for Hitomi Tanaka.

I first came across Darwinia and Introversion Software in the book "1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die" back in 2010. I couldn't afford the book let alone the games listed inside of it, but it was Darwinia and DEFCON from Introversion Software that caught my attention. I watched the trailer for Darwinia and was blown away by the free camera in an RTS (Most RTSs limit the camera and even Total War's debug camera didn't look this fluid).
In 2013, my first purchase on Steam was the Introversion Bundle. I played the prologue for Darwinia and then moved on to DEFCON and Multiwinia. It has been forgotten for 5 years now.
So in the closing days of 2017 I felt this game deserved to be completed as it introduced me to Steam.
Should you play this little 2005 game that is just a footnote in the history of videogames?
The story of a young world of Artifical People being rapidly introduced to a virus that  destroys their society is interesting although about as simplistic as the Darwininans themselves.
The enemies are diverse and extremely frustrating to fight. Combat finds itself reduced to brute force but decisive strikes are needed or the virus will "regrow". Later in the game, the initially defenseless Darwinians can become a better combat force than your own combat Programs. This is rewarding if a little tedious at times.
The problems with the game come from a very basic tutorial so here is what is not properly explained

I liked the game and it tried to make an RTS that went wider (like God Games) instead of narrower (like MOBAs). The story was enough for me and the enemies were challenging for the whole game.
Play Darwinia and experience a little world of gaming history in only 87mb of HD space.
excrement

An absolute blast. Some sections could have been a little harder, but I think it was absolutely worth the pittance I paid for it and I would pay a great deal more. I loved the mix of action and RTS it featured with regards to the unusual but worthy control scheme and the frantic pace.
I am proud to be a customer of the hard-pressed Introversion Software - especially when they release gems like this! Darwinia is definitely worth your money, whether you are an RTS or action game fan.

The game is halloween themed old-school point & click adventure game. Main plot is that your friends have been trapped in a board game ( Jumanji ? ) and you have to find a way to save them. The game is just clicking various objects,  solving tricky puzzles and playing hidden object minigames. This can be turnoff for someones but I personally recomend to try this game.

Shadows is a nice hidden object game. The search scenes contain have some items that require you to solve some very minor puzzles to get them, giving them a little extra flair. Throughout the game you also find other puzzles, including a sudoku-clone and various brain-teasers.
The graphics themselves are very nice and colourful for this type of game and the story is sufficently interesting. The game contain quite a few interesting backdrops and the cutscenes are nice if a little basic.
My only negative is the game offers quite a lot of help. The help-function for some of the puzzles don't tell you the purpose of the puzzle, it actually contains the solution. And the map will tell you where you have things you need to do. So you no longer have to backtrack to see if you missed things. One click on the map and you know where you have to be next.
All in all though, Shadows: Price for our sins is a solid hidden object game. If you like this kind of games, you'll like this game.

TLDR: I highly recommend Among The Sleep.  It's beautiful, immersive, thought provoking, and genuinely creepy.
There are few games like Among The Sleep, in fact as of now it may very well be entirely unique.  Not only does it put the player into the unique perspective of a two-year-old, it actually manages to maintain that perspective by never forcing you to do something that the average toddler couldn't.  In fact, it could well be said that this provides a significant portion of the game's difficulty.  While the challenges and puzzles are simple, so too are the actions you can take to complete them.  You can't throw a ball more than a few feet, you can't even reach doorknobs without finding something to stand on.  If something comes out to get you, you'd better believe you can't fight back, in fact you can't even run very far without tripping and falling on your face.
While we're on the subject of running from something that's come out to get you, I should mention something else that isn't nearly common enough among games: the ability to present both sections which are adorable, and sections which are downright chilling.  For instance, the character Teddy ranks very high among the cutest I've ever seen, while the Water Woman is easily one of the creepiest and well made out monsters I've ever seen.
Speaking of exceptional design, the entire game fits that category to a T.  The levels are beautifully surreal, often melding bright colors with deep shadow to stunning effect, all the while employing an excellent soundtrack with plenty of auditory cues to help the player along.  The voice acting is superb; it's as good as, or better than, most AAA titles.
Of course, nothing is perfect, and Among The Sleep is no exception.  There were a few minor glitches, ranging from a small section of wall in a closet which didn't display properly, to a case where my toddler failed to enter a closet and was subsequently caught by one of the beasties.  In all fairness, I'm not entirely sure I was supposed to be able to get in there in the first place.  Regardless, another issue I had was that there were a few times where I was pretty clearly supposed to be listening for the current monster to avoid it, and, well it sounded like it was coming from everywhere at once.  Honestly though, all that is very nitpicky stuff, and I've ignored far more glaring errors in games which had two orders of magnitude more development staff.  By far the most significant flaw is, in my opinion, the length of the game.  I probably took about three and a half hours to get entirely through it, and I spent a good bit of time smelling the proverbial roses along the way.  I'm pretty confident that I could do a speed run in half the time if I tried.  But before we judge it too harshly for its length, let's take a moment to consider that, so long as you take your time to enjoy the game's art and ambiance (and if you don't then I don't know why you're playing it), the price you're paying per unit time-being-entertained is no more than for a trip to the movies.

Now that the game is launched I came to review it again.
The EA review is under spoiler.
While it is not the 1on1 conversion of the tabletop, as the developers kindly answered, it has a keen sense of the tabletop campaign with all the appropriate mission generation, after battle casualty rolls and most specifically the injuries which are effectively represented if you lose a limb for example.
Miniatures combat is still the health points attrition system, unavoidable and must live with it.
I change my review to recommended because it is a solid tactical turn based game with a good warband and campaign design. Oh and it happens to be named Mordheim. In the end the devs did stunning locations.
If you are a Mordheim grognard you will feel a bit lost in the character sheet. It has many things which one must learn that can only be excused as a balancing mechanic for this specific product iteration of mordheim.
On the other hand, if you are comfortable with WHF RPG, try to think 2D10 on everything instead of D6 system and it starts to make a bit more sense - that is apart from the health points system...
Buy it if you want a good warband management game with nice tactical combat ( it is repetitive without getting dull ) and good options from campaign to skirmishes.
Think very well before you buy it if you are looking for a computerized representation of tabletop Mordheim.

This game was REALLY good in many parts, and is actually a game that had me laughing almost the entire time, it also made me realize that I probably need help regarding my obsession with tanks. This is the first visual novel that actually had me more invested in the convrosations and other humor in the center of it rather than the ending. Which is quite frankly just awesome in so many ways. Ive played quite a few VNs and frankly this comes in 2nd for me just under Katawa Shoujo (a game that will likely never be toppled in the fact its so amazing and well done).
This game does have a rather cheapish vibe to it. If you're a fan of Kevin MacLeod's music you will instantly recognize just about any soundtrack in this game during the chill moments. The art is solid, but I feel it could indeed be improved upon with future updates, but the artstyle does kinda grow on you the more you play this game, just dont expect God Tier work.
Finally.... DEVGRU-P if you are reading this.... do yourselves a colossal favor with the next patch and
Warning! Spoilers ahead regarding the endings! Which may or may not make or break your experience with this game!
Ending rant over. Onto the final bit of this:
+++Actually alot of fun to play tbh
+++Devs have said they're planning to continue working on this game and add content via Non paid DLC, which opens alot of possibilities!
++Great Humor, especially for tank fans
++Some legit moments where if you know old slang and the sort you will go speechless at "did she REALLY just say that?"
++Solid characters, nothing amazing but theres potential
++Devs are working on an H-Patch for those who want it (You guys rock)
+Has that little quirk to it that not many games typically do
---
--Game feels a tad closer to a Beta almost ready for release than a full game in a variety of areas
-Not Particularly worth 10 dollars due to the above
-Art could use a bit of improvement
-Sound track budget seems to be Free.99, Kevin's music is nice, but some basic "feel good" music made by someone in FL could have given this more personality....
-The game DOES NOT play nice with the Steam UI at all, cant open the interface and any requests to watch the game will get permanently stuck in the bottom right corner.
-Seems to lack a fullscreen option (falls in line with the "Unfinished feeling" of this game combined with the above)
-This game gets a bit buggy at times, at one point a bunch of text just raced by and i missed about 30 dialouge boxes for no clear reason which stopped when I clicked again.
-Only 5 save slots :/
-Your friends will probably never look at you the same again.
This game has ALOT of potential to be a great game, but right now, its a good game. And good games arent really worth a 10 dollar price tag especially when you get hit with the endings. This game is best around the 5 dollar range, and even then a full 10 bucks isnt wasted if you play through the lines and get your dose of tank humor out of it. However, if you wanted to see yourself marry a tank
The game is really solid despite all the cons listed above and I dont regret my purchase, especially since there is promise of content patches up coming, so anyone who has this game better support the devs so we can get some more tanks, tank humor, a Maus, and better endings.

An excellent game! I've played this since the 0.95 version came out, and it's been great ever since. The base game is actually free and will take about 1-2 weeks to complete. The Corporate Command and Eternity Port expansions add lots more ships, systems, enemies, missions and plot-lines to follow, and are well worth the 8 bucks. This is like Escape Velocity, but better. And a lot more difficult. One caveat though - you can't switch ships, so you're stuck with whatever you picked at the beginning. There's a mod called "Playership Drones" I remember installing some time ago, it allowed you to buy new ships and even use them as wingmen.
This is really an open-world sandbox, where you can make your own decisions and do whatever you feel like doing. You can escort freighters, mine asteroids, work for the military, engage in piracy, smuggle drugs, even become a gladiator. Be warned though, your actions and choices will always have consequences both good and bad. Gameplay can be very challenging at times, especially the combat which requires good reflexes. Pick the Wolfen gunship and you'll see what I mean. There can be quite a steep learning
cliff, and you'll get blown up. A lot. You can resurrect and pick up from where you left off, with no penalties apart from a lowered high score. On my first play-through I died about 25 times.
Some tips: Learn the trade routes, and how to profit from the black market. Don't hesitate to use exploits like sitting on a planet (they're invulnerable) while waiting for your shields to recharge, or luring enemies to a friendly station to be killed. When about to die, press (I>1). You can attack salvager nomads (big brown ships) and smugglers (gray transports with small escorts) with no penalties. They are easy to defeat and carry good loot. Don't attack the Huari. And definitely don't feed the Teraton fabricator radioactive waste :) Also, remember to have fun and don't get discouraged by the amount of times you get blown up. It's very rewarding when you complete the game at last. Just resurrect and try again. And again.
10/10 would die again.

So, Transcendence has a long term development plan. New versions are going to be released with no end in sight, as far as I know. Transcendence, the base engine, allows you to play adventures in the Transcendence universe. This base engine is free.
The primary adventure
is that of a character who hears the voice of a hyper-intelligence calling them to the centre of the universe, and listens to the voices in their head -- this adventure is called "Domina and Oracus", and is also free. Currently, Part 1 of the story has been released, along with a content expansion pack called Corporate Command, but the expansion pack is not free.
There is another official adventure that has been released, and this one is called "Eternity Port". It is about a character who is left for dead in the depths of space after an attack on their ship, only to be saved by a selfish (I saved you, so *obviously* you owe me) entity representing the virtual citizens of Eternity Port. They want you to do something for them, starting off the adventure. This adventure isn't free. If you want to see how Eternity Port fits into the lore of the Transcendence universe, check out
I mentioned earlier.
The
, as you can see from screen shots. Starry space backgrounds, mixed with the foreground composed of ships, planets and stations with textures that fit in perfectly. Even though this is an independently developed game, it doesn't skimp out on graphics by pretending to be "retro", or trying to get into the good books of old-schoolers with trashy UI design. The game's graphics are modern, and suit the gameplay.
The game

, and most gamers will feel at home right away: the arrow keys move your ships around in interesting ways, and major buttons like the spacebar or control keys handle the firing of weapons. Keyboard shortcuts usually make sense etymologically (e.g. "D" for Dock, "J" for jump), and there is an excellent help infographic that is accessible any time in the game that lists out all the keyboard shortcuts.
The storylines, depending on which adventure you are playing, give some background as to why you are setting off in space, and then some occasional guiding structure throughout. What do you do in between? Well, it's up to you.
You can trade: there are minerals to be mined, the ore sold or forged into useful armour, which can be sold for an even higher price. Or, you can go about simply buying low and selling high, making a living for yourself that allows you to buy fuel and the ammunition needed to stay safe. Maybe you decide you're interested in also running a side business in the black market. Well, as long as you have a murky sense of morality, the connections to get started, and the know how to hide your goods from the authorities, maybe you'll be successful.
You can sign up with the Commonwealth Forces, or some of the other regional powers (depending on which adventure you are playing), and rise up through the ranks. You can meditate in the halls of the Sisters of Domina's temples. Maybe you can figure out what this voice in your head wants. Maybe you are interested in donating items to the Sisters' cause, and helping the needy that you meet in beaten down habitat stations that are nothing more than cargo containers strung together.
Maybe you free slaves held in living stasis inside coffins by the Sung Slavers, as you attempt to make sure you aren't squashed by them. Maybe you get involved in story of the Sung and the Huari, the Aztec/Maya-esque space culture that was decimated by the Sung's relentless ruthlessness. Maybe some zoanthrope buddies tag along because you beat their masters, and thus are next most powerful thing they know to follow. Maybe you willingly submit yourself to the nasty experiments of humans who have genetically modified themselves to such a degree that they might as well be aliens.
Maybe you actually bump into aliens, and other creepy-crawlies. Maybe. It's your call. The game is detailed enough to waste hours of your time, with nice flavour text to spice up every piece of the universe. Bring your imagination along, and go for a ride.
: everything in the universe can be described and programmed with XML files and a custom LISP variant (TransLisp). The C++ guts of Transcendence are completely open as well, and available for viewing and participation on GitHub. Modding documentation is sparse, but community participation makes up for it.
So, if you're into modifying games, Transcendence will give you lots to do. If you like playing with other people's modifications, Transcendence won't disappoint you there either. Popular mods include a complete revamp of the mining system, AI based modifications that allow the game world to be even more dynamic by randomly generating conflict and rebuilding stations, content packs that add new weapons or features such as the ability to craft new weapons from components, and so on.

This hidden object game drew me in with it's Halloween-themed story. At first it starts as a basic haunted house story and then it turns into Jumanji junior in a sense. The entire plot revolves around your friends being trapped in a board game and the ghosts of the game's last victims haunting the farm. They send you on a bunch of fetch quests, so only a fraction of the game is about finding hidden objects. I managed to finish the game in around 6 hours, so that's not bad for the $4 or so I spent for this on sale, but I also lost interest about two-thirds of the way through. I stopped reading the diary pages, for example.
The fetch quests were grinding on me. Some of the objects in the hidden object scenes didn't look anything like I would ever imagine them to look like. Some of the puzzles didn't have clear directions and if you hit the "?" to get an explanation, it focused more on telling you how to beat it than explaining the objective. Some of the later puzzles are very generic like they ran out of ideas near the end. For example, two of the last puzzles are a Sudoku puzzle and a sliding tile puzzle.
There are some good animations that might look like a puppet show starring silhouettes, but the simple visual style had its charm. The voice acting over them is pretty bad. Early in the game, there are a few animations with higher production value. The graphics are nice for a hidden object game, though those animations are a bit hazy. Maybe they just didn't like the HD resolution.
Each location is interesting enough and works with the Halloween theme for the most part.
The developers made this game very easy to complete. Can't find a hidden object? Use a hint. Can't solve a puzzle? Skip it. Not sure where to go next? Just look at the map. It shows you. It'll be hard to get frustrated with the game when it provides you so many bypasses.

Brothers in Arms Road to Hill 30 is an WW2 , FPS and Tactical shooter , and a great combonation. This game stands out from other tactical games , most of them you are given a straticic veiw of the map and you command various different units to take out enemy units. But in this game you jump into the role of squad leader of a paratrooper regiment taking part in the 1944 DDay operation , and the aftermath to take Normandy. Instead of the stratigic overveiw , your in First person , commanding your men realisticly throughout the battlefeild , trying to keep your units alive and yourself. Not only is the there out of this world gameplay style different from normal tactical games , There is an actul story line , where each unit has a name , a backstory and a personality and when certain characters die in the story , you might atuly feel upset over what just happend. Also the story line is presented in a unique way which was pulled off with pure class , The protagonist of the story (Sgt.MattBaker) narates and tells backtories and stories of characters inbetween missions , and how he feels about them , and this can change throughout the story. Overall i think this game has a Brillaint and unique gameplay style , using to concept of miilitristic , tactical shooter , with a story plot we actuly care about , unlike most shooters we shove the storyline in the corner and rush through the game then complain the game was too short. This game changes that. Also i think this game is the thinking man's shooter , where he must plan his aproach through the harsh battefeilds then watch as his plan is executed and see if it works or doesn't. Only one complaint can be made about this game , that is the artificial Intelligance can somtimes (not always) be worse that a goldfish. Overall i think this is an exelent game. 9/10

Resident Evil 7 is the fantastic entry in the legendary franchise that's been around for the past 21 years. To be more specific, Resident Evil 7 is the franchise's return to its survival horror roots, but rather than sticking to the typical third person view, it's first person. Though this isn't the first time this was done in the overall franchise, it is the first and successful attempt with a main franchise entry. Despite being an old school Resident Evil fan, I must say the use of FPV was a brilliant move by the game's creators due to the fact that it leads to better immersion and an overall heightened sense of fear when playing through the game.
In Resident Evil 7 you mainly play as Ethan Winters, an average joe looking for his missing wife in a derelict Louisiana mansion. In searching for his wife, Ethan stumbles upon a family of murderous psychopaths and other ghastly monstrosities that he never would've expected to deal with. In attempting to escape in one piece, he discovers what caused this hellish situation to come about. What's great about Resident Evil 7 is that it doesn't shy away from showcasing its gruesomeness, everything is intensely graphic and up close right from the start.
Resident Evil 7 is a highly detailed game, just about everything you see is lifelike, interactive, and in general well done. To be more specific, for a short period of time you are granted the use of an axe and swinging it against certain objects will lead to it being momentarily stuck. Another instance that showcases great attention to detail is during the numerous fierce moments of combat encountered in the game. It's not surprising at all to shoot at an enemy and see blood/guts fly around, but seeing these fluids/matter splatter onto your weapon/arm and stay there for a brief period of time, that was truly eye opening. Even something as simple as the main character resting his hands on a wall/pillar near him during gameplay reveals the attention to detail found in this game.
It may be a silly thing to bring up, but I also love the fact that despite the FPV you are able to see so much of Ethan. It isn't always noticeable, but there are moments in the game where you can see Ethan's feet, legs, and torso. I bring this up because it's a pet peeve of mine to play an FPS that doesn't show anything at all as you're walking or standing, it's limiting and robs you of total immersion. I'm not totally sure, but if I had to guess as to why this was done, it was for the benefit of PSVR users. Besides that, the extra body parts that are seen can be used to convey body language that isn't always utilized in an FPV game.
There were many moments in this game where dim or even no lighting was used to manipulate the player's emotions. As you play through this game you eventually reach a point where you're ready for anything, especially when walking through a dark area. I found myself in many situations where I'd walk slowly anticipating an enemy to strike, but nothing happened at all. I guess you can say that the fear/expectation of something was just as frightening if not more frightening than the actual enemy encounters. It was when I least expected it that enemies would strike and it was a great way for the creators of this game to keep you in a constant state of discomfort/fear.
Resident Evil 7 didn't just stick to jump scares to frighten the player, it was done in very calculated ways. For example, it was a normal occurrence in this game to be overwhelmed by enemies and you'd have to run away to be able to safely reload your weapon, but this wasn't always possible. In one instance I was confidently running towards an open door because I knew I'd encounter no enemies, having already been through there, but as I approached the door an enemy jumped out of nowhere. Despite being initially frightened by the sudden appearance of this enemy, I later realized that this brief interaction was well done.
In its game design Resident Evil 7 has numerous features from the classic Resident Evil games that series veterans will immediately notice. Initially, the areas in Resident Evil 7 feel really distant from one another, but as you advance through the game, shortcuts will reveal just how overlapping these areas are. Another throwback Resident Evil feature is the use of item boxes and having to juggle what you carry or even having to waste bullets just to make space. Despite being an overall hassle, the inclusion of the item box/item juggling is certain to bring back fond
memories.
Despite having immensely enjoyed Resident Evil 7, I wouldn't say it's a perfect game. I've previously mentioned that this game is well done, but that's not 100% true. It's nice that there are numerous puzzles in this game, but a few of them are lazily used more than once and they're generally not that challenging. Resident Evil veterans will easily go through these puzzles, the series has offered more of a challenge in the past. Besides that, there are also moments of stagnation in this game. Though this could also be said of the highly praised Resident Evil 1, the main house feels a bit empty for long stretches of time and during these moments you are mainly hunting for items from room to room. I was eventually bored of this and wanted something to happen.
I really enjoyed the combat in Resident Evil 7 and it offered a great deal of variety with the weapons that were offered. From the game's beginning you'll mainly use a handgun plus a knife, but as the game progresses you'll eventually get to use a magnum, a flamethrower,  a shotgun, a grenade launcher, remote bombs, and a machine gun. The weapons variety is a good asset in this game because it offers different playstyles so if for some reason you dislike one weapon, you can always rely on another.
For the most part, the combat/boss battles in Resident Evil 7 are neither easy nor hard, but challenging in an entertaining way. You generally know what to do when it comes to defeating one of the few bosses in this game, but that doesn't prevent you from dying. You can easily expect to die once or twice per boss battles until you learn their patterns/weaknesses, it's not that big of a deal. This is mostly attributed to having to be very precise with your aiming in hectic situations. The enemies in Resident Evil 7 were designed in such a way that being shot in specific parts of the body will lead to certain reactions. As a result, you'll mainly want to dish out as many headshots as possible, but it isn't always doable. Maybe it's because I played this game with an Xbox 360 controller, but this was highly noticeable with one of the many handguns used in this game. The recoil was a hassle to deal with at times because after every shot you had to readjust your aim to maximize the damage you dealt.
Though the combat was fun, at times it also got to be a bit repetitive. The main enemies in this game are visually well designed and there are three variants, but at one point it got old fighting the same looking enemies over and over again. At the same time, I feel as if the main humanoid enemy wasn't too original, I was constantly reminded of previously used enemies from other Resident Evil games. At least with the classic Resident Evil games the zombie models offered a decent amount of variety and there was much more to deal with as you progressed through the game.
Overall, I truly enjoyed Resident 7. The story was good and it goes beyond what it initially appears to be, but towards the end it felt hastily thrown together and a bit disjointed. It was a great entry in a series that has lost its way over the years and I appreciated that. It wasn't a perfect game, but what it offered was highly entertaining. I give Resident Evil 7 a 4.75/5 and I highly recommend it.

You've heard the name before, and there must be a reason why the series has lasted 10+ years.
The expectation is a generic fps that requires you to kill the enemy by barely peaking around an edge with a sniper. And while Far Cry is definilty a generic fps in this regard, it takes it to the next level. Not only must you master precision shooting to succeed, you must also become a master tactictian if you plan on reaching the end. When the objective is something within a guarded base, what plan best suits your skills? Is storming the front the call? Perhaps sneaking around through the surrounding jungle using your thermal-vision in hopes of finding a secret way in? Maybe a little of both in order to confuse the enemy? This combination of battle strategy and weaponry gives Far Cry a very Deus Ex feel, so if you're faimilar with that type of gameplay you'll be right at home. Far Cry opts for more of a shooter experience than a spy one, however.
I can't recall a more challenging fps that took me more than 40 hrs to complete on max difficulty. At times I was struggling on one measley part for hours, but rather than get disheartened, I realized that I just had to keep reworking my strategy to find the one that fit.
Skepticism at first turned into a memorable experience rife with difficulties and satisfaction. Excellent graphics (for its time), sounds and gameplay all provided the perfect frame for one of the best fps' I have ever played. Can't wait to get my paycheck and purchase the next in the series.

Overall, I probably have about 16 hours worth of gameplay in Kingdom. I played the old edition, loved it, and was so excited when I heard everyone who had kingdom previously was getting a free copy of Newlands. Kingdom is a simple yet beautiful game, with its fantastic music and aesthetically pleasing art style. You claim a piece of land with some coins, you gain more coins, you build up your city with coins, you give those coins to the homeless, you get the homeless to work for you, they gain more coins for you, you go out to find more homeless people to put to work, they help you expand your empire, you gain more coins, you defend your empire, you win. What is awesome about this game:
- One of the more moody and atmospheric medieval games out there, where you rule some villagers among dark forests and foggy banks that really feel like your new dangerous home
- Extremely simple to jump into
- Open sandbox: you must explore and learn how the world's logic works on your own (experiment to try and unravel the puzzles).  DON'T let anyone spoil the game for you if this is a game feature you like
- Exemplary use of graphical style and music
Those things combined create a formula for the most immersive medieval game I've played in a long time.
What some folks might not like:
- Although a procedural game, it's not the "infinitely replayable" variety where there are massive combinations of random content.  There is a point when you've explored everything to offer and most probably won't consider it replayable past that.  This isn't a flaw, I just mention it because some folks have specific expectations for procedural games.
- I understand that there is no plot that reveals more about the mystery of the islands, although I haven't played far enough to confirm
- You don't have 100% control.  You must learn how your villagers behave and adapt your strategy around it. You can't undo mistakes, and you must live (more likely die) from them and learn for the next ruler.
- Anyone who must have a wiki or hint guide to complete games is probably the opposite of who this was intended for, since a feature of the game is learning its mechanics through experimental trial and error.  There will be times where you are faced with a decision and you won't have enough information to know the right choice.  I personally like that in this game since I think they have the mechanics to support this style well.  You feel like it's the tragic story of that ruler's failed reign.
A few are complaining about the price / content ratio.  I spent enough hours (LOVING it) that I feel it was worth the $15.  I believe most of these folks had incorrect expectations that the game would be more replayable.  It's not that style of game.
Note that although this is also a mobile game, I prefer it on a bigger screen and speakers for the atmosphere.  It's not some desparate port.
WARNING: If you read hints/spoilers you will negative impact the best this game has to offer.  Be careful what reviews you read.

It's an interesting idea, but I was not really a fan.  The game is extremely short (as of writing this, I have beaten the game, but not even played it long enough for a single card drop), and fairly predictable.  Plus, there was no real sense of urgency.  It wasn't even until near the very end of the game that I even knew you could get a game over.  The atmosphere is more nonsensical than spooky.  And the concept of playing as a toddler is lost rather quickly when you're solving puzzles, rather than picking up the toy plane and shoving it in your mouth.
The underlying idea, of trying to piece together what could be a rather mundane occurrence, as seen through the warp of a child that does not understand what's going on, is a highly interesting one.  The execution here doesn't quite pull it off.
It doesn't do a terrible job of it, and there's plenty for people to like.  I'm just not one of those people.
On a more technical side, the game qualifies for an "auto fail" for me in that I cannot change the movement controls to arrows.  Fortunately, I was able to play the game with an Xbox 360 controller, but being left handed, I cannot use a standard WASD setup.  Nor can anyone with a different keyboard layout.  Preventing us from rebinding movement controls in game is something that no PC game should do.

Give it a try and don’t start yelling pay to win until you have actually played a while. I am sure some older players would laugh at my measly 70+ hours in this game but I have a lot of fun and still haven’t spent a penny. I would recommend that you verify the game files after you finish installing it because after doing that I haven’t had any issues with it crashing like some people have. I have also seen people say it doesn’t work with windows 10 but it works fine for me. If you don’t know how to verify the game files go to your library, right click on Blacklight, go to properties, then go to the Local Files tab, and at the bottom of the list is a button to Verify integrity of game files.
To be honest Blacklight has it’s fair share of problems
-older players can be bit op (they should be seeing as they are a way higher level)
-sometimes you just can't sign in (after I verified the game files I have not had this problem again)
-Sometimes in the onslaught aka zombie mode players will spawn without their gun (you can get it back by being downed, not getting revived, and then when you respawn at the start of the next wave you should have it)
-There are not a ton of players (I have always been able to find a match though so there are enough)
That being said I think the pros outweigh the cons
-I have yet to personally find a hacker
-The starter guns are not actually that bad (rent or buy a scope with GP and you’re set)
-Most of the players I have run into are fairly nice
-It’s a free game

I forgot to mention hardsuits but in short they are mechs which can be a pain if they are on the other team. So long as your team focuses on them they are not to hard to take down. Definitely recommend giving this game a shot and if you don’t like it hey it was free.

Expect to be mining and tunneling... If you don't like the idea, don't play this. Easy right?
Is it good game? Not in the common sense
Is it good simulator? HELL YES
Is it worth 10 bucks? Nope, but in bundle or a discount, it is good buy
Would I play this for an hour a day? No way, I'd rather take up knitting
Would I dig another tunnel? Yes, I think I would.
There are some minor technical issues like wrong texture clipping when frantically moving the camera inside the tunnel or when driving trucks close to some objects, but nothing critical.
Tunnel creation stages
1) Strip mining the entrance
Driving in the van and setting up dynamites. Driving model is just HORRIBLE. It does not take too long, so its bearable. But hey, it's not a van driving simulator, right?
2) Cleaning up the debris
With an excavator you must load stones onto a truck and then drive with them to dump them. This part actually is not one big 'Physics, what physics?' mess and it's fun to do. Also kinda frustrating, because the rocks are not very cooperative. And again, it does not take very long, just about the right time to do the work
3) Digging the tunnel
Last part which is both the most interesting and the most frustrating. From a control room you control the TBM that diggs the tunel. The controlling part of the TBM is complex and requires some practice. Thats the interesting part.
But you have to supply the TBM with concrete. Loading the blocks onto a train was difficult at first and was fun to learn it. But then I find out A LOT of LOTS of concrete. For a tunnel of 6 kms you need to load like 7 FULL trains. First train was to learn, second to practice, third to try some cool moves... Fourth started to be tedious.... For a tunnel of length 89 kilometers, I'd have to break something. So how'bout nope....

Let me begin by asking a question to those of you who have not played Devil may cry 4 or just devil may cry in general...
WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH YOUR LIFE?!? SCREW YOUR DAMN GOAT SIMULATORS AND GET THIS GAME! IT'S LIKE 20 BUCKS OR WHATEVER! So as you may of guessed I'm a pretty big fan of the series with Dmc4 being my favorite of the series and 1 of my favorite games of all time.
To boil it down this game is a action hack and slash game. In my opinion this game has the best hack and slash mechanics of the DMC series and any hack and slash game I've ever seen. At no point in playing this game did I feel like I was pressing one button to win. Reaching SSS mid combo will probably leave you feeling pretty impressed with your self. The cut scenes range from cheesy to holy crap that was awesome.
The story is about Nero a new character of the series who works for "The order of the sword" A hot head swordsman who just so happens to be voiced by the same voice actor who voices  Ichigo from Bleach (Keep that in my mind as you rip demons in two). Kyrie is also new character of and is also voiced by a bleach voice actor(Orihime) Even her dress is a referrence to certain ark in Bleach. Utimately though she's a walking plot device. Although if there ever is a DMC5 I would love to see this character again maybe trained by Trish and Lady.
As for Dante if you liked him before you're gonna love him in this game. He's funny and fun to play as and fun to fight against. Not only is his character wonderfully developed but he also referrences (Story wise and gameplay wise) past dmc games in not only a awesome way, but in a way were nothing is spolied for new comers or redundant to veterans. Not only that but he also does all this without using flashbacks (Take notes 90% of animes).
One last thing to mention. The part where you back track half the game as Dante. This really isn't as bad or lazy as you think it is... Hear me out before you down vote. Back tracking has always been this lurking element of DMC but it's definitely more noticeable in this. Especially Dmc3 were you just play through the whole game as Vergil. Having Dante finishing what Nero started and giving back tracking a story purpose rather than just doing it for the sake of back tracking was kind of a nice touch. This was probably Capcoms way of killing 2 birds with one stone(aka Story and two playable characters) Don't get me wrong Dante could of just went to new ares with new Hell gates to fight the demons that survived Nero, but I'd like to give Capcom some credit on putting some thought into this. They could of easily just rinse and repeat dmc3.
A quick note before I forget. If you were wondering about rebuying this game for pc and was worried it would be a bad port. Let me assure you this is a wonderful port, it feels just as natural as the console versions and looks godly on highest settings.
In the end I give this game a 9 out of 10. In the words of Egoraptor "YOU SEE THIS?!? THIS IS A SEQUEL, THIS IS A ♥♥♥♥ING SEQUEL!!!"

I remember when this first came out. I was in 1944 Germany.

I am a full time soldier in the Canadian Army. I love my job, I work with some terrific people, get to do some really cool things and there really is no life like it. The military is also what helped bring me out of side scrollers and into the world of 3D gaming that we play in today, As a teenager I was raised by military parents, and retired military Grandparents. I watched movies about The Great War, World War II, Vietnam, went to the War Museum in Ottawa, Ontario and listened to my Dad as he told me about my Great Grandfather and his role in Vimy Ridge.
It only made sense that, eventually I’d find myself purchasing a copy of Gearbox’s Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30, when I bought my first Xbox. I’d played other World War shooters on the Playstation and PC prior to this, but it never really stuck. While it was cool to play as an Allied soldier working undercover for the OSS, I was never convinced it was a very good representation of the life of a soldier.
Brothers in Arms had me from the start. When I first popped in the disk and heard the Brothers in Arms theme, the music just hit me right to my core. The beautiful, sad but powerful marching music in the menus made me pause and sit for a few minutes to just soak it in, and I realized right then that I was going to be in for a journey that I’d never been in before.
However, I’m going to skip forward a few years. See after being in the military for a few years, I found myself coming back to Brothers in Arms. This time when I started the game, the haunting words of Sergeant Matt Baker struck me and really made me feel and understand why this game had me from the start. I find that most military shooters are just “bang bang explosion, pow pow Nazi!” Brothers in Arms makes you feel the soldiers pain, joy and regrets as they evolve from gung-ho soldiers at the start of D-Day to their final showdown at Hill 30.
As Soldiers in the field, every decision made can have horrible consequences. Many of us have lost friends, have our loved ones leave us to come home to empty houses and many of us have even lost limbs or the ability to have a good nights sleep, all in the name of our flag and freedom. Most of us do not regret these decisions as we recognize that they must be done in order for others to enjoy the freedoms and rights that we have. The life of the soldier is almost never glamorous. It’s a job and we do the very best we can with whatever scenario that is given to us. This is shown in Brothers in Arms several times over the course of the series. One character at one point in the game loses his mind over the grief of losing two squadmates under his command. Another character finds himself running into a burning building to rescue a soldier who himself was trying to rescue an innocent. Characters are killed, others hurt to the point of having to be sent home, and yet the rest soldier on. They do what needs to be done and that makes this game very special.
The words that open the first game in the Brothers in Arms series still give me pause whenever I hear them. They are the words of a man who has lost his friends and lost his sense of youth and vigor to get the job done. Matthew Baker is tired of this damn war and everything that led to where he is and just wants it to be over. Read these words and imagine you’d been in hell for over a week, each day feeling longer than the last.
“My dad said something to me after the divorce. He said that every soldier has two families, those you raise and those you raise Hell with. I’ve spent eight days here, eight days commanding a squad I wasn’t ready to lead, eight days watching my men – my family – kill and be killed. Eight days wishing it would stop.”
From there you open up to a Brutal shootout with Matt’s squad pinned down by enemy fire and tanks. The screams of squad mates calling for support on the radio with no reply. The shouts of the company First Sergeant barely keeping the fear out of his voice as he tried to keep his men calm and focused. The disbelief of a soldier as he tries to rouse his fire team partner who has suddenly dropped dead. Finally, mercifully a tank shell explodes near you and everything gets hazy. The last thing you see before everything goes black is a soldier – having finally snapped from the pressure – expose himself to enemy fire, calling for death, and taking a blast from a tank as a result. It’s a very shocking and sudden introduction to a game that introduces you to amazing characters. Then one by one they are taken away from you as you begin to feel like they are holding your sanity together while you fight your way through hell.
Camaraderie is a big thing in military life. The constant razzing of your buddies, supporting them when they are down and picking on them when they goof up. There are several moments like this in the Brothers in Arms series that really cement that feeling of camaraderie for the player. In the first game, two of the most memorable characters are some guys named Allan and Garnet, who met up in boot camp and became inseparable. The chatter that they have between (and sometimes during) missions is some of the best dialogue I’ve heard in a military shooter, and it would be a great loss to lose these guys in a firefight. In particular there’s an awesome argument between them and another soldier about Batman VS Superman that cemented their awesomeness in my mind forever.
Of course I’m getting away from myself with comparing my life to that of characters in what is still in the end just a videogame. In my opinion it’s a damn good one too. One which spawned two other games that were great as well. Aside from authenticity, one of the big things that I really enjoyed about these games was the challenge and the tactical gameplay. Your squadmates were very smart and did their best to keep you alive, they followed direction but also knew better than to let you get them killed by ordering them to do something silly like attack a tank head on. The enemy functioned the same way making strategy key to victory. You had to be very careful with this as well because your men and you were very vulnerable. In Brothers in Arms, one very well placed shot could kill you in an instant, there are no magic health packs or regenerating health and running out in the open was suicidal. This made it the first shooter I ever played where making use of cover not only made sense, but was essential to survival.
Brothers in Arms has been without a new entry for some time now, with Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway hitting stores in 2008 and ending in a bit of a cliffhanger. Gearbox Software announced a spinoff called Furious Four a while ago which was supposed to make the series similar to Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds. This enraged a rather large number of BIA fans though and Gearbox ended up removing it from the Brothers in Arms name. A couple years ago Gearbox’s Randy Pitchford told IGN that another authentic Brothers in Arms game was on it’s way but that the wait could be up to five years. However, my hopes are high that we will see something in the near future , as I personally think that Brothers in Arms is the best shooter series I’ve ever played and I am looking forward to seeing what’s next for these characters.
