What is awesome about this game:
- One of the more moody and atmospheric medieval games out there, where you rule some villagers among dark forests and foggy banks that really feel like your new dangerous home
- Extremely simple to jump into
- Open sandbox: you must explore and learn how the world's logic works on your own (experiment to try and unravel the puzzles).  DON'T let anyone spoil the game for you if this is a game feature you like
- Exemplary use of graphical style and music
Those things combined create a formula for the most immersive medieval game I've played in a long time.
What some folks might not like:
- Although a procedural game, it's not the "infinitely replayable" variety where there are massive combinations of random content.  There is a point when you've explored everything to offer and most probably won't consider it replayable past that.  This isn't a flaw, I just mention it because some folks have specific expectations for procedural games.
- I understand that there is no plot that reveals more about the mystery of the islands, although I haven't played far enough to confirm
- You don't have 100% control.  You must learn how your villagers behave and adapt your strategy around it. You can't undo mistakes, and you must live (more likely die) from them and learn for the next ruler.
- Anyone who must have a wiki or hint guide to complete games is probably the opposite of who this was intended for, since a feature of the game is learning its mechanics through experimental trial and error.  There will be times where you are faced with a decision and you won't have enough information to know the right choice.  I personally like that in this game since I think they have the mechanics to support this style well.  You feel like it's the tragic story of that ruler's failed reign.
A few are complaining about the price / content ratio.  I spent enough hours (LOVING it) that I feel it was worth the $15.  I believe most of these folks had incorrect expectations that the game would be more replayable.  It's not that style of game.
Note that although this is also a mobile game, I prefer it on a bigger screen and speakers for the atmosphere.  It's not some desparate port.
WARNING: If you read hints/spoilers you will negative impact the best this game has to offer.  Be careful what reviews you read.

Resident Evil 7 is one of the better and more definitive titles in the series.  It took a series that, in my opinion, had strayed from its roots, and brought the very things we want in a Resident Evil game back front and center.  From the visuals, to the gameplay mechanics, to the sounds and musical score, to the storyline, everything about Resident Evil 7 looks modern, polished, and fixes everything you may not have liked about the series in its more recent action oriented titles.
First the visuals.  Resident Evil 7 adopts a new "RE Engine" with photo-realistic graphics, lighting, etc.  When I say photo-realistic, I MEAN photo-realistic, not just high resolution, photo-realistic.  The people, the walls, the lighting, the water, even the way your flashlight refracts off your weapons, it all looks absolutely incredible.  There are plenty of moments when you first enter a dark room with nothing but your very dim flashlight, and it FEELS like you really are in a room that dark.  There's none of that artificial light that's just bright enough for you to see an item like in a lot of other games.  If the lights are out, it gets DARK, and when there is light, it looks incredibly natural, especially against the photo-realistic people and textures.
The audio is just as awesome as the visuals.  The soundtrack is usually very quiet and subtle, but is present enough to set the mood.  The music is high quality in terms of audio fidelity, and it's not loud or abrasive enough for you to "notice" it, which is a very good thing in a game where you want to be engrossed in a moment and not distracted by the musical instruments playing in the background.  The voice acting and sound effects are well done, and there's lots of audio cues to help you stay alert of what's going on around you.  The virtual surround sound worked really well with my headphones.  If something was behind me and on the other side of a wall, it actually sounded correct; I could tell the direction, and its presence behind the wall, because of the quality of sound.  Paired with the great visuals, the quality audio work does a really good job, especially if you're wearing headphones, of making you feel like you're actually there in that moment.
The gameplay is another area where this game has done a lot of things right, and even made some positive changes.  You don't feel like you're playing Gears of War with zombies.  Ammunition is rare enough that you find yourself fighting with your knife, or avoiding fights altogether when you can in order to conserve it.  It keeps some staples of the series like the "safe room" with a storage box, save point, etc.  For the first time I am aware of in the series, the game is first person, which really helps put you in the game when paired with the photo-realistic visuals and quality audio work.  You don't feel like you're controlling somebody else, you feel like you are there.  Movement was fluid and responsive with no noticeable input lag even with VSync enabled.  Combined with the realistic and often sparse lighting, the first person view also lends aid to the occasional jump scare where you may enter a room and there's something hiding in the dark just outside your field of vision, waiting to jump right up in your face in the light of your flashlight; something that's harder to accomplish when playing in over the shoulder 3rd person mode.  Inventory management is improved over older titles as well.  You no longer have to manually move items around in order to make sure two spaces are next to each other so you can hold a larger weapon.  If you have enough spaces for an item, it will automatically move things around if necessary to accommodate that item.  You can craft ammo, potions, etc., or you can even break them down into their base components again using another special item if you really want to.  There's plenty of puzzles to exercise your brain, but none that are too difficult to reasonably accomplish, and thank goodness there are NO SLIDING PICTURE PUZZLES! (I hate that kind)  You might have to find a lockpick, or a special key, or fit some insignias together into a door, etc., but most of the puzzles can be solved simply by paying attention to details in your surroundings as you play.  The puzzles are enough to keep things interesting and give you objectives, without being too difficult to be enjoyable.
The story in this game is a unique and interesting tale.  It does a good job misleading you, making you doubt your own decisions and assumptions, and expands on the story of some well known icons in the Resident Evil series.  As soon as you think you know what's going on, something happens to make you doubt yourself just a little bit, and things that may at first seem harmless or inconsequential, may turn out to be the complete opposite.  One of the weirdest parts about this story is that I finished the game sort of feeling sorry for even the villain.
In summary, Resident Evil 7 has done what it was supposed to, it brought Resident Evil back to its survival horror roots.  From the amazing visuals and audio, to the first person perspective with realistic lighting and sparse ammo, to the intriguing story line, Resident Evil 7 was an enjoyable game that legitimately scared the daylights out of me at times, and left me with some new questions regarding the role of certain players in the Resident Evil drama.  For those who are a fan of the series and thought some of the newer games felt a little too much like 3rd person shoot-em-ups with zombies, Resident Evil 7 is the perfect example of how to return to your roots when you've lost your way.  I highly recommend this game not just for fans of Resident Evil specifically, but for fans of the survival horror genre as a whole.

Holy ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥balls. And all of that first sentence is stars immediately. This game is absolutely incredible. If only sheerly for the perspective not only in gameplay, but in narration...
Just like the more well known FNAF, there's a lot of stuff hiding in plain sight that reveals some history and the going ons that lead to what's happening right now. Although this time you're not a security guard and they aren't animatronics. You're a very very young toddler of 2, and your life is depicted in drawings. Crude ones, as you'd suspect. As you make your way through hell and back you get tidbits of information that lead suspicions to reality. Soon enough, you live that reality.
Some say the imagination of a child is the strongest. Perhaps that is true, as is depicted in this game. What is real and what isn't real doesn't matter any more. You're 2. The world is a big scary place and you're... You, in comparison. Tiny. Dfenseless. Horrified.
I found my self mesmerized, comforted, calmed... Then was thrust head first into hell. With incredibly atmospheric gameplay and stunning music this game had me balls deep before the ♥♥♥♥ing tutorial ended. Sucking me in quicker than a whirl pool. Before I knew it the world was like I said, big, terrifying... And I'm all alone... Well, not entirely. Teddy comes  along to aid you but ultimately does nothing other than exposition and plot driving through the stuff that can't be explained so well with out actually telling the player.
Teddy tags along and acts mainly as your flashlight. And my god was it comforting to have some ♥♥♥♥ing light. Keep the gama down, play in the dark, keep the sound a little high.
It can be rather hard to see and actually explore with the gama too low and too high it ruins the experience. Finding the right balance of both lighting and sound is a bit tricky at first but once done the game is that much more amazing.
Its a bit hard to find places to hide when you can't see though, and you can't use Teddy's flashlight ability when crawling and you can't run when using him. You have to stand and meander, which makes it even more stressful when running from the pants fillingly terrifying monsters chasing you. Don't forget, this game is incredibly immersive. If you get immersed, you'd be filling your pants too.
The game is a cocktail of smooth relaxing and haunting moments of serenity while momma hums for you, or a music box alludes to peace. Then you get to a puzzle. The puzzles in this game are exceptionally well done as they force the player to explore places they may not have explored. Although it can cause backtracking and a bit of confusion. The game looks, sounds, and feels great though so meandering through the dark, in the dark, scared out of your mind can't be all that bad. After, and sometimes durring, puzzles there's sections of horror. Your little tiny baby legs take you in and out of the gates of hell over and over as the nightmares of the real world /are/ your real world. Constantly being stalked by gargantuant shadowy beings that are seemingly always 3 steps behind you. Always on your heels. Always around the corner.
The screen gets a weird loopy filter and its Amnesia all over again. "Runrunrunrunrun! OOOH FUUUUH-UUCK!" Sometimes escaping is easy, sometimes not so much as you bump your baby head into the upper part of a hidey hole and get eaten by a hellish nightmare.
If you liked Amnesia but want something a little different, this is the game for you. Had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ childhood? Want to relive the terror of said childhood? This is the game for you. New to horror? Want to try horror? This is the game for you. Want a cream pie on the outside, but on the inside its the heart of Chtulu? This is the game for you.
Pros: Stunning atmospheric gameplay elements and music creating instant immersion. Simple control scheme that's easy to get used to. Pulse pounding horror as you run for your godamn life. Kinda casual. Best when played alone in your room with all the lights off. And no wall pressed against your back... Don't worry, daddy's comin'. Just don't look over your shoulder.
Cons: Climbing and general mantling is a bit wonk and a bit hard to get used to. Perfect lighting is hard to balance because some areas are just so damn dark, which makes hiding a little tedious at times. Maybe a little too forgiving as each death starts you 15 feet from where you died with all of your previous inputs, that means everything- including enviornmental changes, still in play. Some puzzles are a little too ambiguous with what they want out of you. The answer is sitting right in front of your face, but that's the problem. Its sometimes a little too obvious. Sometimes a little too hidden.
Either way it was an absolutely incredible game. If you have the money laying around I would suggest picking it up and giving it a go. If you have headphones you're in for a treat. Definitely one of my best, if second or third, horror experiences.

I'm actually a sissy when it comes to horror games - especially if they are in 1st person.
However, the overall concept of the game caught me and after some while fearing, that I just couldn't get through the game, I snatched it using a humble bundle and tried.
The game is just great. The main theme is the fear and awkwardness, children have in a world they don't fully understand. They tend to "interpret" things they see, so that they somehow make sense in their eyes. And that's what the game's doing.
If you would be a grownup character, you wouldn't find any of the events in "Among the Sleep" terrifying, but through the eyes of a toddler, even a simple flash can be horrifying. And that's what the game really does well: It puts you in an atmosphere and plays with the surroundings, the size of the main character and its large amount of fantasy.
So the creeps don't come from blood-dripping corpses or something like that. It comes from sounds, voices, height, eerie shadows, lonelyness and helplessness.
The sound is aiding this pretty well and the overall sound composition is fitting in any minute.
I, too, have to say, that the game is pretty short considering it's usual price. But after about 2,5h of creeps, I was kinda happy to really finish the game and get on with more milder themes. ;-)
I highly recommend this game to people, that like to get some good shivers now and then, but don't actually want to be creeped out. Horror-Pros might find this game not so creepy, but may find the concept rather interesting.
I hope, that's not the last game we see from Krillbyte.

I've been playing this since 2004 and am getting quite good at it now.  One day I might even manage the last level without cheating, though this depends on a race between my slowly improving gaming skills and the onset of old age and its associated decline in reaction times and motor skills.
Positives:
It is still a great game after all this time.  It's from that era before game designers decided it was their responsibility to bore you half to death padding out brainless story lines nobody cares about with excruciatingly dull and overly long video clips.  It is a brainless story line but it's a good, simple, fun one that doesn't pretend to be anything else.  Perfect for a game in fact!
I seem to remember Far Cry was a big deal at the time because it was one of the few "open world" type games that let you explore and complete levels in whatever non linear way you prefer.  I think that is why it can still be enjoyable to play today.  It looked amazing in 2004 and is still OK now.  It is somehow still very entertaining, having a wide selection of weapons and vehicles and lets you mix stealth and raw chaos as you like.
Negatives:
The thing that shows its age the worst is the AI of the enemies but I don't really care as it's a bonus for me not to get killed as often as my skills merit.
I never did warm to Val.  She's terribly bossy and not once does she offer to make a nice cup of tea or get her top off.  This bit is a lot like real life.
In conclusion, I would definitely recommend Far Cry to other fat persons who would like to shoot tough guys and monsters and feel big and macho and cool.

I won’t bore with a long review it’s a total war game with all the good and bad aspects that come with the line we love and hate, I’ll just tell you why I like it. I highly enjoyed playing this version of total war, mainly for the scope of area you can conquer (the world minus Africa and Eastern Asia) and scope of battles you can fight (with good unit variation). Highly recommended for any strategy and total war fan.

Probably the most hours I've spend on any computer game. It's an old game but still worthwhile! Especially if you love warfare more than the management part of Total War. OH and one more word: GUNS.
The only downside is how the AI behaves on the map. It doesn't seem that active, ofcourse I've lost battles but when I count the number of battles I've won it's a bit off. But then again, playing as the United Provinces (nowadays The Netherlands) and achieving world domination is why you're playing Total War.

Although not everyones cup of tea, if you love mass scale micromanagement this game will deliver.
The odd thing which I think I have been fortunate to have experienced is that over the time I have owned this game I can count the crashes on one hand.  Others have not been nearly so fortunate.
You'll also want to turn up the difficulty or you will wonder how the whole world wasn't conquered by this or that faction.  In the battlefield the AI is fairly poor despite if you turn up the battle difficulty and is made up for by padding the AI stats.  Still there will be times when the enemy will sit there and be happy to let you blow them appart with long range artillery fire.  I generally autoresolve as I play for the big picture.
The naval battles are nice to watch but fairly limited in tactics.  Basically you are trying to set up favorable fields of fire but generally I was able to manage favorable engagements on the campaign map eliminating the need for advanced tactics.  Essentially two lines staggered will completly crush their fleet every time.  Unless of course you failed on the campaign layer.
Haven't tried MP yet because I'm an anti-social gamer.   So can't say about that one.
I can see why many think this is the weakest entry in the TW series but not for me I enjoy the original Shogun and Medieval the least probably due to their age respectively.  Namely the much more limited options available.  This one looks good but does have some issues but it is also the only TW game with such a massive scope and for me, sometimes that's all that matters.

Note: Many many more hours played than recorded on Steam, for a long time I played this without an internet connection.
There is simply no game that compares with this one for me, and is the second greatest game ever released by the Creative Assembly. The campaign is epic and the scope is truly global, and represents the times and strategies of the day better than any other game.
No franchise has given me as many hours of enjoyment as the Total War series, and this one is my favorite after Medieval 2. Now that the kinks are worked out, no game can compare.
10/10 for all your line of battle needs.

Dragon Rising is the result of Codemasters' attempt to focus the open world, squad based, combined arms, realistic tactical shooter "Operation Flashpoint" series development around gaming consoles rather than personal computers, in contrast with Bohemia Interactive's "Arma".
As a result, the command menu was simplified into a more controller appropriate quadral rose, the group size was reduced from a 12 man squad to a 4 man fire team, and the number of entities permitted on a map at one time was reduced from hundreds to around 60.
Compared with Arma or OFP:CWC & R, the OFP:DR AI move slower and more cautiously, are more alert, flank more effeciently, and yet are less likely to hit the player (exception given to AT weapons). Voices are clearer and more natural. Physix, a more advanced tiring system, thermal optics, and individual medical kits were used in this before being incorporated into Arma. Overall, the Arma games have more to offer though, with an easier to use mission editor, greater mod friendliness, continued support, the ability to lean, customizable faces and voices, free editing software for a user to produce their own content, aiming without having to constantly depress the aim button, and much more.

The game is challenging, sure, but I wouldn't call it fun.

I learned more about D-Day from the extras menu then I have ever learned from High School History Class.
But honestly, this game is a sublime gem for a history nut like me.
Going back to 2005, I picked it up on the old Xbox and got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked on the first few levels. It was unlike any WW2 shooter at the time and even now it's something of a special snowflake amongst a horde of FPS's on steam. Seeing it on sale I decided to pick it up again, this being the THIRD time I have purchased Brothers In Arms in some manner (got a beat-up CD-box set from amazon. I think the guy who sold it to me sat on it).
So how does Brothers in Arms stand out from the crowd, especially from a time when we were once tired of WW2 shooters?
Deploying tactical charges and employing cunning tactics are your only surefire way to make it to the end of the level with yourself and your men intact. Everything from rifle sway, debris and the unforgiving difficulty keep you from reliving memories from Wolfenstein or Medal of Honor and force you to focus and pin enemies down with relentless fire.
This method of gameplay has been a turnoff for some, as it is very hard to actually get through some skirmishes, but I find it fascinating. I can't recall many games utilizing supression fire to achieve victory over an enemy, who come at you in increasingly large numbers. Through this method of gameplay I've found it to be oddly satisfying to land a kill-shot on a Jerry and send his body ragdolling across the pavement. Landing that final blow is far more rewarding then in most games, where the enemy stands out in the open doing little in terms of self preservation.
Of course, another major selling-point for BIA is the story. Unlike MoH or CoD, the fighting is a lot more personal and evocative. the main character, Sgt Matt Baker, is fleshed out, poetic, caring and loyal. Not to mention the characters of your friends and squad-mates are equally endering. Going back, I was astonished by how much character was present in this game compared to games at the time and even today. None of these soldiers are cigar-chomping, hardened veterans. They are optimistic young men, brash yet friendly, stressed yet humorous. They feel like genuine human beings, a refreshing take on Soldiers compared to the nihilistic shouting and brooding from many Modern-Military shooters of today. Sgt Matt Baker and friends see through the patriotism and have first-hand experiences of the horrors of war, yet they strive forward with wit, humor and optimism to reach the end of the day.
However, even at the time, BIA falters on the graphical front. Many textures are muddy and blurry, especially up-close. The levels are rather drab as well. Even at the time they weren't exactly eye-candy. However, they serve the gameplay well, and some special effects such as dirt clogging your vision and muzzle-flashes help reel you into the atmosphere.
Speaking of which, much of the game is played against a silent soundtrack with nothing but machine-gun beats, wind and bullet-impacts riddling your ears. The sound design is top-notch for a game like BIA and creates a fantastic atmosphere against the set-pieces of D-Day and skirmishes that followed.
With all that being said, I can't exactly say I can recommend BIA to everyone. Those looking for a challenge might be pleased but a few may be turned off by the cumbersome controls and lack of modern FPS features like sprinting, prone positions or cover-vaulting. For someone like me, who is a bit of a history nut, I was ecstatic to play this once more on steam and experience the story again.
If this game is right up your alley and are itching to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by rifle-totting krauts, then look no further then Brothers in Arms and it's fantastic sequel!

Pros: Great pixel art.
Cons: The game sucks.

In the original Kingdom there was one land which immediately contained all of the available content and indeed, there wasn't a lot of it. So the developers went and came up with some new stuff. Hermits, which upgrade archer towers into highly specialized ones, more mounts, additional statues, tweaked merchant NPC, a new banker NPC. They also split the play area into five islands and renovating a ship and getting it to shore to sail away is the new victory condition. Sounds great, right?
The problem is that now, having any random realm features requires first grinding to unlock the possibility of them appearing. Even the ones that could be considered the most absolutely basic (and critical) - such as the archer statue, builder statue or upgraded horse - are initially locked. And you unlock (at best) one thing per escaping an island. And it's completely random what you'll unlock. It takes about as much time as what it sounds like; even someone not familiar with Kingdom gameplay might see where this is going. A huge miss.
They also added a winter mechanic where after some time spent on an island, permanent winter will set in. Crops can no longer be grown (farmers discard their scythes and revert to peasants), wild animals no longer spawn. The gold starvation it creates is meant to force the player to leave the island or slowly wither under the continuous onslaught of Greed. I consider this the second key design failure committed in the expansion. I can only guess what were they thinking, but none of the things I come up with are adequate justifications.
Speaking of Greed, they also tweaked the balance a bit to make them more of a challenge. Early waves are more numerous so it's harder to survive around day 10-15. The endgame waves are about on par with the original. And all the small problems I mentioned in
are still present. You still can't order units at all, none of the game mechanics are adequately explained and the game pace is glacial. By the end of it, I had it running at quadruple speed via an external tool because... seriously, I ain't got time for that.
Kingdom: New Lands is still a pretty cool game, they fumbled with a lot of stuff but didn't manage to ruin it. As a whole it deserves a thumbs up. If, however, I were to judge solely the changes made in comparison to Kingdom: Classic, the result would've been a thumbs down.

What I liked:  the graphics are really something special.  At first glance it just looks like a retro-styled game, but it's much more.  There are a lot of subtle atmospheric things going on as you traverse different parts of your island and as the season, weather, and time of day change.  Light is used well as it plays off of objects and is reflected in the water.
But, that's about all I liked, the graphics.
What I didn't like:  Everything is just hard to figure out.  It gets repetitive fast.  Permadeath is not great for a game like this in my opinion.  It felt like torture going through the first couple of islands over and over due to permadeath.  Islands (at least the ones I got to) are basically the same.

you just try to run away.
- The game itself can be speed run in around 1.5h, while 20 min just being unskippable scenes.
- The characters are annoying as hell. In RE3 we had Nemesis, in Deadspace we had the Regenerator, both wonderful
frightening creatures. In RE7 we just have some crazy rednecks that I cannot take seriously. You just ignore them until
you have to fight them in the scripted boss battle.
- The only part I really liked is the ship scene (endgame).
Maybe I just have played to many horror games and have seen to many movies to be impressed by this game …
I finished it once for the story, started it a again but got bored before the first boss and have no intension to finish it a second time.
No replayability. You get some boni after finishing the game on different difficulties, but they are not worth it compared to all the nice upgrades you get in RE4/RE5, or even the boni of RE1-RE3.
I have much more hours on RE6 ... yes  RE6 ...
So my preferences for the main series are as followed:
RE4 > RE2 > RE5 > RE3 > RE1 original > RE0 > RE1 remake > RE6 > RE7
RE7 would be okay for a side series but even here I prefer the RE Revelations series since they offer a good mix of horror and action parts. And a lot of replayability. Especially with Raid Mode.

Being a somewhat old school Eve/X3/spacejesus gamer, I was really interested in trying KV when I heard a few details in passing, Of course, I have the memory of a gnat, and forgot about it for a couple of weeks, I just bought and downloaded it now,.
You start out with a deceptivly simple looking ship; cockpit, engines, guns and superstructure, however all these parts are modular, so you can move stuff around, have it at a different angle and so on, to personalise your ship as much as you like.
I'm really happy to have got this now, as the developers have some great Ideas, and are planning to develop this game for a while after release, So, I can see myself puttering around in the galaxy for a long time to come.

Kinetic Void is a very Early Alpha game. A few annoying bugs and glitches which hopefully get fixed sooner rather than later. The ship building is amazing. despite the bug and glitches. It is fantastic. Easily the best part of the game with me. Space flight is not too bad. I think as and when future updates come out then it will improve. Right now you just fly around shooting stuff, mining asteroids, selling the ores and building bigger better ships. Would like to see the planned economy come out. That should improve the gameplay a lot, Would also like to see the ability to start a factions, take space stations, mining stations, claim systems, Have NPC ships fly around the galaxy mining, and defending territory.
Performance of the game is very good. On High end hardware the game runs over 110 FPS on maxmimum settings.  Graphics are very good in most places. In some places like the engine trails, they are pretty poor, at least to myself.
Should you buy this game? In my opinion yes. While right now there are bugs and glitches, which is to be expected in an early alpha game, The future looks bright, with the developers looking well into the future with possible multiplayer and DLC content.

Far Cry is a classic game from 2004, WOW how fast 13 years can fly by!! It can still hold its own today, especially as one of the classic PC games of our time and it is well worth taking a look at. For its time, the graphics were stunning, still are, but what makes this FPS stand out from all the other FPS flooding the market in the early 2000’s is the way you get from point A to point B each level.
Unlike many FPS where the A to B journey is quite linear and exploration is often restricted by buildings, mountains and darkened corridors or walkways, Far Cry contains huge wide open spaces, oceans, desert islands and jungles. In addition to this, how you get from level start to level end is also varied, whether that be the long stealthy exploratory detour through the impressive scenery, using the different types of transport available or simply rushing head first into the enemy; the choice is yours.
Sadly the online multiplayer servers I believe are no longer available, as this would have been fun to try out with modern broadband compared with snail paced dial up around the time the game was released.
Whether you have played the most recent title in the Far Cry series or not, the original is well worth trying out for the beauty of the scenery, the gameplay and also as a piece of FPS history.

As someone who has played the actual tabletop game, and still keeps several Warbands on hand (y'know, just in case)... I can very much reccomend this game to anyone that is a fan of the tabletop version. It has it's flaws, and there are bugs, but please keep in mind that this is an Early Access game. They are barely in alpha and aren't even finished making all the warbands.  I admit that the limitations of the program now do make it something that would be hard to play often, but as more features are released to people that have already bought it, the game will get much better.
There are currently four warbands to choose from (June 2015) and they are Humans, Skaven, Sisters of Sigmar, and The Cult of the Possessed. The units included are all quite faithful to the source game, and the equipment loadouts are fairly self explainatory to anyone familiar with Mordheim, and easy enough to figure out for new players. Lack of leveling system is disappointing, but that will come in future updates. When the game is more complete it will have a lot more appeal to newer players, or people unfamiliar with the source material.
Gameplay is fairly easy to figure out.  Move your character, perform action, etc. Combat animations look decent, the city has some nice detail and the maps look pretty good. Fun overall to play, though definately more fun with other players than against bots. The bots are fine if you just need a quick game, but for the best experience, play with friends.  All the best multiplayer games are ones that can end friendships. lol.
TL:DR VERSION:   Good game. Currently would rate 6/10, only for limitations of early access version, but well worth investment. Great game, faithful to the source material, and fun to play with friends. 10/10 would buy again.
UPDATE - Full Release Patch 2 -  Having played the campaign and had a chance to genuinely enjoy the game a bit now that it has hit full release, I can say that I still do not regret my decision to purchase this game. It remains a very playable, faithful adaptation of the classic tabletop game that still gets played in my house. Looking forward to the addition of more warbands and expanded content in the times to come.

Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 has truly earned the title of "cult classic". It's one of the best underrated games out there, as well as one of the best of the old days. It's not like your normal Medal of Honor-s or your Call of Duty-s that you see so much of around the time of when this game was in it's hey-day. It is, at it's core, a rather linear tactical first-person shooter. But there are a few distinguishing qualities that set it apart from the crowd.
Concept: BIA: Road to Hill 30 was designed as a tactical first-person shooter with RTS elements set during Operation Overlord (D-Day) in World War 2. You play as Sergeant Matt Baker: a platoon sergeant in the 101st Airborne Division tasked with completing various objectives around the French countryside that will, in turn, help to further the Allied war effort. You'll be taking command of Paratroopers from all over the division. Sometimes even taking charge of platoon-sized elements, as well as combat support and force multipliers such as tanks. You'll need superb tactical know-how, a disciplined trigger finger, and quick wits if you want to succeed.
Story: You are, as stated above, Sergeant Matt Baker. A Paratrooper and platoon Sergeant of America's 101st Airborne Division. Without spoiling too much, you'll take part in the massive Airborne invasion of Normandy, France with a single objective in mind: complete the liberation of the country, and make it out alive. Unfortunately, not all will be able to complete this objective. War is hell. And BIA wants you to know it. If you're looking for an old-school Band of Brothers style war drama, you've come to the right place.
Graphics: As this is an old game, it's understandable that it's visual fidelity hasn't held up to the highest standards. But being as old as it is, it's entirely playable, and enjoyable from start to finish. While the overall texture quality of certain objects show some age, there are some areas where the game still looks rather good with vibrant colors, brilliant lighting, and oooooh...god-rays...
Gameplay: Unfortunately, while the game's graphics have aged well, that doesn't mean the the entirety of it's gameplay has. While the majority of the game is entirely playable without frustration, there are some aspects that can be rather annoying, or just plain stupid at times. The movement and shooting mechanics of Road to Hill 30 are by far the weakest aspects of the game. Movement feels rather clunky and slow, especially when lacking the ability to sprint or jump over 2 foot surfaces. The ballistic mechanics are also pretty terrible considering that when using ADS mode, your weapon sways around like drunk rhino. Weapon variety consists of what you might expect from an early 2000s WW2 shooter. Your standard tried and true M1 Garand, the oh-so familiar M1A1 Thompson SMG, a Colt .45 M1911, the BAR, and an assortment of German weapons. You'll also occasionally get to hop onto some emplaced weapons such as a Browning .30 Cal. or an MG42. Most likely just in time to cut down a few company's-worth of Nazis. Thankfully, these handle much better than the standard "in-hand" weapons. There are certain points in the game where you'll be required to fight enemy tanks in order to progress. These are some of the most frustrating encounters in the game. For one: the damn things take around three shots from a Bazooka or Panzerfaust to destroy. That's hitting them anywhere on the tank. Even the backs and sides. And a lot of the time, the caches where you aquire said anti-tank weapons are partially in sight of the tank. Exposing you to enemy fire. But don't let these design choices fool you. While the game is challenging, even on lower difficulties, I felt that it was fair enough to keep me playing. Now, on to arguably the most important aspect of the game: the squad control system. Not much to say about the system that the game was sold on, to be honest. Most of the time you'll be in control of a squad of Paratroopers that will help you in battle by suppressing and flanking enemy positions. You'll also occasionally get control of a tank that works roughly the sam way, but is immune to small arms fire, and can take out fortifications with ease. But don't expect a free ride. When you get control of a vehicle, it's almost inevitable that a tank battle is near. Thankfully, you can use your squad on the ground to draw the ememy's fire whilst you hop onto the back of your tank, and monut the MG before counterattacking and destroying your opposition. It's moments like these that make you just love this system. And it works well-enough, too. I found it to be very fluid, and useful throughout my playthrough.
Conclusion: BIA is my personal favorite WW2 franchise. And with good reason. And while the graphics and some gameplay elements of the original; Road to Hill 30, may not be some of the most polished in the world, it stands the test of time in every other aspect. The story and writing is masterful. As is the game's pacing, theme, and voice acting. If you're looking for a true cult-classic WW2 nostalgia trip to live out your Airborne fantasies in, you can't go wrong.
Final Rating: 9/10

Before you decide to blindly criticize my review keep in mind I have 377.1 hours invested into this game.
Ah Airmech, where do I begin? I used to absolutely love this game. I first heard about it when Huskystarcraft played it on his channel. Yea, Huskystarcraft. This was a loooooooooooooong♥♥♥♥♥time ago. Back then I didn't have a PC that could even run the game, so I just watched gameplay of it. Eventually, I realized the sad truth that I just wouldn't be able to play this game, so I gave up. A couple years later I bought a new PC cuz my old one broke down, and I made my steam account. It was then that I realized that Airmech was on Steam and that it was free to play. I played the hell out of this game, and almost became completely obsessed with it.
The game had everything I could ever want out of it. Competitive PvP, unique gameplay, people throwing around premium currency like they don't even care, and most importantly, customization. You could choose your airmechs, pilots, units, items, upgrades, and you could even change around the core stats of the airmech with parts.
To me, the parts system seemed absolutely perfect. Most parts had different tiers, ranging from mk1 to mk4. Higher tiers weren't stronger than the lower ones, they just modified your stats more. If you did it right you could almost completely change the playstyle of your airmech. You could be anywhere from a slow tanking beast, to an agile glass cannon.
The free to play model was spot on too. Most of the essentials were bought with credits. Credits being the main f2p currency. The few non-free essentials were mostly parts, items, and pilots. Most of them were relatively cheap and could easily be earned by any f2p player like myself with just some well accumulated active playtime. The expensive stuff was the cosmetic stuff. Things like skins for your airmech and fancy pets and decals.
That's not to say that you didn't get much for paying. Aside from awesome skins and decals, you could also purchase units called 'ultimates.' The were obscenely strong units that were ridiculously OP and not allowed in regular PvP play. You could use them to shred your way through ruthless AIs, destroy survival mode, and have good fun with your friends in custom matches.
But everything changed that one faithful day...
The devs came out with an update that pretty much ruined everything I discussed in this review.
The update split PvP into two different modes. One where parts were not allowed, and one where they were allowed...along with any ultimate units, pilots, or parts. To make things even worse, parts became a direct upgrade to your airmech and higher tiers of parts were direct upgrades. Furthermore, Higher tier parts could only be obtained from farming or trading with other players on the player market for premium currency. Players were left with a terrible choice, play a watered down version of the game for free, or farm for hours upon hours only to be dominated anyway by ultimate units.
RIP balance, RIP f2p, RIP customization
And this isn't even the end of it. Remember how I mentioned "unique gameplay" as one the game's good traits? Well ever since that update the game slowly began to veering towards being just another MOBA. The game slowly stared to steer away from the RTS aspect of it's formerly great concept. Now the game mostly mostly favors an autobuild system AKA creeps or minions.
RIP unique gameplay
For me, that was the dagger to the heart for this game. Don't waste your time. This game has been in beta for years and is shrinking more that it seems to be growing. Just don't bother.

What a sad, sad story this is.
I played the original Blacklight: Tango Down on the 360 when it was released (A decent F2P multiplayer game back in the 360 days, that ACTUALLY has players? yes please!) and it was fantastic fun. Whilst being slightly overcomplicated in both its UID and mechanics; it was a tight, tactical and fast paced shooter that seemed quite well balanced.
Many uncounted hours were sunk into this title, and I especially enjoyed the interesting implementation at some form of 'legit' wall hack, where the game was fascinatingly balanced for its inclusion. I liked this as a future prospect due to it possibly deterring the sweaty inbred degenerates that we now commonly call 'cheaters' in other prominant titles like CS: GO now, or CS: Source at the time. I wanted this game to do well.
After some time - and the 7th gen being surpassed - there was a void for a while where there was no updated Blacklight game, and it dwindled in my interest. Eventually, this sequel was released. I installed it - this time on the garbage PC that I had - played it briefly, and had to wait due to my system simply being too rubbish to actually function with most games at the time. However, though my time with it was brief, it further increased my interest in the series and I 'shelved' it for a planned PC upgrade.
I then came back to it again a short time after, and it had completely changed. Everything was different, sluggish (Even though I had FINALLY properly upgraded my PC) the pace changed and the mouse precision and feel had changed in almost every way. Everything had lost its recoil and skill bracket. The economy was different and alienating. It felt weird and clunky. Boring even. Each frame was taxing on my eyes and mind. I couldn't figure out what had happened!
Reading about the PS4 version, and what the develoment team had decided to do with the PC version following its release, I saw droves of similar minded people that shared my exact same experience with this alien version of the game that had suddenly popped up. I installed it again, furious that after all this time; the game I was so excited to upgrade for and play seriously had simply been fisted by its own development team in the prime of its life.
So, I am sad about this and will be for a long while. It really is hard to believe that a title like Blacklight, which in 2010 showed such promise and innovation, could have its sequel fall victim to such a bizarre and easy avoidable state of affairs. It was inconceivable!
The only hope I have for this game is that the bullshwaz 'Parity Patch' is EXTERMINATED from the currently live build of the game, and it is reverted back to the state it was in mid-late 2014. At that point, and only that point, could you hope to see some resurgence in the player base and friendly community.
Zombie Studios, or now Hardsuit Labs - probably due to the former name having so many blunders associated with it - has a lot of self reflection to do on their failures up until this point, but I know they can create a good game when they keep their♥♥♥♥♥♥together and actually try.
Pre-Parity: 8.9/10
Post-Parity: 4.4/10
P.S To watch the Gaming industry develop over a long period of time can be both incredibly depressing and exhilarating. This is by far one of the most depressing stories that I have witnessed to date.

The very first Far Cry game holds up in a number of surprising ways and is worth checking out, but be prepared for some hair pulling.
The first half of the game (6 hours or so) is consistently enjoyable, especially once you get the silenced MP5, which allows you to sneak effectively and exploit the enemy AI. There are some difficult parts that will result in a series of deaths, but the challenge is pretty consistent and I was having a great time.
It's in the second half that Far Cry will lose some people. Stronger bullet-sponge enemies that are introduced and thrown at you in large groups, the base enemies are upgraded to have tons of body armor and there are numerous set-pieces that require tons of trial and error. While the first half of the game had consistent challenge with some difficulty spikes, the later half frequently has these spikes, many of which just feel plain unfair. Getting through some sections can be a desk smashing chore.
Even with that way weaker second half, the good still outweighes the bad and I would recommend any fan of the series give it a shot. Perhaps you'll even have the patience to finish it!

I'll be honest, this is the first horror game I have completed. But even so, this game is amazing and one of the best First Person Shooters I have played.I got this game after I decided to try the demo and enjoyed it greatly. Before considering getting this, I highly recommend you try out the demo. But onwards:
Pros:
+Visuals are disturbing and creepy
+Little cheap scare tactics or jumpscares, instead relying on creepy visuals and gameplay
+Great antagonists, especially the Baker family, who will be hunting you down throughout the game. Jack Baker is especially good, managing to be Scary, Insane, Hilarious, and sympathetic by the end. Easily on par with other great villains like Vaas, each part you go against him is intense and easily the best parts of the game.
+ Gameplay is challenging and fun with great progression. You start out with zero weapons, relying on stealth or running like a madman. But later, you get a knife and some guns which you can use to keep the Bakers off your back and deal with the Molded (which I will talk about later). This also goes along with the fact that as enemies will get more dangerous, you will too, making unfair difficulty spikes  non-existant. The game also somehow manages to make backtracking rewarding, to the point where I actually wanted to go back and look for what I might have missed.
+ Most boss battles are amazing, making you think outside the box to win, and is not afraid to not take things seriously.
+ the game actually has a good, fully explained story which keeps you engaged and interested.
+ Their is a firm division in the difficulty levels, I have found this out by playing a game of all (exept I have not uflly completed madhouse). Easy: did not die once. Normal: good balance between challenge and fun. Madhouse: Highly self-explanatory.
+ Decent replay value with rewarding collectibles and unlockables.
Cons:
-The Molded are easily the worst part of the game. They are sludgy, zombie-like creatures. They start out creepy, but then they become annoying to fight as you realize how poorly programmed the AI for them is. THEY CAN'T EVEN OPEN OR BREAK DOWN DOORS! This also leads to very little diversity in enemies, as when you are not fighting the Bakers, these are almost always what you will face.
- The game has a good story, but it has several cliches. Crazy Hillbilly Murderers? Check. Creepy little girl? Check. "Redshirts'? Check.
- The last third of the game is easily the worst section. You will be fighting a lot of molded and their is an exposition dump near the end of the game which gets pretty annoying.
- I have to say this since no one else seems too, but the final boss is GOD AWFUL. It requires almost no strategy, or thinking, its not very interesting, feels very out of place, highly scripted, and is basically just a bullet sponge, in heavy contrast to the rest of the bosses.
- If you remain undetected, you can tell the Bakers have a 'somewhat' pre-set AI path. This can make them predictable if you remain cautious enough.
Despite its cons, RE 7 is one of the funnest games I have played in a while, and I highly recommend you to get it. There is also free DLC that will come out at some point in the future, which few games (much less ones by big companies) bother doing, I might make a review for that when it comes out,

Firstly, I always enjoyed Mordheim and have been very excited at the prospect of this game. I really want to enjoy it and want to see it reach its potential.
If you and a friend, who were both really into Mordheim have a couple of days free, you will get hours of enjoyment out of the game in its current state. The customisation is fairly extensive and the developers have stayed loyal to the feel of mordheim, without limiting themselves to a straight adaptation of the dice rolling version. Some players might be turned off by this, but the devs have done it right and the game feels great to play. If you like the warband managment side of things, you can currently spend hours just trying out different warbands and setups.
The bad side is that playing against the AI gets really old, really quickly. In addition to the AI being really bad in its current form, the CPU warbands you fight in exibition are significatnly weaker than those made by the player. CPU warband rating is generally around 2k, while player made is ~3k. While I find little satisfaction in beating the AI in any game, such a lack is far more pronounced in this game currently.
There are alot of bugs, but this of course is to be expected and does not overly concern me. I am confident the devs will work through them in time. Most notably and obvious is the camera angles - AI and camera seem worse on proceduraly generated maps, as does people being able to attack through walls - this should really be addressed before new maps are created, there are plently of maps at the moment, and good replayability due to specific parts being generated differently each time.
Somewhat worrying, is the lack of an in game bug report system. I feel like this would benefit the devs no end, and really help focus their attention on getting the game into a better state. It would also soon remove many of the minor issues which can turn players off a game forever. Chaos spawn getting stuck in a doorway two games running is irritating. I know it will be fixed, but others are not so patient. This is doubly so where people have paid for the game, it is not a beta.
I am recommending this game, the hours of enjoyment I have gotton so far have been worth the money, and there is the promise of many more hours to come if the Devs continue their hard work. Note however, that online games are uncommon so you really need a buddy to play against.
Finally, and if everything else I have said is ignored, I really hope the Devs will pay attention to this point. The planned future updates make no reference to an online matchmaking system. Single player in this game will simply not keep anyone interested for long. Even if you extensively overhaul the AI in advance of the single player campaign, the joy of Mordheim is, and has always been playing against other players. I envisage a perpetual campaign where players are matched against other warbands based on their warband ranking which would effectively act as an ELO. Players will also need the ability to make their own private campaigns. I want to be able to take 6 friends and sit for a weekend starting from scratch.
Private multiplayer campaigns and an ongoing online campaign should be given priority over any single player campaign. Even in the games current state, the ability to create your own league (aka bloodbowl) with friends would dramatically increase sales. This seems comparitavely simple compared to making loads of new maps and scripting 32 single player missions for the single player campaign, which will still be dull unless you plan on DRASTICALLY overhauling the AI.

The setting of this game is one that really piqued my interest, who would've thought that mining and tunneling in a post-apocalyptic European Union would be so immersive?
The main story behind the game, which the developers subtly drop clues and hints about, is that a group of individuals, cloned from the same template, are made to mine and tunnel for one of the many enclaves that emerged from the ruins of a nuclear war on a global scale, in a ragtag prequel to the famous "metro" series.
The gameplay is very symbolic of how we are all trying to burrow ourselves into a little hole to escape the pressures of society. You don't just move rocks - you move hearts. The roar of the machines is the only motivation you need. They're there not just for manual support - they give more approval to you than your boss-bailiff, whom you never meet face-to-face. Your frustrations are almost literally blown away by the satisfaction of moving masses of earth, which is as simple as T...N...T.
I was amazed at the concept of using gentically identical clones as manual labourers, and the subtle argument for its' establishment in the workplace portrayed by the game. While I disagree with oligopolistic conglomerates cloning its' own workforce, the game makes a convincing argument for the "pros" side of the argument.
Oh and P.S., this game is boring. Really boring. You must detonate, pick up, and move gravel until your fingers, eyes, and brain bleed and you have the brain activity of a tomato. If you buy this game, I will call Interpol and notify the international criminal court of your heinous act.

I love simulations... Sim Ant, Sim World, Sim City, Sim Life etc.
I had luck, this game was in a bundle so it came quite cheap - but, if you look closer to this simulation you can see that it goes without the merits of the old time simulations that fans of the simulation genre fancy so much. It isn't as bad as some other simulations that were published over the past few years, but still it isn't a good simulation - it lacks the long term motivation thing, that kept us playing Sim City, the novelty of Sim Ant, and the complexity of Sim World and Sim Life.
I even have to ask myself, is this a "Simulation" in the original sense of the meaning? I had to say: No. It is a "drive around a site of civil engineering and mining and try out the construction site equipment. I like building machinery, I like tractors - mostly because I grew up on a rural town, were you had those things as "toys" to play around.
Thus the game fails the descriptor - "Simulation", at least in the most obvious ways.
And then, is a game that simulates day to day routines of a "everyday"-job a good thing to simulate? Do you want to be a construction site worker for real (I have been for three years after grammar-school), or a trucker, a farmer or forester? And to what extend do you wish to "simulate" the job?
If you answer any of this three questions with a denial, this game clearly isn't for you. If you answer just two of those with a no, or say you don't like simplifications on sims - be wary of this game. If you answer all those with yes, or say that you want a casual, simplified sim - you might have a hit here; there are no calculations of quantities required, no structural engineering calculations and no insurances for your workers... so much for the Sim Part of the game ;-)
Since the user base is very limited, I won't recomend the game - though I sometimes might enjoy that kind of "simplification"...

Kingdom: New Lands
"Everything you wanted out of the flash version years ago, but you have to spend inordinate amounts of time on it."
Pros: Cute pixel art style with decent animations. Really good atmosphere and decent music. Simple and engaging.
Cons: Nothing in the game is explained at all, although that was an intentional choice on the part of the designers. It's not particularly balanced in any way, and the player lacks any sort of direct control over NPCs. The game is designed so the player cannot achieve any sort of balance or status quo; the enemies get tougher and more numerous indefinitely and your defenses have a limited number of upgrades. The objective is to find a broken boat, build a new one in its place, and escape the island with a few people before you are eventually overwhelmed. The main portals from which the enemies spawn can be temprarily disabled, but not destroyed. The final level leaves no escape option and you die.
Summary: Simple fun for a few hours. Wouldn't recommend spending money on it.

You can't control where any of your subjects go, you can't reassign them to different jobs, and you can't remove things you no longer need. What you can do is ride, drop coins for people and to build, and upgrade your kingdom. Unfortunately, it's really difficult to keep your walls in good shape because you can only build them on randomly generated spots, so they may be waaaay far from your defense towers, which will mean your archers can't shoot the enemies until they've already destroyed the wall. All you can do is rebuild it constantly.
This game would be much, much better if there were some hotkeys to control different types of subjects, the ability to plan your kingdom more deliberately and remove things you don't need, and get people to follow your character. I can recommend it now that it's dirt cheap - the only way to have fun here is to finish the game for the developers. If Codemasters spent their time and money fixing Dragon Rising instead of making Red River, they would have fared a lot better. It really depends on what you are looking for - if this game did not bear the "operation flashpoint" name, it wouldn't have gotten so much flak. The main downfall of this game is that a) they marketed it wrong - taking a name no mainstream player heard of and sticking it on a game that will clearly offend the fans of the original, and b) they didn't care about the community post-release. The fact is, the game has a lot of potential - AI responds fast and feels smooth (kinda like in the original OFP and unlike ArmA2), although friendlies are useless; weapons feel nice and weighty; simplistic graphics don't cause too much strain on your hardware; and the missions have the capacity to be as massive and diverse as the original OFP (now ArmA: Cold War assault - actually, go get that instead). However, once the engine and models were finished, nobody bothered creating a decent long campaign, and the paid DLCs were similar in quality to what I could make in the editor in a day. Vehicles, commanding a platoon, variability of weapons - all could have been used for an awesome DLC, or even in the original campaign, but someone, in his infinite retardation, decided to just make a bland generic 10-mission campaign. But if you're willing to learn some LUA scripting, you can have a lot of fun with a reasonably realistic military sandbox with quite a variety of gameplay. Maybe it lacks the capacity of ArmA3, but I still feel weirdly charmed by its atmosphere.

I would like to say with the my opening to this review, it is very hard to say without a doubt that this game is for sure a recommendable or disrecommendable game. It stems from those people who have experienced the 3rd person view of the prior Resident Evils, as well as the static view from the other prior titles. So this title with its first person view will certainly throw you for a loop. There are plenty of jumpy and teeth gritting moments in this game, but overall most of the scares feel scripted. Plenty of gore for the kids. Overall our classic horror genre game. The element of defense is no new idea for Resident Evil, although I personally feel it really makes the fear factor really dumbed down, less about hiding and more just spraying down the family members. I felt quite honestly inticed in the story, and new direction for the Resident Evil genre, but I just felt it lacked a very deep or long narrative, and the gun play just felt really out of place in some parts of the game. Very little enemy variance, lots of backtracking (although its needed). The DLCs do add a bit of depth to the narrative, but that of course adds pay walls to people who should've recieved this information without these DLCs. Although there are some fun modes in the DLCs. I would overall say for those people who have not experienced a wide variety of horror games, its certainly a fun pick me up, and easy to get around, otherwise I would steer clear of this game until a sale, for $60 is a little sharp for the amount of story and gameplay here excluding the DLC.

I bought KV because I wanted exactly as it was described:  “Kinetic Void is a 3D space adventure with a focus on customization and enjoyable space simulation.”  And it was, it was a lot of fun.  Open ended design-build of ships of any size, kind, and configuration.  The graphics were beautiful, you could seek out battles or just cruise through the stars.  At times it was like a living, ethereal journey through space with nice music (and if you shut off the HUD it was like a living screen saver).  It was wonderful.  I took full advantage of the developer's description that “our in game ship builder allows players to construct their ship piece by piece.  Ships can be as simplistic as a cockpit, a single hull, a single engine and a single gun, or as complex as a player wants” and that ships can be “creative (unlimited components)” and I did build these.  Small fighters to huge Dreadnaught size.  But now, with recent mandatory patches, this has all been for nothing.  The advertised “open world sandbox” KV is purported to be is now becoming a concrete, high requirement game just like all the others out there.  All the ships I spent much time building I can no longer launch, and I'm not spending three months rebuilding a single huge ship because of the new “disconnected  components” requirement the developers have instilled (despite their allowing a freeform creation of ships) that came through force-fed updates even when I was opted out of this.  Even upon re-install the changes were there.  This game, in fact, used to be “customizable and enjoyable” but because of the forced changes now it has simply become a chore to play.  This game has gone from my “highly recommend” list to my “highly avoid” list, and the game's description now needs to be changed because it's no longer what it was.  The only questions left is for me to ask steam how to delete it from my games list.

This is my first review on Steam so excuse any formatting mistakes or any lack of coherence, but I want to start by saying that this game is really worth it if you're a competitive spirit or a hoarder or maybe even both. Learning all of the moves, learning how to put them together to form an efficient deck and having the ultimate satisfation when using it properly together with your defensive tools to defeat someone is the most satisfying feeling that I've ever had in a competitive PVP game.
If you are worried about the rumors you heard about that shabby servers, worry not, as the guys at SLOCLAP got it all under control almost as soon as the issues were pointed out by the community, unlike let's say For Honor where matchmaking and match stability is still a steaming pile of Bantha Fodder.
The game follows the fighting game formula with all of its concepts including blocking, parrying, dodging, super armour, guardbreaks, high/medium/low attacks sweeps and more, but the fact that it's a third person fighting game adds the amazing 3d element to it where moves actually have dodge capabilities against other types of moves.
If you're into Fashion Souls, you won't be dissapointed either because here you have Fabsolver, not only can you customize your moveset, you can also gather gear of different qualities that will alter the appearance of your character. Wanna go for the shaggy drunken master, go ahead. Maybe you want to look like a baddass Shaolin monk, you can do that as well.
The PVE I gotta admit is really the weakest point of the game, BUT do not lose hope as the awesome developers at SLOCLAP have this in mind and are planning on a lot of free content that will improve on this aspect of the game.
Overall I must say that I personally am addicted to this game and sincerely recommend it if you are into competitive games and I can say that it's a must have for fans of the fighting game genre.

In the genre of real-time strategy, every game touts complete 3D units, maps, effects, etc. and it seems hard to really distinguish between them and see any innovating features. But along comes Darwinia that decided to simplify both the graphics and gameplay and created a wonderful game.
Darwinia stars the player as a internet wanderer that stumbles upon a network filled with little A.I. creatures that Dr. Sepulveda created in order to research how they grow and evolve. But at the time the player enters, the network has been almost completely overrun by a virus and nearly destroyed the entire environment. And through the rest of the game the player must help the Dr. eradicate the virus and find the cause in order to bring back the world of Darwinia to its former glory.
Anyone that has played a real time strategy game will notice that Darwinia is a really simplified RTS were instead of managing resources, dozens of unit types to choose from, and hundreds of units to organize the player only has to manage a couple of "programs"; soldiers, gatherers, airstrikes, transport/machine gun nest and the Darwinians themselves through a task manager so that the player can take control over.
Graphically the game is a interesting one as it's the not the graphical power house that every game out today is but is very simple and is a bit of a throwback to old school pixelated games, there is even a setting in the games options that read "I need a upgrade." Really it is very possible to run the game on high settings while on a netbook or 5-6 year old computer.
The sound is a soothing electronica, which I'm not a fan for but fits the game exceptionally and the effects of the surroundings and weapons are loud and powerful and isn't bad for digitally created.
For all RTS fans, Darwinia is a no brainer. But for players that have never played any or very many RTS's, Darwinia is simple enough to pick up and play and are sure to have fun.

This is a fairly good game. In 2004, when it came out, it was met with great opposition. I'm not referring to the critics either. 2004 was probably the biggest milestone in first person shooters since 1992ish. The same year this classic Far Cry title came out, the world was also met with Half-Life 2 and Doom 3. All 3 of these titles managed to stun and impress the gaming community with not only some of the greatest visuals seen at the time but some of the most innovative gaming engines and gameplay features we had seen in many years.
Where Half-Life 2 had the phenomenal Source engine and its spectacular physics and Doom 3 had the unbeatable dynamic lights and shadows, Far Cry had the best feature of them all: a (semi) non-linear game map style with proper jungle based stealth.
Unlike the typical first person shooter of the time (and still ever present today) this Crytek title brought the player choices. Not choices in how the game evolved or ended story-wise, but choices in gameplay STYLE. You didn't have to run and gun the entire game if you didn't want to. For once, the player could crouch or go prone in tall grass and sneak up or around enemies without being detected. The player could get in close with a machete and perform stealth kills. The player could also throw rocks to distract the enemies so further the effect.
To add to this amazing stealth based (optional) approach to the gameplay, the player could also choose roughly which path they wanted to take as the levels progressed. The levels always have a point A and a point B. The player could however, choose how they reached point B. You can fly half the way in a hang glider. You could speed your way there in a truck. You could work your way around the edges of the map in a boat. You could sneak through the jungle. You could flat out mow everyone down with machine guns and waltz the heck right in. The point is this; you weren't forced to do as the game wanted you to do as though stuck on rails.
The gameplay made this one of the top titles for years. This was also one of the first if not THE first title to experiment with a 64-bit executable. I don't recall if this Steam version has that executable but I DO recall not being able to get it working properly and without texture glitches on an Intel CPU. Regardless, this was a monumental release, even if the story was lame and the gameplay has since grown tired for me. Frankly, I much prefer the Ubisoft Far Cry titles nowadays as they have evolved very well without losing the character of the original.
This is a game all FPS fans should try so they can experience FPS history at one of its finest moments.

Full detail:
Was a great game but something happened that I really can't explain. It was great once with good gunplay that felt challenging and at the same time managable with huge amounts of customization that worked and actually affected weapons and gear so you could literally created your perfect playstyle. The the parent company Zombi Studios hit a point of low profits so they invested heavily in a last ditch effort on a game called Daylight which was a horror sim and unfortunately the game didn't sell well so Zombie closed. During that time they were investing in Daylight Blacklgiht (BLR for short) was left unupdated and server maintance wasn't done often enough. Form that point on the game started losing players this was around 2013-2014. When Zombie shut down the devs of this game spintered off with rights to the game and continued as Hardsuit Labs (HSL) and focused on porting the game to PS4 again leaving PC mostly un updated. The did eventually come back and they tried to come back hard wtih a patch in 2015 if memory serves me right, called Parity which would bring all the features that was in PS4 version which was the primary focus at the time. And it did but at the same time it ♥♥♥♥ed up the balance that was on PC and a lot of mechanics and gear was changed to have console stats. Nothing wrong with that in essence but in reality PC handles a lot tighter and more precise than console. That's simply the nature of the avaliable hardware and interface (such as high end precision gaming keyboards and  mice) and software (that changes a mouses DPI or ability to control polling rates of mice and keyboards). I know all this stuff sounds Stupid and like marketing but keyboards and mice really do tend to be more precise and with all the variations, adjustability, and overall controls that are usually superior (sometimes) and more complex than consoles, making all the stats the same or similar to consoles destroyed the game's gameplay. Nearly all weapons began to handle and play extremely easily and almost identically. This meant that the most veteran players who spent time learning the curves, developing the skills and knowlege of how the game, gear, and weapons handled and worked were set on almost exactly equal terms as a fresh player. Basically progression was ♥♥♥♥ed and you felt like you weren't really achieveing anything anymore. Even all the gear was made avaliable to any and everyone without level restrictions (to an extent of course) but for the most part everything was accessable easily and early on so the game got boring quick especially when gameplay felt samey despite what you used and who you played against. And of course with everything easily accessible for free early on the game doesn't make that great of a profit. I mean it could have because all cosmetics were the only things that you couldn't earn with in game currency but the fact that the gameplay was so dumbed down that no players ever stuck around once they reached what they felt was the pinicale of what the game had to offer. I understand closing the gear, skill, and learning gap between old players and new ones in attempt to attract more new players but the way the game did it made it end up losing new players quickly and old players almost instantly. The core mechanics of the game hasn't been changed much at all from Parity back in 2015 and the devs announced that they don't plan to make anymore updates for the whole of 2017.

As most reviews have said up to now, KV is in Early Access, and thus has a long way to go. That being said, the fact that it does have a ways to go is less of a reminder than something to look forward to(as is often the case in Early Access games) as this game is remarkably whole. You generate a universe, build a ship(or if that's not your thing there are plenty of perfectly fine pre-built ships), and launch it into space. You fly around vaporizing enemies(or getting vaporized...you'll learn your limitations very quickly) and completing missions, and, if your hull is about to crumble or you decide you can do better with the design, you return to the ship yard and make adjustments. As it stands, the missions do need work, as they are random and can become repetitive, and the help center and be opaque to people starting out, but for those looking for a space sim because of exactly what it is: a sim, this game is excellent.

I played the other Resident Evil's and I was dissapointed as to where the franchise was headed after RE:6. I saw the reveal and genuinely thought it was just going to be another action FPS game. I was very dissapointed by the initial reveal When it launched I was highly skeptical about paying $60 for a game that is purely singleplayer. Something about it didn't sit right and against my own judgement I opened my wallet and chugged in my credit card info. The first thing I noticed when I first started playing was how nice the game looked and how well it ran. On my RX480 I never dipped below 60 FPS on the highest settings. Everything was smooth except for the controls. The game overall feels rather clunky but that is to be expected in a Resident Evil game. If anything it adds to the experience, the slow and clunky feeling controls make encounters truly feel engaging and important. The difficulty of the game can leave some to be desired. There's an easy mode which is genuinely too easy. You would have to be lame not to be able to complete the game on the easiest difficulty, however the normal difficulty can really just kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you don't know what you're doing. This is just me being picky and I had no problem with completing the game, but less experienced players might find some issue with finishing on normal and easy is just too easy.
The story overall is great but it suffers some plot holes near the end of the game that aren't really explained. The game lets you make choices in the game which is nice and when you're playing it feels like you're really in control of what happens to Ethan, but the game takes the choice you make and pretty much flushes it down the toilet and proceeds to give you pretty much the same ending. It's a shame because I really thought that my choice would significantly affect the outcome. I think this was a missed opprotunity.
The music in this game was great! I really liked the sound in the game as well. The voice acting would at times get a little bit corny but never at intense times where it ruins the overall atmosphere. What's a Resident Evil game without a little cheese anyways?
On my first playthrough, it took me about 9 hours to complete the game on the normal difficulty. This seems to be around the average time for the first playthrough, although there are some speed runners that have completed the game in an hour and a half. There is a lot of replayabiltiy though with the addition of ability rewards for completing objectives during a playthrough.
Overall I loved this game and do not regret throwing $60 at it. I am going to recomend this but it may not be worth that $60 for everyone. If it is on sale for $40 then there is no reason not to get it. This game is great!

Darwinia isn't an RTS, because there's not a lot of "strategy" to it.  There's no tech tree, and you only directly control a few units or squads at a time.  It's mostly "action tactics": player skill is applied in unit positioning/movement/targetting on 3D terrain, and in switching your focus around.
Darwinia is also mostly about its theme, if a game is allowed to have two mostlys.  It's a Tron-like journey into a retro cyberspace.  The goals of each mission are set in varied and beautiful techno landscapes sparsely populated by artifical life, friendly and otherwise.
So it's a sequence of setpieces really, with a small-scale hands-on feel.  It's not too frantic.  Compared to a traditional RTS like StarCraft 2 it is downright leisurely.  Which is fine with me; I like to be able to take a few seconds occasionally to watch an Engineer cruising across a digital seascape with a string of glowing souls in tow.
The demo is a good sampling of the game's content & mechanics.  Try it!
