I've had great moments in this game, even though at the time of writing this review, the game is far from complete. But I can see myself playing this game, until it is complete and allows me to manage my troops through an evolutive process.
Mordheim is a game in the spirit of the many Warhammer themed games that already exists. The World of Warhammer is a grim world where life has no value and everyone, from the greatest hero to the lowest of the low, can die in an instant. It shall be the same with your troops. They will get hurt, light and grave, they will die. You will loose your Champions, but if you play your cards right, you will prevail ... at least that's how I hope the game will shape up to be ... like its tabletop equivalent, up there with tabletop Bloodbowl !
Edit: I have now come back to Mordheim: City of the Damned after its launch. This is the game I expected so this review remains positive ! I'll give you my pros and cons:
PROS:
- Turned based epic fights
- Character progression coupled with injury/death system that can be ruthless if you really are unlucky (your favorite hero/leader might die or have permanent injuries each time they are put out of action ... of they might get lucky and miraculously recover) ... don't put all your eggs in the same basket and you might want to wait until your characters are better equipped before training them for this 200 gold skill ...
- The maps are fun. There's a lot of terrain to cover and you'd best remember to manage movements tactically.
- Warband progression is, overall, very slow but I consider this a pro since it rewards long term planning and strategy. Bad luck can really mess with your plans ... but we accept that as one of the reasons we play such a game in the first place.
CONS:
- Long loading times. I understand the scale of the map and that warband generation is a complicated process but ... I can't imagine people at minimum requirements not ending up losing patience.
- Random numbers generation (dice rolls) is weird. This game gives us percentages but I feel like it rolls d4s in its tests. It's come to the point where I started rolling dice as I made my throws for a couple games, to compare and I wish I could play with dice ... they never gave me 6 misses in a row twice in a game on 84% chances to hit, my dice respect statistics a lot more than the game seems to be doing. I mention this only because I'm usually very good at risk assesment in such games but I'm now almost convinced I have to threat a 75% chance of success more like a 40% chance of success when taking decisions. Is that only me ?
- The user interface and user experience could easily be vastly improved. Menus could be arranged differently so that there's no counter intuitive stuff such as a list of incoming events in the Mission Selection screen (there could be a "general information" menu for that and other informations spread around different menus). The "Warband management" menu where you pay for treatments and characters upkeep is a button just like other buttons. It could have its own menu or be a bit more evident, since it opens a menu which is different from the menus opened by other similar buttons in the same page. I'm sorry that I didn't bother suggesting that before the game was released.
- A lot of randomness which you cannot influence. For example, sellswords and shop inventories. I don't dislike the current system, I just wish there was a way for me to have a way to influence those. At times, my progress was slowed or my warband subefficient simply because I couldn't find anything good in the shop or because available sellswords didn't fit what I needed (when I could afford them, sometimes I had kickass sellsword worth 40 gold !!! Other times, I have over priced leaders who really aren't worth the price they ask ...)
- Hard to navigate the map, to gain knowledge about it to better strategize. Sometimes I wish I could get out of my characters' perspective to inspect something he can clearly see even if the range was limited (it would have to be). I always have so much trouble finding building entrances ...
- I wish there were more different warbands to chose from. DLC !
Overall, this is the game I hoped for with longer loading times. It is a challenging game, but also a rewarding game. Don't get frustrated at your losses, learn from them ... and if you lose again tell yourself you can't win them all. Bury your warband, remember them and start a new one.
Good hunting amongst the damned !

Mordheim: City of the Damned isn't ready - Even for early access - plain and simple.
While everything looks promising, I would not recommend anyone purchase this game until it's either released as the full game, or some significant advancements are made with the game as is. Right now, it's a $30 demo with extreme loading times, and most elements of the game missing - which might be forgivable outside of the fact that those elements are what would make the game worth investing any time in to at all right now.
When I say extreme loading times, we are talking 3-5 minutes for a skirmish vs. A.I.
The core components of the game are looking promising, but the camera clips constantly through the scenery, often placing the camera awkwardly below the ground behind your current unit during an attack. The U.I. is in desperate need of some revisions. Attribute checks, for example, are identified on one end of the screen, and display the result on the far end of the screen. This is poor design and should be a unified element in the center of the screen tying the attribute check directly to it's result. a tip should also be included to explain what a failure or success means - this feature should be enabled by default, but allow veteran players to turn it off to reduce screen clutter. This might seem a bit strange to say, but this game is so obsessed with hiding things from obvious view that it's overly streamlined.
That said, if you turn on everything, it's certainly a lot of info so there is a balance to be struck, but the radial menu feels pretty good to use and would be where I would focus my attentions as the UI designer.
The map needs work also. Getting the cursor over an element should identify that element - as is, the strategic value of the map is very dependant on how well you know each and every icon. Memorizing icons is not an edge which should exist.
The lack of game modes is pretty egregious for a game they are asking $30 for - certainly it's understood that this is a game in Beta/Early Access, but as is, this is not a game experience, it's a demo that isn't worth playing in it's current state.
The graphics are fine, but the models require some level of enhancement, especially on the highest settings. The rat ogre, upon whom I seem to get focused during opponent actions, is quite disappointingly rendered. There is no separation on the large front teeth, the fur and skin textures are flat and outside of the life you see in the armour, everything looks pretty dull.
It's not all bad, of course. The game play is pretty spot on (even with the UI deserving a bit of a reworking) and the strategy of the game has been captured well in this digital interpretation. The movement of the Skaven is well animated, and the management/advancement element of the game which is only implemented in a skin-deep "level your warband to 10 immediately" demonstation, does look like it's going to do the job well and fulfill the needs of the Mordheim fans to level their warband up and craft it in their own unique ways.
Long story short, pop this promising game on your follow or wishlist and wait for quite a few patches and updates before you throw any money down on it. Based on potential, this game is highly recommended for a future purchase. For early access, I would say skip this offering and find something that will give you a little more return on your investment.

My nostalgia got ruined by playing this game again. I first played it back when it came out in early 2005, and I remembered the game all of these years and decided to get it again, with all of the BiA games.
It turns out that this situation is where the nostalgia was better than the actual game (to be honest, that doesn't actually occur as often as people think it does). Back when I first played it, I was a big WW2 game buff, way more than I am now. I think that's the biggest reason why I had such good memories of it.
But later that year, Call of Duty 2 came out, and looking back (and even looking at right now, since I've played CoD 2 again recently), that game is much better. Out of all of the WW2 games that I've played (and played again recently), I have to say that BiA: Road to Hill 30 has disappointed me now. I loved the Medal of Honor and Call of Duty series about 2007 or 2008 and before. I do NOT like the CoD or MoH series after those years.
My favorites are Call of Duty 2, Medal of Honor: Allied Assault, and Call of Duty: World at War. Turns out that I enjoy all of them more than I do this game.
To go into more detail on the game itself, I mostly remembered the characters and what happens, who dies. The game is known for being very historically accurate and also based on real people, but other games are very historically accurate as well. The game is often compared to Band of Brothers, but after having replayed BiA, I would rather watch or read Band of Brothers than play it. Gameplay-wise, the mechanics are rather bad, really, especially in comparison to other games released at the time, especially of CoD 2 which was the exact same year. I snuck up behind soldiers many times in the game and shot them in the face, and they didn't die. Some soldiers I shot point-blank about 5 times before they died.
I can't tell if the mechanics are just from running it on a modern machine or not. I was able to run on Windows 8.1 with no problem whatsoever, no extra installations or settings needed. I also downloaded the popular group of mods for the game, which you can find the forums easily. I would recommend them if you do play.
But honestly, the only thing that struck me was the cutscenes of the characters dying, because I remembered them dying the exact same way. Those scenes stuck with me, because you are with the same people the whole game, mostly. But in terms of the overall environment or progression through the game, it actually didn't feel as life-like as some of the other better WW2 games.
It turns out that my own nostalgia overrated the game.

I'm recommending this game, but keep in mind that there are glaring issues with it at the moment. The servers are down pretty often (I'm in the U.S, I've heard the situation is worse in other regions), the game has a long progression system yet saves are only kept on your computer, there's a higher chance of hackers because they can easily edit those saves without a server check, and there's not much of an endgame besides the 1v1 arena (but they have confirmed they will be adding free content later on). The developers interact with the community a lot and have been promising they are working on these issues, so I'll probably edit this review as they get fixed.
Despite those problems, this is easily one of my favorite fighting games now. I still had a great time fighting NPCs when the servers were down, and once I got to test myself against actual players the combat became even more satisfying. I'm not going to give an in-depth overview of the mechanics since other people have done it a lot better than I could, but I just wanted to add to the praise of this game. It was made by a small team but the combat system has more polish than anything I've seen in a long time.

If you like pvp fighting games with good mechanics, balance, complexity, and ease to grasp on a basic level then this game is for you.  If you want a long and satisfying singleplayer experience then don't buy this game.  Content will also be released for free in the future and the Devs have been quick to respond to bugs/server lag issues considering their small size.  Not only am I having fun with the game, I feel good supporting SloClap.  I recommend this game.

I was having a good time, playing the game and slowly learning the mechanics until it slowly started to move towards frustrating. The main "difficulty" in Kingdom: New Lands is that it's a race against the clock. The downside to this is that it doesn't outright tell you, and lets you keep going after you've gone past the time. Winter comes, and slowly erodes your economy and wittles away your resources. This would have been fine, if, especially for a newer player, it wouldn't be so easy to keep playing a doomed run for several hours before realizing you're not supposed to survive this.
Browsing the Steam user forums, I found out the developer made statements saying winter is supposed to end your run. I don't mind perma-death mechanics. But I do mind a game requiring lots of restarts dooming you without you knowing and letting you continue that way for several hours. There's one thing in not telling players information and letting them learn for themselves, but being entirely obtuse to the point you can't know about this with just in-game information is absurd. Even if the run is supposed to end at winter as a state of failure, the game doesn't communicate this in any meaningful way to a point people struggled their way to keep playing through it anyway, despite it being entirely against the function of the game.
I dunno, after struggling through one winter I'm just soured on a game treating me like this entirely. Most of my favorite games on Steam have perma-death and require you to experience things to understand the concept fully, so that in itself is not a problem. But they also function as intended, and I don't get the feeling this game does that.

I got this game as part of the Humble Bundle monthly.
Although I like the underlying premise of the game, some of the game mechanics make it terribly frustrating to play. If you have a single bad night, it can take weeks to recover. This was true of Kingdom: Classic as well, but the addition of a winter mechanic that negates your farmers means that if you have a bad night during winter, you might as well quit and restart. Also, since the daily money chest is now a merchant you have to send (pointless busywork that adds no enjoyment to the game), if you forget to send the merchant during winter and run out of money, there's literally nothing you can do but restart or sit there and wait for winter to end.
As mentioned in other reviews, combined with poor AI (archers that run into a crowd of baddies in the middle of the night trying to repopulate towers, construction workers that just saunter towards home at dusk or stand just outside protective walls) it makes this game an exercise in frustration.
It's a shame, as I feel the basic idea of the game is a good one, but the mechanics need some work and winter needs to go. I would not currently recommend this game at any price point. The previous Kingdom: Classic is OK, but only worth it at a steep discount.

Ah, Kinetic Void. What can I say about this beauty? For starters, the ship building is easy to use an monumentally powerful. While I have encountered some games that give you about 20 pieces and 20 spots to put them, Kinetic Void's ship builder truly lets you build whatever you want. If you don't like using the node system to place pieces, there is a freehand mode that lets you put anything anywhere. There are tons of pieces and all are resizable. On the largest setting, the pieces are insanely massive, and the more creative will find many pieces to build full size replicas of some of sci-fi's most famous ships. But this game isn't just space ship builder simulator. It has an incredibly well made space exploration portion. The ships to show their size quite well, as maneuvering a giant capital ship take much longer than a small agile fighter. There are tons of weapons of different damages and types and there are also preset ships for new players to use. In conclusion, Kinetic Void is an absolute masterpiece and I cannot reccomend it more.

Echoed World is a very interesting game with a very interesting story. Its gameplay reminds me of games such as Limbo, a 2D-meets-3D, story-driven adventure in which the plot unfolds itself before you. The narration is strong and the game manages to establish a world of power and magic that's deeply intriguing and captivating. The art style is a mix of dark and light, with a magical essence pervading through the world you explore. The transition from level to level, with blackness enveloping your screen from the foreground, is both immersive and calm on the eyes. The game is comfortable.
While the art style is an enjoyable aspect of Echoed World, the way in which it displays itself and its story is quite disappointing. Its script is very unnatural, possibly written by someone who doesn't have English as a first language - I picked up on Indian? Itts captions are, likewise, a minefield of typos and unfitting words and improper turn of phrase. The game's animations and character rendering are another downfall, with the main character's avatar being a lump of shaped pink plasticine; scarily badly rendered and unpolished. At times, the narration was quite overpowering, and I found it did not mix well with the calm ambience of the soundtrack. I can see that the soundtrack picked up at times to mirror the emphasis of the male narrator, but it was too little and didn't sync very well.
I fell on spikes and the game froze up in a black screen. I restarted the level and got stuck on a bouncing pad. I feel this game could use some time in Beta, or perhaps apply a quality assurance period to your future games. Echoed World is brisking the line of unplayable.

is a fairly short 1st person, on rails game. You play the part of an unnamed toddler who is accompanied by his best friend. While this game is on rails, it does allow to explore the game world quite a bit. The game is simple to play, yet provides a bit of a challenge by the way of puzzles and interactive items. The store page has
as one of the tags for this game. I would categorise it along the lines of being "heart pounding inducing". There is no blood, no guts, no real violence, but it's still enough to get the heart rate up.
*
*
In
, you play as a small toddler who wakes up in the middle of the night. Accompanied only by a teddy bear, you must brave the monster filled darkness to find the source of True Comfort - your mother.
The game is in 3D first person view and (I believe) is Oculus Rift supported (though you don't need it in order to play). The in world graphics have been beautifully rendered, with a lot of the items you find throughout the game interactable, allowing you to pick up, throw, push, and pull almost everything in the game. Well, everything that a one year old would be able to handle that is.
Another huge plus for this game is its haunting music and sound effects. They're really well done, to the point where I cringed every time I accidentally broke glass objects while exploring the world.

is not very long at all. Saying that, the plot is done so well that it doesn't need to be long. Indeed, my opinion is if the game was any longer, it would actually be to the games detriment. You don't always need a game to last for hours on end. Often, short and sweet drives the point of the story home more than long and drawn out ever could.
Unless you want to go for 100% achievements or want to speed run the game after leisurely playing it through the first time, there really isn't any replayability to this game.
Overall,
is a short game with a really deep story. I highly recommend this game for that alone. The superb graphics and unforgetable music are just icing on cake, really.

Very nice horror game with truly eerie atmosphere. The music, the suspense, the gore, and the supernatural elements blend well. Being trapped in a dark house with limited ammo and sometimes completely defenseless is way scarier than in the open with big guns. It's a survival horror after all. Sometimes you can simply hide and wait out instead of fighting the enemies. A radical departure and major step-up from RE5 and RE6's action-packed shooter. Also, I have to admit I had some doubt about the first-person perspective (not a big fan of), but it works really well in RE7.
Nicely combines elements from other titles, like the safe room (Evil Within), fungus infection (Last of Us), "molded" (crawler, puker, slasher) (Dead Space), with RE signatures like quick turn, herbs (no red herb this time though...).
To challenge yourself, I recommend turning off the HUD, which makes it much more realistic but way harder: finding ammo requires sharp perception, and sometimes I even missed key items because they are not glowing like in other games other hinted with the arrow. I looped around forever in the ship until I found out what I missed.

Empire Total War is a great Strategy game. I've been playing this game for many years now and still believe it to be one of the better games in the Total War series.
Whilst it lacks the political or economic fidelity of later Total War games such as Rome II (which itself has it's own problems I won't elaborate on), or the direct focus on real time military strategy like its successor Napoleon Total War, Empire Total War manages to expertly balance both the turn based and real time strategy the Total War franchise is loved for.
This is not to say the game is flawless. Glitches in the real time battles do occur and can be frustrating, especially I've found with defending during sieges. Likewise the AI don't necessarily play smarter at high difficulties, but seem to instead just be immediately more aggresive and gang up on you at the start of the game, which can make playing a smaller nation that plays the long game as opposed to early expansion (i.e. the Dutch) quite frustrating.
However in the grand scheme of Empire Total War these complaints are relatively minor. Not many games are truly dictated solely by a players ambition, but Empire is one of those games. If you're bold enough and have the strategic and fiscal skills to back it up you can take a smaller empire like the Dutch or Marathans and forge an empire, and having my Polish Hussars spreading out to the Americas and India after crushing the European powers was a nice bit of irony compared to real historical events. It's nice to be able to set your mind to doing something unexpected and, whilst being challenged, be motivated to finish it off regardless of the absurd amount of time it will take due to how much fun you're legitimatly having.
Empire Total War is an awesome game and I would gladly recommend it to any gamer out there who simply wants to set their mind to something and do it however ridiculous it may seem.

Picked it up today and haven't stopped playing it all day. It is definitely in early release stage but by far one of the better early release games on steam. At this point it's more playable than most fully released games!
Being a big fan of the Warhammer series from everything to lore and the table top (both Warhammer fantasy and 40k) I was really excited when I first discovered this a while back. Most of the games made with Games Workshop are usually the 40k space marine type or Dawn of War. This was obviously a delight because it looked like a “real” attempt at the fantasy style instead.
I was a bit hesitant to pick it up at first mainly because of the bad wrap on early releases lately and from everything I read it was meant for a console and was still pretty rough for PC users. As I watched it though it went from “mixed reviews” to “Mostly positive” the developers were releasing some awesome new content and watching some game play on youtube it looked like it might actually become a real game instead of another early release disappointment (here's looking at you Day Z).
The game play itself is pretty solid. You have the 4 factions all of which are pretty balanced and at this point pretty simple. At this point in the game you really on have the tutorials (4 of them which really do cover all the game and take less than an hour) and skirmish. You create a map and choose the opposing faction if it's against AI or you can randomly pair with another person for some PVP. The unique thing I liked about setting up the game were the vast options for starting locations or scenarios. For example you can can do standard set up (both teams start at opposite corners) you can do Ambush (one team starts all inside a building and the opposing team is surrounding the building) Fog of War (Both teams are completely scattered across the map) and the list goes on and on. The maps even at this point are impressive and I love that they randomly generate so you hardly ever get the same map twice.
The combat is pretty simple which might be a down point for some, but personally I enjoyed I. It keeps the game play fast and allows you to focus on other strategy rather than micro managing each character during their turn. You basically have two types of points for each unit Strategy Points and Offense Points (SP and OP respectively) your SP points allow for movement and your OP allow for combat which you can see pretty decently in the game play video. Depending on the skills or spells your unit has you are allowed to cycle through your available options each turn  by hitting Q or E. This helps make the combat smooth and quick. Most of the strategy is in placement of troops and sight. Much like in the tabletop game the first few turns are setting up your units in defensible areas or in getting the enemy in line of sight. This may seem tedious for those who want action but it is incredibly fun to run around as an Ogre or Cultish Wizard looking for positions of advantage.
Outside of the match you do have the option to micro manage your troops which was also fun from a looting, leveling, and buffing standpoint. You can customize your squad with gear which can be looted from battles and eventually purchased, you can spend points and level skills, spells, or abilities, and you can enchant your weaponry (Hammer of Sigmar +5 awesomeness). This makes you invested in your war band but keep in mind this game also has perma-death so don't get super attached to your beloved hero.
Some awesome things that stand out:
The overlord view during a match that allows you to plan and scope the whole map was really a cool idea and works very well.
In game log for all actions so you can see why you missed that hit or miscast a spell.
Dark fantasy art and feel is seriously awesome as hell. They did a fricken epic job making Mordheim seem like a city of dark magic corrupted by chaos.
Lore (though limited) is all accurate and pretty intriguing. It will be appreciated by fans of the genre and at the same time new players won't be confused or lost without background.

You can carry two primary weapons, one secondary, lots of other equipment, and also loot the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s you kill. Buildings are destructible. Missions are your typical war game missions, what would you expect? Eliminate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, blow up radars and things that pose a threat to friendly vehicles, secure a place and hold it, etc. Occasional stealth, too.
There's not much weapon variety, but most of them have several variants with different attachements. I guess that's something that makes up for it.
Story is pretty average, but I'm OK with that.
AI is stupid, as with any game. Sometimes radio lines are not heard (but show in the subtitles). Sprint speed is pretty pointless as there's barely any difference from the normal speed. Sometimes enemies take about 15 rounds (half a mag for most weapons) to take out, even at point blank. This seems to be random, as sometimes I kill enemies with a single shot on the foot. In short, not the best there is, but not that bad. It's interesting. If you like war games that are a bit more realistic than usual, you should give it a shot.

I really enjoy this game so far. While I understand the points of the people who complain and dont recommend the game, I really dont understand how such small issues can make them not recommed it.
TL;DR: Dark Souls of the fighting genre.
THE GOOD PART:
Now, I feel that Im deep enough into the game to give out my thoughts finally. So far Im really enjoying because this game isnt your typical fighting or hack and slash game. At its core its a simple fighting game, that totally disgregards the simplicity with its unique combat and deck building. With deck buidling you can pick your own moves so its suits the way you wanna fight.
Yes, you can make your own combat deck and EVENTUALLY your combat style. That itself is amazing and the fact that you will never see a single player or an npc fight the same way just adds in more to the depth. What also makes this game really good is that its like Dark Souls. You are free to explore the each part of the world the way you want and you chose who to fight.
I must not forget that eventually when you feel confident with your deck, you can create your own school out of it and teach it to other players as well. Really cool system that I havent seen anywhere else.
The athmosphere is also really nice. Something about that lolenly, silent ambience really draws you into the game. The game itself is also very pretty and stylized which is what makes it pretty.
THE BAD PART:
Now, I understand why some people would complain about learning new moves. It can be hard as all you do is block and use your class ability, so it can get pretty hard.
This game also lacks music in some part, while the existing soundtrack is BEAUTIFUL, I cant help but think that this game needs some more music that can add to the lonelyness and intensity of the world.
There are also some issues with the servers as well. When someone enters the same area as you, I found my game chop a few times but then returned to normal. That should get fixed asap. I also had a problem 2 times when the 1v1 wouldnt load so I had to reopen the game.

In this game, you play as Erwin Lommer, a recent American recruit attending a prestigious military academy in the Akihabara district of Tokyo, Japan. When he shows up for his first day of "Tank School" he is surprised to learn that the students themselves are literal tanks who just-so happen to look exactly like Japanese schoolgirls (it makes about as much sense in context). Now Erwin must navigate the life of a Japanese high schooler all while being confused at his circumstances, but maybe he can also find love at this unusual school.
If you are reading this review, you are probably already aware of the fact that this is a parody game. Specifically, it is a parody of Japanese-style visual novels/dating simulators. Like in a visual novel, you make choices along the course of the story that dictates the player-character's relationship with the various characters in the game.
Being a parody, the main attraction here is the writing and humor. In this case, the humor is excellent. I found myself cracking up all the time playing this. The game itself contains parodies of the visual novel genre and anime in general. Many of the characters in the game are parodies of the usual anime clichés such as the yandere, the tsundere, the otaku, and so on. Not only that, but the military theme of the game contains many references to the tanks and events of World War II, giving the game even more of a variety of jokes. In addition, the Gunnery Sergeant Heartmann character was a hilarious parody of the similarly named character from the 1987 film
. The game never stops being aware of just how stupid and silly the entire concept is and, as such, never stops being funny right up until the end.
The other aspects of the game necessarily take a back seat to the humor, but it mostly works well. The sprites were well-drawn and distinctive. I also thought the music used was pretty good.
However, my only real criticism of this would be the interface. There is an option to skip text, but no separate option to skip only text that has already been read. Plus, the skipping does not include scene transitions which means a longer wait to get where I want to go. This was frustrating when I was trying to see all of the game's content. There is also no option to go back to previous text in case I missed a line. Plus, there was only five save slots which does not seem enough when trying to explore all of the game's routes.
I am not sure if this game is worth the full $9.99 asking price, but I was able to buy it on sale 50% off and I think I got my money's worth. If you are looking for some great laughs in a rather unconventional parody, look no further than this.

Although I like the underlying premise of the game, some of the game mechanics make it terribly frustrating to play. If you have a single bad night, it can take weeks to recover. This was true of Kingdom: Classic as well, but the addition of a winter mechanic that negates your farmers means that if you have a bad night during winter, you might as well quit and restart. Also, since the daily money chest is now a merchant you have to send (pointless busywork that adds no enjoyment to the game), if you forget to send the merchant during winter and run out of money, there's literally nothing you can do but restart or sit there and wait for winter to end.
As mentioned in other reviews, combined with poor AI (archers that run into a crowd of baddies in the middle of the night trying to repopulate towers, construction workers that just saunter towards home at dusk or stand just outside protective walls) it makes this game an exercise in frustration.
It's a shame, as I feel the basic idea of the game is a good one, but the mechanics need some work and winter needs to go. I would not currently recommend this game at any price point. The previous Kingdom: Classic is OK, but only worth it at a steep discount.

Great game for casual and hardcore gamers alike.
It's a mix between games like Starcraft and Dota / League of Legends.
You are given a Mech of which can transform between ground and air forms, both of which has it's own advantages/disadvantages and special uses. There are 9 different types of mechs in the game. All are specified for a certain playstyle and all have unique designs and stats. In addition, you are given control of a "Command Center" that allows you - on your command - to build infrantry and vehicles such as Tanks, turrets, etc. that will be vital to capture other outposts.
The AI oponenets themselves have varying degrees of difficulties, ensuring you the time to learn the mechanics in order to fully get into the game.
You can either play with other players, Ai or both in gametypes such as: Player(s) vs Ai, Player(s) vs Player(s) and so on.
Gamemodes include Skirmishes - standard battles to capture the most outpost and eliminate enemy command post(s) that you can play with the gametypes stated aove.
There is also a Survival mode of which you can play solo or online to up to 4 total players (including you).
As for the online community, from my experience, they have been generally helpful, willing to answer questions you may have.
For those worried about the "Free to Play" nature of the game, do not be alarmed. The game has a matchmaking system to prevents high level players from fighting low level players. There are also "Ultimate" equipment that can only be used on higher level games.
Overall, this is a fun game that anyone that likes games like Starcraft, Dota or robots (mechs) in general should atleast try out. Also, since it's free, there really in't anything to lose from trying it out.

Pretty good considering this is a student project. Show promise and combines story telling and level design. Overall it was pretty good but rough around the edges, as is to be expected. Things that these students need to work on (for their next project):
- better blend of characters and background. The backgrounds and objects have a 'hand painted' aestetic whereas the main character has a very smooth CGI appearance. These two styles don't blend well together.
- better character animation. The running animation is good, but when you turn around, bump into stuff, jump onto ledges and the character has to go from one animation to another, it looks very raw. the animation that is used when you're hanging on a ledges and flip yourself up look weird. He should either pull himself up or make a small jump.
- some near instant deaths. At some places you suddenly face an obstacle or enemy that you didn't expect which meant an instant death. Luckely the game autosaves and you don't have to redo much of the level, but there should be clear signs of oncoming danger. If this game was longer these kind of encounters would get very tiresome very quickly.
- puzzles are okay but also very standard. The giving life, taking life, pushing boulders onto buttons, I've seen it all before.
- the platforming is very standard as well, nothing really sets it apart from similar games.
The last two points are not important for this student project. But for a more elaborate game it will be important to think of some game mechanics that are more interesting. I see many people compare this to Ori and the blind forest. Which is a good example of a game that takes the platforming/metrovania genre into new directions and does this very well.
But all in all this game shows promise and it's very wise of these students to start with something small and get feedback from the gaming community before commiting themselves to a large project.

One of my favorite games, The story line is amazing, I can't stop playing this over and over.
Graphics - Especially for a 2010 game, the graphics are amazing, you can get some really amazing scenery in this, Not quite on the level of Skyrim, But looking over the map is very nice to do :)
Gameplay - The gameplay is very easy to get used to, from stealth missions to full out combat, this game gives you some brilliant gunfights, robberies, boss missions and car chases. The police evasion is a very tedius, but over all more fun method, Unlike games like GTA where, you loose the police and you can then drive past them with a car thats smashed up, covered in blood with bullet holes in it and they won't beat an eye, this game requires you to get your car fixed up, new plates added, and a change of clothes to get the police to not suspect anything next time they see you.
Controls - The controls are very nicely done, as far as combat is concerned, the aiming, the slow motion, everything is brilliant. Story - One of my favorite stories of all time, I can't really describe it, but you will have to play it to find out. Its a whole story of betrayal, emotion, sadness but at the same time, partying, trust, money. The story is a crazy mix of family life and gang life. The best way to describe it, is sort of on par with Breaking bad. A hardworking man taking up illegal tasks to help support his family.

Definitely a lot of potential here, a fantastically charcterful and good looking game, but I have some frustrations about it:
-Clipping on scenery is a pain. Sometimes it takes an unnecessary amount of walking to get around a corner. I've also had henchmen get inside a building, then not be able to get back out, as there was a slight clipping issue with a piece of scenery (rubble) just inside the door.
-Warbands look superficially different, but statistically behave almost identically in battle, there is very little differentiating between the different troop types and playstyles, even having a massive two handed weapon has the same effect as having a weapon in each hand.
-AI tends to rout a bit too easily, meaning you dont get to loot their wagon or corpses (although I believe you will be getting access to all the remaining map loot in the full campaign).
-Magic and missile weapons are a bit underwhelming, considering the extra effort to use them effectively.
Some of these gripes are bugs that will (hopefully) be ironed out by release, but some are game mechanics which make the game less interesting to me. I still think it's a fun game with a lot going for it, and a lot of potential to be even better, and recommend giving it a go.

The game is early access (<--means the game isn´t close to be finished yet, so if you want to buy the game, be sure to do it to support the development and not really to play a finished game) and its very clear, that there is still much more work to be done. In this "Early Access Review", I will focus on what the game currently has and not what it currently lacks.
-The graphics are quite nice and the character models look like the tabletop figures i know and love from my Warhammer Army.
-When you built your Warband you can choose their weapons, the abilities and uprade certain qualities like strength/intelligence/initiative etc., name them/change the name of your warband,   adjust their looks.
-Skirmish Mode: You fight against human enemies or CPU and you are able to determine the starting conditions of the game (like: all troops in one place or spread all over the map/the winning conditions etc.), however you are not able to choose what CPU army you want to fight, so if you want to fight a specific CPU army you need to make a private lobby and click on the CPU button till you have the enemy of your choice.
The game is turn-based, in your turn you...:
however there are no phases like in the Warhammer tabletop game, so you have more freedom in what to do when you wanna do it.
-The Campaign mode is now in the game (it´s the main game focus): In this mode you built your Warband from the ground up, equip their weapons etc., then you choose one of the 2 randomly generated missions, you earn experience, you can loot dead enemies to find new weapons etc. After you finish your mission, you have to pay your soldiers and pay the treatment of their wounds. However if one of your soldiers needs treatment, you can´t use him for a period of time (4 days for example), which can really f**** up your Warband, so you need to play very carefully. Your main objective is to smuggle a certain weight of your warpstone out of Mordheim to your contractee, you earn warpstone by winning missions, but you have only some days to gather enough warpstone for the next shipment. You can go to the shop to purchase armor, weapons and potions etc. for gold. When you are done end your day by clicking on a tent, your warriors will lern skills and the treatment days for the injured will reduce by 1. Then you go on your next missions, or a story mission, that has different objectives and conditions.
-The CPU is challening, but combat against other players is much harder.
-The game costs plenty of money in early access and it will even become more expensive after early access. Maybe because the Warhammer license is really pricey, but however it limits the people who will buy the game strictly, because no one who doesn´t love the Warhammer universe  will buy this game. (<--At least that are the reactions, that I saw when talking and reading about the game).
-The tutorials are only battles with text sometimes and you can´t just read the text in an extra menu (<--Might be improved in the future)
-
-Although the game is still in Early Access, it seems nearly finished and progressed in the right direction.
[I´m German and only made the review in english because the whole game is in english, so there is the possibility of grammatical errors in this review]

Let me make this clear. This game is by no means finished. I would recommend waiting until it is a little further along in development before purchasing straight away.
With that out of the way let's begin. Mordheim City of the Damned is the electronic and spiritual successor to the tabletop franchise that spawned out of Games Workshop's very own tabletop world of fantasy Warhammer. You take control of a band of warriors and proceed to try and outwit and eviscerate your opponent.
The gameplay is a nice blend of a turn-based RPG with elements from the tabletop game itself. In my opinion this is the game Relic should have been making for the Warhammer franchise all this time. And once it is finally completed it will be a real gem. There is talk of adding more warbands, adding to the original four. These new bands will supposedly include Undead, Dwarves and Elves.
This game has tons of potential, and once all these features which are currently locked in game start working, it will get even better. Plus who doesn't enjoy watching their Commander fall flat on their♥♥♥♥♥from trying to climb a 6ft wall.

I'm kind of upset that the second video says "campaign features blah blah blah" and then I buy the game and the campaign still says coming soon. I'll change my rating when the game is more fleshed out.
edit: I am 100% for Mordheim and know this will be an amazing game in the future. I was sincerely surprised that the video mentioned a campaign that wasn't there and my review ONLY reflects that I would not normally buy or recommend a game in this state (Random battles only, practically no customization, no leveling, no story). I am looking forward to turning my no into a yes in the near future, specifically when warband management comes into play and also the campaign. Only buy this game now if you're ok with random battles that have no effect on your warband.

I've put enough time into this game to know almost everything about it... until I gave up on it. 429 hours of play, most worth the investment.
I'll start with pre-parity patch and move up to the last time I played.
I started playing years ago, and the gameplay was frighteneing and suprising at every virtual corner. I grew accustomed to the players being so varied and the permutations of guns being as numerous as stars in the sky. Everyone had a different build, and 95% of them were usable to some extent. After playing daily for 6 months, I had found a niche between mid-long range pseudo-sniping and CQC. The number of attachemnts was only dwarfed by the precision of tuning you could do with them. The game mechanics were as solid as bedrock, and the weapon stat balance was as good as the orbit of planets around our sun. There were ~5 attachments that were purely drawbacks, and 1000s of others that made the gun different, but not better or worse.
Then came Parity.
This patch was by the original devs, who had signed away the game long ago and then came back. Everyone was excited, and they were adding new functions to the game and shaking it up. When the patch arrived, I likely had 400 of my 429 hours logged. Parity took everything about the game, and threw it away. It was a port of the PS4 version to PC, and it was terrible. The guns with the strongest recoil (LMG) were like staplers, with everything else being a laser pointer (as shaky as your controlling hand). Weapon balance was thrown off to the point that it was a joke.
I put in 29 more hours trying to convince myself it was still good, to no avail. I started seeing the same people in 2 of 3 matches I played. Pre-parity players were like gods to new players, since the currency was HEAVILY skewed toward pay-2-win.
This game was "THE BEST FPS" I had played, pre-parity. It used to stand out like someone who played S.T.A.L.K.E.R. playing Battlefield (literally hunting down players and destroying them unseen). Now, this game is like Call of Duty for Wii.
Here's a TLDR:
Game was fantastic, diverse, impressive.
Parity patch arrived-made game a bad console port
Game now stinks like a corpse after a few months.

It's a really neat idea and a unique experience that's overall a good, relaxing game. However, I absolutely cannot recommend because the entire thing is overshadowed by the horrendous winter system. Not only does it essentially remove all income (i.e. your ability to play the damn game), but lasts significantly longer than the time inbetween winters.
It's a mechanic so obscene that I had to double check that this wasn't still in Early Access. It would be one thing for the winters to be brutal and short, or last as long as they do and just apply some pressure to your income. If you just AFK when winter rolls around, the end result will nearly be the same because youre not allowed to do anything in the meantime anyway.
Quite the shame. It was really quite fun up until that point.
Second Opinion: I gave the game another chance only to be reminded that it's still a title that never really left Early Access. Even if you just consider winter to be an implicit "You lose" screen, the fact is that you have no control over which side your people go to. So hypothetically, if you were to have just cleared the portals from one side and turn all your new recruits into archers, only to watch them all flock to the wrong side and throw the game away at no fault of your own isn't just awful design, it's a bad gameplay experience.
Fortunately things like this can be easily added into the game later on, however since the devs are producing content now it suggests that they're not interested in changing that part of the base game.

A fun diversion, but I would not suggest it to others. There are too many ways the game will seemingly arbitrarily choose to leave you high and dry, and in ways that aren't readily apparent.

Well this game isn't bad and should be played.
Based on a true story, set during the famous airdrop before the invasion at Normandy, where Sgt. Matt Baker and his squad of 101st Airborne Paratroopers are scattered over the French countryside.
There are 20 chapters to play through and with the action and story, you'll really want to know whats going to happen next.
Controls are easy enough for anyone who has played FPS on PC but it does have a little bit a getting used to. Why? Because player not only controlling Baker, but the squad thats with him. Player control two fire teams and can place one team to place covering and suppressing fire while Baker and the other team flanks the enemies. The game does have a tutorial build in so that player can learn to lead their brothers to victory.
Music in game is the pretty standard fare of orchestral but the sound FX of the gun fire and squad members yelling at the player were so life like and is really immersive.
The game just looks great as every house, plant and character are all textured wonderfully and bring the game a gritty realistic feel.
The only draw back is that the team AI isn't smart enough sometimes and continually says that they can't see or shoot a target and don't move to get a better shot and sometimes gets shot and dies so the strategy part is mandatory most of the time.
Really the game is fast, furious and a blast to play and the story is compelling to continue to the end.

I honestly don't get everyone going on about how amazing this game is, particularily how realistic it is.. because it's far, far from it. If you're looking for a realistic WWII shooter, don't even touch this game.
Sometimes this game is easy.. but when it's hard, it's what I call "artificial difficulty". That is, difficulty due to poorly implimented and/or repetative actions, or difficulty due to bad design.
The checkpoint save system is annoying. It doesn't add challenge to the game. It forces you to re-do the same easy, mundane parts over and over to get past the one odd difficult part. I just spent 10 minutes taking on a pair of Panzer IVs. Tanks in this game are a joke.. find rocket, shoot it ad infinum until it blows up. A Panzer IV should be shredded by a single Panzerfaust. I wouldn't have an issue with the liberties taken here if I could see a point to it, but there isn't any. It isn't "difficult" getting rid of tanks, just time consuming (once you get your squad somewhere where they won't get mowed down). After I killed the one tank, another appears. Wash, rinse, repeat. Then a squadmate kills me with a grenade. Thanks, bro. Checkpoint? 10+ minutes earlier before I dispatched the tanks. That's not difficulty. That's not a challenge. That's tedious. And moments like that happen numerous times throughout the game. Actually, come to think of it, this game is very repetative overall. Every chapter plays out almost the exact same way with slightly different scenary.
The small maps are atrocious. This game is suppose to be about maneuver and flanking, yet many, many times the maps design is such that it feels like a railed cover shooter more than anything else. Your squad AI is so stupid you end up spending more time babysitting them to make sure they don't do something dumb and get killed than actually PLAYING the game. Many of the maps are too small to actually maneuver realistically, and winning becomes a matter of "gamey" tactics. If you want a game with tactics, play Combat Mission.
And the story? Uh.. what story? Maybe it's because I've actually read Band of Brother by Ambrose I'm finding this game incredebly light on the story. I don't give a hoot about any of the characters. Nothing makes me want to like them. If you want the story of the 101st in Europe, go read the book or watch the movies. They're both more entertaining and much heavier on the story than this game.
I can forgive the issues I have with the game because of the technology at the time it was developed. But frankly this just isn't that good of a game. I think a lot of people let the content simply colour their ratings.

Let's just start this off with one simple statement: This game is a joke.
Now, although this game does have a good amount of content and can be replayed (Though only if you're with a few friends and can find some fun tactics to try) somewhat for at least 50 or 60 hours. After that and you're probably going to want to invest in their "VIP system..." Which just seems to be ever so slowly growing so that this game is less and less of a free to play and more of a, "Free to try some of the content." game.
I started playing this game quite some time ago, and although I can't say I'm the most experienced player, I have had the chance of seeing this game grow, change, and (d)evolve. It started as a rather unique game with a good basis and a lot of potential. Updates rolled through occasionally bringing new content, maps, features, etc. and the community grew rather well. And much like many games, everything changed
when development seemed to slow to a halt. Now the game was much more cosmetic driven and it seemed to simply be held together by a few regular players, the newbies that flowed in at a constant rate, and the seasonal items- which was really the only "content" added.
From here the game shifted... as I said, from a nice game that some people would play and toss, having had their fun, and others would find much joy into something much worse. It became a pay-gate game. Slowly features left, like the market listings and ability to sell your
loot for a few measly diamonds (The in-game common currency that has a oh so familiar real world transaction rate) or market chats, etc.. There were levels of VIP too, bronze, silver, gold, and diamond. Obviously paying more meant you got a better rank (Going up as appeared), allowing you to gain wonderful bonuses, like increased funds from games, more experience, and access to useful features like the market.
So where does this leave us? Well, ever so intelligent me gave in after putting what felt like many, many hours into the game and having a lot of fun, though the magic was lost and I was losing interest, I decided I would put down my fifteen dollars during the winter sale and get silver VIP and unlock these cool features. Originally I was on the fence, but upon seeing that
would I get diamonds, market chat, market listings, better plots (A cheap gimmick that deserves to be in a mobile game, though that's not what I'm here to discuss.) among other things, and the cherry on top, the tipping point for my decision, an incredible all access map editor and creator. So I slapped my money down and felt good about my purchase.
I worked on and off on multiple maps, finally ending up with one super map that I intended to be incredible. A map that would rival any other map that had been created by devs or fans in size and quality... With this new dream map in mind I set off to create it, working as much as possible, when time allowed. During this game I noticed more and more things shift towards this "VIP" experience and saw more and more things fall off the "F2P" model.
And here we are, as of writing this, I logged into Airmech fully excited to work on my map now that school finals were over and I could return to my glorious map that was nearing completion. I clicked towards the map make, paused deciding first to check the store as I noticed an update had released recently changing and adding some things. Nothing new, not at least in the
content section. Nothing that added gameplay value or made me want to terribly come back. But none the less I checked and curiously noticed that there was a plot item for map creation (That I had already purchased) to my surprise and it said I needed Diamond VIP for access. Concerned I navigated over to the map creation section and
it was gone. The only thing I cared about in this utterly trash game that the devs seem to be driving into the ground for the sole goal of making money, no matter how much it screws their fanbase (Who has already payed for this game, though they- I - Probably shouldn't have.) over.
So I guess what I'm trying to say is, don't expect anything out of this game. Don't pay money unless you are 100%, absolutely, without a doubt, convinced that you will be playing this game for ages, putting down hours on hours consistently. Make sure you are willing to pay for diamond VIP and that you are willing to have everything you
payed for taken away at a moments notice. If not, then sure play the game but keep in mind what I have said and you'll do find. That's all then, it's a mediocre game with failed potential and a dying fan base and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ developers.

...ONLY if you can get it for the right price.  As others have been saying, this game is quite short.  I myself beat it - with the DLC - in less than 5 hours.  And unfortunatley, there's not a lot of replay value.  It's barely worth $10, let alone $20.  I was lucky enough to get it for $5 during the Steam summer sale.
That said however, this game is quite clever.  It's unique in its approach to the horror genre, and it touches upon themes that I haven't seen any other game do.  I give the developers major credit for that one!  The storyline is unique and quite emotional, especially toward the end.   I had to take a moment and think about what was really going on, but when I did, I said to myself "man, that is heavy!"
As far as gameplay itself, the levels are not very challening, but they are fun (which is what counts).   However, I almost put the game down because through most of the beginning, there's no real threat to you.  Scary games aren't nearly as scary if you can't fail or die, and it looked like that at first.  Without saying too much though, that does change later on, and I was happy to see it.
In summation, I DO recommend this game, but try to get it on sale if you can (unless money is no issue to you, which in that case, go for it).

Echoed World is more of a short concept of a game made by students than a complete experience. It barely stands on its own and still lacks a lot of everything, especially polish and more fleshed out mechanics. However, for what the intentions are, as stated in the description, it's overall idea holds promise.
The fairy-tale background graphics are quite beautifully drawn. But every moving thing sticks out like a cardboard cut-out due to the rather stiff and sometimes glitchy animations. The narrator's voice is surprisingly good and fitting, only the mastering of the sound in general except for the background music seems to be lacking here and there.
The story is little more than a basic idea and barely goes beyond what is presented in the opening exposition. Nevertheless, it ties in with the gameplay, despite its limitation and offers a potential basis to further the narrative. Yet the ending comes quite abruptly and leaves the player stumped.
Echoed World's gameplay doesn't deviate from tried and tested puzzle platformer mechanics or level design. However, there's enough game shown here to build upon. It's certainly worth a try for curious players with contained expectations regarding the game's overall execution though.

Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood is the start of the downward spiral for the Call of Juarez series before Gunslinger pretty much singlehandedly saved the entire franchise. It's less fun than the first game even although it features a character choice between either of the McCall brothers for added replayability value. The thing is though, that gameplay isn't as fun, duels aren't as fun and the game actually looks slightly worse than the first game regarding texture quality, although I have no idea how they managed to do that.
Dualwield pistols were a lot better in the original game. Both the feel and the mechanic to pick them up, to be able to assign weapons to either hand manually instead of automatically, the way concentration mode worked, the bible mechanic, the refreshing stealth levels with Billy, all the things you could do with the whip, the bow handling and the extreme fun of riding on a horse which was completely cut from the second game.
I liked Bound in Blood and it has more replayability than the original, but the original is better in most elements in my personal opinion. I liked the art, sound and level design more than in Bound in Blood as well. The writing of McCall was better too.
In the end it comes down to opinion, but Call of Juarez was amazing when it came out, Bound in Blood was partially more of the same and instead of improving and evolving features, they devolved in an attempt to streamline the gameplay to be able to target a broader audience. Therefore, even while it technically can be enjoyed, I don't deem it to be recommendable.

Looks to have potential. I am excited about playing this game as of Sept. 27 2015. It has a very good feel to it. Like playing one of the Games Workshop minature tabletop games. You can change a ton of bits on each model and paint it several different colors and schemes. The game is almost like the table top game as well with the item selections, the spells, skills, attributes, and perks all adjustable and customizeable.
There is now progression and consequences, in my first battle my hero was surrounded and defeated, in the after action report it was revealed that the hero had been mortally wounded and lost an arm. The model was forever afterwards missing a limb and could not hold a shield anymore. There are objectives during combat and the AI isn't terrible at ganging up on you and isolating single units. (not certain at this time if the AI will complete objectives of it's own or if it has them) but the game has a sense of RPG to it now.
Money well spent as the developer keeps pushing out new content and seems to be working on something that could be unique in the Games Workshop videogames; a digital version of the table top game. 4 races at this time and hoping to see undead, orks, and elves, but a very solid game at this point with most bugs stompped out regularly as they creep up. I would recommend this game to any GW fans of the old mordheim and inquisitor games.

Crytek is a developer that knows how to create near perfect first person shooters. Far Cry is another of those examples from their repertoire. This is some great, solid stuff, despite the bugs and glitches. A game to remember. Far Cry is hard. A true challenge even at the easier difficulty settings. Performance is an issue even for today's hardware standards. The game seems to need a fresh system restart to run at its full potential. There are plenty of bugs and glitches. Some were so major that I was forced to reload a save point several times. The game engine and physics is different than most other games, and this takes a little getting used to. The main character's voice acting is pretty bad. Almost to the point of making it sound like a comedy. For whatever idiotic reason, the game alters the Windows audio settings to its liking without setting them back to their original state. This is extremely annoying. Staying in the subject of sound, do a Google search and you will see the massive amount of sound problems people experience in this game. To access the multiplayer portion of the game, one is forced to register and create an account with Ubisoft, which is absolutely ridiculous. The developers clearly reward players who specialize in stealth and skill shots rather than running and gunning. The atmosphere, mood, and setting are superb; providing a tense and exciting experience almost every second of the game. The tension you will experience is not often produced by other games at this same level. There are many parts where you will be spooked and surprised by what comes around the corner or appears suddenly. It is all done very well. Level design in this game is outstanding. The AI is good, and there is always a challenge. Far Cry is all thriller, no filler. It took me about 17 hours to complete.

Imagine my thumb pointed straight to the side for this one. The concept, atmosphere, and gameplay fundamentals are great - certain levels make you feel like you're seconds from being overwhelmed by German soldiers, and good art design helps distract you from the game's age.

When you make mistakes in leading your squad, your losses are earned, but when questionable level design and bad botpathing mean your squad gets chewed up because they go somewhere you never intended, it's just frustrating. The difficulty spikes you come up against aren't because the game's too hard, they're because you must play through a map where your squad's A.I. is plagued with bad pathfinding. In fact, I find the broader, more complicated maps are done very well, while the simpler, tighter maps will find your squad regularly running to the wrong side of a wall and getting cut to pieces. I like difficulty when it's part of the design. I don't like having to fight a game to make it work properly.
It's a phenomenal game when it works, but you'll come up against a few levels that so badly implement the gameplay that playing through turns from a joy into a chore.

Here's my review on "Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30".
As far as I know this is the first game of the series. You play as Sgt. Matt Baker, a troubled soldier that was never ready to lead men in combat. But as this was forced upon him on the night of 6th of June 1944 on D-Day. Throughout the game, you'll lead your men (everywhere from one man up to 3 men and a tank or 6-7 men) and defeat the German Warmachine in Normandy before you'll face the ultimate test of Hill 30.
I first played this game way back when it was on PS2 and one of the best shooters I had ever played. Now you kinda ought to have prior experience with this game in order to really enjoy it. Because, face it, the graphics are somewhat hard to look at with modern technology available.
The idea behind the game is rather simple: you're usually given 1 or 2 teams. You use them to overcome what the german forces might throw at you, that being normal infantry, AT-guns and MG's, mortars or tanks. It's all first person, except a tactical map you can check every now and then.
You use f.ex the fireteam to pin the enemy down and then flank with your assault team. (and yes, this game has a rather well done "suppressive fire"-system, which has come to be something BiA is known for.) It sounds very simple, but sometimes it can be a little tricky.
It has very outdated graphics, decent voiceacting (a little better in later games), very good soundeffects, excellent story/plot, but a little repetetive gameplay. Controlls are good.
So:
Graphics: 6/10 It's old, so give it some slack
Sounds: 8/10 Sometimes the voiceacting and dialogue are a little awkward
Gameplay: 7/10 A little repetetive, but challenging and brings a new factor to FPS' that's very rare. Try to suppress the NPC's in the campain on BF4 f.ex...
Controlls: 8/10 They're good enough. Twerk it to make it 100% the way you want it.
All in all: 7/10

Road to Hill 30 separates itself from most WW2 games by having interesting strategy-shooter mechanics, a tighter focus on a smaller theatre, and a good amount of writing that makes you feel for the characters and their situation. The main bulk of the gameplay consists of you ordering squads around so you can outfire and outmaneuver your enemy. There's a heavy focus on suppressing enemy squads so they can't return fire, then swinging your soldiers on to the flanks to finish them off.
The gameplay is challenging and engrossing, and allows the campaign to separate itself from games like CoD or MoH  by having long challenging missions that take place over realistically-sized engagement zones and against a reasonable amount of enemies. You won't be securing all of Stalingrad in eight minutes while mowing down three hundred Germans, but you'll feel even more satisfaction after liberating a small farmhouse from a defending Germany company.
Another unique thing about the game is the fact that its story, while hammy in spots, is pretty engaging. Soldiers have personalities and you feel for them once the squad starts taking casualties. It's not the best out there and there's some VERY obvious cut content, but it's good to see a war game have an actual engaging story with relatable characters.

It's a really neat idea and a unique experience that's overall a good, relaxing game. However, I absolutely cannot recommend because the entire thing is overshadowed by the horrendous winter system. Not only does it essentially remove all income (i.e. your ability to play the damn game), but lasts significantly longer than the time inbetween winters.
It's a mechanic so obscene that I had to double check that this wasn't still in Early Access. It would be one thing for the winters to be brutal and short, or last as long as they do and just apply some pressure to your income. If you just AFK when winter rolls around, the end result will nearly be the same because youre not allowed to do anything in the meantime anyway.
Quite the shame. It was really quite fun up until that point.
Second Opinion: I gave the game another chance only to be reminded that it's still a title that never really left Early Access. Even if you just consider winter to be an implicit "You lose" screen, the fact is that you have no control over which side your people go to. So hypothetically, if you were to have just cleared the portals from one side and turn all your new recruits into archers, only to watch them all flock to the wrong side and throw the game away at no fault of your own isn't just awful design, it's a bad gameplay experience.
Fortunately things like this can be easily added into the game later on, however since the devs are producing content now it suggests that they're not interested in changing that part of the base game.

You can use your Mech to harrass other units, or to carry yours straight to their base, or just to fire homing missiles at any enemy players you see.
Never mind that you can also get pet jetpack cats, Companion Cubes, flying trains, bombs, roasted turkeys, giant furry dice, bald eagles, fat bats, and cakes, or that you can play as a Gothic flying saucer which abducts enemy units.

So, I came into the store one day, and while I was looking through the gaming archives for a new passtime, this popped up. I looked at the reviews, they didn't turn out too bad, so I took an immediate interest due to the pictures and effective wording done by the game developers of how it works, and also because of its' high praise by other players. So I bought, and downloaded it.
After starting the game, a series of menus (the game played without much lag at all, it seems to be very effectively coded) that brought me to the ship creation menu. The whole thing was obviously still in development, as is the whole game, so I wasn't fazed. So far, it seems to have a solid menu system, and I love and hope that they try to make a little more sense of the icons, numbers, subsystems and such, because it wasn't all clear as to what they did, or meant, or how they affected the ship.
So, after a few minutes of confused silence, I decided to choose one of the pre-made ships, and set off on my journey through space.
I had fun. The distances were ridiculous, and the slip-space mechanic was a bit underdeveloped, but hey, it's a still-in-progress. What do you expect?
Then I went into the fighting mode, in which I was destroyed in seconds, and had a good laugh at how horrible I was at simulators, and confused as to how exactly the weapons functioned. Once they did fire at the enemies, however, their power was surprisingly underwhelming.
I see a lot of promise in this recently-aquired game, though I've barely tapped into its' evidently deep wells of entertainment. I do reccomend this game as it will continue to develop, and the onward march of progress is a brilliant thing to behold.

After completing this game, there's only one verdict I can possibly come to. About time Capcom! Resident Evil was a pioneer of the survival horror genre. While RE5 and RE6 were indeed fun to play, clearly those two entries lacked horror. However, this is not just a return to horror. This is the next stage of evolution for the series. Bringing back familiar gameplay features we remember from the good old days, while uplifting the franchise to a whole new level. The first person perspective has made this entry far more intense than it's predecessors. It felt like I was a part of a horror film, while retaining the well developed RE universe. A new story and a new kind of protagonist. Yet ultimately still connecting to the rest of this well crafted horror universe. From beginning to end, I had no complaints about this one. In fact, I'm looking forward to what's coming next. I would go as far to say that the first person viewpoint should be used from this moment forward. At least until Capcom revolutionizes the survival horror genre yet again. Knowing Capcom, I wouldn't be surprised if they do years down the road. But for now, we have much to look forward to.
Final Verdict: Resident Evil 7: Biohazard not only goes back to the survival horror roots, this groundbreaking entry into the series seems to be just the beginning of a brighter future for the Resident Evil franchise. Or due to the circumstances, a terrifying one. Either way, the previous mistakes made by Capcom have clearly proven to be nothing but the past. With Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, Capcom has achieved redemption. Well done!

Bound in blood feels like one of those games where the devs overlooked a major feature during its release. You play almost the entire game alongside your brother helping out in various ways even directly interacting at times via helping one up onto a platform, covering them while they place explosives etc...it gives a very solid feeling that this game was intended as a CooP game but it feels like the dev backed out of the idea at the last minute.
The older of the McCall brothers uses brute force and is a bit tougher, he can duel wield, throw dynamite etc while the younger of the two prefers long range tactics and precision shooting. The mechanical differences between them seem minor but they'll influence pretty heavily how you'll play. On the note of mechanics shooting seems be pretty solid once you get the hang of it and it's fairly unique cover system.
The game is really starting to show its age at this point but still manages to stay entertaning throughout and with a pretty decent story that makes for a solid prequel if you were ever a fan of the original CoJ.

Ignore the scrubs that couldnt handle the FOV or were too slow for the dueling system, this game is great. Best Call of Juarez in my opinion, improves on the first one in many ways, and is significantly better than the two that came after it.
But it looks like Techland must have been pressured by Ubisoft to release it early, because many of the systems in the game are half-formed at best. The open world part could have been done so much better, imagine a red dead style campaign in first person, instead we get a couple of piddly missions that take no time to do. It just felt slapped on, like take the time to flesh out the open world, or dont put it in at all. Because of Techlands indecisiveness some of the on rail portions felt cheesy and rushed as a result.
Another thing i noticed, you put all the effort into having explosives and molotovs and fire effects, why not add some destructablity into it, like make consequences to your actions. It would have tied into some of the themes in the game well and added credibility to the story. Still the story is somewhat interesting and with the exception of the whiny narrarator i never really felt bored with it. Its definitaly not up to par with say Witcher 3 standards, but this is the series where you murder people with a gun while quoting scripture. But all that said i think they did a pretty good job, the guns feel solid, the missions though linear are fun and well put together. And yes, the dueling controls could have been tweaked a little bit, but i didnt really have any problems until the last duel (which is supposed to be hard anyways).
I think, like with Red Dead the best character is the West. The scenic vistas are many, and they are gorgeous. Techland did a great job of making you feel like you are visiting actual places, with actual real distance between them, even if the human characters are mostly just forgettable stereotypes. Overall its a solid game, but it could have been so much better.
I think if you were to start at the series this would be the best one. The first one was a entertaining game for 2006, Cartel is unplayable trash, and gunslinger was completely linear and boring. Heres to hoping that the success of Red Dead 2 will make techland pick up the mantle once more.
