Pretty fun game, certainly not the worst "indie" title to have ever come out. The price point is about accurate for what you're going to get out of it, because the game itself is VERY short. You can finish it in an afternoon if you want to, though that will depend on how good you are at managing the combat system.
7/10 Graphics
They're cartoony, sort of Guild Wars-esque in the sense that the devs intentionally didn't try to make it realistic.
4/10 Sound
There's nothing to it. You'll hear the same boss track play for one minute, every time. One area's music is no different from the next. It's minimalist, and I tend to disable it. Punching impacts all sound roughly the same, as well. I feel like the devs missed the mark on this one, because quality sound design could have really pushed Absolver a lot further.
1/10 Story
Plotline is non-existent. You fight a handful of bosses and then you scale a tower and fight the boss of the game. She's not particularly hard either, she just has a lot of HP. Your reward for winning is a cutscene and then some old guy throws a robe at you. The end.
6/10 Customization
The loot is a barebones equivalent to Dark Souls. There's no real "I WIN!" items, thankfully. Everything affects your weight and how much blunt or cut resistance you have. You try to balance these stats however you can so that your stamina refill doesn't slow down. Other than that, gear is purely cosmetic.
10/10 Combat
This is really where the game shines. When there isn't any server lag, you're able to engage in some pretty hair-raising PvP and PvE. Few gaming moments are as satisfying as the moment you're able to pull off a winning Tornado Kick and knock someone off a bridge into a chasm. I had to log out after doing this, because I knew I wouldn't be able to top it.
Now here's issue:
The end game is purely PvP. You can roam and try to help newbies if you want to, but again, even if you don't help they're going to beat the game themselves within a day or two. That just leaves "Combat Trials". This might be some people's bread and butter, but from my experiences with it, everyone chooses the fastest attacks possible in order to stun-lock you into a corner. After that, it's just X -> X -> X -> X-> X-> etc. I hope this changes in the future, as there's not much reason to plan your combat deck right now. I also don't like that you're forced into 1v1 PvP immediately. I wish there was more of an open battleground setting similar to Guild Wars' PvP (why does this game remind me of it so much?)
Anyway, yeah. It's fun. Buy it, but you might get bored within a week or two.

Empire: Total War is an edition in the Total War series consisting of the titles Rome: Total War, Medieval: Total War 1/2, and many more.  Empire: Total War, if I am not mistaken, is the first Total War game in the series to introduce gunplay in battles along with user controlled naval warfare. I suggest playing the previous installments before jumping into this game.
Now let's talk about this game.
You start off like most Total War games by selecting who you want your faction to be. Depending on who you choose will place you on a certain part of the map. An addition to this game from the previous installments was that it used more than just Europe and a few surrounds areas. Instead it incorportated parts of Africa and North America. You could travel to the different sections of the world on your power for conquest.
The gameplay consists of the player controlling cities, armies, and special units. Same as other Total War games:
-Cities: Generate Revenue, Can Create Units, Expand Your Empire, ect..
-Armies: Can Conqour Cities, Defend Against Enemies, Build Forts, ect..
-Special Units: Spy For Subertufuge, Assassin For High Targets, Generals, ect..
The main goal is the take over a certain amount of Cities before you hit a designated time period. You can fight the battles over an instant computer generated decision or you can manually control your troops on the battlefield.  Diplomacy can be made with other factions for things like trade, alliances, and much more.
I enjoyed this game for the most part. While on the other hand I would recommend buying the other Total War games. Namely Rome: Total War the original and Medieval II: Total War.
Thanks for reading.

Con:
- The UI is a disaster. It feels like it was built for the console in mind and not at all for PC. UI is VERY cumbersome for a PC user. You can't use mouse to select different things directly in UI which feels extremely frustrating. The map is also cumbersome to use. Not at all user friendly.
- In skirmish you will not be able to level up your characters which is a really negative thing as it's what I hoped to do. You can only level them up if you play multiplayer game. So you are indirectly forced to play multiplayer games even if you would like to play skirmish to have some fun. I don't know what the plan is here. I was quite disappointed because of this.
- The game could have been more polished when you think about the price tag they sold it for and what you got. $20-$25 would have been a better option.
- It's hard to see which character will do next turn in "Initiative ladder" as the color is not that easy to see (clear) in all environment. I hoped they make it easier to see the color of each character there. Clear blue color for characters in your army and enemies in clear red color. Neutral can have yellow color (if they are there).
- Lack of information. You have for example an action to switch weapons, but you have no clue to what kind of weapon you will switch to. Also if I could hover the cursor over an ability or spell so I can get more information about that ability. I can't do that today as it's designed to be a console game in mind.
Uncertain things:
- Gameplay could have been more diverse. It feels you do the same thing over and over again regarding combat. Maybe it's because my character have not leveled up. My guess it's because of that.
- It looks there is a risk they will add a cash shop in the game also. They have something called "shop" in the game which isn't included yet. But I really hope I am wrong here.
Pro:
+ It has great potential being something fun if they fix most issues I have with the game.
+ I like the different factions and how they look like. Ravens looks very cool.
+ They add from time to time new factions. I hope they will add some more.
+ If you like Warhammer it's a must buy game for you.
However I recommend you to buy the game when it's more polished. Right now it's not that fun to play. However I will probably change this review if they change/improve most things for the better I complained about.

I got Road to Hill 30 after playing Hell's Highway to completion on my PS3, and boy are there significant differences. My biggest issues with Road to Hill 30 stem from the game design, so if your the kind of person that sees "classic" and "old" as meaning "timeless," you should probably ignore this recomendation.
Aiming reliably is a huge pain, to the extent that I found myself relying on my AI squad. Trouble is, the squad AI is so dumb it will walk in front of bullets, throw gernades at your legs, and take cover right on explosives. If you don't do your best to lock your team down, they will freely walk in front of you during a firefight. You can try to coordinate stratigicly through a special top-down mode, but this mode is unreliable for doing more than getting your bearings.
I have rarely so noticed the absence of any ability to stick to cover or sprint. Hell's Highway has both these things, in addition to better aiming, and the severe loss of freedom I felt as I tried despirately to manuver in Road to Hill 30 is so bad its almost funny.
In the absence of good controls or gameplay, the story has to pick up the slack. Unfortunitely, I knew going into this that I probably wasn't going to like the story. WW2 and the endless massacre of the mostly-white soldiers bores me to death at this point. In other games, the tired WW2 cliches are often mixed up by the introduction of new elements, such as the alternate timeline of the new Wolfenstien. Road to Hill 30 is a full-on historical drama, however, so expect no mercy for non-enthusiasts.
At the end of the day, you'll probably like this game if you like WW2. Trouble is, Hell's Highway has better gameplay. You will miss out on some of the story if you skip ahead (these games are a fully realized drama, after all), but such is the cost of fun.

I can remember being incredibly frustrated by this game as a kid because it wasn't a Medal of Honour/early CoD corridor shooter and I actually had to think things through sometimes.
But now I found it really enjoyable, at times still frustrating and  a really good story to it.
BiA series is a great, if slightly underrated/overlooked WWII shooter series!

What makes Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 is how authentic it is. When Gearbox advertized it as being the most authentic and realistic WWII game to date, they meant it. With the help of retired Army Col. John Antal, Randy Pitchford and the creative team at Gearbox researched hundreds, if not, thousands of files and photos from WWII at the National Archive and Records Administration in DC, in order to accurately recreate the towns of Normandy, Carentan, and the surrounding farming areas using recon photos from 60 year old, now 70 year old aerial photos. The files don't go just from that, they photocopied written reports from Col. Cole and other military leaders on the tactical actions that are accurately recreated in the game. And how are the tactical movements accurately recreated in the game in an environment context? Amazingly, as Gearbox artists traveled and photographed much of the area shown in the game. The houses you will see, the buidlings, industrial areas, fences, hills, even the friggin hedges, they all exist in real life and were placed accordingly from research photos and recon maps. It's amazing and profound.
The game is remarkable not just for the authenticity, but the true to life story of the soldiers. While the likeness and names aren't what they were in real life, the actions of Matt Baker and his squad are based on the actions of the 502nd Parachute Regiment of the 101st Airborne during Mission Albany. I shouldn't have to explain the story, as it's based on real events, but Matt Baker leads his squad from Normandy after the events of D-Day to secure nearby land and the town of Normandy. The in-between narrative is what really makes Baker's character profound though, because it's evident that the war is effecting him emotionally as some of his men die.
The tactical movements from the files mentioned above are use as accurate movements of the linearity of the levels. Because these movements actually happened, that means the game isn't very open, but that doesn't detract from the quality of using your squad to suppress fire and flanking the enemy with your assault team. The gameplay is a hybrid of being an FPS and a strategy game. You command your squads, fire and assault teams. You can place your team into cover and then order them to suppress fire. Rather simple, but intuitive and fun. There's also the strategy view, which is supposed to simulate recon maps a Sgt. would have studied and memorized beforehand, but being a videogame, Gearbox doesn't strain this on you and allows you to view the area in a semi bird view, getting a strategic idea of how to move on.
I'd like to say that the graphics are decent enough. I just can't believe this game came out nearly a decade ago, 2005, and how they compare now. The levels are designed perfectly, just play the sniper level, you get to see all of Carentan. But only two years later, the first Crysis would come out. I just think Gearbox could have spent a little more time in the textures. Otherwise, the animation was made using motion capture as a basis, and it does look good. The sound design is insanely well done. This game puts you in the battlefield without some soundtrack playing Hans Zimmer for no particular reason. As for the music that is in the game, the pause menu music or the music played over some of the cutscenes are remarkable and true to WWII films. The Prague Philharmonic did a fantastic job in the orchestration.
I think I covered everything. Absolutely my favorite WWII shooter, next to Brothers in Arms: Hells Highway.

It's hard to describe this game in a short sentence or by lumping it into a category. I feel it is very different from what is already on the market, sometimes in a good way, sometimes not. But it does have personality, despite the initial impression you might get of it being
retro pixel art side scrolling genre mash. Jezus I'm getting so tired of pixel art.
I think the important thing is not to approach it expecting certain mechanics or features. If you're going "oh cool a 2D city builder, I like city builders", that's not a good way of starting. If you're going "oh cool a 2D real time strategy", that's not it either. "Management game!" - nope. What it provides is actually it's own kind of experience and I think it's important to go into it with as little expectation as possible.
The main things that come into mind when thinking about this game are "exploration" and "aesthetic". The "exploration" part is both about the game mechanics and about the game world itself and is one of the main themes - you need to figure stuff out on your own, the tutorial is very limited. But I think this might also be the game's weak point, because the mechanics are simplistic and once you figure them out (or read a guide) a big part of the exploration part is gone and then you're left with watching a pixelated character riding a pixelated horse across a pixelated landscape from a parallax viewpoint. Which can be pretty soothing, I guess, but I don't really see that as compelling gameplay.
About the aesthetics - even if I normally loathe this kind of retro look, there are a lot of nice small details that make the game very aesthetically pleasing: morning fog, lighting effects, reflections in the water, animations. The little world that you're playing in is very nicely created and full of life. But this also wears off after a while.
I'm probably not part of the target audience however, since I'm more interested in games that provide deeper mechanics, more control over what happens and a lot of content to play with. It got me intrigued enough for an uninterrupted 2 hour play session and it actually has a pretty addictive cycle built around day time/night time, but I don't really see myself spending a lot more than that (maybe I'll try getting off the first island, my first attempt failed spectacularly).
So, yea, I'm recommending it because it is a very interesting experience, although be aware of the fact that it feels very different from most games out there and it definetly is not everybody's cup of tea.

This is hands down the best military game I've ever played. The interface is and the gameplay works almost flawlessly compared to other titles in the genre (military simulation FPS).
Many people wrongly compare the game to other good games like Arma and such, and opt to take sides in the clonflict between the two gaming companies. I find this silly, as one could easily enjoy both games and simply be glad to have twice as much game.
The game presents very realistic military scenarios and gives the player a lot of choices about how to handle their objectives. The levels are quite huge and the bullet drop in the game works quite well.
The few things that work poorly would be (as always) a fairly limited AI (still decent), weird driving physics (avoid cars, or stay on the road! Off-roading even a little can be fatal - it's not a big deal if you just use cars to get from A to B quickly, using the roads, but don't let the AI drive. Only the enemy AI can drive properly) and the lack of ability to pre-select equipment, despite it seeming like this feature was meant to be implemented.
Also, on the multiplayer part of the game, it seems like it was intended for it to be possible to me quite a few players in each mission, some taking a more "RTS" like stance on the game, as they play officers, but this also seems to have been cut from the final release.
Finally, several missions in the game are only available by essentially typing in certain codes, which is weird... These codes can only be found on the internet.
Also, it took me and my friend that I play with months to figure out that the game had a few non-campaign related missions that you could play when playing co-op. They're tricky to find, but they are there.
The game is best played co-op with 3 friends.

Best horror game I have ever played so far. Beware of spoilers.
It has an incredible atmosphere, when you are passing the same area for the fifth time just because you forgot something or wanted to check something, and you hear this crackling floor sound behind you or somewhere aside, a piano button was pressed in the next room that you checked twice, footsteps behind the wall you are passing by, strange roar
and many more, and even if you know there is nothing going to happen since you cleared this area, watched walkthrough or even cleared the whole game on your own, it still will be scary. At the beginning game made me to take a few breaks for 5 minutes, just to take my balls and get into the game.
It has a really strong plot, maybe with a little lack of choices,
, but aside from that it's still a great story with its own characters with their own stories, part of which you can find in the different documents. The whole story is on plain sight, but you are always footstep away from getting it, you can't catch it till the very end.
Gameplay is awesome, there are a lot of different puzzles, various enemies, even a lot of death traps! And what is more interesting and impressive - each boss has its own unique tactic,
, and you don't lack on weapon choice, there a lot of different weapons like different shotguns, different pistols, burner, or even grenade launcher. Game itself reminds me the first game in the RE franchise, especially with the inventory management, safe rooms and cassette recorders, since its the only way you can save the game. On madhouse difficulty it's a way different game, which makes replaying way more efficient. Enemies not only hit harder, they are more tough, they walk faster, you can meet them at different places, or vice-versa, they are missing somewhere, for example basement fridge. All lockpicks, coins and items now can be found in different places.
And the sweetest part of madhouse difficulty is cassette tapes, or simpler, the only possible way to save the game for you is find cassette tape and put it into recorder, meaning that you can save your game fixed amount of times.
Somewhere you can go full John Wick, somewhere you have to play hide'n'seek, especially with Jack, and if he finds you, you have to outrun him in order to hide again, I'm not afraid of chases, but chase from daddy was really tense for me, especially with the face grab, and somewhere you can take a break and explore surroundings.
All of that above is accompanied with beautiful soundtrack, which at the same time can be really spooky, truly amazing and well-designed locations, moreover,
, they are absolutely different from each other, and each of them makes you feel differently. It makes you play the whole game in one shot, like instead of Ethan it's you, who will face all of the upcoming events.
Aside from the main game, it has a few good dlc, which are worth buying it, since it gives you interesting game modes, like 21, Nightmare, Jack's 55th Birthday or Daughters, which can shed some light on what actually happend before Ethan's arrival.
11/10, I'm really grateful to capcom for their product, and I would gladly wipe my memory out to play this game one more time and get all of these feelings again. It could have a hude potentian as a separate game with separate universe, and I hope that someday it will happen.

Generally I don't write reviews, because I'm not very good at them but this time I felt compelled to do it. Resident Evil 7 was an unexpected surprise for me. The first time I heard about it and watched the very first reveal trailer I thought: Jesus dudes, what are you doing? What's wrong with you? But in the end, a couple of weeks ago I decided to buy it, just because Capcom deserved the benefit of the doubt... Well I can say now that it was the best choice I could have made. Resident Evil 7 is absolutely revolutionary. It has everything we all needed from a RES game, plus the innovative gameplay which some had turned their noses up to – however, I can tell you that this is its strength and it will surely make you feel like part of the game.
I’ve watched every video that I could find on the net about the creation process of the game and I was amazed by Capcom's hard work, especially the work on sound design - which, honestly, is outstanding. They‘ve put considerable effort into it and they‘ve recreated every sound and noise paying great attention to detail. The voice acting is amazing too. All of characters are very well dubbed and characterized, and last but not least, the soundtrack, which corroborates every aspect of the gamesound and gameplay.
Now, let's talk about the graphics... (I apologize in advance for my "nontechnical" opinions :] ) The "RE Engine" does an excellent job. It's not very demanding, so you will be able to easily play the game without resorting to too many compromises. The atmosphere and locations are very well designed thanks to their great textures, but I warn you that you will rarely encounter very low res textures, however, if you do they're not that big of a deal - as in they won‘t compromise your experience. I really loved the lighting effects and I think you will appreciate them as well. Physics are good too but sometimes, like for the textures, you will find some effects that are not made perfectly, but they're not a biggie either. I don't want to talk about the story, you need to discover that by yourself and I promise... you won't be disappointed :).
As for the gameplay... Resident Evil 7 is a survival horror adventure with all the typical elements of RES games. The innovation is the "first person perspective" which has never been used in any of the previous games in the serie. This is driven by the concept of Resident Evil 7, which is a "return to horror". I want to quote Capcom team's words about this:<< At this particular time in games, it was determined that first-person was the most advantageous way to present horror to the player. When confronting the enemy, there's no barrier between you and the enemy. This also applies to exploration and gimmicks and traps and things like that. We felt that it really gets you up close and personal with everything, which adds to that horror element.>>. I can tell you that it really feels like this. Every aspect of the game and especially this one, makes you really feel like an integral part of the game. You will feel the terror and anxiety rising up in you.
In conclusion I can say that this was the best choice that they could make to bring Resident Evil back to its roots, while being innovative at the same time. But remember; this is not a "Survival horror walking simulator" where you just need to run, run and run over and over to reach the end of the game. Here you’ve gotta kill, solve puzzles, explore, craft, face and survive the horrors that the whole game and especially the Baker's house will offer you. I don't think I need to say anything else, also because I don't think it’s necessary to go into detail. You’ll have to discover the game by yourself :). I hope that you all will enjoy this review and I wanted to thank you for taking time to read it. I just wanted to share the intro of the game, because I think it really deserves to be appreciated. It looks like a trailer for a big-budget movie or TV serie and it's very well done. There is no a better presentation than this intro :).

With it's fluid combat mechanics, astounding character models, and level and enemy variety, it's hard to see why Devil May Cry 4 has been overlooked and underrated. The game allows you to take on the role of Nero, and later Dante, the latter being the main protagonist of the series, having more weapons, however in DMC4, you are playing the role of Nero instead, who has comparitevly less weapons and movesets. The story of DMC4 unfortunately is not there. Although lengthy at around 12 hours, you will find yourself stuck in a cliche of Nero's love interest being snatched away, and he must rescue her (Mario I'm looking at you). You'll hack, slash, and shoot your way through hordes of varied enemies, across semi - linear levels. The latter part of the campaign however, is where you might see it getting repetitive, with you playing the story essentially in reverse order, but this time as Dante. Aside from the story, something that DMC4 does do right (and in my opinion, makes it worth getting), is the combat system. As mentioned before, fighting in DMC4 is like no other, and is smooth as butter. Both Nero and Dante are equipped with 2 categories of weapons: ranged and Melee. Nero having a double barreled revolver named Blue Rose, and a motorcycle engine sword, Red Queen. While this may seem little, each weapons has its own unique moves, and can be executed using combos on the keyboard. These moves can be linked with a little practice (I recommend learning how to Jump Cancel first), and can make for a very fun time. If that's not enough, Nero also has a special melee/pseudo ranged weapon named the Devil Bringer, allowing you to smash enemies into the ground WWE style, drag enemies closer to you, and pull off various high damaging finisher moves. On the other end of the spectrum, Dante is the one with the absurd amount of weapons, ranging from his signature pistols Ebony and Ivory, to a transformable suitcase called Pandora. What's more is that Dante has various styles to choose from, ranging from Gunslinger, to Sword Master, Royal Guard, and Trickster. Each has its own unique abilities to manipulate certain weapons. Gunslinger allows free play of Dante's ranged weapons, such as and aerial spinning top move with his pistols, rapid firing his shotgun Coyote-S, or adding new forms to Pandora. Sword Master allows Dante to perform special moves regarding his sword, Rebellion, his rocket-fist Giglamesh, and the explosive spear dealer, Lucifer. Royal Guard allows Dante to heavily mitigate damage from enemies, building up his rage bar, and eventually allowing him to release devastating counter attacks, and even transform into an invicible armor. Finally, Trickster allows Dante to move faster, short range teleport, and perform other stylish moves to better evade, and gain a position on enemies. All of these styles can be switched on the fly with no delay (unless you're standing still), and can be employed very effectively. All of this combat is rated by an in game on the fly letter grade system, ranging from a D-SSS. Overall, get DMC4 if you enjoy hack n' slash games with fluid combat, but prepare to be dissapointed should you buy it for the story. P.S.: For those who are wondering, there is indeed a "endless combat" mode, deemed Bloody Palace. While not exactly endless, its 101 floors will provide plenty of challenge and replayability.

Mordheim City of the Damned is an excellent game.  Because I have crummy Internet I am not able to download it as quickly as I would like.  However, the patches for the game have been amazing.  I would reccomend it to anyone who likes nitty gritty turn based games.
My thoughts on the different warbands:
Cult of the Possessed: So far they are my favorite warband to play as.  They have good attacks, but lack in defense.  That is okay considering their henchmen start with two handed axes.  Thier leader starts out with a decent spell and their hero does have the chance of random mutations.
Clan Eshin: They are my second favorite to play even though they lack physical prowess.  They are not able to hit very hard, but their leader does start out with a poison weapon.  On the other hand, they are all excellent at dodges from the start making you harder to hit.
Sisters of Sigmar: The Sisters of Sigmar are the absolute worst warband to face in my opinion.  I have yet to win a battle against them and they all seem to be overpowered even at low levels.  When I try to play them, they always end up doing awful.  They seem to have a pretty good chance of doing well later on down the road though.
Mercenaries of Reikland: I have honestly not played them as I have never been a huge fan of the Empire.  I don't know all that much about them.
Overall, the game is very difficult to start, but it the game is very rewarding to players who do well.  The game itself is a little clunky, but it is a very good game.

You asked for feedback, so I thought I'd give as much feedback as possible.
Overall, good game. I like the puzzle concepts, and the resource management aspect of it. I would love to see more of it, and to have the story reach a conclusion.
Biggest pros for me are the graphics and the music. I love the feel of the world and the stark contrast that the red provides with Algiz's purple. And the soundtrack is ambient, inspiring, and well done. Give Mr. Sokol my regards.
I also particularly enjoyed the narrator's "Algiz, what are you doing?!" when I stood idle for a few moments.
That said, several things could use improvement. Beyond being a fraction of a game, it has several features which I noticed throughout my playing it that made it less than perfect.
> Getting close to any of the boxes triggers the pushing animation and makes controlling Algiz difficult. He should only be pushing if you move toward the box while next to it.
> The character feels like he is walking above the ground. As the terrain moves up and down, he continues on a straight line, sometimes near the top of the graphic and other times not.
>The voice acting is a bit bad. Unprofessional, at least, in that it sounds like a person reading  script.
>When climbing or jumping, even a slight move to the right or left can send you quite far. I was able to tap the A key and fly clear off of the vines when climbing them.
>The sound of the enemies running does not decrease when you get further away from them. I jumped over one of the enemies, and when he got caught on a wall, he just kept plodding like he was right behind me no matter how far away I went.
>After dying, I respawned next to a door lock that would not accept my energy to unlock, even though I had 5. I also then died while touching the rolling stone on the ground. Both of these happened only once.
>In the ending text, there should not be commas after any of the uses of the phrase "The world".
I also thought there could be a few improvements which, while not necessary, would help greatly in my opinion.
First, the chases often feel like "how long can I hold the move button until spikes appear?" I would appreciate some way of making them more interesting. In addition, I was able to consistently end each episode with about 1-3 spare energy, and feel it would be nice to include some sort of reward for the amount of energy you can end with. Lastly, the boxes sort of seem like random boxes conveniently placed in the world for no apparent reason. If you could make them less square, they would likely fit in much better.
Keep up the good work, however. This has a lot more potential than lots of the games I've seen make their way onto Steam.

A phenomenal tactical shooter that still holds today. This game actually captures the feel of WWII combat, unlike Call of Duty or Medal of Honor, which simply are shooters set in WWII. The squad mechanics are deep yet extremely simple to learn and use, and the enemy AI is some of the best I've ever seen. The combat model is very realistic, with weapon recoil keeping the player from running and gunning most of the time. The health system is one of the most original things about the game; instead of you losing health gradually before dying, the game accumulates danger based on how close you are to an enemy firing, and when the danger reaches a certain level, you get shot and die. This mitigates much of the frustration involved with waiting for your health to regenerate, and establishes a realistic disparity between how much danger you're in engaging enemies close up and far away. The sound design is also ridiculously good, with patriotic melodies that really bring out that "Murica" feel to the game, and convincing weapon noises that make you feel like you're shooting a gun. I only have two problems with the game. One is that the visuals have not aged well at all, and even for 2005 this game looks meh. The other is that sometimes I found my shots being blocked by invisible cover boundaries even though I had my sights on the enemy's helmet; this is likely a contrivance designed to make the player use flanking tactics, but it was still annoying.

Brothers in Arms has the Band of Brothers feel from the start to the end of the game. Great story, lots of actions and actually requires some strategy on giving your squads commands to out-flank and outmaneuver the enemy.

The first game in the Brothers in Arms series, (Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30, Brothers in Arms: Earned in Blood, Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway, and eventually Brothers in Arms 4: The-game-gearbox-studios-will-make-when-they-get-off-their-lazy-asses-and-realise-that-their-fanbase-has-wanted-this-game-for-a-very-long-time), Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 is effectively HBO's Band of Brothers the video game. If you have ever wanted a serious WWII game that tells a touching and thought-provoking story, this is it. Don't be fooled by the game's age, it's gameplay is engaging and challenging, and the story is, in my opinion, the best story ever told through the medium of video games - REALLY. If you have never played it, or the other titles, you won't understand the perfection of the story-telling that goes on in this series. To top it all off, the game is based upon real events, people, and actions, and so feels very realistic. Overall, this and the others in the series, are incredibly immersive video games, with an important, exciting, touching, gritty, at times humerous, and bleak story around the horrors experienced by the 101st Airborne 502PIR during WWII. 10/10 would rank 10/10.
An old classic, but the story and immersion in the game are hardly matched by anything even today. The BiA series is one of my favourite for the WWII era. Highly Recommended

Kinetic Void - I originally bought KV for the ship building as I just enjoy playing Lego star ship building. Alas at the time I bought KV actually flying the ship was not that good, But!!........
(EDIT 5th August 2014 : Dev Build 14 ship control is quite good, totally enjoying flying  my crazy designs)
Things have changed for the better as patches came along. Now its fun to get your creation made and out into the galaxy, Combat has come a long way since release, and I myself find it fun whilst I fly my ship and bombard the unsuspecting with my weapons. Oh and Combat drones actually do their job, nothing like seeing a wing of my drones attacking the enemies along with my ships weapon systems.
Building your ship, at times looks tedious. But its actually quite fun and simple once you understand its mechanics. There is a snap to grid type of mode and freehand mode for fine tuning a module of your ship for that certain look. I can literally spend all my time building a ship save it and begin another as I find it a ton of fun - It is my personal starship lego in my pc - Just a big kid at heart I think.
Mining has also came quite a long way, drone now mine the asteroids etc, harvesting ores for selling (A lot more to come I am sure on mining, buts its off to a good start)
Updates/patches come fast (I have noticed most Mondays there is an update) which shows the team dedication to KV. Some of the latest updates included some nice new backgrounds for the galaxies (Which I found to be excellent)
Dev support is quite good, I think this is one place where any game company (AAA or Indie) can excel or die from. Thankfully KV's team is quite good at letting the game players upto date on things coming and patch information. I myself have posted a comment or two and have had the Dev Team reply auite quickly on the topics  (This is something I look for in an Indie Team/Alpha release games - A+ guys/gals)
KV is still very alpha and most of us by now know what "alpha" means and if your unsure maybe wait a little longer, but I have not been disappointed with my purchase. KV has a long way to go with what is planned, but I think its going to be a fun ride as KV progresses into a full release.
I own pretty much every space game from Elite on C64 to the latest flop by a AAA developer, and all I can say is:
KV is another space game that I am happy to of added to my list of games I play each time I log into Steam.
If space games are your genre, I recommend adding this Indie title to you collection, for the price you will get your moneys worth out of it indeed!!!!

Bound in Blood is a rootin', tootin', lasso throwing, chairs-being-smashed-over-peoples-heads Wild West Adventure.
Playing as either one of the McCall brothers, we are treated to a breakneck adventure through the classic spaghetti western locations - a Civil War battlefield, saloon shootouts, a Mexican border town, gold mines, native American camps and an Aztec treasure haul. Coupled with the usual plot of a lust for gold, betrayal by a business partner, two brothers falling in love with the same woman and it could have been written by the WesternFilmBot2000. Its probably an unfair joke, as for all its predictability the plot and interaction between the brothers is pretty good - at least you don't have to pick flowers like some other games set in the wild west.
Its got some replay value as each brother has different skills with which to complete the level, which means their paths branch to provide unique viewpoints on the current scenario. Ray can duel wield pistols and can look thoroughly impressive firing away his six shooters whilst being unable to hit a barn door, whereas Thomas can accurately shoot rifles and throw lassos but takes damage like he's made of crepe paper.
The level design is a cunningly disguised linear path, but it has the feel of an open world. It does attempt to become almost a sandbox style at times with various side missions available along with a trip to the gun shop but it does this twice before throwing it out of the window. I'm not sure why they bothered with it, it almost reeks of plot filler.
It is a shame that the multiplayer servers are no longer available as I remember the multiplayer being good fun on the Xbox 360. There are some graphical glitches and performance issues, for some reason if you are running Windows 8 or above the game does weirdly play upside down. However, for me it was only the opening cut scene and menu background that displayed upside down so didn't really detract from the experience.
I'd turn the auto aim off, as its like your gun barrel is being moved around the screen by an over protective parent. It makes shooting whilst moving damn near impossible - see the referenced stagecoach section by others. The frame rate does tank occasionally and severely, so I suspect with the issues outlined above its probably just a really naff port to PC.
Overall though, its an enjoyable but slightly flawed experience. Just don't expect too much from it.

If you are worried that Capcom is turning Resident Evil into Amnesia, well, you can rest easy. It's still RE and even more than RE6. The switch to first person hasn't eliminated what made the first RE games so effective. The atmosphere is well crafted, and though it sometimes relies on clichés, I found it massively contributes to the immersion and horror factor. The story is engaging and at times shows depth you rarely expect in a RE game. It is however bogged down by a short duration and a predictable and anticlimactic ending. The gameplay is satisfiying and has not lost its action elements, the choice of running away or shooting your enemies is present and mild stealth elements are too. While the Molded become boring enemies really fast, it is the Bakers' invincibility and creepiness that really makes the game shine. All in all, RE7 is a worthy entry in the beloved series and a game that can be enjoyed by survival horror purists and new fans alike.

The combat of this game is fluid, fun, and rewarding for both players with good reactions, well thought out combat decks, and people that can adapt to their opponents playstyle. In my opinion, the most fun and fair combat I've seen in a game. When the servers went down I just ran around beating up random enemies for no reason other than it was simply fun. My only complaints right now about the combat is that there is too much insentive and not enough risk for players to simply put very fast attacks in their deck and then spam them (still counterable but very annoying) and playing defensivley to flee/heal when out of stamina is too easy, there should be a stamina penalty for running or backing away from your opponent to properly punish people when they run out of stamina.
The PvE of this game is fun and intriguing, I just wish there was more of it. The bosses are not too difficult but still the most entertaining AI the game has to offer. There isn't much of a real story and the main bosses are the only people with real dialogue but the lore of the game is mysterious and interesting, and to be mostly put together from NPC text and item description, similar to the souls series. It does not bother me much at all, but I think the biggest flaw in the PvE is forcing players to progress through PvP levels to fight the bosses again without starting a new character. A simple fix would be to allow players to duel difficult AI in place of players so progress can be made offline or without having to fight players. Most of the gear in the game is obtained through PvP as well so some workaround
Finding your way through the world can be confusing and somewhat frustrating, but using the map to figure out which direction is which, and then venturing ouy to find and defeat the bosses was rewarding, and gives a reason for exploration. After some time, you get the hang of the map and memorizing the pathways is easy. However easy it may be, I still think that some sort of fast travel should be added for after you beat the final boss, as currently there is none.
Overall, I'd give this game an 7/10, but once more content is inevitably added to the game, that score would definitely go higher. I have a lot of faith in the developers, they've done some good work and after talking to them on the official discord server, I know they care a lot about this game. I think that the mixed reviews currently are a misrepresentation of the game's quality. I know there were server issues that prevented a lot of the game from being playable, but upgrades have been made and everything seems pretty fine right now. Most of the other negative reviews are from people that were expecting more PvE from the game (it was always intended to be multiplayer-focused), and those that think the game is too hard. Avoid some of these angry negative reviews and watch gameplay online to see what the game is about. It's a gem.

I remember my first teddy bear when I was a little girl. His name was Rufus. He was actually my best friend for a long time until I was able to imagine friends without the need of a physical face.
He still huddles among the boots of my closet, negotiating with all the sock-monsters in there.
For many children, the security of a soft, cuddly friend can really make or break their day, and there is something incredibly endearing in being able to experience this through the eyes of a toddler, as an adult.
The knowledge that such simple things seem so terrifying at such a young age, makes complete sense when you understand that a child's mind is bursting with unbridled creativity.
- I recommend you play with headphones for full immersion.

-This game, In comparison to other /Total War/ franchises, Is still my no.1 favorite alongside Rome II: Total War. The campeign still runs on who to conquer over the course of the game, But the idea of being a good/bad tactician within the campeign itself is complex, even down to your own home infastructure. For example, You cannot contain a surplus of soldiers in reseves somewhere without having lots of farms/high-level estates. Although, I've yet to see a vantage gain/loss over altitude in the battle mechanics themselves.
-In the combat mechanics, it's generally simple, but great once you get used to it through it's simple complexity. In the early game, with no tiered units or elite units, it somewhat feels like rock/paper/scissors (unless you fight against Sweeden with their little rapid-fire rifles). But, It's not pure rock/paper/scissors, AS if you were to run a battalion of calalry infront of a fresh batallion of Line Infantry, Say goobye to the cavalry; Whereas if you use cavalry "rightly"(flanking from the side or rear, preferably with wedge or diamond formation), You will destroy the infantry.
-Politics, on the other hand, is a bit wierd. EA Games still hasn't mastered the ability to put emotion into political leaders, But they have made an actual treaty system/alliance system. It all depends on ratings of percentage of negative/positive, with every negative being on the opinion of that nation. Quite nice, althout I've yet to meet a rouge ally in-campeign.
The only negatives I see in this game are that... 1. There's no official co-op campeign, and 2. Military mechanics are a bit wonky, still. Although they were improved in Rome II., only by a margin. Overall, a great game for those musket line battle savy.

So let's begin
Empire Total War is the 5th part of the Total War franchise. (if we don't count the Standalone Barbarian Invasion).The game  was released on 4 March 2009 by the Creative Assembly and Sega. It is a (less dificult) Grand Strategy and RTS hybrid. We will controll one from the 11(+USA) factions who fight for the total controll of the world in the 18th century.
THE PLAYABLE FACTIONS in the grand campaign are: Britannia , Austria, France, Maratha Conf (it is an indian empire)., Ottoman Empire, Poland-Lithuania, Prussia, Russia, Spain, Sweden, United Provinces (Netherlands)
We also have a little "Campaign" (toturial) mode where we can look trhough the more important keystones of the War for Independence. ( Honestly I never played it through).

In most RTS games, resource-gathering and military power are two mostly separate things. In Darwinia, your resources are actually the souls of dead units and you need to harvest them soon after you kill them.
This choice between harvesting and military is very dynamic. You can and have to change your tactics fast to deal with the situation. You have a low maximum number of units but there is no build time. However, you can only build at certain locations, so waiting time depends on where the battle is taking place.
Third, micro-management is quite different from what you're used to: You don't just click to attack, you decide exactly where your soldiers shoot. Macro-management is really narrative-driven. Levels have very different goals with each other and winning feels more like solving a puzzle than managing and allocating resources.
Darwinia is a weird little game, it's one of those things that broaden your horizons. That's why it shouldn't be missed.

I purchased this game in the 2017 steam summer sale for $4.99. It was worth every penny!
My first time through the game, I played it on the "hard" setting (standard procedure for me). While it often provided a challenge, it wasn't overbearing. The story took me 9 hours to complete, and it appears to have a fair degree of replayability due to the variety of locations, the number of hidden secrets, and the fact that most of the levels can be played as either of the two main characters, who have their own combat styles as well as differing paths/objectives in certain story locations.
The story is simply oozing with flavor, hearkening back to the historical moments and the best of the western genre. That said, I highly recommend that you play the original Call of Juarez (despite its heavily-aged graphics and mechanics, and the fact that it technically takes place later in the timeline) before you pick this one up, or else you may be disappointed by the ending. With the context of the first game (which takes place later in the timeline), the story makes a lot more sense, and truly becomes a triumph.
Some notes:
Overall, a fine western shooter. I had a few quibbles here and there, but if you're looking to pick up a good single-player shooter for a good price, this is a great choice.

Pros:
+ Game runs quite well for the most part

+ The story, while tearing half the script out of
, is still pretty good

Cons:
- The driving manages to be somehow worse than
, and you essentially have the mobility of a motorized bar of soap
- The cops will go after you for almost anything, which gets annoying very quickly and makes moving across the city a chore
- The gunplay is infuriating as either your enemies stand in place and let you shoot them, making the game a shooting gallery, or you have the durability of wet tissue paper and can die way too easily, not to mention the fact that the guns feel weightless and the guns either do too little damage or two much, making combat either boring or frustrating

At the end of the day, I give this game a thumbs up because it's not a terrible game by any means, and you can have fun while playing it. It's obvious the devs put a lot of effort into this. Disclaimer - played about up to Chapter 10 before quitting.  Maybe something changes later, but I lost patience.
The game does indeed have a good story and dialogue, but I got turned off after playing far enough to realize something that I kind of wish I'd known before I paid for it: this is NOT an open-world game.  The entire game is the story missions; you do them one by one, with no real opportunity to make choices or go on side quests.  Yes, there's a nice big city to drive around in, but unlike in a real sandbox/open-world game, there's almost nothing IN that city to interact with.
In addition to being frustrating if you, like me, bought the game on the premise that you'd be playing an open-world game, this has the added effect of making a great deal of the driving you do in the game a pointless time-filler.  Most missions you do have extended sections that are just "drive to this location where the plot will happen," with no real opportunity for anything interesting to happen along the way unless you deliberately drive like a moron and get the cops to chase you, which loses its charm fast.
TL;DR - if you want a linear game with good story and dialogue, and you're prepared to do a lot of pointless driving around to get to cut scenes that the game could have just skipped to directly, this is your game.  If you wanted GTA meets the Godfather, that's not actually what you're going to get.

Among the Sleep is a cleverly written survival horror game developed by Norwegians. It is a unique little game in the sense that the protagonist is a two-year-old little boy who's aided by his Teddy bear in order to go through various horrors that are lurking in their house.
The story begins with a birthday celebration that reveals Teddy to be the gift. However, he is taken from the boy and in chapter 1 we need to retrieve him quickly only to realise that the real protection from the dark can only be offered by mom. The journey then continues to find mom and along the way we encounter some monsters and cleverly thought out puzzles.
The game has a great atmosphere and for full immersion a headset is required - similarly to the Amnesia games. The Unity engine does its job properly and the visuals look great. The only downside is the game's short story: it can be completed in a mere 2 hours including its DLC content which is a kind of prologue and is meant to be played after the story is done.
Overall, Among the Sleep is a good game that I can recommend mainly to the fans of the genre. Hopefully, the guys at Krillbite Studios will develop a - much longer - sequel or another game with similar level of quality.
UPDATE: The latest update (version number 2) introduces some new achievements (all related to collectibles) along with some nice graphics enhancements thanks to the new version of the Unity engine.

Okay so here it is:
Graphics:
1. They aren't pushing any limits with textures but the coloring is on point as well as the shading. If you're thinking of buying this game for high end graphics then thats a no go here.
2. There is also a mechanical issue with the game that kind of hurts the graphics as well... What I mean by that is you character is a visual representation of the style of play you've chosen. If you are going light armor then you really have no options on how to look. I'm not saying I want to have a panda mount, just that you really hurt your optimization in order to look cool.
2a. The best character for speed is basically wearing nothing, you'll do more damage with certain moves as well as dodge much further and faster. So if you want to be badass and look the part then this isn't the game for you... unless you go with strength in which case then this is the game for you.
3. There are a few bugs graphically where certain items will stretch across the screen. What I mean is a shoulder pad another player is wearing may graphically strech across the screen. It doesn't happen very often though but is pretty bad when it does.
4. Level design is deceptively simple in this game, and each map has a lot going on in its background... probably more than whats going on in the area you are in. It left me hoping that eventually they would expand on the content.
5. Animation is mostly on point there are a few transition problems but this is by far some of the better animations for characters out there. I'd love to see a full on mmo with this kind of combat. I could picture D&D working with this.
Music::
1. Again nothing to write home about, its transic background fluff mostly, even in combat amazingly as most of your energies will be bent on reading your opponents attacks and raging when you timed a dodge perfectly but they attack so fast you get hit by the 2nd attack before you could finish your dodge animation... Anyway, the music doesn't hurt the game either and its noticable and for me at least missed when it isn't there.
Gameplay::
1. The games genre says fighting game so I'll judge it accordingly. If this was an mmo or an rpg with a strong fighting component then I'd be far more forgiving here but it isn't saying all of that and is branding itself as a fighting/action game. Without going into the definition of "Action" in gaming history I'll note that any leniency in my game play review comes from that and that they are still updating this game... and with that said I will add that I do miss the days when games were launched completed.
2. For the price this game offers still too little, what I mean is the content can be cleared in a matter of 2 or 3 hours. The worst that could happen is you go up the stairs or to the left from the first interesting looking area with the tablet. If you do that and are not using a guide figure in another 3-6 hours until you realize going to the right exit would lead you past areas you could handle more in line with the learning curve. So yes there is a actual design to the game that introduces you to enemy mechanics (and in turn your own) but there is no attempt to help new players on getting on that path.
3. Multiplayer is there as well and its... a mixed bag... friendly fire is fine but it doesn't do anything to benefit the gameplay experience, you kind of just end up having to deal with teammates who actually want to help but are doing more harm than good sometimes. Single player is well lonely and reveals how lonely the world is very quickly to put it plainly the adventure part to this game has no consistent narrative and as such the world in single player feel like a lonely place.
4. Difficulty, this is either a good or a bad thing, there is no aoe finisher style moves like assassins creed, enemies have no qualms about putting the "ganging" in "ganging up". While it really comes down to decks certain styles just do not work when facing multiple opponents.
5. Controls are pretty solid its amazing how they got everything to fit to 2 buttons, there are things that need work with the game mechanics but controls are not a problem.
6. Stances, this is the games selling point as a fighting game so how does it work? Very well actually... as a fighting game this game does a very simple job of letting you fight. Is it imbalanced? Name me a fighting game that wasn't imbalanced. Imbalance isn't the issue, the issue is wether low tier builds stand a chance against high tier? The answer sadly is no not really. Some styles are amazing by comparison one that gets you super armor, one that slows the enemy when you counter them are amazing enough next to the two that let you dodge. Combine that with things like super armor attacks and quick fire attacks that can be further sped up with timing and looping and you have a pretty big issue.
6a. Above I alluded to dodging not really being so effective, well lets use the stagger stance (drunken boxing) dodge for example. At the end of each of its stances it has an attack. This attack is very predictable and easily parryable. The whole dodge takes long enough that in most cases you can respond to it with a parry or super armor. In the case of parry you can then punish them with whatever you want really. Also with stagger, dodging back gives you an invincibility frame, except that the frame is about 1/5th the animation. The game rewards you crystals for sucessful dodging which can be used as a way to verify if you've dodged... unless you use the stagger stance dodge back which can still get pummeled by certain special attacks that may be longer in animation. Apply the same situation but to fast attackers who will throw out 3 attacks before you finish that dodge.
6b. There are folks who say that the meta is counterable and are advocates of that finding a stronger deck combo will counter the various meta people use. In truth if two different meta were to meet however most already know which would win. I wont spoil it here but a quick google search will be up people begining to realize it.
6c. The good thing is the developers are paying attention to things like this and are updating the game.
7. Grinding is present but it is not korean mmo level. You can hit cap level in about 10 hours, but it isn't worth it. Enemies scale and they are after a point deadly no matter what. So in my honest opinion the game punishes you far more than rewards you for gaining levels. Enemies essentially become hp walls later. The good thing is you get to see first hand which builds are far superior because at 60th level enemies start doing things with those builds at a stupid level... I mean if I could use windfall like the boss npc could and jump over high attacks or duck under low attacks... I'd be god of windfall... or a hacker.
Overall is it worth it?::
As an adventure game no not really, it has some level design quirks that lends itself to a bit of exploration despite being linear in most cases.
As a Fighting game average, it has moments of high adrenaline higher intensity but if you are going with the meta then it comes down to luck at the end of the day.
As a Martial Arts game; ya, oh man you know it has a lot of martials moves and he sound of the impact is great some of the moves don't really make sense with the styles they are in but thats fine, after all thats what schools are about.
Base Line::: 6/10
Still better than most other game out there right now and it is quite unique. If they expand on the game some more down the road then I'd expect I could only enjoy it more and more.

This game got my MMO hopes up so high...and then utterly destroyed them. Like, set them on fire, watched them burn out, and then set them on fire again.

"Finally!" (I thought naively) "An MMO centered around REAL combat, martial arts, and looting!"
I was a stupid, stupid child for believing they'd do something great with this. So here we go, Pro's/Con's time.
Pro's:
- It's not another tab/target MMO, so there's that at least.
- Combat is kinda fun, AT FIRST.
- Martial arts styles and animations are pretty cool.
Con's:
Oh dear god, where to begin...
- This game feels EARLY ACCESS AT BEST.
- Combat. Interesting at first, then becomes really, really, really, annoying. Really. I have no idea how they settled on THIS as the final version.
- There is no story. None. There's a very vague-ish premise that you can kinda guess at, but other than that, nada.
- I was annoyed at the PVP over PVE focus, but was willing to try go through it, til I realized there is virtually NO PVE. In fact, the PVE part may as well just be the Tutorial. I mean, seriously? I get that you wanted to make a PVP heavy game, but to this extent?
- Gear System. At first, I was excited about fighting random AI mobs and picking up pieces of their gear, but then you find out that every time you make your Attack/Defense better, it WEIGHS YOU DOWN and you become incredibly slow. Annoying as hell.
- No map, at all. You don't really need one after a couple hours, because the entire place is ridiculosuly small, but still. It's pretty annoying.
- The art style. I keep seeing people compliment it, but I don't get it.
I guess? But nothing noteworthy, just different.
- Could go on and on.
This really could have been a great game, the core concept was there and some of the game mechanics had a lot of promise. Then I assume they all just said "F$%# it" and gave up halfway through the development and slapped together whatever they could to make it functional. Truly disappointing.

Far too glitchy for me to waste time on. Mission critical doors not opening, NPCs shooting through walls etc.
Edit: I don't think I've played Far Cry before so I don't have that nostalgia "burden" many probably bear. In 2017 there's so many alternative shooters that this one just seems too clunky to bother with (from older games something like Crysis was way more functional even today).
The game where enemies can see you through solid objects

As a warning to fans of the more recent Far Cry games, I'll start off by saying that this is NOT an open-world game. It's a linear game that has much larger maps than most FPS games and allows you to approach your objective in a variety of different ways.
The plot is simple, but no one plays Far Cry games for their plots; you assume the role of Jack Carved, an ex Special Ops operative with a terrible sense of fashion who becomes stranded on an island while transporting a reporter named Valerie there. You eventually discover that a mad scientist named Krieger is experimenting on primates and turning them into some of the most annoying enemies you'll ever face in a
After playing for awhile, you may notice that this game had a heavy influence on Crysis, and they share many similarities. Both games:
As I mentioned before, there's many ways to approach each objective and battle despite the game's linearity. This is helped by the wide variety of weapons you can use. You can kill foes from medium range with assault rifles, eliminate them from afar with the sniper rifle, let the enemies come to you and peak from behind cover to get quick kills with the automatic shotgun, and more. The only strategy that doesn't work is going in guns blazing, as you can killed in seconds on even Normal difficulty if you're not careful. Even if you're an FPS veteran who thinks that anything less than the highest difficulty in a game is child's play, I'd strongly recommend playing on High difficulty or lower, and I can explain why in one word: Trigens.
Trigens are the aforementioned mutated primates, and they are a the game's weakest aspect. On Normal difficulty, the unarmed Trigens can kill you in just a few hits when you have full armor and health, and half the time they may not appear to even hit you when you take damage from them. Things only get worse later in the game when you must face humans that have become mutated and are capable of wielding guns. Some of them are simply tankier soldiers, and you occasional encounter massive brutes with a rocket launche arm that can withstand multiple grenades or several shotgun blasts to the face at point blank as well as invisible Trigens. Making this even worse is the fact that this game uses a checkpoint system. This game will be much more enjoyable if you take advantage of the console command "\save_game". It essentially allows you to quicksave, and will save you loads of trial and error.
While the Trigens are certainly more annoying than the human mercenaries, they can be pretty irritating as well due to their impossibly good vision which NPCs in the other game in the series thankfully don't have. Even in this dead of the night, enemies will be able to instantly spot you from several hundred meters away if they face your direction. This isn't a problem for the most part since their chances of hitting you with bullets are pretty much zero, but be prepared to die A LOT if they have rocket launchers.
It's worth noting that for its time, Far Cry looked fantastic. Even to this day, the models and water look fairly decent in my opinion, and I was especially impressed by the dynamic shadows that are cast on your weapon by foliage. I have no clue how well optimized the game is or if it runs well on the recommended hardware, as I have a GTX 1070 GPU which was unsurprisingly able to run the with settings turned up beyond their in-game menu limits at 1080p 60 FPS without any issues aside from the game sometimes freezing for a second or so when I threw a smoke grenade.
Despite my frustrations with the Trigens and the weak plot, I'd still recommend Far Cry. When there's no mutants involved, it's an absolute blast, and anyone willing to put up with its shortcomings will likely have fun with the majority of the decently lengthy campaign.

Funfact: The gameplay of Airmech is lifted directly from the classic Genesis game Herzog Zwei, right down to the transforming robots:

That's not a bad thing-- Herzog Zwei was an incredible game, way ahead of it's time, and laid the groundwork for a lot of RTS games to follow. On its
you can see the list of all the developers who called it an influence. It was much in need of a remake, and I'm happy that it has such a good one, I just think it should get some credit.
So if you spent hours of your youth playing that early Genesis cart, if you nearly lost friends over the intense split-screen battles that could last so long that you'd have to call a temporary truce to eat lunch, if you still have the cherished faded cartridge in a box of nostalgia somewhere, then this game just might scratch an itch you've had for a long time.

This game is awesome, as long as you remember that it is in Beta...
There have been several updates (eg: Auto Deploy Arm) that have caused the playerbase to fall from time to time, but these changes - even those you may not like - are a part of playing a Beta state game.
Some Great things about the game itself:
- Dota meets RTS (with prebuilt buildings to capture/deploy from).
- Massive Unit list to fully customise your loadout (from Infantry to Tanks to Artillery/Turrets and Support).
- Increasing list of Parts to customise your AirMech performance with.
- Pilots and Items to enhance your play style.
- CO-OP & PVP Leaderboards for weekly prizes.
- Simply an insane amout of purely "cosmetic" flair and pets to show off your personal Style (obtainable with premium "Diamonds" currency, generally bought with real cash).
- Seasonal Promotions in the Shop.
- Player Market.
- A Basecamp to build, with crops to generate free "Kudos" - also earnt just by playing (free ingame currency).
- Nanoforge (the crafting craze continues in AirMech...).
- All critical gameplay Units & AirMechs obtainable with Kudos.
Some Great things about the Community in AirMech:
- Helpful & Friendly.
- MODS keep faction chat in check (Plus the ingame Swear Filter option helps).
- Diamond Rolls (sponsored by players) share Diamonds via a Chat minigame - Click those Dice! Highest and lowest numbers win Diamonds!
- Factions help newer ones to learn the game
I am the Leader of "[Rise]" Faction, contact me ingame for an invite to [Rise], there i am known as Dartis.
Some Factions also have Joining requirements, something to strive for.
- For those that sign up to the Forums, there are Giveaways hosted by Generous AirMech Members and Players.
Some things new players confront when just starting:
- Diamonds! As said, these are the Premium currency obtainable with real money (generally).
- Market. There are Distinctive benefits (like reduced Tax) for those that are at least Silver VIP ($5USD) over those that are unable to (or choose not to). This makes selling on the Market (and earning those precious Diamonds) harder for those F2P'ers (however this isn't necassary to play or be good at the game itself).
- Kudos. Even though you will gradually earn Kudos, some players find it takes too long to buy everything they need to play (but please don't spend your early Diamonds on these things, you may regret it later).
- PVP. Ranked PVP doesnt allow Parts or Ultimates but Unranked PVP does. This has led to some believing AirMech is now P2W as Ultimates are only available with Diamonds. However Ultimates were 'nerfed' a few patches back and are not as OP as they used to be, they now only give an advantage. As an incentive, "Honor" was released for those who play PVP Without Ultimates against those that Do - earn enough Honor and you'll unlock some exclusive stuff...
Overall, I love Airmech. Between playing CO-OP, learning PVP, playing the Market, "ChatMech", "FarmMech", Diamond Rolls (or the Ever OP "Black Diamond Roll") there is enough content here to have kept me entertained for years! Just remember its a Beta state game and so will you!

Terrifying, horrifying and awesome. "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" is one of the best Resident Evil game this year.
Despite its decision to make it from third-person to first-person perspective, it still my favorite game.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic game. It kicks things off right away by immersing you in a horrific atmosphere akin to Outlast, keeping you on the edge of your seat as the story is introduced and the scares commence. While having a large focus on puzzle-solving and combat mechanics, I wouldn't hesistate to call Biohazard a story-driven game. As you progress, new clues and hints will constantly be appearing, allowing you to slowly piece together the mystery behind the Dulvey Haunted House and the Baker family. Without spoiling too much, I will say that the game features a major plot twist, one which enhances the story tenfold and gives it an extra layer of depth.
If I had one gripe about Resident Evil 7, it would be the difficulty. I played on normal, and I found myself dying multipe times in many sequences throughout the game. A challenge is obviously fun and exciting in a video game, but when you must die over and over just to progress, it can become irritating and detract from the atmosphere. Similarly, the puzzles can be excessively difficult, giving you no real direction or clear objective and essentially leaving you to figure out everything on your own. As I said about difficulty, a challenge is fun, but this ends up killing the mood after a while.
Who knows, though. Maybe I just suck.
If you're considering this game, go for it. Buy it, get immersed in its story and atmosphere, and marvel over it for days after you've finished playing it, just as I have. It's 100% worth it.

I really like this game a lot--it's short, sad, and sweet. What makes it unique is the perspective; it's a first person perspective horror game where you play as a 2-year-old toddler. The game really makes you see the world through the imagination and fears of a little child. The visual design of the game succeeds in making benign everyday objects look menacing when in the dark. Is that some sort of monster standing there watching you? Or is it simply a coat on a coat rack with some boots sticking out the bottom of it? Even your own toys can sometimes seem unsettling. I liked how, whenever you see written text in the game, like in an open book, for example, it looks like gibberish, since your character can't read. Sound effects are used effectively at the right times to evoke a sense of dread and fear.
In my opinion, the star of the show here is Teddy, your imaginary friend teddy bear who seems alive and who is with you you traverse the dark, avoiding a monster and looking for your missing mother. Teddy is an ambiguous character; cute n' creepy. Is he there to help you or is he not to be trusted? He is well voice-acted, but there are long sections of the game where you almost forget he is with you because he doesn't have much to say. I realize this is under the pretense that you both have to be quite so as not to alert the monster to your presence, but I just feel like Teddy could have been used more in some of the middle sections of the game.
I'm not going lie, this game can really get you into the mindset of a small child and I did find myself weeping after the climax and at the end. The game can be scary, but there's no blood and guts or anything. But be aware that the game delves into issues that kids shouldn't have to face, but sometimes do. The evidence to me that this game successfully told a story with some emotional impact was the fact that it gave me the feels even though I had a pretty stable and happy childhood.

SPOILERS FOLLOW
the atmosphere in this game is top notch. amazing sound track, visuals, and puzzles that all inspire feelings of suspense and terror. A frightening and compelling nightmare world, made all the moreso by the fact that you play a two year old child.
that said, I felt like the twist in the end wasn't well realized. I was sure that things were going a certain way because, in my view, the entire game was setting you up to believe in a certain scenario. when it turned out otherwise it didn't have the impact it could have, because there is exactly zero foreshadowing in the beginning of the game. all of the foreshadowing portends the scenario I thought was going to take place, but didn't. frankly sometimes I think games nowadays try to shoe horn these twists in because it's the thing to do, but (and I felt this a little with The Vanishing of Ethan Carter) it would have been just as good if not better if played straight.

Interesting marriage between For Honors combat system and Original Dark Souls like level desing ( NO, NOT LIKE CRASH ♥♥♥♥ING BANDICOOT ). Levels interweave really well and there are hidden short cuts sprinkled around the map. On occasion you will get lost in this game because it doesn't have a map. But unfortunately the game area is some what small and the "story" can be quick run through really quite fast ( My first play through took 6 hours to complete but I didn't rush it at all ). This does have one positive side, loading screens are very rare.
Combat system is the most balanced I've seen in a while. Learning curve can be a bit steep for someone who is new to difficult third person action games. Where the games combat truly shines is 1v1 combat and the freedom player has to create your own combos and even own school of martial arts ( Requires PvP ). Combat system isn't really desinged for taking on multiple opponents, and it quickly becomes frustrating. On the other hand all of the boss fights are great( There's 3 proper bosses and 10 "minibosses" ). The minibosses are pretty decent too but the actual bosses are much better and much more interesting to fight.
Absolver also has system where other players will occasionally come into your game and it's up to you whether you fight them, ignore them, or help them. Most of the time people seem to be more interested in helping each other then killing each other. And I have to say that community in this game has been really friendly so far ( In my game time I've only ran into 3 people who have been more interested in fighting you then the NPCs, and I've played PvE with maybe 15 different people ).
Replay value is also a bit of a an issue with this game since the PvE content is quite limited. There has been statement from the devs that they are going to add some RNG based end game elements into the game.
At best Absolver is a really fun & difficult game with a great 1v1 combat, where you get lost and end up discovering some thing new.
At worst you get ganked by multiple NPCs because you couldn't switch targets easily.
On overall I'd say this game is decent buy if you are into intricate level desings, difficult combat, and want to create your own style of combat.
PS: if you only want play this in PvE then wait for a sale, since the PvE content is so limited.
