Absolver is a game with a great art direction, interesting mechanics and tight, responsive and fun gameplay. The PvE content isn't too long, but with a very customisable skillset and unique mechanics for three or four styles, you can really tailor your fighting style to suit your preferences, and progress by learning new moves and building on what you learn as you play. The game is pretty, it runs smoothly, and the combat features a intuitive and interesting enough to provide a great PvP experience.
...so why am I not recommending?
Because Absolver suffers from just about every woe you would expect it to, given the context of its release. Sloclap is an indie developer, and this seems to be their first big title. Absolver has also garnered enough attention to gather a reasonable playerabse, and there's no shortage of players to fill their servers. The servers just can't handle it, and the core mechanics of the game, polished as they might appear, do not handle the lag well. Not at all. As you enter new areas you might find parts of the world failing to load in, or loading in far too late; you can become stuck, walk into what turns out to be a wall, or areas you shouldn't be. You can discover enemies, both NPCs and players, that have yet to load in properly; they will be invisible, or warp randomly around, still able to hurt you, whilst sometimes being impervious to damage themselves. Sometimes new players will enter your instance and cause sudden immense framedrops as they load in. You might try to team up with your friends, only to be greeted with errors and infinite loading screens; one of you will inevitably have to log out and back in again for it to work, during which time the game might just outright crash
Absolver is a game that is very clearly, and openly oriented towards PvP. Account for the above issues with poor server support, game-breaking lag and loading screens that lead to crashes, and you just don't end up with a good experience. As a game, it's fantastic. It's wonderful. I could forgive a few bugs here and there. I could forgive the minimalistic explanations, the oddities in the labyrinthian map design and the occasional design oversight. ...but as an -online- game, Absolver just isn't well-supported enough right now. It's close, It's REALLY close. ...but it is just apparent that there are just too many bugs and too few good servers available.

As was the case with The Long Dark, Mordheim: City of the Damned is in early access and will be reviewed as such. At a later date (when the game is officially released) we will come back and update our review of it. The score we will give at the end of this review is the score for the game as it is right now. And, on that note, let’s get rocking.
I – Story [8/10]
Mordheim: City of the Damned is a turn-based strategy game (with some RPG elements mixed in) from Rogue Factor. It is a digital adaptation of the tabletop game Mordheim from Games Workshop. Set in the city of Mordheim (part of the amazing world of Warhammer) a comet has crashed and turned the whole city into a horrific battleground for bands of mercenaries from across the land. The prize? Fragments of Wyrdstone that came from the comet and that are scattered throughout the city.
It’s not the most intriguing of stories (and, let’s face it, this was originally a tabletop game), but I rather liked it. Not to mention the gorgeously morbid setting in an absolutely immersing universe.
II – UI [5/10]
There were very few things I didn’t like about the user interface as it sits now. Accessing individual unit stats and action menus is easy as can be, but (again, this is still in early access and will hopefully change) the lack of functionality in the tactical overview map is disappointing. It is often times hard to plot out your strategy on the overview map and then attempt to put it into action in real time. A minimap would definitely alleviate this problem to an extent, but increased functionality of the overview map should definitely find its way into a future update of the game.
The really troublesome thing about the user interface is the incredibly awful camera angles during your opponent’s turn. I can’t stress enough how annoying the camera angles are during action phases that are not yours. Sometimes you’ll be looking at a unit in a completely different area of the map that has nothing to do with what is currently happening and that is if you get lucky. More often than not, you’ll be looking at some scenery. While that isn’t necessarily a bad thing in and of itself (the environment is fascinating), it gets obnoxious in a hurry.
As far as actual action animations go, the camera angles need some work, but the animations themselves are pretty nice.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
I love the gameplay in M:CotD. I’m a newcomer to the Warhammer universe for the most part, especially the fantasy side of it, but M:CotD is genuinely fun.
There are currently two modes of play. The first mode, “Battleground Only”, is essentially a deathmatch. The object of this mode is to either kill all of the enemy’s units or cause them to rout, effectively forfeiting the skirmish. This (alongside the tutorials) is a good way to become familiar with the mechanics of gameplay.
The second mode of play is “Extra Objectives”. In this mode you can win the skirmish in the same way you can win a “Battleground Only” match or by being the first to complete a secondary objective. There are three secondary objectives: “Marked For Death”, “Crush Their Will”, and “Wyrdstone Rush”. To complete “Marked For Death” you will need to kill specific units of the enemy’s warband and collect their belongings as proof. To complete “Crush Their Will” you will need to steal the Idol of the enemy’s warband and stash it in your chest. To complete “Wyrdstone Rush” you will need to gather a certain percentage of all the Wyrdstone on the map. Also, your team and the enemy team could have different secondary objectives or you could have the same one. It keeps things interesting.
You also have the ability to alter the roster of your warband. Other things you can manage is what equipment certain units have and how their skills are being developed. You gain experience the more you play with your chosen faction.
IV – Content [7/10]
For M:CotD to be in early access, it has a fair amount of content already. There are four playable factions to chose from currently (Empire Mercenaries, the Cult of the Possessed, the Sisters of Sigmar, and the Skaven Clan Eshin), four playable maps, a good diversity of units for each faction, and a good smattering of items to equip your warband with. As it is now, is there enough content to justify the price tag? Probably not. At least, not quite yet. There is still more than enough to keep you going for a good long while though.
V – Visual [10/10]
Now we’re coming to the aspects in which M:CotD really shines the brightest. The graphics are beautiful; both character models and the landscape. Everything is dark and gloomy and the atmosphere is to die for. Every unit is intricately detailed and wonderfully animated. The environment may be the best part about M:CotD. It might be Hell on earth, but it is an unforgettable place to visit.
VI – Audio [10/10]
We have now reached what I consider to be the greatest part about M:CotD: the music. The music in this game is perfect. It really sets the feel for every single battle and incursion into the cursed city. Not only this, but the sound effects are incredibly well done. As far as sights and sounds go, Mordheim should be your next tourist destination.
VII – Overall [8.3/10]
Overall, Mordheim: City of the Damned is off to a great start. This one has serious potential and I cannot wait to see where it ends up in terms of it’s completion.

If your warrior or a unit is injured, they can lose an arm, leg, or eye. This injury is permanent and each has a profound effect on gameplay.
The story has been expanded but it's still a bit week, that's the only complaint I've got after HOURS of gameplay.

So I've been a long time fan of Devil May Cry, and I'm probably the only person I know that is. I picked up the first game around the time it came out and died terribly all the way to the second or third-to-last mission, and then I was stuck there for a while. I eventually finished the game, and I stayed a fan of the original even after playing through 2 (note: it's bad...really really bad), and became a bigger fan after playing 3 (my favorite so far). Oddly, 2, 3, and 4 were all directed by the same person, Hideaki Itsuno, though 2 was very different from the rest of the series. After 3 I was definitely willing to give it a go again, so I was very excited when 4 came out. Here I am FINALLY playing it in 2014, almost 6 years after the game came out in 2008, and I thought I'd write up what I thought of the game overall.
In Devil May Cry 4 you play as Nero instead of Dante. Nero is another white-haired sword-wielding Devil Hunter like Dante, but he's younger, likely around Dante's age in 3 which was a prequel. You start out the game with a scene that looks like it came right out of Spider-Man 2 where Nero's on his way to see a girl on stage and gets interrupted by demons. He manages to make it there as the performance ends, and the girl is so happy to see him that there's no real conflict that arrises from it.
Nero acts really aloof and stand-offish right away which makes him seem really unlikable, and even whiny. Shortly, though, Dante shows up guns blazing and Nero rises to the challenge of trying to fend him off while everyone else is running around in a panic. From then on Nero seems more and more like Dante himself. Starting with the scene where he's given his sword, and going on to each major demon he faces, Nero keeps up with the wise-cracks Dante is known and loved for, and I actually really ended up liking him as a character as the game went on.
Halfway through the game you actually end up playing as Dante for a few missions. There's a lot of fan service here with Dante showing off in every cut scene he's in, with a bunch of silly over-the-top scenes evey time he gets a hold of a new weapon. There's a particularly funny moment when he and one of the villains act like they're in a play when they meet to fight on a stage.
Overall I thought the story and characters were well written with the exception of Kyrie, the love interest. Kyrie is the classic damsel-in-distress and you never really learn much about her because she's always either captured and hidden offscreen or oddly mute. The actual plot surrounds a group of people wanting to use Sparda's power to become gods and take over the world which is somewhat similar to the main villain's goal in 3, but there's a little more going on here with more exposition and more characters.
The world design and character design is very similar to the previous games. There are gothic ruins and a city that seems to have a Vatican City vibe to it, as well as a jungle (oddly enough). Characters look similar to what you'd see in 1 and 3, though Dante is sporting a goatee now and a set of boots that look like they may be a little too big. Every female character seems to have spontaneously become extremely well-endowed for some reason, including a couple of returning characters.
Creature designs in this game are the best in the series in my opinion. One of the bosses is a giant frog with two lures similar to an angler fish, but the lures are shaped like human women. My favorite design is the Blitz which is a blind demon that uses lightning.
The weapon designs are interesting, the two most interesting and ridiculous being Pandora and Lucifer. Pandora is a demonic suitcase that can transform into multiple different guns including a ridable missile platform; yes, I'm serious. Lucifer is a very strange shoulder-mounted weapon that looks like a demon head with bat-like wing/arms. Lucifer allows Dante to create blades that explode a while after being stabbed into enemies, and he can throw the rose he holds in his teeth to manually detonate all of the blades at once; again I'm not making this up.
The gameplay in Devil May Cry 4 is similar in feel to the rest of the series. Nero has almost the same moveset that Dante does for his standard sword with a few differences. The ability that replace Stinger has an area of effect when it lands, for instance. Nero also gets an ability that gives feedback when there are secrets nearby which is absent when you play as Dante.
Nero has two new special abilities that change up combat a little bit. The first is his Devil Bringer which is his demonic right arm. The Devil Bringer allows Nero to pull enemies towards him and perform special grab attacks when their guard is down. This mechanic is easily my favorite addition to combat in this game.
Nero's second ability is the EX Gauge which the player has to rev up like an engine to perform more powerful attacks with the sword. I found this ability to be lacking because the extra time taken to charge attacks up didn't seem worth the little bit of extra damage you supposedly got from it. I got into trouble more often than not when using this ability either while revving it up or by missing my charged up attacks.
Dante's gameplay is similar to Nero's but it drops the two extra abilities I mentioned previously. Instead of the Devil Bringer grab system Dante gets access to the Style system from 3. This allows him to switch through a larger moveset for swordplay or guns, the Royal Guard style that adds a guard system that gathers energy from blocked attacks into an attack Dante can use against enemies, and the Trickster style that increases movement.
Dante gets access to more weapons than Nero, filling in the standard Devil Arm quotient for the game. Overall Dante is the more versitile character, and it feels a little jarring to get used to Nero's fighting style that focuses heavily on the grab-and-throw Devil Bringer, then change to Dante's extended moveset which drops the grab system entirely, and then back again.
To unlock new abilities in this game you use proud souls instead of red orbs like in previous games. Red orbs are still in the game and used as currency for items in the shop, and red orbs are still awarded from every enemy defeated and found floating around in missions. Proud souls are only awarded at the end of a mission. A convenient feature is the ability to unpurchase any ability any time you're in the shop which allows you to change your loadout between fights or missions if you would like to try out different abilities.
Devil Trigger is available after a few missions, and it is basically the same as usual. Nero gets a couple of extra moves to use.
Secret missions return in the game, and remain, in my opinion, uninteresting. They are usually very difficult to complete and give a reward of a blue orb fragment. Occasionally you will come across a secret mission as Nero or Dante that can only be completed by the other character. The game doesn't let you know this is the case, and you have to learn it on your own which can be a little bit annoying.
The difficulty curve in this game is high, like the others. There's a point when you have to fight Dante as Nero that took me 2 hours of tries to complete on Devil Hunter difficulty. There's also a couple of strange sections where you roll a die to move yourself around a gameboard to continue on, and because of the randomness of the die this is easily frusterating, especially at the end of the game. There's also a few times where it's hard to figure out exactly what the game wants you to do, but overall I was happy with the gameplay.
Overall I really liked this game, and I would recommend it to anyone that would like to try it out. Currently in the series I am ranking 3 at the top, trailed closely by 4, with 1 at the bottom. 2 doesn't get to be on the ranking.

This was my second Devil May Cry game I've played, for some reason I'm working backwards through the franchise. So, the story is fairly simple you start off playing as Nero, who I enjoyed playing more than I did Dante, but I enjoyed watching Dante's scenes more though, you find out the Order is evil and they eventually use the girl Nero loves as leverage to try to stop him from messing up their plot to essentially rule the world. Nero is a fun character to play because his arm gives him the ability to slam enemies and grab and pull them Scorpian style (Mortal Kombat). I didn't really use the ability his bike engine sword gives you where you can rev it up and make the next attack to powerful, I found the time to rev up the meter wasn't worth it. Dante on the other hand is fun to play since he has different stances to choose from (each stance has different attacks and combos), and he also gets a whole arsenal of weaponry, 3 ranged weapons and 3 melee weapons. This gives him more variety in combat and makes getting S ranks way easier. I really enjoyed the conversations between these two characters, Dante the funny, outgoing, laid back guy, Nero is more determined and out to prove himself yet a little disrespectful in a good way. The environment is beautiful, every piece of architecture is amazing and very detailed. The Bosses are pretty well done as well, every boss you fight starts off as a puzzle to figure how you're going to attack and then excuting it. But it also brings up what is bad about this game.
I love this game but it does have some things that I could do without or could be improved on. First the Bosses, the first time you play them it fun and challenging, but they make you fight each one of them 3 times, 2 with Nero and 1 with Dante. I feel like they got lazy and decided just to throw the same bosses at you instead of new ones. Another thing that bothered me and sort of ruined the game for me alittle was the Boss fight with the huge statue and then the level after that. The fight with the statue was sort of weird, if he destoryed the platform you are on you float down then a cutscene which leads you to being a different platform magically. The whole fight took me out of the experience, but then the level after that is where they bring back the Dice game that you play on an earlier level. It would've been fine if you had to do it once or twice but it felt like a good 30 minutes of rolling the dice over and over again, this is also where you fight the Bosses for the third time. One last thing that bothered me was the camera, for the most part it wasn't bad but sometimes it would be your worst enemy, floating behind walls or having the worst angle for a fight.
Overall I enjoyed the game and definitely recommend it to anyone who is interested in Devil May Cry or any good action game. I've read bad things about this game like Capcom didn't put much effort into this game and its not really that good, I can see where they're coming from but to me it was a pretty good game. I also didn't mind playing as a new character and Dante sharing the spotlight, maybe because I haven't played the past games yet but I played and reviewed this from a unbiased point of view which I think other people should do the same.

Now, in order for a tactical, squad-based shooter like Brothers in Arms to succeed, three key elements need to work: level design for allowing tactical choices, the squad commands for being able to efficiently tell your squads what to do, and the AI for being able to actually do to what you tell them to do.
The level design is open enough to allow for flanking and other such tactical strategies. You'll get a spot for one squad to lay down supressing fire while your other squad or yourself gets a path to flank them. It also doesn't get too repetitive in repeating that formula through every level though, so it keeps things fresh. In some levels, for example, you get to command a tank and you and your squad have to use the tank as cover while moving down empty streets towards the enemy. The level design also provides a decent challenge for players who enjoy that, like myself, though two or three of the levels do ramp up the difficulty quite unexpectedly. The level design isn't as open as I hoped, as you usually get only one or two ways to flank an enemy. I would have preferred lots of ways to get around the enemy so there are more options available to the player. However, the level design is good enough that it emphasises the main mechanic of the game, that is supressing and flanking, and keeps it fresh throughout.
Controlling squads is very easy and very quick, both of which are very important if you're in a firefight. Telling one squad to suppress an enemy then switching to your other squad and telling them to move to a certain postition is very simple and straightforward. No complaints here.
The AI is probably the most important aspect that needs to be good in a game like this, and for the most part, the AI was good. Your squads will follow your commands quite well, be it suppressing an enemy or charging they're position. They listen well and react quickly to whatever you tell them. Occasionally though, the AI had it's hiccups. A couple times one of my squadmates would be killed because they took cover on the wrong side of a wall and twice I had to continue the rest of a level without a squadmate because they got stuck in a bush and couldn't move. The enemy AI could have been better, as they usually stick only to their cover and never try to flank you or try any other aggressive tactics that could have added a little more to the gameplay. For the most part though, the AI is good and does its job very well.
As for the rest of the game, the voice acting and writing aren't awful, but they're not that good. I am SO glad to see you guys! - Jospeh Hartsock, Brothers In Arms Road To Hill 30
THE GOOD
Authentic environments range from visually stunning (In the sense of scope) to downright ugly. Some of the character animations are a bit awkward, and one particular glitch sent a German rifleman across the map where he promptly caught himself on barbed wire and ruined the mood. The textures could be worse, but that's like saying that Duke Nukem Flopped could've been more hyped. For 2005, graphically speaking, it's mediocre. Not great, not terrible, not a benchmark for games and not something you'll want to recycle for toilet paper. While being failry realistic, it suffers from having people die very quickly, which can be frustrating when you need that person for a particular job, as shown perfectly by Objective XYZ. The multiplayer has two players who each command two teams to try and eliminate the other team. While not a straight up shooter, it would be nice to see some other objectives rather than just kill everyone else. This is BiA, not Quake.
THE GREAT
The story is fantastic. Not Half Life fantastic mind you, you do not have a wide range of ways to be attached to the game. Be that as it is, BiA is still worth playing just for it's story. Gritty, depressing and a bit too real at times, BiA is not for children, those with a weak stomach or those who get attached to characters quickly. The gameplay is solid and fair, giving you advantages when you constantly fail, but also giving you the choice wheather or not you take that extra. You will get attached to characters, some quicker than others, and if they die in combat, or via scripted event, it can be a real pain, due to the fact that you cannot save whenever you want. This can be good though, it pushes the story along and makes character deaths even more shocking than in games such as Halo: Combat Evolved.
THE UGLY
Most players will die a few times during this game, myself included. The introduction of a few characters can feel a bit strange when they either die or are never mentioned again during later missions. One death in particular was shocking, although it did seem a bit pointless, as I had been involved in the game quite a bit and hadn't gotten a grasp on who he was or why he was there. The following mission had you sniping from a tower while you sent your soldiers to work down below, but this personally felt like it wanted to be an RTS for a mission. For half the mission, either the enemy soldiers are too far away or the bloody tanks get in the way which make it feel less team oriented, and more like a straight up FPS while still keeping the same mechanics, which means that getting killed instantly by a tank shell is not impossible. Thankfully it only lasted one mission and was not seen again.
THE VERDICT
This is the best game in the series so far. Earned in Blood shows a different perspective, which is fine, but storywise the third game Hell's Highway has an intro cutscene which basically sums up Road to Hill 30 and Earned in Blood, which may make you wonder why you bought RtH30 and EiB, but you bought them because you are a good boy and played the first ones because they were better games.
SIMILAR GAMES
-Earned in Blood, Hell's Highway to a lesser extent
-Star Wars Republic Commando

I played BiA: Road to Hill 30 when it first came out in 2008 and really enjoyed it. Since I recently bought the BiA pack from the recent Steam sale I thought I'd revisit it before continuing on with the other two. So how well did it hold up five years later? Not well I'm afraid. The graphics haven't aged well at all but they are serviceable. Level design is pretty bland. Grasslands with a few humps are the order of the day,  My biggest issue was the gunplay.  You can be point blank range from an enemy and there's a very good chance you will miss. This goes for using the iron sights as well. I can't remember another shooter where the guns were so inaccurate. Mission variety was okay. Escort this guy, take this house, typical military mission fare. There are some positives though. The ability to control your squads is very easy and they do their job okay. The scope of the game is cinematic and the sound design is wonderful. The level protecting the church was a good time, especially since you get a scoped rifle that is very accurate.  The banter between your squad before the level starts is realistic and adds some humanity to the proceedings.  Overall, BiA gets a recommendation from me. It's a shooter that any fan of WW2 should play at least once. Welp, onto the next installment.

After beating Resident Evil 7 twice now, I can assure any doubters that it is the perfect modernization of the original game's themes and concepts. It's not RE4, which was a masterpiece in its own right, but its still fits into the current plethora of horror games.  Instead of taking the action focus of the last two release and puts it back in the background.  Avoidance and preservation are going to be big focuses of your play time.  The pistol is very weak and it takes quite a few shots to down most of the enemies with it and its the weapon your going to find most the ammo for.  The shotgun on the other hand feels like a tank, when you shoot it, you can expect something to tobble.  Ammo is on the low side for it and the other speciality guns you run across, so you will get used to just running around the enemies you can.
As far as graphics go, I thought most of the game is breathtaking.  The textures are all really good and by narrowing the focus of the game to just a few areas, I feel like they were able to invest more heavily in making sure each one works. This of course goes with the overall tone and theme, which is another thing the game gets right.  It feels dark and harrowing in the mansion and around it.  As you repeat the same areas with new spins, you will be able to navigate it like your own house.  There are so many little details that make it feel fully realized as a place (photographs, small things like lighting being in realistic places, etc.), it was a joy to see how each new area would look and feel.  The sound should also be applauded since I feel like it was a huge factor in the experience.  Everyone has meaty footsteps and guns are like cannons, but small details like hearing bugs when your outside made it also a joy to listen to.
I would recommend anyone buy and give this game a chance if your interested in horror or puzzle games, the only reason  you may not enjoy it is if you are looking for something where you want to kill more.

RE7 is a triumph and a real comeback for the series after the forgettable RE6. The game takes modern lessons from Outlast and Alien: Isolation while making sure that a 'classic' Resident Evil feel is present throughout. Expect puzzles, tense exploration, backtracking, freakish enemies, and impressively detailed levels. Pacing and tone shift throughout, which makes sure the game doesn't become repetitive or overbearing.
RE7 is an instant classic for the survival horror genre and gets a very strong recommendation from me.

Marginal game disguised as a good one.  Spam <square> to win. It all depends on who can stagger lock who first.
*edit*
I think i need to clarify since I really want (and trying hard) to like this game.
I should also note that I have not, and have no plans on uninstalling this game and getting my money back even though I have issues with it.  I think sloclap should be commended on what they did here.
This applies to pvp (and lets be honest, that is 98% of this game's appeal):
This also assumes that you have put together at least a somewhat coherent deck.
There is a smaller stamina penalty for spamming attack vs blocking/dodging--so generally that is what you get in 1v1 fights.  Spam attack, staggerlock and win (especially the drunken boxer style which offers both avoid and attack at same time.  Lock on, spam attack and profit.  I have litterally locked on, and spammed attack while talking to my girlfriend, not paying ANY attention and won a round in 1v1).
There is a heavier stam penalty for blocking/dodging--so if your goal is to win rounds, why bother?  Just start mashing attack.
Ever watched a boxing match?  Ever seen the end of rounds when both fighters are gassed?  They dont swing a lot. It takes a lot of energy to swing--less to block.  But in this game, if you block you will burn stam way sooner than when swinging.  Its just unrealistic.
The 1v1 fights where you actually get an opponent who is anti-spam (who actually dodges, uses special ability, blocking and attack all combined with a strategy) can be extremely entertaining.  Yes they do exist.   These encounters alone have given me hope for this game:  Do a few attacks, block a few, disengage and either try a different opening moveset or use the same one (depending how you did against your oppenent in the outset)--you know, like a real fight.
But unless depletion of stamina on attack is forced in game mechanics (see: Dark Souls/Nioh) these encounters are rare, and you have to depend on your oppenent to play like its a real fight.
So hopefully they balance the stamina use a little better and this game will be around for awhile, otherwise I think people are going to get bored as it takes little skill (see putting toghether a coherent deck) to win.

A sequel to Kingdom, New Lands is an interesting rogue-like/town-management-lite game that ALMOST work as a game.  They have added a small number of new content since the original, but unfortunately the gameplay remains unchanged for the most part, and the same issues that plague the first game are still present, most notably the wonky AI.  Copy/pasted below is my review of the original game.
"You are a prince/princess. You have nothing but a horse. You have to fend of evil monsters, and build a kingdom.
I actually quite enjoyed the semi-relaxing, minimalistic but borderline-just-one-more-turn-addictive gameplay.
You can choose which buildings to upgrade, and VERY loosely guide your AI followers (by buying your choice of weapon, building tool, or farming tool and leaving them for to pick up), but beyond that only other gameplay consists of your character running PRAYING the AI will do something useful with your followers. And there lies the problem - the AI.
The problem is, the gameplay is perhaps a wee bit TOO simplistic, providing the player with next to no control, with too much reliance on an AI, which, sadly just isn't very good. While you can buy weapons and tools for your followers, you can't actually control what they do or where they go with them. It is frustrating once you realised after a few games that the AI followers will NEVER do what you expect of them, that they will infact NEVER do what is needed."

TL;DR: Kingdom: New lands is a game with stupidly simple mechanics shrouded by a nice pixel aesthetic and sound design. Watch the first 45 seconds of the main trailer. That's basically what you do for a vast majority of the time spent in this game. No joke, just holding left or right.
This game has great aesthetic but is ubelievably boring and does little to none in order to keep your attention. Everything is so overly simplified that I question why the game made me touch the keyboard.  The controls make the game tedius as all hell. Left arrow, Right arrow, Down arrow on a 2D plane. That's all you do, all game. Your objective is essentially the same every level. Build a camp, recruit some archers/builders, build defense, expand, start making income in order to escape on the boat and do it all over again. And it's a chore. You spend most of the time running back and forth collecting money.
The amount of things you can actually build are extremely limited. You are given locations to build walls and towers for the archers. Note that I said "given" locations. Which can be a little inconvenient. So if you wanted a wall to cover a certain area or be closer to your tower and there's no plot for it, you're SOL. Also, when you build an archer tower, one of your archers will automatically garrison it. Cool, right? Except it's not very cool when you no longer need that archer sitting in that tower because you have more outer defenses that need him but he won't budge and you can't do anything about it. So the optimal strategy I've figured is to simply not build defenses for as long as possible.
Without taking the time to figure it out or read a guide. You will mess up. There's no real challenge to the game. No real strategy. You either know what things do and play correct. Or don't understand how things work yet and make mistakes. One good source of income, the merchant, has a small shack that he slowly walks in between to give you money. If you chop down a tree near his shack, he's gone for the level. That's a decent source of coins gone because you were just chopping down trees because you weren't sure if you needed to do that or not.
It's basically a walking simulator. You're just on a horse going back and forth. Need some money, go run over to your farmers, hunters. Then run back to the area you were attempting to upgrade and expand. Then you need more recruits for your expansion. Run all the way out to a vagrant camp and get some recruits. Which if you get recruits at the wrong time, they may just get attacked by the night creatures. So you have to make sure you're timing it and only going out to grab new recruits in the morning.
And then there's the creatures that come out at night. This sounds like the fun part, right? Nah, it's really the most painful and non-sensical of it all. You cannot judge what nights you will be attacked and from which direction (2D plane, left or right). So, you generally want to have some decent defense on both sides. Which the defense is pretty pure RNG. Earlier in the game, you have archers and maybe catapults behind your walls lobbing arrows and rocks at the monsters. The catapult is great, as long as it hits. It can take out an entire enemy attack in one good lob. Or just keep missing and be useless. So, good luck with that. The monstes also arbitrarily do and don't attack things. They'll attack any walls or units they are able to get to. But they won't bring down any defense towers or break many buildings. They're really just meant to be a nuisance and make the whole thing take longer. Because if you lose people, you gotta then go run to get more recruits all while your income is now shot.
When you have a good setup and defense going, coins coming in from multiple sources, it's time to set up the boat. The boat requires a lot of coin and for you to sit there pressing the down arrow key over and over again until you purchase about 30-50 little pieces that your builders put together. Then the boat get's built and is pushed into the water and you have a slight sense of accomplishment before the next painful realization. Your workers littlerally push the boat to the dock (while it's in the river) while some archers sit on top for defense. And they push this boat slowwwwwww
So if you've got the time, like a lot of time, and losing these workers, archers essentially doesn't hurt you too much then they may eventually reach the dock. Then you can round up some more units and leave. Then you kinda just do it all over again with a couple unlocks that don't really make the game much more exciting. This game is just not really fun and feels like a slow, painful waste of time.

This really is one of those games that I want to like. The concept is great, the art style is fantastic, and the music is relaxing, what more could you want?
But the game mechanics are lacking, enough that it will get increasingly frustrating if you really want to win this game. Every time I lost in this game, moreso than any game I can remember in the recent past, my insticitive reaction was 'no fair, that wasn't my fault,' and I have trouble getting absorbed into a game that creates that kind of feeling while playing.
Most of the complaints have been said already, but while most of your tasks revolve around raising money and followers, you have little to no control over any of those things. You can designate where things are built, but only sort of (specific things can only be specific places, and sometimes not in the places that make the most sense), and you can designate what role your followers fill. But you can't tell them where to go or what to do. So you can raise troops, only to have all but a couple of them wander off in the opposite direction of where you want them, and you have absolutely no way to get them where you need them.
Simply put, you have no way to control your kingdom, and this game advertises like that is the whole point of the game. You set things up in more or less a preset layout, and hope your minions cooperate. But they probably won't. And there won't be anything that you can do to change that.
But hey, it looks great, and it can be a relaxing play for a while. But it will start to get frustrating, I promise.

DISCLAIMER - this is MY PERSONAL OPINION. As with all opinions from internet randos, take it with a grain of salt.
(My review "spoils" a few game mechanics. If you only want the general opinion, read only the last paragraph.)
When you start out, you get a very basic explanation - this is your camp, this is how you get builders & archers, these are walls, enjoy. You need to guess that stone-piles will be watchtowers, that the strange hut you get after a certain camp upgrade is a siege workshop that produces catapults, that the wooden relic will allow you to get stone walls, that giving money to the castle makes knights, that knights will take your archers as entourage and PREVENT THEM FROM HUNTING, that giving money to the flag in front of your outer wall will send the knights towards the enemy portal. This and some other things are HUGE money sinks, that neither explain their functionality, nor the downsides of having them. Wanna know how much money the financier stored in your castle? Well you're just out of luck, because, apparently, monarch don't get clearance for that information.
There is nothing you yourself can actively do. Once your hire your people & commission the upgrades, there is no way to directly influence what your underlings are doing. You can't even get them to change the side they're standing on, so when one side doesn't need guarding, the subjects standing there just twiddle their thumbs while the other deals with the invasion. And you yourself can't attack or do anything, which is a good lead-in into the last problem :
This game wastes your time on every turn. Your horse (latter steeds can apparently be better, but the game is so repetitive that I don't see the point in playing until that point) is slow, it's sprint is rather short, so traversal is a pain. You're a sitting duck during the night, as you can't do anything. Winter wastes your time even further, by severely limiting your income, thus limiting your already small pool of interactions during the day. I don't even know how long it takes for the boat to reach the pier, because I have no patience for rebuilding during winter after two large attacks and a bloodmoon. I tried sending the knights out, but they would reach the portal a few seconds after the enemy starts spawning, and fail, because as soon as a knight dies, his entourage just hightails it outta there, getting picked off one by one in the process.
I got Kingdom in a bundle, and am happy that I didn't buy it separately. While some of my misgivings might've been simply because of bad luck, enough of them were, in my opinion, due to bad game design, to encourage people to hold off from buying it. It's a pretty looking foundation for a potentially good game, but there's too little to actually do, and what's there quickly gets boring & irritating.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
@Raw Fury (I haven't seen a way to respond to a dev response, and I wrote too much to fit into a coment, so I hope this update will suffice)
First off, thanks for your kind response.
You're probably right about it just not being for everyone. It's not like I totally dislike the game, and with some more patience, like Melar suggested, I might have gotten into it. Having said patience takes time though, and considering how spoiled for choice we are nowadays, and how fast-paced live can be, giving up that time isn't always an option a person has and/or wants to take. (But that's a bit off-topic.)
While I understand the idea of mystery, I think that, when interacting with said mystery can set you back, it's better done in a more fast-paced gameplay style. Most rogue-lites have the possibility of fairly short game sessions, where experimenting with loadouts & unknown modifiers happens very quickly & doesn't set you back a lot. The problem I had in this case was that the setbacks I suffered through the slow discovery of mechanics, rather than resulting in my swift demise, resulted in a long, drawn-out path to a snowed-in poor man's grave. While I could very well utilize what I had learned for a better next playthrough, the process of rebuilding would have, because of the slow pacing & the periods of down time at night where you can't take meaningful actions, been a bit too slow to be enjoyable for me.
In the end, as I've mentioned, I might've just had a bit of bad luck in that I survived for far too long on my first try, and might have enjoyed it more if my death-respawn cycle was a bit shorter. But, for my personal taste, the pace was just a bit too slow. And not knowing how much money you have in the bank hinders your decision-making, which is unfortunate. I mean, I could count myself, but apparently he also multiplies the money by a tiny bit? And without numbers, that was just not really possible to gauge without a lot of experimentation.
The way the pixelart is utilized is very nice though, and I liked the soundtrack & sound design, and the general idea of the game was interesting, and certainly eye-catching.
Enough people like it , so I guess you just can't make everybody happy.
I wish you good luck in your future endeavors =)

UPDATED 7/8/2014
Since a number of people were asking me to re-review the game in its current state, I finally relented and decided to try the game again.  These are my thoughts.
I find that many improvements have indeed been made.  This is to be expected, and very much welcomed.  I find that many of the features such as the shipyard and flight models have been improved with more easy-to-use controls and additional features.  A quick rundown of some of the key features and improvements I noticed:
* Better inter/intra-system navigation and map
* Slightly improved combat gameplay
* Improved flight model and warp systems
* Missions, Cargo, and semi-functional stores
* Semi-functional "career" mode.  More on this below.
Some things that are still issues:
* Not developer's fault, but many workshop ships no longer function out-of-the-box due to creators failing to update them for new patches.
* Overall, game still feels quite clunky and difficult to use.  Somewhat high learning curve unless you're wiling to read a lot.
>> Documentation has been improved.  Just be prepared for lots of reading.
* Crash to desktop is common.  Crashes more as your ship's # of modules increase
>> Relatively decent auto-save means you won't loose too much progress.
* See more below
The game is still quite confusing and you often still don't even know what's going on.  There's still a lot left to be desired I think.
Overall, the game has improved. Though I can't say that this is something to get especially excited about.  "Why are you being such a debbie downer" you ask?  Well, it's an alpha.  It is SUPPOSED to improve.  If it didn't, it's not worthy of even being sold.
I still do not recommend this game.  There is a "But" however... Here are my thoughts
Many critical features have been added and improved to a more usable state.  The warp mechanism has been tremendously improved.  The shipyard build system also deserves a mention as a vast improvement.  More customizability and more controls to fine tune your construction.  Though this can make things a bit more confusing to the new person or returning player, as with some of the other expanded features.  This is made up for with the improved documentation.  But beware, decent amounts of reading is required.  There are also some tweaks and improvements to the combat system.  It makes more sense but can still be awkward.  The galaxy map has also gotten a big makeover and is MUCH easier to understand.
There are many things that still are confusing and unfinished in this game.  The "career" mode is clearly unfinished and requires more attention.  From what I can tell, it's a misleadingly named "survival" mode at the moment.  However, it fails at that as well.  You have credits and the idea is to earn more through cargo or more "illigitimate" means. Basically, you start out by picking ANY ship from the workshop or stock selections.  No cost.  If you run out of money buying cargo to load into your mega-freighter you downloaded and didn't have to pay for, then just select any of the ship-part categories and sell any number of the "999" parts you somehow own from the start.  Just sell a couple Tier 5 weapons or ship bridges and you immediately have so much cash that the display has to use exponential notation (e.g. 1,000,000^E10).
Verdict:  Not recommended.  The game is still definitely unfinished.  There is not much polish. While there are a number of great improvements, I still cannot justify this game as a purchase.  It's confusing for new/returning players unless you're a quick learner or wanna read all the documentation.  Without developer input, I estimate this game is less than 50% done; though considerably more than the 6% quoted by the dev around the time of my original review 7 months ago.
My point still stands.  Do not buy the game unless you want to support the developer or really like the idea this game stands for.  It is playable now, so if you just really wanna get into space and do things, then go for it. I recommend waiting until a sale, however.  It is not worth $19.99 to me.  If it had a price-tag of about $10, it may be a good price if you're willing to put up with the downsides of a relatively mid-level-alpha.

Devil May Cry 4 PC is a damn good game, and it definitely shows that japanese devs can made a good PC release when they try. While the story is a bit meh, and has definite plot holes (kind of par for the course), it's serviceable enough to not be too much of a negative. While I can see why people hated on Nero before this was released, he's definitely a likable character, and he's pretty fun to play, definitely acting as a nice Sakura to Dante's Ryu and Vergil's Ken gameplay wise. On top of that, as mentioned, this is an exceptional PC release for a company that primarily makes console games (especially compared to the crap ports that DMC3 & RE4 apparently are). I see Bound in Blood as a total reversal from its predecessor - with the sequel now having significantly better mechanics at the cost of one of the blandest stories in the franchise. If you played the first and liked the story, you’re going to buy and play this to see how Ray ended up being the total bada** he was. But even still, you’ll feel tempted to skip through a lot of cutscenes to skip bland character stories until the end.
The game follows the story of two brothers who desert their army force to defend their family home. When they get there, they get back in touch with their other brother. To rebuild their home and get rich beyond their wildest dreams, they set off to Mexico for the sake of that golden treasure. Along the way, they run into some cool and not-so-cool indians, the big wigs of the army they abandoned, a foxy mamacita, and numerous sketchy Mexicans that meet and exceed stereotypical expectations. I will say that the writing was passable and focused primarily on the brotherly bonds, but left something to be desired in terms of wanting to be interested in other subplots and its characters.
As for the actual gameplay, I just can’t get over how fluid the cover system was in this game - it was perfectly responsive to tense shootouts. The game focuses on two styles of gameplay based on the two brothers. Both have similar styles - one plays to a run and gun style while the other relies on  long-ranged combat with some elements of stealth. But because both classes have pistols that you’ll use more than anything else because of the ubiquity of ammo, there’s little that sets them apart. Sure, there’s missions that involve each brother going into certain zones for a few minutes. But that’s about as differing as it gets. Weapon upgrades are based on the money you collect in sidequests. I’ll say that it’s worth it - since its rare for henchmen to drop great weapons, and they don’t drop the best guns in the game that have one shot capabilities.The grind doesn’t take as long as you think, and the rich quasi-open world environments (at that time). Again, you want to complain about the barren world, but it’s like late 1800s to early 1900s Mexico. There’s nothing there.
Levels are designed well, but the AI’s not so great. But in the instance of laddergoat (where you can force animals to walk up ladders), it can be hilariously bad. But it doesn’t detract from the difficulty. There’s also quick draw duel mechanics they just happen to shoehorn into every single battle. It’s cool, but definitely overdone. You don’t get a sense of progression - they’re all just the same and easy enough for you to beat in less than 3 tries.
Bound in blood should satiate FPS fans that crave a decent shootout. Just don’t expect the story to work wonders.

Ok, let me say this first. I went into this adventure with high hopes based on the reviews this game received. I wish I hadn't. Im going to go ahead and start with what worked with this game (Sorry if this portion seems lacking); Quick paced story and setups, you can tell from the get-go this game will be mostly about trying to immerse you directly into Vito's view of the world. The textures in this game are smooth and pleasing (though maybe too much so, more on that later) and overall it feels well polished, though a bit "Thin". Gun fights in this game are actually pretty good.
Told you it would be a little sparse. Ok, heres what doesnt work so well and things i just genuinely did not like. The world you are dropped into feels so EMPTY! I mean, i see people wandering the streets yet they might as well be cardboard cutouts or mannequins like an episode of The Twilight Zone, nobody interacts with Vito, they just sort of exist. Youre basically stuck on rails in order to advance the narrative, there are no (worthwhile) side jobs to encounter, money feels useless in this game (i spent maybe 2% of ALL ACQUIRED MONEY in this game because there was just no point. The style feels too...cartoony? i dont know how to describe it, its as if youre viewing all of these events through rose tinted glasses, its all just too "Crisp" for a mafia game with the content this one utilizes. Driving in this game is a joke, yeah the cars of yester-decade werent exactly ferraris but come on, it feels like im driving a powerwheels car on a frozen lake, its horrid. Then theres how crime can occur in this game, im talking non-narrative crime, its really superficial. You sideswipe a car? cops chase you. You speed? Cops chase you...its supposed to be realistic i suppose? but it feels cheaply setup. And you cannot for the life of you, run anyone over in a comical fashion (think GTA) they suddenly receive super human reflexes and strength and the most you can hope to do is knock them over (which somehow kills them?). And then theres the whole point of this game, which is the story...oh boy, does this story BBLLLOOOOW
I like a good mob movie/game, i enjoy twists and drama and bloodshed for the sake of the family but...this story feels so sloppily thrown together, its like someone saw Goodfellas once, got his drunk friends together and tried to make their own movie with a shoestring budget and cliched ideas. If it were on sale for less than 10 dollars, i would say "buy it, its a decent enough game in its own world" but stand it next to GTA or anything similar and it feels hollow.

This game was absolutely incredible when I first started playing it in July of 2013. At first it seemed like just another Call of Duty ripoff that decided to take the free-to-play route, but as I invested more time into the game, I began realizing how distinct this game is from others. Just pressing the V key is enough to see that.
In all honesty I don't know where to begin. The weapon balancing was pretty good, but that kinda changed later. The customization options were, and still are, broad and lets you really personalize your character. The community was fantastic for the most part, and as time went on, the playerbase decreased, which led to each lobby being like those old towns you hear about where everyone knows each other.
There was a time for about a year and a half where the developers did not update the game due to internal problems, and the game's functionality certainly reflected that. The servers didn't work too well, constantly crashed, were rather laggy, ect. A lot of the playerbase died out at this point since the game was having these problems, but it just made the loyal parts of the community closer.
Then they updated it after all that time with the Parity patch. They took all of the new content from the PS4 version and brought it to PC, which everyone was excited for at first. What ended up happening was we got a game that felt really strange and unlike what we were used to. Recoil was reduced greatly, which limited the viable builds to be damage-focused builds for the weapons. The question for moving further into the game changed from "how can I build this gun to fit my playstyle and comfort?" to "how can I build this gun to do more damage?". To me, this lack of diversity ruins the fun for me, especially considering the amount of diversity before the Parity patch.
If I were to have written this three years ago, I would have said that this was the best multiplayer FPS game available and that if you are willing to grind a bit to find equipment that matches your playstyle, you will enjoy this game greatly. But sadly I can't say that anymore. I would not recommend this game to anyone looking for a fresh FPS experience.

I build for accuracy and low recoil on my weapons, and I don't tend to play at the breakneck speeds that some folks like to. I used to like the game, I've put money into it, but I'm done with it.  It is free, so I'd recommend giving it a shot, but I can't recommend it as any sort of a fun game anymore.

Disclaimers: Completed the playthrough in 9 hours, medium settings. Haven't played any of the previous Resident Evil games. Not a follower of the Resident Evil movies. Lets get to the review!
First person perspective in a survival-horror setting. The gameplay mechanics are not vast or complex but they are done right. Conserving ammo and health potions is a must. You can craft items in game and they it is smartly implemented. Some items share components, so you always have to see which item you need more at that time. There are some puzzles to be solved in between, which I really liked.
For this type of game, the story is more than half of the reason why it can fail or succeed. Here, the story delivers. From the trailer you can see the main character is in search of his wife and he ends up in a remote house in the middle of a forest. And the horror entails. The best part of the story is that there is no expedition or motage of events shown to tell the story. It is all done through video tapes and memories, which you basically see from 2 characters. The whole story does not unfold till the very end and it keeps you gripped the whole time.
In a horror game, the scare does not work if you don't build up the tension. In this game, as soon as you take your first step, they start building the tension and it piles up till they give you a scare which makes it really effective. Another great thing about the level design that even though it is not vast, but made available in bits and pieces so even after going through the same area after 4 or 5 times you can get into new stuff.
The main character is Ethan. He starts the game with the main objective of finding his wife, but then as he finds out new things, his objective changes. This makes for a good character development. There are only a bunch of characters in this secluded house, but all of them really takes the spotlight when it is their show. The voice acting is great and the animation is well done.
The game do have two different endings. But apart from that, the scare only works for the first time. When you know, when or how something is coming at you, the surprise factor is not really great which lessens the experience.
Whether or not, you have played or watched the Resident Evil games or movies, this one is a must for every fan of a good single player campaign. At the time, when every game is turning to a money printing machine and is delivered in pieces through DLCs or micro transactions, this game keeps it real and takes it back to good old days of single player games.

Welcome to the family.
After playing through the campaign twice, and playing through most of the already released DLC, It is safe to say that Resident Evil is back! This game is awesome! It is not for the faint of heart, but if you love survival-horror, get yourself a copy, because RE7/Biohazard 7 delivers.
I haven’t enjoyed a survival horror game this much since I played RE4 for the first time. RE7 delivers on all fronts. I really enjoyed the switch to first person view, which made the horror feel a little more real to me. My heart got some good cardio workouts in.
Also it is a great jumping in point for players who are new to the Resident Evil universe/story. It has a few subtle nods to the old game storyline, but is a new enough story that new players will not be lost at all.
Aside from a few unanswered questions in the story (which perhaps the future DLC will answer), it has great graphics, great atmosphere, great gameplay, and great story. I give it a 9.5/10.
All in all a must have for Survival-Horror fans.

Two years ago, if someone told me that it would have been possible to create a game so short, yet so genuinely horrifying and gritty to the very end, I'd have referred them to the likes of Alien Isolation, which also won bonus points for length and originality. Now, we have a contender, one that I genuinely believe to be worthy of comparison to legends such as Alien Isolation in this regard: Resident Evil 7.
Fast forward to the present, Resident Evil 7 returns to the roots of the Resident Evil series: Slow paced, exploratory, puzzle-based gameplay that empasizes on a slow-paced and exploratory gameplay style. No longer do we have heavily armed combatants with serious skills such as Resident Evil 5 and 6, where stealth and discipline were eschewed. Here, we have true , pant-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ horror played out in a first-person angle.

"Amongst the Sleep" is a surprisingly good little survival horror game that invokes your primal fears by placing you in the body of a small toddler that can barely walk upright. What may seem amusing at first quickly becomes outright scary as the child's unique perception of reality turns seemingly mundane objects and locations (such as a closet or a playground) into pure nightmare fuel. Even when the twist at the end of the story reveals the toddler's terrors to be relatively normal from an adult's point of view, the anxiety and uneasiness you will experience throughout the game will not simply fade away, as it merely replaces the imaginative fear with a real one.
Unfortunately, the enjoyment you can get from this game is drastically limited by it's very short length, with a walkthrough taking little more than roughly two hours. It is perhaps something to be expected from a game that evolved from a student project, but still, by the time the credits roll you may feel extremely disappointed and longing for more. For what little it's worth, the game still manages to scare the hell out of you for these two hours.

Mordheim has come by now a long way and it can keep up with many AAA Titles I saw over the years, it came a far way and I can tell you it was a joy of a ride to see the game growing together with the community.
It has its flaws, but these flaws are what makes the game charming to me.
---RNG---
The RNG can be very brutal like in the old X-COM games where a critical hit just keeps missing, but the moment when you still manage to pull off a victory despite the odds can be so much more rewarding.
---Difficulty---
The difficulty of the game is very high and it affords a lot of tactical thinking to make progress, your warband will get injured, insane or might even die on your way of progress. In this regard it keeps itself a bit more roguelike that you progress in a veteran System to permanently unlock feats for existing and future Warbands.
---Fun---
A big part of the Fun to me comes to me from the difficulty and so does the rage I feel in some moments, but let me tell you it is glorious to do. The Atmosphere is certainly there being in the dark grey alley's of Mordheim and to see the destroyed buildings and Chaos influenced area's all around.
To build up your own Warband from Scratch, seeing them rank up and life or die to tell their own stories really makes this game to me. I have a little Skaven (Verminkin) named Nirk that lost his arm in the first Mission I set him into. But this little Henchman survived up to the point of writing this review and pulled himself through despite so many times where I thought him lost. He won a special place in my heart and I will cry the day he won't make it home.
You will get easily attached to your Warband and mourn the loss of your favorite Units, as you customized them with 4 color and 2 skin variations on each body part, as well the several skin tones to choose from.
The Campaign Missions are brutaly hard and very fun to play in my opinion, something anyone who enjoys a challenge will love.
The Development team is small and for their size of 20 dev's what they created here is truly astonishing and you can tell by my review that I'm simply in love with the game and wish them only the best for its future lifespan!
---Recommendation---
I recommend this game to anyone who loves a challenge like in the old X-COM games and loves the rage enducing nature that RNG can have with your plans. The fact that the tide of battle can shift in one moment to the next will keep you on your toes throughout the battle, while you scavange for loot and wyrdstones to keep your Boss satisfied and rank up not only your warband but also in the Veteran System and Factions to unlock Units and other Bonus.
The games difficulty is certainly not for everyone, but if you love a challenge and don't mind the game being Early Access, in the current state it is one of the best I played in the last year.
It easily happens that you find yourself at 3 am wondering what happened to your time, as the "one more round!" is very present in this.

Not without merit, but thoroughly mediocre.
The good:
The ship builder is the primary draw of this game- very versatile, can design whatever manner of ship you wish. The shipbuilder in Kinetic Void is more of a creative endeavour than anything else- unlike Kerbal Space Program, you do not need to worry about engineering constraints, efficiency, or performance very much. Perhaps that is appealing, perhaps not.
The matter of taste:
Even in campaign mode, the game is very very sandboxy. You are given very little direction, just let out into the galaxy and accosted by radio about missions. Absolute freedom, but absolutely no story or direction.
The ugly:
This game is utterly lacking in polish. Campaign mode opens up with an interminable tutorial, a series of pop-up text boxes listing what each button does- this is not a good way to present information. The interface looks awful, combat is unexciting. Space is ugly, a starless void with only waypoints as defining features. It is an exciting concept with utterly mediocre execution.
TL:DR Buy this if you want to make model ships, or really like sandbox games

Ok, let me say this first. I went into this adventure with high hopes based on the reviews this game received. I wish I hadn't. Im going to go ahead and start with what worked with this game (Sorry if this portion seems lacking); Quick paced story and setups, you can tell from the get-go this game will be mostly about trying to immerse you directly into Vito's view of the world. The textures in this game are smooth and pleasing (though maybe too much so, more on that later) and overall it feels well polished, though a bit "Thin". Gun fights in this game are actually pretty good.
Told you it would be a little sparse. Ok, heres what doesnt work so well and things i just genuinely did not like. The world you are dropped into feels so EMPTY! I mean, i see people wandering the streets yet they might as well be cardboard cutouts or mannequins like an episode of The Twilight Zone, nobody interacts with Vito, they just sort of exist. Youre basically stuck on rails in order to advance the narrative, there are no (worthwhile) side jobs to encounter, money feels useless in this game (i spent maybe 2% of ALL ACQUIRED MONEY in this game because there was just no point. The style feels too...cartoony? i dont know how to describe it, its as if youre viewing all of these events through rose tinted glasses, its all just too "Crisp" for a mafia game with the content this one utilizes. Driving in this game is a joke, yeah the cars of yester-decade werent exactly ferraris but come on, it feels like im driving a powerwheels car on a frozen lake, its horrid. Then theres how crime can occur in this game, im talking non-narrative crime, its really superficial. You sideswipe a car? cops chase you. You speed? Cops chase you...its supposed to be realistic i suppose? but it feels cheaply setup. And you cannot for the life of you, run anyone over in a comical fashion (think GTA) they suddenly receive super human reflexes and strength and the most you can hope to do is knock them over (which somehow kills them?). And then theres the whole point of this game, which is the story...oh boy, does this story BBLLLOOOOW
I like a good mob movie/game, i enjoy twists and drama and bloodshed for the sake of the family but...this story feels so sloppily thrown together, its like someone saw Goodfellas once, got his drunk friends together and tried to make their own movie with a shoestring budget and cliched ideas. If it were on sale for less than 10 dollars, i would say "buy it, its a decent enough game in its own world" but stand it next to GTA or anything similar and it feels hollow.

The statement above is what I imagine the captain of my ship would say after I sent my crew in to kill those damn giant alien spiders. In
you control your very own spaceship, your ship carries information containing a crucial weakness of the encroaching rebel fleet and you must deliver it to your superiors. To do this you must travel through several sectors each with their own distinctions and inhabitants. Each sector you vist will contain twenty or so beacons, these beacons are how you maneuver through the sector and reach your destination.
In these beacons you will encounter ships looking for a fight, trading posts, asteroid fields, nebulas, stars, and ion storms. Occasionally you'll also meet someone friendly. Some of these friendly occurences will give you quests, these quests lead you to new ships for later playthroughs or upgrades for your current ship. Most battles and quests reward you with precious scrap. Scrap is the currency of this game and with it you can purchase new weapons, crew, systems, passive upgrades, ammo, fuel, and repairs. When you can't find a store you can spend you scrap on system upgrades like improved shields or stronger blast doors. To succeed you must balance your scrap between new weapons, crew, system upgrades, hull repairs, and ammo.
Most of the time in FTL you'll be fighting. Combat is the most exciting and difficult part of the game and beating another ship is very satisfying. Combat largely consists of waiting for your weapons to charge up before choosing where to aim them at the enemy ship. Should you damage their engines to knock down their evasion chance? Or should you take out their weapons first to prevent hull damage to your ship? These questions can take a lot of time to think about which is why Subset Games implemented a pause button. It allows you to pause all actions and give you time to think and direct your crew so that when you unpause everyone commits their orders (as best they can). However, when your weapons are charging you may also be sending your crew to board the enemy ship, launch a drone to repeatedly attack the enemy ship, or hack one of their systems to temporarily shut it down. The fighting is easy to learn but difficult to master. It will suprise you how much depth there is when fighting another ship. Combat leaves a lot of choice open to the player which makes it new and exciting with every playthrough.
FTL is challenging, it took me dozens of attempts to even reach the final boss. Luckily FTL features different difficulties to suit different players. When you do reach the end of a playthrough (which takes about two hours on average) you will meet the rebel flagship. A behemoth compared to what you'll be used to up until that point. The flasgship is a real challenge and will probably take you multiple attempts to destroy. But when you do, there is very few video game moments as satisfying as being victorious over the rebel flagship. Don't spoil it for yourself by looking up a video, the shock of first seeing and then having to eradicate the flagship is indescribable.
In terms of your crew, their race varies. You may have a human or a zoltan, a rockman or a mantis. There are quite a few different species of crew and they all have diffrent characteristics. The engi, for example, repair at twice the normal speed but do half the regular damage to enemy crew. A lanius will drain the oxygen out of a room slowly but doesn't need oxygen to survive. This is useful for boarding automated ships which have no oxygen system. You can also name each crew memeber you attain, some players might not care about this feature but I really enjoyed roleplaying as the captain and thinking of what each of my crew members did in their spare time. When it comes to your crew the possibilities are endless.
FTL is not all fighting and strategizing though. Sometimes you may travel to a beacon with nothing at all. During these more serene beacons, you may just appreciate the view of space. The game puts it best with "you spend a good deal of time staring out the window. It is, you must admit, rather beautiful here." These beacons and all the others too are carried by the superb soundtrack composed by Ben Prunty. Each track conveys a different emotion. Whether it be the thrill and tension of combat, or the loneliness of space.

Among the Sleep is a First Person horror/puzzle game in where we play as a toddler trying to find his mother in a dark and twisted world. We start off in our birthday party, eat some cake with our mom and are given a terrifying teddy bear as a gift. The bear teaches us the basics of the game such as picking stuff up and climbing but you may be half expecting it to murder you at any given moment. Surprisingly that creepy as sin stuffed bear turns out to be your best friend throughout this ordeal and doubles as a flashlight whenever you hug it. The voice actor that plays the teddy bear has a very calm and soothing voice which ironically enough adds to the creepiness of it.
Everything is all well and normal until you go to sleep and have your crib flipped over by an invisible entity. From there on out the world turns pretty twisted and has no sense of coherency sort of like a dream as the ways the areas connect to each other make no sense. Not much will make sense actually as the story is quite cryptic and you will have to piece it together yourself. As strange as the world is the level design is linear and well thought out so you should never find yourself lost. Most of the story is also told through the environment so there is a reason to pay attention to your surroundings other than the possibility of death.
A large portion of your time will be solving very simple puzzles to be able to progress to the next area but there are a few stealth sections where you must hide and avoid monsters. These are definitely the low points of the game as it can be hard to indicate when the monster is near until you catch a glimpse but by then you will be killed. They just hold you up in the air and show a game over screen so don't expect violent baby executions buying this. Another problem with having to avoid the monsters is that your fat baby legs are nowhere near agile enough to move to cover quickly. As mentioned before these sections are few and far between so it doesn't really have much of an impact to the experience.
When you are standing you will be able to run shortly before falling down and reverting back to your crawling stance. Crawling allows you to fit into tiny locations and is much faster than walking but you are unable to hug the teddy bear for light and since you can also run when standing there is little reason to crawl. You can also climb on objects to reach places. An example being pulling up a chair and climbing it to reach a door knob. You can also pick up objects and throw them but throwing doesn't really become a factor until much later on. The baby is surprisingly strong considering how hard he throws objects and is able to move chairs without a problem.
I'd imagine you are not considering purchasing this game for the cool physics or the puzzles but for the horror. Among the Sleep pulls it off pretty well and being a toddler really helps as everything in the world seems big and scary. This isn't really the kind of game that will throw jump-scares at you around every corner. Jump-scares are rare for the most part and the game instead relies heavily on subtle psychological horror such as dimly lit rooms, objects falling and distant noises. One thing that I found separated it from most horror games is the lack of blood, gore or violence. It is definitely a breath of fresh air and shows you can make an unnerving experience without resorting to gross out tactics.
The audio in Among the Sleep really amplifies the horror. It does a very good job at making you paranoid through use of sudden thumps, braking glass and just tense ambient music. Without such good sound effects and ambiance the game would have been much less effective at horror. Environments are unique and have the advantage of really making you feel like a small defenseless toddler in a over-sized world. Graphics are pretty good as well and I found it impressive how environments went from breathtaking to horrifying in some areas. Levels don't actually interconnect in any real way other than you sliding down a rusty pipe into a new location but it does end up adding to the surreal nature of it all.
Overall this is a pretty good horror title. It does lack in gameplay and the puzzles are so easy that they will not offer any challenge and may feel like they are there just to give you something to do. Though considering the game is only two hours you will likely finish the game before boredom or repetition sets in. The horror does stay unpredictable throughout and they do a really good job at sparingly using the monsters to hunt you. Among the Sleep doesn't feel like a glorified game of hide and seek like other modern horror titles, instead it feels like a very personal experience through the warped mind of a toddler. It really does feel like a walking simulator with puzzles thrown in to slow you down but if you are fine with that there is a truly memorable and unique experience here that will remain in your mind long after you beat it.

I'm extremely fond of indie horror titles in general, having seen the old classics turn slowly into action titles (Resident Evil comes to mind) and as an original oculus rift kickstarter backer I watched this one with keen interest.
All I can say is: wow.
True horror makes you feel vulnerable, it doesn't give you any way to fight back, it makes things hopeless - and what better way to do that than to put you into the fears of childhood. This game really pulls that off well, a formal analysis would find lots of little psychological tricks used to generate an intense atmosphere and I heavily recommend playing with headphones on and the lights off.
If you have one, the oculus rift is a must, but there is one annoying issue: it didn't work on Linux. This is something that should be fairly simple to fix, and may just be a problem with my setup (i'm using SteamOS inside a docker container), but it still annoyed me as setting up the rendering view for the rift should be a fairly trivial task to do cross-platform.
That said, it's still got plenty of atmosphere played on a normal LCD monitor in a dark room, the whole game reminds me of the otherworld in Silent Hill, but far creepier due to the vulnerability it induces.
If you enjoy horror, just get it.
