INTRO:
After playing Far Cry 3 a few years ago, I went crazy.
I loved that game so much that I decided to be curious and look forward trying their other game series.
Since yesterday, I finally finished Far Cry 1.
I finished every Far Cry games on PC (except for Far Cry Primal that I can't afford for now x.x;;) and I decided to make a game review for each of those games. So I hope i'll do fine as in, English is not my first language :P
________________
GAME'S STORY:
The Story is about a guy named "Jack Carver", that got paid by a journalist (aka Valerie Constantine) for some specific mission.
They traveled on a boat and some soldiers shot the boat with a Rocket Launcher, which made you wake up on the beach, with no clue where did Valerie go.
Your main mission will be to rescue her and you will receive help from Doyle.
Other things will happen in the game but I won't spoil in that part :p
The Scenario is kind of decent. I am not a huge fan of this as in, we already saw a lot of those in this early years because it was very popular to make sci-fi games // games with scientists and creatures like Half-Life but since it's a old game and that it was popular at this time, we can forgive them about that. :P
________________
PROS & CONS
PROS:
- Graphics are beautiful for how old the game is
- Gameplay is decent for their very first game release
- Different types of weapons (Shotgun, Snipers, machineguns, grenade-launcher, etc..!)
- The story is okay! Not the craziest, but it's okay :P
- A good amount of interactions on the radio for the Story, making so the game is not empty at some parts
- You can find some funny magazines that they customized, giving more interactions with the player if you ever decided to discover stuffs around and not only play the game
- There is 20 levels to do in the game. (Levels, chapters, whatever you call that :P)
- The game is fun overall
CONS:
- The scenario can get dumb at some part, and somewhy you'll see Valerie randomly almost naked at some point lol
- The gameplay can get terrible: There is some part where you can't do multiple things at once (Moving forward while shooting, then you can't move to the left or right anymore, somewhy)
- In some maps, NPCs can shot you through walls (mostly Army Tents) and it is pretty frustrating to die from someone that you can't even see.
- The difficulty is insane.
I am very good at video games, and I died A LOT on most levels.
I played in Standard, which were the 2nd difficulty out of 5.
I got forced to use some cheats at the very 2 last chapters because they were no way to win for me:
7 rocket launchers shooting at you and you instantly die, rare checkpoints to heal you / get shields and/or ammos.
I never had to cheat to win anygame in the past and I played tons of games, difficult, or not.
- Some levels can seem very very very long while some can be short
- Some levels are extremely hard to pass just for a small part of it that is insane to win
_________________
Overall, it's a great game to play.
Probably the scariest of the 4 games (by that I mean, that there is a moments where you are in the dark with obscure ambiance, and out of a sudden monsters jump on you)
I'm not saying that Far Cry games are scary in general, though :P
MUST PLAY. Peace. <3

Wow, now
is a perfect example how nostalgia and hype by its time can make a game better than it actually is.
I remember the media and gaming community back then in 2004 going
nuts about this game, declaring it as one of the best first person shooter experiences to ever have seen the light of the world. Especially in German-speaking countries the fan circlejerk was out of this world, since Crytek, back then still a small German developer team, was now seen as the new Valve or iD.
But playing this over ten years later AT MOST charms a worn-out smile from me.
Yes, the outdoor firefights against mercernaries are pretty good at first. Driving around in patrol boats or buggys is fun too. The island surroundings are still nice to look at, even nowadays. These parts hold up about 6 hours into the game.

Just to get it out of the way, *no* the game is not worth 20-30 dollars in it's current state. It's less an Alpha and more a 1v1 combat demo of the four warbands with no campaign or warband management that made the original Modheim, Necromunda, and Blood Bowl games so fun.
Is it worth the 20 dollars as a pre-order for the full game? I'd say yes.
The game is fun. I wasn't sure when I first saw the original videos, but it's a lot more of a tactical RTS game then you would think. Instead of player turns you go by unit initiative turns, and map vision is 100% based on your troops line of sight. They have changed the looting system to an almost scavanger hunt while in the middle of a PvP match - You now search for the warpstone and enemy chests during the fight, instead of getting a list of rewards after the match. Looting is also a team effort as each warrior of yours has 2 open inv spots, plus 1 extra spot per 4 str. So the entire warband will need to work on gathering the loot instead of having 1-2 packrats. The movement system is really simple to get the hang of as each point of movement your character has opens up a set distance shown in a blue ring, and as long as you don't run into an enemies range, you can always revert changes and move him in a different direction at any time. Combat reminds me of Fallout - each trooper seems to have 3-5 action points, and different combat maneuvers cost a different amount of your pool. When your warriors can actually gain xp and purchase skills and new equipment I could see this system being a helluva lot of fun.
I can't say anything about the magic as you basically get an attack spell and a buff spell and that's it. Again, when the warriors can be developed more I could see this system being fun, but right now it's just a fancy bowman.
Multiplayer is less fun. It's a bit buggy, it's full of a lot of rage quits right now, and since there is no warband progression 99% of what makes these types of games great is missing. In a patch or two when they hopefully have the xp system working and people start forming leagues, multiplayer will be worth it. Right now, I can't say it's a selling point.
The fact it's shipping with only four warbands (more will come via paid DLC I am sure. :/  ) is dissapointing as well. With all the great races and backstory the Warhammer world has, you would at least have hoped to see one of the Dwarven warband types, along with one of the Elven warband types, included in the base game. As it stands you basically get the Germans, the Joan of Arcs, Humans-but-cultists, and the awesome Skaven (rat assassins).

Well.
This game shows a lot of potential.
Of course it's early access and so some of my critique may quickly become obsolete .
Strategy combat around city scapes where you can climb, drop and leap is a lot of fun.
Even though I am ignorant to Mordheim I greatly enjoy fantasy and this game has bucketloads of it.
A nice choice of starting warbands although I am a bit unsure about the lack of female mercenaries ( I wouldn't use them anyway but I find it odd) Perhaps there is a lore based reason?  Great potential for future growth.
The ambience and atmosphere of the game is great however I am not too sure about the suitability of the soundtrack.
While I think the soundtrack is quality it sounds like the drums of war and great battles at points. But these aren't great battles: they are skirmishes for ones life in the dregs of a corrupted world.   Anyway it seems insignificant. Stylised music for each warband would be great also. Ironically the opening menu ambience is fantastic but it does not seem to be replicated in skirmishes.
At the moment the games engine doesn't seem quite capable of supporting itself and I would highly recommend the coders get their butts in gear as to fixing critical game glitches for example playing versus  player seems to get stuck and 4/5 times will not get unstuck and you are left thinking of what might have been. Load times that don't seem to be done justice by the in game content.
There are some minor graphical glitches  mostly in chraracter models. The human impressive unit looks bald from some angles if he has no headgear. The ogre has an invisible buttcrack when he's stunned. Sisters are miraculously empty on the inside of their armour and it's particularly evident when they fail a drop check. Brethrens robes spazzing out.  Overall the graphics are solid, stylised and make a positive impact on the game.
Quite a few quality of life problems and glitches that need to be fixed up. There are spots in the map that are bugged one way or another. For example in the sewers of the church of sigmar there is a reddish tentacle-ridden area that one of my sisters got stuck in. There are multiple places where, as a ranged attacker, you can walk up a wall and get stuck in it for an added height boost and sniper spot particularly in houses of the merchants quarter. Seems to be a few problems with characters magically falling down walls they just climbed.  And the menus in skirmishes could really do with full mouse capabilities.
There are people who are griping and giving this game a bad rap. You must understand that there will always be people who give a game a bad rap and in the last 5 years they seem to have crawled out from under every rock and basement known to man.  If you have a reasonable intellect you can master the keyboard menus quite easily. The game is quite the very definition of early access and an excellent early access game with the promise of great growth potential for 2v2 and great customisation and strategy.
However I'm extremely fearful that this game will collapse or I will have to boycott it because it will become a left right and centre cash grab. Indeed, the game already shows omens of it in the form of currencies of wydrstone and coins. The "Smugglers Den". The potential to buy boosts for your characters for exp and expedite their learning of new spells.
Purchashing mercenaries (Priest of Morr etc),
While the wyrdstones and currency and upkeep are all in tune to the rules of the game it does not mean a player should have to fork out unreasonable amounts of real cash to manage them.
The seeming potential for your warriors to become incapacitated or injured for periods of time, while realistic, is probably more about the potential for customers to purchase boosters that let them recover completely or faster.
Depending on how overboard the group goes with cash grab if they do and I imagine they will. ( And come on, it's sanctioned or run by Games Worskship the people that sell, while of good quality, small figures of tin or plastic at prices going beyond twenty dollars and then squeezing you for the paint($36 for 2 medium pieces), the glue($12) and the tools(32+18) as well. Bless them.)
Considering that the base game is not free to play they will be walking on thin ice with me and I imagine a lot of players if there isn't a
means for those who can't fork out money to build their warbands up and give them a sanctuary to play and enjoy the game where they don't constantly get stomped on by someone who has already learnt grand true comet of sigmar and  has 200 damage weapons. Sigmar forbid they make it so you have to WAIT because your lack the funds to pay for your warband or you don't have enough warriors and can't afford to buy a new one.
That will drop the game to the status of a glorified facebook game and I would be
disappointed.
That aside I will try and remain positive for this game and hope to see it blossom into a popular title of its genre or atleast become a cult classic.
For those of you considering the purchase of this game in early access please consider the following.
o The PvP is not thriving yet
o You can't build up resources or exp at this point
o There are some fatal game errors
o The game requires more resources to run than it appears

Genre - Games Workshop Board Game Conversion
Disclaimer - I have only played one skirmish game. Although that is really all you can play at the moment. I saw people moaning it was targetted at console users. I used a keyboard/mouse and it as fine (you just need to get used to using Q & E to flick through abilitys). A controller can be used just as well if not a bit better though. The skirmish was hella' fun and left me wanting more. So why haven't I played it more? Because this is such an early build I want to wait and enjoy it properly.
You move your 'pieces' with nice 3D graphics in real time, that actually counts as a turn. You engage the enemy and try and rout them or complete optional objectives. My optional objective was collect 16 warpstones, but due to restricted capacity there was no point in this so I just engaged the enemy. You can climb to higher ground with the risk of falling and the various units are unique (such as a stupidity check for a Rat Ogre, spell casters etc.). There is loads of potential here with a campaign, progression and equipment for your squad. There are four diverse squads at the moment. I used the Skaven and they stayed true to the Warhammer universe. So a great game is lying in wait here, but don't get it just yet, unless you can get a discount or a Games Workshop obsessive like me.

Some of the most fun I've had in recent weeks. Honestly despite it's flaws it's a joy to play and makes you feel like a bonafide badass. But there are flaws that are fairly prevelant at times.
Including but not limited to:
-Rubberbanding- Although only experienced a couple of times it can get to be unbearable if not fixed and is a severe interruption in the otherwise fluid fighting
-Short story- Finished the game in 6 hours though there is still much to be explored and done. Here's hoping to free updates in the future!
-Steep learning curve- This game isn't one you can just pick up, play for 2 hours, and expect to master. You need to invest time AND I CAN'T STRESS THAT ENOUGH
-Fairly small map-  Although lovingly crafted, the map is somewhat lacking in size. Still enjoyable though (As they say "Not about the size but how you use it ;)")
But now onto the pros-
-Entrancing art style- The world is absolutely stunning and the art style and vivid colors are set to stun you throughout your entire experience. I found myself stopping to enjoy the scenery much more than I probably should have, yet couldn't seem to stop myself
-Fluid and innovative combat controls- The Four stance combat system is extremely fun to use and experiement with, and by using it you somehow feel your skill growing in the game
-Combat Deck- Another innovative feature that makes the game feel custom to you. You can basically make your own fighting style and make tweaks as you go along to make your character stronger, faster, or more agile, all depending on how you want to play
-CUSTOMIZATION!!!- Character creation is lacking with a handful of haircuts, colors and the choice between male or female. But that doesn't really matter as you're wearing a full face mask throughout the entire game and do not see your characters face except for a few glimpses here and there during cutscenes. But god, oh GOD is the gear abundunt and diverse.
-Soundtrack- Music is beautifully crafted and immersive. Not once have I found myself wishing that I turned the music setting down before I entered combat
-Player interaction- Outside of combat trials I'm not usually hostile towards other players, yet find find myself helping players who are struggling with combat. And the occasional duel here and there really spices up the environment.
Summary- I would reccomend this game 9 times out of 10 for anyone and everyone. This game is as equally rewarding playing solo as it is playing with friends, and the beautiful world is going to entertain you for hours on end. I would give this game a 8.5/10 because of it's small map and short story, but guarantee your entertainment because of it's seemingly endless combat customization and mentorship feature.

I recommend the game if you're happy to do that, but if you're only interested in more single player content, for now I would go elsewhere

A good horror game leaves the player feeling powerless in the face of something truly horrifying, so how much more powerless can you get than playing as a toddler? With amazing atmosphere and a true sense of dread throughout, Among the Sleep is an amazing horror experience that any fan of the genre should traverse.

Among the Sleep is a prime example of why horror is my favorite video game genre. The story is great, the monster encounters are exciting, unbearably tense, and are actually challenging unlike Amnesia The Dark Descent. Above all, Among the Sleep is incredibly creative and, despite its dark atmosphere, is very sentimental and succeeds in making the player feel like a little kid again.
PROLOGUE DLC REVIEW:
Among the Sleep comes with free DLC, which is a prologue which adds about an hour of gameplay mean to be played after the main campaign. Prologue is a skillfully designed addition to Among the Sleep and makes itself stand out from the campaign in several ways:
- A chilling winter atmosphere, which is refreshingly different
- Improved puzzles which require more thought to solve than what was seen in the campaign
- Thoroughly creepy dolls to collect
Prologue also expands upon the campaign's story, although since it's a prequel there is sadly no Teddy to keep you company. Prologue is actually very similar to Penumbra: Requiem, a mission pack/sequel to Penumbra: Black Plague. In Requiem there are no monsters to encounter, only environmental hazards and puzzles to solve. Prologue's only fault is that is pointlessly throws in a new monster which is a complete joke and takes the player out of their immersion. Considering that is all Prologue does wrong and the many other things it does right, it is a great bit of free DLC. Give it a go if you've played the campaign.

I do want to recommend this game.  Well, this story.  There's no actual game here.  The choices are largely irrelevant and have no impact on the actual outcome other than who shows up where - and even then, only sometimes.  Some of the humor is pretty good, and the characters are likable enough for what is effectively a harem anime.
But this game just feels a bit lazy overall.  It has a strange theme that makes people curious, screenshots of a few of the jokes, it's enough to make some people (myself included) decide to buy it - on sale - and see what it's really like.  And it delivers, to a degree.  There are some references to the actual tanks the girls are named after.  Some of their personality traits can be assigned due to their country of origin.  But the personalities have about as much depth as a saucer of milk.  And the writing, unfortunately, contains several plot points that get immediately dropped that COULD have actually gone somewhere.  That and some things in the game really should be explained.
It's short, it's sloppy, it goes nowhere, and it ends rather abruptly.  And, while it contains a "skip" feature, using it will likely crash the game as it can try to forward faster than the engine can actually handle.
Also, the jokes in the screen shots?  Not actually in the game.  There are similar jokes told by other characters, but never the ones you see like that.  The world doesn't make sense - which at least your invisible protagonist self points out a few times - and the characters largely don't behave in any reasonable way.  Which is a shame, because you see hints of a good idea here and there, something that COULD be explored in depth.  Instead, they just hope you know about Kancolle and think this is similar enough to pay for.  It's not.  Sorry.  Put some more time in the writing, make decisions MATTER, give some logic and actually follow up on the plot threads you keep leaving around and there could be something unique and special here.  As it stands, this is the "visual novel" equivalent of Buzzfeed clickbait.  "Top 15 tanks turned into high-school girls, you won't believe number 7!"
Edit: It occurs to me that there IS another game out there, with an equally silly theme, that shows that good writing is still possible.  Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth 1.  Don't let a silly theme make you shy away from telling a good story.

If you are looking for a realistic, intense WWII shooter, you won't find anything better than the Brothers In Arms series

Brothers in Arms Road to Hill 30 was the beginning of one of the best World War 2 shooter franchises in history. Great characters and action keep this game unique from all the other WW2 shooters out there. This game feels so authentic, and it's probably due to the recreated locations and the stellar voice acting. The squad tactics in this game can get a little annoying due to dumb AI every now and then, but overall, it's not really a hassle. This game actually takes strategy, as you'll more than likely have to flank and suppress your enemies at every encounter. Health doesn't regenerate either, so you'll have to stay behind cover. Well, enough talk, here's the deal: if you want a good shooter with fantastic characters, story, and gameplay, get Brothers in Arms. Now. Best WW2 franchise out there.

It may be part of the WWII shooter genre that's been overdone, but Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 is not your typical linear "Call of Duty" styled game. It heavily relies on the concept of flanking, which is helped by a vital system known as "Situational Awareness" view, which allows you to plan your movements accordingly. You have to rely on tactics and the use of your fireteam to survive.

Brother’s in arms Road to hill 30 is the first game created under the BIA franchise.  Oddly I played Earned in Blood before I played this game. There is virtually nothing different between this and the sequel. Combat feels extremely shallow, it’s like rainbow six and call of duty 2 had a baby and decided to call it Brothers in Arms. The squad play is there and the WWII feel is there, but the gun battles are atrociously boring. The story is top notch and the voice acting is very convincing. If you like story-time FPS games, you’ll really enjoy this game. If you’re the COD4+ generation that loves senseless shooting nonstop don’t even bother wasting your time.

Not a bad game, but not a good game either. It jumps between FPS and RTS in the middle of battle and I have to admit it's fairly fluid, but the wonky controls, the faulty AI, and the bad voice acting really put a damper on the whole experience. And while it doesn't do any of the RTS or FPS sections poorly, it all seems fairly washed out and generic.

10.1 hours of playtime and completing the campaign on normal difficulty leads me to conclude that were I Sgt. Baker, I'd have died many, many times. If you've seen HBO's Band of Brothers, parts of this are going to look familiar. That's fine, it's epic. While not totally realistic - for instance, penetration of cover is not modelled, so the real advantage of blasting at ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s hiding behind a fence with a .30-06 is not represented - it is a damn sight better than any other WWII game with the possible exception of Red Orchestra: Ostfront 1941-1945, which models the same sort of behaivours but has no AI to speak of. There is some replayability here, but it is a good thing the price is fixed at ten dollars at the time of this writing. Solid squad-level combined-arms gameplay circa D-Day to D+8.

Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30 is a game-changer first-person shooter that introduces a tactical element into the FPS genre. BiA spoiled me for years on FPS games since I began to crave control of squads in a tactical environment. FPS gamers should certainly tryout the BiA series to experience a new tactical play versus the typical run-and-gun game.

In terms of story, as many say, the first half is pure survival horror, and the second half is more action oriented, however, unlike most, I actually like both parts, because the story makes a natural progression to it, you start finding more and more about how things got so ♥♥♥♥ed up, and sure, its a little cliche but its a good kind of cliche, you get a little development on characters that you wouldnt even think of, and I liked that, ive endured some♥♥♥♥♥♥on this mansion and i deserve to feel i am part of the whole thing.
The game also knew how to keep the environments varied and interesting in a believable way, going to a "new area" in a way that makes sense, every place you find has a purpose that makes sense lore-wise, and for the mansion every part shows which baker rules over it through good level design.
Which takes me to one of the last areas of the game, where the game stops the action again for a while, and gives you a tense situation of resource management under a waaaay more stressful environment
I like it, its tense, stressful, puts you in an uncomfortable position and you have to basically try to gain a little bit of that comfort again, while this helps towards feeling the urge of the antagonists, really good if you ask me
All in all I do love the whole thing, it didnt make me feel like i got used to it the whole time cause the level of tension and management did increase and decrease accordingly when the action became faster or slower.
Get it if you come for the horror, but be open minded for the trigger happy bits.

In regards to general gameplay this game quite a shift in a series that tends to focus more on the melee combat of the European and Japanese middle ages. Takes a little getting used to as battles are fought rather differently on land and actual naval battles being introduced into the series for the first time. But once you get used to the changes this game is a blast to play.  Watching battles unfold in this game is rather enjoy able, as you see your battle lines form up, open fire, and march through volley after volley of cannon and musket fire over piles of dead soldiers.  It's also very amusing how you can get so engrossed in watching your infantry that you forget that there is still calvalry in the game until they come crashing into your flank and endanger your entire battle plan. In terms of looks and playbility I can go on all day about why this game is bloody awesome.
That said it does have some downsides. Occasionally the enemy generals will suicide charge at the start of the battle resulting in an easy win as their army's moral plummets in response. Then the enemy units will sometimes start moving non-stop randomly, running back and forth until the entire army is exhausted and has been demolished by cannon fire.(An everlasting bug in all Total War games sadly) Unlike other games of the series your generals are no longer unique. You can create them at will from another unit, and keep both, making them just another unit instead of something you worked to earn, develop and preserve; losing one of them doesn't threaten to unhinge your plans in the slightest outside of the battle they die in.  You also have no real control over your government personel except for the option to sack them, really your government seems to effect the game even less than losing your generals now. Lastly, there is paid DLC that should have been in the game from the start. Other than the warpath campaign there is no excuse for this obvious cash grab.
Overall though, this is a very good game and is very fun to play. I have truly enjoyed this game and would recommend this to anyone without a second thought. And like all Total War games that it's available for I highly recommend Darthmod after you've played this game and seen what it has to offer by itself. The mod ramps up the replay value and gameplay immensely. It also helps eliminate or reduce the frequency of the few bugs I've seen in this game.

The game takes place on the fictional island of Skira, based on the island Kiska which is located in Alaska. The Global Economic Crisis makes China seize control of the island from Russia, just to be able to grab the oil on the island. Of course, the russians are not very fond of this and they put their army on taking back the army from the PLA (People's Liberation Army). As they already encounter the PLA on the chinese main land, they call to the USA to retake Skira for them. And so... you're playing as two different squad leaders in the struggle of reclaiming Skira. Nothing too fancy.
I thought it was a really good game and the player must be careful when playing, can't play it like a Call of Duty game where you just run in to the fire fight and kill everyone "Rambo style". No, that'll result in death very quickly. Instead, the player need to take it slow, think about what route to take and if he/she really need to kill that one soldier, why not go around the enemy? That might make the mission a little easier further on.
Anyway... I really recommend this.

Alright everybody just relax. We do still have a solution to be able to play mp matches and best of all, it's built right into the game. I've made a post on moddb regarding the issue and included instructions on how to start a multiplayer match without the dependency on any third party servers. The post can be found at
Many of us have been able to enjoy online matches simply by sharing the host ip address with all of the match participants. The process is really simple and has existed the entire time, but most players remain entirely unaware of the solution.
To make this work, the player that hosts the session can simply obtain their ip address from one of many websites that give you your ip. Here are a couple:
Once you have your ip address, share it with all of the players you are going to have in the match.
Start up your game and select multiplayer from the menu.
Select LAN
For the host, you must simply create a server for the match. Once you have done that, the other players can join your server and will appear in the lobby after doing so.
For the clients, go to the ip address menu selection and enter the ip address that the host gave you. Press enter and if the server is set up as described above, you should connect and enter the game lobby awaiting the start of the game.
It's as simple as that!
This is something we've known was coming so we shouldn't be quite this bent out of shape about it. We lost much more when they pulled the plug on the forums. In comparison, this is a much lighter blow to the community than that was. Look over the instructions above if you're not familiar with the process. The biggest challenge will be to find other gamers to strike up a game with, but I'm confident we'll be able to find a solution for that too.
If anyone is having a problem getting this to work, post it in the Tech Support area of the forums and the answers to your questions will start to roll in.
For goodness sake, cheer up!! :D We've survived much worse than this ;)

Mordheim: City of the Damned is a turn-based, squad-level tactical game set in the devastated city of Mordheim. You begin by choosing a warband - the current choices include four different warbands with (what is currently) a basic variety of units, spells, and abilities. You manage what units from your warband you will take into combat within Mordheim. Some are more capable than others overall (heroes) and their inherent unit statistics vary leading to variety in capability - in other words, units with higher agility have higher dodge and hit chances, higher toughness means shrugging off damage, intelligence affects spell-casting, so on. The unit statistics can be viewed from your warband management screen, along with equipped weapons, armor, abilities. Currently you can only change armor and weapons (from some basic choices with differences in combat effects) and swap out your warband units. The plan is for your units to gain experience as the game's development progresses, thus making your units more powerful (and mitigating some of the RNG effects). Most units can currently carry two sets of weapons for tactical variety. Weapons such as swords allow the user to parry while halberds hit hard but suffer an accuracy penalty. Some weapons apply debuffs when they hit enemies (poison blades, warplock pistols, etc.) that can stack and ruin someone's day.
Each unit has two types of points - blue points for movement actions and red points for offensive actions. Blue points allow your units to move, climb walls, jump down ledges, reload ranged weapons, flee from opponents, swap weapon sets etc. Red points allow you to attack, cast spells, etc. Some actions require combinations of both (for example, safely disengaging from an enemy without provoking an attack of opportunity requires the use of both types of points, or taking full aim with a ranged weapon).
The turn order for units is displayed at the top of the screen but since units of the same type utilize the same icon the information provided isn't as useful as expected. Turn order is determined through initiative based on unit statistics. You can also zoom out from a unit by pressing the LALT key, giving you an overview of where your units are currently stationed, any visible enemy units and previous known locations of currently out-of-sight enemies (marked with a ?). This is extremely useful as Mordheim's devastated and maze-like city streets can be difficult to navigate otherwise.
Action success is percent-based, so you can clearly see your chances prior to performing any action. This is of course where RNG effects can be extremely frustrating, but again, once experience gains are implemented stronger units should help mitigate this. Like a lot of turn-based tactical games with these mechanics risk management is an extremely important aspect of the battlefield.
There are lootable points on the battlefield and dead enemy soldiers will sometimes drop 'special' weapons (in other words weapons with different statistics, or essentially 'magic' weapons). You can't permanently keep them in your inventory at present but in the future this should impart a sense of unit progression and reward the player for succesfully defeating opponents.
Graphically the game is well-done - on the highest settings the game is crisp, runs smoothly and has nice effects. The music is suitably dark considering the setting and lends an appropriate 'doomed' quality to the atmosphere. Those who don't enjoy the Warhammer universe's grimdark grimdarkness might have to overlook these items to enjoy the gameplay.
There's quite a bit more to be done in Mordheim. I personally am looking forward to unit progression and the loot system. As it stands the game provides you with one-off skirmishes between warbands to give you a taste of the game's combat and gameplay.
If you love games such as X-COM, Xenonauts, UFO: Afterseries, or essentially any squad-level turn-based game you'll definitely enjoy this. Keep an eye on it - if they don't fug it up this could be great.

Echoed World seems like a really great game. However, this is a review. There's going to be some problems.
I don't think the player/entity models look good with the background artstyle. The contrast is just a bit too much, to the point where it's extremely noticable (and not in the good way).
The controls are pretty okay. If I could use some other button, like Q or E, instead of X to take and distribute life, that would be nice. The dialogue could use some work. In the first level, I think, the player has to run from some sort of rock monster. The player "defeats" it by running it into a hole filled with spikes. The speaker then says, "You did it!". It just sounds off to me. The player didn't do pretty much anything but run. Plus, he gives no explanation as to what we just ran from.
The biggest problem I have, though, is the feeling. The feeling of running, jumping, grabbing, taking/giving life...Every action feels off to me. The running just feels and looks awkward; I don't know how to explain it. The jumping is really bothersome. When you jump, you barely go up, and it just feels too...real. These architects are supposed to be ethereal...mystical being, correct? I can see where you may want to go, but maybe you could go a bit farther into lore, and have Algiz jump a little higher. When I jump near a ledge there have been and overwhelming amount of times where I just...fall. I don't grab or anything. I fail to grab and I fall. There have been times where I get stuck in the falling animation whilst still attached to the ledge. The biggest problem I have is the taking/giving life. It just happens too quickly. It seems like it doesn't matter too much. "Oh yeah, this is just a normal thing. Just ripping the life out of something thats florishing and handing it to a decaying plant. Happens everyday." tl;dr There are very few features currently in the game, but what's there is very good and very promising.
So, point of mention: I never played Mordheim before this; I'm familiar with the game and its concept, but never had a chance to actually get in a campaign. Also note that this review is current as of the second content update
Currently the game only really has the combat more or less. There's 4 warbands (essentially Skaven, Empire, Warrior Priest Empire, and Chaos), and they all have unique units with different skills and abilities, including a powerful Leader unit and 1 impressive unit (Ogre, Chaos Spawn, Rat Ogre, or Super Sister) The rest of the options are fairly simple as to be expected from a starting warband, usually with only a skill or two differentiating them besides their different stat lines. Unfortunately, this does make the units feel very generic, but that's how I imagine they are until level ups and injuries anyways.
Surprisingly, combat/movement does not take place on a grid, but in 3D environments using circles to mark how far you can move with each movement point. This does create some weirdness moving around objectives, because you can end up eking out a lot more movement in some situations, looping around obstacles without leaving your circle, but largely looks really nice. The movement is also interestingly handled by WASD, so you actually get to run around with your guys, which was a refreshing change and felt really good. A nice side effect of this as well is that the entire game is playable with a gamepad, hinting that they may move into consoles at some point. Circles also dictate enemy threat zones and ally "control zones", which is an area that keeps other allies from performing actions. It sounds strange, but basically its simply to keep you from stacking 30 guys on one enemy. Nice to note that although there are many missing features currently, the game does include a fairly polished 4-part tutorial that also gives you a chance to see all the factions. Load times were a bit of a bother, but that could also be my machine. Lastly, the interface during the game was very nice. You're able to easily open windows with a single button press that will allow you to see a summary of your active character's stats/buffs, the target character's stats, or a breakdown of what modifiers are on certain actions (explaining why your success chance is higher or lower than expected). All in all, it allows the player to only be confronted with the information they feel they need without requiring lots of popping back to a settings menu.
Insert standard comment about bugs and it being in early access so hopefully they will be polished out.
Currently, the only form of customization that exists is choosing what weapons your guys have equipped. Dual wielded weapons can be equipped in any combination, so there's actually some nice variety here in, even just with equipment, deciding and executing specific roles for your dudes. As warband management is the newest feature, it's pretty light, but there's lots of promising space on the screen to be filled in. Notably, there's something like 12 locked equipment slots, hinting at lots of consumables and magic items coming in the future (one of the tutorials actually mentions something about enchantments). The Skills page is broken up into something like 10 different tabs, also hinting at lots of customization incoming (currently you can only skirmish with the starting armies, and loot + XP are not applied).
Graphically, the game is, frankly, amazing. I'm running it on a 3-year-old laptop and I was getting decent FPS on the "good" setting, which is better than the vast majority of games I've played. Surprisingly optimized for an early access game. I'm not a huge fan of the maps and environments, but that's mostly a question of taste; I'm not one who really enjoys OMG SO GRIMDARK!!!1 all the time. That being said, for that vein they do look absolutely fantastic. They also sport lots of points of interaction, allowing you to climb and leap through different elevations. Nice level design so far from what I've seen. Traps and looting are in, though can't really say how big a role they currently play.
All in all, I have to say that I am very impressed. Like I said, the game still has lots of missing key features, but the thing is that they seem to be taking their time and making sure that they do everything right the first time around rather than spit out a bunch of features and try to massage it into a playable state. Personally I won't be playing a whole lot of it right now (since I'm mostly looking forward to the warband growth aspects of the game), but it is totally playable and, compared to almost all other Early Access games I've played, seems to really be starting on the right foot.

Kinetic Void is a stellar example of what many space related games should be.  Mind you while in early access many things are bound to change.  This game has a ship design system very akin to that used in Galactic Civilizations 2 which should be counted as a good thing.  The amount of customization that is offered to players in the design of their ships is a welcome sight as it’s something I have seen lacking in several games with the same feature.  From building the fastest fighter to the most looming dreadnought the experience of testing out different parts and experimenting with style is a great joy.
Players are allowed to name their galaxy and select how many sectors and factions exist within, giving them some level of control of the environment that they start off with.  There is plenty of room for expansion in this area of the game’s development as further options in creating the play environment would add to the overall experience.
The combat system is decent but could use some work.  While offering a manual mode of firing your ships weapons, there is a means of auto fire via the lock on, and pressing the assigned weapons group number.  In this early build I recommend avoiding the use of the auto fire as my weapons seemed resistant to firing let alone hitting.  However due warning, there does not appear to be any form of aim assist for now, and larger ships will have issues contending with smaller vessels you just cannot seem to hit.  (I am sure that these features will be ironed out in the future)
Other than that there really isn’t that much left to do within the game, yet currently you can see the foundations for what have the potential to be engaging and immersive systems.
I full heartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys building ships from the ground up and actually being able to use them, as well as to anyone who enjoys space simulation games.  For what this game could be twenty dollars is a fair investment into seeing the developers get the chance to finish this game.  Yet to be fair it should be mentioned that in its current state Kinetic Void is arguably worth its asking price, while I love building ships and taking them for a spin there is just not enough to do currently.  With the occasional frame rate issue and bugs, for those on a budget or those who are not willing to drop twenty dollars on an incomplete game I would still recommend getting this game but when it is on sale.  This way you can still support the game, get a great ship builder, and access to what has the potential to be a great game.

Absolver is a fun game with a relativly unique game mechanic in it's combat built into a intriguing world with a somewhat unique art style. This is both a comment on the game and my opion as well as a list of all problems with balancing, game design and bugs that I personally came accross.
In my opion Absolver is an enjoyable game with a lot of potential. If you like MMO's with a focus on combat then pick it up if you have the money. However i would suggest that you hold off for now as the game is a bit of a bug ridden mess at the moment so wait for the Winter Sale or something and get it then when most of the bugs will be fixed (hopefully).
Absolver is a game that struggles with a combination of two game genres that go against each other. It is basically an MMO fighting game, however this comes with a set of problems which Absolver suffers from. The main problem that comes with this is balancing the games enemies. If you make the enemies to easy the game is boring because it lacks any challenge and you can pretty much one-shot every enemy with a single combo. If you make the enemies too hard, you can't beat any of them if you are forced into a 2 v 1 (or more) situation because you get stun locked.The best way to descibe fights like those is this, imagine playing a fighting game, like Street Fighter, but instead of one opponent you have two, sure you can win but it won't be easy and you most likely won't unless your really over leveled (remember this is an MMO). Absolver is at the latter of the spectrum, the enemies are too strong to reliably kill any of them solo if you are attacked by two or more. This wouldn't be too much of a problem but the aggro system is also badly balanced, you either attract all of them or none.
Another problem with the enemies in Absolver is there AI. They wil always pull off a parry or dodge, etc. if the attempt one because they dont have a programed thinking time (at least in my experience). I also had a problem witht the game design itself, Guidance Bridge is the tutorial island for the game and the first area has three exits, the big obvious door to your left is not the way you are suppoesed to go first (just a little tid-bit really). I would make a list of bugs I encountered now but the list would be long so here's two of the most game breaking ones; you can lose all input capabilities randomly execpt moving (the animations play halfway then end) and sometimes two sets of enemies will spawn, including the mini bosses.
In conclusion, Absolver has a bug and balancing issue at the moment, but most new MMO's do so just wait it out and join later when they have been delt with (unless you don't care, in which case pick it up it's a really fun game).

Absolver suprised me. Bought it on impulse, Went in expecting something mediocre and was completely and utterly blown away. If you're the sort that enjoys challenging skill based combat, buy it. NOW.
And dont worry about those online issues or lack of content, they are sure to be fixed over time...

Kingdom is a work of gaming art, and one of the finest RTS games I have ever played.
Imagine trying to teach your three-year-old to control an army in a Total War game, or attempting to explain the diplomatic options in a Civilization game to your seven-year-old. Imagine trying to explain the advanced build orders and timing attacks in a bronze league Starcraft 2 match to a thirty-year-old adult, who's never played a strategy game.
Now, imagine that same three year old, making the descision to shift her primary income to agriculture, due to the degredation of hunting grounds after expanding.
Kingdom: New Lands creates an engaging, and complicated strategy experience with a few extremely refined tools and concepts. These concepts are surprisingly simple; there are only three resources(player attention, money, and timing), only four in-game keyboard imputs(left, right, up, down), and you interact with your units and buildings only one way. Yet, the depth, and challenge that the developers squeeze out of these basic comcepts is phenomenal, and unlike anything I have seen in a game.
You start every round of Kingdom the same way: a monarch astride a hours, a few coins in hand, and a ghost telling you where to go. You find a few vagabounds around a fire. Here, you learn how to spend your first resource.
Coin. By spending coin on things you build your units and buildings: the vagabonds become serfs, the snuffed out fire becomes the base of your camp, and merchants provide weapons and tools for your camp. Serfs become hunters and a source of more coin, and builders improve your structures, but only if you have to coin. As you spend coin your settlement grows, and you learn about the second resource.
Player attention. There are only two directions you can move in Kindom: Left, or right. As you build your settlemet, the distance between all your sources of income and tools become larger, and the time it takes to get there becomes longer. You soon find that managing a larger settlement requires you to choose what is most important at that time. Do you move left and harvest the coin from your farmers, or spend time recruiting more vagabonds? Do you go back every time the merchants arrive in your settlement with coin, or do you skip a few visits to clear more forest during the day? The sense of urgency, and choices you make due to have to be there to manage everything is amazing, and soon you are faced with the hardest resource to manage.
Timing. The ultimate goal of Kingdom is to rebuild a boat to escape from the Island, in order to save your monarch from the night time enemy of the game, the aptly named "Greed". These gray, zombie-like creatures will break your walls, rob your serfs, and try and steal your crown. As the game progresses, their attacks become more and more dangerous, and  your time and coin is stretched. The trick, is that they only attack at night. You have to learn when it is the right time to spend coin on strengthening your position, and when you can spare coin for the ship to win. Victory is not always sure, and one strong attack can strip you of much of your power. You have to time your spending of coin, and your visits between the crucial parts of your settlement, in order to overcome the Greed and escape.
All of this takes place on carefully rendered and randomly generated maps. These three elements are complicated by layout of the land, where everything is important, from the positions of wall and tower sites, to the richness of farming lands. This conflict is so well executed, there is depth and delima to every game. You have to reall pay attention to where you build things, or whether or not you build them at all.
Kingdom: New Lands is wonderfully executed, simple to learn, and yet full of depth. My three-year-old learned to play in about an hour, and with a little help from me was able to manage a settlement and make choices that affected her playthrough. It's an amazing game, and worth your time if only to see what can be done by a few well implimented concepts.

DISCLAIMER:
Obviously, reviewing horror / thriller games is tricky at best since fear is subjective; some find FNAF terrifying, others don't. For the record, I am a horror game veteran with games such as Silent Hill 1 & 2, Resident Evil 2 & 3, and a ton of indie horror games under my belt. So it is entirely possible that my tolerance for terror is forming a bias on opinion.
TLDR:
+ Brilliant atmosphere, pretty much spot-on
+ Great environment design, cohesive and consistent with the theme
+ Decent Audio Design, even if the ambience sfx is a tad over-recycled
- Horror? What horror?
- Tone and atmosphere is very jarring, changing dramatically as game goes on
- Gameplay is very textbook, and is altogether unchallenging
REVIEW:
Forget those shadowy nightmares, that teddy is 10 times scarier than anything else this game will throw at you.
I really, REALLY wanted to like Among The Sleep. I'm always on the lookout for innovative ideas, and the concept of a horror game through the eyes of a 2 year old was certainly intriguing. The story, without going into spoilers, is essentially that of a toddler who awakes in the middle of the night, and upon hearing noises downstairs decides to go investigate and look for mummy. Controls are the standard First-Person control scheme, with the nice added touch of crawling for increased movement speed as opposed to walking.
Personally, I think the level design is where the game does really well; the environment is designed to be really up-scaled and large, and it does a great job of portraying a toddler's perspective of the world. Chairs are giant obstacles that take effort to climb onto, fridges feel like a giant white pillar, and getting from point A to B is an arduous task.
The atmosphere is unnerving and subtly sinister, reminding me of the foreboding and evil vibe I got from Dead Space or Alien: Isolation. Lighting is sparse, casting shadows on everything, and at one point a flash of lightning made a tree seem like a monster. A nice touch showing the power of a child's imagination. All this combined gives us a first hour of feeling really tiny and vulnerable, exactly how a horror game should do. I was nervous, I was jumpy, and I was really looking forward to how the rest of the game would play out.
And then, well... the game kinda gave up trying.
I had assumed the suburbian home environment I saw in trailers and screenshots would continue throughout the game, and since it was up-scaled to be so large this would have been entirely possible. But for some reason, the the game turns into the Adventures of Alice In Wonderland opening with a literal tumbling down the rabbit hole. We start seeing the atmosphere's creepiness being traded in for whimsy and wonderment, and any sense of danger just drops out of the game with an audible thud. It occasionally tries to remind us of its spooky ways with whispers, moody lighting and the occasional shadow, but by the third act I was so comfortable and complacent with the game that I just lost interest.
I will give a tentative thumbs-up for the story (still spoiler-free), which is intriguing enough that I may play more of the game just to see its conclusion. But again, the fact that I lost all interest points to an indication that the opening hook for the mystery was not strong enough for me to keep me invested. Most horror games either keep you engaged via mystery (Silent Hill, Amnesia) or survival (Resident Evil, Dead Space). Since Among The Sleep isn't about a baby struggling in post-apocalyptia, it has to rely on mystery. Which, unfortunately, isn't very mystifying; it's rather predictable and overall feels kinda cliche. But like I said, it is intriguing enough that I'm willing to play more in the future. And since most horror games aren't actually that complex in the story department anyway, I'm willing to let this aspect of the game go unpunished.
Gameplay-wise there's not much to talk about. It's a very standard exploration puzzler à la Amnesia. You find a locked door /  staircase / see-saw, so you collect X keys to open said obstacle. It's not challenging, it's merely time-consuming, and the puzzles involved in getting the keys are mildly difficult at best, downright trivial at worst. This wouldn't be so bad if the story was interesting enough to carry the game on its own, and turn the game into more story-focus rather than gameplay-focus. However, as established previously the game isn't exactly strong in the story department, so Among The Sleep falls down on both fronts.
Apparently there is also a persistent enemy within the game that hunts you down in each level, but if there was I didn't encounter it. I didn't even realise there was an enemy, which is a failure of design if you ask me. You want a persistent, omni-present monster to hunt the players down and scare them? Great! So make sure the player is aware of the enemy's presence at most / all times. You can't have an oppressive, nemesis-type antagonist if it's so passive in its oppression.
Overall, I can't recommend Among The Sleep. I really WANT to, since it's such an fresh concept. It's also visually interesting, the level / audio design is pretty great, and the initial atmosphere is damn-near perfect. But the writing and gameplay design let it down for things to remain engaging, especially for a horror game. I would recommend this game when on a discount, but otherwise it's just not worth the regular asking price.

There were some really good scary moments in the game that gave an interesting vibe of unease that was compounded by that fact that you're playing as only a toddler. It's short but I felt that worked to its benefit although I'm not sure how I feel about the ending. Though it's not perfect, if you're looking for a unique, GOOD horror game on Steam, this is one you should try out.

In 1706, I, leader of Russia, conquered Crimea with General Ivan Mazepa leading my troops into battle.
In 1707, the Crimean people rose up and overthrew the garrison I placed in their lands.
In 1708, with Prince Anikita Repnin leading a second army while General Mazepa was tied up in Dagestan, I marched against them and besieged their holdings in Bakchisaray. Rather than give up without a fight, their forces left the city and attacked my army. I placed my troops on a sloping hill nearby, entrenching my infantry and cannons while my cavalry lay in wait at the crest, ready to charge. I had over 1900 battle-hardened troops at my disposal, veterans, all. They had over 2000, but were mostly comprised of peasant militia, with only a single troop of cavalry with their leader. With the elevated and fortified position at my disposal, I waited for their army to cross the valley below. Their leader rode out ahead of their infantry to scope out the battlefield. As soon as he saw what was waiting for him and his men, he turned and ran all the way back to the city, without so much as a word to his infantry, who kept marching up the hill in the face of artillery barrage from my cannons. By the time the Crimean army reached the top of the hill, two of their regiments were already routed, peppered by my infantry's guns after they were too close for effective bombardment. After 5 regiments of my cavalry charged along their flank, their forces were shattered completely and routed.
By the end, over 75% of their forces were dead on the field, with less than 25% of my own joining them, most of whom were merely injured and would live to fight another day.
Empire: Total War called this a "Heroic Victory". It did not feel heroic. Perhaps granting them a period of tax exemption will take the edge off…

RE7 is a PT clone coneptually albeit not nearly as frightening. The material Silent Hill touches on are truely horrifying i.e.♥♥♥♥♥♥victims attacking you with their nightmares, or a man brutally murdering his entire family, and their daughter being this terrifying ghost creature.

But all together it is much better than anything that has come out in recent memory. The graphics are really well done. I can't really recall any bugs, but I'm sure some exist.
Very well optimized, very original format ( since Silent Hills was canceled).
The story though is just kind of stupid. I was hoping for a reboot, because the Resident Evil story just frankly doesn't age well. The original RE biohazard games were a bit more mysterious, and you felt very against the odds.
RE7 definitly touches base with this appealing game design type. That is making you feel like you are the actual character. Just some normal dude or girl helpless to a large degree. That you aren't some super hero action star.
Thats the problem with this game in its ending. It takes a very human experience and then it goes all indiana jones crystal skull on you. Leaving you feel like, wtf is this. The ending is just stupid, really stupid.
I think the ending was just placed there to a large degree for those ignorant fan boys, who can't bare to think outside the realm of possibilities, and cling to these old story tropes. Maybe, even a younger audience who have never played the first one and experience that sense of helpless fear you had the first time you saw a zombie.
Good horror movies, books, comics do not have happy endings, they don't have super heros, unless we are speaking of the cheesy, yet entertaining movie tropes like Evil dead. You see there in lies the problem. That ending, that sort of fantasy based crap mixed in with this dramatic story, just end up making it cheesy. Any RE after 2 suffers from this same issue, and it just gets progressively cheesier with RE5 and RE6.
It was like they had a very intelligent cast of writers, just mold this anti-cheesy RE game, and then production probably stepped in and was like lets plant this cheesy ending so we can create sequels.
That is so dumb. First of all, you can do the formula similar to what outlast has done (and been very successful at bringing horror back to its roots. We need endings that are sad, terrifying and leave you satisfied and impacted by the realities and struggles of being a basal human being. You don't need continuity in your story. Hell, even Edgar Allen Poe knew this. You can make other productions using the RE name and the zombie stuff etc. But you dont have to have heroes, you don't have to follow some story arch as such. So, I just finished playing Resident Evil 7's story. And oh boy, was it a rollercoaster. So, I'll break the game down into the parts and give them ratings, and rate the DLC released of now.
[SPOILERS AHEAD]
----
[STORY]
----
Introduction: Rather boring, but it has the atmosphere (and the same start of a plot as Silent Hill 2) Not really great, but oh well. 6/10
Home Sweet Home: The house is quite an interesting place, and stumbling onto the Sewer Gators tape was quite enjoyable. Definately set the scene for what was to come. 10/10
Time For Marriage Counseling: Psycho wife tried to kill you for some unknown reason, but ends up taking an axe to the neck and surviving. Not very Resident Evil. Very shocking though. Maybe this is the new formula? 7/10
Welcome To The Family Son: Shoot wife after losing hand. Get suckerpunched in the face. Have dinner. Sets scene beautifully. 10/10
Snooping Around: You look around for stuff being persued by Jack Baker. Small claustrophobic spaces included. Well done. 9/10
Filler Moment #1: Oh my GOD THESE DON'T COUNT AS PUZZLES, EVEN FOR A 5 YEAR OLD! 2/10
The Fight With Baker: So. Many. ♥♥♥♥ing. Times. I. Died. Unfair and buggy. His attacks clip through the walls. Not enjoyable and I didn't feel rewarded when I killed him. 3/10
Goin' Out For A Walk: So, it's night time and I found this sweet trailer. And found these cages. Pretty cool too. Not really a "hub", but it's alright. Only got the steroids though... Oh, and this dumb ♥♥♥♥♥ on the phone 5/10
Visting Momma: Huge chunk can be summed in a few words. I ♥♥♥♥ing hate bugs, but this was done almost perfectly. 8/10
Lucas' Trials Of Denial: Possibly one of the best parts of the game. Love it to bits. Love Lucas too. Great Character. 9/10
Jack's Back: JUST AS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T AS THE PREVIOUS ♥♥♥♥ING FIGHT! Didn't take me as long though. 3/10
The "Important Choice": "Who else was I going to choose?". ♥♥♥♥ing cheap moment. 2/10
The Boat: IT WOULD OF BEEN SO GOOD, IF IT WASN'T JUST JAMMING IN THE STORY AT THE LAST MOMENT WITH A LONG DRAGGED OUT, TEDIOUS, UNINTERESTING SECTION LIKE THIS! 0/10
Shrek's Swamp: Not nice looking. Looks like a 12 year old designed it when he got threw into a washing machine and let out, and he tried to spell "mysoginistic" with a pile of dirt, while on a little bit of cocaine. 3/10
Mines: Didn't expect this. Lucas must've been there. Reminded me to check the boxes... Wait a second... Where the ♥♥♥♥ is Lucas anyway? They didn't just drop him from the story, right? Right?! 7/10
Monster House: Somehow ended up in the house again... This seems kinda... rushed... 4/10
Time For Your Shots: Bringing it back home... Not my home, but their home. Cool scenes to build up to the finale. 9/10
Eveline: YOU'RE TELLING ME THE OLD WOMAN WAS EVIE?! HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ IT WAS SO OBVIOUS! WHOA! 10/10
The Last Boss: Oh great. It's Resident Evil 5 all over again. Atleast it isn't a cutscene... 2/10
Finale: That Chris Redfield? Well, he looks different, but atleast he doesn't look like he can suplex an apache attack helicopter or a boulder... 7/10
The End: Wait. Thats it? Atleast the rest of the story is FREE DLC. Take notes Mass Effect. 9/10

[DLC]
----
Firstly... The Tapes.
NightMare: Huh... Clancy... I guess I'll play as hi- OH MY GOD WAVE MODE?! YAAAAAAA- 8/10
Bedroom: Awesome, but finished it my first time. 7/10
21: And the winner is... CLANCY!!!! 10/10
Origins Crap: Why is this DLC. It explains it atleast. 7/10

Ethan Must Die: Wow. Never been so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and entertained at the same time... It's fun. 10/10

In my humble opinion, the Call of Juarez series is rather hit or miss- pulling one game randomly out of the bunch is 50/50 as far as you getting your money's worth, and that's saying something given that there's currently only four games in the series. Glad to say, this is one of them.
Sound- Voices sound like they were recorded with a potato, yet the gunshots are crisp. Explosions look flat, though dynamite and oil lamps scattered around the environment are effective enough. This is a western, though- the focus is on the gunplay.
Gunplay- Just a touch tricky with some of the special moves, but once you get the hang of it you're damn near unstoppable playing as one of two brothers- Thomas, the sneaky and lithe long ranged specialist with knives and a bow, or as Ray, the guns-blazing, dual weilding muscle bound♥♥♥♥♥kicker. The game rarely limits your approach as far as what weapons you're actually allowed to utilize- as Ray I often found myself picking off people with a long rifle, and with Thomas I've blown away many an outlaw with a double barrel- the differences lie in how you utilize these weapons, and also, what perspective you experience the story from.
The Story- It's well written and engaging as any good western should be- not reinventing the wheel by any means, but satisfying to see unfold- and given the different perspectives of each brother through these missions, it's worth a second go just to see what exactly is going on when the other brother is out of sight. How you determine the quality of the ending and how everything get's tied together will ultimately be a rather subjective thing, but I personally enjoyed it.
I can't speak for the multiplayer- I haven't tried it, but there's a community however small it may be dedicated to keeping it alive, so it must have some merit.
If you're new to western themed games but enjoy first person shooters heavily focused on story and gameplay, definitely give this one a whirl- if you're already a fan of such things, don't even wait for it to go on sale like I did, ten bucks is already a steal, minor little quirks and flaws be damned.

However the development team behind Kinetic Void are working on the game at a decent pace and patches appear within a time span of 1-3 weeks between each other. It wouldn't be surprising to see the game toting more features a few months down the line.
In the game's current state, it's great for anyone who wants to recreate ships such as Serenity from Firefly, The titular Battlestar Galactica or an X-Wing from Star Wars. And indeed, that is in it's own right an entertaining thing.
As a result, I find that Kinetic Void is an entertaining video game that, even in it's unfinished and somewhat unstable format that it's currently in, is worth the admission price.

The first thing I want to do is address the premise of the game, which I feel is being missed when people look at the tags for the game:
You are a student and your entire goal is to learn more about martial arts and teach those who are less experienced than you are. Your journey is to become an Absolver and become the best that there ever was. That's it. That's the entire premise. Wandering around and exploring the broken world is just icing on the cake. Fashion is extra. PvE just exists to teach you the game and give you more moves to play with.
Pros:
Great diversity of movesets from various styles
Surprisingly technical in how moves are used and how they flow with other moves
The tension shard system is an interesting take on powers and weapons
Picking fights with other players can either be done in the open world or through the queuing system at any Altar you visit
Dark Souls' level design distilled to its essence makes for most of the explorable world
You get armors from PvE and PvP
Grey:
Netcode is very hit or miss, but usually more hit than miss
Your PvP rank unlocks higher difficulty versions of previously defeated bosses. This is great if you're good at the game, but raising your PvP rank is very slow if you're not able to beat your opponents.
Powers in general. Some are simply not worth using.
No way to increase your weight limit. It's not too much of a problem since it prevents hardcore min-maxing of stats, but at the same time it hampers your fashion ability if your Combat Deck needs a high Mobility stat.
Cons:
Servers can be finnicky but otherwise the developers have been very fast with supporting them. Since having the MP is so integral to the game, a big chunk of the game is lost if you can't be online.
There's no way to delete duplicate armors at the time of this review.
You can receive visual bugs depending on how bad the latency is, such as stats not being properly represented on your moves.
Some moves have questionable balance practices.
This game is NOT for solo players. IF YOU INTEND TO PLAY SOLO, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. This game by its nature is very social and without the MP feature the PvE is very shallow.

For new game developers, this is a great start. This felt like it had the possibility of being fun, and the story line was very intriguing. The art, while very intriguing and interesting, lacked a sense of cohesiveness - it was obvious what was 3D and 2D and it felt like it was fighting against eachother instead of working together to create an interesting environment. I did see a spelling error with "soulless" and heard a mispronunciation of laybrinth at one point, I got stuck on that for a little bit and looked through to see if everything else was as polished. Overall, I do think this game requires more polish. I wanted more gameplay with tighter controls (felt frustrated by the jump and by the camera at times because it kind of made me feel sick). The enemies did not feel incredibly meaningful to the gameplay experience or unique in aesthetic style compared to the rest of the game, though I'm sure they were more in there to coincide with the story, and I mostly felt frustrated by them.  Also, the sound that triggered when transferring energy felt cut mid-length, like it was being cut off or interrupted. The rest of the sounds/music were good. Maybe the narrator's voice could be a tad softer in-game. But for a first-time developed game on what looks to be a broad team, great job! Look forward to more possible iterations of this game.

My brother gave me a Mordheim tabletop starter set for my birthday long ago so I was really excited to see a video game version of it. So far reading about the game and playing a couple of hours of it I find this game manages to capture the spirit of the tabletop game pretty well.
- The game has great visuals from the dark Chaos touched ruins of the city, to the look of units and their abilities. The visuals really put you into the world of Mordheim. More variety  of maps would be good but I am sure more will come out with release.
- The frustration of your units failing time and time again to hit an opponent while the opponent wails on them! 100% Game Authenticty.
- The current Warbands are pretty fun. I love we get female characters and they aren't wearing bikini chainmail. And any game that lets you play as Skaven is an automatic win. One of the biggest things I think will make or break this game is how much will available on release and how much will be DLC later. If they give us a decent selection range, more then 4 just warbands, off the bat the game could be pretty great! Hopefully within each Warband there will be some some diversity to choose from eventually, Clan Pestilens instead of Clan Eshin for Skaven for example.
- I am excited they brought the customization of your Warband to this game. I can't wait to have a unique group to despair at as the die off in combat. Have battered veterans with new skills and missing limbs. Not much of this is in the game yet so I will have to hope it delivers what is promised.
- Scenario games with plenty of interesting objectives similar to the original game! I haven't delved into these too much yet but I am hopeful that the game will feel less like a bunch of pointless battles with a little bit of lore behind each one.
The game is currently glitchy and a little bare bones but that is to be expected for early access. But it is still a fun game to play in its early state so I have high hopes for the game.

I really liked Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood; the prequel to the first Call of Juarez game. Set in 1864, and then 1865, and later, 1866, Bound in Blood revolves around the McCall brothers. You might recall Ray McCall, the badass priest from the first game. And you might remember Thomas McCall, the "father" of Billy Candle from the first game. Well, they're the stars of Bound in Blood, and their youngest brother, William, shares the adventure with them as the good shepard, a preacher.
The game begins in 1864, when the Civil War is coming close to an end. Ray McCall is a member of the Confederate Army, and works to make sure Thom is safe. Ultimately, the two brothers desert their ranks to save their family from the Union army. They manage to save WIlliam, but their mother has already passed away. This is where the game's story really picks up. Their commanding officer is Barnsby, and he is rather♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that the McCall brothers fled. He's also delusional and thinks that, despite the Union army winning the war, he can help revitalize the southern army and win the war.
Anyway, the McCall brothers follow what I like to call the "classic Western format." The classic Western format is when a group of people, the people here being the McCall brothers, travel a great distance with a single goal in mind, to make some money in order to rebuild their family home. They travel, and run into a great number of characters, some of which are in the first game, set some 18 years after the events of this game. Without getting into the plot, the gist of the McCall brothers traveling involves getting into plenty of gun fights.
The narrative of William is easily the centerpoint of the game. It's strong and well written. It emphasizes the various themes of the game, and his narrative will ultimately lead Ray to become the man he becomes in the first Call of Juarez game. I will say that the writing and story in Bound in Blood is quite strong. What's not strong would be the animation. I'm not surprised either, it's a Techland game and most of their games have animation that's not terrible, but not great, like Naughty Dog or Remedy or Rockstar great. However, the vast openess of the game, despite being a linear shooter, is remarkable, and does more to make up for the games few technical shortcomings. The scope of the world that Techland made is quite something. It's not surprising considering how they've transitioned into the open world genre with their more recent games. Hell, even Bound in Blood has some "intermission" parts where you can do a few side quests in a semi-open world zone.
Pretty tight game overall though. Voice acting could be better from a few characters. And some of the visual effects weren't executed that great; most post processing effects really, specifically depth of field.

So, I have played every RE to date and I have almost every horror game on Steam. RE7 has its good qualities and its bad qualities. Lets start with the good;
- First person is actually somewhat refreshing in this series and enhances the horror aspect.
- The mechanics are pretty solid. Combining items, puzzle solving, ammo conservation etc etc. These are all still present, as they should be.
- The Bakers are pretty damn scary especially Jack. He makes the early part of the game the most memorable.
- Decent graphics.
- Fantastic soundtrack.
- Keeps you on your toes from early to mid-game.
Alright. Thats the good. Lets get to the bad;
- Very small game area. RE series has always had this but I really feel that this is even more the case in RE7 and first person actually enhances this negative aspect.
- Short. *So* short. I mean I get it. Its a new engine but come on.
- The Bakers make the *early* part of the game the most memorable. Then they take a backseat to the mould which is just insane to me. They clearly should have been persistent threats like Nemesis seen as they were the most flaunted aspect of the game.
- The mould are *not* scary past the first time you see them. They're brown sludge. Are you frightened by brown sludge? No. Me neither. Its not even as though they couldn't have gone a different way with it. If you have a monster that converts biomass into more of itself you could have something like John Carpenters "The Thing". (The original, not the remake.) Now *that* was scary and it could masquerade as people you knew.
- Theres a choice you're given before you get on a boat. Its a pointless choice with results that make little sense. Its pretty obvious which choice is canon and which isn't. If you're not going to make that choice matter just don't offer it to us, its not like people look to RE for this stuff anyway.
- The second half of the game is considerably weaker and turns into an FPS rather than a horror game.
- The final fight with Eveline is basically a cutscene. Why? I mean isn't she meant to be the big bad? Also, why turn her into just a big monstrosity? Wasn't part of what made her scary the fact she could insidiously ♥♥♥♥ with peoples minds? It feels like an opportunity was missed here and I just don't get why.
Conclusion; I want to recommend this game and you know what? I would have but the rose-tinted glasses are off now and I look back and for the life of me the only parts I can remember fondly are the earliest parts of the game. Because that was the most similar to what I was sold in the trailer; a horror game. The rest just felt like "oh look, uroboros again" as if that was a part of the RE series we wanted to revisit. It isn't.
