Coming from a background laden with the likes of Mordheim, Necromunda, Gorkamorka it is safe to say that I am no newbie to the Warhammer universe, albeit somewhat disenchanted with the recent developments at Games Workshop. I was originally thrown into the wargaming hobby whilst young and grabbing up a copy of Space Crusade and Warhammer: Quest and I personally always favoured the Games Workshop adaptations that featured tonnes of "fluff", whose being warband campaigns that did not count on you buying the latest or greatest mini's but really becoming immersed into play system that demanded tactics.
Over the years Games Workshop has failed to meet the bar with many of its video game adaptations of its franchises. Blood Bowl was an epic example of how to mismananage, annoy and isoloate an entire sub culture of gamers away from your product by failing to meet basic demands.
Mordeim: City of the Damned is however a massive step in the right direction! The gameplay is immersive as ever with rich environments and fantastic graphics, the W,A,S,D controls in third-person rather than a strict "overhead only" approach layer upon another dimension of interactivity and narration. The actions and cut scenes have been carefully crafted to actually look good! The controls are consistent and easy to use, along with being able to grasp the basic rules for the game.
What I must commend Rogue Factor on the most is the balancing of the game. Many players threw the Mordheim original rulebook out of the window, because of many broken atrributes, the favoured the fan moderated and constructed 'Coreheim' rules. Rather than using the broken original rules, or further breaking or basterdising rules to fit, Rogue Factor have balanced this gameplay beautifully, making it a pleasure to play.
Please Rogue Factor, once you have completed this, do Necromunda: Tales of the Underhive.

I generally despise early access titles, from a pragmatic point of view and a philosophical view. That being said, Mordheim is an incredible game, especially in this early version. Allowing multiplayer skirmish and warband items management makes this more functional than many other full games.
The High Points:
-AAA Graphics and Terrain. This team is one of the few that actually gets the central aspect of cover in a WH game.
-Skaven and Sisters of Battle. Not since dawn of war has there been a focus on allowing multiple races, and not just the ones that make GW the most money. I hope they expand to Undead, but having these two factions in early access is huge.
-Good Tactical elements, bringing the core ruleset to life. There are a lot of GW games that are not worthy of the name, but Mordheim is a shining Paragon of what a good WH game can bring to video gamers.
-Blending AAA Third Person movement with a tactical game. This is one of my favorite things, and i would love to see more AAA Strategy games take this and modernize the RTS genre. One of the worst things is that the RTS Genre hasn't really improved over time. This isn't technically an RTS and more of a Tactical game, but the point is it is an innovative style.
-The possibilities: This game has HUGE potential, and I pray dearly to Sigmar that they will follow through and get the support they need and dont rush this.
The low points:
-Its early access. The better parts of leveling up your warband has yet to come, but if implemented fully, it will be amazing. That being said, I don't really have faith in gaming companies, and I hope they can deliver.
-Only 3 races and 4 planned as far as i know. I would love to see all the races being implemented, even if quality does trump quantity.
-Camera issues when attacking. Pretty annoying but not game breaking. It is immersion breaking though.
-Not sure if they can manage to implement all the features that will truly make it Mordheim but its on a roll right now.
-Not for pure action junkies. It is for tactical and strategy junkies. Warhammer is a cult phenomenon, and they have yet to come out with a title that competes with most AAA titles like CoD, Mass Effect, etc.
Overall, if you like tactical games and warhammer, get this even in early access it is fun. Probably not worth the money until warband management and levelling is in play, though. I have faith in this title and you should too. Unless we are proven wrong.

I have to give this two scores.
Warhammer Tabletop Score: 9.0/10
Video Gamer Score: 6/10
As a player of Warhammer 40k, and newcomer to Warhammer Fantasy, I have to say this was an amazing and thoroughly enjoyable introduction. I'm a fan of Space Hulk (The original board game, not the steam version, we're talking 1990's here), it was my introduction to Warhammer and Games Workshop. The version on steam comes highly recommended by me. This game is shaping up to be an evolution of that direction, and it's absolutely fabulous. Developers, keep up the good work, as my hat is off to you.
Lets break it down, the following scores are for video gamers, not warhammer fans. If you are a warhammer fan, your excitement and imagination will already see this game is possibly one of the most immersive and enjoyable tabletop simulators in existence, with expansions that evolve elegantly into the video game format. A bit of RPGish element, and a threat of permadeth of hard-won characters adds new layers to a style of gaming we've all come to love. And the FX and animations bring the world to life, like I've only seen in it my imagination.
Realize, no game exists I have ever given a 10 to... yet. That is a perfect score.
Graphics: 9.5/10
While not completely triple A, it comes incredibly close. Atmosphere and character models are high resolution and the modular qualities of the world are hidden behind well crafted layers of detail. I expect this to improve, but even if they don't, they're far beyond anything a TBS or RTS has ever attempted before.
Sound: 7/10
The sound effects are admirably done. The atmospherics are up to the task of providing the player with combat awareness. I am expecting, as they progress, for more sound effects to be added, atmospherics, and other aspects along with the dynamic qualities planned. While doing the job, it doesn't make you terrified. And this is Mordheim, ask a Warhammer player, you should be terrified.
Level Design: 9/10
Once you're done navigating the narrow alleyways and threading your way through the rubble of a house, you'll find plenty of advantages to be had above you from sniper nests to byzantine catwalks, while below your feet lie sewers and pits with murder holes a plenty. Whether your climbing over rubble to take a shot, holding back enemy at a choke point, or slipping through ruined walls and cover to flank, the maps of Mordheim are complex, layered, balanced, and ever changing. The procedurally generated map methods they use have provided me with a puzzle at the beginning of each game as I am forced to reassess and explore. I see lots of replay value.
Controls: 8/10
While I heard problems about using a keyboard and mouse, I found the controls to be tight and smooth. Movement is elegant, a huge step forward from X:Com and Space Hulk, giving players unprecedented options and a fluidity of play that I've never expected in a TBS. Movement is a simple WASD affair, looking is with your mouse, and all combat is done through action selection. Elegant and intuitive.
Gameplay: 6/10
The game is Turn Based Strategy. Two teams called warbands, each consisting of up to ten units. Units are varied, and have classes, and these will be developed as the game goes along, allowing for many options that are not available, but should give you a wide variety of customization when it comes to your characters. Currently, warbands are pre-selected.
Basically,  its an evolved game of X:Com PVP, two teams, go at it. Initiative is by character not side, and action points are a bit more complex. At the moment, there is enough to keep you playing, but online I have not seen many players yet. The AI is very enjoyable to fight, I have not gotten bored of it yet. It's on par with X:Com without any singleplayer, and a lot of shiny new aspects to add some fun.
Content: 2/10
A lot of content is planned, a lot simply isn't there. For you who aren't warhammer fans, you may wish to hang back until more content is coming out... however... it is worth the sale price for early access, I would easily part with the full price for this game when its finished.
Optimization: 5/10
LONG, LONG, LONG loading times. And the game tends to freeze, in combat, without any progress being possible until the game is restarted. It is early access. 3-4 minute waits are not uncommon at this point for me in my playing. Longer are rare, but have happened. Once the game has started, aside from the above bug, the game runs smoothly, quickly, and is quite enjoyable. The slowest aspect of this game in a multiplayer setting will most likely be waiting on the other human being to make up their mind.
Final Thoughts:
Get the game. If you're a video gamer and love Tactical/Strategic RTS/TBS like me? If you're a fan of tabletop games of ole, or modern video game emulations of them, or if you're a Warhammer fan. Everything in the feature list is already worked into the menus. The game looks professional, it looks promising. While Early Access is always a gamble, I already consider my 32.00 well spent. And that's what it comes down to. Is this worth the money. Will it be fun for the time you spend on it and for what you spent in cash on it? The current content is worth easily 20 dollars, 30 dollars with their most recent content update. If they keep it up, you'll be buying it on sale effectively after this point.
Enjoy and see you in the streets of Mordheim.

Disclaimer: I had fun playing this game, so this is why I put Thumbs up (Recommend) But I'd put a ''meh'' thumbs for the rest.
The game is really short (about 2 hours) and the ending is... really disapointing. I won't spoil anything, but I expected more than the cliché it delivered.
You are a 2 year old child, and it feels charming. The game, in itself is gorgeous I believe. The controls are simple and ok and I just love the Teddy. But the game is a bit ''too simple'' and too easy. The only part I had a hard time with is finding the last exit after running around an hour (I was really tired, so it's not even the game's fault).
This is clearly meant to be a game that you see the world from the eye and the mind of a child and I get that the world he sees is not really the world as it is.
The real con is... The game is not scary... in any way. It's not scary as an experience (I didn't felt helpless), it's not jumpscary (yes, there are monsters... 2 times) it's not freaky. I mean, there should've been emphasis on the child's feeling and how it changes his perception of the world, and no emphasis on the child's body. We get it... he's small and can't climb a lot of things. I want to know how he/she feels (I am still not sure about the sex of the infant) not how it moves... we pretty much all know how a baby moves. A child sees his furniture big: MAKE IT BIG! Don't make it real size, make it like the baby sees it!
Also, the Teddy, while being cute, puts too much emphasis on the ''It's dark here, I don't like it'' and... nothing happens.
The ''puzzles'' are too simple (yes I know, it reflects the child's capabilities... but as a player I would've like to be challenge in a new way like ''What would a baby do in that situation''. Not... ''Oh... there is 6 holes here... there 6 owls to find... I am not sure what i am supose to do''
So I would kind of recommend it, because it is fun... and that the adventures worth the game. But... THE PRICE! This game isn't worth 19.99$. There is no exploration per se (the only places you ''explore'' are to find ''keys'' to put in ''switches'') and the rest are just narrow spaces that you go from point A to point B.
The overall design is great though. The music is awesome, the visuals are great and the sounds are also great. The word ''Atmospheric'' really pin point the game, as it surrounds you with beautifulness.
But the story... and the gameplay are a bit disapointing. Not BAD, disapointing! It could've been more (Well, every game could bee more, but I mean, as this game in itself, it could've been more)

I purchased Kingdom: New Lands early this week and I've already logged over 30 hours on it. This game is extremely well designed, and I've had difficulty putting it down!
The controls are as simple as it gets-- so simple you can play the game with only one hand (the arrow keys are the only necessary controls, however you can hold shift to sprint if you don't like to double tap the left and right arrow keys), making it a great game to play at leisure.
The gameplay is fluid and easy to get accustomed to. I also cannot praise K:NL enough for avoiding heavy-handed tutorials. The game tells you the basics, and then leaves you to your own devices. It's awesome to see a game that lets you learn mechanics fluidly as you play, rather than forcing explanations down your throat.
I'm normally not the biggest fan of side-scrolling games, but the style of K:NL drew me in. I absolutely love the graphics for this game-- especially the lighting, which is so detailed that you can see the world around you dim as you go deeper into the forests. The game's music is just as beautiful; I'm especially fond of a bouncy track called "Meadow" that fits perfectly with bounding along on the elk mount.
I'm very happy that I purchased this game. I'm not exactly great at it-- I've let many a kingdom fall already-- but It's been great fun.

Devil May Cry 4 is a hack&slash action\adventure game that focuses on combat,
difficulty, Boss fights and a little humour in the long and amazing cutscenes.
DMC4 starts with a new protogonist named "Nero" as he battles his way through demons to get to the church and witness to Kyrie sings and the ceremony that being held for Sparda.
When everyone starts to pray Nero got bored or innoyed by it and wanted to leave when Kyrie tries to stop him but then a "mysterious" character Interrupts the ceremony and kills the man who's in charge of the ceremony.
in the confusion the guards tries to stop the mureder, Nero tries to get Kyrie out of the place and when she almost got hit Nero Interrupts the murder and battles with him,
after their fight the mureder escapes while making fun of Nero and this is where your journey starts.
Gameplay : Devil May Cry series has always being popular especially for its deep and complex combat, you won't be able to button mash you way through and because of that you will need to learn how to make combos\special attacks and more, you will learn every single attack that your character can do.
The game won't be easy on you and you will find yourself dying
( even on normal difficulty ) especially in boss fights
( if you won't be able to find your enemies weak spot )
that being said theres also a couple of puzzles that might frustrate you,
also unfortunatly you will find yourself battle with the same boss two times if not three times. The game also will repeat the same map twice in which it shows that the developers were too lazy.
Graphics : the game delievers an impressive visuals and art, there were times where I just stood there ( even though it ruins the main score at the end )
and looked how beautiful the game is. I really liked the enemies art style which was combined with demonic look and humour.
the game will look at its best when you will deliever and outstanding combos at the poor demonic creatures. The cutscenes are just amazing and you will be entertained as if you watch a movie in the cinema.
Story : Devil May Cry storyline isn't his strong side... I would say the story is predictable, sometimes stupid or illogical but non the less entertaining.
the good part are the characters which are funny in the second half of the game.
AI: the ai in the game aren't really special or anything its just that they are sometimes unpredictable and when you raise the difficulty you will be encountering many diffrent foes which has diffrent abilities and thats where you will put your skill in to the test, and because they will be coming at you together it will be harder for you to fight and defeat them.
Summary : DMC4 isn't the best game but non the less its a great game
while the game has its down sides like reused maps\bosses\enemies and the puzzles are just annoying the game also delivers a fun combat, an entertaining cutscenes, funny characters ( and moments ), a hard challenge and great boss fights.
I myself completed DMC4 more than 3 times which in total I spent over 45 hours ( on pc 15 hours on xbox 30 hours )
and there is a reason to come back and play the game again with a higher difficulty ( there are 7 diffrent difficulties ).
Overall I give this game a 8.5\10

Quite a brilliant game. It's small, but well crafted and deserving of praise.
But it is greatly wasted potential. Few games have such a masterfully crafted combat mechanic or has such a decently decorated enviroment, yet Absolver is disappointly short. That is to say, it lacks content, a lot.
I delibaretedly avoided reading up anything about Absolver on forums because I didn't want to get my hopes up, maybe if I did I would have at least waited for a sale before buying it because quite frankly (what was to me) a 5 hours experience isn't worth its current price. Though I should specify that it took me those 5 hours to complete it's entire quite short "story missions", if I can even call it that. The rest of my playtime is entirely grinding through the combat trials pvp system.
Absolver advertises a "relationship-binding online experience", but so far my experiences with other players in the pve section of the game was rather passive. Most players were content with ignoring me entirely as long as I showed no aggression, whilst a very few attacked me on sight, and sometimes when I revived them (or they revive me) they simply attack me again. On very very few ocassions we engaged in some manner of co-operative action, but it was always short-lived.
The trailers and various images showed off swordplay and staff combat as well as martial arts, but I was greatly disappointed to discover that weapons are only present in the game as quite temporary, either breaking after being used a while or knocked out of your hand if you get hit too hard. And the Bo staff simply doesn't exist in the game, far as I know.
Imagine if Absolver's brilliant design and mechanics were incorporated into a fully-fledged grand title, instead of a 4 gigabyte novel arcade game?
While I enjoyed the game (and I hope I'll continue to when and/or if further content is added) I firmly believe it needs a slight price reduction. In short; it's a good game, just get it during a sale.

It's Resident Evil 1 if it was released in 2017.
Basically original Resident Evil is multi-layered puzzle game with arcade gameplay mixed with exploration, ammo conservation and movement planning set in horror-flick themed setting.
Resident Evil 7 is exactly the same game at it's core. It still a multi-layered puzzle game with arcade gameplay mixed with exploration, ammo conservation and movement planning set in horror-flick themed setting. The difference is in it's form, not function. Functionally it is still the same game as first. Capcom used all modern tech and design doctrines to recreate the core Resident Evil experience into new generation. They used it to create the most immersive, scary and polished package in recent gaming. It is what PT (Silent Hills) was to Silent Hill: reimagination in new era of gamedesign while keeping the essence of series. And while Silent Hills was canned, Resident Evil 7 got to release in absolutely glorious form. Not to mention that PC version is the definitive one with great visuals and optimisation.
Also proper story DLCs are free, and paid DLCs are not required at all - they are all experimental and standalone mini-games for fans, they don't affect core story and game. It's DLC done right - they pushed away content that is not required, but won't work standalone. So you get complete package even without buying DLCs.
The king is back baby. And now it's finally scary.
PSA: One thing: the game requires a lot of high speed vram to be played on high settings since whole engine was designed around current gen hardware with a lot of high speed vram. For high settings your GPU need to have proper 6Gb of vram and for medium GPU needs proper 256bit bus. Otherwise it'll stutter. So, sadly, Nvidia folks with their midrange 128bit cards and 3.5Gb 970 got shafted. But that's not exactly the problem of the game itself tho

Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising is one of those gems that is overlooked by most players.  Personally I think the way to get the most out of this game though is running multi-player Co-op.
This is no Call of Duty or Medal of Honor shoot 'em up, but rather a tactical combat simulator.  If you are a solo player I would probably skip this title.  However if you like to roleplay and really get into your job, then team up with up to three others and run this game in multi-player campaign mode (Co-op).
There are four roles to choose from. Engineer, Medic, Sniper and Squad Leader.  There is only one squad leader and he sets up and calls out the waypoints and strategies through the missions.  The game can be a bit glitchy at times, but the fun factor far outweighs the technical glitches.  The first mission is probably the worst, so if you pick up this game don't let the beginning stop you.  By the third mission you will be wading through the foliage calling out targets for your sniper while your engineer sets some demo up on an enemy APC.  I cannot emphasize enough that this game is best played with others and is definitely not a solo affair.  You will need to use 3rd party software for headset chat.  You will need to use a headset as well as the in game communication is very poor.
I always played Squad Leader, as I was the host for our game sessions.  One of the most memorable moments in this game for me was when our sniper got pinned down behind a wall and was getting hammered by a .50 cal from an enemy technical.  I sent in the engineer with this heavy weapon and before he reached the wall he went down hard.  He was still alive so I instructed the medic to lend support to the engineer while I drew fire from the technical.  The screaming going on over the headset was intense.  The medic got the engineer back on his feet and behind the wall while our sniper bugged out of the area.  I was getting attention form that .50 cal and hiding behind a tree and was also drawing fire from some infantry that heard the ruckus and started closing in on my position.  Just when I figured that I was going down the technical blew up thanks to our engineer's heavy weapon and the inantry closing in on my position started dropping like flies from our sniper.  We were back in business doing what we did best.
When it comes right down to it, it's times like this that I game for.  I would highly suggest this title to anyone that likes to game with friends.  Operation Flashpoint: Red River is even better and provides a smoother ride.  If you can pick this title up on a steam sale with Red River I wouldn't hesitate.

Overall, it looks like this will retain the feel of the original game while making a reasonable transition to modern computer capabilities.  That said:  right now (December 2014) it's no where near complete.  That's to be expected in an early-access game, so I'm not counting it against them, but it's something to be aware of.
A few thoughts, both positive and negative:
- I really, really, REALLY hope they hire a copy-editor before the final release.  Bad use of tenses, plurals, and all kinds of bad grammar.  I hope it gets fixed, because it's annoying.
- The large creatures FEEL huge, which is fantastic.  It's not just having a larger model:  they move differently and act differently, which is as it should be for a 10' tall Ogre (or rat ogre, or demon...).
-  The graphics are good, and the feel of the space is perfect.  It's meant to be a run-down rat-warren of a destroyed city, and it is.
-  The downside of that is limited sight-lines, and not just in game terms.  The enclosed spaces mean that I frequently can't see who is attacking, because they're on the far side of the wall from a camera.
Overall, I'm excited by the game.  I look forward to seeing what Rogue Factor can accomplish as they get closer to release!

Blacklight Retribution.
A supposed still-born, that defied the odds. BLR was a great, probably the greatest, game that had a level of customisation that was almost perfectly balanced, you could make your weapons in any way you wanted and it would work just as well as the so-called 'meta' builds that were floating around. I played Tango down and BLR and loved every hour i spent on the games, I had over 300 hours in Tango down and 600 in BLR. The games were perfect, a good balance between a futuristic shooter and a competitive game that allowed anyone to play as anything and go anywhere on the map AND still make a massive impact on the flow of the game. The maps were well designed and the clever spawn system allowed teams to get back on their feet if they had just been aced by one guy(possible). This was what BLR was like before PS4 was introduced. When PS4 was introduced everything went downhill, the parity patch was due to hit. Hardsuit labs attempted to revive the game, as it was in decline after 2 years, and they did bring hope back into the community, there was definitely a jump in the number of players on at any given time after the community heard a new company was taking over, but then we heard of the 'parity patch'. Anyone who played pre-parity will know what this update did to the game. no offence console players, but please learn to use/counter recoil or just plug-in a damn keyboard and mouse for your console as that is exactly what hardsuit labs removed, recoil. So now after recoil had been removed you know what else they did, they added more cosmetics, included a pay-to-win system and in my opinion ruined the game. BLR will be sorely missed especially after i spent many hours getting my builds perfect and participating in many a scrim with my clan/friends, and many others will agree with me in what i said above. Hardsuit labs, i hope you know what you are doing.

Funnily I got into this game due to the Cyber-Punk vibe, as I used to play another game (well, mod) known by the name of "NEO-TOKYO", the game (mod) is sadly dead now, however saddened by that news I was determined to fill that empty void with something similar. This is what I found. To me, Blacklight: Retribution is definately a solid FPS. Its mechanics are definately non-unique and modern except for one little exception; the HRV. I will go over that in more detail, as with other topics I feel compelled to cover. Lastly I have to say I spent very little time typing this review/overview, please forgive me if I make any mistakes.
Aesthetics
The game is set roughly half a century in the future, in what appears to be cities in some Asian country going through a epidemic and political crisis, the prime candidate being Japan as the maps leaves me with a "Neo Tokyo" impression. Everything in it, whether it be the map design, or the overall look of the agents, fit in well and no doubt compliment each other. One small problem to this is with the gun customisation, sometimes aesthetics needs a general direction to head in for it to look natural, by making components non exclusive to a certain weapon some parts put together will look odd, or out of proportion.
Mechanics
Nothing much to say here, apart from being an extremely plain modern shooter with an interesting twist. The HRV is basically a legallised wallhack you can use to see opponents. This is one thing that could've ruined the game outright, but instead it grew into one thing that defines this game. the HRV is not overpowered. Here are the reasons as to why:
1. It can only be turned on whilst the energy is full
2. The energy needs to be recharged over time
3. Energy is depleted fairly quickly, even if you use the HRV for half a second
Customisation/equipment
Everything your agent hold can be customised, and for each part their are dozens of types you choose from. As is with every F2P game you can have the option to buy everything with real money, this is nothing new. However never have I felt certain items were overpowed, every item will boost a certain stat by a small percentage, and take away another stat's potency. This is what makes this game balanced, you want to armour up like a tank with 240 HP? sure, but your stamina and speed is reduced porportionally. This applies to guns as well, if you install a barrel which increases accuracy, perhaps your recoil kick and spread will rise. As of this writing however not all will have this trade, but most does. This is exactly what a customisable game should allow, granted that certain builds/loadouts will prevail, just look at any FPS games with a competitive scene, quake pro players dictated which way it is more efficient to move about the map, and how map control can be acquired the most effective way, CS players figured out the most viable gun is the AK47 and M4A4, and manners of usage which will produce the greatest efficiency, if you bother looking at any CS competitive matches you can see those two guns are the only guns being used round after round consistently. This criticism is something I tolerate, because there are many ways to play the game, but often times there is only one single efficient way to play. This mentality is something you'll definately find less of in casual servers, often times I'll play with and against players with loadouts so bizzare I'll question their sanity.
Equipment is something that requires more focus from the devs as it is one thing that can potentially upset the balance. However I will argue everything here are still incredibuly well tuned. To name an example, HRV blockers will block out vision of the player in HRV mode, the single most useful equipment I argue, but its area of effect is minute, and players in normal vision will easily notice the odd blue bubble forming just some distance away from them. There are things added in just for flair, things such as melee weapons with feel like its main use is to insult the enemy.
In summary, for a free to play game, many have done worse. Give this game a try and see for yourself, the only cost is time spent downloading. I give this game a 7/10

Wow. Just wow. What an amazing game.
So Kingdom: New Lands is an RTS in which you play a Monarch that is trying to rebuild the kingdom of their ancestors. You recruit goons of questionable virtue and build a kingdom from a small fortune you found lying around. Lord knows how it got there but who cares. Use this gold to rebuild your kingdom. But it seems that someone knows of your attempt to rebuild your kingdom because every night you get assaulted by mobs and mobs of goons. But you couldn't, nay, you'd never sully your hands by fighting the goons yourselves. So you have your archers fight the goons for you and you just have to sit back and pray that your walls are thick enough. If you'd like to stem the flow of goons, you can destroy portals using knight squads. Each knight can have three archers following them. The knights don't attack the portal, they just hold the line so their archer squads can do the work.
Every few nights a Red Moon appears in the sky and during this night you get mobbed by even more enemies than usual. Normally this wouldn't be that much of a problem but your archers have the accuracy of blind man firing a BB gun at a flea on your cat. The good part about Red Moons is that the enemies will only spawn from one side. I think there's a possible exception if you destroy a portal right before it though.
There are various shrines you can offer gold to if you want to buff your units (and why wouldn't you) but they can get pretty pricey if your income is stifled by... I dunno... the swarms of goons at your door. And then your knights are such♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that if the wall gets low on health, instead of doing their jerb and holding the line they run back to an inner wall. And they bring their archer squads with them! The number of times I yelled at my computer because if the knights had stayed and let their archers keep firing, we wouldn't have lost that wall! Christ.
And don't get me started on the engineers. If you happen to accidentally mark a tree for removal out in the middle of nowhere, your engineers will continually suicide at it until they cut it down! And sometimes your archers will stay out hunting way past their bedtime and get gooned. And sometimes you need that extra gold coin and your archer will shoot like five arrows at a rabbit and miss every time. PUT. ON. YOUR. GLASSES.
The only downside to this game (I would say) is that each level takes like two hours to complete. Oh, and if you want to clear the last island, it's imperative that you set yourself up by beating a prior island (I chose the first island for ease) because the small fortune you find at the beginning of the game is a little tooooo small.
That said, it's very absorbing. I accidentally played through the night until I had to get up for work several times. "Just one more attempt." The game nicely works its way into itself for replays too. After your die, your new monarch will be the ghost that leads you to the new site. There's a war horse you can ride that spawns in a battlefield. One of the background textures for that battlefield is the body of your old monarch. The little touches. 100% recommend.

It is a shame that everything else seems lacking. Not sure there is a story. The level design is passable but minimal. There doesn't seem to be a way to sell off eqipments, even duplicates. Enemy variety is low.

Over a decade ago, when I first tried out Far Cry, I was astonished about the standards FPS gaming had reached and shocked on how good the enemy AI can be. Unfortunately, didn't manage to finish it, cause the spec requirements at the time were insane. Even at low (medium?) settings my PC would howl and come to a not very comfortable fps level to be able to keep up with the game.
Today, even though my laptop can play Far Cry at max res and fps with ease, I still find it hard to beat that dastardly enemy AI. Reliving Jack's moments at the tropical paradise, I thought I was finally experienced enough to easily handle medium Far Cry difficulty level and I was so wrong. After 6hrs and not even a quorter of the way through the game...
And that is the essence of Far Cry. Even after so many years, it still holds its own and provides a worthy challenge, at par with the likes of Half Life 2, Bioshock, CoD4 etc with great level design, plot that is pacing to your progress and an intelligent AI that plans, adapts and responds to each of the player's actions.
This time around, I will be finishing Far Cry for sure and then perhaps re-try at ta higher difficulty level while trying out some of the numerous mods out there that add hugely to its re-playability. Shame about the shutdown of the multiplayer services but still a highly recommended classic to all fps lovers.

- Beautiful landscapes. The scenery is really original.
- Interesting story.

- Algiz doesn't seem to be affected by lighting. He is in full brightness all the time, making him look ugly next to all the good looking landscapes.
- The magma-monster is hilariously cheap looking and it didn't intimidate me at all despite being the only real enemy in the game.
- Despite this being a platformer game, where responsive control is crucial, it felt kinda bad. Algiz jumped without any acceleration and when I jumped at a box he kinda just sticked to it. The "bouncyness" of the controls felt very bad at the dodge-the-projectiles sections.
- The game crashed when I tried to exit.
- The game once didn't reload the map when I died. It was black until I restarted the map, which brings me to the next point:
- If you restart a map, the game totally forgets about how many collectibles have you already got. It restarted from zero.

Tompi is a fine example of a diamond in the rough - the two developers behind this game have added a lot more gameplay and exploration elements than most larger dev teams have over the past decade.
Secrets, collectibles, multiple gameplay mechanics; "AMBITIOUS" sums this game up nicely
But unfortunately Tompi met with a couple of highly aggrivating misfortunes along the way - namely lost data due to hard drive failure and a bundle site (now shut down) that refused to pay up for Tompi's participation.
I've just had a go since Desura and quite a bit has changed in the first level so I'm happy to see the game was cleaned up a bit more before it was deemed a closed case.
The developer assured me that, despite the bugs, all stages are finishable right up to end credits so I look forward to playing this game through to finish.
At the current retail I recommend this game to anyone wanting to support a small team of two who have tried desperatley hard and have churned out some highly intriguing game concepts (also see 'Match 3 Revolution') that perhaps might prove more lucrative if sold as concepts & prototypes to larger design houses.

OFDR is an attempt by Codemaster to reviveits Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis, originally developed by Bohemia Interactive (who created their own "Arma" franchise). Using their own "EGO" engine, OFDR is an attempt to bring back the "sandbox military shooter" genre, in trying to get away from the tightly scripted experience of MOH or COD franchise. The result is a bit hit and miss, due to unforgiving difficulty, a tightly scripted experience on an open map, and clunky interface that was not even optimized for gamepad.
Set on a fictional island just off Russia, which has the potential of large oil reserves, China, with some historical claims, chose to invade it for the oil to fulfill its own energy needs. Russia, busy with its problems, requested US for help, and US marines landed, and soo ncame into direct conflict with the People's Liberation Army. You will get to play two characters... a Marine Sgt with his own fireteam, and a special forces lieutenant leading his own fireteam. They have different missions on different part of the island, but together they will find a way to kick the PLA off the island.
The game is realistic in that you can be wounded by a single bullet, and a head shot will likely kill you. You will need to use the medpack on yourself to staunch the bleeding (else you'll fade out and die), and/or summon the fireteam medic (or anyone else) to bandage you. However, the interface to do so is clumsy and impossible to use during combat. Same with grenades. You have them, but throwing them is a real PITA.
The game does retail a lot of the open feel. If you can get at a vehicle, you can probably drive it. A jeep, sure. Tank or APC? No problem. Helicopter? Why not, if you catch one on the ground. Killing armor, on the other hand, is a different problem, as clearly they are invulnerable to your bullets, and you have to find anti-armor weapons (Queen Bee AT rocket, Javelin AT missile, etc.) . And you will occasionally get to shoot Stinger or Strela SAM at helicopters.
The actual shooting, however, leaves much to be desired. You will barely spot the enemy at all, even through the various target scopes, unless you happen across a sniper rifle (usually by killing an enemy sniper, or special ammo crates). There's also plenty of foliage and terrain features. Add it to a very... bland color pallete (it's almost all autumn yellow) and you'll NEVER spot the enemies without a little help from the threat indicator (which is only active at the "easy" difficulty level).  And no, there's no "radar" showing you where the enemies are. This is a sim, not a "game".
The missions are long and the progress saved at checkpoints. However, the checkpoints are not always placed at logical spots, and you often don't know what exactly you did wrong last playthrough. So you end up repeating the checkpoint over and over until you throw your controller through the monitor. The missions also fail to allow the open-sandbox style map to work its magic, as most of the missions are tightly scripted and often with a TIME LIMIT, such as "you must eliminate the SAM teams before our own gunships arrive in X minutes". Obviously there's going to be a ton of enemies between you and the SAM teams, all wanting to shoot you dead.
All in all, OFDR is extremely disappointing. It has plenty of potential, as its sequel, OF:Red River showed. However, the execution is marred by timed mission triggers, impossibility of acquiring targets in the scopes, and very clunky interface, even on a gamepad.

The very first time you get into this, you will think "oh what a simple game. Just power this, aim this and I'm ready!". Give it 20 more minutes and your eyes will be dashing back and forth on the screen in order, your mouse will move at incredible speeds, and you, well, let's just hope the wall next to you doesn't end with a hole.
It's a complicated game, and very annoying. But nonetheless, you will get to a point where you just want one more run.
The art is amazing, pixelated yet so precise, the battles are hard but none of them are impossible (generally speaking). It drags you in by the amount of work you need to put in. Micromanaging is key, but once you have that down, it's just praying to RNG-esus.
Pros:
1. Great looking art
2. Huge variety in between classes and ships, each one has a different playstyle
3. Deep secrets and easter eggs
4. Easy to get into, hard to master
5. Once you do get to the end, it will be one of the best feelings ever
Cons
1. Truly, a hard game
2. You will die, many times, before you may even get near the end.
3. Everything is RNG
Other than the game being RNG based (which for me, really isn't a con) and being, quite unforgiving. It is incredible, and unique. You have one ship, one crew, make it yours.

Wow. Just wow. What an amazing game.
So Kingdom: New Lands is an RTS in which you play a Monarch that is trying to rebuild the kingdom of their ancestors. You recruit goons of questionable virtue and build a kingdom from a small fortune you found lying around. Lord knows how it got there but who cares. Use this gold to rebuild your kingdom. But it seems that someone knows of your attempt to rebuild your kingdom because every night you get assaulted by mobs and mobs of goons. But you couldn't, nay, you'd never sully your hands by fighting the goons yourselves. So you have your archers fight the goons for you and you just have to sit back and pray that your walls are thick enough. If you'd like to stem the flow of goons, you can destroy portals using knight squads. Each knight can have three archers following them. The knights don't attack the portal, they just hold the line so their archer squads can do the work.
Every few nights a Red Moon appears in the sky and during this night you get mobbed by even more enemies than usual. Normally this wouldn't be that much of a problem but your archers have the accuracy of blind man firing a BB gun at a flea on your cat. The good part about Red Moons is that the enemies will only spawn from one side. I think there's a possible exception if you destroy a portal right before it though.
There are various shrines you can offer gold to if you want to buff your units (and why wouldn't you) but they can get pretty pricey if your income is stifled by... I dunno... the swarms of goons at your door. And then your knights are such♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that if the wall gets low on health, instead of doing their jerb and holding the line they run back to an inner wall. And they bring their archer squads with them! The number of times I yelled at my computer because if the knights had stayed and let their archers keep firing, we wouldn't have lost that wall! Christ.
And don't get me started on the engineers. If you happen to accidentally mark a tree for removal out in the middle of nowhere, your engineers will continually suicide at it until they cut it down! And sometimes your archers will stay out hunting way past their bedtime and get gooned. And sometimes you need that extra gold coin and your archer will shoot like five arrows at a rabbit and miss every time. PUT. ON. YOUR. GLASSES.
The only downside to this game (I would say) is that each level takes like two hours to complete. Do not buy this game if you are looking for the following:

PVE content.  Yes, the game has PVE content, however, it should be considered a fairly large tutorial for the end game which is PVP.
Do buy this game if you are looking for the following:
PVP - This is a hardcore fighting game.  The depth of this game comes from collecting various moves to put into your combat "deck" at which point you will challenge other fighters in a 1v1 combat.  You will earn experience points and random unlocks that reward you along the way.  They are also going to institute a 3v3 fighting mode coming soon which I feel will be a nice change of pace as well.
Simply put, Absolver has the framework to really be something special but you need to understand what you are buying.  You are buying a game that has the primary focus of PVP.  Do not buy this game for any other reason.  A simple comparison would be buying Street Fighter for the arcade mode.  You just wouldn't.  You buy Street Fighter for the online competition and the same holds true for Absolver.
Side note, for those of you who have put several dozen hours into For Honor like I have, I feel this game trumps it in almost every facet.  For Honor was plagued by the turtle meta which rewarded players on just focusing on counters.  In this game you cannot do this as your stamina is drained with each block.  Since this game is really not focused as much on "Classes" as For Honor, and focuses entirely on your "deck" it will not have the horrific balance problems that ruined that game as well.
TLDR - The combat is amazing, buy this immediately if you are interested in a pulse pounding pvp game.  Skip it if you are looking for anything else.

Summary: Currently Absolver feels like it is in beta. Lacking substantial content, needing bug fixes and balancing changes, but the core mechanics and gameplay are there.
Absolver definitely fulfills in it's combat. One on one duels feel great and you can learn moves from opponents just as expected. There seems to be a good amount of different combat moves you can learn as well.
The game is built with the explicit intent of one on one duels, and yet regularly puts 3-4 NPCs against a single player at every given encounter.
The class/school abilities do not feel entirely balanced as of yet. I myself started with Kahlt, and the absorb does little more than a precise timed block, still allowing opponents to continue chaining attacks on you. Meanwhile the parry of the Forsaken interrupts and completely turns the tide in favor of the user. Windfall appears to just be timed dodging. I find myself (a Kahlt user) using the normal dodge more regularly anyway, it'd likely be a better choice.
There also appears to be many server crashes (though to be expected immediately following the release) and assets in the game not loading properly. Other players with less than optimal performance in your area can also cause you connection issues, latency delays, teleporting, and other networking issues. It is also possible to aquire repeats of the same item over and over, with no way to discard duplicates and this bulking your inventory.
Finally, Absolver makes a habit of presenting you with decisions that will prove vital to later gameplay: your choice of school/style, and attribute point distribution. These choices are given to you before you can understand the effects they will have a part in, and given that you make a wrong decision there is no way to correct it without restarting your character from scratch.

Well, this is WAY overdue, but here goes: My CoJ: Bound in Blood Review!
This is a liner(mostly) Old-West FPS with a fantastic story and some tragically under appreciated multiplayer. Here's the pros and cons for you, just to make it a little simpler.
PROS:
-Fantastic atmosphere and setting. I personally love the Old West, and this only amplified that love. From the cutscenes to the running-and-gunning, to simply staring at the scenery, the game perfectly captures that old school cowboy vibe many games fail to achieve.
-Incredible story. It seems simple at first, two brothers, on a trail of vengeance and glory, but the narrative, and a stellar performance from the cast, send this story soaring, even to it's heart-breaking (if slightly predictable) ending.
-Solid, entertaining combat. There's not a ton of weapons to choose from, but hot damn if they're not fun to shoot, especially in the games many set piece combat areas.
-Great level design. The levels make great use of height ad cover to provide some truly entertaining shooting action.All but a few of the levels are fairly linear, but that handful of non-linear levels show the possibility to make an incredible open world CoJ, with detailed environments, plenty of side-quests, and a great sense of scope.
-Stellar multiplayer. Sadly, the community is no longer active, but Bound by Blood had some truly spectacular multiplayer. The controls carried over from the campaign quite well, and the map design made for some fun and frantic action.
CONS:
-Runtime. The game is too damn short. I mean, it has a reasonable runtime, but still, it's so great, I easily could've sunk another 10 hours into the singleplayer if it was there.
So there you have it, a truly fantastic game with a great story, awesome combat, a spectacular atmosphere, and some sadly under rated multiplayer to boot.

I bought Panzermadels because it looked weird and interesting and was on sale, and it delivered. It was both weird and interesting in a very fun way.
The characters follow some common tropes (ex: tsundere) in anime, VN, and manga. However, the way these tropes were tied into the tank framework was very interesting and made the game light hearted, and very enjoyable. The game contained numerous references to variety of subject matter, but mostly to WW2 and tanks in general. Many of these references were quite funny.
Overall, Panzermadels was a blast to go through the first time and contained a lot of choices which made it feel engaging. Subsequent readings definitely feel lacking as the game doesn't change very much depending on your choices, and some choices appear to have no impact at all and were used to create an amusing moment. The characters were well written and it made me want to see more of some of the secondary characters to see how they would turn out. The biggest downside to this game is that the ending is quite bizarre and I felt didn't live up to the rest of the game. At the end, I was definitely a bit dissatisfied. Now that the game has left early access and been out for a month, it's time to update my review.
First of all, most bugs have been fixed. There's still some that pop up now and then, but rarely anything that will impact your gameplay in any major way, and they will presumably be worked out too.
Now the two major points: RNG and difficulty.
A lot of players complain about the RNG. Not because it's broken or rigged, because it's not (several have tested it and confirmed that it's working fine).
No, they complain because they either do not understand how RNG works (it's a "Random Number Generator", and a big clue is in the "Random" part), the gameplay mechanics or do not like it when they lose.
First, for those not understanding the gameplay mechanics, here's how an attack works:
-you attack a target, and a "Hit Roll" is made (based on your Hit chance)
-if it's a Miss, you miss
-if it's a Hit, your target gets a Dodge/Parry roll (if they are in Dodge/Parry stance)
-if they pass their Dodge/Parry roll, they Dodge/Parry the attack and take no damage
-if they fail the Dodge/Parry roll, you deal damage
Simply put, you need to first Hit, and (if they are in a Dodge/Parry stance) they have to fail their Dodge/Parry roll.
That's where a lot of people get confused or frustrated. The hit chance displayed does not take into account Dodge or Parry, only your chance to "Hit" (or not Miss) the target. So you'll find a few individuals claiming this makes the Hit chance shown is wrong.
Yes, you can potentially miss 3 hits in a row when you have a 95% chance to hit. And yes that can happen in a short span of time. But over the course of 10,000 rolls, a
. Conversely, sometimes you'll also manage to hit 3 times in a row with a 5% chance. And it's exactly the same for the AI. I can't stress this enough:

Streaks will happen on all sides, both good and bad.
If you can't accept that sometimes RNJesus will screw you, then you can't stop reading. You will not enjoy this game, and I highly recommend against buying it.
Then there's the difficulty.
Is it a hard game? Yes. It's hard in the same sense that Mario Bros. was hard. Make too many mistakes and it's Game Over, start again.
But if you look at most of the negative reviews, they are form people with very little time played. Few have more than 50 hours and the majority seem to have less than 20 (even as low as 0.1).
And there's a good reason for that: This game takes time to get into properly. It's not a "Jump in, kill some things, log off and have a biscuit" game. This game requires a certain amount of patience.
You'll most likely fail spectacularly with your first warband. Maybe even your second and third.
It really can be a punishing experience at first.
But when you start understanding the mechanics and taking some time to plan your warband and unit builds, things suddenly get a hell of a lot easier. Those mobs you needed 3 units to take out first time around, you can suddenly take on 2 at a time with only 1 unit.
And the more time you spend planning and choosing your stats, skills and equipment, the better your units get.
And then you get screwed by RNG, and your favourite unit dies. And when I say "dies", I do mean that the unit is dead and gone. No medical kits. No Revival spell. No Phoenix Downs. Your treasured Hero is lost forever.
So you buy a new one and make him even better.
That's how the game works. Your units are always replaceable, and you will replace them for better ones. Managing to get to Rank 10 without losing any units (not to mention without injuries) is supposed to be an achievement, not the standard.
So in the sense that there's always a chance you'll lose units, or even your entire warband, all while trying to make sure you can fulfill shipping demands, it is indeed a hard game.
Personally, I find it a nice change from the way more common mechanic of not actually losing anything if you fail. The Arkham series is a great example of that. Fall to your death? Nope. Automatic Bat-Grapple to a ledge. Get shot or beaten to death? Nope. You simple resurrect at the last Auto-Save. Nothing wrong with that type of mechanic, but it is not what you'll find in Mordheim.
There are no backsies here. Consequences are permanent.
It's certainly not for everyone, but I like it. Makes things more exciting when you know you can lose something.
So, the positive things about Mordheim: CotD.
-Warband and unit customization is vast and can keep you occupied for hours and hours.
-The 4 warbands play very differently, and themselves be played in very different ways.
-Single-Player is large enough to keep you occupied for a long time, with both random missions and 8 Story mission per warband. There is no end to the ranomd missions, so you can keep improving your warband as long as you like.
-Multiplayer is really fun and engaging. It offers two different versions, one with consequences (injuries, death, loot gained, etc) and one without (no loot gained and no injuries or death). In both cases the match can be heavily customized to suit your preferences.
-4 mission difficulties (Normal, Hard, Brutal, Deadly) let's you choose what kind of risk vs reward you go for.
-Random monsters can appear and attack both sides, but are restricted to Brutal missions above rank 5 (so if you don't want to meet them, you don't have to).
-Singleplayer and Multiplayer are tied together, so you can rank up your warband vs the AI then go fight other players.
-potential for expansions (maps, warbands, etc) is huge.
Now for the negative parts.
-Multiplayer, while great fun, is lacking. No servers means no rankings, matchmaking or anything. There's only a lobby and inviting others. It can make finding matches a tedious process.
-AI is dumb as a brick. As soon as you learn it's behaviour, you can easily beat it.
-Visual customization of units is a little lacking.
-Singleplayer and Multiplayer are tied together. Yes, it's also a negative, because it limits a lot of tweaks and additions to Singleplayer because it would affect multiplayer too. A "PvE only" option where you can Save at any point (or restart macthes), or "PvP only" where you can't buff up fighting the AI, are two highly requested features.
Overall, I'd recommend this game to those who enjoy strategic and tactical games where you plan ahead, and spend time with warband and unit management, as well as fighting.
I would not recommend it to players who want quick-paced action or easy games that don't require much thought.
Just be aware that things take time and will not always go your way.

You should not buy Absolver, and it pains me to say that. Absolver has one of the best concepts going for it. It's an online melee action game with RPG elements, items to  earn and equip, and over 100 different martial arts moves to learn and use in a fully customizable combat deck that you can use against the AI and other players. Most fights against players feel unique against players since everyone is using their own customized deck that can string together stylish and devastating combos. It is incredible fun and exhilirating when it works.
The problem is, 9/10, it doesn't.
The network architecture in the game is poor. For an *online* melee action game, that's a problem. Apparently, Austrailia connection problems are catatrophic but even here in North America, I rarely get a good match. Players in 1v1 duels teleport everywhere, attacks and defense moves are delayed, which makes the main crux of the game downright frustrating. You'll feel you're getting spammed, that players are abusing the system, but the fact is the networking is just poor right now.
Unfortunately, this also extends into the combat with the AI. Other players may instance into your game, which lets you and two other players walk around the area kicking butt. Unfortunately, when you connect to another player, this can cause significant problems especially for newer players. NPCs will occassionally double spawn as the instance reloads, you may be in a fight and then an NPC's health replenishes once another player connects, or the NPCs might teleport like the players. This is incredibly frustrating for new players who need to learn moves (by blocking or using abilities) from the NPCs, only to have a tough fight reset, have the NPC kill them, and then lose all their progress (you only earn experience towards moves if you win the fight; this system, while acceptable in theory, leads to extreme frustration as the game essentially jerks you over with its own faults).
In fairness, the developers and publisher have claimed to have a fix for these issues and will be out the week of  9/4/17. That's nice, but doesn't change whether you should buy it now. The networking is the big issue, aside from the fact that you can cheese through the game's fairly empty world in < 8 hours. It's a fun jaunt when played offline, but thats not what the game was supposed to be.
It'd be a game I could recommend at 30 USD for the content on offer.  The game just doesn't work right now, and you'd be better off saving your money unless the networking is fixed.

Crystal Caves is a simple, old-fashioned 2D puzzle platformer, bearing some similarity to the very first Duke Nukem.
Each level, you need to figure out what order to do things in so that you can take out the baddies, grab all the goodies, and make it to the exit alive; it's easy to die or sometimes to get trapped so you have to quit and re-enter the level, but if you're fast and clever enough you may be able to succeed without taking a single hit for a massive score bonus. You can take as many tries as you need to beat each level (no lives limit), which makes the challenging puzzles much more forgiving, and if you get frustrated, you can go back to the main map and platform to a different level for a change of pace.
The story is silly and the action simplistic, but with Steam automatically setting up and configuring a dosbox for it, this is an easy way to relive the old days.
From a modern perspective? It's not all that exciting, but if you like retro simplicity, or are craving nostalgia, it's not bad either.

Overlooked as the actual best single-player stealth FPS of all time.  No gimmicks or stealth-designed levels, just open-world environments and very challenging enemy AI make sneaking in this game feel realistic and terrifying.

I've played plenty of Old-School FPS, so I like to think I know how shooters are supposed to work. The player runs around at a frankly irresponsible speed, shooting tons of enemies with lots of guns and avoiding at least five simultaneous attacks at any given moment while being hit by two more. It's a good system that's proven its worth many a time. Far Cry, however, completely avoids this formula. You can only carry four weapons at a time, you won't survive more than a couple of hits, you spend most of your time crouching or crawling, cover is the most sensible option for avoiding fire, ammo and health are rare, there's a stealth system, the enemies all seem to be tougher than you are, and you're expected to spend most of your playtime sneaking around avoiding being spotted and trying to shoot one guy before someone sees you, calls over his five friends, and tears you into lead-laced lunchmeat. It's Vulnerability: The Game, and it's the antithesis of everything that makes an FPS fun.
So why do I want to keep playing?
Somehow, Far Cry manages to make being the weakest guy around engaging and interesting. The player has to be intelligent, making use of whatever resources are available, locating enemies before being located, and putting together a weapon loadout that has something for every situation. Sure, it takes some getting used to after a few hours of Unreal Tournament, but once you get in the mindset, it's really an excellent experience. My only issue is that plants don't seem to lower your visibility and some solid-looking buildings actually provide no cover whatsoever, but other than that, I'm actually having...fun.
Unusually for me, I wrote this review before actually finishing the game. I've only clocked in a paltry 2-3 hours thus far over the past few weeks (I've been busy). I'll update this review when I beat the game.
EDIT: At long last, I've finished the game. My thoughts and opinions have changed quite a bit about this game. First, however, a summary of the plot:
Jack Carver, the biggest♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on Earth, is hired by a woman named Valerie to take her to an uncharted island in Micronesia for some reason. When they get there, Carver's boat is blown up in the world's most unintelligible cutscene. He then realizes that there's an entire hostile militia on the island, and, with the help of some guy named Doyle, eventually rescues Valerie. At this point, 1/3 of the way through the game, Carver is informed about what's actually going on: an evil scientist named Krieger is making mutants to take over the world, and Doyle and Valerie (who claims to be a CIA agent but only seems to hack things, get captured, and pose gratuitously in skimpy wet clothing because this is a game made in 2004) want to stop him. From there, lots of adventure that I won't spoil happens, and Jack is a part of it because he can't seem refuse an order from anyone.
I got through a good chunk of the game with the graphics set to Low, because apparently the system specs detector was not programmed with the technology of over a decade later in mind. I eventually realized this and turned them up to High, and was amazed at how good the game looks, especially for 2004. I did kinda like them on low, though, because it was doing that "everything is made of weirdly angle-y Play-Doh" aesthetic that Unreal Tournament 1999 has, which I really like for some reason.
My loadout throughout most of the game was as follows: Shotgun for close range because it's ridiculously powerful, P90 SMG for midrange because it's accurate, high-damage, and armor-piercing (occasionally switched out for the OICW or Machine Gun when ammo was scarce), Sniper Rifle because this game captures the fun of sniping really well, and Rocket Launcher because nothing else is good against helicopters. You probably don't care about this, but I'm just proud of the fact that I came up with a sensible and well-rounded weapon set all by myself.
The gameplay and my opinions on it are the same as they were previously, with a few additions. Being able to push grounded boats into water is a nice touch, and it turns out vegetation actually does provide cover. The game, unlike its sequels, is not actually open-world; instead, it's just a linear series of massive levels with many openings, secrets, and optional areas. I like that there's a freedom to pursue alternate strategies on the fly, allowing seemingly hopeless situations to be saved by a reckless change of strategy. One time, I was storming a base on a beach, but a lack of cover and an abundance of enemies was impeding my progress and slowly lowering my health. Getting desperate, I ran up a nearby exposed hill and stumbled upon a mounted turret; after killing its occupant, I was able to gun down my attackers and gain the upper hand. It doesn't seem that exciting, but in the context of the game it's exhilarating to be able to do something stupid and have it turn out really well.
The game does have one major flaw, though, one that at times brings the entire game to a standstill. I still have no idea why developers constantly omit the ability to be able to save at any time in favor of just putting in checkpoints at certain areas, and it is a decision that I will protest until the day I die. It's just awful in Far Cry, as some sequences that are particularly difficult on their own merits are made even more frustrating (not harder, just more frustrating) by absurdly sparse checkpoint placement, forcing you to redo the entire thing if you make one mistake. I cannot overstate the annoyance of killing every single enemy in an area large enough to house a small town—including some that take a full clip of shotgun shells to the head to defeat—over the course of about half an hour, only to slip on some janky level geometry and fall in lava, forcing you to do ALL OF THAT AGAIN. Some especially poorly checkpointed sections made me stop playing for days on end, and that does not reflect well on the game as a whole at all.
Overall, Far Cry is quite a long game with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ beginning, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending, and a pretty damn good middle, with core gameplay that's tense and fun let down by a few awful design choices. That's not a recipe for being remembered fondly, and many today find the game to be impenetrable and unfun. If you can get past that, however, you're in for an excellent experience. I still recommend it.

Bound in Blood is a much smaller game than Red Dead Redemption, but it is still one of the best wild west themed shooters.
The Good:
-Decent story with good voice acting.
-The gameplay mechanics are solid, and not too repetitive.
-Graphics: While many things look average, some of the environments are truly beautiful (at times on par with Crysis 1).
-This game does not shy away from christian themes, which fit well with the story. And it does so without seeming unpleasantly pro or anti christian.
-A good manual save system (no annoying checkpoint reloads).
-No Ubisoft Uplay account required!
The Bad (mostly minor):
-A very low Field-of-View (not fixable) due to being optimized for console TV screens.
-The first level (tutorial) has clumsy scripting and mediocre graphics, but it gets better with later levels.
-Bodies disappear the moment you look away, due to silly Xbox360/PS3 RAM limits.
-AI is mediocre (not a big problem since most things are scripted)
-screen vibration effects severely overdone during scripted explosions.
-Enemies move like ants (no movement inertia), making aiming a pain sometimes.
The Ugly:
-No COOP mode! With the two protagonists working together, this game would have been perfect for co-op, and yet there is no co-op mode! What a missed opportunity!
Overall, I can easily recommend this game, especially in a sale.

Gosh, where to start with Panzermadels? I guess it's always nice to start with all the lovely things you can say first, and then move on to the problems.
First and foremost, I do really do love this game's idea. It's cute, and silly, and very interesting. The idea that there's a school in Akihabara filled with girls who are also famous tanks throughout time? It's definitely odd, but it quickly becomes endearing. And the backgrounds of all the different tankgirls, and the things they talk about are great sources for tangential learning. I did quite a bit of wiki spelunking on this one. Before this game, I did not know New Zealand's first homegrown 'tank' design, or what 'tovarich' means. Those are just small examples.
The art, and most of the writing, are cute and snappy, helping to immerse you in a very weird world, but also in making it feel (somehow) quite real.  It does not quite manage this quite as well as NekoPara, or Highschool Romance, but considering the massive amount of suspension of disbelief required, it's still quite amazing how well they make you believe. Some of the human characters do more to derail this universe than the tankgirls do...
Unfortunately, the game is plagued by a few issues. Two of them objective, and one of them very subjective. Objectively, the game has several bad grammar - or pheraps, writing - errors that can impede understanding. A few times I thought I'd missed a line in a conversation. This came up more often near the end. Second, the game is apparently not bug free. During one of my playthroughs, I lavished all my attention on the IS-2, and somehow, the end of the game had me with the T-34. While semi amusing, I can't figure out exactly what went wrong there. (A lack of guides or information for this game doesn't help in that regard. Maybe it IS functioning as intended, but I have no way to verify that.)
Finally, the ending of the game. Ending, singular. Which tankgirl you decide to date has no apparent bearing on said ending; which may have been meant to be darkly comic, but instead, falls completely flat. Instead, it seems to take a cute, silly game, and move things into way too serious and depressing a direction. It was quite a shocking 180 for the game, and I played several times just to be sure this unfortunate ending was there every time.
In summation, I'm not sorry I spent the money on it, as I do love the premise. Rather, I feel the game needs more polish, and a much better ending. If you're a hardcore fan of wacky games, or dating sims, Panzermadels is worth a look, particularly on sale. But for the vast majority of STEAM users, this game is best passed up for better visual novels.

Gosh, where to start with Panzermadels? I guess it's always nice to start with all the lovely things you can say first, and then move on to the problems.
First and foremost, I do really do love this game's idea. It's cute, and silly, and very interesting. The idea that there's a school in Akihabara filled with girls who are also famous tanks throughout time? It's definitely odd, but it quickly becomes endearing. And the backgrounds of all the different tankgirls, and the things they talk about are great sources for tangential learning. I did quite a bit of wiki spelunking on this one. Before this game, I did not know New Zealand's first homegrown 'tank' design, or what 'tovarich' means. Those are just small examples.
The art, and most of the writing, are cute and snappy, helping to immerse you in a very weird world, but also in making it feel (somehow) quite real.  It does not quite manage this quite as well as NekoPara, or Highschool Romance, but considering the massive amount of suspension of disbelief required, it's still quite amazing how well they make you believe. Some of the human characters do more to derail this universe than the tankgirls do...
Unfortunately, the game is plagued by a few issues. Two of them objective, and one of them very subjective. Objectively, the game has several bad grammar - or pheraps, writing - errors that can impede understanding. A few times I thought I'd missed a line in a conversation. This came up more often near the end. Second, the game is apparently not bug free. During one of my playthroughs, I lavished all my attention on the IS-2, and somehow, the end of the game had me with the T-34. While semi amusing, I can't figure out exactly what went wrong there. (A lack of guides or information for this game doesn't help in that regard. Maybe it IS functioning as intended, but I have no way to verify that.)
Finally, the ending of the game. Ending, singular. Which tankgirl you decide to date has no apparent bearing on said ending; which may have been meant to be darkly comic, but instead, falls completely flat. Instead, it seems to take a cute, silly game, and move things into way too serious and depressing a direction. It was quite a shocking 180 for the game, and I played several times just to be sure this unfortunate ending was there every time.
In summation, I'm not sorry I spent the money on it, as I do love the premise. Rather, I feel the game needs more polish, and a much better ending. If you're a hardcore fan of wacky games, or dating sims, Panzermadels is worth a look, particularly on sale. But for the vast majority of STEAM users, this game is best passed up for better visual novels.
