After a very satisfying Early Acess period, Mordheim finally reached the Full Release, so it's time to update this review.
"Mordheim:City of the Damned" is a tactical squad based game with battles set in the dark Warhammer Fantasy setting of the tabletop spinoff called Mordheim.
This game builds close to its tabletop foundation and focuses on delivering intense round based tactical battles between mercenary warbands in the streets of a city fallen to chaos. While for our grown casual gaming community this might seem to be plain flavor text someone would write on a box of the store shelf version, the game is not to be taken lightly as it definitely keeps its promises.
While any misstep or just plain bad luck could cost you your hard earned equipment, the lives ouf your men or the whole warband the game expects you to handle critical situations like a commander would do, by sticking trough and minimizing losses instead of running away. Loading a different savegame is impossible as this principle is enforced with an automatic savegame system ala Darksouls. Still trying to dodge fate (Alt+F4 or just aborting a mission) will result in punishment for leaving behind your troops on the fields of battle. They return injured and broken, if they ever return. The immersion is further increased by permanent effects that can be aquired by your Troops at the end of battle which are an essential part of the progression system. While XP and resulting Level Ups provide skillpoints and attributes to be spent, permanent Injuries or Mutations span a wide range of effects that will sometimes change the use of a warrior or even render him useless (e.g a Blind Archer).
The Missions are played on very open maps that all have random factors that could change between loadouts thus giving the wide range of different city settings even more variety. Outside of missions the game provides a lobby or hideout for your warband, giving a chance to trade and manage your warband as well as play against real players.
As PVP goes, it is tied to PVE progression. It is possible to do matches against players as an alternative to playing against AI, but to gain any XP from this for your troops you have to play by the standard PVE rules. Without consequences are only the so called Exhibition matches that give you a chance to try stuff out, but as mentioned they give no XP.
Now as someone who started playing almost a year before release my level of optimism towards this game is higher than average and it has been met with over the top amounts of dedication from the devs. I do feel bad for wording criticism but I need to be fair about the amount of masochism required to play this game ... Let me phrase it like that: I doubt you want the game to be keeping its promises.
In certain aspects this game is suffocated by its many design choices to value atmosphere over quality of life. It's like the polar oposite of modern AAA+ titles that deliver a fun experience without soul. Most of the things that give Mordheim it's "soul" are things that you probably will hate quite a bit.
The sometimes long and mortifying battles have to be played in one session, no way of saving and continuing later on even in Singleplayer make it impossible to slowly digest this game and force you to choke it down in bites of undeterminable sizes. You never know how long the next mission will take and there is no way to tell because even the easiest loadout available can become a hell of a nightmare.
When already demoralized from sitting trough a loosing battle, you are forced to watch your people die until your warband drops below a certain moral value. There is no way to retreat or disengage, you are locked in a slugfest until one has lost roughly 60% of the warband, no way out.
When you are on the receiving end of the beating the game can quickly reach a point of no return, after this you are condemned to patience for the game to end. The only motivation to sit trough this is that the punishments for abandoning the mission will count all your warriors as knocked out while otherwise one or two might be spared before the morale value sinks low enough.
After reaching the mission recap, the real headache starts when your units roll for Injuries if wounded. The chances range from miraculous recovery to lost limbs and mental problems. While it can be fun to adapt to changes in your warband, after spending alot of time to train a mercenary loosing him to debilitating injuries that render him useless can be demoralizing. Attachment sooner or later just become frustration. This is true for any efforts you put into the game, as it is very quick to ruin them. That exactly is the real difficutly of Mordheim. It revolves more around how well you can stomach bad news, rather than how well you can solve difficult problems.
Maybe you get the feeling the game wants to punish you for loosing games? So there is more to your assumption than you'd think. It's the warband management element. It requires you to pay your mercs after every loadout, pay for their treatments after injuries and fullfill deadlines for certain shipments of wyrdstones, magical stones you plunder while inside the missions. If you should happen to fail several missions in a row you will struggle to pay all those bills. The consequences can be dire enough to stop your campaign progress.
Something i wanted to save for last is the terribly clunky interface and HUD. I just got used to playing with an Xbox Controller while still using mouse and keyboard in the menus. The interface did get improved over time going from functional to usable. Warband management is overall impractical without clear look and feel in the menus mixing console and PC designs - failing hard at both - some buttons being unreachable with controller or alternatively being laggy with the mouse. In the missions you notice that over the shoulder perspective is not really practical for gaining insight in the possible layout of the city behind the next cover. The game substitutes this with a birds eye view map screen you can activate to get overall orientation of your units and enemies you might have spotted. Sadly there is no way to gain insight on entrances and exits of building from the map view and you must rely on backtracking while looking for an exit. Especially annoying in PVP, eiter for you with a turn timer or for the opponent without one. Talking HUD, to activate the different abilities of your units you use a circle menu that reminds me of "Baldurs Gate" or the first "Neverwinter Nights", they feel equally strange to navigate with mouse or controler.
But well the UI and HUD are probably not what will make or brake the game for you ... judging by the early acess period I am positive the UI will get improvements sometime soon.
To be fair, for me personally all the good and the bad (and the queen) this game does is lost to the fact that I can barely find time to play it. This game requires me to dedicate a whole afternoon to it as I find it impossible to break it down to smaller sessions. Add to this the rather slow progression and many elements that setback your progress makes it take forever to see some improvement with little room for experiments.
Still I have alot of fun with this game and do highly recommend atleast trying it out. This might be interesting not only for Warhammer fans but aswell people who know nothing of the franchise, general tactical game enthusiasts, people who want to play something good, slow and different or plain old masochists ... they will love this.
As with most games like this one there is a good community surrounding it, many dedicated players (e.g. search for the group "The Gentlemen of Mordheim").

Resident Evil 7 is a welcome change after the fiasco that was known as Resident Evil 6 (aka. The Evil Giraffe BJ.) RE7 strips away a lot of the over the top action compared to previous games, and returns to claustrophobic close quarters horror with some intense item management reminiscent of the first three RE games.
In the beginning, you are completely defenseless, which means you'll have to sneak or run from enemy encounters. You'll eventually get a knife and even firearms, but you'll have to spare ammo and juggle using your weapons depending on the situation. Health also doesn't regenerate, so every hit you take is something you have to live with.
At around midpoint the game starts to have some annoyingly bullet spongy bosses, and towards the very end the game started feeling almost more like Doom than RE, but luckily the game didn't delve too deep into the shooter territory. The survival horror elements could be felt throughout the game.
Technically the game seemed quite solid, but as always, your mileage may vary. Not once did the game crash on me or corrupt my data. My potato (1st gen i7, GTX 960) runs this game at 60 fps at fairly high settings on a 1080p resolution. Only towards the end did I start to occasionally dip below 60fps, but that was mostly because of larger events happening. Loading times on SSD were barely noticeable.
While I have my minor gripes, RE7 is definitely a damn good game, and a long needed renewal of the RE series.

text:
Build. Expand. Defend. Oh, and watch everything you love crumble before your eyes.
When you spawn into your first land as part of the tutorial, you are a solitary king on horseback. As you ride past the massive stone letters introducing Kingdom, they splinter and collapse. The withered ghost of your predecessor leads you to a small hoard of treasure, an extinguished campfire, and a handful of unemployed vagrants in the middle of a forest, and as King, you wield the power of money to set the vagrants to work building your empire.
Kingdom is a resource management game in a gorgeous low-res sidescrolling format. You don't get the coins unless you run over to pick them up, giving a very personal feel to the dryness of many management games. And those coins will be needed to build defenses against nightly raid by Greed Trolls, an army of little gremlins who will steal your coins and equipment by night. For all the joy of expansion and natural beauty, there's an equivalent horror at the constant decay of your walls, men, and gear as the attacks grow stronger and stronger with the passing days. If the trolls should knock to the crown from your head -- "No crown, no king."
Kingdom quietly dances a fine line between total serenity and creeping terror. Sure, the one-button interface has the peasants doing most of your work for you -- but you must carefully manage your horse's stamina as you run back and forth across the countryside. Amassing coins is easy. So is watching all your ivnestments melt away the night of a bad raid. The end-goal of rebuilding a shipwreck and sailing away devolves from noble ambition to desperate escape...
Will you be able to keep your crown?

"Far Cry" is arguably the toughest FPS I've played. Ever.
Even on a completely subjective terms, I'm openly admitting that my review here is far from being a valid measure stick for how the game truly feels in the hands of an average FPS gamer as the RPG genre is what I usually prefer the most. That being said, my favorite shooting games until now were still those so-called "old schools" like "Return to Castle Wolfenstein", "Soldier of Fortune" and "Vietcong".
Nonetheless, "Far Cry" is the game that doesn't allow you to simply run through your enemies and shoot them down mindlessly, but rather requires application of some real-life tactics and forces you to play like you truly
there on the islands as even a minor mistake could cost you most of your health bar. Enemies are tough, extremely intelligent and highly perceptive (especially on higher levels) to the point where you would almost consider it a bug - let's just say they can spot you from afar through dense undergrowth and even through tents... not to mention shoot you from miles away with like 90% precision. On the other hand, you're unable to tell where they are shooting at you from most of the times. However, that's not what makes this game hard in my opinion.
Lack of manual "Save game" option
.
It's quite frustrating to stealth around and take your enemies one by one for like half an hour... only to get shoot by some fodder your radar failed to spot (or even worse - your radar
spot him, but you were still unable to tell his exact location due to vegetation or whatnot). Briefly, distances between checkpoints on some levels seem painfully long.
Despite that, this game can be passed without a single cheat, indeed. In order to do that, rely heavily on binoculars and cry vision goggles the whole time and you'll be fine. Oh, and make sure you don't miss to pick weapons like G36 or OICW because it's next to impossible to pass a couple of the last levels without them.
Overall, story of this game seems pretty generic and predictable (with main character not being so particularly interesting); I'm giving it a solid 8/10.

This one is thought to enjoy. Far Cry has without a doubt some nice moments and some nice open levels. Many elements of it have been recycled in Crysis as well as later Far Cry games and it's nice to see how it all started. But Far Cry does have a few to many fatal flaws to recommend.
Most prominent would be the insane difficult, most enemies can kill you with two or three hits. By itself that wouldn't be a problem, as stealth would be the logical answer, but stealth doesn't work here. Enemies can spot you from miles away and will instantly shot at you when you use your sniper rifle. There is a silence gun in the game as well, but that doesn't work long range. Enemies are also far too fast on their legs, so you can't really play hide and seek, the enemies will have you surrounded you long before you can find cover.
To make this issue even worse, the game frequently moves away from the open island levels and into buildings and bunkers. In those settings you are often confronted with enemies right in front of you after you open a door, leaving no room to do anything from a distance. Your binoculars, that help to detect and mark enemies on open terrain, become useless here.
The next problem is the lack of quicksave, despite being at times pretty open, Far Cry sticks to a checkpoint system and linear progression, but when exactly you will hit a checkpoint is unpredictable due to the openness of the levels. They are scattered more or less randomly throughout the levels. Luckily the the lack of quicksave can be fixed, as quicksave function can be enabled by editing a config file, it's just not exposed in the GUI.
The game has it's moments where things click, but those moments don't last very long. One moment you might be impressed by the level of foliage the game presents you with, but the next moment you might already be shot dead from an enemy that you didn't see coming.
After now quite some hours into the game my frustration with the game, despite having quicksave, is getting a lot bigger than the enjoyment I am getting out of it. There are just too many situations where the game doesn't communicate what you have to do and you have to trial&error yourself through far too many enemies. The game never manages to establish a proper flow.
On top of all that I also had plenty of problems getting the game to run in Windows10. Lowering lighting settings to "High" and installing the AMD64 patch made the game start properly, but even after that it's still hanging when you exist it.
Edit: I finished the game now and some of the later levels, especially when you run around with a companion NPC, tend to be more fun and interesting than fighting in caves against monsters. However the basic combat still stays quite frustrating as there just isn't a good way to attack enemies in a stealthy way. It always ends up chaotically with a lot of trial&error and a lot of dying.
The weapon balance and control also seems out of whack. The RPG is drastically underpowered and slow moving, requiring four or more rounds to kill one of the bigger enemies, assuming you can hit them in the first place. Moving with a weapon while watching through the scope will disengage the scope, but only after a short delay and it won't reengage the scope when you still hold the button. Some weapons also require a hold for the scope while other do it as toggle. Getting a good zoom level on the scope also requires some additional button presses. All this makes scope use rather cumbersome.
The story also isn't anything special. Good guy vs evil doctor and his monsters, with a few minor twists and turns thrown in.
So overall this just isn't that good of a game. Has it's moments, but also far too much frustration and annoyance.

At only 3 hours of gameplay (including the very short prologue DLC), some might consider Among the Sleep a poor investment for their gaming dollars.  To those, I ask, how much did you spend on your last trip to the movie theater, and after you watched it, did you find yourself thinking about the deeper meanings of it, or wanting to talk to others to explain how moving it was?
That is this game.  Short, true, but longer than an average movie, and definitely far more engaging.  Among the Sleep manages to do more in those few levels than most big-budget franchise games have accomplished in their entire series.  Playing from the perspective of a toddler, from the difference in size, to the inability to jump, to the general sounds and movement styles, is the key element that makes this game different, but not what makes the game great.  The fascination that you see repeated over and over again in reviews comes from the subtle, yet powerful, story-behind-the-story.  Yes, you're a toddler, wandering around the house with a teddy bear.  But the real story lies behind the "why."
Fans of horror games like Amnesia will enjoy this, while fans of action games will probably want to pass.

The single player experience of Absolver is fairly well done with combat that generally feels rewarding and an art style with a rather unique look.  It does what it tries to do well enough on a mechanical level but the "story" part of the game is not nearly engaging enough for that to make it worth the asking price.  To the developer's credit, the game isn't just about the story though and much of the effort has been spent on the multiplayer component.  Unfortunately, that multiplayer component has been absent or malfunctioning for much of the week I've been playing it and even the single player portion suffers for it due to some design decisions.
Servers were unavailable for me on launch day and have only come back online 3 days later- at which point I had completed the very short story campaign.  When playing in the world of Absolver with online mode active, other players are seen in each of the dozen or so zones.  These zones are often quite small so the game will frequently hang as it loads these players into your game.  Once in, connection quality obviously plays a role in how well they are represented in your game but it also affects NPC's since their positions and actions need to be synchronized.  The result is that even AI-controlled characters are absurdly laggy, making for an unplayable experience.
There are problems I have with the single player portion of the experience as well.  Manipulating your combat deck makes for a very personalized experience in that you are the one that determines your character's movesets.  The problem is that, while the game offers several slots to save different decks, they are locked.  I have not seen any indication that they will unlock due to story or character progression so I suspect this is tied to the aforementioned dysfunctional online component in some way.  I cannot understand why a simple quality of life function like this would be locked.
Then there is the combat itself.  1v1 fights are fantastic with my only gripe being that it seems like blocking isn't instantaneous even from a neutral stance- it takes time for your character to raise their arms into a guarding position.  While this might make sense, it has the effect of making the controls just feel sluggish.  Where the combat fails though is in 2v1 or 3v1 fights.  The game will frequently tie enemies together in that if you aggro one, they will automatically bring friends.  This is about the only way to increase the difficulty of trash mob encounters (short of just giving them more health) but it happens far too often in my opinion.  Fights against multiple enemies are usually quite frustrating due to the fact that your character's stance is dependent on the targeted enemy's position when you target them and will usually change when you switch targets.  These encounters also effectively nullify the combat deck as you will be lucky to get more than a single attack out at a time.
Maybe Sloclap can eventually resolve the server issues and smooth out the online portions of the game.  From the sound of things, they have every intention of supporting the game post-release with additional content.  Unfortunately I'm not sure if that will be enough to make me want to come back after I've moved on to other games.

Don't waste any time on this "game", it's not worth it and neither is any Perfect World Entertainment title, not even at the cost of free. Ignore my Steam hours, they are incorrect (BLR and Steam running simultaneously caused issues for me), I've logged thousands of hours in BLR as this game was my life for at least two years. Most NA players from 2012-2014 would recognize my IGN because I was playing all the time and active in the community.
As of 2017 the server quality is so poor it basically killed the community run competitive scene, there's been no remarkable content in over a year, balance is still terrible and meta is very select and boring, staff haven't communicated with players for months now (nearly a year in some cases, and this isn't the first lapse in communication for this long of a time period), the store hasn't been updated in about the same amount of time, and many game breaking bugs (still) exist while the head cheese's response is "Those issues that remain will probably stay in the game for life at this point". All signs point to this title being dead.
This game had potential in 2012, but it all was squandered by a neglectful publisher, Perfect World Entertainment (PWE), and by two inactive development teams, Zombie Studios and Hardsuit Labs (HSL). Now this game is just a placeholder, retaining ownership of the title while gaining awareness of the franchise by being "playable", prolonging advertisement until the next edition arrives. Everything that was once unique and cool to this title is being copied by Titanfall, CoD, and everyone else, and quite frankly it's done better there. Blacklight as a series will die without fresh ideas; there is no story to really care about, development is too slow to compete with bigger titles that do the same features better, and BLR population can't compete with AAA. Given the game's track record, this seems impossible.
PWE is inept as a publisher and I have seen them commit offenses that I can't mention in this review due to Steam rules. When the actions of the game's publisher fall under Steam's "Off-Limit Topics/Replies" section of the rules and guidelines concerning this review (6/10 bullets hit!) you know that something is very wrong with the company. See also: DeathMogui, or contact me for further information. I'm heavily considering contacting the BBB at this point. I've had PWE customer support issues take over eighteen months to be resolved despite constant contact, PWE community managers ignore my direct messages concerning violations, multiple profile bans against me were overturned by PWE on account of no proof, and between $100-$140 worth of unused in-game digital goods removed from my account with no compensation for the removal (most expensive item is $100). PWE customer support has never solved any of my numerous (over 12) issues correctly; the company is next to impossible to deal with. I once had a ticket that was immediately closed for being filed incorrectly; I had never typed anything in the ticket personally,  it was initiated by a PWE live chat representative, who did all the typing. Check out other player's reports of losing their entire profiles and ARC not doing anything without the player providing proof. Exploring forums of other PWE titles mirrors the same complaints I've found, proving the problems are not specific to this title, but more likely company-wide. PWE neglect sometimes borders on questionable business practices.
In 2012 it was made known that the female model was visually smaller than the male while allegedly retaining the same hitbox, which is advantageous. The cost to switch model sex was $10 USD. This issue still isn't "fixed" as the female visual representation is still smaller, but changing model sex is available free since parity patch. That's a little over three years that PWE profited from a well-known bug that was left in the game. It's anyone's guess as to the conversation PWE had with Zombie over this, but the "solution" took far too long and I can only blame PWE directly for the delay without knowing what went on behind closed doors.
HSL biggest sin is inaction. Countless game breaking (rendering it unplayable) bugs have existed since 2012, parity patch only added more. Check any BLR forum you want and the story is the same: multiple issues going on and the solutions can be hard to find, if there is one. HSL took over after Zombie Studios gave players a year-long content drought, and HSL promised more frequent updates, yet it's been a year again since anything significant has changed. HSL VP LordAlf likes to brag "we're darn good at porting" but if you use BLR parity as an example I'd have to argue otherwise, the job is largely unfinished. Parity patch removed more content on PC than has been added since, and you'd have a hard time convincing me of any improvement to the game that was made with parity patch, everything from graphic performance and sound to game play and balance suffered. Community map editor was supposed to help with development shortcomings, but hardly anyone from a once dedicated community wants to spend time making something if the game isn't going to improve. HSL makes great promises and hopeful timelines when they choose to communicate, but rarely are the promises impressive/as promised and the timeline is overshot much more often than it is met. I recognize that HSL is a small studio, but there are smaller studios that regularly provide frequent content updates that HSL has so far proven to be incapable of.
Population changes suggest that parity updates were not appreciated by the community, neither was the most recent price hike. Instead of trying to open dialogue with the community about what needs to be changed HSL has been mostly silent on all official channels, while the Steam chart shows the lowest numbers ever. BLR's advertising has always been community driven, and treating the community to silence has paid off in kind. Community run HUD customization, tournaments, websites, and countless other labors of love have long left the game due to HSL seeming inability to communicate with their customers.
HSL has stated that BLR PC makes them no profit, and that ARC forums are toxic, I can't really blame them for not having a greater interest/presence there. But when Alf responds "Never been discussed, but interesting idea" to a topic that has been brought up multiple times over the course of four years it becomes clear that the developer's are very out of touch with their audience. I've made personal attempts to reach out to Alf on the ARC platform and some of my private messages were deleted, Alf claims to have never seen them. I question whether PWE's site "losing" messages is accidental or more dubious.
To top it all off HSL and PWE are "thought police" who scrutinize those that have issues, even if they politely suggest a solution, and are not accepting to constructive criticism on any platform: ARC, Steam, Reddit (while it lasted), Blacklist, and Twitter. Keeping your community in constant fear over inconsistent policies is no way to draw people to the platform. Around May of 2014 the servers started having serious disconnect issues at the end of rounds. PWE asked for community input, we responded with over 35 pages of responses, which is now edited down to just 3 pages.
The only way I'd consider playing a Blacklight 3 is if PWE isn't involved, and at the very least, two years into the game's life so I can judge HSL's community involvement and update schedule at that time. I'd need HSL to show me they've learned from their mistakes and are trying to correct them before I'd think about investing my time with them again, let alone any of my money.
PWE doesn't deserve the privilege to operate, and HSL hasn't earned your money until the studio proves they are capable of better communication with customers of their F2P titles, and more frequent actions based on said communications.

This game has the classic survival horror charm that made the first Resident Evil amazing. I was afraid that the game was just going to be like any other game in the survival horror genre except with the Resident Evil title slapped on it. As the story progresses, you'll find out that this is in fact reminiscent of the classic RE games. From resource management to limited saves, it was a great callback to the original game. I actually didn't mind the first person view because it made the experience immersive and much more terrifying. Not knowing what's around the corner adds to that element of terror, and believe me, there are a lot of narrow halls and corners lol. My main complaint, which many others I've seen would agree with me, is that the game is too short. First playthrough only took 10 hours. With that being said, the game does offer a lot of achievements and unlockables which add to the replay value. I'm currently working on my 6th playthrough as I write this review xD. Capcom does offer some DLC content, but in my opinion, you probably won't be missing out on much unless you really can't get enough of RE7. Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to any Resident Evil fan or survival horror fan.

The down side is that it is relying on online pvp which doesn't appear to be balanced (I had a fight as a level 6 against a guy who was already max level somehow).
Also, the servers are really suffering right now, I haven't experienced lag like this for years. Players and NPCs randomly jump about the screen, someone 10 foot away from you can suddenly have their feet in your face in a nano second, and I have on a few occasions seemingly died of a heart attack.
And as other reviews have mentioned, most people just hammer their experience points into stamina and spam attacks, so if you've tried putting points into different things evenly, you'll end up on the defensive until your stamina breaks.
And trying to solo run takes a lot of patience. Some mini boss fights usually involve one boss and two other fighters attacking you, and they will just keep hitting from all angles so you have to focus on one, and usually take them out one at a time then get knocked out, and run back to the fight.

As a fighting game this can certainly appeal to more casual as well as skilled players, excecuting combos is an art you develop as you craft your deck. The casual player will spam, miss timings thus not properly connecting hits and will have an underdeveloped deck that you can beat 3 to 0 all the time. I love watching them just press buttons for the sake of it, it all looks fancy and appealing even if they're not quite sure what they are doing.
To the skilled fighting game community, this is not a mash and spam game. The technical aspects of the game in high level gameplay are based on spacing, perfect timing of attacks, blocks, parrys and dodges. Crafting a deck of your own is very fun, each stance and the attacks you choose for each individual stances are correlated to speed, range and strength of a move that can even break guards, massively reduce stamina, avoid high or low attacks and counter against rush tactics. You cannot underestimate the use of weapons in the game as you develop the ability to materialise your own weapons out of thin air, of choice of course, with its own movesets and style at any point in a fight.
What makes this game even more complicated is the idea that you can mix fighting styles together, making for some badass mui tai like kick combos or drunken wing chun style punches as well as learning other fighting styles
The DIY aspect of making the perfect form of martial art is awesome when you consider you can be a mentor for an infinite amount of people, thus creating a school or a closed group of people who practice and use your own fighting style by influence.
Yes there is a short story but amazing map where you can revisit all the bosses at any point to learn their moves or steal their clothes, alone or in co-op.
In truth it has taken me four days for me to be a mentor which is the pinncle of the game, beforewhich you complete the story and then have to focus on PVP and learning moves to graduate and be a mentor yourself. I found myself kind of lost after that, it was pvp or helping people, finding disciples is not easy.
I would give this game a 9/10, it took 35 hours for me to become a mentor and for the £20 price it is definetely worth it. We just need to wait for DLC for this game for it to really become relevant for more than a month.

The controlls aren't perfect--I did get stuck on a few tree roots here and there--but overall, they suffice to bring the player a deep, memorable experience with very few hiccups.  It took me an hour and a half to play this game all the way through, but let me tell you, it was a briliant trip.  I would wait for it to go on sale, since $20 does seema bit steep, but if you can catch it for a decent price, grab this gem.  It can easily outdo any horror flick.

This game is how sequels should be - it takes everything that was good about the first game and improves it, builds on the old characters, and smooths out the rough edges of the original. The two brothers play differently enough to give an incentive to play through it twice, so there's plenty of value to it. The only reason I ever had to not recommend it before was because the field of view was extremely low (46 degrees) with no way to fix it, but thankfully a mod has finally fixed that recently, allowing you to go up to 75 (which is still pretty low, but a lot more manageable).
I don't recommend using the date-changing part of the mod (the read-me and description explains how to only apply the gameplay changes), but everything else about the mod is great. With this mod, I can finally completely recommend this game.
Also, on another note, if you have problems with the voices sounding like they were recorded in a bad microphone, you may need to lower the audio quality of your sound device in Windows. It probably won't be a problem for most people, but if you have a high quality sound system and use 24-bit audio, you may need to switch to 16-bit, 44100 Hz for this game.

Every creak and rustle of the environment; every groan and word uttered by the Baker family add a striking dimension of fear as Ethan explores his environment.  I do wish the game was a little longer; In all honesty I could have finished it in seven hours, though we're talking all content and no filler.  While I think $60.00 is a little expensive ($39.99 is right on the money w/ DLC included), Capcom is releasing some free DLC so that is something of a redeeming quality.  All in all, a very well-crafted experience.  4/5

Let me start this off by saying I don't write reviews. Ever. I always read them and I always base my decision in getting a game on them. Today, I come to you as a humble man who has, for the first time, truly enjoyed an early alpha game. I've played other titles, Starbound and other fancy early alpha titles, and I always had the sense of regret in them. Saying to myself, "Damn! Another $## wasted on a game I'll look at my library gathering dust." (Trust me, I own tons of those titles) But this one...
This title has made me enjoy sinking in the cash, supporting the growth. Why do I love it? It gives you EXACTLY what you pay for: A Tabletop game with tabletop attributes. There have been other projects that I've seen as ambitious as this title, but nowhere near as close as fulfilling as this one.
I do warn those who aren't as interested in table tops as I am in: This game is quite a stone to pass if you don't have some time dedicated to learn the game. I was quick to frustration at the numerous spells in the game, mainly for Skraven, and I didn't understand half the time what was going on simply because there was no tutorial (Till I found it later) on screen. If I had to compare the experience of this game to another, the Valkyria Chronicles titles are an easy match.
Tl;Dr Version:
Not sure? Ask yourself:
- Are you into Table tops?
- Do you like RTS?
- Do you like Valkyria Chronicles?
If you answered yes to two of the three, I consider buying this early alpha.

Confession: I have not beaten FTL despite hundreds of hours of play. But I keep playing. It’s so easy to get caught up in the little details that I always lose sight of the big picture—you’re meant to be equipping your ship to take down the final boss. That seems straightforward, and online strategy guides can help guide you—but procedural generation of encounters and stores means you may never find what you need (or you may be tempted to stray when you stumble on some crazy weapon you’ve never seen before). The encounters stay mostly fresh even years later, and spaceship combat, while fairly simple in essence, gets richer and deeper the more you explore. I reckon I’ll keep playing long after I do finally beat it.

OK, this is a very cool game that has excellent graphics, & beautiful backgrounds.
I see that it has loads of potentials ... so let me just say that in general everything is OK. I liked it, although the difficulty of the game is too high... for me at least...
Pros:
+ The movement feels good
+ Weapons are fun to use
+ Music is awesome
+ Enemies are fairly varied
+ There's a lot of good stuff for such a cheap game
Cons:
- The aiming system needs work.
- The red cursor is WAY too small and blends in to the environment and surroundings.
- Mouse input is buggy.
- The blue laser enemies will kill you the moment they show up in the corner of the screen.
- No way to change options when you're in the game, you have to end your mission and go to the main screen to change things like sound or video settings.
My final rating would be 7/10 very recommended.

There's a lot of potential here, but there are a few annoyances that really hindered my experience.
Pros:
+ The movement feels good and fluid
+ Weapons are fun to use (when they respond to your input)
+ Music is good
+ Enemies are varied enough
+ Making an enemy explode and having its torso fly up and hit the screen feels really cool.
+ There's a lot of good stuff here for such a cheap game
Cons:
- The aiming needs work. Aiming at enemies sometimes makes the red laser-sight jitter up and down and bullets just fly off randomly.
- The red cursor is WAY too small and blends in to the environment too much. I shouldn't have to search the screen for it after dodging a bunch of rockets. If the cursor was more visible, then using your periferal vision to aim and focus on your character to dodge stuff would make the gameplay feel much better and smoother. Either making the laser sight a solid red line, or the red cursor more opaque/changed to a larger crosshair would definitely help. Maybe even allowing us to change the color of the cursor.
- Mouse input is buggy and, while I'm pressing down and trying to shoot... sometimes it just won't respond. Holding down the fire button, letting go and firing again sometimes would result in a 2-3 second delay before you start firing (this is for the regular primary gun, not the one that overheats). Once I even had a bunch of lasers and rockets but NONE of them would shoot at all, and I was stuck with an overheated minigun which just takes way too long to cool down.
- The blue laser enemies feel cheap and just stun-lock you and kill you the moment they show up in the corner of the screen. (This is a small annoyance, sure you can memorize their locations after a few runs and avoid them easier)
- Getting stuck on pieces of the terrain on the floor, or a broken part of a building is really annoying and doesn't feel like it should happen.
- No way to change options when you're in the game, you have to end your mission and go to the main screen to change things like sound or video settings. (I didn't know how loud the game would be so I started a mission, it was too loud, so I tried to change the sound but had to end the mission to do so)
If it wasn't for the first 3 negative points, I would have recommended this game easily.

Add garlic, tomatoes, tomato paste, tomato sauce and water.
Add basil, parsley, brown sugar, salt, crushed red pepper, and black pepper.
Stir well and barely bring to a boil.
Stir in red wine.
Simmer on low, stirring frequently for at least an hour. A longer simmer makes for a better sauce, just be careful not to let it burn!
Cook spaghetti according to package directions.
Spoon sauce over drained spaghetti noodles and sprinkle with parmesan cheese.

Far Cry was designed as the dream-come-true FPS game of some ambitious newcomers at gamedev stage - Crytek studio. Their first known project turned out as the real bomb when it was released. The hype was immersive - and after all those passed years, I have to say, this game is worth its reputation.
"Thunder in Paradise" rich setout unleashes badass oldschool shooter (like Doom or Half Life) - with so many fixes as one could imagine 12 years back: outstanding visuals and physics, witty and challenging level design, clever AI behavior... And level editor for icing the cake.
I remember playing (and ending) this game in 2004-2005, with the hardest difficulty possible. The last level was utterly hard, and it changed my mentality forever. Seriously. Now I have but one fear in my life. My only fear is about ammo depletion. So far as I'm locked and loaded, let'em come!
Well, sadly, my skill was decreased since those times, so now I am good enough only at "challenging", medium level difficulty. For the newcomers, however, I suggest to start from the basic level of difficulty - the standarts was really different then.
I've read many depressing comments about this game from people who decided to give it a try, but was not ready for the outcome. Enemy soldiers are not aim-bots, that's I know for sure. If you're good with positioning and tactical movement in the rough terrains, if you're lucky... and if you're ready for constant reloads... Try it on!
The game is selling for such a low price, that every FPS devotee should have no problem with adding this brilliant to the collection. The only real question before buying should be - are you really bad enough for this? You can't hide behind chest-high wall here and recover health. The enemies, once you'll allow them to spot you, will be engaging until you'll finish them all or die trying. Some of them will be crying for backup (and usually, they'll get one), some will be cornering you, while others will rush on you, using supressive fire, grenades and strafing moves... And all that you'll see right from the beginning!
As for downsides: saving only at checkpoints is really annoying! Sometimes those checkpoints too far one from another, sometimes, when you crouch your way around enemy, you can not activate any checkpoint at all! And sometimes checkpoints are saving the game just the second before enemy sniper blows your head off. Some levels, otherwise quite well-performed, could become total clusterfunk due to those fixed savepoints. Like the upper level of the tanker, where you have only about 0.5 to 1 second to hide once you've climbed there, before bullethell breaks loose. Or later, in the second half of the game, where some enemies are getting on another level of the food chain... My advise there is to find tweakguide with using console around this problem. Or get over with it as it is!
My mark is 8/10. Clever engine and gameplay, nice physics. We don't have scarcity for FPS games, that's right. But if you need FPS where you are not tied to corridor shootouts... Where you exploring the area around before engaging - or instead of it - to learn enemy's routes, behavior, weakpoints... Where you have to worry about not being hit more than about fragging another dozen of dummies - now, there's still not many good games like this.
Do you like fresh, meat-packed action like Serious Sam? Well.. you get it right here, in the middle of Tajikistan, with numberless help of our Chineese friends :)
